fix(daemon): drop pending Telegram backlog on connect (#23)

grammY long-polling was started with no options, so on every (re)connect it
resumed from Telegram's last un-acknowledged getUpdates offset and replayed the
buffered backlog. Because a fresh top-level @mention keys a new session on its
own message_id (canonicalizeTelegramThread), each replayed stale mention minted
a duplicate session — observed as two sessions (tg:26 + tg:92) from what the
user saw as a single "hello".

Start long-polling with drop_pending_updates: true so a reconnecting daemon
skips anything Telegram buffered while it was down. Trades at-least-once for
at-most-once: messages sent during a brief restart are dropped rather than
answered late (and duplicated).

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(skills): shared skills — GitHub sources, per-agent (per-skill) enablement, npx install (#21)

* feat(skills): shared skills P1 — GitHub sources, per-agent enablement, npx-skills install

Implements the shared-skills design (docs/designs/shared-skills.md) end to end.

protocol: AgentSpec.skills — self-contained AgentSkillEntry[] (source/ref/subDir/
skill filter) rides inline on the agent spec, no separate frame.

control-plane: SkillSource registry (Prisma model + migration, repo, ports,
container wiring) + /skill-sources REST (list/get/preview/create/patch/sharing/
delete). The per-agent enable-list lives in runtimeOverrides.skills[] as
"<source>/<skill>" / "<source>/*"; agentSpecAssembler resolves it against the
registry into inline AgentSpec.skills entries. Editing a source fans out
agent/upsert to every referrer; delete 409s while referenced. Preview does a
best-effort GitHub Trees scan for the SKILL.md manifest + tag/branch choices.

daemon: agent.json gains a top-level skills field (write-agent persists it like
mcpServers; the old workspace.skills is deprecated). install-skills runs

 ERROR  Missing required argument: source

  Usage:
    npx skills add <source> [options]

  Example:
    npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills per enabled entry after clone / before session start —
non-blocking, timeout-bounded, fingerprint-cached in a workspace marker, git-
excluded, with a runtime→CLI-agent map (claude-code/codex/opencode/gemini-cli/
cursor).

web: Tools & Skills page swaps the mock library for a real SkillSourcesCard
(import/edit/delete); agent detail gains an AgentSkillsCard toggling sources;
api/data-context/swr wiring; the dead AddSkillModal + SKILLS mock are removed.

Tests: CP skillSource resolver + daemon composeSource/runtime-map units; existing

* fix(skills): address review — filter fidelity, reconcile, move-safety, authz, name grammar

Six findings from the automated review on b1bf542:

- resolver: a whole-source wildcard now honors the source's own skill filter
  instead of emitting [] ("install all"), and specific picks that intersect the
  filter to nothing omit the source rather than falling back to all.
- daemon install: reconcile stale copies. The marker records exactly the skill
  dirs this daemon created; a changed run removes those first (disable / narrow /
  runtime-switch / zero-desired) without touching manually-authored skills.
- git exclude: resolve the real repo root (walk up for .git) and cover both
  .claude/skills and .agents/skills plus the marker dir, anchored under a nested
  agentDir — so codex/cursor/opencode/gemini targets and subdir cwds stay clean.
- move-safety: the move bundle snapshots resolved skill entries and passes them to
  project(), so agent/activate no longer clears skills on placement moves /
  workspace edits.
- authz: agent create/PATCH reject enabling skills from a source the caller can't
  see (mirrors the MCP enable-list gate), closing a restricted-source leak.
- grammar: SkillSource name is a slash-free slug and skill enable-refs are
  validated, so a name with '/' can't corrupt <source>/<skill> parsing.

Tests: resolver filter/omit transitions; daemon reconcile (disable, manual-skill
preservation, unchanged-skip, unmapped-runtime cleanup).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(skills): harden daemon installer — path-traversal, arg-injection, install-presence

Three findings from the second review on b8974db1 (the prior six are confirmed
resolved):

- path traversal: the workspace marker is untrusted (repo content / the agent can
  write it), so reconcile removal now only accepts a single non-dotted segment
  directly under a known skill root (isTrackedSkillDir); a poisoned '../victim' /
  absolute / nested entry is rejected and never drives rm.
- argument injection: skill/source values become npx args, so a leading '-' (e.g.
  '-s --all') is a flag, not data. Rejected at the wire boundary (protocol
  AgentSkillEntry) and the CP DTOs (SkillFilterName / SkillSourceArg / enable-ref
  grammar), with a defense-in-depth drop in the daemon installer.
- install presence: a fingerprint match now also requires every recorded target to
  still exist and (for a non-empty desired set) at least one owned target to have
  been recorded — so a deleted/never-created install repairs instead of caching a
  phantom 'unchanged'. The fingerprint is committed only when the pass produced an
  owned target.

Also made AgentSpecAssembler.project()'s skillEntries argument REQUIRED so no
authoritative move/activation path can silently default to a skills clear.

Tests: protocol arg-injection rejection; daemon marker path-traversal guard.

* fix(skills): address review — install-before-spawn, CLI-cache, manifest scope/filter, default branch

Resolves five of the six findings on cc7abc10:

- install before host.start(): session-manager now runs prepareWorkspace (clone +
  npx skills install) BEFORE acquiring the host, so skills land before the runtime
  spawns — not after. cwd is resolved once and shared by the new-session/resume paths.
- AC_SKILLS_CLI now part of the install fingerprint (resolved before the fast-path

- manifest scan honors the source's subDir + ref: scanSkillSource scopes discovery

- manifest honors the source's own skills filter: GET /skill-sources/:id/skills

- subDir without ref no longer assumes 'main': create/patch resolve the repo's real

Tests: AC_SKILLS_CLI fingerprint-invalidation. Remaining: private skill-source repo
authorization (dedicated gitcred grant) — the documented P3 item.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(skills): address review round 2 — warm-turn prep, PATCH ref clobber, subdir ref

Three more findings on a5b1756a:

- warm-turn mutation regression: hoisting prepareWorkspace before the host made it
  run on EVERY turn, so pullOnNewSession + skill reconcile could mutate a checkout a
  live ACP session was using. Now prep-before-host runs ONLY for a brand-new session

  warm turn on an existing session no longer re-prepares.
- PATCH ref clobber: an unrelated partial PATCH (e.g. skills-only) on a subdir source
  no longer overwrites the explicit ref with the default branch — the default-branch
  resolve only runs when the EFFECTIVE ref (body or existing) is absent.
- subdir without a resolvable ref: create/patch now 400 instead of letting the daemon
  assume 'main' when the owner has no org GitHub App installation.

Remaining: private skill-source repo authorization — deferred to a follow-up PR.

* fix(skills): resume-cold-start ordering + reject private sources (scope to public)

* feat(control-plane): memory dreaming REST surface

Adds the CP REST routes proxying the memory/dream/* frames to the owning

it relays — staged store bodies are proxied live, byte-sliced like memory/read.

- orchestrator/outbound.ts: dreamStart/Cancel/List/Get/Adopt/Discard/Files/

  admin calls.
- http/dto: DreamDto/DreamListDto/DreamFilesDto/DreamFileDto + StartDreamBody/
  AdoptDreamBody/DreamIdParam.
- http/routes/agents.ts: POST …/memory/dreams (start), GET …/dreams (list),
  GET/…:dreamId (get), POST …/cancel|adopt|discard, GET …/files, GET …/file.
  Each is documented for OpenAPI (tag/summary/operationId). BAD_PAYLOAD→400,
  CONFLICT→409 (fence / wrong state), offline daemon→503; a non-managed agent
  is a 400.

Skill accept/dismiss routes are deferred to D-3 with the daemon side.
Unit tests cover the REP→DTO mappers. CP unit suite: 601 passed.

feat(daemon): memory dream runner and staged consolidation pipeline (#16)

* feat(daemon): memory dream runner and staged consolidation pipeline

Implements the daemon side of memory dreaming (docs/designs/memory-dreaming.md,
D-1): offline consolidation jobs over the managed store.

- agents/memory-dreamer.ts — the pure pipeline pieces: dream policy prompt
  (orient → gather signal → consolidate → prune & index), bounded prompt
  builder over the store snapshot + mined transcripts, hardened proposal
  parser (topic regex, size caps, dedupe, file cap), and the store digest
  that fences adoption.
- agents/dream-runner.ts — the job engine: one dream per agent, snapshot,
  extraction via an injected isolated-session runner, staged output under
  <agent-root>/memory-dreams/<dreamId>/ (the live store is never modified by
  a running dream), fenced + reversible adoption (timestamped backup,
  .history carry-over, per-file 'dream'-source provenance rows), discard,
  cancel-wins semantics, and boot-time crash recovery.
- cp/dream-reader.ts + cp/client.ts — the memory/dream/* frame surface; job
  metadata only crosses the wire freely, staged bodies ride byte-sliced
  correlated replies exactly like memory/read. Violations map to BAD_PAYLOAD
  and lifecycle conflicts to CONFLICT.
- store/local-store.ts — dreams metadata table (never staged bodies) plus the
  transcript-source queries, scoped like transcriptPageForAgent so a peer's
  private rows never enter a dream prompt.
- daemon.ts — runDreamExtraction: fresh isolated ACP session per dream;
  trusted runtimes carry the dream policy via _meta.systemPrompt (+ best-
  effort read-only mode), others get the policy prepended to the user prompt,
  acceptable only because dream output is staged and human-reviewed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): address dream-runner review — safety and atomicity

Resolves the CHANGES_REQUESTED review on the dream pipeline:

- (P1) Fail closed on extraction permissions. runDreamExtraction now REQUIRES a
  verified read-only/plan mode and throws if the runtime has none or the switch
  is rejected — an injection-exposed extraction never runs with the runtime's
  native write tools. The trusted system-prompt channel stays soft (policy
  prepended to the user prompt otherwise); only auto-adopt is gated on it.
- (P1) Serialize starts and reserve synchronously. start() takes a per-agent
  lock and sets the in-flight reservation before the first await, so two
  concurrent start frames can't both pass the one-in-flight check. cancel() no
  longer releases the reservation early; the run's finally releases it once the
  extraction promise settles, so a canceled dream's late extraction can't
  overlap a replacement.
- (P1) Atomic, serialized adoption. The replacement store (carried-over
  .history + one dream-source provenance row per file) is built in a sibling
  temp dir first; the visible window is a single rename with rollback, not a
  multi-write span where readers could see a partial store. adopt/discard run
  under the same per-agent lock. (Full live-writer serialization — the
  distillation-rebase rule — remains D-2, per design §8.)
- (P2) Pending failures are terminal. A failure before the pending→running
  transition (e.g. the input-snapshot write) now marks the dream failed instead
  of leaving it stuck pending forever.
- (P2) Oversized output stays adoptable. Staged file/index content is clamped on
  a UTF-8 code-point boundary with a byte reserved for the trailing newline, so
  the final string never exceeds writeMemoryFile's cap (which would make a
  "completed" dream un-adoptable).

Adds tests for concurrent-start serialization, pre-extraction failure
terminality, and byte-cap adoptability; updates design §2/§5 to document the
hard read-only gate. Full daemon suite: 1933 passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): close dream adoption fence race and cancel-during-staging

Second review round on the dream pipeline:

- (P1) The non-force adoption fence was stale by commit time — the dream lock
  didn't exclude console/tool/distillation writers, so a writeMemoryFile that
  landed after the digest check was silently overwritten by the swap. Add a
  shared per-memory-dir mutex (withMemoryDirLock) that every writeMemoryFile
  caller now holds; adoption builds the replacement in a temp dir first, then
  re-validates the digest and commits the swap *inside that same lock*, so no
  live write can interleave between fence and swap. A post-snapshot write now
  reliably makes a non-forced adoption refuse rather than lose the write.
- (P2) A cancel landing during stage()'s awaited writes could be overwritten to
  completed. Re-check lifecycle state after staging: on cancel, drop the partial
  staged output and preserve the canceled status (cancel-wins).

Tests: a concurrent write racing adoption is never lost; a cancel that fires
right after staging (via an onStaged test seam) yields canceled + no staged
output. Full daemon suite: 1935 passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(daemon): use const for the dream-runner test's self-referencing runner

The onStaged closure reads `runner` only when invoked, after the const is
initialized, so the forward self-reference is safe — satisfies prefer-const.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): abort the ACP extraction on dream cancel

Third review round: cancel only marked the record; the fresh ACP session
running the extraction kept going, and because the one-in-flight reservation
is held until the extraction promise settles, a hung or long prompt pinned the
agent and blocked every replacement dream indefinitely.

Thread an AbortSignal through DreamRunnerDeps.extract: the runner holds an
AbortController per in-flight dream and aborts it on cancel; runDreamExtraction
drives the host session-cancel path (host.cancel(sessionId)) when the signal
fires, so the prompt stops and the promise settles promptly (releasing the
reservation). The status-recheck guards stay as defense in depth.

Test: a cancel aborts a hung extraction (signal observed), the dream lands
canceled, and a replacement dream can then start and complete — proving the
reservation is no longer pinned. Full daemon suite: 1936 passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): make stagedFiles tolerant of concurrent staging removal

The cancel-during-staging test flaked in CI: run()'s post-cancel `rm(output)`
races the test's stagedFiles() call, so readdir listed a file that stat then
found already gone (ENOENT). Skip files that vanish between readdir and stat —
a cancel or discard can remove the staging concurrently — and poll for the
async cleanup in the test. Stable across repeated local runs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): harden dream cancellation — setup-race guards + bounded backstop

Fifth review round on dream cancellation:

- Setup-time race: an abort landing during ensureHostAsync / newSession /
  setSessionPermissionMode could fire session/cancel before any prompt exists,
  then still proceed into host.prompt with a spent one-shot signal — launching
  an uncancellable turn. Guard on the aborted signal after each awaited setup
  step and immediately before dispatch, so a canceled dream bails.
- Missing hard backstop: a runtime that ignores session/cancel would leave
  host.prompt (and the runner's `active` reservation) stuck forever. Two bounded
  backstops now cover it:
  * Runner (DreamRunnerDeps.cancelGraceMs, default 30s): abandons the await and
    releases the reservation a grace period after the abort regardless of
    whether extract ever settles — the hard guarantee, unit-tested with a
    never-settling extract.
  * Daemon (DREAM_CANCEL_FORCE_MS, 15s): stops awaiting host.prompt after the
    abort so the `finally` discards the isolated ACP session instead of leaking
    it. host.stop() is deliberately not used — the dream shares the agent's host
    and must not kill its real sessions.

Test: a runtime that ignores cancel (extract never settles, never honors abort)
still lands the dream canceled and frees the agent for a replacement dream.
Full daemon unit suite: 1937 passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(feishu): support international Lark region via a per-integration switch (#37)

* feat(feishu): support international Lark region via a per-integration switch

Feishu and Lark are the same ByteDance product on two open-platform gateways
(open.feishu.cn vs open.larksuite.com) — same app model, SDK, event shapes, and
rendering; only the host differs. Rather than a fifth platform, add a
`region: 'feishu' | 'lark'` field threaded end to end (defaulting to 'feishu',
so existing installs are unaffected):

- protocol: IntegrationFeishuConfig.region (FeishuRegion)
- daemon: consolidateFeishu carries region onto the per-app group; the SDK
  factory sets `domain` on both Lark.Client and the WSClient long-connection
- control-plane: persisted on the integration row (feishuRegion, NULL ⇒ feishu);
  integrationToSpec emits it; verifyFeishuBot exchanges creds against the
  matching gateway (a Lark app verified against the Feishu host would be
  spuriously rejected); exposed on the integration DTO
- web: region selector in the Add-integration modal; the console link + copy
  switch between the Feishu and Lark developer consoles

Tests: protocol codec region default + explicit 'lark'; daemon region→factory
forwarding; CP verifier gateway selection (unit) and a 'lark' install route
(int) asserting the verifier region, wire spec, and persisted row.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(feishu): make Lark region survive uninstall + reconnect on region change

Addresses two lifecycle gaps from PR review:

1. Region was stored only on the integration row, which uninstall deletes while
   keeping the bot + credentials. Reinstalling a freed Lark bot by botId then
   produced a region-less integration that defaulted to the Feishu gateway,
   sending retained Lark credentials to the wrong host. Region now has its
   durable home on the bot row (like slackAppId/discordAppId, survives uninstall)
   and is mirrored onto the integration at install time (as integration.name
   mirrors bot.name) — so integrationToSpec stays a pure read. The reinstall-by-
   botId paths copy the region forward from the durable bot.

2. The daemon identified/reused Feishu connections by appId alone, so a region
   change on the same appId stayed bound to the old-domain client. FeishuConnection
   now exposes `region`; the reconcile prune drops a conn whose region changed, and
   the reuse match requires appId AND region so the open loop dials the new gateway.

Tests: CP int — reinstalling a freed Lark bot preserves region 'lark' end to end
(durable bot row, mirrored integration row, wire spec). Daemon — FeishuConnection
exposes the region the reconcile compares on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(feishu): make daemon connection identity fully region-aware

Follow-up to the review's second-round findings — two remaining wrong-domain
windows when a region changes on the same appId:

1. The per-integration routing map (`fsConnByIntegration` / `botUserIds`) was
   evicted only when `conn.appId` differed, so a same-appId region flip left the
   integration pointed at the stopped old-domain client if the replacement start
   failed. The eviction now keys on appId AND region (feishuConnKey).

2. The in-flight guard was appId-only, so a NEW-region reconcile skipped behind an
   already-running OLD-region handshake, which then published its old-domain
   mapping. The guard now keys on appId+region, and after the handshake the connect
   re-checks the live desired region (desiredFeishuRegion) and self-discards if it
   was superseded mid-flight — so only the current-region connection ever binds.

Test: daemon reconcile drops the stale mapping and stops the old-domain connection
when the same appId switches region.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(daemon): dream auto-adopt gate and distillation rebase (D-2a) (#48)

* feat(daemon): dream auto-adopt gate and distillation rebase (D-2a)

Two of the D-2 adoption items from docs/designs/memory-dreaming.md §6/§8.

Distillation rebase — additive per-turn capture landing while a dream runs used
to trip the adoption fence and starve a busy agent of ever adopting. On fence
mismatch the rebase now gets one chance to explain the drift, splitting the
question in two:

- Authorization from `.history`: every record after the snapshot must be
  `source: 'distill'`. The window is delimited by a new `snapshotHistoryLines`
  (the log's line count captured WITH the store snapshot under the shared
  memory-dir lock), so it's exact rather than timestamp-approximate.
- Content from the files, not `.history`: a record's `after` is clamped to
  MAX_HISTORY_VALUE_BYTES, so a large file's row can't be replayed faithfully.
  Distillation is additive, so diffing the live file against the dream's own
  `input/` snapshot yields exactly the added lines; they're appended to the
  staged store and deduped against everything already there.

Any tool/console/other-sourced write still hard-fences to manual review.

This also fixes a latent tear: the snapshot read in `start()` wasn't under the
memory-dir lock, so it could interleave with a concurrent write and produce a
digest matching no actual state. It now shares the lock with the history count.

Auto-adopt — `dreaming.autoAdopt` adopts a completed dream without review, but
only when the runtime carries a trusted system-prompt channel (the same
`trustedExtractionMode` gate distillation uses); an untrusted runtime keeps the
dream reviewable. It runs after the in-flight reservation is released (adopt
refuses while a dream is in flight), never forces past an unrebasable fence, and
never throws — a conflict just leaves the dream awaiting review.

Tests: rebase applies distill-only drift, hard-fences a mixed window, and dedups
a line the dream already folded in; auto-adopt is an A/B on the trusted gate and
declines to force past a console write. Daemon suite 2013 passed, protocol 180.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): authoritative rebase ledger, bound trust, persisted marks, caps

Addresses all four blocking findings on the D-2a review, plus a production bug
the new tests surfaced.

1. (P1) LocalStore never persisted the snapshot counter, so every real rebase
   hit the fail-closed branch while FakeStore-based tests passed. The column,
   mappers, insert/update SQL and a migration now carry it, with a LocalStore
   round-trip and an end-to-end runner regression.

   While adding that round-trip, it caught a bug shipped in D-1 (#16):
   `updateDream`'s UPDATE never referenced `triggerKind`/`createdAt`, but
   `dreamToRow` binds them — better-sqlite3 rejects an unknown named parameter,
   so EVERY dream status transition threw against the real store. The statement
   now assigns every column dreamToRow produces, so the two can't drift.

2. (P1) `.history` cannot authorize a rebase. `appendHistory` is best-effort by
   design (it swallows its errors so logging can't fail a write), so a tool or
   console write whose append was lost is invisible there, and a later distill
   append makes the window look distill-only. Authorization now comes from an
   in-process write ledger bumped inside the write under the same lock, counting
   total vs non-distill writes. Counters that moved backwards (a daemon restart
   cleared them) are unprovable and fail closed, as is a digest change with no
   recorded write. `snapshotHistoryLines` is replaced by `snapshotWrites`.

3. (P1) Auto-adopt re-read the agent's CURRENT host, so a host replacement
   between extraction and adoption could let a new trusted host authorize an
   untrusted proposal. `extract` now returns `{ output, trustedChannel }` and
   the runner binds the producing host's verdict to that dream.

4. (P2) The rebase appended to staged files without re-checking the store's byte
   caps, so an at-capacity proposal plus one distilled line could adopt a store
   later managed writes couldn't update. It now re-enforces the index/topic cap
   and hard-fences instead.

Also corrects §3, which claimed an untrusted `autoAdopt` is rejected at
admission; it saves fine and simply leaves the dream reviewable.

trust flip during onStaged, an unlogged console write followed by a distill
write, and an at-cap staged file. Protocol 180, daemon 2018.

   moves backwards and any older snapshot is eventually caught up by new writes,
   which would reclassify a pre-restart tool/console edit as post-restart

   requires an exact match before comparing any count.

fix(control-plane): guard against unhandled promise rejections (#80)

The control plane runs one process for every tenant's BFF REST surface,
daemon WS gateway, and relay WS gateway, but it was the only service
without a process-level `unhandledRejection` handler — the daemon and the

terminate, so any floating rejection took the whole control plane down
and, under a supervisor, kept taking it down on each restart.

fix(daemon): stop memory reads from following planted symlinks (#81)

* fix(daemon): stop memory reads from following planted symlinks

#79 hardened the memory write path but left reads lexical: both
`readMemoryFile` and `nativeMemoryRead` validated the relative path and
then called `fsp.readFile`, which follows symlinks. The daemon runs
outside the agent's sandbox while the managed memory dir is inside the
sandbox's writable set, so an agent could plant
`memory/<topic>.md -> <any file the daemon can read>` and get the
contents back through the `readMemory` tool — the read-side mirror of the
write escape, and a way out of the sandbox's read confinement. The same
link under `MEMORY.md` is injected into standing context at session
start, and the dream runner reads every topic file.

Add `readContainedMemoryFile`, the read-side twin of the write path's
containment: walk and canonicalise every parent without creating
anything, reject a symlink or non-directory component, then open the file
itself with O_NOFOLLOW and require a regular file. Both providers route
their reads through it, so a link anywhere on the path fails closed
instead of resolving. Listing was already safe — it filters on the
dirent type, which reports a symlink as neither file nor directory.

fix(relay): keep webhook capability tokens out of the request log (#85)

* fix(relay): keep webhook capability tokens out of the request log

The generic-webhook ingress authenticates on a token carried in the URL
path (`POST /webhooks/in/<token>`), and that token is the only
authenticator when a hook has no HMAC configured — the default. The relay
builds Fastify with `logger: true` and no request serializer, so every
delivery wrote the token into an ordinary access log. A log stream is a
strictly lower trust boundary than the hook's owning org: anyone who can
read it (an operator, a log-shipping vendor, a crash bundle) could replay
the hook with a body of their choosing and wake the bound agent.

Redact the token segment in a `req` serializer rather than at the route,
so unmatched paths are covered by the same rule, and replace Fastify's
built-in 404 handler, which logged the raw URL back out — an unknown or
typo'd token is exactly the request that 404s, so the serializer alone
still leaked it.

fix(cli): stop an upgrade version from being re-read as --root (#91)

The daemon runs `upgrade --to <version> --root <root>`, where the version
comes from the Control Plane over `daemon/upgrade`. `parseRootFlag`
scanned every argv token, including other options' VALUES, so a version
spelled `--root=/elsewhere` was taken as the CLI's root before commander
parsed anything. `selfHealCliEntry` then created that directory tree and
wrote `cli-entry` into it, and `runUpgrade` took its version lock there
instead of the real store — a write primitive outside the AgentConnect
root, and a silently voided lock. `mkdir -p` on a path that must be a
regular file (an authorized_keys, say) replaces it with a directory.

Fixed at three layers, none of which relies on the others:

- `parseRootFlag` moves next to `firstPositional` in route.ts and skips
  option values the same way it does, so the two cannot drift. It also
  learns the CLI-owned subcommand value options — `--to` is the
  load-bearing one.
- `resolveTarget` rejects a `--to` that is not a plain version token, so
  a value shaped like an option never reaches any scan. It is now `async`
  so that rejection is a rejected promise, matching its declared type.
- `DaemonUpgradeBody.version` constrains the value at the boundary where
  it enters the system, where `min(1).max(64)` accepted any bytes.

* fix(daemon): stop materializing accepted skills beneath an agent-writable path

Third attempt at this, and the first two were wrong for the same structural
reason. A bespoke copier, then identity-pinned re-validation, then delegating to

indirection changes who writes, not the authority or the containment (the
installer does its own path-based reconciliation removal).

all. Acceptance now stops at the daemon-owned copy under `<agent-root>/skills/`,

rather than silent. `workspace-manager` is back to its original behavior — this
PR adds no workspace writes whatsoever.

Making an accepted skill visible to the runtime needs a containment-safe
materialization step (a hardened installer, or execution under a filesystem
sandbox that cannot follow workspace links to host paths). That is genuinely
larger than this PR and is tracked with the CP/console wiring this feature
already needs; `mineSkills` is off by default and unreachable from the console
until then, so nothing ships half-wired.

The previous revision closed the sandbox escape but left `skillAccept` returning

fix(protocol): bound git-repo normalization instead of backtracking on it (#92)

`s.replace(/\/+$/, '')` looks anchored but is not: the engine retries the
greedy `+` from every offset, so a long run of slashes that does NOT end
the string is O(n²). Three helpers used it, and `normalizeGitCloneUrl`
runs inside CP request validation — a `gitRepo` of ~1 MB of slashes plus
one trailing character stalled the single event loop the whole
deployment shares, blocking every other tenant's REST call, daemon
heartbeat, and relay frame for the duration. `GitRepoInput` had no length
cap, and the checks that would have rejected the value all ran after the
strip.

Strip trailing slashes with a linear scan, and bound the input twice:
`normalizeGitCloneUrl` refuses an oversized value before any check reads
it, and `GitRepoInput` caps ahead of the transform so an oversized body
is rejected without normalization running at all. `normalizeGitUrl` and
`gitRepoLabel` also take stored values that never passed the clone-url
cap, which is why the strip itself had to become linear rather than
relying on the bound.

fix(daemon,cli): create the state store and CLI root with restrictive modes (#98)

Two artifacts inherited the umask while everything else around them is
explicitly 0600/0700.

`<root>/state/local.sqlite` holds every platform message body, agent
reply, tool payload and durable inbox blob the daemon has seen — the same
material the console serves behind authorization — and was created 0644
inside a 0755 directory. config.json, agent.json, materialized
config-file secrets, runtime homes and evaluation artifacts all pass an
explicit mode; this one did not. The WAL siblings carry the same rows, so
they are narrowed too, and the directory is chmod'ed after creation
because `mkdirSync`'s mode does not apply to a path that already exists —
a container image `mkdir -p` or a systemd `StateDirectory=` (0755) is
exactly the case that bites.

`selfHealCliEntry` runs before anything else on every invocation, so it
is normally the first code to create `<root>` — at 0755, while
`cli/login.ts` and the daemon's `config/load-config.ts` both pass 0o700.
The loose mode is the one that persisted, leaving the store and the
daemon logs traversable by any other local account. It now creates the
root 0700 and repairs an existing looser one, skipping win32, which has
no enforceable POSIX mode semantics (same carve-out as
`protectCredentialsFile`).

`selfHealCliEntry` moves to `src/self-heal.ts`: `index.ts` executes
`main()` on import, so the permission handling was not reachable from a
test while it lived there.

* fix(control-plane): stop activation redeem from 500ing and from burning bearer links

Two bugs on the new optional-email activation link path:

   violation. That is fine at signup (no surrounding transaction) but fatal inside

   transaction, so the next candidate died with 25P02 — not P2002, so it was
   rethrown and surfaced as `internal server error`. Pick the free slug with a READ
   instead; the last candidate is derived from the (unique) user id, so it is free
   unless the user already owns an org, which the early return covers.

2. An already-activated account consumed a one-time BEARER link. It gains nothing
   from the link, so redeem now reports success without stamping `redeemed*`,
   leaving the invite available for someone who still needs it. A BOUND link is
   minted for that exact person, so it keeps recording its redemption (audit).

activated account opens it, then a fresh user can still redeem it; redeem succeeds
with every preferred slug taken).

* fix(control-plane): allocate the personal-org slug conflict-tolerantly

Read-then-insert still loses a concurrent race: two activation transactions with the
same base slug can both pick the same free candidate, and the loser's failed INSERT
aborts its interactive transaction — the very 500 this branch removes.

concurrent regression — three redeemers sharing an email local-part all activate and

feat(daemon): install accepted dream skills under symlink containment (#108)

* feat(daemon): install accepted dream skills under symlink containment

Unblocks `skillAccept`, which PR #86 shipped refusing with "not available yet"
because every materialization attempt was escapable.

Why the earlier attempts failed, and what is different here. Runtimes only read
skills from project-scope dirs under the ACP cwd, and that cwd is AGENT-WRITABLE
while the daemon writes with daemon authority from outside the agent's sandbox.
A bespoke `rm -rf` + copy followed a planted `.claude/skills` symlink; so did
delegating to `npx skills`, because process indirection changes who writes, not
the authority or the pathname containment.

The answer was already in this repo: `agents/memory.ts` has shipped a discipline
for exactly this — walk each path component with `lstat`, REFUSE a symlink
instead of following it, `realpath` and re-check containment after every step,
and publish through an exclusive temp + rename. This extracts that into
`fs/contained-path.ts` so both users share one implementation rather than
maintaining two subtly-different copies of security-critical logic, and builds
the skill materializer on it.

- `fs/contained-path.ts` — `containedTarget` (read/write) and
  `containedRemoveDir`, which refuses to delete through a link. Documented as
  narrowing the TOCTOU window, not closing it: Node has no `openat`.
- `skills/dream-skill-install.ts` — copies accepted skills into `.claude/skills`
  or `.agents/skills` by runtime, every path contained, bounded file count and
  size, non-fatal like `installSkills`. A containment refusal warns as a
  security event, not a routine miss.
- `skills/dream-skills.ts` — the canonical accepted copy under the agent root;
  never lists a symlink, since the name is handed to a copier.
- `skillAccept` now COPIES staging into the agent-owned tree, so discarding the
  dream later cannot uninstall a skill the user already took.

Tests: both reproduced escapes (a skill-root symlink and a per-skill symlink)
are refused with the outside tree provably untouched — verified to FAIL against
the naive implementation — plus runtime-root mapping, replacement of a prior
copy, and malformed-skill skipping. Daemon suite 2108 passed.

* fix(control-plane): reject MCP provider deletion while agents still enable it

Agents bind an MCP provider by name (runtimeOverrides.mcpServers), so
deleting a provider that agents still enable left dangling name-based
selectors — recreating a provider under the same name later would
silently rebind those agents to the new (possibly different) upstream.

DELETE /mcp-providers/:id now 409s while any org agent's enable-list
still contains the provider's name, mirroring the skill-source delete
guard. The OpenAPI description documents the rule and the 409 response
schema is declared. New integration tests cover the 409-while-referenced
flow, exact-name matching (daemon-local server names don't block), and
release via agent unselect or agent deletion.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): serialize MCP provider delete with agent enable-list writes

The reference guard read its agent snapshot outside the per-provider
serialization, so a concurrent agent create/patch could enable the
provider name between the check and the row delete — DELETE returned
204 and left exactly the dangling selector the guard exists to prevent.

The check now runs inside the serializeByProvider critical section, and
agent writes that ADD registry provider names join the same chains
(new serializeByProviders, entered in sorted id order so multi-name
writers cannot deadlock). A concurrent write now either commits before
the in-chain check (delete 409s) or waits until the provider row is
gone (its name then resolves as a daemon-local server, never a dangling
registry binding).

Regressions: two integration tests park the DELETE inside its reference
check and assert a concurrent agent create/patch blocks instead of
slipping into the check→drop window; unit tests cover mutual exclusion
and opposite-order acquisition of the multi-chain helper.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): close the diff-bypass and connector-rollback holes in the provider delete fence

Two orderings still produced a deleted provider with a live agent
reference:

1. The agent-write fence keyed off an added-vs-before diff, and ordinary
   agent edits overlap — a stale full-replace PATCH re-asserting a name
   it believed unchanged computed added=[], skipped the chain, and could
   restore the name inside a concurrent DELETE's check→drop window after
   another PATCH removed it. The fence now keys off the SUBMITTED list:
   any write whose resulting enable-list names a registry provider joins
   that provider's chain.

2. The connector create flow commits the provider row before the
   upstream save, so an agent can enable it while the save is pending —
   and the failure rollback deleted the row without the reference guard.
   The rollback now re-checks references inside the same per-provider
   chain and keeps a referenced row (the caller still gets the error;
   reconnect repairs the connection, or delete it after unselecting).

Regressions: a parked stale-PATCH restore ordering asserting the DELETE
queues and then 409s, and a parked-save connector rollback asserting the
referenced row survives.

* fix(control-plane): row-lock the runtimeOverrides read-merge-write in agent update

PgAgentRepo.update merged runtime-override patches onto a bag it read
without any lock, then replaced the whole JsonB column. Under
overlapping PATCHes that read-replace loses concurrent edits — and
worse, a PATCH that OMITS mcpServers (e.g. model-only) could carry a
stale mcpServers key back after another PATCH removed it, restoring a
provider reference behind the delete guard without ever joining a
provider chain.

The read-merge-write now runs in one transaction with the bag read done
via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, so concurrent bag writers fully serialize: an
omitted key always merges onto the committed post-edit bag and can never
resurrect removed entries. Callers through PgAgentConfigWriter compose
under its existing transaction; direct callers get their own.

Regression: an external row lock parks a removal PATCH and a model-only
sibling PATCH so both queue and serialize behind it; asserts the sibling
edit lands while mcpServers stays removed and the provider then deletes.

* fix(control-plane): key the provider lifecycle fence by (orgId, name) and guard create against name capture

The fence was keyed by provider row id while agents bind by NAME: an
agent write could resolve old row A, queue behind A's DELETE, and — once
the delete dropped the row and released A's chain — a same-name create
could commit replacement row B inside the window, silently rebinding the
queued agent onto an upstream its authorization never saw.

Three changes close this:

- Chains are now keyed by (orgId, name), the durable binding key, so
  lifecycle events on different rows under one name (drop A, create B)
  serialize with each other and with agent enable-list writes. Agent
  writes chain directly on their submitted names — no resolve-to-row-id
  staleness exists at all.
- Provider create (both POST /mcp-providers and the connectors create
  flow) joins the chain and is REFUSED with 409 while any agent already
  enables the requested name — the mirror image of the delete guard, so
  a name can never be captured out from under existing selections.
- Agent writes re-run the enable-list visibility gate INSIDE the fence,
  so authorization always holds for whatever the names resolve to at
  commit time (mapped to 403 via McpEnableDenied).

Regressions: the reviewer's full ordering (delete 204 → parked queued
agent writer → same-name re-create blocks on the chain, then 409s), the
simple create-while-enabled 409 on both create surfaces, and updated
chain unit tests.

DELETE /skill-sources/:id refuses (409) while any agent's enable-list still
references the source by name — but the check-then-delete was not serialized
against agent create/patch, so a concurrent write could commit a new skill ref
between the check's agent snapshot and the row drop, letting DELETE return 204
while leaving a dangling name-based selector.

This mirrors the final MCP-provider lifecycle fence (#136) for skill sources:

- Chains keyed by (orgId, name) — the durable binding key — in
  serializeBySkillSource / serializeBySkillSourceNames, so lifecycle events on
  different rows under one name serialize with each other and with agent
  enable-list writes.
- The DELETE reference check runs inside the chain; source create gains the
  mirror-image name-capture guard (409 while any agent references the requested
  name); sharing flips join the chain.
- Agent writes join the chain of every source their SUBMITTED skill-refs name
  (not an added-vs-before diff — a stale full-replace PATCH may be the write
  that restores a ref), via withSubmittedSkillSourceChains nested inside the
  MCP fence in a fixed order so the two chain families cannot cycle.
- The skills visibility gate re-runs INSIDE the fence with the keep-exemption
  derived from the agent's committed refs, evaluated in the row-locked update
  transaction via the new AgentUpdateOpts.authorizeSkills hook (twin of
  authorizeMcpServers). One skills-specific difference from MCP: a skill-ref
  has no daemon-local fallback, so a NEW ref to an unknown source is refused —
  a write queued behind a delete gets 403 instead of committing a dangling ref.

Unit tests cover chain mutual exclusion, opposite-order acquisition, and org
scoping. Integration regressions mirror the MCP suite: the parked-delete
create/patch racers, the stale full-replace fence (no diff bypass), restricted
same-name replacement not grandfathered (queued and route-entry orderings), the
row-locked hold check, the sharing flip queuing behind an in-flight enable, the
sibling-PATCH bag merge, and the referenced/capture guard basics.

fix(web): never redeem an activation link under a stale session (#160)

* fix(web): never redeem an activation link under a stale session

An activation link redeemed in a browser that still held a previous console
session redeemed as THAT identity — the wrong account, or one an admin had
since deleted (whose `sub -> userId` mapping the CP's auth memo still served,
so `/me/access` reported no email and joining the waitlist failed with
NO_VERIFIED_EMAIL).

Two independent fixes:

- `/activate/[token]` now always starts from a clean slate: sign the existing
  session out through Logto's end-session endpoint, then redeem under a freshly
  established identity. A per-tab marker (checked with a single-shot effect
  guard) resumes the flow after the sign-in round trip instead of logging out
  again, and falls back to the old behavior when sessionStorage is unusable so
  the link can never loop.
- The human-auth plane confirms the resolved user row still exists, drops the
  dead memo entry, and answers 401 `ACCOUNT_GONE`; the console signs out on
  that code. The row is deliberately NOT re-provisioned: an account an admin
  removed must not come back to life under the old session — the next sign-in
  is a normal JIT signup.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): keep a deleted account rejected, and fail closed without storage

Addresses both review findings.

1. Evicting the `sub -> userId` memo alone let the very next request with the
   same still-valid bearer re-run JIT provisioning and recreate the account an
   admin had just deleted — a retry or a parallel console poll could resurrect it
   before the client finished signing out. The auth plane now tombstones the
   subject with the time the deletion was observed and refuses every token issued
   at or before it (a token with no `iat` cannot prove it is newer, so it is
   refused too). Only a demonstrably newer authentication clears the tombstone
   and signs up afresh. Entries expire after 24h — far longer than any access
   token — so the map stays bounded.

2. Activation no longer falls through to the current session when its resume
   state cannot be stored: that reproduced exactly the stale-session redemption
   this change exists to prevent (Logto keeps a completed session in
   localStorage, so "no sessionStorage" and "already signed in" coexist). The
   flow state now tries sessionStorage, then a short-lived cookie, and reports
   failure; the page fails closed with a recoverable message plus a sign-out
   button. `/auth/callback` reads the same helper so a cookie-resumed flow still
   returns to the link.

Tests: the integration case now asserts the rejection PERSISTS across retries
and across a write route, that the row is never recreated, and that only a token
issued after the deletion provisions again. New `flow-state` unit tests cover
the cookie fallback and the both-stores-unusable path the fail-closed branch
depends on.

* fix(control-plane): record the identity boundary from the deletion itself

The durable cutoff still depended on a request reaching the CP between the
deletion and a restart: delete the row, stop the process before anything observes
it, and the next process saw an unknown subject and JIT-provisioned a replacement
account for a still-live pre-deletion bearer.

Evidence has to be written at deletion time, and the CP does not perform the
deletion — the external admin app does, and it must not have to change for this
invariant to hold. So the evidence is written where both meet: an AFTER DELETE
trigger on app_user records the cutoff for any deleter, CP included, with no
cooperation from the deleting application. The auth plane's own recording stays as
a second path (a row that vanished without the trigger, e.g. an older restore).

subject-less invited rows when merging an invite into a claimed account, and
fencing there would lock out the person claiming it. GREATEST() on conflict keeps
the boundary monotonic; TRUNCATE does not fire row triggers, so test teardown is
unaffected. Still 24h-expiry-limited, mirroring TOMBSTONE_TTL_SECONDS.

* fix(daemon): collapse Discord threads into channels, collect user names

Discord channel discovery listed one row per THREAD. A session keys on the
concrete channel a message arrives in — the thread's own id, and the daemon
opens a thread off every top-level mention — so approach-A discovery (observed
session history IS the reachable set) surfaced "#general" once per turn.

(server name, channel name): a channel reported under several ids collapses,
while same-named channels of two servers stay separate rows. Rows with no known
server (DM conversations, unresolved scopes) dedupe on id alone, the only key
that cannot merge distinct conversations. Scope is learnt from the inbound
gateway message (no API call), when the daemon opens the thread itself, and
from the TTL-cached channel lookup, which also backfills stored sessions.

The reported id is now the channel rather than a thread, so channel-scoped
routing rules and the §14 gating checks accept `parentChannel` too — a trigger
set on "#general" now governs the threads underneath it, where before it
stopped applying the moment the bot threaded.

Discord user names were never collected: only Slack ran sender/mention
resolution, so `display_names` held no Discord user and the console fell back
to the raw snowflake. ChannelNameResolver gains noteMessage/resolveUser
(Slack-parity, bot senders skipped), and mention tokens humanize through the
gateway message's own mention cache — "@acp-tester", not "@1524225313192542270".

fix(daemon): give the agent the message a Telegram reply quotes (#166)

* fix(daemon): give the agent the message a Telegram reply quotes

Telegram nests the replied-to message inside the update, but the normalizer
typed `reply_to_message` as `{ message_id: number }` and threw the rest away.
That id only stitches the reply into a session, so an @mention that quotes a
message the daemon never recorded reached the agent as the mention text alone —
it could not see what the reply was about. Unlike Slack there is no history
backfill to recover it (`fetchThreadHistory` is Slack-gated, and the Bot API
cannot fetch history after the fact), and the unrouted-message transcript path
only records a thread that already has a live session. So the update itself is
the only chance to keep the content.

Normalize the quoted source into `NormalizedMessage.quoted`, preferring the
Bot API 6.9+ `quote` selection over the full source (an explicit statement of
which part the reply is about) and folding an attachment mention in so a
media-only source still says something. Prompt assembly injects it just before
the reply text, framed as context rather than instruction — the quoted author
is a third party.

Suppressed when the quoted message is already in this session's transcript:
it either rides the catch-up context or was delivered on an earlier turn. That
covers the bot's own past posts, so the common "reply to the agent" case adds
nothing and cannot duplicate.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): suppress a quoted reply only when the runtime can see it

A stored transcript row is not proof the model has the content, so keying
suppression on one dropped the quote in two states where it was the only carrier.

A user-SELECTED passage (Telegram `quote`) states WHICH part of the source the
reply is about. Having the full source in context cannot supply that, so "what
about this?" stayed ambiguous. Track the selection apart from mere partialness
(`selection` vs `excerpt`, which truncation also sets) and never suppress it.

When a persisted ACP session cannot be resumed, `handle` mints a fresh session
with empty context, and replay filters the agent's own rows — so replying to the
bot's own prior message suppressed the quote AND omitted the message. Key the
check on what actually reaches the runtime: the row is in this prompt's replay,
or it predates the unread window on a CONTINUING session. A recreated session
suppresses nothing.

Both paths now have regression tests that fail against the previous condition.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): prove quote visibility from delivery receipts, not cursor order

The previous suppression asked "is the quoted row outside this turn's unread
window", which is unsound twice over.

Ordering: `transcript.ts` is TEXT and `transcriptSince` compares it with SQL
`ts > ?`, but Telegram ids are ascending integers — `"100" > "99"` is false. A
quoted human message at id 100 with the cursor at 99 falls outside the window,
looks "delivered earlier", and gets suppressed although it never reached the
agent, leaving a bare "what about this?". That defeats the point of the PR.

Own messages: the bot's reply is recorded after the inbound cursor, so it lands
INSIDE the next window while replay filters it out as an own message. Quoting it
back therefore duplicated content the continuing runtime authored itself.

Replace the window test with three order-free facts: the row is in this prompt's
replay; or, on a continuing session, this agent AUTHORED it; or, on a continuing
session, it has a delivery receipt. The last is what `transcript_recipient` (plus
the row's own `recipient`) already records for every inbound append, so ask it
directly instead of reconstructing delivery from a cursor. Two new store readers
expose those facts; neither compares timestamps.

The lexical `transcriptSince` comparison is a pre-existing issue with a wider
blast radius (it also governs Telegram catch-up replay); this change stops
depending on it rather than fixing it here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): always deliver a quoted reply source unless the prompt repeats it

The delivery receipt is not proof the runtime saw the message either. It is
written at the TOP of `handle`, before any prompt, and `dispatchOne` can still
bail in between — the `readyGate` cancel returns after the row, the receipt, and
the advanced cursor all exist, with nothing ever sent to the agent. Own
authorship is no better: it says some PAST session produced the text, while a
recreated session starts empty and `freshSession` describes only this turn, not
earlier recreations.

The daemon records no fact that implies "the current ACP session has seen this
message", so stop asserting one. Emit the block whenever a reply carries a quote,
except when the quoted row is among the rows THIS prompt already replays — the
one case that is verbatim duplication inside a single message and provable
locally.

The trade is deliberate and asymmetric. Suppressing wrongly drops the subject of
the reply and leaves a bare "what about this?"; echoing back a message the model
already holds costs one bounded, labeled block. On Telegram the echo is often
useful anyway: reply-quoting is how a user says WHICH earlier message they mean,
and after a compaction the agent may no longer hold even its own words.

Drops the two store readers added for the receipt check, now unused.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): match quoted replay by content, and gate selection on is_manual

Two ways the quote block still misrepresented its source.

Replay suppression matched the quoted message id alone, which does not establish
that the replayed body IS the quoted text. The connection consumes `message` but
not `edited_message`, so a recorded row can hold pre-edit text while Telegram's
inline source carries the correction — an id match then handed the model the
stale wording and dropped the current one. Require the replayed body to still
contain the quoted text (whitespace-collapsed, ignoring the ingress ellipsis);
a miss costs one duplicated block, a false match loses content outright.

`quote` was treated as a deliberate selection whenever it was non-empty, but
Telegram's `is_manual` is what separates a passage the sender CHOSE from one the
server added by itself. Without that flag the block told the model "the user
selected exactly this part" about text no user ever picked, and bypassed replay
suppression on that false premise. Reserve selection semantics for
`is_manual === true`. A server-added quote stays useful as content where the
source has no text of its own, marked partial but never as intent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): require exact equality to suppress a quoted reply source

Containment is not equivalence. A stale row reading "do not deploy now" contains
an edited source reading "deploy now" while meaning its opposite, so the matcher
could suppress the current instruction and leave the model only the inverted one.
The lossy normalizations that made containment look workable were unsafe for the
same reason: collapsing whitespace hides an indentation-only edit to quoted code,
and stripping a terminal ellipsis hides a short message that genuinely ends in
one.

Compare for equality, and normalize nothing except the separator before a trailing
`[attached: …]` mention — the transcript writes it on its own line while the quote
joins it with a space, a difference in OUR rendering of identical content rather
than in the content. Partial quotes never reach the comparison at all: an excerpt
cannot equal a full row, so a chosen passage, a server-clipped excerpt, and a
capped body are all delivered unconditionally.

Also refreshes the `NormalizedMessage.quoted` docs, which still described every
Telegram quote as user-selected and claimed injection happens only for
never-recorded messages. Both stopped being true two commits ago.

fix(daemon): deliver a finished background task back to its session (#176)

* fix(daemon): deliver a finished background task back to its session

`run_in_background` promises the model it "will be notified when the task
completes" — a harness guarantee, not an SDK one. Under ACP the foreground turn
has already returned `end_turn` by the time the task exits, so nothing delivered
the result: the model ended its turn expecting a notification, and any obligation
riding on that task went with it.

Observed end-to-end: agent test asks test2 to answer after 30s with
`needsReply`; test2 backgrounds `sleep 30; date`, ends its turn, and the reply
never arrives — `needsParentReply=1` stays set forever while the parent waits.

The runtime is not idle in that window: it re-enters a `running` cycle to drain
the completion. That cycle is NOT a delivery — it carries no `Pending`, so
`onAcpUpdate` returns early and discards every chunk, tool render, transcript
row, and webchat frame it produces. Its MCP tool calls do land (that socket is
not `Pending`-gated), which is why the wake tells the model not to repeat a
report it already sent.

So on a non-subagent task settling, the daemon now injects a turn into the
session with the completion. It defers to the runtime's self-drain cycle only
while that cycle runs (bounded re-arm), then delivers regardless. The wake is
`source: 'agent'`, carries no `CallMeta` (it is not an agent call), and keys
`msgId` on the task id so a duplicated settle edge cannot dispatch twice; a child
woken this way still reaches its parent through the origin persisted on the
session. Unlike the §5 channel notice it is not gated on output mode — that notice
is for the human, this is for the model. `MAX_BG_TASK_WAKES_PER_SESSION` bounds a
self-feeding loop, since a wake has no hopCount to cap.

Also logs the accepted SDK lifecycle edges at debug: that feed cannot be
reproduced offline, and it was the only way to establish the sequence above.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): fence and agent-scope the background-task wake

Addresses both P1 findings on #176.

Fence automatic reclaim while a wake is armed. `settle()` deletes the task before
the timer is armed, so the session read as SDK-quiescent for the whole grace/re-arm
window. A task that outlived the session's idle TTL therefore let a sweep landing
in that window close the session and drop the lease; the wake then took the "host
reclaimed" branch and the completion was lost again — the exact failure §5.1
exists to prevent. The lease now counts `armedWakes`, which joins `tasks.size` and
`sdkState` in the quiescence predicate and in `agentHasLiveSdkWork`. Arming takes
the count, the fire path releases it before deciding anything, so delivered,
skipped, and gave-up all leave it balanced, and the re-arm path takes it again.

Key leases by (agentId, acpSessionId). ACP session ids are runtime-local — the
reason `pendingTurnKey` and `getSessionByAcpIdForAgent` exist — but the lease map
was keyed by session id alone, so two agents each exposing `acp-1` shared `tasks`,
`sdkState`, and `bgWakes`: one agent's live task could suppress the other's
completion, and a colliding task id overwrote the wrong record. `closeIdleSessions`
now passes both ids to its exemption predicate for the same reason.

The `armedWakes` count also fixes a case the `tasks.size` guard could never catch:
an empty `background_tasks_changed` snapshot settles every task on one edge, arming
a timer each, all of which then see an empty `tasks`. The last armed wake now
delivers for all of them instead of one turn per task.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): hold the wake fence through async turn initialization

Third P1 on #176, reproduced by the reviewer: releasing `armedWakes` when the
wake dispatches still left a gap. `dispatch()` claims the serial gate
synchronously, but `dispatchOne` then awaits thread history, attachments, and
managed-memory recall before `SessionManager` writes `state = 'prompting'`.
Through that window the row is still `idle` and has no `Pending`, so an
already-expired session reads quiescent, and a sweep landing there TTL-closes it
and stops the host mid-initialization — the same loss the fence exists to prevent.

The count is now handed to the dispatch promise and released when it settles,
which is turn completion rather than admission; `finally` covers rejection so a
failed wake cannot pin the host, and a turn that never settles is still bounded by
the absolute `agentMaxLifetimeMs` ceiling. Release moved into one idempotent
helper so skip, give-up, and deliver each release exactly once; the re-arm path
takes the next count before releasing this one, so the total never dips to zero.

Holding past dispatch also widens the multi-settle guard: the surplus count can
now mean "a wake turn is in flight", not just "another timer is armed". Skipping
is right in both cases — a task settling during a turn is handed to the model by
the runtime in-turn, which is what the session-state guard already assumes.

The budget test no longer drives 20 real turns; with the fence outliving each
dispatch that sequencing was timing-dependent, and the property under test is the
refusal at the cap, not the arithmetic getting there.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): defer a wake behind an in-flight turn instead of coalescing it

Fourth P1 on #176, again reproduced by the reviewer. `armedWakes > 1` had come to
mean two different things, and only one of them is safely coalescible:

  • another timer armed — an empty `background_tasks_changed` snapshot settles every
    task on one edge, arming a timer each, and all of them then see an empty
    `tasks`. None has run, so one turn can cover them all.
  • a delivery in flight — the dispatch promise deliberately outlives
    `host.prompt()` while renderer/finalization runs. By then `sdkState` is already
    idle, so the model has stopped and cannot observe a newly settled task in-turn.

Folding the second case discarded the task permanently: its timer skipped as
"already delivering", the older dispatch then released the last count, and the
session was left with no timer, no delivery, and no prompt for it — the same
stranded-result class this PR exists to remove.

Split the fence into `armedWakes` (timers) and `deliveringWakes` (dispatches), so
the coalescing test can name exactly the armed case. A wake that fires while a turn
is in flight for the session now DEFERS: it retries the same attempt once that
session's `activeDispatchDoneByKey` promise resolves, taking the replacement fence
slot before releasing its own. Aggregate progress stays bounded by the wake budget,
which caps deliveries.

Deferring on any active dispatch (not just a wake's) also covers the same
post-prompt window after an ordinary turn, which the `rec.state !== 'idle'` drop
would otherwise lose for the identical reason.

Regression: `delivers a task that settles after a wake prompt returned but before
its turn settles` — holds wake A's prompt open while reporting the model idle,
settles task B in that window, and asserts B is still owed (not discarded) and is
delivered as a third prompt once A's turn completes. Verified to fail with the
deferral removed: 2 prompts instead of 3.

that point, not after.

drift-guard test:

message.mpim subscription plus routing work: both the daemon and the
relay currently skip mpim conversations when listing channels, and treat
only channel_type === 'im' as a DM.

* feat(slack): route group DMs as their own conversation kind

Group DMs were not a supported surface: without the message.mpim
subscription an agent never sees an un-mentioned follow-up in one, and
without mpim:history / mpim:read the thread and conversation lookups it
needs fail with missing_scope.

conversation kind end to end (protocol IntegrationChannel.kind, the
ConversationKind enum, DTO, console).

conversation between people that the agent happens to sit in, not a room
addressed to it. So it follows a channel's rule, not a DM's — the agent
answers when @-mentioned, thread follow-ups need no further mention, and
"every message" stays an operator's opt-in. isDm therefore stays false
for mpim; the new isGroupDm flag only classifies.

Slack never lists a group DM as bot membership, so it is surfaced the way
a DM is: on observation, when an inbound message names the bot, never
through a membership snapshot. Consequences carried through:

- a gated agent's group DM is created Off and stays unroutable until a
  Console editor enables it, and an authoritative channel snapshot (which
  can never contain one) does not delete the row;
- an app_mention payload carries no channel_type and Slack's "G…" ids are

- that channel-to-mpim conversion resets the trigger to Off: the trigger
  the row carried was a channel's default, not an operator's choice for
  this conversation.

The console lists group DMs beside DMs under "Direct messages" with a
distinct glyph and label, but keeps the channel's three-way trigger
rather than a DM's binary on/off.

Non-gated agents need no configuration: their unscoped mention rule
already covers a group DM once the events arrive.

* test(cp): stop the usage series test crossing UTC midnight

Unrelated to this PR's Slack work, but it is what is failing CI here.

`GET /usage?range=d30` buckets the spend series by DAY on the requested
tz's boundary, which defaults to UTC. The test seeded three rows at 10,
20 and 30 minutes ago and asserted all three land in the FINAL bucket —
true only when the suite runs more than 30 minutes after UTC midnight.
CI ran at 00:27 UTC, so the 30-minute row fell into yesterday's bucket
and the last point summed to 0.30 instead of 0.35.

Clamp each offset to the time actually elapsed since that boundary, so
the rows stay in today's bucket whatever the hour. They remain well
inside the 30-day window, so the totals and the tz-shift sums are
unchanged. The sibling test that spans two buckets is unaffected: `now`
and `now - 24h` are always in different day buckets.

* feat: review mined dream skills from the console

Closes the last gap in D-3: the daemon could mine, stage, accept and dismiss
skills, but nothing reachable from a browser could drive it. The protocol frames
have existed since D-1, so this is the CP relay plus the console surface.

- control-plane: `dreamSkillAccept` / `dreamSkillDismiss` on the outbound sender,
  and `POST …/dreams/:dreamId/skills/:name/accept|dismiss`. Both are edit-gated
  and capability-gated through the same guard as adopt/discard — a viewer gets
  403 and a pre-dreaming daemon 409 + DAEMON_FEATURE_MISSING, with nothing
  forwarded in either case. The `:name` param carries the miner's own kebab-case
  regex, so a traversal-shaped name is refused at the schema before it can reach
  a filesystem path.
- web: `acceptDreamSkill` / `dismissDreamSkill`, and a "Suggested skills" block
  listing each still-`proposed` candidate with its description and Accept /
  Dismiss.

The recommendations render OUTSIDE the store-review block on purpose: a skill's
review lifecycle is independent of the store proposal (design §7), so candidates
stay actionable whether or not the store was adopted and after its staging is
gone. Copy says acceptance installs the skill for this agent, since that is the
consequence a reviewer is agreeing to.

Tests: console asserts nothing is installed without an explicit click, that
already-reviewed candidates are not re-offered, and that a viewer sees the
actions disabled; CP integration covers forwarding, the traversal-shaped name,
the viewer 403 and the version-skew 409 — each asserting the daemon was never
contacted. Suites: CP 668 unit / 683 integration, web 372.

fix(daemon): stop a skill's own code fences from truncating the dream (#185)

A mined skill body is Markdown, and a procedural skill exists to show its
commands — so it almost always contains fenced code blocks. Those inner
fences live inside a JSON string, but the reply parser matched the outer
fence lazily and stopped at the first ``` it saw, handing JSON.parse a
truncated object. The parse failed and the whole dream was discarded:
the store proposal and every mined skill, not just the offending one.

Every test passed because each fixture was hand-written JSON with no code
block in a skill body. Running the real prompt against a real model is
what surfaced it: the model returned exactly the right candidate, cited
two distinct sessions, and correctly ignored the one-off session — and we
threw all of it away.

Recover the JSON by trying the plausible readings in order (outermost
fence, brace slice, innermost fence) and keeping the first that parses to
an object. Regression covers a fenced reply whose skill body carries code
fences, plus a reply that trails prose after the JSON.

* fix: address review — atomic org provisioning, fenced revocation, durable revoke reports, real install signal

Five review findings on the M0 + platform-Slack-app PR.

1. Org creation is now genuinely atomic (§3.2). `ensurePersonalOrg` only
   composed under a caller's transaction; the ordinary JIT-signup path passes
   the root client, so org, membership, `PgAgentRepo.create` (its own tx) and
   the `preset_agent` marker each committed separately. A crash between the
   agent and the marker leaves the reserved slug taken by an agent no marker
   describes — the next boot's backfill sees a collision and writes a PERMANENT
   `skipped`, with no repair path. New `withAmbientTx` opens a transaction on a
   root client and composes under an ambient one; the compensating org delete
   is gone (rollback does it). The no-auth default tenant uses the same seam via
   the new idempotent, collision-aware `ensurePresetAgentsProvisioned`, which
   the backfill now shares. `prisma/seed.ts` opts OUT so suites keep their
   known-empty default-org baseline. Regressions: fault-injected marker failure
   proves full rollback + re-runnability, an ambient-tx rollback proves
   composition, and the default tenant proves idempotence across boots.

2. Revocation is generation-fenced. Slack does not order `app_uninstalled` /
   `tokens_revoked`, so a delayed event from a replaced install could revoke a
   freshly re-authorized bot and kill its live integrations. `Bot` gains
   `credentialRevision` + `credentialInstalledAt`, advanced together by the new
   `bumpCredential` (also the only un-revoke path — a bare `setRevoked` is
   removed so no unfenced back door remains). The revision rides `rc/bot-assign`
   and is echoed on `rc/bot-revoked` along with Slack's envelope `event_time`;
   `revokeIfCurrent` applies the stamp in one CAS and `revokeBot` skips the
   whole teardown when it refuses. The timestamp arm is the load-bearing one: a
   relay that already applied the re-install's assignment would echo the NEW
   revision, so only the event's own occurrence time reveals it is stale.

3. `rc/bot-revoked` is no longer droppable. Slack acks the HTTP event before the
   relay's async handler runs and never redelivers it, and no CP-side probe can
   discover a dead token — assignment reconciliation just republishes the stale
   active state. The manager now buffers the report per bot and flushes it on
   READY beside the thread-assign and channel-snapshot queues, replayed verbatim
   so the fence still sees the generation that observed the event.

4. The platform install has a real completion signal. The callback settled by
   DELETING the row, so the console watched the integration list for growth —
   but a re-authorization of a workspace the agent already has only rotates the
   token and creates no integration, leaving that path polling forever. The row
   now carries `status`/`failureReason`/`botId`, survives as the signal behind a
   new `GET /integrations/slack/platform-install/:id`, and stays single-use (a
   replayed callback is refused rather than re-running the install and bumping
   the generation again). Failures settle with their reason, so the modal
   reports them instead of hanging; a TTL-reaped row (404) ends the poll too.

5. The design docs no longer carry contradictory current-tense requirements.
   preset-agents.md's active sections are rewritten for the single general
   preset, with §4 behind an explicit superseded boundary that names the
   successor shape; agent-assistant.md gains a reading guide, keeps MCP/OAuth
   active, and fences the assistant-agent sections. Section numbers are
   preserved — source comments cite them.

* fix(slack): fence the unassign, acknowledge the revoke, close the reuse path

Three review findings, all confirmed.

1. The post-commit re-read in `revokeBot` narrowed the TOCTOU window but did not
   close it: revoke commits N, the read returns N, a re-install commits N+1 and
   broadcasts its assign, and only then does the old revoke broadcast an
   unfenced `rc/bot-unassign` — which wins at the relay and removes the LIVE
   ingest. Moved the decision to the point of application: `rc/bot-unassign`
   carries the revoked generation and the relay drops a release older than the
   assignment it holds. Only a revocation stamps it; a transport flip / un-share
   / last-install-removed stays unconditional.

2. The dead-token probe still could not guarantee delivery. The queue cleared as
   soon as `WebSocket.send()` succeeded, while the CP handler caught and logged
   DB failures without telling anyone — with the link up and the one startup
   probe already spent, the bot stayed active indefinitely. `rc/bot-revoked` is
   now the one acknowledged rc/* report: new `rc/bot-revoked/ok` REP, the relay
   queues FIRST and clears only on that ack (`applied:false` — the fence refused
   a stale report — is equally terminal), and the CP propagates handler failures
   as a retryable error instead of swallowing them.

3. The "always non-shareable" invariant was enforced only where the bot is
   created. A freed platform bot has `inUseByAgentId === null`, so the generic
   picker offered it and `POST /integrations` would `setShareable(true)` on the
   http branch — widening it AND, after an uninstall, minting an install on a
   token Slack already rejects. Generic reuse now refuses a revoked bot and any
   platform-app identity (`teamId`), and the console filters both out of the
   picker rather than offering what the server rejects.

Regressions: relay drops a stale unassign but honors a current one; the revoke
report retries until acked and only then drains; generic reuse refuses both the
platform bot (still non-shareable, still zero installs) and a revoked bot.

dead-credential backstop deliberately reports the exact current revision with

unconditionally. The ordering treated a missing timestamp as merely unfenced,

credential and be refused terminally) could displace the queued probe report
and drain the only retry source.

* fix(cp): make platform-bot membership admission atomic with the bot row

Review #196 flagged two races in the widened Slack platform-bot path:
the callback admitted membership on a stale `shareable` snapshot (a
concurrent sharing disable could commit alongside a second-agent
admission, ending non-shareable with two agents), and its
check-then-create was not idempotent (two concurrent callbacks for the
same new agent could insert duplicate active rows).

Both sides now serialize on a bot-row lock: IntegrationRepo.
addBotMembership re-reads `shareable` and the active membership set
FOR UPDATE in the same transaction as the insert, admitting at most one
active row per (bot, agent) — a duplicate callback's loser reports
'exists' as success; BotRepo.setShareable(false) recounts active
installs under the same lock and throws BotStillShared (409) when >1
remain, so the route's optimistic pre-check can no longer be bypassed.
Deterministic interleaving regressions cover both: concurrent duplicate
callbacks admit exactly one membership, and a disable racing a held
admission lock is refused with both members intact.

winner commits; READ COMMITTED re-reads then see the winner's membership
and the call degrades to the idempotent no-op.

org/membership/preset; it fails with a duplicated org when the lock is
