fix(web): remove redundant Discord checklist (#244)

fix(auth): link social identities through the Account API (#243)

Linking Slack from Profile always failed: the CP returned 502 and the card
showed "Something went wrong."

Root cause is upstream. Logto's `POST /api/connectors/{id}/authorization-uri`
runs the connector with no session context -- it passes `notImplemented` as the
session store -- so any connector whose `getAuthorizationUri` persists state
fails inside Logto with a 500. Slack's connector does exactly that
(`setSession({ redirectUri })`, read back by `getUserInfo` for the token
exchange). Logto documents the limitation as Management-API-specific and names
apple / standard OIDC / standard OAuth 2.0; Slack belongs in that set too. Both
legs are affected, so this could not be fixed by moving only the first call:
the session is what carries `redirectUri` between authorize and verify.

Verified against a live tenant with the same connector: the Management API
returns 500, while the Account API returns 201 with a real Slack authorization
URI.

So linking and unlinking now run over different Logto surfaces, split by
whether they need a connector session:

- Link is driven by the browser against the Account API with the user's OWN
  token. This restores the pre-#225 flow. Note it does not weaken #225's
  rationale: that path never involves the M2M credential at all, so the
  credential still does not reach the browser.
- Unlink stays on the CP, because it enforces a server-side invariant the
  browser cannot be trusted with -- the last sign-in method may not be removed,
  serialized per user by SocialIdentityMutationGate -- and needs no session.

The browser still cannot discover a connector id, so the CP keeps that half:
`POST /me/social-identities/authorization-uri` and `POST /me/social-identities`
give way to `GET /me/social-identities/connectors/:target`, and the two service
methods behind them collapse into `socialConnectorIdFor`.

Also logs the upstream status/code in logtoFailure. Diagnosing this took far
longer than it should have because the 502 fallback recorded nothing at all --
the CP had swallowed Logto's 500 without a single log line.

* fix(sessions): settle a whole pending A2A chain, not just its first level

Review catch on #241. Two linked gaps let a 3-level delegation chain that
arrives root-last strand its deepest session:

- A child whose parent row EXISTS but is itself `inherited_pending` copied that
  parent's placeholder values and stamped itself `inherited` — which looks
  settled, so the settlement scan (`inherited_pending` only) would never revisit
  it once the real ancestor landed. It now stays pending.

  handed its own placeholder down to its children. A pending row now settles

permanently hidden.

* fix(sessions): close six review findings on the visibility gate

Review on #241 found six current correctness/privacy gaps, all fixed here.

1. The capture gate covered only automatic post-turn distillation. An agent can
   also write agent-scoped memory EXPLICITLY — and the session prompt encourages
   it — so `writeMemory` and the record-memory mutations now consult the same
   gate at CALL time (which also covers a session tightened mid-life). Reads stay
   available: recalling what the agent already knows is not a disclosure of the
   current conversation. Native runtime memory persists inside the runtime per
   AGENT, with no per-session lever, so it cannot be gated here; the product docs
   now narrow the guarantee for that backend explicitly instead of implying one.

2. A tightening cascade skipped descendants that were already private, leaving a
   different owner on a transcript that holds text copied from the tightened
   session. Every descendant is now re-owned.

3. The reconnect snapshot was a bounded newest-first window, so a session
   tightened while the daemon was offline could sit past the cap and keep a stale
   `org` gate indefinitely. The snapshot now orders unacknowledged revisions
   first — those are exactly the rows whose gate may be stale — and logs when the
   cap still bites rather than reading as full convergence.

4. The visibility PUT authorized against an unlocked row: a concurrent ancestor
   cascade could re-own the session in between, after which the former owner's
   in-flight request would still widen it. Authorization is re-checked inside the
   write transaction, against the locked row.

5. A placed-but-offline daemon was reported `applied`. Daemons keep serving
   established sessions while the CP is down, so its gate may genuinely still be
   `org` — that is now `pending`. Only an unplaced agent is vacuously applied:
   nothing runs it, so nothing captures.

6. The detail endpoint polled only the root session, so the UI flipped to
   `applied` as soon as the root daemon acked while descendant daemons were still
   behind. It now evaluates the whole subtree.

* fix(sessions): route retryable snapshot failures into the replay continuation

Review follow-up on #241. `sendSnapshotChunk` returned a bare `false` for every
failure, so `replayPages` treated a correlator timeout or a failed
`recordVisibilityAck` exactly like a disconnect and returned normally —

fix(web): prove account ownership before linking a social identity (#252)

Linking Slack got as far as Slack's consent screen and then failed on the
callback with "Your sign-in session expired. Sign in again and retry."

Two proofs meet at `POST /api/my-account/identities`: the social verification
proves the NEW identity, and `logto-verification-id` proves the caller still
owns THIS account. Logto requires the second whenever the account has a
security verification method and answers 403 without it. #243 sent neither,
following #225's "no second email-code step" stance -- which held only because
#225 wrote through the Management API, where the M2M credential was the
authority. On the Account API the user's own token is, so the account has to
re-prove itself.

The proof is collected BEFORE leaving for the provider and carried across in
the flow record: on return the identity is saved immediately, with no UI left
to ask in. Accounts with nothing to re-prove keep going straight out.

Also stops reporting that 403 as an expired sign-in session. It sent this
investigation after the wrong thing; while linking it means the identity change
was not proven.

Restores `requestEmailVerification` / `verifyEmailCode` and the
`hasSecurityVerificationMethod` + `primaryEmail` fields dropped in #225.

most of it. A second call then fetched the Slack workspace separately.

next to the provider: ~240ms, most of which is the client's own round trip to

  projects from too. A profile load costs ONE upstream fetch, not one per
  projection. githubLoginFor keeps its own cache deliberately: it sits on a live
  authorization gate and must not shift because a display read was added.

  OIDC payload -- stops reaching the browser at all. It only ever went there
  because the browser was the one calling the provider.

single replica, so a shared cache would buy nothing that the existing in-process
one does not; and persisting mirrored provider data would make us own its

* docs(auth): record the Slack identity keying rule

Reviewing Slack sign-in raised a question nothing in the repo answered: is a
Slack `U…` safe to treat as an identity on its own? It is not, and the answer
was living only in a chat log.

Slack documents the user id as unique to its workspace and says to use it
together with the team id. So any map, comparison, or column identifying a Slack
human has to be keyed on the pair. `SlackIdentity` returns both for that reason,
and taking only `userId` off it compiles, reads naturally, and is wrong -- which
is exactly the kind of mistake a doc alone will not stop, so the type carries the
warning too.

Audited the two places that compare Slack user ids. Both are safe by
construction and the doc says why, so nobody "fixes" them later:

- allowedUserIds is per integration, and an integration is bound to one
  workspace, so both sides of the comparison come from the same workspace.
- slack_user_config is keyed on the CONSOLE user, not a Slack one.

Nothing maps a Slack sender back to a console user today. Whoever builds that is
the first caller who has to honour the rule.

Also records, in the same place, that Logto's own connector keys on the bare
`U…` (verified against a live tenant), and the two Logto behaviours this
investigation cost the most time to discover: why the provider needs a second
callback registered, and that configuring a connector does not enable sign-in --
a tenant can have working account linking and a dead sign-in button at once.
Setup steps stay in .env.example rather than being duplicated here.

workspace containing the user" and concluded that Logto, keying on the bare

be authored from another workspace while the normalizer keeps only

has to carry the author's team id first.

feat(daemon): tell an agent when its root post forked the conversation (#301)

* feat(daemon): tell an agent when its root post forked the conversation

A channel-root post opens a NEW session on that post. That is the right thing
for a deliberate new topic, and the wrong thing for the case agents keep hitting:
asked to relay an answer back to whoever asked, an agent posts to the channel it
can see, so the asker gets a detached top-level message and the answer's session
forks away from the conversation waiting for it. Nothing told the agent — the
call succeeded and returned `ok`.

Return a `notice` on the result when the root post landed on a conversation this
agent is ALREADY part of, naming the address that would have replied instead:

- the parent session's channel ⇒ name the `{"to":{"sessionId":"…"}}` to answer;
- the current session's own channel ⇒ its ordinary turn reply already goes there.

The post is never blocked — a root post elsewhere is a legitimate new topic and
stays silent, as does a threaded post (it joins a conversation rather than
forking) and a run with no daemon to seed the session. Feedback lands in the same
turn as the mistake, where the agent can still answer the right way, instead of
in a prompt rule written long before it.

`parentSession` resolves the parent from the current turn's trusted call metadata
when present, else the durable origin persisted on the session row — the latter
being the load-bearing half, since relaying an answer happens on a later,
human-triggered turn that carries no metadata at all. It widens nothing: the
notice fires only when those coords MATCH a channel the caller itself named.

* fix(daemon): let the daemon judge which conversation a root post landed on

Review found three ways the notice could speak falsely, all from ops deciding
something only the daemon knows:

- A Feishu caller could never resolve its parent: the lookup keyed the session
  through `narrowPlatform`, whose fallback folds `feishu` onto `slack`, so it
  searched for a row that does not exist.
- Identity compared raw platform + channel, while the daemon deliberately scopes
  channel ids by physical bot (Telegram DMs reuse a user's id across bots). A
  post through another bot to a same-looking id read as the parent's conversation.
- The notice claimed a session opened whenever the callback existed, but the
  daemon declines the seed at the agent-call hop limit.

Replace `parentSession` with `rootPostRelation`, which answers the question
itself — parent, self, or neither — using the caller's platform string verbatim,
comparing transport scope on both sides, and reading the parent's coords from its
own row (the only place a scope is recorded). `spawnChannelRootSession` now
returns whether it seeded, and the notice is gated on that.

Tests cover the Feishu caller, a scope mismatch with an unscoped control so the
silence is provably the scope's doing, and a declined seed.

fix(runtimes): stop leaking probe temp roots when a runtime outlives its adapter (#309)

`probeAllRuntimes` removed its temp root with a single best-effort `rmSync`, which
loses a race: a runtime whose process escapes the adapter's process group can still
be writing when `AcpHost.stop()` resolves — omp registers its own daemon under the
private runtime HOME, so the group-wide SIGTERM/SIGKILL never reaches it — and its
next write re-creates the tree we just deleted. Each orphaned root holds a private
runtime HOME (~270MB once omp has materialized its natives), so a busy host
accumulates them until the disk fills: 213 roots / ~57GB inside one hour.

Cleanup now observes a schedule of checkpoints (250ms / 1.25s / 4.25s after
teardown) and keeps going even once the root looks gone — stopping at the first
empty stat would only move the race window rather than close it. Only the initial
removal is synchronous, so callers still see the root gone on return while the
observation window runs in the background and never delays a probe result.

`sweepStaleProbeRoots()` backstops it at daemon startup and on the recurring idle
sweep (15-minute cadence), reclaiming `ac-probe-*` roots older than an hour so a
root re-created after the last checkpoint is collected within the same process
lifetime. It lstats rather than stats, since the OS temp dir is world-writable and a
symlink planted under the prefix must not be followed out of it, and skips roots a
live probe still claims so the timer can never reclaim one mid-sweep.

Not addressed: omp re-materializes 269MB of natives into every private HOME because
seeding deliberately skips large files, so each probe still writes and deletes that
copy. Fixing that needs omp's natives-cache env var, which the private-env table
does not cover.

* fix(daemon): give a posted message one canonical thread key

#295 fixed the Telegram session key inside `spawnChannelRootSession` and named
the residual itself: the peer-wake path in ops.ts still anchored to the raw ts.
One post therefore produced two different session keys depending on which
consumer read it — the mark of a conversion living at a call site instead of at
the seam where a post becomes a thread segment.

Move it to that seam. `threadKeyForPost` (messages/normalized.ts) is now the one
place that conversion happens; ops computes `postedThread` through it once and
hands the same key to the spawn, the peer wake, and the transcript row. The spawn
takes the canonical `thread` plus the raw `postTs`, because those genuinely
differ off Slack and the transcript row must keep a real, comparable platform ts.

Having one place made it clear the old rule was only right for two platforms, so
it now follows each platform's actual conversation model: Discord conversations
ARE the channel (every inbound message keys the channel id, so a post cannot open
a thread of its own), a DM is one continuous stream that a post joins rather than
forks (`dm` on Telegram, the chat on Feishu), and Telegram groups keep threading
off the root message. Only the platform knows which chats are DMs, so ops asks it
— once, and only where the answer can change the key; a failed lookup falls back
to the non-DM key rather than failing a send that already happened.

Also fix the row that conversion was papering over: `recordOutbound` fell back to
the CALLER's thread for a root post, so a cross-channel post wrote a row keyed to
(target channel, caller's thread) — coords belonging to no session at all, and a
trap for `telegramThreadForMessage`, which resolves a reply's owning thread by
`ORDER BY seq DESC` over that same ts. Whether the reply landed in the right
session depended on the async seed row winning that race. The outbound row now
carries the thread the post created, so it collapses onto the seed's row
(INSERT OR IGNORE, delivery recorded separately) exactly as the toAgent path's
`transcriptTs` already does — one row, one key, no race.

An explicit thread is left alone: a numeric Telegram thread is a forum TOPIC id
that drives message_thread_id at post time, and canonicalizing it would silently
move the post to another conversation.

feat(web): reuse one ownership proof across consecutive links (#313)

* feat(web): reuse one ownership proof across consecutive links

Linking a second sign-in method asked for a second email code, even seconds
after the first. Logto does not require that: a verification record lives for
10 minutes and may authorize more than one change in that window -- its docs
list identifiers, credentials, social account linking, and MFA.

So the proof is kept for the window instead of being spent on one round trip.
Only the record id is stored, in the sessionStorage the in-flight link already
uses; the code itself is never stored.

Two things this has to get right:

- A reused proof must still be valid when the CALLBACK saves the identity, and
  the provider's consent screen sits in between. Spending the tail of the
  window is how someone who pauses there gets a 403 instead of a link, so a
  proof is only handed back while five minutes remain.
- A proof Logto refuses is dropped rather than retried, or every later attempt
  in that window would fail the same way.

The trade, stated plainly: one code now authorizes any link for the rest of the
window rather than exactly one. The id was already parked in sessionStorage for
the round trip, so this widens an existing window rather than opening one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): anchor the reusable proof to Logto's own expiry

Review was right on both counts.

The record's clock starts when the code is REQUESTED, not when it is redeemed,
and the verify step returns that same record. Timing the reuse window from
redemption therefore credited a slow reader with minutes the record did not
have: four minutes spent finding the email left six, not ten, and the
five-minute callback reserve silently became one. The request response carries
`expiresAt`, so that is what is stored now -- the guessed TTL constant is gone.

A proof also outlived its session. It is tab-scoped, so signing out and back in
as someone else left the previous user's proof in place; Logto rejects it, but
only after a wasted trip through provider consent. clearLocalSessionMetadata()
now drops it, covering logout, session reset, account-gone and dead-refresh.

feat(auth): pick the ownership-transfer recipient by org tenure, and show it first (#314)

* feat(auth): pick the ownership-transfer recipient by org tenure, and show it first

A restricted resource is reachable only through its ownership arm, so when a
member leaves, "which owner inherits it" decides whether anyone can still find
it. Two things made that outcome arbitrary and invisible:

- `membership` carried no timestamps, so the recipient came from `ORDER BY
  "userId"` over timestamp-prefixed cuids — effectively the OLDEST ACCOUNT among
  the remaining owners, a fact about the platform rather than about the
  organization being left. The console's "joined" column borrowed
  `app_user.createdAt` for the same reason, and was wrong the same way.
- Nothing surfaced the transfer, before or after. From every other owner's
  console, a departing member's private agents simply stopped existing.

Adds `membership.createdAt` and re-bases both surfaces on it. Pre-existing rows
are backfilled from the cuid in `membership.id`, whose leading base36
milliseconds are that row's own creation instant, so historical ordering is
accurate rather than merely well-defined going forward; rows with a non-cuid id
(seed fixtures) fall back to max(account, organization) creation.

The recipient rule is now stated rather than incidental: an owner removing
someone else inherits their resources, and a member leaving on their own hands
them to the organization's longest-standing owner. A transfer still never widens
visibility.

`GET /members/:id/removal-preview` returns the prospective recipient plus the
departing member's owned-resource counts per kind, with the restricted subset
called out, and the leave/remove dialog renders it as a sentence. It shares the
removal's authorization, takes no locks, and is never an authorization input —
the transaction re-derives its own recipient, so a race can only make the dialog
stale, never the transfer wrong.

feat(collab): authorize agent discovery and A2A by call policy, not channel (#186)

* feat(collab): authorize agent discovery and A2A by call policy, not channel

A2A delivery has been postless since #854 — a `sendMessage` with `to.toAgent`
wakes the peer directly and leaves nothing in any channel — so a shared channel
stopped being evidence of anything while still gating both peer discovery and
peer wakes. That left two legitimate populations unreachable: peers sharing no
channel, and agents with no IM integration at all (webchat / hook / dream /
memory-only), which a channel-keyed table cannot even express. It also crashed:
`listChannelAgents` from a webchat session made the CP throw in `toDbPlatform`,
and a throwing WS handler closes the whole daemon↔CP control socket.

Authorization is now the directional call policy alone, org-scoped: caller A may
discover or wake B iff both are known in the directory (fail CLOSED if either is
missing), same org, A's outbound admits B, and B's inbound admits A. Discovery
stays the authorization surface — a peer failing the predicate is omitted, never
listed-then-rejected. `Agent.visibility`/`sharedWith` is deliberately not
consulted: it governs human console access, so a `restricted` agent is still a
callable peer.

- protocol: `CollabRoutesSnapshot` gains a flat, channel-free `agents[]` (the
  only structure that can express an integration-less agent);
  `ChannelAgentsReq/Ok.channel` becomes optional.
- control-plane: new `AgentRepo.orgDirectory`; `handleChannelAgents` serves both
  scopes over one org read and one `visibleToRequester` filter (a channel is a
  literal intersection, never a wider grant); binds `requesterAgentId` to the
  authenticated daemon; feature `agent-directory-org-scope-v1`.
- daemon: `CpCollabRoutes` gains a flat by-agent index + `admits`; tool renamed
  `listAgents` with `listChannelAgents` kept as a deprecated alias; `channel` is
  an optional filter, no longer a default.
- relay: same flat index; `agent-msg-router` binds org from the caller entry.

Channel checks did not disappear — they moved from authorization to COORDINATE
INTEGRITY. `coords` is still the woken peer's session key, so an unchecked
assertion would let a source daemon name a channel its agent cannot reach,
compute a bit-identical `childSessionId`, resume the target's existing session
there and read it back via `needsReply`. `coordsAdmit` enforces this identically
on all three wake paths, keyed on (orgId, channelId) and deliberately
PLATFORM-FREE: `narrowPlatform` collapses unknown platforms to 'slack', so a
platform-keyed check could be dodged by asserting e.g. 'feishu' coords.

Rolling upgrade is feature-negotiated. A new daemon never sends a channel-less
request, nor a session-identity-platform channel, to an old CP — that payload is
what triggers the close(1011); with nothing answerable to narrow to it answers
locally instead. An old CP's snapshot has its flat directory derived from the
channel entries.

Behavior changes reviewers should notice: an unknown or unplaced target now
yields `not_allowed` instead of a misleading `offline`; `introduceOnJoin` fan-out
regains a code-level bound (the joined channel rides the trusted `CallMeta` and
is forced as the filter, instead of only being asked for in the prompt).

hardening; DM/group-DM coordinates and departed-bot channel rows on the
`coordsAdmit` pass branch; removing the now-dead `hasMembers` / `channelOrgFor`.

feat(integrations): let any agent switch a channel off (#318)

* feat(integrations): let any agent switch a channel off

The per-channel trigger only offered "off" to a restricted agent, whose
ingress is scoped-rule-only so Off was free. An org-visible agent reaches
every conversation through unscoped defaults (@-mention anywhere + DMs),
which no channel-scoped rule can subtract from — so it had no way to say
"not here" short of deleting the whole integration or removing the bot on
the platform.

Off becomes a control every agent has, expressed as a subtractive fence:
`mutedChannels` on the integration spec for a daemon-arbitrated bot, and on
rc/bot-assign / rc/routes for a relay-arbitrated one. Both arbiters apply it
ahead of every rung, so a muted channel answers nothing — not an @-mention,
not a thread it had already joined, not a control command, not a shared
bot's slug or default-dispatch fallback. A gated integration leaves the list
empty; its Off remains the absence of a scoped rule.

Direct rows still never mute: a preserved DM row of a now-org-visible agent
is hidden in the console, so honouring it would be behaviour with no visible
control. A channel row is different — it stays on screen — so it now keeps
its Off across a restricted → org transition instead of decaying to mention.

fix(messages): never split a streamed reply mid-sentence (#323)

* fix(messages): never split a streamed reply mid-sentence

The ~2s idle-flush timer fires on a pause in the ACP stream, which says
nothing about whether the reply's text is complete. Text deltas are
token-sized, so the buffer routinely ends mid-sentence — even mid-word —
and flushing it verbatim posted one answer as two chat messages cut at
that arbitrary point.

A time-triggered flush now emits only up to the last paragraph break
outside a fenced code block and re-buffers the rest, so the tail settles
into the next flush, the next semantic boundary, or the turn's final
message. Semantic boundaries (tool call / plan / thinking) and turn end
still drain the whole buffer: the model really did finish a text block
there, and holding would push the body below the tool chrome.

its channel output is one streamed card, and only its transcript records
are chunked.

* fix(messages): keep a full drain for the terminal failure path

flushBuffered() is not only the idle timer's entry point: when
host.prompt() rejects, the daemon calls it to publish an error the
runtime narrated into the message stream before failing (codex-acp

single-line error, and each converger has coverage for a boundary-less
body and a paragraph-plus-tail body.

Adds the wire contract and the daemon half of leaving: `integration/leave` is a
REQ with a reply, because unlike every other channel control it changes the
outside world — the operator is told what the platform said, not what we hoped,
so a missing scope or a `last_member` channel comes back as `ok:false` rather

The three platforms disagree in ways the design has to carry rather than hide:

- Slack leaves one channel and then emits `channel_left`, which re-lists
  membership authoritatively and retires the row by itself.
- Telegram leaves one chat and tells nobody — no self-event, and its bot API
  cannot enumerate chats — so the row survives unless retracted by id. That is
  what `IntegrationChannels.removed` is for: absence from a non-authoritative

fix(sessions): stop reporting ordinary access outcomes as faults (#351)

* fix(sessions): stop reporting ordinary access outcomes as faults

The Settings > Session access card raised two everyday situations as
degradation, and neither could be cleared.

Enabling a provider policy hides every candidate whose source scope the
migration could not reconstruct. That scope is unrecoverable — only new
activity on the same session rebinds it — so deriving `degraded` from
that count pinned any organization with pre-existing history to a
permanent fault state and buried the one signal worth acting on. The
policy row now carries `legacyUnresolved`, the low-water mark of the
unresolved count since enablement: `degraded` means the live count
exceeds the mark, i.e. a candidate went unresolved AFTER enabling. The
mark is adopted at enable and ratchets down as legacy rows settle; the
migration backfills it for already-enabled policies and clears the stale
`degraded` they were pinned to. The backlog stays reportable to owners
as `hiddenSessions`.

The Slack resolver treated every `ok: false` as "could not answer", so a
deleted private channel — or a bot removed from one, which is the same
response over the wire — raised "external access checks are unavailable"
on every list, and the 5s unknown TTL re-asked Slack about that channel
on every page. `channel_not_found`, `not_in_channel` and `user_not_found`
are Slack answering, so they become a plain deny at the deny TTL with
`degraded` false; auth, missing scope, rate limiting, outages, unknown
codes and transport failures stay `unknown`. Access is unchanged — deny
and unknown both refuse — and a re-invited bot recovers within the deny
TTL because no scope is revoked. GitHub already drew this line.

The card reserves amber for `degraded`, renders the hidden count as a
muted fact, adopts the platform tile the Bots and GitHub rows already
use, and moves the full access policy behind the row's info hint so each
provider reads as two lines instead of four.

fix(webchat): stop initialize/tools-list losing the session-registration race (#360)

On a live deploy every new webchat conversation on the general preset got its
`agentconnect-admin` descriptor installed and STILL showed no administration
tools. The remote-grant authenticator required a private current session for
every method, but that predicate cannot hold when the adapter connects: the
descriptor is installed into `session/new`, the adapter's `initialize` (and its
immediate `tools/list`) fire while that call is still running, and the daemon
registers the session with the CP only after it returns. Observed on test:
`initialize` at 10:26:28.257 got 401 `session_not_private`; the `session_meta`
row landed at 10:26:28.368 — 111 ms too late, every time. Adapters do not retry
a failed connect, so the server stayed dead for the session's whole lifetime
(until the ~25-minute grant rotation forced a `session/load`).

The private-current-session predicate now gates only `tools/call`. That is the
step that actually wields the delegated authority, it is issued mid-turn when
the registration has long landed, and it still fails closed the moment the
conversation's current session is not private. The handshake reaches no tool
and `tools/list` serves the static curated catalog with no org-scoped data, so
admitting them on grant + live-authority checks alone gives up nothing.

Not caught by #357's tests because the fixture always pre-registered the
session; the new tests cover the registration window (initialize/tools-list
admitted, tools/call denied) and the widened-session denial.

released the write mutex. A concurrent reporter could settle generation N+1

replace `actions` on every update.

that fence means a newer generation owns the Check and writes its own name
and actions, so the stale write is dropped.

write into an ambiguous state mutation: the Check's settled state is the one
the create wrote, so the fence is released with that observed value. The
recovery path renames only, through a helper that asserts nothing else.

feat(cli): launch the service daemon through the user's login shell (#373)

* feat(cli): launch the service daemon through the user's login shell

Moving the daemon from foreground to an OS service broke npx-distributed
ACP runtimes (e.g. claude-acp probed as "not installed"): systemd --user /
launchd give units a minimal PATH and never source shell profiles, so
version-managed node/npx and ~/.local/bin binaries vanish from the
daemon's environment.

Fix at the process-tree root instead of guessing env vars:

- The unit now runs the CLI run shell (ExecStart=<node> <cli-entry> run).
  In service mode the CLI launches the daemon THROUGH the user's
  interactive login shell ($SHELL -l -i -c 'exec "$0" "$@"' ..., fish
  variant included) — the daemon is born with a fresh terminal-equivalent
  environment and tracks profile edits at every restart. `-l -i` matters:
  distro .bashrc guards return early for non-interactive shells, and
  version managers append their PATH exports below that guard.
- Readiness watchdog: the daemon writes its pid to <root>/daemon.lock
  first thing, and the shell exec preserves the pid, so lock == child pid
  is a precise came-up signal. A hanging or exec-hijacking profile is
  SIGKILLed at a deadline and the run shell falls back to direct spawns —
  a broken profile degrades the environment, never the service. Shells
  with no safe template (tcsh &c.) go direct from the start.
- Static floors: an install-time PATH snapshot baked into the unit
  (Environment="PATH=..." / EnvironmentVariables) keeps the CLI itself
  and the fallback path working, and the daemon prepends its own Node bin
  dir on startup (covers legacy direct-ExecStart units and docker).
- Upgrade semantics unchanged: the run shell re-resolves <root>/current
  at every respawn and handles RESERVED_RESTART_CODE itself; legacy units
  keep working and migrate on the next install-service.

Verified end-to-end on a live host: with a systemd-like minimal env
(no nvm on PATH, no $SHELL), claude-acp probes ok and the full login
shell PATH reaches the daemon.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): single TERM on service stop; group-kill hung login-shell attempts

Review findings on #373:

- systemd's default KillMode=control-group TERMs both the CLI wrapper and
  the daemon; the run shell then forwards a second TERM, tripping the
  daemon's second-signal force-exit mid-drain. KillMode=mixed delivers
  TERM to the main process only (exactly one TERM reaches the daemon via
  the run shell) while keeping cgroup-wide KILL escalation.

- The readiness watchdog killed only the direct shell pid; a profile
  hanging in a child command (sleep, credential helper) survived the kill
  and leaked alongside the fallback daemon. The login-shell attempt now
  runs detached in its own process group and the watchdog SIGKILLs the
  whole group. The ready daemon's signal path is unchanged (pid-targeted).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): a requested stop wins over login-shell fallback and respawn

Review finding on #373: with KillMode=mixed, stopping the unit while the
login-shell attempt is still pre-readiness forwards TERM to the shell,
which dies not-ready — and the fallback branch then launched a
replacement direct-spawn daemon while the service was stopping, leaving
systemctl stop to hang until the cgroup SIGKILL.

Track stopRequested in onTerm and give it precedence over both the
not-ready fallback and the reserved-code respawn. The loop decision is
extracted into pure decideNext() with a stop-before-ready regression
test.

fix(control-plane): serialize cross-instance writes with pg advisory locks (#377)

* fix(control-plane): serialize cross-instance writes with pg advisory locks

Rolling updates give the CP a bounded two-writer window (SIGTERM -> readiness
flip -> WS drain -> http.close), which voided three process-local serialization
mechanisms. Migrate the two that fit a transaction to Postgres advisory locks,
taken inside the write transactions so they hold across instances:

- skill sources: replace the per-process (orgId, name) promise chains with
  blocking pg_advisory_xact_lock scopes (persistence/skill-source-lock.ts).
  Source create (name-capture scan), delete (reference scan), and sharing flips
  run their check-then-write pair in one repo transaction under the scope; agent
  enable-list writes carry an AgentSkillSourceFence so the name locks, the
  viewer-visible source read, and the row-locked authorize all happen inside
  the agent write's own transaction.

- external memory: delete ExclusiveMutationGate and move its fail-fast 409
  semantics onto pg_try_advisory_xact_lock scopes
  (persistence/memory-connection-lock.ts) inside a new PgMemoryConnectionWriter
  (connection create/update/rotation-prepare/delete + installation delete, each
  a single transaction; secrets sealed before the tx, daemon/relay pushes kept
  post-commit best-effort). Agent create/update/delete transactions try-lock
  the touched connection scopes and re-verify a newly bound connection in-tx,
  closing the check-then-delete race around the FK-less JSON binding. The move
  handler intentionally drops its gate: staging pushes self-heal via the
  post-commit re-push, usage-checked removal, and reconnect snapshots.

- AgentMutationGate cannot ride a transaction (moves span daemon RPCs across
  transactions with unbounded drains): document the rolling-update exposure and
  the lease-row design in the class comment; follow-up tracked in #376.

Integration tests now wedge the fences by holding the real advisory scopes
from an independent transaction (the shape of a concurrent CP instance), with
a pg_locks waiter probe for deterministic FIFO ordering.

* fix(control-plane): pair memory projections with their committed revision

Review follow-ups for #377: ending the connection advisory scope at
transaction commit left two commit/push interleavings where the relay's
strictly-newer revision gate pins stale state until reconnect.

- Secret pairing: the writer now returns the secret snapshot read INSIDE
  the committing transaction (sealed in-tx, decrypted after commit), and
  the PATCH/rotation pushes publish exactly that — a config-only PATCH
  that read secrets before a concurrent replacement can no longer
  republish the old credential under its newer committed revision.

- Grant retirement: rotation gains a fenced second half
  (finalizeGrantRotation) that revokes the retiring grants AND bumps the
  revision in one transaction, then republishes the whole post-retirement
  allowlist at that strictly newer revision. The per-hash relay unassign
  is gone — it only applies at the exact current table revision, so an
  assign landing between the overlap push and retirement made it a no-op
  and left the revoked grant relay-authorized.

Both interleavings are covered by tests that stage the exact commit/push
orders (a parked pre-transaction secret read; a racer assign between the
overlap push and retirement), not just contention while the lock is held.

* fix(control-plane): derive the delete tombstone under the connection scope

Review follow-up for #377: the relay tombstone was computed from the
route's pre-transaction connection read (+1), which a completed rotation
(now two revisions per rotation) can outrun — the relay drops a tombstone
at or below the revision it already holds, leaving the deleted
connection's upstream binding and grant hashes live until reconnect.

deleteConnection now returns tombstoneRevision (current revision + 1,
read from the row inside the fenced delete transaction) and the route
publishes that value. All mutations serialize on the connection scope, so
it is strictly newer than every assignment that could still be in flight.

Review follow-up on #393. The disable gate was built on the wrong signal and
contradicted the authoritative design.

`authRequired` is not launch admission. The daemon sets it from a probe
rejection AND from a live turn rejected with ACP auth-required
(`noteRuntimeAuthFromTurn`), and both land on the same wire field — so an
admitted, perfectly launchable runtime that had one turn rejected for login is
indistinguishable from an unadmitted curated candidate. The gate therefore
disabled legitimate choices.

"deliberately does not require readiness — an agent placed on a logged-out
runtime is an ordinary, supported state", and creation and placement never
gate on it. And the gate leaked anyway: with every reported runtime logged
out, the fallback selected the first one, which RuntimeSelect exempts from
disabling as the current value, so it saved regardless.

So surface the state instead of blocking it. `loginRequiredRuntimeIds`
(renamed from `unavailableRuntimeIds`, with the semantics written down) feeds
a "Login required" tag on the menu row and a warning mark on the closed
trigger, where the field is too narrow for the text. Every row stays pickable
and keyboard travel stops on all of them.

What survives from the gate is the part the design itself endorses: the
DEFAULT prefers a signed-in runtime, mirroring how auto-placement picks a
preset's runtime, falling through to the first reported id when all are logged
out. Add and Onboarding now seed the runtime as '' so that default applies to
a fresh form while an explicit choice always survives.

* fix(web): render peer agents on the left in session detail

In a session's transcript every sender other than the owning agent rendered
as a right-aligned human bubble — including other AGENTS (webchat peer
participants, trusted a2a bots on Slack). With a third party in the
conversation that misreads badly: the right side means "you" in every chat
UI, so a peer agent's answer looked like the viewer's own message.

Rule now: the right side is reserved for humans; any sender that resolves to
an org agent (and isn't the viewer) renders as its own left-side agent block
with its icon, name, and timestamp — matching how the owning agent renders.
Applied to all three turn-building paths (real transcript, live steps,
adopted-webchat live tail). Owner-turn grouping gains the same speaker
identity check so consecutive owner/peer rows no longer merge into one block,
and FmtStep learns an optional image so peer attachments survive the move.

Also: the composer placeholder says "Message everyone…" in multi-participant
conversations — post-#409 every participant responds, so "Message review-bot…"
implied a private reply that isn't what sending does.

Humans other than the viewer keep the current right-side rendering for now:
Slack sender ↔ console identity linking is deferred, and flipping them left

Addresses the three v2-round blockers:

1. Conversation scope is the protocol's DURABLE workspace/tenant scope —
   EventSession.transportScope (Slack team id / Feishu tenant key / stable
   mint, filled for Socket Mode and HTTP alike) — persisted at C1 as a new
   nullable SessionMeta.tenantScope column (today it is only folded into
   ownerIdentity). Explicitly NOT the daemon session key's credential-derived
   physical scope, which is hashed from tokens and rotates with them; v2's

   cursor's full (lastActivityAt, startedAt, id) tuple (millisecond ties
   cannot double-emit), and the exists-newer probe runs under the outer
   scan's own org/visibility predicate (a newer invisible or cross-org row
   cannot suppress a visible conversation). C1 index becomes
   (orgId, platform, tenantScope, channel, thread, lastActivityAt, startedAt, id).

The mined transcript a dream consolidates is attacker-controlled, so the
dream model must never run where it can read provider credentials. Give
every dream its OWN one-off host with the OS sandbox FORCED on, instead of
reusing the agent's warm (possibly unsandboxed) host — a sandboxed runtime
is denied provider credentials (HOME + runtime-state dirs are denyRead) for
both Claude and Codex. Fail closed if the host has no sandbox mechanism:
refuse the dream rather than mine the transcript next to credentials.

  (behaviour-preserving; the warm path is unchanged) so the dream can build
  a host with a different sandbox/cwd without touching the warm host cache.
- runDreamExtraction now builds a dedicated host via buildDreamHost (sandbox
  forced, fail-closed, not memoized), runs the extraction on it, and tears
  it down in a finally — which also kills a runtime that ignored session/cancel.
- A dedicated dream host never reaches stopHost's per-agent quarantine
  sweep, so clear remaining extraction quarantine tombstones at shutdown.

Does NOT re-enable dreaming: dreamOperationsAllowed() is unchanged, so prod
stays blocked (Phase C flips the gate after the security review + RC).

  torn down with a bare `host.stop()` and never reaches `stopHost`'s per-agent

  (`memoryExtractionQuarantines`) accumulated one entry per dream for the life
  of the daemon. Thread the dream's session id back to the caller and reclaim
  exactly that session's tombstone once the confined host is stopped (a stopped
  host can produce no further stragglers). The whole-map clear at shutdown stays
  as a backstop.

  needs only its materialized inputs, but the host was built with the ordinary
  launch, materializing `*_DATA` config-file secrets (KUBECONFIG/DOCKER_CONFIG)
  to disk and wiring the github-app/gh credentials — exposing them to the
  attacker-controlled extraction, and (since the dream host never populates
  `hostConfigFiles`) never calling `cleanupConfigFiles`. `buildAcpHost` gains an
  `excludeAgentToolCredentials` option that `buildDreamHost` sets, so the dream
  launch skips config-file materialization and git/gh credentials entirely.

Addresses a TOCTOU in the Phase B skill review fence. `skillAccept` verified the
staged directory with `inspectLocalSkillSource`, but `publishAcceptedDreamSkill`
then took its OWN independent snapshot — a concurrent writer between the two
could get a different (un-reviewed) digest pinned and activated. The reviewed
bytes were therefore not actually bound to what got published.

compared against its own capture snapshot's digest before the bundle is renamed
or `accepted-skills.json` is updated (the temporary capture is discarded on
mismatch). The digest verified is the digest published, so a swap of staged
bytes after review can never publish un-reviewed content. Regression test mutates
the staged skill after minting the token and proves acceptance refuses.

Also documents the sandbox-availability convention in docs/product-conventions.md:
every feature is supported with or without a sandbox, trusted agents may run
unsandboxed, and no feature fails closed on a missing sandbox mechanism.

Production regression: on a host with no supported Linux SRT/bwrap sandbox, the
daemon's fleet-wide skill-authority requirement threw during reconcile
(`activateGlobalSkillSandbox`) and in the single-shot chat CLI, so the daemon
could not reconcile or complete the CP handshake — it failed closed and never ran.

Per the sandbox-optional product principle (any feature is supported with or
without a sandbox; trusted agents may run unsandboxed), skill confinement is no
longer forced fleet-wide. A host is sandboxed only when the agent itself opts in
(`agent.runInSandbox`) or the operator sets `security.requireSandbox`; skills run
wherever their agent runs. The daemon boots, reconciles, and connects on hosts
with or without an OS sandbox.

- Remove the forced `globalSkillSandboxRequired` boundary: `agentRunsInSandbox`
  drops the skill-authority term; delete `activateGlobalSkillSandbox`, its boot
  establishment, its callers, and the now-unused skill-sandbox-policy imports.
- `cli/chat.ts`: the single-shot host follows the agent's own sandbox decision
  instead of throwing when no mechanism exists.

The residual exposure (an unconfined ACP child could tamper with the skill
registry/ledger/bytes on an unsandboxed agent) is a documented, owner-accepted P2,
to be revisited with per-runtime credential/authority brokering. `docs/product-conventions.md`
already documents the sandbox-optional invariant.

Tests: daemon-smoke now asserts a default agent is NOT force-sandboxed (and is
sandboxed only when it opts in) and that boot/reconcile do not fail closed with no
mechanism; the chat single-shot test runs on hosts with or without a sandbox.

fix(web): stop the session rail from shifting the page when it lands (#451)

* fix(web): stop the session rail from shifting the page when it lands

The session detail page painted in three different geometries. The rail's
list is a second round-trip behind the session itself — `railQuery` is only
derived once `session.agentId` resolves — so at the paint that first shows
the title the rail holds one row and `total: 0`, tripping its own "fewer
than two rows, nothing to navigate to" guard and collapsing to nothing. The
880px body is centred in whatever horizontal space the rail leaves, so when
the rail's page landed a moment later the whole transcript slid 125px to the
right under a reader who was already reading it.

Give SessionRail a `pending` flag and an empty `SessionRailSlot` to hold its
224px column while the answer is still in flight, gated on a live query so a
session with no agent (which never fetches, so `isLoading` never flips)
cannot hold an empty gutter open forever. Fixing only that would have moved
the jump one step earlier, since the loading branches centred their spinner
in the bare wrap, so route them through a shared SessionDetailFrame that
draws the same two columns as the loaded page.

A session that genuinely has no rail still collapses to a centred 880px
body, and the not-found branches — dead ends that grow no rail — keep
centring in the bare wrap.

Verified in mock mode at 1440px: the loading frame, the held-open slot, and
the fully rendered rail all measure the column at x=270 w=224 and the body
at x=525 w=880, so nothing reflows across the three states.

Review caught that the pending-slot approach moved the shift rather than
removing it. `railQuery` goes non-null as soon as `session.agentId` resolves,
whatever that agent's session count turns out to be, so a genuinely rail-less
session reserved the column through loading and through the in-flight list
request and then lost it when the fetch settled at `total < 2` — a new reflow
for the one case the previous commit claimed was untouched.

There is no state that both predicts the rail early and stays correct: the
answer only exists once the agent-filtered page lands. So stop making the

survives navigation rather than remounting, so clicking from a busy agent's
session to a quiet one already re-centred the transcript mid-read.

The cost is an empty gutter on a rail-less session — a single-session org, or
an agent whose only run has no lineage. Worth it for a body position that is a
constant of the route.

Verified in mock mode at 1440px, viewport-absolute: session with a 4-row rail,

feat(platforms): chronological event time + merge adapters for Telegram, Discord, Feishu (#454)

* feat(platforms): chronological event time + merge adapters for Telegram, Discord, Feishu

The merged conversation view assumed Slack-shaped timestamps; the other IM
platforms' message ids broke both halves of §6 (merged-conversation-view.md):
Discord snowflakes overflowed the µs axis to 0, Telegram sequence ids parsed
as 1970s seconds, and none matched the Slack decimal dedupe predicate — so
multi-agent threads on those platforms rendered duplicated and mis-ordered.

- protocol: NormalizedPlatformMessage gains platformTimeMs (provider send
  time, epoch ms); SessionMessage exposes the daemon's eventTimeUs axis.
- mappers: Telegram stamps message.date; Feishu plumbs create_time through
  FeishuRawEvent → MessageLike → normalize; Discord decodes its snowflake's
  embedded time (BigInt — snowflakes exceed Number's safe range).
- daemon: TranscriptEntry accepts an explicit eventTimeUs override — the
  inbound append stamps platformTimeMs onto the normalized axis; ts
  coordinates, primary keys, and replay comparisons are untouched.
- read chain: session reader → CP DTO → web DTO expose eventTimeUs; the
  merge orders by the stored axis when present (falling back to deriving
  from ts, which now handles snowflakes) and dedupes text rows on
  per-platform native id shapes — Discord 16-20-digit snowflakes, Telegram
  ≤9-digit sequence ids, Feishu om_ ids — none of which a 13-digit
  monotonicTs local stamp can match.
- fixtures: snowflake dedupe + embedded-time ordering, Telegram
  stored-axis-over-id ordering, Feishu om_ dedupe, per-platform predicate
  matrix.

Legacy rows written before this change keep their old (wrong) stored axis
until re-observed; new rows are correct end to end.

* fix(web): keep the rail one row per conversation, and order the filter by name

Seeding the filter from the whole roster made the rail read the FLAT view
with every member agent selected, so a thread two agents worked in listed
itself once per agent. One row per conversation is what the rail always
showed — that only happened to be true while the filter named a single

which also collapses superseded ACP sessions the flat view kept.

A conversation row links to the merged page rather than a member session
that would bounce through the §5.3 redirect, and the open conversation is
dropped from the listed rows by KEY: both sides name the newest member,
but the list names the newest member the FILTER still covers, so removing
one participant's chip would otherwise put it on screen twice.

Neither the roster (last-activity order) nor the org agent list is ordered
by anything the reader can see, so the chips and the picker both read
alphabetically, and the seed holds its ids sorted — an agent taking a turn
used to be enough to reshuffle the filter.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): identify rail rows by conversation, not by their newest member

Two ways the "one row per conversation" rule still came apart, both because
a grouped row is named after whichever member is newest — and that is not a
stable name.

Removing one participant's chip narrows the grouped query to one agent, and
the projection dropped the key for a single-member conversation, so the row
could no longer be recognised as the conversation the reader had open; with
the remaining agent not being the overall newest, the two ids survived the
merge as separate rows. The key now rides along whatever the member count —
it is IDENTITY — and what marks a row as a merged VIEW is `participants`,
which is what the links now test.

Pins were stored against that same moving representative. Pin member B,
let A answer, and B is no longer on the page: hydration refetched it as a
flat session beside the grouped row it already belonged to. Rows now
answer to every member id, so a listed conversation counts its members as
loaded, a pin on any of them lights the row, and unpinning releases the
member that was actually pinned rather than adding the current one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp,web): report conversation membership independently of the agent filter

A grouped row's `sessions` are scoped to the requested agents, so reading
membership off them made a conversation's participants a property of the
query rather than of the conversation. Filtered to A, a shared A/B thread
looked like a conversation of one: a global pin on B missed the loaded set
and hydrated as a flat row beside the group it belonged to, the same
conversation then rendering twice; with B as the open representative the
layered row kept A's membership and read B's pin as unpinned; and the row
linked to /sessions/A, bouncing through the §5.3 redirect this is supposed
to avoid.

The CP now reports `memberSessionIds` over every agent the caller may see —
`memberAgentIds` widens the member backfill while which conversations
qualify, their order and the rows returned all stay on the filter — so the
client no longer infers membership from what it was handed. Visibility is
unchanged: a member the caller cannot see is still absent, and its
participation still leaves no trace.

The web reads membership from that field for pins and for the merged-page
link, and the open row carries the roster resolver's members, which are not
agent-filtered either.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): resolve external scopes over the membership agents, not the filter

Widening the member query was only half of it. The viewer snapshot every
query is authorized against comes from `listExternalScopes`, which still
read the FILTERED agents — so a member visible only through a Slack,
GitHub or Feishu audience had no allowed scope, and the widened membership
query could not admit the very row it was widened to find. That member was
dropped again, for having been filtered out rather than for being
invisible, and a pin on it hydrated the duplicate row this field exists to
prevent.

`memberAgentIds` moves onto the filter query so scope resolution widens
with membership, and the key-addressed resolver now splits one widened
lookup into filtered `sessions` and full `memberSessionIds`, so addressing
a conversation by key and paging to it no longer disagree about who took

* fix: address review on organization variables and secrets

Five findings from the PR review bot, all legitimate.

[P1] configRevision now covers DERIVED spec inputs. `AgentSpec.skills` and
`AgentSpec.managedSkills` are resolved from the skill-source registry and
managed-skill bundle revisions, so a skill-source edit, a managed-skill
archive/restore, or an accepted bundle revision changed spec CONTENT while
the agent row stood still. The daemon then saw new content at a revision it
had already applied and — correctly — refused it as an invariant violation,
repeating that refusal on every reconnect until an unrelated agent edit
happened to move the revision. Those mutations now bump the referring
agents in the same transaction. A skill-source rename bumps both the old
and new name's referrers, since agents bind by name.

[P1] The daemon-compatibility preflight no longer discloses a restricted
agent. It ran before `resource.edit` was applied and answered a guessed
agent id with a 409 naming it, proving existence and name where a 404 was
intended. A preflight over caller-supplied ids now examines only agents the
caller may edit and leaves the rest to the authorization decision; a
preflight over already-bound agents still covers them all (the write does
reach them) but omits the name of one the caller cannot view.

[P1] A retarget that omits a replacement value now counts the STORED value.
`selected` → `all` treated the omitted value as 0 bytes, so a large stored
value could enroll agents whose resolved environment exceeds the frame
budget.

[P1] Admission measures ENCODED bytes and the whole spec. The old counter
used raw key+value lengths and a flat 8 KiB reserve, so JSON escaping
(quotes double, control chars expand 6x as \uXXXX) and the rest of
AgentSpec were unaccounted: values passing a 240 KiB check encoded to
~480 KiB, past the 256 KiB codec ceiling. Values in memory are measured
with the frame's own serializer; stored values are measured Postgres-side
via octet_length(to_json(value)::text), so size is known without returning
the value or opening a cipher inside the transaction. The reserve is now
32 KiB for the envelope, scalar fields, and the resolved skills/managedSkills
entries. Under an encrypting provider the stored measurement is of
ciphertext and therefore approximate — documented, and deliberate, because
a transaction must never wait on a cipher.

[P2] The Console can set the empty-string secret the API accepts. The sheet
used `value !== ''` as the "replacement supplied" sentinel, so an owner
could neither create nor rotate a secret to ''. A saved secret now shows a
mask plus an explicit Replace value action, with a Keep the current value
instead link to back out; intent is tracked separately from content.

The design doc is updated for all five, including the encoding/reserve
rules and the non-disclosure requirement for pre-authorization checks.

fix(web): follow the newest transcript output in the session view (#492)

* fix(web): follow the newest transcript output in the session view

The session transcript only ever APPENDED rows — nothing moved the viewport.
The console's single page scroller (`.content`) stayed wherever it was, so a
live session's newest output, and the reply to a message just sent, landed
below the fold.

Add `useStickToBottom`: one ResizeObserver on the scroller's content box, which
covers every growth source (tail merge, live ACP steps, an image finishing
decode, the typing dots) with no dependency list to keep in sync with the
transcript's internals.

Two orderings make this trickier than it looks, and both are pinned by tests:

- The stick decision is latched on `scroll`, never read at growth time. Once new
  content is in the DOM it has already pushed the bottom away, so a measurement
  taken then always reads "not at the bottom" and the follow would never fire.
- A pin dispatches its own `scroll` event, and the browser delivers it AFTER
  React has flushed the rows that prompted the pin. Measuring that echo un-arms
  the follow one beat after arming it, which is the same growth-time
  measurement through the back door. So the echo of our own pin is swallowed —
  and only when the pin actually moved the viewport (read back after the
  browser's clamp), or the flag would eat the user's next real scroll instead.

Sending re-arms the follow regardless of scroll position: someone who scrolled
up to read history and then writes is done reading, and scroll position cannot
express that.

Reading back through history is never yanked forward. Opening a session does
land at the newest message — the view arms while the transcript is still empty,
so an empty container reads as at-the-bottom. That is what makes the follow
reachable at all, since a reader dropped at the top of a long history would
have to scroll all the way down to earn it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): identify the pin echo by position, not by turn

Review catch: the self-scroll guard assumed the next `scroll` event belonged
exclusively to its own pin. Scroll events for one scroller COALESCE, so anything
that moved the viewport before the pending echo was delivered — the `?focus`
scrollIntoView after the transcript renders, or a quick flick of the wheel —
arrived as that same single event. The boolean flag discarded it and left the
follow armed, so the next row dragged the focused reader back to the bottom.

Record where the pin actually landed (read back after the browser's clamp) and
swallow only while the viewport still sits there: if it moved, something else
moved it, and that scroll gets measured like any other. A pin that moved nothing
still records nothing, so it cannot eat the user's next real scroll.

Regressions for both orderings — the `?focus` centring and a user scroll beating
the echo — fail under the old boolean guard and pass under the position check.

* fix(web): only pin the transcript on an accepted send

Review catch: `onPgSend` re-armed the bottom-follow and pinned BEFORE `pgSend`
decided whether the send was valid. Enter on an empty composer, or Enter while a
turn is already streaming, sends nothing — but still yanked a reader out of
history, contradicting the guarantee that reading back is never pulled forward.

`pgSend` now reports whether it ACCEPTED the send, and the composer pins only on
true. Keeping the condition in the provider rather than restating it in the view
means the two cannot drift: the empty/whitespace/busy test lives in exactly one
place, and every entry point (the "Start with" chips, textarea Enter, the send
button) inherits it through the same `onPgSend`.

Covered by PlaygroundSend.test.tsx against the real provider — empty, whitespace,

acceptance; the busy rejection stays per session. The busy case flushes a commit
between the two sends, which is the real ordering for two keypresses. All four
acceptance assertions fail if `pgSend` goes back to returning void.

(peer fan-out on delivery, silent referee after the start message, the
regeneration path active): count upward from 1; each participant must post

refactor(daemon): key-driven connection registry (S2 §7.5) (#526)

The five connection pools and their in-flight guards move behind one
`ConnectionPool<C>`, and — the part that actually removes branching — every
per-platform IDENTITY COMPARISON collapses onto an opaque key.

Before, reconcile and prune compared credentials field by field, differently
per platform: `c.appToken === g.appToken && c.botToken === g.botToken` for a
Slack socket, `c.botToken === g.botToken` for Telegram/Discord,
`c.appId === g.appId && c.region === g.region && c.mode === g.mode` for
Feishu. Each platform now states its identity ONCE as a key function, and the
shared lifecycle only ever compares keys — it cannot know, and never asks,
what a key is made of. Feishu had already been forced into this shape (the
daemon carried a private `feishuConnKey`); that helper moves to the platform
and the other three join it.

The five prune blocks become five calls to one `prunePool(pool, desiredKeys)`
with the same rule: a live connection survives iff its identity is still among
the keys consolidation asked for. The Feishu case that used to need spelling
out — a region or transport flip must drop the old client — is now just
another key that stopped matching.

Key functions take the shape BOTH a consolidated group and a live connection
satisfy, so "the connection and the group that wants it hash to the same
string" is type-checked rather than a convention.

Two modes per platform are first-class (§7.5): Slack keeps a socket pool keyed
by (appToken, botToken) beside a send-only pool keyed by botToken, because a
shared bot has no app token to key on.

Deliberately NOT in this PR: the four per-integration binding maps. Their read
sites call concrete methods (`postBlocks`, `startStreamingCard`), so they
generalize when Layer 2 — the renderer seam — replaces those calls, not
before. Pools are generic in their connection type, so every read site keeps
its concrete type today.

Behavior-preserving: same consolidation inputs, same open/close decisions,
same in-flight semantics (Slack's socket pool keeps its retry-timer guard
rather than gaining a claim it never had). White-box tests that seeded the old
fields now seed pools. daemon 2793, full typecheck green.

refactor(daemon): turn-output surface — converger + applier + opaque state (S2 §7.3) (#527)

refactor(daemon): move Slack turn output into its platform module (S2 §7.3) (#530)

as platform-specific — it simply was "how the daemon posts". The other three

a chat.delete for the status bar.

they stayed, Slack's host port would be eight functions wide against Telegram's

name only. Two groups move:

the Telegram / Feishu state shapes already extracted.

record. They look like Slack state, and most of them belong in the opaque slot

human-input paths (attribution alone has 30+ readers). The structural SlackTurn
view names that surface exactly, which turns the follow-up into a mechanical

refactor(daemon): GitHub poster implements Layer 2 as a turn-final surface (S2 §7.6) (#531)

§7.6 lists the GitHub poster as `Layer 1: no, Layer 2: yes` — no connection, no
ingress, no read port (its ingress arrives through the core hook seam and stays
there permanently, per §12), but it does produce output for a turn.

Extracting it surfaced a real finding about the contract: GitHub does not fit
the Layer 2 shape the four chat platforms defined. `TurnOutputSurface`
(converger + apply + state) was derived from four STREAMING platforms — text
arrives in chunks, each chunk becomes an action, each action becomes an API
call. GitHub has none of that:

  - no converger: it consumes raw ACP updates directly, because its production
    rule is "select the final answer", not "chunk the stream";
  - no apply: there are no per-action calls to make. The core streaming path is
    deliberately BYPASSED for a GitHub turn (isHeadlessGithubFinal), precisely
    so no intermediate output escapes before the single public post;
  - one comment, published once, at the very end.

Forcing that into `apply` would mean inventing actions nobody emits. So Layer 2
publishes a SECOND shape, TurnFinalSurface, and GitHub is its first implementer.
The four chat platforms are untouched. The two shapes are independent — a turn
may carry a chat surface AND a final surface (a GitHub-reply hook has both), so
their state slots are separate and neither reads the other's.

What moved: GithubTurnState (poster + collector + deferredFinalTranscript),
isGithubFinalChunk (which ACP update is GitHub's final), onGithubUpdate, and
finalizeGithubTurn (final-text selection, the deferred transcript row, publish).

What deliberately stayed in core: the hook durability barrier. Publishing is
wrapped in a state machine — `in_flight` recorded before any public POST,
`settled` after — and a replayed `in_flight` is what stops a retry from
double-commenting. That is the HOOK's durability contract, not GitHub's
rendering, and §12 keeps hook machinery in core. The surface gets
beginPublish() / endPublish() instead; `false` from beginPublish means the
barrier could not be made durable and the surface must not POST. Fail-closed
stays fail-closed, as one rule in one place. The formal-review fork is likewise
decided by core from hook state and passed in as one boolean.

Behavior-preserving, verified against all four edges of the original control
flow: formal-review-owns-response, output-suppressed, no-github-turn, and a
non-`end` final phase (which still publishes an undefined final, as before).

platform DOES; Layer 2 (turn-output.ts) is what it renders; the registry keys
its connections. The manifest is what core reads BEFORE a dispatch target
exists — which is exactly D2's dividing rule for what earns a manifest field.
If core can wait until it holds a connection or an adapter, the answer belongs

Two fields, each named from what its call sites actually ask:

  - membershipEnumeration: 'bulk' | 'per-conversation' — whether the platform
    offers one cheap membership snapshot for the whole bot (Slack
    users.conversations) or none, in which case core discovers reachable chats
    from traffic and resolves each stored session's channel individually.
  - statusSurface: 'turn-bar' | 'on-demand' — whether the platform supports one
    editable session-scoped status line, or answers /status when asked.

Branch clusters retired: backfillChannelNames' three-way exclusion, the
first-seen-chat observed-channel refresh, and four status-bar conditionals.

refactor(daemon): loop-guard scopes become a §7.4 adapter strategy (S2) (#533)

First of the class (c) strategy extractions. A strategy, not a manifest field,
and the distinction is the one #532 got wrong once already: core reads this with
a normalized message in hand, i.e. AFTER the dispatch target is known. D2 sends
everything post-dispatch here.

What it decides: the loop guard is one durable circuit shared by every agent on
a physical bot, keyed by conversation coordinates. That keying works only if a
conversation's coordinates are STABLE across its messages — and on Slack they
are not. A Slack top-level post is normalized with `thread` set to its own event
ts, so every fresh root mints a brand-new scope; two bots alternating top-level
posts would each get a virgin guard forever and the circuit would never trip.
Slack answers that with a channel-wide coarse circuit those roots collapse into.

No other platform needs one — their thread roots are stable, so coordinates
alone key the circuit correctly. That asymmetry is why this was three
`platform === 'slack'` literals rather than a shared rule, and why the DEFAULT
strategy is "no coarse circuit" rather than "Slack's, disabled".

Two facts, one lookup, because core always asks both about the same message:

  - coarse — the channel-wide circuit this conversation ALSO belongs to, checked
    alongside the coordinate scope (a trusted !resume anywhere in the channel
    must be able to reset it);
  - isRoot — this message IS a fresh root, so coarse REPLACES its
    coordinate-derived scope instead of sitting beside it.

Behavior-preserving; each of the three call sites was checked against all three
cases it can see (Slack non-DM, Slack DM, non-Slack). A platform with no
strategy returns { isRoot: false } and every site degrades to the pre-existing
coordinate-only path.

refactor(daemon): member-id recognition becomes a §7.4 adapter strategy (S2) (#534)

Second class (c) extraction (`mentionIdPattern`).

What it protects: an agent-call's `toAgentId` is an AgentConnect id — from
listAgents or the trusted agent-call envelope — never a platform member id. A
model that copied the human-facing mention out of a transcript hands over a
platform id instead, and accepting it publishes a visible `@U…` fallback into
the thread before the relay can reject the unknown target. Core fails before
publishing, and to do that it must RECOGNIZE a platform's member id. Only the
platform can say what one looks like.

Why only Slack is registered, and why that is not an oversight: Slack member ids
(U…/W…, plus the <@U…> wrapper) are the only ones core rejects today.
Registering Telegram's or Discord's numeric ids would be a BEHAVIOR CHANGE — ids
that route fine today would start being refused — and a risky one, since a
numeric pattern cannot distinguish a Discord snowflake from a legitimately
numeric AgentConnect id. The strategy makes that extension possible and
reviewable one platform at a time; it does not make it automatic.

The default is therefore "not recognizable", which is exactly the pre-existing
behavior for every non-Slack platform. Two call sites, both behavior-preserving.

session resolution, sticky overrides. What was NOT core was the last inch — how
a short control reply, a /status line, or a tappable select card is PRESENTED —
and that inch was four inline forks inside handleCommand:

Verification (§4) requires all of: an authentic provider event, a sending app
that belongs to AgentConnect in this org and conversation, a claimed author that
app actually backs in THIS channel, and a usable integer source depth. The last
one drops the whole claim rather than defaulting to 0 — coercing an unverifiable
depth would hand a runaway mention chain a fresh loop-protection budget on every
hop. A shared bot with no exact author claim fails closed.

Agent traffic takes its own ladder, placed BEFORE control commands and gated
discovery. That placement is the enforcement: thread affinity, DM, keyword,
channel `auto`, and default-agent fallback are structurally unreachable, so
activation can only come from an explicit verified recipient — and a bare
shared-bot mention, which resolves to no agent, cannot become "the default".

The hop transition (§4.1) puts a platform mention on the SAME budget as an
internal call: one +1 per agent-to-agent edge, computed once (by the relay when
it forwards, by the daemon otherwise) and installed on the admitted turn as
trusted call metadata, so an A -> B -> A chain advances by one per hop and stops
at the shared cap across queue replay and restart.

A durable activation rendezvous (§8.6) collapses the internal wake and the
visible echo of a paired `toAgent + channel` call into one admission. The wake
is the authority — it alone carries lineage, correlation, needsReply, external
origin, and the privacy gate — so a platform-first record is claimed `pending`
and can never reach `admitted` without an envelope. A pairing whose envelope
never arrives expires transcript-only and is reported as a delivery failure,
never downgraded into an envelope-less child; an admitted key answers every
retry with the child it already opened.

* fix: close five delivery-correctness gaps found in review

All five findings from the review of 2f4ef49 were real; each is fixed with a test
that fails without it.

**1. The relayed mention path dead-ended.** `handleRelayIm` suppressed every
AgentConnect-bot message before reading the trusted `RdMsgIm` envelope, so a
shared-bot mention the relay had verified, capped, and forwarded was acked and
woke nobody — the entire relay half of the feature was unreachable. It now runs
the verified-agent ladder, terminal-verifying org, policy, and the conversation
gate against this daemon's own snapshot, and INSTALLING the relay's depth rather
than incrementing it again (§4.1 step 4 gives the relay the one `+1`).

**2. The pairing id was never minted.** `sendMessage`'s visible half carried only
`agentAuthorId`, so the platform-first rendezvous could not recognize it and the
documented pending-before-envelope path was unreachable in the real send flow.
Both halves now carry one minted `agentCallDeliveryId`; the post is stamped
`final` because, unlike a streamed reply, it is complete when made. Its recipient
set is deliberately empty: the peer is woken by the wake's authoritative
envelope, and listing it would invite a second, envelope-less activation.

**3. Only the first recipient was activated.** One finalized response addressing
two agents woke one of them, with nothing to tell the sender. Every admissible
recipient is now dispatched.

**4. The conversation Off/gated fence was skipped.** The verified-agent ladder
bypasses `routeRules`, which is where the human path enforces Off — so an agent
mention had become the one way into a silenced channel, contradicting
product-conventions ("not to an @-mention"). Re-applied on both the daemon route
and the relay's `agentTarget`, including the §14 gated-agent scope rule.

**5. Activations went terminal before admission.** `admitActivation` ran before
dispatch, so a rejected turn, a persistence failure, or a crash in that window
left a claimed key with no child and deduplicated every retry — exactly-once
becoming never. The record is now settled on the admission barrier and released
on failure. Fixing that exposed a related race: `attachActivationEnvelope`
granted `dispatch: true` on every call until admission, so two arrivals inside
the (now genuinely async) window would both dispatch. The envelope itself is the
claim, granted once.

deduplicated against a child that was never opened. The sweep now separates the

* fix(daemon): tie the activation claim to the durable inbox row

The remaining blocking finding, which I had deferred and should not have — the
reviewer was right that the claim and inbox admission needed an explicitly
reconcilable relationship before exactly-once holds across persistence failure
and restart.

Two holes, in opposite directions:

**Admitted without a replayable turn.** Rendezvous dispatches did not request
`requireDurable`, so a failed inbox append still reported `accepted: true` and
the activation went terminal for a turn that could never replay. They now
require it, making `accepted` imply a durable row.

**Released a delivery that was already queued.** The previous fix released every
expired pending-with-envelope row, which is right when the dispatch never
persisted and WRONG when the inbox row landed just before the crash: startup
replay runs that turn, and deleting its claim lets a later retry deliver the same
thing twice. The two cases look identical in the record, so the record now
carries the inbox id its dispatch will write, and the sweep reconciles against
the inbox instead of assuming:

- inbox row exists -> replay will run it, so the claim COMPLETES (`admitted`)
- no inbox row     -> nothing will replay, so the claim is RELEASED
- no dispatch id (legacy row) -> not reconcilable, released; same answer as
  "never persisted", and the safe one, since the alternative strands the key

Closes the crash chain a sweep-based reconciliation structurally cannot: crash
after the inbox row lands, restart replays the turn, the turn completes and its
inbox row is removed, the activation TTL expires, and an inbox-existence check
now reports "never persisted" and releases the claim — letting a retry deliver
the same thing twice.

single admission point instead of at each call site. That one move covers live
dispatch, queued dispatch, and startup replay alike: the replayed turn completes
its own record, so by the time any sweep runs the record is already terminal and
the inbox row's fate stops mattering.

whose dispatch never persisted at all, which is the one case with no turn to
carry the key.

asserts the key is still taken at the end.
