feat: let agent messages continue a conversation without naming a recipient (#549)

* feat: let agent messages continue a conversation without naming a recipient

§2.3 previously said an unmentioned agent message never activates through any
implicit rung. That made agents respond only when addressed by name, which is not
how a conversation works — the counting-relay test stalled after one round
because "1" / "2" / "3" name nobody. Reverses that rule: a verified
agent-authored message now takes the SAME arbitration ladder a human message
takes, with the author removed from the candidate set.

The author exclusion is the one absolute and is applied once, before any rung, on
both the daemon (`routeRules`) and the relay (`arbitrate`). An agent's own reply
always matches its own rule, so self-activation would not be a loop the hop cap
slows down — it would be unconditional.

Everything else the explicit path checks still applies to an implicitly-selected
edge, because those are properties of the edge and an implicit edge is still an
agent call: the shared hop budget, directional call policy, the conversation
Off/gated fence, exactly-once admission, final-events-only, and the ban on
agent-authored control commands. Verification is still what separates a
participant from anonymous bot traffic — an unverified bot, third-party included,
still stops at the explicit-mention rung.

Relay thread affinity is deliberately NOT rewritten by agent traffic: an agent
continuing a conversation is not a human establishing who owns the thread, and
letting agents move the binding would hand ownership back and forth away from the
person who started it.

Recorded prominently in the design and in product-conventions, because it changes
what operators should expect: a multi-agent conversation now ends by reaching a
limit rather than by an agent declining to address anyone. The hop cap and the
durable loop guard become the ordinary terminating conditions. With dedicated
bots this compounds — each app receives the same channel event on its own
connection, so one agent message can wake every other agent present — and the
loop guard is a latch that only an explicit `!resume` clears.

* fix: keep implicit agent continuations subject to `!stop` and explicit addressing binding

Two routing regressions in the implicit-continuation change, both found in review.

An agent-authored message returns from `onInboundOutcome` above the `!stop` gate,
and the activation helper stamped `trigger = 'mention'` unconditionally. That was
sound while every delivery on this ladder WAS an explicit mention; making the
ladder implicit invalidated the premise. The result was that `!stop` silenced a
conversation's humans while its agents kept waking each other — the one control a
person has over a running exchange, disabled precisely where the hop cap and loop
guard became the ordinary terminating conditions.

The route cause is now threaded to the point of admission on both edges. The relay
is the only party that knows which rung it used, since the frame is pre-addressed
to one agent either way, so it says so through a new `RdMsgIm.trustedRouteVia`;
absent reads as 'mention', because a relay old enough to omit it only ever
forwarded explicit mentions. An explicit agent mention now actually clears the
mute, which this ladder's comment already claimed but the code never did — done
after the delivery commits, so a deduplicated or paired observation cannot lift a
mute without waking anyone.

Second, the implicit ladder was reachable from two states that are not "named
nobody". Emptiness is now judged BEFORE the author is filtered out, since a
response whose only name is its own author is the one self-address every response
can produce and was indistinguishable from an unaddressed one. And a message whose
named recipients are all refused stays transcript-only on the direct path instead
of falling through, matching the relay: answering "the agent you asked for is Off
here" with a different agent substitutes a recipient the author never asked for,
and the Off fence must not become a redirect.

A response that mentions only humans still continues implicitly. That is the same
ladder a person's `@someone` reply takes in the same channel, which is the premise
of the change; the design line saying otherwise was stale and is rewritten, along
with the implementation map, checklist, and the source comments that still
described mention-only routing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: stop agent continuations at any unmatched mention, and scope the mute to its target

Three findings from the second review round.

The direct and relay ladders disagreed about a response that mentions a human.
`mentionedBots` holds every `<@U…>` token, not only bots, and `routeRules` stops at
an unmatched mention in a channel — for human senders too, so a person's `@alice`
reply already wakes nobody there. The relay had no such rung, so the same event
woke an `auto` peer over the relay and nobody over a direct connection. The relay
now stops as well, DMs exempt on both sides as before.

That resolves the semantic the previous round got backwards: addressing anyone is
binding, and only a response naming NOBODY continues implicitly. An unmatched
mention, a self-mention, and a named-but-refused recipient are the same case with
three surfaces. It also restores "a bare shared-bot mention does not select the
default", which the implicit fallthrough had quietly broken.

The direct-path `!stop` key was built from the OBSERVING connection's transport
scope while the activation rendezvous three lines below deliberately uses the
target's. Every dedicated app sees the same post, so the author's connection could
win the target's rendezvous, look up an unrelated scope's mute, dispatch anyway,
and leave the real tombstone standing — after which the target's own copy
deduplicates before it can clear it. Both now use the target scope.

Finally, `trustedRouteVia` needed a rollout gate. A daemon that predates it reads
every agent-authored delivery as an explicit mention, which CLEARS a mute, so a new
relay talking to an old daemon would silently disable the human's stop control.
Added `RD_AGENT_IMPLICIT_ROUTING_V1` to the existing fail-closed hello capability
set; the relay refuses to forward an implicit continuation without it and degrades
to the pre-change behavior instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: carry the complete response's "addressed anyone" fact on the final event

§5.5 marks only the LAST physical section `final`. `mentionedAgentIds` is already
computed from the complete response for exactly this reason, but every non-agent
mention survives only as `mentionedBots`, which is reparsed from that last
section's visible text. A long answer that addresses a human in section one and
ends without a mention therefore arrived with BOTH mention sets empty and read as
unaddressed — so whether "addressing anyone is binding" held depended on where the
splitter happened to cut.

The final event now carries `addressedAnyone` for the whole logical response,
resolved from the complete reply text at turn end beside the recipient set, and
both ladders consult it. The predicate lives next to the regex `mentionedBots` is
built from, so an author's claim and a reader's own parse cannot disagree about
what counts as a mention.

A boolean rather than the full provider mention set: it is everything the binding
rule needs, and publishing each mentioned human's user id into Slack message
metadata would put identifiers on the wire for no routing benefit.

Absent ⇒ false, matching the rest of this metadata. An older author daemon splits
the same way but cannot report the fact, and its finals must stay routable exactly
as before rather than becoming silently unroutable; only an explicit `true`
asserts an address, so a malformed value degrades to "named nobody" instead of
blocking every continuation.

Retention GC (#485) deletes a session's local row and worktree, but the CP's
metadata row survives — it is all that remains of the session. Until now nothing
told the CP that, so the console rendered a permanently unreplayable transcript
as a session that said nothing.

The daemon now reports each purge over a new `event/session-purged` D→C REQ and
the CP stamps `SessionMeta.contentPurgedAt`. Correlated rather than
fire-and-forget: the local row is already gone, so an unacknowledged report can
never be re-derived. The receipt is written in `deleteSession`'s transaction,
survives restarts and CP outages in a `session_purges` table, and is released
only on the ACK — with a 30d TTL (logged, never silent) bounding a daemon that
never reaches a CP advertising `session-purge-v1`.

CP side keeps the metadata and applies the stamp first-wins, so at-least-once
redelivery cannot move the date the content went away. A report whose agent is
not placed on the reporting daemon is still ACKed: the daemon's row is gone
either way, and an error would make it retry a claim that can never land.
`GET /sessions/:id/messages` answers the empty page directly for a purged row
instead of round-tripping to the daemon — or 503-ing when that daemon happens to
be offline, which would read as "try again later" for a transcript that is never
coming back.

"no messages yet" card with the retention explanation.

refactor(daemon): cursorOrdering becomes a platform strategy; routing knobs become an envelope read (S3 Appendix A) (#589)

Two Appendix-A clusters, both pure strategy extractions — same behavior, the
platform name stops being core knowledge.

**cursorOrdering (class c).** Seven sites across the session manager and the CP
session reader asked one question — *do this platform's message ids carry a
native total order, and how do two compare?* — and each spelled the answer as
`platform === 'slack'` beside a Slack-timestamp parser. Adding a platform with
ordered ids meant finding all seven; missing one leaves a read cursor that
silently skips or re-delivers messages. `platforms/message-ordering.ts` now owns
the question: a platform supplies only its coordinate parser, and the total
order, the synthetic-coordinate rule (a real follow-up must never look older
than the legacy anchored-cron UUID that created its thread) and the wall-clock
cutoff test are shared, because those are daemon facts rather than platform ones.

Not a §5 manifest axis, deliberately: the manifest's rule is that a field is
earned by a PRE-DISPATCH read, and every read here happens inside a turn that
already exists. It is a §7.4 strategy, registered exactly like `threadKeyForPost`.

Fail-closed by ABSENCE — `messageOrderingFor` returns `undefined` where ids are
opaque (everything but Slack today) and the type system forces each call site to
say what that means there. There is no neutral default object on purpose: a
comparator that quietly answers 0 would turn "not comparable" into "equal", and
the resulting cursor bug is invisible. Every `undefined` branch reproduces
today's non-Slack path — nothing re-sorted, no ids compared, cursor advances to
the trigger.

`slackTsForWallClock` deliberately stays put: its callers are the warm-thread
snapshot cutoff and the daemon's final-fence checkpoint, which the audit assigns
to `threadBackfill` (the Layer-1 read port), not to cursorOrdering.

**routing-rule core knobs (class b).** `integrationRouting` switched four ways on
`int.platform` purely to reach three identically-named fields, so a new platform
had to edit the router to be routable at all. §6.4 makes those knobs the core
envelope, so this is now an envelope read (`platforms/integration-config.ts`)
plus one registered strategy for the value §6.4 leaves OUT of the envelope on
purpose: the bot's own id, which Feishu spells `botOpenId` because its bots have
an open_id, not a user id. The config block is read at the integration's own
platform id, which is the same read after §6.4 renames the slot to `config`.
`resolveAgentIntegration`'s same-platform preference stays platform-keyed and
says so inline — it is a platform-vs-platform equality with no literal in it.

Tests pin ordering and cursor behavior PER PLATFORM by running one activation
shape twice with identical message ids: Slack re-sorts the replay gap into
microsecond order and discards a coordinate-less cursor; an opaque-id platform
leaves the store's text order verbatim and honours the cursor. Same contrast for
the reader's tail page (event order vs mutation order). All four bite when a
second platform is temporarily registered. The core knobs are pinned against
today's values for all four platforms, including Feishu's differently-named id.

refactor(daemon): the MCP tool surface reads Layer-1 capability ports (S3 Appendix A) (#596)

Four Appendix-A rows, one seam. Same runtime behavior throughout — the platform
name stops being core knowledge.

`contract.ts` already declares the OPTIONAL half of the connection contract, and
the audit calls the `typeof conn?.x === 'function'` probe over it "the sanctioned
Layer-1 read-port mechanism". What was missing is the other half of the same
question, asked where no connection exists yet: does this PLATFORM offer the port
at all? The MCP tool surface asked it three times and spelled every answer as a
platform name.

`platforms/read-ports.ts` now owns both asks, and they are deliberately not one
ask. `offersReadPort` probes a live bearer — a connection, the `MessageGateway`
slice the tools hold, a duck-typed fake. The registry declares for a platform id
before a connection is in hand. Deciding tool injection by live probe instead
would silently drop `readSlackFile` from a session opened while the socket was
reconnecting, so the pre-connection declaration is load-bearing, not a shortcut.
Absence is the fail-closed arm, as with `messageOrderingFor`: an unregistered
platform declares no ports, which is exactly the old `else` of every branch.

**Tool injection (mcp/tools.ts).** `integrations.some(i => i.platform === 'slack'
|'telegram')` becomes `attachmentReadToolsFor(platforms)`. The two descriptors
moved to `platforms/{slack,telegram}/attachments.ts`, so the platform contributes
its own tool by declaring the port and core no longer knows either name exists.
Emission walks the REGISTRY, not the agent's integration list, so an agent whose
integrations were stored the other way round does not see its tool list
reshuffle. `ALL_TOOL_NAMES` enumerates every platform's tool the same way — the
auto-allow set is about names, so a name a platform can inject must be listed
even for agents that never see it. The MCP dispatcher likewise stopped
case-matching the two names and runs one shared body for whatever is declared.

Tool names are FROZEN. `readSlackFile` / `readTelegramFile` are what agents have
learned, what shared resource_links point at, and what warm ACP sessions already
carry. The mechanism generalized; the names did not move.

**The `toUser` DM form (mcp/ops.ts).** `directMessage ? 'slack' : ctx.platform`
becomes `directMessagePlatformFor(ctx.platform)`: the session's own platform when
it can open a DM, else the platform that can. With Slack the only declarer, that
is bit-for-bit the old literal, including for a session on a platform that cannot
DM at all — it still resolves to Slack and still fails on the caller's own "no
slack integration" error, because gateway resolution runs before the port gate.
`wantPlatform !== 'slack'` becomes `!offersDirectMessages(wantPlatform)`, and the
error keeps naming the capable platform ("only supported on Slack (not telegram)
yet") — which is why a declaration carries a label instead of core carrying the
literal. The narrower live probe stays where it was: a gateway that lacks the
method still reports that THIS integration cannot open direct messages.

**The final fence (daemon.ts).** The provider-snapshot gate had already collapsed
to a duck-typed probe, but reached it through a `Partial<SlackConnection>` cast —
audit blind spot 3, where the cast, not the test, is the coupling. It now asks
`offersReadPort(conn, 'getThreadReplies')` and needs no Slack type at all.

`ReadPortBearer` is `object` rather than `Partial<Record<ReadPort, unknown>>` on
purpose: the latter is a weak type, so TypeScript rejects exactly the connections
implementing no optional port — the arm the probe exists to answer false for.

Tests pin the injection matrix for every combination of connected platforms
(none, Slack, Telegram, both, both orders, two bots on one platform, and Discord
/Feishu which declare no such port), the DM path off Slack in both its DM and
channel-mention arms, the missing-integration ordering, the live-probe failure,
and that the final-fence snapshot follows the port rather than the platform — a
non-Slack pending whose connection answers the port gets one, a Slack pending
whose connection does not, does not. One test pins the registry against the real
connection classes, since a declaration that drifts from its own adapter is the
failure mode this seam introduces.

refactor(web): AddIntegrationModal becomes the host chassis; the four wizard bodies become platform fragments (S3 §10) (#591)

* refactor(web): AddIntegrationModal becomes the host chassis; the four wizard bodies become platform fragments (S3 §10)

The install wizard was a 3794-line monolith in which every platform's pane,
probe, poll and validator lived in one component's state. Adding a platform
meant editing that file in a dozen places, and the platform name was core
knowledge: `platform === 'slack'` decided the footer, the identity chrome, the
transport default, the reuse input and the free-bot predicate.

This lands the wizard half of `WebPlatformModule` (the seam published in #573).
The chassis keeps exactly §10's list — picker tiles and their
`daemon.caps.platforms` gate, the existing/create mode cards, the generic
free-bot reuse list, the share toggle, the error banner, the footer, and the
webhook/github sections, which mint an inbound trigger rather than a bot
identity and are therefore CORE fragments, not modules. Everything per-platform
moved to `platforms/<id>/`, reachable only through `WizardHost`.

WHY THIS SHAPE

- Two publication channels, not two-way access. A fragment drives host-rendered
  chrome via `setFooter` / `setIdentityChrome` instead of reaching into modal
  internals. Both keep the CALLBACKS in a ref and only the RENDERED fields in
  state, so a Body may republish on every commit without looping the host — an
  unchanged publication returns the previous object and React bails out.
- The platform-switch reset seam disappears. The chassis mounts
  `<wizard.Body key={platform}>`, so a switch unmounts the old fragment and its
  state goes with it. The monolith's two hand-maintained 20-line `set*('')`
  reset lists are gone; they can no longer drift from the fields they reset.
- One deployment probe. `GET /slack/config` is Slack-NAMED but
  deployment-SCOPED, and the monolith called it from two effects. It is now one
  shared SWR key: the chassis reads `relayAvailable`/`relayPublicUrl` for
  `WizardHost.relayCapability`; the Slack-funnel flags on the same DTO stay
  Slack module state.

BEHAVIOR PRESERVED, DELIBERATELY

Every derived flag was moved arm-for-arm, including the awkward ones:

- `(!b.teamId || b.shareable)` applied to all platforms in the monolith but is
  Slack-only in truth — `Bot.teamId` is the Slack workspace id and no other
  platform ever writes it — so it became Slack's `freeBotFilter` and the other
  three add nothing.
- Telegram/Discord reuse spread `shareable` under `wantShared`, which was dead:
  `wantShared` required `platform === 'slack'`. Their `buildReuseInput` drops
  the spread and commits the identical payload.
- The busy-label swap (`'Creating…'` during auto-config, else `'Connecting…'`)
  is reproduced inside the Slack fragment's own publication.
- `nextTransport = transport ?? (relayAvailable ? 'http' : 'socket')` relied on
  the pick being NULLABLE. The host hands fragments a resolved value, so the
  Slack Body tracks `transportPicked` to keep the same three-way outcome.
- The one pre-existing `isMobile` fork (the walkthrough disclosure) moved
  verbatim into `wizard-chrome.tsx`. No new fork was introduced; the wizard
  stays one responsive tree of base + `desktop:` classes.

Mock mode rides on `WizardHost.mockMode`, and the monolith's Slack-only mock
branch became `MOCK_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIG` with the same four flags, so design/dev
with no CP still reaches every pane.

WHAT THE TESTS PIN

`platforms/reuse.test.ts` covers the pure half of the facet — `freeBotFilter`
and `buildReuseInput` per platform, plus `affordances` and the
region-parameterised copy. Nothing renders these, so an arm could drift
silently; the assertions state each platform's rule explicitly (Slack's
not-yet-shared workspace install, Feishu's region match and its legacy
region-less bot, the absent `shareable` key vs `shareable: false`) and pin the
registry's id set and picker order.

Verified additionally by extracting every multi-word string from the monolith
and from the refactored tree: no user-visible copy was dropped and none was
invented.

1. Funnel retraction. The monolith read the endpoint once per modal open and

docs(design): reconcile §5 identityScope and the §8 relay contract with what S3 shipped (#597)

Three sections of the integration-plugin design have been overtaken by their
own implementation. Recording the deltas now, while the reasoning is still
recoverable, so the remaining S3 adoption work reads the amended contract
rather than the sketch.

§5.1 — `identityScope` is per-ASSIGNMENT, not per-platform. The relay demux
work found a per-platform constant cannot express Slack, where both shapes are
live simultaneously: a distributed platform-app install is tenant-scoped (many
installs share one app id AND one signing secret, so only the composite
identifies the bot), while a legacy sibling may carry an app id alone or none
at all. Declaring the platform `'tenant'` would strand the legacy bots or, far
worse, license a signature scan that resolves a callback to a sibling install
of the same app — one workspace's messages delivered into another tenant's
bot. The amendment states the derivation (tenant id present ⇒ composite only,
never learned, and a re-assign that gains one must evict the stale app-only
entry; app id only ⇒ learnable, bounded; neither ⇒ bounded verify-scan) and
keeps at manifest scope only the weaker claim that the platform's identity
vocabulary has a tenant axis, which the CP still needs for §11 column choice.
§11's sentence that "the manifest's identityScope tells core which shape to
persist" is corrected the same way.

§5.2 — what actually shipped, and why it is a third of the published list.
The manifest carries `membershipEnumeration`, `botSenderRouting` and
`dmChannelPattern`; the last is not in the published candidate list and was
earned by a pre-dispatch read the audit surfaced. Records the discipline that
kept it small, including the field the rule rejected in review (status-bar
shape reads like a capability but is only ever read from an existing turn).

§8.1 — the relay contract as it shipped after three review rounds: plugin is
per-platform and stateless while the per-bot ingest is what it builds; verify
returns the plugin's typed product rather than a verdict (Feishu decrypts, and
the decrypted payload must reach handle exactly once); challenge is not a
third arm (Slack's is answered pre-candidate, Feishu's is encrypted and must
flow through verify); handle returns only a sync body because events are
ACK'd inside the platform window; the host forwards normalized messages, not
pre-addressed deliveries; the directory has three distinct trust models;
`getDaemonOnline` became `canDeliver` because a shortcut's trigger id is
one-shot; revocation reports carry the observing generation; egress is
`{ notice, lookupUserName }`.

§14 gains the four defects the S3 work fixed en route: revocation fenced with
the wrong generation, an offline daemon eating a one-shot trigger, Slack
event/interaction discrimination by absence, and the relay ignoring the §6.7
ingress bag it was already being sent.

refactor(cp): spec assembly and rc/bot-assign project through the providers (S3 §9) (#603)

§9: "the CP still assembles the wire payloads (it holds the rows and the
decrypted secrets), but through `projectIntegrationConfig` / `projectBotAssign`,
so `placement.ts` / `httpBot.ts` stop branching per platform and merely await
and forward provider output." The providers and their equivalence tests landed
in #574 (telegram/discord) and #580 (slack/feishu); the create DTO adopted the
registry in #592. This is the flip on the reconcile path — the last place core
knew a platform's field names.

WHY THE SHAPE CHANGED

`integrationToSpec` / `httpIntegrationToSpec` lose their per-platform arms and
gain two arguments: the registry, and the BOT ROW. The bot row is a required
projector input by contract, and passing it whole retires the three positional
bot fields the shared assembler used to take (`shareable`, the provider app id,
`botUserId`) — the very fields three call sites had drifted apart on. Both
assemblers now funnel into one private `projectSpec`, so the ONLY thing that
distinguishes direct from shared is the core envelope core still owns; the
payload behind it is entirely the provider's.

`buildAssign`'s `feishu ? … : slack` ternary becomes one awaited
`projectBotAssign`, and the method returns `RcBotAssign | null`.
`projectBotAssign` is OPTIONAL by design (the #580 erratum): a platform with a
daemon-owned long-lived transport declares none, and the create route already
refuses `transport: 'http'` on exactly that signal, so no such bot row can reach
the assign builder. Absence therefore neither fabricates an empty assign (the
relay would arm an ingress it cannot verify) nor throws (that would take down
`syncBot` for every other bot); it joins the two existing "cannot assign"
outcomes — `syncBot` logs and returns, `replayTo` skips the bot.

WHAT THE INVARIANTS COST

Everything on these paths is async now, so every call site was audited for a
missing await and a lost rejection. `reconcile` already mapped inside
`Promise.all`; `agentMove.snapshot` likewise; `pushSpecs` awaits inside the
loop's existing `NoConnection` try, which re-throws a projector rejection rather
than swallowing it. In `replayTo` the assign is built OUTSIDE the dead-socket
`try` on purpose: that catch means "the socket died", and a projector rejection
swallowed there would be a lost error rather than a dropped send — outside, it
propagates to the register handler's `.catch(log.error)`.

The registry reaches `Placement`, `HttpBotOrchestrator` and `AgentMoveService`
through a late-bound façade in `buildContainer`: the providers close over
`httpDeps`, which does not exist yet when those three are constructed, so the
existing `get platforms()` getter is generalized into one stable object every
holder captures. No secret material moves: the projectors receive the decrypted
`BotSecretMaterial` and return it inside the wire payload exactly as before —
nothing is persisted into `platformConfig` JSON.

BEHAVIOR THAT MOVED (two previously-unreachable arms, plus one convergence)

- An integration row whose platform has no registered provider is refused
  instead of falling through to the slack arm, which would have shipped a
  slack-shaped config under `platform: 'slack'` for a foreign row. Writes are
  fenced by `toDbPlatform` and the create route admits only registered ids, so
  that arm was dead code; `toDbPlatform` — the repo's existing persistence
  fence — now also narrows the open registry id back to the closed wire union.
- A missing bot row skips the spec instead of emitting a direct-mode one. The
  integration→bot FK is non-null with `onDelete: Restrict`, so this cannot
  happen; the guard states it rather than fabricating an identity.
- `agentMove`'s move bundle now carries `botOpenId` on a shared Feishu spec. It
  alone omitted the bot's open_id while the reconcile roster and the live
  HTTP-bot push both sent it, so the bundle now equals what the daemon receives
  by every other route. Activation fingerprints are computed and compared
  in-process, never persisted, so no rollout window sees a mismatch.

WHAT THE TESTS PIN

The four provider equivalence suites can no longer compare the live path to the
provider — the live path IS the provider now, and that comparison would prove
nothing. Each grows a GOLDEN LITERAL of the payload its pre-adoption arm emitted
(direct for all four; shared for slack and feishu), and the permutation cases
switch to equality with the extracted helper bodies those arms called, unchanged
by this commit — which is what catches core threading the wrong envelope,
secret, bot row, or direct/shared arm into the seam. Slack's shared golden also
asserts the appToken is absent (credential domaining) and feishu's that the
region default survives.

`httpBot.test.ts` pins the absent-`projectBotAssign` path three ways: `syncBot`
resolves, broadcasts NOTHING at all (not an empty frame), and pushes no
send-only spec; `replayTo` skips that bot instead of failing the whole replay;
and a provider that does declare the member still assigns. `placement.test.ts`
pins all three fail-closed fences — unregistered provider, unserved platform id,
session-identity id.

refactor(web): marks, settings fragments, channel semantics and the platform helper libs move into the modules (S3 §10) (#604)

#591 made `AddIntegrationModal` a chassis and moved the four create panes behind
`WebPlatformModule.wizard`. This moves the rest of §10's per-platform web surface
against the same seam (contract.ts, #573), so the console's platform knowledge
lives in `console/platforms/<id>/` rather than in switches spread across four
views and five `lib/` files.

WHAT MOVED

  Mark          — `PlatformMark`'s chat arms become each module's own component.
                  The `fillPct` box rule is now one shared helper
                  (`components/mark-box.ts`): 60% by default, capped at 80% for
                  the full-bleed square glyphs (Slack, Discord, GitHub). Losing
                  that cap is a silent visual regression, so `platform-set.test`
                  renders every module's `Mark` and the host's `PlatformMark`
                  at four fill values and asserts byte-identical markup.

  settings      — the Slack transport badge, the three provider deep links, and
                  the whole refresh/reinstall machinery (~180 lines of
                  card-scoped state) become `settingsFragments`. `DeleteBotModal`
                  takes its provider block from the same place.

  channelList   — `roomNoun` / `roomGlyph` / leave granularity / the cannot-leave
                  hint / the footer tail. The ALGORITHMS stay host-generic; only
                  the per-platform values moved.

  helper libs   — `slack-manifest`, `slack-refresh-notice`,
                  `use-slack-platform-install` → `platforms/slack/`;
                  `discord-invite` → `platforms/discord/`. The Lark/Feishu region
                  axis (brand word, console origin) becomes `feishu/region.ts`.

  display names — three divergent tables (`platName`'s substring chain, the
                  picker's `BOT_PLATFORM_LABEL`, `IntegrationChannelList`'s
                  `platformName`) collapse into one, `lib/platform-labels.ts`.

TWO LOOKUPS DELIBERATELY DO NOT READ THE REGISTRY

`platforms/registry.ts` eagerly imports every wizard `Body`. `PlatformMark` lives
in `components/marks.tsx`, which the login, waitlist, join and activate routes
import for `Wordmark` / `Spinner` / `SocialLoginMark`; `platName` lives in
`lib/data.ts`, which nearly every view imports. A registry read from either would
drag the install wizard into those bundles, so `platforms/marks.ts` and
`lib/platform-labels.ts` are small standalone lookups. They list the platform ids
a second time, and `platform-set.test.tsx` fails the build when the copies drift.

CONTRACT CHANGE: `WebBotSettingsFragments` LOSES ITS `TCardState` PARAMETER

The published shape had `useCardState()` return it and the fragments take it as a
prop, "flowing opaquely through the host" like the relay's `TVerified`. It cannot
be built: the registry stores modules as a homogeneous `WebPlatformModule[]`,
which resolves `TCardState` to its default, and `ComponentType<{card: SlackCard}>`
is not assignable to `ComponentType<{card: void}>` — component props are
contravariant under `strictFunctionTypes`, so the erasure a registry performs is
exactly the one the parameter cannot survive. (The relay's generic works because
each route binds it at its own call site; a React registry array binds nothing.)
Only `any` rescues the prop version. So the state stays inside the module behind
its own context: the host mounts `lifecycleActions.CardProvider` once per platform
tab and the module's fragments read from it. The host still never learns the
shape — it just no longer carries it. `TApi` is unaffected; it appears only
covariantly.

Exact-id lookup replaces the substring chains for chat platforms (those ids come
off the wire, where the vocabulary is closed); the core kinds keep theirs, because
`playground`/`webchat`/`schedule`/`github` are synthesized locally and the order
is load-bearing — `hook` must still be tested before `web`.

Deliberately NOT here: `textRenderer`, `messageIdentity` and `transcriptOrdering`.
All three are transcript-domain members of the same module objects, and the
renderer registry ships them together as one explicitly-reviewed behavior change.

TESTS PIN: the Discord invite URL's client_id, scopes and 292057893952 permission
bitfield plus the base64url token decode (new — it feeds a real external install
and had no coverage); mark/label registry parity and render-parity at
fillPct 60/70/100; the channel-card footer tails, room glyphs and the
platform-named cannot-leave sentence, including the unknown-id fallbacks;
`platName`'s chat arms and core-kind ordering. Slack's manifest and
refresh-notice suites move unchanged.

refactor(cp): the platform slot owns route mounting, the background lifecycle, env keys and the create tail (S3 §9) (#605)

§9 calls the CP slot "behavioral, not declarative" and lists what a descriptor
cannot express. #574/#580/#584 published the four providers; #592 moved the
create BODY and the live credential check behind them. This moves the rest of
the behavior core was still holding by name.

- **Route mounting.** `server.ts` no longer imports five funnel-route
  factories: it mounts `provider.installRoutes(scope)` at both scopes, and the
  public-callback scope stays deliberately double-mounted (`/api/v1` + the
  public `/v1` alias). Every path is unchanged — verified by diffing the whole
  331-row route table before and after, and pinned going forward by a new
  suite that asks each plugin what it declares and Fastify where it landed.
- **Background lifecycle.** The three hand-listed `SlackInstallReaper`
  instances and the reconciler `start()`/`stop()` calls become a fan-out over
  the providers' `pendingInstalls` / `backgroundLoops` declarations
  (`platforms/lifecycle.ts`). Same three labels, same TTLs, same instances.
- **Env fold.** `AppConfigSchema` composes `platforms/env.ts` instead of
  spreading two provider shapes by name. The fold is a static declaration, not
  the registry: `loadConfig` necessarily runs before a provider, which is
  constructed FROM the parsed config, can exist — a test pins the declaration
  against what the four providers actually declare, so the two cannot drift.
- **The create tail (#592's explicit leftover).** The four
  `req.body.platform === …` arms — each casting the opaque credential block
  back to a per-platform type and writing its own rows — collapse into ONE core
  skeleton (`http/install-bot.ts`) driven by a new provider member,
  `buildNewBotInstall`: which bot/integration columns this platform fills, how
  it packs the shared secret row, and the D6 external-identity it claims
  (id, tenant sentinel and 409 copy, so core runs both halves of the fence).
  `installNewSlackBot` now delegates to that skeleton, so Slack has one
  implementation across the manual install and both funnels. The
  post-create avatar/profile pushes run as `sideEffects.postCreate`, and the
  exhaustiveness guard #592 added ("no create tail for registered platform")
  is gone — there is no tail left to be missing.
- **`daemon-platform-capability.ts`** drops its hand-copied closed
  `IntegrationPlatform` union (audit Appendix A) for the open id the registry
  vouches for; the daemon's advertised list was always the real authority.

One deliberate behavior change, argued in the PR body: the `transport: 'http'`
relay-availability 409 now precedes the provider round-trip on every platform
(Feishu already did; Slack checked after), so the deployment-level blocker wins
over the credential verdict when both apply.

No public callback path, env var, or gateway/secret-store input changes.

refactor(web): transcript text rendering becomes a registry keyed by platformId (S3 §10/§14) (#614)

The last web unit of the S3 platform adoption. #604 moved marks, settings
fragments, channel semantics and the helper libs into the modules and left the
three transcript-domain members behind, because they live in the same module
objects and needed their own call-site work. This lands them.

textRenderer. `MessageText` resolves the renderer from the ROW's platform key
and no longer hardcodes one global renderer. NO MODULE DECLARES AN OVERRIDE —
that is the state §10 asks for ("ships with the Slack renderer as the default
for all chat platforms, then per-platform overrides land separately"), so every
row still renders through the core Slack-mrkdwn pipeline and the rendering
itself is unchanged. The default stays core rather than becoming the Slack
module's member because three other platforms render through it; it moves into
platforms/slack/ with the first real override, which is also the first change
here with visible pixels.

The lookup is per row, inside the memoized per-row component — not hoisted to
the page or the turn. A merged conversation interleaves sources by event time,
so a hoisted lookup would render one platform's rows with another's semantics,
silently, and only for the users who merged two platforms. `mergeConversation`
now carries each row's `sourcePlatform` out with it so the view cannot pair a
row with a neighbour's key, and the transcript threads it through FmtStep and
the user turn.

The published member keeps its ComponentType shape rather than §10's sketched
`(text, ctx) => ReactNode`: the memo boundary has to sit outside the
per-platform work or every transcript re-render re-runs each row's remark
pipeline, and no call site has a ctx to pass.

messageIdentity / transcriptOrdering. Both moved into the modules. #604 recorded
them as test-only; they are not — `mergeConversation` and `mergeSessionMessages`
are both live through SessionDetailView, whose NUL byte makes plain grep skip
the file. `transcriptOrdering` is a pure relocation (Slack event-time, everyone
else seq, unknown ids seq as before). `messageIdentity` is not, and the change
is deliberate: Slack used to be the fall-through arm for every unrecognized
platform id, while the contract says an absent member never dedupes. Dedupe is
the only step in the merge that can delete a row, so an unclaimed id now dedupes
nothing rather than borrowing Slack's decimal-ts rule.

`session-transcript.ts` takes the resolved ordering instead of the platform id:
it is shared with PlaygroundProvider, and a registry import would pull all four
platform modules and their CP bindings into the playground's graph for a value
it never reads — the same trade lib/platform-labels.ts documents.

Tests: 26-entry mrkdwn corpus pinned against markup captured from the
pre-registry renderer and asserted for every platform key; per-row resolution
with stand-in overrides across an interleaved merge; the unknown-id and known-id
arms of all three members.

refactor(web): the Profile card and the two Slack-flavoured bot-row sentences move behind the contract (S3 §10) (#616)

#591/#604/#614 moved the wizard panes, marks, settings fragments, channel-list
semantics, helper libs and the transcript members into `platforms/<id>/`. This
closes the three leftovers those PRs named, and sweeps the tree for the rest.

**`SlackConfigCard` gets a home.** It was the last direct core caller of a
platform-named `lib/api` export — #604 left it because it is a PROFILE-page card
while `settingsFragments` is scoped to Settings → Bots, so it had no member to
land in. It lands behind a new `ProfileCredentialCard`, not behind `apiBindings`:
routing it through `apiBindings` would not have removed the platform-named import
from core at all (the Slack-named component itself stayed in
`components/console/`, now importing `platforms/slack/api` instead of
`lib/api`), and it would have made the host the single caller of the one member
the contract documents as opaque to the host. What the card was missing was a
home, not a client seam. `ProfileView` now renders `PlatformCredentialCards` —
identically in both of its responsive branches.

**The revoked badge and the Sharable toggle stop describing Slack to everyone.**
Both are host chrome rendered for every platform's rows, and both spelled Slack's
model: a Telegram bot's `revoked` badge said "The Slack workspace uninstalled
this app", and a Discord bot's disabled toggle told you to switch to an HTTP
transport Discord does not have. `settingsFragments.copy` supplies the wording;
the host keeps owning the elements and the conditions. Slack declares both
strings unchanged to the byte and is the only module that declares either —
because it is the only platform that can reach either state. `revokedAt` is
written by exactly one path, `rc/bot-revoked`, whose reason enum is Slack's own
`app_uninstalled`/`tokens_revoked`; and multi-agent bots are Slack-only at the CP
("multi-agent bots currently support Slack only"). So the honest copy for the
other three IS the generic sentence, and inventing provider prose for states they
cannot reach would have been fiction. The default `shareHint`'s two arms are
deliberately the same sentence: the host still picks an arm by transport, but on
a platform that cannot share, transport is not the reason — two sentences would
promise that switching it helps.

**Sweep.** Six dead CSS custom properties (`--slack`/`--telegram`/`--discord`
and their `-soft` twins) had zero references anywhere in `src`; and
`.slack-hint-blink` was byte-identical to the generic `.step-blink` that Telegram
already used, so it collapses onto it and the keyframe loses its platform name.
Everything else the sweep found is platform-keyed routing, another feature's axis
(the session-access provider set, the OIDC connector catalog), or a comment — the
PR body lists it. `IntegrationChannelList` and the modals are already clean.

Every sweep used `grep -a`: `SessionDetailView.tsx` carries two raw NUL bytes in
composite-key template literals, so plain grep reports it as binary and silently
omits it — the same trap #614 documented.

Tests: 108 files / 832 passed (from 106 / 822). `tsc --noEmit` and eslint clean.

core dep slot IS a platform.

* fix(cp): the Slack tooling-credential facet takes its API client by name (review)

BLOCKING REGRESSION, caught in review. The facet was constructed from the route
dep bundle — but this same unit deletes `slackConfigApi` from `HttpDeps`, and
`resolveUserConfigAccessToken`'s first branch is `if (!deps.slackConfigApi)
return unreachable`. `SlackUserConfigDeps` declares that member OPTIONAL, so the
bundle kept satisfying the parameter type after the member vanished: the compiler
stayed silent, every suite stayed green, and the PRODUCTION graph resolved every
Slack App Configuration token as `unreachable` before the stored row was read —
quick-install 502 on a perfectly good token, manifest refresh degraded to
`unknown`, stale credentials unable to rotate.

Why nothing caught it: `test/fakes/build-http.ts` composed the facet DIFFERENTLY
from `container.ts`, giving it an explicit API-client getter. The fake was testing
a composition production did not have.

THE FIX makes the mistake unrepresentable rather than just correcting the call.
`createSlackToolingCredentials` now takes named `{ configApi?, store }` instead of
a bundle: no dep object in this codebase has a `store` member to donate, so a
bundle can no longer satisfy it by accident, and the API client must be passed by
name. Absent `configApi` keeps its pre-existing "funnel off ⇒ unreachable"
meaning, but is now an explicit omission.

ANTI-DRIFT. Both composition roots call that one factory with the same two named
arguments. In the harness the client comes from ONE source shared with
`slackSeams.configApi`, so the fake cannot hand the facet a client the routes do
not see. And the container graph is now exercised directly: a new integration
case builds the app through `buildApp` — the real `buildContainer` graph — and
asserts a MISSING credential resolves as `not_configured` (⇒ 409) rather than
`unreachable` (⇒ 502), with a companion case proving a stored row is actually
read. Verified to fail on the broken wiring (`expected 502 to be 409`) before the
fix. `container.test.ts` exists for exactly this failure mode; this is its
integration-scale sibling.

Also from review (non-blocking): the `GET|PUT /slack/config` status projection
stops re-reading the row through `usableNow` and applies `configUsable(row, now)`
to the row it already holds. The single-authority property comes from that PURE
PREDICATE — the facet's `usableNow` is a thin wrapper over it — so nothing can
drift, while the second round-trip and the split-snapshot response both go away.
§9 puts the store's entry/rotation/status routes on `installRoutes` and reserves
the facet for the platform's OTHER flows (the funnel start, the manifest refresh),
which is where it stays.

A unit case pins that an omitted `configApi` yields `unreachable` without touching
the store, and that `usableNow` still answers from the store — the asymmetry that
made the regression invisible to the status route.

docs(design): no conceptual line separates the hook and platform seams — only timing; Linear is a Platform on its own merits (#627)

§4.1 justified Linear-as-Platform by contrast with GitHub, and every version of
that contrast has failed scrutiny in turn. The section now leads with Linear's
positive case — Linear's product hands us the Bot/Integration shape natively
(the OAuth app IS the assignable identity, one per agent, §4.3) — and then
records why each candidate conceptual line between the seams is false, so
nobody re-derives the split from a bad premise:

- Conversation: falsified by the GitHub-events work (perThread session keys
  resuming the same ACP session, @-addressing, follow-ups in-thread).
- Streaming: a point on the output-mode axis; the GitHub poster already
  implements the Layer-2 output surface (§7.6).
- Shared posting identity: one App installation fronting many agents is the
  Slack shared-bot pattern, and Slack is a platform module.
- Authorization direction: both seams share "installation grants presence,
  per-event policy decides who may address". GitHub's write/admin gate against
  comment.user is a policy DEFAULT tuned for a public repository's
  internet-wide audience, not a structural property — a public Discord server
  poses the same exposure class inside the platform contract, and "anyone may
  address" is the same knob as chat-side conversation gating.
- Resource rows: HookDef ≈ Integration + subscription filters; one installation
  fanning out to many hooks ≈ one shared Bot fronting many Integrations.
  Migration is feasible, not conceptually blocked.

What keeps GitHub on the hook seam is two-implementer discipline and migration
economics: the platform contracts were settled from four chat implementers,
and reshaping them around a fifth, non-chat implementer would extract an
interface from one example for zero user-visible payoff. The convergence point
is GitLab — §7.6 already admits facet-subset implementers, so the expected end
state is one module system where chat platforms implement the full facet set
and code hosts a subset plus their own facets. One consequence does not wait:
the "who may address" knob (conversation gating ≍ the write/admin gate) is one
policy family implemented twice, and its next change should be designed
cross-platform.

The borrows-from-hooks list now names the assign-rule/CP-replay table as a
restatement of platform routing rules — duplication that merges in the same
GitLab-time consolidation.

feat(auth): link without a code when the provider allows it (#632)

Linking any provider asked for an emailed code. That was collateral from #243:
it moved every provider to the Account API to escape the Slack 502, and the
Account API requires an ownership proof because the user's own token is the
authority there. On the Management API the CP's credential is, and no code is
needed -- which is how #225 worked before Slack broke it.

Only Slack was ever broken. Its connector stores state while building the
authorization URI (`setSession`), and the Management API runs connectors with
no session. GitHub and Google do not: both build a plain URL, and GitHub's
getUserInfo reads no session either. So they never needed the code they got.

Rather than keep a list of which connectors need a session, the CP ASKS: it
tries to have Logto build the URI, and reports `direct` or `verified`. Logto's
own published list omitted Slack, and a list that is wrong here is exactly the
502 this used to be. A failed probe is not an error -- every connector is still
linkable the other way -- so the fallback is always correct, merely slower, and
a new provider lands on the right path without anyone classifying it.

  GitHub, Google  -> direct   -> no code, link completes server-side
  Slack           -> verified -> browser drives it, ownership proof as today

The verdict is cached per target for an hour, so only the first attempt pays
the probe; `direct` deliberately is not cached, since each link needs its own
state and redirect in the URI.

* test(evals): the automatic-turn budget, not the hop cap, now bounds the chain

Rebasing onto main picked up #628, which raised `MAX_AGENT_CALL_HOPS` from 8 to
20. That changed which protection binds, and the arena caught it.

**Measured:** the A→B→A chain advances one hop per edge in strict alternation,
exactly once per finalized response, and stops at **16 edges with 4 hops still
unspent**. Each agent spent exactly its 8 automatic turns
(`MAX_AUTOMATIC_TURNS_PER_WINDOW`, 60 s window, durable latch). Attribution was
confirmed by construction, not inferred from arithmetic: raising only that budget
lets the identical chain run to hop 20 and stop on the cap instead.

So after #628 the hop cap is not the operative limit for a leaderless two-agent
room — the automatic-turn budget is, at 2 × 8 = 16 edges. Raising the hop cap
alone does not lengthen such a conversation. The same budget is what saturates
under 4-bot fan-out, so it now bounds agent-to-agent conversation in both the
narrow and the wide regime while the hop cap binds in neither.

The test pins that behavior instead of the design's "until the cap" wording. It
stays an ordinary assertion: main still carries this as `it.fails` blamed on
`session_source_mismatch`, which #568 fixed — the transport property is green,
and what stops the chain is simply a different protection than the design
assumed.

bounds and which one binds, §2 no longer claims "until the cap", §6.3 tied to

* fix(dream): stamp baseline before source query; refresh stale docs

Review-bot flagged a cutoff race in the automatic window. The dream's
`createdAt` is the cutoff the next automatic dream filters on

whose `updatedAt` landed between the query and the stamp was then in neither this

time; the worst case is a thin band of sessions mined twice (safe, idempotent
consolidation) instead of dropped. better-sqlite3 is synchronous/single-threaded,
so no session write interleaves between the stamp and the query. Adds a
regression test asserting `createdAt` precedes the source read.

feat(evals): make Werewolf's day a natural sequential discussion, and measure where it dies (#659)

* feat(evals): make Werewolf's day a natural sequential discussion, and measure where it dies

Werewolf's day phase broadcast one prompt to every living player at once, so
everyone spoke concurrently and then voted. That skips the core of the game:
players speak IN ORDER, and each speaker hears everyone before them.

The day is now sequential and carried by the players themselves. The referee
opens each day exactly once — deaths, living players, the speaking order, and
the rule "speak only after the player before you has spoken" — and then says
nothing until the order finishes or dies. From there the round advances
agent-to-agent: the production Slack echo (now installed on the public room)
fans each delivered speech back to the other members' connections, and the
daemon's own arbitration ladder decides who wakes. Nobody is nominated —
speaker N+1 is woken by speaker N's ordinary message, which is the PR #549
behavior. Players who are only listening answer with the product's own
AC_NO_RESPONSE silent branch, so a listening turn posts nothing.

The vote is unchanged (structured `vote` tool calls once discussion ends); a
vote attempted during discussion is rejected with `discussion_in_progress`.
Private roles, the wolf den, seer results as private control, canary/leak
assertions and win detection are all preserved.

Every day is now instrumented: the announced order, who spoke, who never got
their turn, out-of-order speeches, how the round ended, which loop-guard
circuits latched, per-player peer-wake accounting (admitted/gated/suppressed),
and whether the round reached the vote.

What that instrumentation measures, scripted and reproducible:

  A day costs every participant one automatic turn per other participant's
  speech, so position i must absorb i automatic turns before its own turn
  arrives. With MAX_AUTOMATIC_TURNS_PER_WINDOW = 8, the ninth speaker is the
  last the budget can carry. Tables of 7/9/10 complete the order; 11 and 12
  stall at exactly 9 speakers, every latched player showing `admitted: 8` then
  `gated`. The bound is per ROUND, not per game: the referee's DAY/VOTE
  broadcasts are trusted human turns, and a human turn resets the automatic
  counter. The latch is durable, so a latched player cannot even receive the
  VOTE broadcast — the day reaches the vote with fewer ballots than living
  players.

Also adds a contained real-subject preflight (`preflightRealSubject`), because
both real-run failures found here were silent: a runtime that cannot launch
makes the game produce zero effects for its whole deadline, and a wrong
`AGENTCONNECT_DAEMON_ENTRY` brings the ACP session up with no AgentConnect
tools at all. Both now fail loudly with an actionable message.

Werewolf's table scales past seven players (two wolves, one seer, one doctor,
villagers for the rest), which is how the order-length bound is measured.

Verified: pnpm typecheck, pnpm lint, pnpm format:check, pnpm eval:validate,
pnpm eval:collab:contracts (15 files, 107 tests). Real local Claude Code over
ACP, five trials, recorded in the baseline.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(evals): terminate the preflight runtime's whole process group, not just the wrapper

Review finding on this PR, verified and reproducible.

`npx -y <adapter>` runs the REAL ACP adapter as a GRANDCHILD of the npm
wrapper — measured here as pid 9895 under wrapper pid 9825. The probe killed
only the direct child, so the adapter was orphaned and reparented to pid 1,
still holding its inherited stdio pipes and a credentialed process open. Every
preflight leaked another one.

The adapter this PR names happens to exit on stdin EOF, which hid the leak in
practice. That is luck, not cleanup: a wrapper whose grandchild ignores stdin
demonstrates the orphan surviving, and that is the regression test added here.

Fixed the way the daemon already solves this exact topology in `AcpHost`: spawn
detached so the child leads its own POSIX process group, signal the group
(SIGTERM then escalate to SIGKILL) instead of the direct child, and sweep group
survivors on the leader's exit while its pgid provably cannot have been
recycled. Falls back to the direct child on win32 and on ESRCH.

The regression test was confirmed to FAIL against the previous implementation
("preflight orphaned a grandchild") and pass against this one.

Also closes the reviewer's non-blocking note: a latched circuit makes the daemon
post its loop-protection notice into the room, which echoes and wakes peers. For
a player that had already spoken but whose successor had not, that wake
satisfied the scripted host's visible-transcript turn rule and bought a second
speech. The notice is not conversation, so the host now treats it as no
activation.

Arena gate: 15 files, 108 tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(evals): cancel the preflight kill escalation once the leader exits

Second review finding on this PR, and correct.

`finish()` scheduled a SIGKILL against `-child.pid` two seconds out and never
cancelled it. When SIGTERM worked, the exit listener swept the group and the
pgid became empty — and an empty pgid can be recycled, so the late
`kill(-pid, SIGKILL)` could land on an unrelated process group.

Escalation is only safe while the leader is alive, because that is exactly what
keeps the pgid ours. The exit listener now clears the pending escalation before
its sweep, and `finish()` does not arm one at all against an already-exited
child. `AcpHost.stop()` cancels for the same reason and likewise refuses to
signal a pgid whose ownership it can no longer prove.

Arena gate: 15 files, 108 tests.

feat(daemon): auto-approve the evaluation tools this daemon serves on its own reserved MCP server (#664)

* feat(daemon): auto-approve the evaluation tools this daemon serves on its own reserved MCP server

A real ACP subject in a headless arena run could never take a game action, so no
Werewolf game could ever reach a winner: no lynch, no night kill, no win
condition, `acceptedActions: 0` in every trial.

The mechanism, measured rather than assumed — and it is NOT what an earlier
revision of the baseline claimed. The daemon records ZERO `permission.*` events
for a whole real run: the ACP `session/request_permission` is never sent, so
`isBuiltinSystemTool` was never even consulted. Claude Code was denying locally,
24-31 times per run: "Permission to use mcp__agentconnect__protect has been
denied because Claude Code is running in don't ask mode."

Three subject-side pre-approvals were tried and all failed (workspace
`.claude/settings.json` + `settings.local.json`, both rule shapes, written and
confirmed surviving the run but not honored; `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` takes the
runtime's authentication with it; `permissionMode: auto` stalls on the
classifier). A headless subject must therefore run in `permissionMode: default`,
where the request does reach the daemon — and the daemon must be willing to
approve a game's own tools without a card, because a headless run has no card
surface and the fallback is to hold the request forever.

So the auto-allow set is no longer the hardcoded product list but the tools this
daemon ACTUALLY REGISTERED on its own reserved `agentconnect` MCP server for
that session. The scoping is the whole point, and every clause is pinned by a
test:

- the extra names come from `evaluation.environment.tools`, injected in-process
  at Daemon construction — no wire, agent, peer, CP or config path can add one;
- that registry is EMPTY in production, so behavior there is bit-for-bit
  unchanged (pinned: verdicts with an empty extra set equal today's verdicts);
- a name only matches under the reserved `agentconnect` prefix — the same name
  on any other MCP server still gets its card (negative test), and a misleading
  display title cannot override a foreign structured server identity;
- startup already rejects an evaluation tool that shadows or duplicates a
  product tool; the runtime's dangerous built-ins are not in the set and still
  prompt.

The product path's matching is deliberately unchanged: `isBuiltinSystemToolCall`
still requires an exact title match, and the extra names are matched the same
strict way rather than by substring.

Measured with real local Claude Code (sonnet), 5 players: a complete game to a
winner — village, 2 rounds, both wolves lynched, 14 accepted actions (9 votes,
1 kill, 2 inspections, 2 protections), every speaking order completed in order,
0 canary leaks, 0 unauthorized or wrong-room effects.

Adds a scripted CI test pinning multi-round play to a winner (night → sequential
day → vote → resolution, repeating), including that the per-round automatic-turn

* feat(evals): make Werewolf actions ordinary messages, and revert the daemon auto-allow widening

Modelling vote/kill/inspect/protect as MCP tool calls was the wrong design. A
tool call is out of band with respect to the system under test: it never
traverses routing, produces no thread message, spends no automatic-turn budget,
and makes the leak assertions weak because role visibility comes from tool
privacy rather than from conversation membership. It also forced the daemon
permission change in #664.

Every action is now an ordinary message in the conversation it belongs to:

  vote     → the public day room, said out loud (it SHOULD be public)
  kill     → the wolf den, agreed by the wolves in conversation
  inspect  → the seer's own private referee DM
  protect  → the doctor's own private referee DM

Parsing is strict and never coached: an action verb must be followed by exactly
one alias inside the same sentence; two different targets is ambiguous and
yields nothing. An actor that spoke in the right conversation but stated nothing
readable is `unparseable`; one that never spoke is `silent`. Neither is retried.
Authorization (phase, role, aliveness, one per round) is unchanged, now applied
to parsed intent. The wolf den also gets a PlatformEcho, so the pack must
actually hear each other to converge — the first clear statement carries.

REVERTED: #664's `isBuiltinSystemTool` / `isBuiltinSystemToolCall` widening and
its five tests, by reverse-applying that commit's exact hunks. It existed only
to make MCP tools reachable for real subjects; with actions as messages the game
registers no evaluation tools at all, so it is unnecessary. The §6 registry
remains a product capability, still covered by evaluation-game-tools.test.ts.

MEASURED — the automatic-turn budget now binds much harder, and the reason
matters:

  Scripted 7p: every circuit latches at exactly admitted:8 and rounds 2+ are
  empty. The wolves absorb more (14) because the room and the den are different
  channels, hence different loop-guard scopes.

  Real 7p (local Claude Code, sonnet), 2 trials: BOTH complete to a winner in 2
  rounds with 91 and 95 admitted automatic turns and ZERO gated, ZERO latches.
  Round 1 spans 90s and 128s of wall clock — longer than the 60s window — so it
  rolls over inside the round and players absorb 11 and 14 without gating.

So the scripted collapse is an artifact of scripted SPEED, not a limit of the
design. It is pinned as its own test because it is a real property of the gate.

Real agents state actions clearly enough to parse (unparseableActions: 0 in both
trials), and the wolves genuinely negotiate — proposal, rationale, "any
objections?", agreement — which independent tool submissions never exercised.
Reported honestly: both trials still left votes uncast (3 and 2 of 6 eligible)
with zero gating, so that is model behavior, not a protection.

Arena gate: 15 files, 113 tests.

* fix(evals): count a failed action statement once, and keep the night victim's owed action

Two accounting bugs found in review, both affecting the headline metrics.

A statement already classified this round — ambiguous, rejected or duplicate —
was counted a SECOND time at phase resolution, because close-out spoke for any
actor without an ACCEPTED action. `unparseableActions` therefore double-reported
a single failed statement. Close-out now stays silent when the round already
recorded a disposition for that actor and action; the pack's kill close-out
carries the same guard, since it is a separate inline path.

The owed-action scans also ran AFTER the round's death was applied, so an actor
eliminated during resolution dropped out of the scan and its missing action
vanished: the lynched player's uncast vote, and the seer's or doctor's missing
night action when they were the night's victim. Both scans now snapshot who owed
an action before the death is applied.

Regression tests for both: one ambiguous kill statement yields exactly one
`unparseable` record, and a seer killed at night still reports its missing
inspect rather than disappearing with it.

Also scopes the day-speech-count assertion to the first day — a later scripted
day can be legitimately silent once circuits latch, which CI hit and local
scheduling did not.

fix(protocol): keep the slack-app-manifest subpath bundler-resolvable (#726)

`pnpm --filter @agentconnect.md/web dev` 500s on every console route with
`Can't resolve './frames/relay-cp.js'`. The web console value-imports
`@agentconnect.md/protocol/slack-app-manifest`, and in dev the `development`
export condition resolves that subpath to `src/slack-app-manifest.ts` instead
of `dist/` — so Turbopack compiles protocol source directly and hits the
NodeNext `.js` specifier on line 1.

Turbopack does not implement TypeScript's `.js` -> `.ts` extension
substitution (verified: it fails for a `./x.js` import inside
`packages/web/src` too, so this is not a workspace-symlink or `type: module`
effect), and Next lists the webpack escape hatch `experimental.extensionAlias`
as Turbopack-unsupported. No `next.config.mjs` setting fixes it, and dropping
the `development` condition would force a protocol rebuild before every web
dev run — which is what that condition exists to avoid.

So make the one bundler-facing entry point a leaf: move
`SLACK_MANAGE_SESSION_SHORTCUT_CALLBACK_ID` out of `frames/relay-cp.ts` and
into `slack-app-manifest.ts`, which now has no relative imports at all. The
constant belongs there anyway — it is the `callback_id` the manifest declares
to Slack, unlike the Block Kit action ids beside it, which name controls on
messages we post. The package root re-exports it explicitly, so the public
surface is unchanged for daemon, relay, and CP.

Add `slack-app-manifest.leaf.test.ts` to enforce the invariant. Nothing else
catches this class of breakage: typecheck, the test suites, and `next build`
(which reads `dist/`) all stay green while dev is broken.

Verified by loading console routes against a running dev server — `/`,
`/agents`, `/settings` all 200, and the Add-integration modal that pulls in
the Slack manifest opens — plus a clean `next build`, repo-wide typecheck,
lint, format, and the protocol/web/relay/control-plane suites.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore(web): stop tracking the generated next-env.d.ts (#727)

Next writes this file from `distDir`, so `next dev` (`.next/dev`) and
`next build` (`.next`) each rewrite it over the other's version. Tracking it
means every switch between the two dirties the working tree with a change no
one authored — you either commit build output or revert it by hand before
every commit.

Nothing depends on the committed copy:

- `next dev` and `next build` both regenerate it, byte-identical to what was
  tracked (verified by deleting it and rebuilding).
- CI never runs `tsc` against web — `typecheck:ci` filters to control-plane,
  daemon, and setup, and the Check job notes the Next build already typechecks
  its own package. The Build job's `next build` regenerates the file.
- `tsc --noEmit` passes on a tree with neither `next-env.d.ts` nor `.next`.

The file itself says it should not be edited, and every create-next-app
template ignores it, so this brings us in line with upstream rather than
inventing a local convention.

Verified: `next dev` rewrites the file and `git status` stays clean; a clean
`next build` regenerates it and succeeds; web typecheck, lint, and format:check
all pass.

feat(cp): per-org secret encryption (scope the SecretCipher seam) (#722)

Scopes the at-rest secret seam per organization. SecretCipher.seal/.open take a
SecretScope -- the deployment's, or one org's -- and VaultTransitSecretCipher
resolves it to a transit key per call, so an org's material can later be
destroyed with its key.

The scope is a parameter, never a field inside the stored value: the stored
string comes out of Postgres, the surface we assume may be read across tenants,
so it must not select its own decryption key. A row of org A handed to code
serving org B now fails to decrypt instead of decrypting silently. The envelope
carries only a format version tag, and open keeps three arms, so the rollout
needs no backfill.

Ten secret-store ports take an orgId first parameter -- not a second fence
(org-scoped-data-layer.md 3.6 already fences these child tables through their
parent) but because only the caller can assert which tenant's key to use. Paths
with no serving tenant use that document's existing *Unscoped convention.

The rewrap sweep resolves each row's owning org and re-seals under that key, and
picks up feishu_app_registration, which sealed values through the cipher but was
absent from the sweep.

Vault key destruction is deliberately absent: the CP only ever records intent.

feat(cp): destroy an organization's transit key when it is deleted (#731)

Completes crypto-shredding. Deleting an organization records the intent in the same
transaction that removes it, and an operator-run CLI destroys that org's transit key --
turning its ciphertext into permanent noise, including the copies inside database
backups taken before the deletion.

The CP never deletes a key. It writes one pending_key_shred row, deliberately without a
foreign key because the row must outlive the organization it names, and only on the
deleted path -- a refused deletion must not schedule the destruction of a live org's key.
The row pins the resolved mount and key name at deletion time, so rotating the mount or
the org key prefix before draining cannot redirect the destroy at a name that does not
exist and be read as "already destroyed".

Deletion lives in secrets/shred-cli.ts, which runs as its own workload with its own
identity and its own minimal configuration. A separate Vault role would not be enough:
roles bind to a service account, so a role bound to the CP's account stays reachable from
the CP. Reusing the CP's config loader would have had the same effect from the other
direction, by requiring the CP's credential before the job could start.

The shredder never enumerates keys -- every name comes from a tombstone this deployment
wrote -- so it needs no list capability, which matters because Vault cannot restrict a
list to a prefix and a shared transit mount would show every other deployment's org keys
as orphans.

Vault's auth plumbing moves to secrets/vault-http.ts so the cipher and the destroyer share
one implementation. They share no credential.

Design: docs/designs/per-org-secret-encryption.md

refactor(daemon): retire the orchestration tools from the agent tool surface (#732)

`startOrchestration` overlapped `sendMessage`: fanning work out to N workers is
N `sendMessage({ toAgent: { agentId, needsReply: true } })` calls, and status
lookup is `viewSessionStatus`. Two tools meaning "give work to another agent"
made the surface ambiguous, so the orchestration triple is no longer offered.

Move the three descriptors out of `COLLABORATION_TOOLS` into
`RETIRED_ORCHESTRATION_TOOLS`, which is injected into no agent's tool set. The
daemon-side machinery is deliberately untouched: durable orchestration/subtask
records, the four correlation checks and idempotent report recording, and the
one-shot session-anchored deadline wake that is re-armed from the store on
startup. That deadline is the one capability `sendMessage(needsReply)` cannot
express today, and it is kept so `needsReply` can gain an optional deadline on
top of it.

`executeTool` still dispatches the three names, and they stay in
`ALL_TOOL_NAMES`, so a session already warm with the old descriptors and any
still-open orchestration record keep resolving without hitting approval, and no
evaluation tool can claim a name the daemon still handles.

fix(web): widen a session rail whose seeded agent filter collapsed (#733)

* fix(web): widen a session rail whose seeded agent filter collapsed

The rail seeds its agent filter with every agent in the open conversation,
and repeated `agentId` asks the CP for the conversations those agents
SHARE. A thread two agents have only ever worked in together once answers
with exactly that thread — so the rail held a single row, the one already
on screen, and `empty` read that as "nothing worth drawing" and rendered
only its invisible placeholder column.

Hiding the rail also removes the chips and the agent picker, which are the
only way back to a wider list, so the reader was left with an empty gutter
and no way out of it. That is the same trap `filterTouched` already guards
a reader's own filter against; a seeded filter had no equivalent guard.

Re-ask the question unfiltered instead of erasing the answer: when a
SEEDED filter's page comes back with fewer than two rows, fetch the
unfiltered list and clear the chips so they describe what is on screen. A
filter the reader touched is never widened — a narrow result is a real
answer to their own question. An in-flight page defers the decision, since
it is indistinguishable from a collapsed one and would otherwise fire the
unfiltered request on every load.

Applies to any collapsed seed, not just the multi-agent case: a single
agent reaches the same dead end whenever the open session is the only one
it owns.

`SessionRail`'s own `empty` rule is unchanged — relaxing it there broke
the test that pins "hold the column, draw nothing", which is correct
behaviour once the caller has already widened a collapsed seed.

Opening a conversation sometimes rendered "Conversation not found — or none
of its participants are visible to you" for a thread the caller can see
perfectly well. That copy states an authorization verdict the console never
actually got.

Two distinct non-answers were landing in the not-found branch:

  console reproduces the message immediately; restoring it brings the
  conversation straight back.
- the resolver answering EMPTY while degraded. The CP fails external access

  budget collapses to `unknown`, omits the very members it could not check,

were never the same thing, and only one of them is about permission.

unverifiable read now renders the existing SessionAccessNotice ("access

and only a healthy empty answer keeps the not-found copy. The roster unwrap
preserves `undefined` = in flight and `null` = answered-empty, so every
downstream reader is untouched.

access check collapses to `unknown` through a bare `catch {}` with no log
anywhere, so a hidden session left no trace an operator could correlate

perf(cp): stop re-resolving session provider access per request (#739)

* perf(cp): stop re-resolving session provider access per request

The console home page spent seconds on exactly three reads — /sessions,
/sessions/facets and /usage — while every other read model on the same
page answered in tens of milliseconds. Those three are the only ones
that resolve Session external access, and each paid its own full
provider sweep: per external scope an uncached GitHub repository lookup
or Slack conversations.info, then the per-user permission check.

Two caches remove the duplicated work without moving an authorization
lease.

One resolver, and so one snapshot, per composed app. Five route modules
build a resolver of their own and a single page load asks several of
them the same question at once, so a per-module instance would defeat
the point. A short window single-flights the sweep and the concurrent
reads share one answer. It is keyed on org, viewer, identity set and the
scope set including aclRevision, so a re-fenced scope cannot hit a stale
entry.

Per-scope resource shape. Whether a repository is public, or a channel
is a public channel, is a property of the resource rather than of the
viewer, yet the decision caches are keyed per user — so every viewer
paid its own lookup, and for a public resource that lookup is the whole
check. These are now shared across viewers, and an allow is leased from
when its evidence was observed rather than from when it was reused, so
reuse cannot stretch the existing 120s window. deny and unknown keep the
wall-clock lease: reused evidence can only ever narrow access.

A failed lookup stays a per-request verdict in both caches, so a
transient provider blip is never pinned as a decision.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor(cp): back the session-access caches with lru-cache

The three caches added here were hand-rolled Map + TTL + in-flight +
eviction, and the eviction was FIFO rather than LRU — a hot entry could
be dropped for having been inserted early. lru-cache does all of it,
including handing concurrent callers of one key the same promise via
fetchMethod, so the machinery goes and the two adjacent per-principal
verdict caches move onto it as well.

Two semantics of the library are load-bearing and worth naming.

The clock is injected through the perf option, so the caches read the
same time seam as everything around them. ttlResolution is 0 because the
default debounces now() behind a real timer that a FakeClock cannot
advance. Expiry stays lazy, evaluated on read, so no background timer
exists either.

lru-cache records an entry start and treats a falsy one as no TTL
recorded, which makes an entry written at time 0 immortal. Clock
documents wall-clock epoch milliseconds and production passes Date.now,
so this only reaches fixtures: the two that used a zero-based FakeClock
now seed an epoch, and the constraint is written down where the caches
are configured.

The evidence lease is now expressed rather than computed: an allow is
set with start at the observation, so the entry expires a lease after
the evidence was read rather than after it was reused.

One asserted boundary moves by a millisecond. The hand-rolled check was
inclusive, lru-cache goes stale once age passes the TTL, so the
120 second refresh lands at 120001ms.

The migration arm read a bare vault:vN: value under the DEPLOYMENT key while
ignoring the asserted scope -- the exact fence the scope parameter exists to
build. It was a hole justified only by being temporary, and it is no longer
needed: all deployments have been swept by rewrap and hold zero pre-scoping

introduced: an older replica meeting a newer envelope now fails loudly instead of
serving the tag as plaintext. The other half is unchanged -- a build predating the
envelope has no such check -- so a future envelope change still owes two releases.

still pass through, PlaintextSecretCipher is still pure identity, and the online
