perf(cp): serve the session-access snapshot while it refreshes (#746)

* perf(cp): serve the session-access snapshot while it refreshes

Collapsing one page load's reads into a single sweep fixed the common
case but not the tail: whenever the snapshot window and a plugin's own
decision lease both lapsed, some unlucky request still wore the whole
provider sweep — every ~120 s for allow verdicts, every ~30 s for deny,
and every ~5 s while a provider is degraded.

Past a 30 s fresh window a read now hands back the snapshot it has and
re-sweeps behind the request, so no console read waits on Slack or
GitHub. Past a 60 s ceiling the entry is gone and the next read blocks
on a real sweep: an unbounded stale-while-revalidate would mean a
revoked user is never re-checked until they happen to come back.

The ceiling is not free and the code says so. A sweep reuses plugin
verdicts already up to their own 120 s allow lease old, so the
worst-case age of the evidence behind a served answer is the ceiling
PLUS that lease — ~125 s before this change, ~180 s after. Every second
added to the ceiling is a second added to the revocation window, one for
one. No setting avoids it: serving anything stale is the price of never
blocking, which is why the ceiling is 60 s rather than the plugins'
own 120 s.

Stale-on-rejection is scoped to the refresh path only. A refresh that
fails keeps serving what it was refreshing, up to the ceiling; a COLD
sweep that fails still rejects, because resolving it to "no external
access" would silently hide every external row instead of reporting an
error.

A refresh started inside the stale window can still be running once the
entry passes the ceiling. `fetch` coalesces the caller that arrives then
onto the SAME promise — its in-flight branch runs before any staleness
check — and lru-cache settles that promise with the options of the fetch
that CREATED it. `allowStaleOnFetchRejection` on the refresh therefore
handed the old snapshot to a caller that was supposed to block: the
ceiling was not hard in exactly the case it exists for, and the evidence
age could pass the ~180 s the constant advertises.

Dropping it while keeping `noDeleteOnFetchRejection` gives all three
behaviours at once, confirmed against the pinned lru-cache 11.5.2: the
reader that never waited still gets its stale value, the entry still
survives a failed refresh, and a caller that arrives past the ceiling
observes the failure instead of inheriting the snapshot.

empty space under the handler bar. Register @prisma/instrumentation so

time in.

Prisma tracing is a globalThis handshake rather than a module patch, and
this deployment runs the v7 queryCompiler with a driver adapter, so a
clean install proves nothing about whether spans appear. An integration
test runs real queries and asserts they do, that the SQL is attached,
and that bound parameters are not. No schema or preview-feature opt-in

* refactor(daemon): replace ad-hoc store upgrades with a versioned migration runner

The local store had accumulated 21 `migrate*` methods, each re-deriving
`PRAGMA table_info(...)` on every open to add a column some pre-v1 daemon
lacked. None of them can fire on a v1 database, and together they were not a
migration mechanism: no version was recorded, so ordering was implicit in a
call list and every step paid a table scan at boot forever.

Delete them and record a schema version instead. `SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS` is empty
at v1; step i upgrades a store at user_version i+1 to i+2, each running once
inside a transaction that commits the version it produced. A store from a
newer daemon is refused rather than "upgraded" by older steps. The daemon's
store holds the user's transcripts and sessions on their own machine, so it is
still upgraded in place — this keeps that path, and makes the next schema
change declare itself instead of being inferred from a missing column.

Three things were riding along inside those methods and are now where they
belong:

- `transcript_agent_tool_call`, `transcript_thread_event_time` and
  `transcript_thread_revision` were only ever created by a migration, so the
  CREATE block alone produced a store without them.
- The `transcriptRevision` counter is in-memory over durable rows and must
  resume from MAX(revision) on every open, not only on upgrade.
- `sessions.conversationKind`, `tenantScope` and `launchCorrelationId` had
  drifted out of the CREATE block and existed only as ALTERs.

Verified by diffing the full `sqlite_master` schema of a freshly created store
before and after: identical.

`adoptLegacySessionScope` goes with them — it rekeyed pre-transport-scope
sessions, a shape no v1 store can contain.

* fix(daemon): gate the store schema version before any DDL

The upgrade ran after the constructor's CREATE block, which broke it in two
directions the empty migration list hid:

- The CREATE block describes the CURRENT schema, so it may index a column a
  future step introduces. Running it first would issue that CREATE INDEX
  against a table the step had not widened yet — the first real migration
  would have failed at boot.
- A store from a newer daemon was refused only AFTER the CREATE block had
  already run against it. IF NOT EXISTS reads as harmless, but on a newer store
  "not exists" is the wrong question: it re-adds this version's objects to a
  database this build cannot reason about, and only then rejects it. The
  refusal existed precisely to avoid touching that store.

Both are fixed by running the version check and the steps before any DDL, and
stamping a fresh store only once the CREATE block has actually emitted that
schema. A step now reshapes what exists; creating anything new stays in the
CREATE block, which runs afterwards and covers fresh and upgraded stores from
one description.

The refusal test now proves the store is untouched — it drops a table this
build would happily recreate and asserts it is still absent, and that the
version was not rewritten.

perf(cp): collapse the session visibility predicate to a fixed three arms (#751)

The predicate was written as one OR arm per provider policy and one per
granted scope, each carrying its own EXISTS. For an ordinary org that is
nineteen arms and ~28 correlated subqueries, evaluated per candidate row —
and the conversation page re-applies the whole predicate to the inner probe
row of its emit-at-max subquery, so every arm is paid again per probed row.

The arms were identical apart from the value they matched, and their EXISTS
clauses referenced only the row (orgId, externalProvider, classifiedPolicyRev),
never the arm. So a set membership plus one shared EXISTS says exactly what
the union of the arms said, in three arms instead of nineteen.

The revision fence rides inside the scope lookup as a (scope, revision) pair
rather than one arm per pair. external_scope.id is the primary key, so at most
one row can match the session's scope id, and the pair check binds that row's
revision to the one this viewer was actually granted.

Both EXISTS checks still read the live policy and scope tables rather than
trusting the caller's snapshot — that fence is what stops a concurrent enable
or an ACL bump being authorized against a stale decision. It is now performed
once instead of once per scope.

Measured against a database with ~2,600 sessions and 14 granted scopes, the
old and new predicates select an identical row set (same count, same id
fingerprint), and:

  session page query (emit-at-max)   13,316 ms -> 132 ms
  grouped COUNT (includeTotal)          846 ms ->   8 ms
  session facet (channels)              393 ms ->   6 ms

The emit-at-max subquery itself needed no change: it was expensive only
because the predicate it re-applies was.

* refactor(control-plane): fold per-platform bot metadata onto the generic bag

Three items the migration squash carried over, closed together because they
share one migration.

**Bot demux identity was fenced twice.** `@@unique([slackAppId, teamId])` sat
beside the D6 successor `@@unique([platform, externalAppId, externalTenantId])`,
with a lookup for each and reads on the per-platform pair. Retiring the older
fence is a no-op rather than a semantic change: Slack is tenant-scoped, so its
projector mirrors `(slackAppId, teamId)` verbatim and writes NULLs rather than
the tenantless sentinel, which makes the generic unique enforce exactly what the
retired one did. `getBySlackAppTeam` had one production caller, now on
`getByExternalIdentity`.

is the console's deep-link to api.slack.com/apps/{id}, and `teamId` rides
`rc/bot-assign` to the relay, whose delivery-time demux reads it to pick the
strict or learnable arm. Their comments say that now instead of calling them
legacy, because that label is what invites a deletion that breaks admission.

**`discordAppId`/`feishuAppId`/`feishuRegion` were dual-written.**
`platformConfig` already existed as the declared fold target and the providers
already projected into it, while the named columns were written and read
alongside. Reads now come off the bag at the repository seam; the named fields
stay on `BotRecord`, because that is a domain type with named platform metadata,
not a column list. A platform now adds a key instead of a column.

**`SessionExternalAccessPolicy.migrationCursor` was dead.** The resume cursor
for the one-time external-access classification pass, never written since.

All of it ships as a FORWARD migration, not an edit to `00000000000000_init`:
that baseline has been released, so rewriting it would fail every deployed
database on its recorded checksum and silently skip the change besides.

The migration backfills before it removes, in that order:

1. `externalAppId`/`externalTenantId` from `(slackAppId, teamId)` for rows that

   NULL generic identity would leave them unfenced — and unfenced here means a

2. `platformConfig` from the three columns, via `jsonb_strip_nulls` so an absent
   value stays absent rather than becoming an explicit null.

Verified by applying the chain with `prisma migrate deploy` against a real
Postgres (the integration harness) and exercising the Feishu registration,
integrations and Slack platform-install suites against the result.

fix(cp): stop serving a platform audience nobody is syncing any more (#755)

* fix(cp): stop serving a platform audience nobody is syncing any more

Turning a provider's session sync off stops NEW sessions binding to
platform access, but the sessions already bound kept their external
classification and went on being served from that platform's audience.
Nothing maintains that audience once the switch is off, and every
session read went on paying the provider's round trips to evaluate it: a
disabled Feishu policy still cost a tenant-token call plus a member-list
page on each list, the slowest observed at 1.7s.

Off now means the synced history stops showing. The rows are untouched
and re-enabling brings them back.

The check goes on the scope arm only. A candidate classified while sync
is off keeps its org baseline but still records externalProvider, so the
direct arm cannot match it and the provider arm is the only thing making
it visible; gating that arm too would hide exactly the sessions that
"sync off, everyone can see" is supposed to expose.

With the scope arm closed, resolving a switched-off provider produces
grants no read can honour, so the resolver skips it. The in-memory mirror
already required a policy entry, so list and detail stay in agreement:
both hide the row rather than one hiding and the other 404ing.

Two settings strings were also wrong. Off was described as visible to
anyone who can view the agent, but the session list reads every org agent
regardless of Agent Team visibility, so it is the whole organization. And
the copy promised already-synced sessions keep following the platform,
which is what this change reverses — turning a restriction off showing
LESS is surprising enough that it has to be stated, not implied.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): re-decide session access the moment the sync switch moves

Review caught that the live SQL fence was only half the story. The
snapshot the in-memory predicate reads keys on org, viewer, identities
and scope revisions — not on whether the provider is syncing — and
nothing invalidates it on the write. So a snapshot taken while sync was
on kept authorizing detail, transcript, tool, workspace and SSE reads
for the rest of its lifetime, while list reads hid the same session
immediately through the new SQL arm. The two disagreed for up to a
minute, and the inverse stale-empty entry delayed restoration after a
re-enable.

Policy state and revision are now part of the snapshot key. Every toggle
bumps currentRev, so both directions re-decide on the next read with no
explicit invalidation to keep in sync with the write path. The policies
are read once per request and threaded into the sweep, so this costs no
extra round trip.

The sweep's closing fence also only re-checked scope revisions, so a
disable landing between its two policy reads kept grants the SQL had
already stopped honouring. It now filters the resolved grants by the
current non-disabled policies as well. That drop is the setting being
obeyed rather than a provider failing to answer, so `degraded` stays
measured against the revision check and no longer raises a spurious
"scopes stopped resolving".

Settings copy now says Everyone rather than "everyone in the
organization": docs/product-conventions.md reserves Organization for
management, membership and ownership, and uses Everyone as the audience
word for the internal org value.

fix(cp): name the Slack error behind a degraded session-access check (#759)

A degraded resolve hides sessions and tells the console "access checks
unavailable", and in production that line fires about once a minute with no
way to say why. Slack refuses over HTTP 200 with `ok: false`, so there is no
error span and no failed request to find; `body.error` is the only thing that
separates `missing_scope` from `ratelimited` from an outage, and every reader
here dropped it before anything could report it. The bot row persists no
granted OAuth scopes either, so the answer cannot be recovered from state.

Carry the reason with the verdict — including through the two caches, so a
resolve riding a cached `unknown` is not the one that cannot say why — and
aggregate it by code in the warn that already exists:

  reasons: { missing_scope: 12, ratelimited: 1 }

Slack's own code when it gave one, one of a fixed set of local labels when the
failure was on this side (no credential, an unreadable body, a timeout, a
non-200).

The privacy discipline of that log is unchanged, and is why the reason is a
code rather than a verdict per scope: counts per CAUSE, never per target. A
reason is admitted only if it matches Slack's lowercase error vocabulary —
every Slack object id is uppercase-prefixed — so an unexpected payload is
reported as its shape instead of echoed. No conversation, scope, user, or team
identifier and no bot token reaches the line.

Diagnosis only. The check still fails closed, and the TTLs, the
definitive-denial classification, and the app's OAuth scopes are untouched:
the real fix is a choice to make once the code is known.

fix(setup): delete the Logto Cloud demo connectors blocking managed social targets (#763)

Logto Cloud seeds new tenants with demo connectors parked on real social
targets such as `github` and `google`. Logto treats them as read-only
fixtures — `GET` and `PATCH /api/connectors/:id` both answer 404, the
listing hides their config — and refuses to create the real connector
while one holds the target (422 `connector.multiple_target_with_same_platform`).

Setup reconciliation picked the demo connector up as the connector for
that target, tried to patch it, and died on the 404, so sign-in setup
could never complete on a Cloud tenant.

A demo connector is now never a candidate to adopt: connector selection
skips it, and reconciliation deletes the one occupying a managed target
before creating the real connector. The replacement is resolved first, so
a missing credential still fails before anything is deleted. For a target
Setup cannot create (a manually configured OAuth 2.0 connector), the demo
connector is left alone and named in the error instead. The setup
inspection reports the pending removal alongside the missing connector.

feat(cp,web): name a short Slack app grant as an actionable access issue (#769)

A Slack session-access check that fails because the installed app's token
lacks a required scope reached the console as a bare `accessSyncDegraded`,
with no cause attached. The only copy that fit was "Session access checks
unavailable — affected sessions are hidden until access can be verified",
which reads as a Slack outage and suggests nothing to do. It is in fact a
configuration problem the organization can fix itself in about two minutes,
and the remedy already ships: the Slack app's refresh action on Integrations
syncs the manifest and names the missing scopes.

The gap was that the Slack plugin never populated `accessIssues` — only the
Feishu plugin did — even though it already classifies every failure into a
`DegradedReason` for its operator log. That classification now also feeds the
requester-facing half, in the same pass over the same verdicts.

Two decisions worth recording.

**A new `reason` variant rather than reusing `authorization`.** Today
`authorization` means the VIEWER's linked identity fell short; they fix it
themselves, on their own Profile, and no one else is affected. An installed
app that is short of a scope is a different actor, a different page and a
different fix — an administrator, once, for everyone. Overloading one label
would have forced the console to render one of the two remedies to the wrong
person. `app_authorization` costs the DTO enum plus its two mirrors, and both
directions degrade safely: a console that predates the variant falls through
to the generic notification, and a control plane that predates it simply
never sends one.

**The issue stays coarse — it does not name which install.** An organization
can run several Slack apps, so "reauthorize Slack" is admittedly only
somewhat more specific than today's copy. Naming one was rejected on
correctness rather than privacy: `accessIssues` only ever sees the apps behind
the sessions on the page being read, so a named app would be an INCOMPLETE
answer, and someone could fix the one named and stay degraded. The refresh
action on the app's own row is the authoritative per-app diagnosis — it asks
Slack which scopes the installation actually granted — so the notification's
job is to route there, not to duplicate it partially. `SessionAccessIssue`
therefore stays a cause and never a target: no channel, conversation, user,
team or credential enters it, and a test pins that.

Transient failures are untouched: rate limiting, outages, timeouts and every
transport failure stay `unavailable` and keep the generic copy. The point is
to separate "we cannot reach Slack" from "your app's permissions are short",
not to relabel everything. `ekm_access_denied` stays transient for the same
reason — reauthorizing the app cannot lift an enterprise key policy.

Fail-closed behaviour, the access-check TTLs, `failureDecision`'s
classification and install-time verification are all unchanged.

`?platform=<id>` is added to Integrations so the notification lands on the
right tab. `?bot=<id>`, which selects the tab AND expands the row, still wins
when both are present; an unknown platform is ignored.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(slack): fail an install whose workspace grant is short on bot scopes (#768)

Slack's initial authorization does not reliably apply every bot permission
an app's manifest declares, and reinstalling is what picks up the rest.
Nothing in the install flow noticed: the wizard reported success while the
bot token was short of SLACK_BOT_SCOPES, and the shortfall only surfaced
much later and looking unrelated — the session-access check calls Slack,
gets missing_scope, fails closed, and conversations disappear from the
console behind an "access checks unavailable" notice that names no cause.

Verify the granted scopes at the end of both install paths and refuse a
positively-short grant, naming the scopes that are absent so the operator
can reinstall while still in the flow:

- config-token / custom app: the finalize step already called auth.test and
  discarded the scopes it returns. It now checks them before
  installNewSlackBot, so a short grant leaves no bot and no integration,
  and answers 409 SLACK_MISSING_SCOPES with a missingScopes list.
- platform-published app: the OAuth callback verifies the workspace token
  it just obtained, as the last fence before the first write, and settles
  the pending row with missing_scopes plus the list (new column) — the
  poll is the console's only channel there, so the reason code alone could
  not say which permissions were withheld.

The scope diff itself moves next to SLACK_BOT_SCOPES as checkSlackBotScopes
and is now the single implementation behind both funnels and the Settings
refresh, which had the only prior copy. It is deliberately tri-state:
Slack does not always send the x-oauth-scopes header, and an unreported
grant stays "unknown" rather than "short", so an install is never refused
for a reason unrelated to permissions.

Console: the wizard's final step renders the failure as an actionable
panel — the missing scopes and a deep link to reinstall — instead of a
generic error line, and Connect stays live so reinstalling and retrying is
the whole loop. The two duplicated copies of the platform-install failure
map collapse into one module alongside the new outcome.

fix(web): stop offering a futile retry for a permanently unverifiable conversation (#771)

The conversation page refuses to render when the roster comes back empty with
`accessSyncDegraded` set. That much is right and stays: reporting "not found"
for something the console never got a verdict on would state an authorization
answer nobody gave.

The assumption underneath it was wrong. The page called every such cause
transient and offered "Try again" — true for an outage or a timeout, and false
for a short app grant, which is a permanent configuration state. The reader got
a blank page, a button that cannot ever succeed, and no hint that the fix is a
two-minute reauthorization two screens away.

It is worse than a dead end, because it does not even look like one. A resolved
verdict is cached — the plugin's allow lease plus the access snapshot — so any
successful resolution keeps the page working for a couple of minutes before it
flips back. The failure is permanent but is experienced as flakiness, which is
exactly the reading "Try again" invites.

So the cause now picks both the words and the way out, the same distinction
#769 made for the notification: a short grant says the Slack app needs
reauthorizing and links to the app's row on Integrations, while a genuinely
transient failure keeps the copy and the retry it always had. Whether a retry
could plausibly answer differently is a property of the cause, not a constant.

`accessIssues` was already on this response and already unwrapped into
`ConversationResolution` — the view simply never read it.

The decision lives in `unverifiedConversationNotice`, next to the notification
that answers the same question, so the two surfaces cannot drift on which
reasons an administrator can clear. Getting that wrong in either direction has
a real cost: calling a permanent state transient tells someone to wait for
something that will never happen, and calling a transient one permanent sends
them to reauthorize a healthy app.

A failed request keeps its own copy and its retry regardless of the issues on
the response — the console never reached the control plane, so it holds no
access verdict to interpret.

refactor(web): collapse the session rail's Related tree to three levels (#770)

conversation", "Delegated by", "Delegated to", "Delegations" — directly
above the rows it described. Each restated the indent beneath it, and
usually the title as well: a conversation is named after its first
message, typically the human @mentioning the very agent that then
delegates, so heading, agent row and open row all carried one name.

open row, the open row, whatever it woke. A cross-room parent and

never had — the §9.2 lift unions parents across every member without
recording which member each one woke, so hanging `wokenBy` under `parent`
asserted a relation nobody computed. `woke` and cross-room delegations
share level 2 for the same reason, and no fourth level is needed.

The words move into each row's hover tooltip — the same two words for the
navigation row and the attribution row — and stay as sr-only text
besides: a tooltip needs a pointer, and indentation is a visual relation,
so neither reaches a screen reader on its own.

`conversation` was only ever the flag that chose between heading wordings,
so it goes with them.

cross-room parents through the `siblingSessions` slot, whose meaning on a

fix(slack): designate one workspace-check credential per realm (#777)

The session-access plugin cached workspace-standing verdicts under
[realm, credentialRevision, principal] — no bot id, no org.
credentialRevision is a per-bot counter (in practice ~always 1), so
every bot in a workspace shared one entry per viewer despite holding
different grants: whichever credential resolved first decided everyone's
verdict for a TTL. A deterministic short grant (missing users:read)
therefore presented as sessions flickering in and out, and two orgs
sharing a workspace could serve each other's verdicts.

Keying per bot alone would break the other way — every short-granted bot
deterministically failing its own checks, losing the accidental fallback
the collision provided. Make "who answers" a choice instead:

- Same-team workspace standing (users.info) routes through one
  designated checker per (org, realm): capability first (must hold
  users:read per the persisted grant; an unobserved grant stays eligible
  but unproven), proven over unproven, prebuilt preferred, oldest
  createdAt tiebreak.
- Cross-team (Slack Connect) checks stay on the recording bot: an
  external user is visible only to a bot sharing a conversation, so the
  checker would answer user_not_found — a definitive deny.
- Conversation-scoped calls (conversations.info/members) stay on the
  recording bot, unchanged.
- The workspace cache key now names the ANSWERING bot and its credential
  revision, closing the org-fence hole as a side effect.
- No qualifying candidate degrades deterministically into the existing
  app_authorization access-issue path (new local reason
  bot_scope_missing) instead of spending a call whose answer is known.

Capability data: new Bot.grantedScopes column (empty = never observed,
never "granted nothing"), written wherever a flow already verifies the
token — config-token finalize, the platform OAuth callback (both arms),
manual POST /integrations validation, and the Settings refresh. Slack's
current reference does not document needed/provided fields on
missing_scope errors, so no check-time scope refresh is attempted.

test(cp): give integration tests headroom over the two 5s timing walls (#781)

`agent-placement-delegation.test.ts > revokes on a real setPlacement
change but not on setPlacement or movePlacement no-ops` failed
intermittently when the integration suite ran with the default 4 workers
under CPU contention (~5.9s runtime against ~0.6s healthy), while passing
reliably in isolation.

That test drives no concurrency and reads no clock, so every assertion is
deterministic given its fixtures — it can only fail on a timeout. Two 5s
budgets sat under it, neither reachable from the test:

- Vitest's default `testTimeout`. The integration project already raises
  `hookTimeout` to 120s but left this at the unit-test default, and it is
  the first wall a test hits: its clock starts before any repository call
  opens a transaction, so a stalled statement surfaced as an opaque
  "Test timed out in 5000ms" instead of the error that explains it.
- Prisma's interactive-transaction defaults (`timeout` 5s, `maxWait` 2s).
  `setPlacement`/`movePlacement`/`establish` open `$transaction`
  internally, so a test calling them on the root client cannot widen it.

This test is the file's canary because it is the only one driving four
separate repository transactions plus three reads sequentially on the
root client; the others wrap their work in an explicit
`{ timeout: 20_000 }` transaction. Its body measures 62-155ms even under
8 workers plus 8 busy loops, so the failure is not gradual slowdown — it
takes a multi-second stall (oversubscribed CI vCPUs, a container I/O
hiccup), which the 5s wall then turns into a failure.

Verified by stalling the agent row for 9s on a second connection: before,
the test died at exactly "Test timed out in 5000ms" with a 6890ms
reported runtime, reproducing the observed signature; raising only the
Vitest budget moved the failure to the internal transaction closing
itself; with both raised the verbatim test body survives and still
asserts the same revocation semantics.

Ordering is deliberate: 20s transactions under a 30s test budget means a
genuine lock cycle now fails with the real Prisma error rather than being
cut short. Tests that deliberately hold a row or advisory lock open pass
their own explicit `{ timeout: 20_000 }`, which still wins over the
client default, and none of them rely on the old 5s budget to break a
deadlock.

No test file changes: the assertions were never the fragile part.

docs(designs): session access for the infrequent visitor (#792)

The console's primary usage shape is occasional visits after external
activity, which inverts the assumption behind every access-check cache:
the typical request arrives with every lease expired. This design makes
the cold visit fast without loosening any per-principal lease.

Three pillars: identity warmed at first authenticated touch (overlap,
not staleness); resource shapes warmed by session activity, valid under
a verdict-split lease with touch-revalidation (a public verdict serves
up to 60 minutes but any read older than the 120 s recheck threshold
re-verifies in the background — viewed content self-limits to first
touch plus the per-principal verdict tail, and the long lease governs
only unviewed windows); and a unified cache policy: one serving
function serve(age, R, S) whose parameters express every strategy on
the path, two operator knobs, and named exceptions.

Reviewed by a five-lens adversarial panel; the revision demotes the
snapshot-ceiling raise from issue #775 to a product option (it is a
per-viewer authorization lease — raising it widens every per-principal
revocation window to ~17 minutes) and adds the putCache redesign the
verdict split forces (an allow anchored to hours-old shape evidence is
otherwise born expired).

feat(daemon): add a --cloud mode switch for cluster-backed runtimes (#821)

* feat(daemon): add a --cloud mode switch for cluster-backed runtimes

A cloud daemon supervises runtimes in cluster sandbox pods rather than as
local subprocesses. Every behavior that assumes "daemon and runtime share
one machine" now switches in one place instead of being re-decided per call
site: no runtime probe sweep or refresh, no SRT mechanism, no self-installing
bootstrap upgrade, and no sandbox capability advertised (the pod is the
isolation unit, and this shape runs with the cluster default runtimeClass).

The load-bearing part is runtime discovery. installedRuntimeCatalog answers
"nothing" in a daemon pod, because runtimes ship in the sandbox image rather
than next to the daemon, which would leave the daemon advertising and running
nothing at all. Under --cloud the runtime set therefore comes from a declared
table at <root>/cloud-runtimes.json (AGENTCONNECT_CLOUD_RUNTIMES overrides):
ids the image provides, optionally with its version pin and a model snapshot.
Commands and arguments still come from the resolved catalog, which is served
cache-first and so can be satisfied by an acp_registry.json baked into the
image.

Declared curated-source runtimes are dropped loudly rather than advertised:
curated admission refuses to launch without a fresh successful probe, and
--cloud does not probe, so they could never start. Declared model snapshots
report modelsSource 'cached' — no live probe confirmed them, so model gates
stay permissive. security.requireSandbox refuses startup with an explanation
instead of silently meaning something else.

Review of #821 found both rules stated but not actually enforced.

A declared runtime whose command is a package launcher (npx / uvx) was only
warned about and stayed advertised and launchable. Its artifact is fetched at
launch, so it is neither the image's build nor what the declared version pin
names, and the fetch fails outright on a restricted egress. Drop those entries
like curated ones; an image shipping such a runtime has to resolve it to a

refactor(daemon): put an ACP spawn driver seam under AcpHost (#822)

AcpHost owned both halves of starting a runtime: the ACP protocol on one side,
and child_process, PATH resolution, sandbox wrapping, process groups and signal
escalation on the other. Only the first half is about ACP; the second is about
where the runtime happens to live, which is exactly what changes when a runtime
moves into a sandbox pod.

Everything process- and filesystem-shaped moves behind SpawnDriver, with
LocalDriver preserving today's behavior verbatim: detached spawn, the pgid sweep
on exit, stdin EOF before SIGTERM, the SIGKILL escalation and its failsafe, and
the already-exited early return that a past regression hung on. AcpHost keeps
what only it can know — env assembly, account-app isolation, argv composition —
and consumes a byte-stream pair plus a lifecycle handle.

Two resolutions move down deliberately rather than staying put: the command
lookup and the CLAUDE_CODE_EXECUTABLE fallback. Both search a filesystem, and
only the driver knows which filesystem the runtime will see, so AcpHost states
the policy ("this runtime wants CLAUDE_CODE_EXECUTABLE from `claude`") and the
driver performs the lookup where it applies.

No behavior change and no caller change: the four other AcpHost construction
sites (chat CLI, runtime prober, model enumerator, evaluation runner) pass
options and never touched the process, so they keep working through the default
LocalDriver. AcpSandboxLaunch moves next to the driver that consumes it and is
re-exported from acp-host, where callers have always imported it.

The new test drives a full ACP turn — initialize, session/new, prompt, streamed
update, stop — against an in-memory agent with no process anywhere, which is the
shape a cluster driver will present. One existing test reached into AcpHost's
private child handle to simulate a terminal Ctrl-C; it now reaches through the
driver's launched target, asserting the same behavior.

feat(daemon): add a thin Kubernetes client for the sandbox API (#823)

* feat(daemon): add a thin Kubernetes client for the sandbox API

The agent-sandbox project ships Go and Python SDKs, and this daemon is
TypeScript — but its CRDs are ordinary REST endpoints, so no TS SDK costs us
nothing. This adds only what the daemon needs, with no new npm dependency.

Three parts. `config.ts` discovers in-cluster access and, importantly, reads the
bearer token per request rather than once: the kubelet rotates the projected
token in place, so a boot-time capture expires under a long-lived daemon. It
fails with the missing piece named rather than returning a half-configured
client.

`http.ts` uses node:http(s) rather than fetch. The API server presents its own
CA, and pinning that CA is a plain per-request option here while fetch would
need an undici dispatcher we do not depend on; it also hands us the raw stream a
watch needs. Rejections become a K8sApiError carrying status and Status.reason,
so callers branch on isConflict / isExpired / isAlreadyExists instead of
matching message text.

`watch.ts` is the part that is genuinely easy to get wrong. The initial LIST
establishes both the snapshot and the resourceVersion the watch resumes from, so
nothing between them is lost; allowWatchBookmarks keeps an idle watch's resume
point fresh enough to reuse; and a 410 / Expired — whether reported as a status
or in-band as an ERROR event — is answered by re-LISTing rather than failing,
which is exactly why `list` is a required verb in this client's RBAC. A cleanly
closed stream is the server-side timeout and reconnects without backoff; a
failed connection backs off through the shared Backoff policy, and the loop
takes an injected Clock so tests drive it without real timers.

`sandbox-api.ts` exposes one method per granted verb and nothing more: the type
surface mirrors the Role, since a method the Role does not authorize could only
fail at runtime. Claim creation treats AlreadyExists as success and deletion
treats NotFound as success, because both are keyed on the agent id and must
converge on retry. operatingMode writes are JSON Patch with a `test` guard on
the value we observed, so a wake racing a suspend decision fails as a conflict
instead of silently overriding the newer one. The Pod API is absent by design —
pods are the vendor controller's to materialize.

* fix(daemon): correct the sandbox wire types, force the patch guard, stop leaking abort listeners

Review of #823 found three real defects.

The declared v1beta1 response shapes were invented rather than checked. A
SandboxClaim's status names the bound Sandbox and carries no uid of its own, so
`status.sandbox.uid` would have read undefined forever — and since the HTTP layer
only casts parsed JSON, nothing would have caught it. The Sandbox UID the spawn
record keys on comes from the object's own `metadata.uid`, which now has a test.
`podIPs` is dropped from both types instead of being restated: the shim handshake
does not trust a source IP, so nothing needs the field, and an unverified shape
is worse than an absent one.

setOperatingMode's guard was optional, which contradicts the invariant it exists
for — and the old test enshrined the unguarded path. The observed mode is now a
required argument and the `test` op is always emitted, so a wake racing a suspend
decision is a conflict rather than a clobber. The documented `expected: null`
case is gone: RFC 6902 `test` does not match a missing member and `replace`
requires the target to exist, and v1beta1 defaults the field to Running anyway,
so an observed value always exists.

The backoff delay registered an abort listener that was only removed if abort
actually fired, so every retry whose timer won left one behind — unbounded growth
on one long-lived signal during an API-server outage. It now follows the
repository's cleanup pattern (named handler, removed on both paths, pre-abort
check that closes the registration race), with a test that advances a fake clock
through three failed lists and asserts the listener count stays at zero.

Also condensed the multiline comment blocks in these files to single lines, per
the repository comment style.

* fix(daemon): classify the operating-mode guard failure from the status Kubernetes really returns

The guard was mandatory but its failure was mislabelled. The API server wraps
every rejected JSON Patch — a failed `test` included — as 422 Invalid and never
409, so `isConflict` was false in exactly the wake/suspend race the guard exists
for, and the fixture hid that by synthesizing a 409 nobody sends.

Classification cannot key on the message either: the text for a failed `test`
comes from the patch library and changes between versions. So `setOperatingMode`
confirms by state — on a 422 it re-reads the Sandbox, and only when the current
mode differs from the observed one does it raise the typed
`OperatingModeConflictError` carrying both values. An unrelated 422 (a schema
rejection, say) surfaces as itself, and a failed confirming read leaves the
original error intact rather than guessing.

Tests now use the real 422/Invalid Status body, and cover all three paths: the
genuine race, an unrelated 422 that must not be dressed up as a conflict, and an
unavailable confirming read.

Refs #811

* fix(daemon): stop inferring why a guarded operating-mode write was rejected

Confirming the guard failure with a follow-up read was itself a race, in both
directions. If another actor set Running (correctly failing the test) and then
set it back to Suspended before the read, the code saw the observed value and
downgraded a real conflict to a generic error — losing the retry signal in
exactly the wake/suspend race the guard exists for. The inverse sequence would
label an unrelated 422 a conflict.

A later snapshot is not evidence about a past failure, so nothing here tries to
be. The 422 becomes OperatingModeRejectedError, carrying what we observed and
what we asked for, and explicitly not claiming what the intervening state was:
the decision behind the write is stale, so the caller re-reads, re-decides, and
writes again. Its doc states the obligation that comes with an unclaimed cause —
callers must bound retries, since a permanently invalid patch would otherwise
loop forever. Errors that are not patch rejections (an admission denial, say)
pass through untouched.

A resourceVersion precondition yielding a structured 409 would also remove the
inference, but this environment cannot verify that Kubernetes returns 409 for
that write shape, and guessing wrong there would silently disable the guard
altogether — strictly worse than an honest unclaimed rejection. Worth revisiting
once #816 can exercise it against a real API server.

Tests cover the change-away-and-back sequence that defeats confirm-by-read, and
a non-patch rejection passing through.

feat(daemon): let Kubernetes supervise restart while refusing self-upgrade (#825)

* feat(daemon): let Kubernetes supervise restart while refusing self-upgrade

Kubernetes stands in for launchd/systemd and for the CLI's version store at
once, but it supervises those two roles asymmetrically, and admitFleetExit gated
both on the same "is the supervisor cli or service" check. A cloud daemon would
therefore have refused the one operation Kubernetes genuinely performs.

Restart is supported: the daemon drains and exits with the reserved code, and
restartPolicy: Always brings the container back in place, in the same pod — the
same shape as a systemd process restart, with re-register plus an incremented
epoch still the completion signal. AGENTCONNECT_SUPERVISOR gains `k8s` as a
shared protocol constant to declare it.

Upgrade is refused with a reason that says the version is the image. The
daemon-side capability is already off in cloud mode, so this is the belt to that
braces — but the message matters: a cli-entry can exist on the root volume, and
"no supervisor" would then send an operator looking in the wrong place.

A declared supervisor is still required. `--cloud` alone does not admit a
restart, because exiting with nothing to bring the process back leaves the daemon
down; the launcher has to say `k8s`.

Draining needs no new code — the existing SIGTERM path gates new turns, awaits
in-flight ones to shutdownDrainMs, and cancels stragglers, which is what both a
preStop hook and a SIGTERM reach. What it needs is stating: a pod's
terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed that deadline or the kubelet SIGKILLs
mid-drain, and since the daemon has no pod read access it cannot check, so it
logs the deadline it will use and leaves the alignment to the deployment.

Section 2.6 of the design records the asymmetry, the kubelet's restart backoff
(which stretches completion versus systemd and should shape control-plane
timeouts), and the grace-period requirement.

* fix(daemon): refuse a cloud upgrade on the mode, not on the supervisor marker

The previous check keyed the upgrade refusal on the marker being exactly `k8s`,
which left the state it was meant to close still open: with --cloud, an inherited
AGENTCONNECT_SUPERVISOR=service and a stale but valid cli-entry on the root

Upgrade is now refused whenever cloud mode is on, before the marker is consulted

supervises the process can bring it back, so only self-install is gated on the

feat(daemon): add the in-sandbox shim and its bind-on-callback handshake (#826)

* feat(daemon): add the in-sandbox shim and its bind-on-callback handshake

The shim is the arm inside a runtime sandbox that performs what the daemon used
to do by sharing a filesystem and a set of unix sockets. It holds no policy; the
channels themselves (materialization, exec, tunnels) land next, on top of this.

The shim dials out and the daemon listens, so the sandbox needs zero inbound —
an empty ingress list and no per-sandbox Service. The reverse would need a
Service per sandbox, an ingress allowance and a readiness probe, all for nothing.

Binding is proved by the pod's own audience-restricted, permissionless projected
ServiceAccount token, reviewed through TokenReview and mapped to a spawn record.
Two shortcuts are rejected in code comments so they are not reinvented: a
bootstrap token in the SandboxClaim (claim env bypasses warm-pool adoption and
does not propagate to a rebuilt pod, so resume would deadlock on an exhausted
token), and reverse-looking the source IP (pod IPs are reusable and the status
mirroring them is asynchronous, so a sibling sandbox could claim a victim's
channel inside the stale window). The source address is a log hint only.

All five invariants are enforced through ONE predicate, authorize(): credential
compared in constant time, expiry, generation, capability. There is no other way
to turn a credential into a binding, so a channel added later cannot skip a
check. This is deliberate — my recent defects have clustered exactly where a rule
had more than one enforcement point and they disagreed.

The shim re-checks the credential, generation and grant before serving rather
than trusting the daemon already did, and rejections carry one coarse reason with
no pod, token or agent named, so the endpoint cannot be probed for identities.

Packaging matters as much as the protocol: adding the shim as another entry of
the daemon bundle made rolldown share chunks, which would have meant copying the
daemon's whole graph — CP client, platform SDKs, credential paths — into the
half-trusted image. It is a SEPARATE tsdown build with its own graph, and the
self-containment guard now fails the build if it imports anything but node:
builtins. One 258 KB file goes in the image.

docs/designs/cluster-spawn-and-shim.md records the seam, the rejected
alternatives and the invariants, and states plainly that this stage has no
hardened isolation and keeps a provider key inside the sandbox.

* fix(daemon): supersede a shim binding by launch identity and keep the channel alive

Two lifecycle defects in the handshake, both of which broke behaviour this PR
claims.

Supersession was keyed on pod UID, but a rescheduled or resumed pod arrives with
a NEW UID — so binding generation 4 for the same agent left generation 3's
credential live and authorized. That is exactly the replay the fence exists to
stop, and it applied to eviction and reschedule, the cases the fence was written
for. Supersession is now by launch identity (agent + sandbox), the superseded
channels are closed rather than left in connectionsFor(), and the test uses a
different pod UID for the replacement, which is what a reschedule actually
produces. The old test reused one UID and so never exercised any of this.

The client had no lifecycle after its first bind: start() resolved and nothing
remained, so a later socket close left the executable running and permanently
detached, and the 10-minute credential expired under a perfectly healthy pod —
a channel that works for ten minutes and then silently never again.
expiresInSeconds was accepted and ignored. start() now resolves on first

and the credential is renewed by re-handshaking at half its lifetime. The
listener closes the channel at expiry as the backstop, so a peer cannot sit on a
dead credential either.

Three hardening items from the same review: the wire rejection is now identical
for every pre-binding failure (the previous distinct reasons let a caller tell
"token not accepted" from "pod not recognized" and probe for launched pods,
contradicting the anti-probing claim); a hello is single-flight while TokenReview
is in flight, so a second one cannot bind twice; and the endpoint uses the
repository's 256 KiB MAX_FRAME_BYTES cap instead of the ws default.

* fix(daemon): make shim binding generation-monotonic and scope channel callbacks

Three ordering races, all in the overlap between one pod's launch ending and the
next one's starting — which is the only time these paths run.

generation-3 pod binding AFTER generation 4 — a terminating pod reconnecting, or
simply a slower TokenReview — deleted 4 and reinstalled 3 as the authorized
binding. Replacement is now monotonic: bind() refuses a generation that is not
newer, mutating nothing, and the listener answers with its uniform rejection.

A TokenReview can also finish after its socket has closed. The continuation then
issued a credential, could supersede a live binding, and published a connection
for a socket already gone. bindFrom now checks liveness immediately before the
registry mutation — its only mutation — and reports an abandoned handshake
instead.

The client's close callback mutated shared channel state without checking which
transport closed, so a delayed close from a transport being renewed tore down the
healthy replacement that had already bound. Every transport callback is now scoped
to its own channel and returns early when it is no longer the one in service.

Writing that third test exposed a fourth defect of the same kind: a close
arriving between binding and the loop arming its channel-end callback was
dropped, and the channel then parked forever on a transport that was already
gone. The channel record now remembers a close that arrived early, and the wait
observes it instead of hanging.

Also addressed the non-blocking finding: a post-bind drop went through no
backoff despite the comments saying so. The channel now ends with a reason —

* feat(daemon): add the cluster spawn driver for per-agent sandbox runtimes

The driver the previous pieces were built for: an agent's ACP runtime runs in its
own Sandbox pod, and AcpHost still sees a byte-stream pair.

Lifecycle stays local on purpose — claim creation, wake, suspend and teardown are
all decided here, so a control-plane outage cannot stop an existing agent from
starting or stopping its runtime. Claims are named from the agent id so a retry
after a partial reconcile converges, and carry only the pool reference and org
and agent labels: a claim with env or volumeClaimTemplates bypasses warm-pool
adoption, and pool pods are stamped before any user exists, so identity travels
over the shim handshake instead. The Sandbox UID comes from the object's own
metadata, since the claim status carries only a name.

Mode writes re-read and re-decide when the guarded write is rejected, with a
bounded budget: the rejection deliberately does not claim what the intervening
state was, so looking again is the only correct response, and a permanently
invalid patch must not spin forever. A pending drain annotation holds the
instance down — one arriving message would otherwise revive the image a rollout
is replacing — and generations increment per launch so a departed incarnation
cannot act.

The ACP stream is its own channel rather than a reuse of exec: framing is open,
chunks, close, because ACP is already a complete protocol and reinterpreting it
in the channel would add a second place for it to go wrong.

MEASURED, not assumed. test/k8s-real-apiserver.test.ts runs the client against a
real k3s API server under the RBAC the design specifies, and settles the two
questions #823 had to ship on faith: a failed JSON Patch `test` returns 422
Invalid and never 409, so the original isConflict would not have fired in the
race it guarded; and a stale metadata.resourceVersion precondition does return a
structured 409. The second is recorded in the client rather than adopted — it
guards the whole object, so any unrelated status write by the vendor controller
would conflict, while the field-scoped test only conflicts when the mode moved.
It also confirms an audience-restricted token is refused for the wrong audience,
which is the entire basis of the handshake.

The suite is gated behind AC_K8S_E2E=1 (it needs Docker and a k3s image) and
skips cleanly otherwise. It exists because every defect in this workstream's
review history reached me through a fake I wrote from the same assumption as the
code; a fake cannot tell me what Kubernetes returns.

Refs #816

* fix(daemon): make the cluster ACP transport actually work, and order its lifecycle

The submitted driver could not carry a turn. It sent open/chunk/close through the
one-request/one-response exec channel, so runtime stdout and exit had no path back
and AcpHost.start() would have hung forever — while the ACP schemas I had written
sat unused. Every unit test passed, because they all checked the parts I had a
model for (claim shape, generations, drain, retry budget) and none ran a turn.

The stream is now a real protocol. A `shim/event` frame carries recurring events
keyed by the request that opened the stream, because one-shot correlation cannot
express continuous stdout plus a terminal exit. The shim serves the ACP capability
through a runner that spawns the runtime, relays stdio, sweeps the process group
and escalates past a deadline like the local driver does. Writes await their
acknowledgement, so a runtime that is not draining applies backpressure instead of
letting the daemon queue without bound.

A runtime no longer pins one physical connection. ShimSession is a logical channel
that re-attaches when the same launch rebinds — the shim renews its credential at
half TTL by dialing a replacement, and the listener closes the superseded socket,
so anything holding one connection for a runtime's lifetime was stranded on the
first ordinary renewal. A different generation ends the session instead, and a lost
session reports terminal exit rather than leaving AcpHost waiting on a stream that
can never produce another byte. Event subscriptions are removable, so a restart
does not accumulate listeners.

Resume now precedes the readiness wait. Suspension deletes the pod, so requiring
Ready before anything asked for Running meant a restarted daemon could never
recover a suspended claim: the wait blocked the only call that could end it.

Mode transitions are serialized per agent. A guarded write protects competing
writes but cannot protect a decision that performs NO write — a later wake could
observe Running and return while an earlier suspend patch was still in flight, and
the older write would land last and reverse the newer decision.

Also: launching while a drain request is pending now fails fast with the reason
instead of waiting out the readiness deadline against a sandbox held down on
purpose.

test/cluster-acp-e2e.test.ts runs a real turn end to end — driver, listener, shim,
a real runtime process — and it immediately found two things the units could not:
the `acp` capability was missing from RUNTIME_GRANTS so the shim refused every
open, and the listener forwarded only response frames, silently dropping every
event. The ordering regression was verified by removing the serialization and
confirming it fails.

Refs #816

* fix(daemon): emit ACP events through the current channel, not the one that opened it

The shim's event sink captured the transport that handled `open`. Renewal closes
that socket at half TTL before dialing a replacement, so every later byte of
runtime stdout — and the exit event — went into a closed WebSocket even after the
daemon reattached its session. Events now go through whichever transport is bound.

Bytes cannot simply be dropped across the handoff: losing an ACP fragment corrupts
the stream. Events produced while no channel is attached wait in a bounded buffer
and flush, oldest first, on the next bind. Overflow fails the stream loudly with a
terminal exit rather than silently truncating it, because a corrupted ACP stream is
worse than a reported failure.

The previous test named "survives a credential renewal" performed one prompt and
never renewed, so the case it was named for never occurred in it — the same mistake
as the pod-uid fixture in #826. It now advances the shim's clock to the half-TTL
deadline, waits for the replacement bind, and prompts the SAME runtime and ACP
session afterwards. Verified by reverting the sink to the captured transport: the
test fails, and passes again with the fix.

Two of the non-blocking findings are real functional gaps, so they are fixed here
rather than deferred. The production shim entry never supplied resolveCommand, so
executable hints — CLAUDE_CODE_EXECUTABLE among them — and path-qualified registry
commands would never have resolved inside a sandbox; it now uses a small local PATH
resolver, written rather than imported because the daemon's resolver drags the
runtime registry behind it and the shim ships as one self-contained file. And a
runtime's natural exit now removes its runner from the stream map instead of
accumulating one per crash.

Remaining follow-ups stay for the integration work: sandbox-to-daemon backpressure
in the event direction, disposing daemon-side sessions when a runtime ends, and
queueing a turn across a drain instead of failing it fast.

feat(daemon): make an upstream credential rejection explainable in direct-connect (#829)

* feat(daemon): make an upstream credential rejection explainable in direct-connect

In this stage the runtime reaches its provider itself, so credentials travel the
paths they always did — runtime env, agent secrets, the shared credential profile —
and only their delivery moves onto the shim channel. What was missing is what a
user sees when the credential is wrong.

turnFailureCode classified on message text only, and failureSignals collects
strings, so a numeric `status: 401` was skipped entirely. A provider reached
directly answers with a status rather than prose, and the wording varies by
provider and SDK version, so an expired key surfaced as a bare `turn_failed` —
true and useless. HTTP 401 and 403 now classify as provider_auth_required,
including when nested under error/data/cause/response.

429 is deliberately NOT mapped to quota exhaustion. Rate limiting is transient, and
telling someone their plan ran out when it did not is worse than a generic failure;
a 429 whose message really does say the quota is gone still classifies as quota,
because that is the message doing the work rather than the status. JSON-RPC codes
are excluded from status matching, so -32603 cannot be read as an HTTP status.

The direct-connect invariant is asserted the strong way: the entire serialized
claim must contain no credential material, rather than a specific field being
checked empty. A claim carrying env bypasses warm-pool adoption, and a pool pod is
stamped from the template before any user exists, so a template env value would be
visible to whoever is adopted next.

Verified by removing the status classification and confirming the 401 test fails.

Refs #817

* fix(daemon): classify provider auth failures by provider signal, not HTTP status

Matching a nested numeric 401/403 was the wrong idea, and wrong in a way worth
recording: K8sApiError — introduced in this same workstream — carries a numeric
`status`, GithubHttpError does too, and turnFailureCode sees failures from far
beyond the model call. A Kubernetes RBAC denial on a SandboxClaim would therefore
have told the user their provider credentials needed attention. A status belongs to
whichever layer produced it, so it is not evidence about the provider.

The signal that does identify a provider is the one providers send: a typed code.
Anthropic answers `type: "authentication_error"` with `invalid x-api-key`; OpenAI
answers `code: "invalid_api_key"` with `Incorrect API key provided`. Those cannot
arrive from an unrelated layer, so provenance comes free. failureSignals already
collected them — the classifier simply was not looking.

The status traversal is gone rather than guarded, which also resolves the unguarded
`Reflect.get` reads: there is nothing left to throw from. The hostile-getter case is
covered anyway, because the classifier runs while handling someone else's failure
and must never replace it with one of its own.

The claim test was vacuous as written — SECRET was never given to the driver, so its
absence proved nothing. It now launches with a real key in the runtime env, so the
assertion is about a value that was actually present to leak.

Both regressions were verified against the defect: with the status matching
reinstated, the non-provider 403 case and the hostile-getter case fail; both pass
with this change.

* fix(daemon): recognise Gemini's auth envelope and stop trusting our own reason strings

* fix(daemon): parse every porcelain-v2 record type, and pass a real env in the contract test

Two failures, and the second is one I reported as passing.

The daemon declares a closed set of git subcommands, but a declaration on the

* fix(daemon): match execution options by prefix and bound the ENCODED result

The reviewer was right on both and my counter-probe was wrong. I tested `-c` in
the GLOBAL position, where git rejects the attached form, and concluded the
attached spellings were not holes. Wrong position: `git clone -c` is clone's OWN
option, and clone accepts every spelling. Measured against git 2.43:

    git clone -ccore.k=v SRC DST                        -> accepted
    git clone --config=core.k=v SRC DST                 -> accepted
    git clone -cprotocol.ext.allow=always ext::HELPER    -> HELPER ran
    git clone -u<program> SRC DST                        -> program ran

So the guard now matches option PREFIXES rather than exact tokens, which is the
only shape that covers separated, attached, and long-with-equals at once. `-c`
and `--config` are refused in every spelling; no argv the daemon sends starts
with either, and `--count` is unaffected since `/^-c/` needs `c` second.

The frame guard was also checking the wrong quantity. JSON encoding is not
size-preserving: `status -z` emits filenames verbatim and each control byte
becomes a six-byte escape. Reproduced the reviewer's case exactly —

    raw stdout:  51,682 bytes   (under the 64 KiB raw cap)
    encoded:    302,976 bytes   (over the 256 KiB frame cap)

— so the raw cap did not see it and the transport dropped the frame. The
authoritative bound is now the serialized size with envelope headroom; the raw
cap stays as a cheap first bound.

Both regression cases are in the suite, and both were confirmed load-bearing by
reverting the guard to exactly the shape the review rejected and watching its own
test fail.

Also states a boundary the argv work does not close: env is a trusted input on
this channel. GIT_SSH_COMMAND, or GIT_CONFIG_COUNT pairs naming an executable
setting, still reach execution — and cannot merely be filtered, because those are
the same mechanisms that deliver credential helpers and pin hooksPath. Making env
untrusted means moving that policy into the shim, which is a design change.

feat(daemon): propagate cancellation into the sandbox and key the clone lock by filesystem (#836)

* feat(daemon): propagate cancellation into the sandbox and key the clone lock by filesystem

The last two items of #815.

**Cancellation.** A daemon-side abort only unblocked this side's wait; the git in
the sandbox kept running. That is the exact failure the local runner's
abort-kills-the-child behaviour exists to prevent — an abandoned git keeps
index.lock and wedges the next session's pull — so the 4.5s pull and 15s
review-fetch budgets were budgets in name only on the cluster path.

Adds a `shim/cancel` frame, fenced with credential and generation like every other
post-binding frame, so a replayed cancel from a previous incarnation cannot kill
live work. The shim tracks in-flight non-ACP work per request id and aborts it;
the exec handler passes the signal to the child and classifies `ABORT_ERR`, which
carries neither `killed` nor a signal and would otherwise read as a spawn failure.
A request timeout now sends the cancel too: giving up locally while the child runs
is the same bug in a different coat.

`ShimRequester.request` takes an options object rather than a positional timeout.
Note that `tsconfig` only type-checks `src`, so the one stale call site in a test
surfaced as a failing test rather than a type error.

**Clone lock.** It was keyed on the textual cwd. For local agents that is the
intent — one path is one checkout, and coalescing is why the lock exists. For
cluster agents the same path is a different filesystem per agent, so coalescing
would hand one agent the other's clone and look like success. The key now includes
the agent id exactly when a resolver claims that agent; local sharing is
unchanged, which the existing single-flight test still proves.

Every guard here was confirmed load-bearing by reverting it. That mattered twice:
the first cancellation test searched for the child by its FIFO path, which lives
in the child's ENV and not its argv, so `pgrep` never found it and one test passed
having observed nothing; and the fencing test first sent a cancel for an invented
request id, which misses the lookup whether or not the fencing exists. Both now
observe a real child by a unique argv marker and cancel the real in-flight id.

* fix(deploy): make the manifests actually start a daemon, and let the probe run

Five real problems, and the first one meant the feature this PR is about had
never executed.

**The probe never ran.** It was kicked off when the execution plane came up, but
it projects onto the resolved runtime catalog, which `start()` assembles ~150
lines later — so it returned immediately, every time. A probe that never runs and
a daemon that advertises nothing look identical from outside. It now starts right
after the catalog exists.

running the example through `ConfigSchema` rather than by reading it.

owner-only permissions on a secret-bearing config and REPAIRS a looser mode; a
Secret volume is read-only, so that repair throws and the daemon refuses to
start. A mode it would accept without repairing (0400) is unreadable, because

volume at 0600 — which keeps the key out of the argument list, the reason it was
not a flag in the first place.

the template by default and an empty egress list is default-DENY, which blocks
the one direction this whole design depends on. Stated explicitly and narrowly:
the daemon's port, DNS, and 443 for direct provider egress — the rule an egress
proxy would later replace. Ingress stays empty; the daemon never dials in.

The direct-connect grant test — "exactly the channels it needs and nothing else"

holding exec, materialize and tunnel. And carries the probed version into the
reported profile, so the image's answer is what reaches the Control Plane.

fix(daemon): send the ACP cwd in the pod's coordinates, not the daemon's (#853)

* fix(daemon): send the ACP cwd in the pod's coordinates, not the daemon's

A cluster agent's `session/new` carried `agent.workspace.path` —
`/var/lib/agentconnect/agents/<id>/workspace`, a path on the DAEMON's
filesystem. The runtime lives in a sandbox pod that mounts its volume at
`/agent`, so the cwd named a directory existing on no machine the runtime can
see. There was no k8s path translation anywhere: grep found the shim's `/agent`
default and nothing at all on the daemon side.

The root cause is that `agent.workspace.path` had quietly taken on two jobs —
"where this lives on the daemon" and "where the runtime sees it" — which are the
same string locally and different machines in the cluster. Fixing HOME (8469aac0)
only covered the half a pod can answer for itself; this is the other half.

The pod is the only party that knows its own mount, so it says so: the shim
reports `workspaceRoot` in its hello, the listener sanitizes it (absolute,
normalized, never `/`), and the driver keeps it per agent across renewals. Taking
it from the pod rather than restating the image layout in daemon config keeps one
source of truth — the image can move its mount without a daemon release. It is
only ever echoed back into the same pod, so a lying shim gains nothing daemon-side.

On the daemon, `runAgentWorkspacePreparation` now resolves cluster agents through
`clusterWorkspaceCwd()` and runs NONE of the local preparation: its mkdir,
`existsSync(.git)` and skills installation all land on this daemon's disk and
describe a filesystem the runtime never reads. `resolvePreparedWorkspace` gets the
same treatment — it is the WARM-session path, and leaving it local would have left
every resumed session on the old daemon path with the cold path fixed. Prefetch
becomes a no-op in `--k8s` for the same reason: it would clone onto the wrong disk.

git-repo workspaces and session isolation now REFUSE loudly instead of half-working.
Both still mix coordinates — the clone target is passed as argv (never checked
against the shim's `/agent` fence), and every local `existsSync`/`realpathSync`
reads the wrong disk, so a git-repo cluster agent would re-clone every session and
fail inside the sandbox. A clear error beats a mystery one from git in the pod; the
remaining migration is the rest of #815.

A legacy shim that reports nothing falls back to `/agent`, which is what every
image with this layout ever mounted — so the fix lands without waiting on a
rollout, and new images stop hardcoding it.

feat(tasks): show a session's background tasks in the dock (#854)

* feat(tasks): show a session's background tasks in the dock

The dock's fifth tab (webchat-side-panels.md §3.5). `task/list` reads one ACP
session's background tasks live from the owning daemon's in-memory lease; the CP
proxies one snapshot and persists none of it, since descriptions are
model-authored text.

Scoped per (agent, ACP session) because the lease already is — ACP session ids
are runtime-local, so `sessionId` is required rather than optional and there is
no per-agent aggregate to answer with but a boolean. Unlike the workspace reads
it is NOT gated on workspace isolation: a lease is not a checkout, and a
session's background tasks exist whatever it runs in.

The daemon's lease gains a `startedAt` and a bounded settled-task history, kept
in a separate `settled` array so no reclaim decision can see it — a task
retained for the panel must not keep its session open or spend the
background-task wake budget (background-task-aware-reclaim.md).

What the design asked for and the runtime cannot supply is absent rather than
faked, measured against the shipped daemon and @agentclientprotocol/sdk 1.3.0:

- No `task/cancel`, frame or control. `CancelNotification` carries only
  `{ sessionId }` and cancels a whole prompt turn; there is no ext-request sender
  for a `_claude/*` kill-by-id; the daemon advertises no terminal capability, so
  the agent owns its shells; and the only hard stop kills the agent's shared
  adapter and every session on it. Worse, the turn-scoped interrupt is a no-op
  exactly when the panel matters, because a background task outlives its turn.
  A per-row control could therefore only cancel unrelated work or report a stop
  it did not perform. The escape hatch is the composer's own stop.
- No `queued` state: the lifecycle feed's only start edge is `task_started`.
- No progress bar and no step line: nothing upstream reports either.

`tracked:false` distinguishes "this runtime reports no task lifecycle" from
"this session has no background tasks" — a non-Claude runtime, an adapter
without the lifecycle extension, and a session that has emitted nothing yet all
have no lease, and the panel says so rather than drawing an empty list.
`subagent` rows are carried on the wire and marked at render rather than
filtered, because the same records fence host reclaim: hiding them at the source
would show "no tasks" beside a host refusing to be reclaimed.

snapshot had nothing running installed no interval at all. What the panel

feat(daemon): serve the daemon's unix sockets inside a sandbox pod (#855)

* feat(daemon): serve the daemon's unix sockets inside a sandbox pod

The `tunnel` capability was declared in the shim protocol, granted in
RUNTIME_GRANTS, and implemented by neither side: the exec handler answered
`capability tunnel is not served by this handler` and no daemon call site ever
sent a tunnel frame. So `/run/agentconnect/gitcred.sock` never existed in a pod
and a GitHub-App workspace's git had no credential helper to reach — the gap
deploy/k8s/README.md records.

The direction is what shapes this. A tunnel exists because a process INSIDE the
pod wants a daemon-side server, while shim requests only ever flow daemon →
shim. So the pod announces each connection as a `connect` event on a stream id
it mints, and the daemon answers by dialling its own socket; bytes then travel
as events one way and `data` requests the other. Listeners belong to the POD
rather than the channel, because the shim re-dials at half the credential TTL
and a socket torn down per renewal would break any client mid-request.

Two fields of the declared-but-unused protocol go away. `gh-token` was a second
in-pod path onto one daemon server (the gh token helper shares gitcred.sock), and
`socketPath` let the daemon name a path that would have to be validated against
SANDBOX_TUNNEL_PATHS on arrival anyway — carrying no information while widening
what a compromised daemon could ask the shim to create.

Both sides bound and re-check independently, in the exec-handler tradition: the
sandbox mints stream ids, so the daemon re-checks the authorization, the
duplicate id and the stream ceiling the shim already enforces.

Policy stays in the daemon (`tunnelsFor`/`tunnelSocketPath`): gitcred for an
agent whose workspace authenticates through a GitHub App, and nothing else. MCP
is deliberately unwired — the in-pod bridge that would dial it is not in the
image, so a listener would be a socket nobody can use.

The image gains /run/agentconnect owned by 10001: /run is root-owned and the
shim is not root, so without it the bind fails and reads as a credential problem
rather than a permission one.

What this does NOT finish: nothing in the pod dials the socket yet. The helper
config still points at a daemon-local path (next) and the helper executable is
not in the image (after that).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): end a tunnel stream whose frame was in flight across a rebind

Review found a real asymmetry. The pod→daemon direction survives a credential
renewal: the shim buffers events with no transport and flushes them on the next
bind. The daemon→pod direction did not. `ShimSession.attach` aborts the requests
on the socket it replaces, and `send` merely logged the rejection while the
proxy entry and the pod-side unix connection stayed open — so a git-credential
reply landing in that window vanished and git waited out the five-minute idle
timer.

Retrying is not available. A rejection means either the frame never left or it
landed and only its acknowledgement was lost, and these tunnels carry
request/response protocols where re-sending the second case is a corrupt request
rather than a retry.

So the stream ends instead, at the moment the replacement channel binds:
`ShimSession` announces each attach, and the proxy drops exactly the streams
that had a frame in flight. The in-pod client sees EOF at once — for gitcred, an
authentication failure git can retry — while a stream that was idle across the
renewal is untouched and its next frame travels on the new socket. A `data` frame
that fails to deliver for any other reason ends its stream the same way.

Two tests, one per half: a live connection keeps working across a real renewal
(a short credential TTL plus the shim's fake clock, which is why the plane now
takes `credentialTtlMs`), and a stream whose frame was in flight is terminated
with the pod told on the freshly bound channel. The second fails without the
attach hook, reporting one surviving stream where there should be none.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): announce a bound shim channel only once its peer can serve

Review caught the ordering my previous fix depended on and did not have.
`ShimListener` called `onConnection` BEFORE putting `shim/bound` on the wire, so
`session.attach` — and with it the tunnel proxy's cleanup of an interrupted
stream — ran while the renewing shim still had no binding. The shim refuses
anything that arrives ahead of its own `bound` as `not bound`, and the proxy had
already dropped the stream, so the close was never retried: the in-pod helper
went on waiting exactly as before the fix.

The send now precedes the notification. Ordering on the socket is what makes that
sufficient rather than merely likely: the peer processes frames in sequence, so a
request queued after the bound frame is served with the binding in place. Nothing
inbound can be missed by registering `onFrame` one statement later either — both
statements run in the same tick, before any I/O is processed.

The test that was missing is the one that proves it: an interrupted stream through
the REAL listener and shim client across a real credential renewal, with a
daemon→pod frame withheld from the pod's socket so it is genuinely in flight. It
asserts the in-pod client reaches EOF. With the old ordering it waits out the full
15s and fails, which is precisely the hang users would have seen; the stubbed
session could not show it, because a stub requester is usable by construction.
