refactor(daemon): make git credential pointers a function of where git runs (#858)

* refactor(daemon): make git credential pointers a function of where git runs

Every value git-injection writes is a PATH, and a path only means something in
one filesystem. The module held one daemon-local `shimPath` and one `runDir`, so
a cluster agent — whose git runs in a sandbox pod — got a `credential.helper`
naming an executable that pod has never had, and a `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` pointing
into the daemon's own run directory. What makes that expensive is the failure
mode: git reports an authentication failure, not a missing file.

`GitCredentialTarget` replaces both variables. `targetFor(agentId)` resolves it
per agent off the SAME predicate `setWorkspaceGitRunnerResolver` uses — the
plane's new `runsInSandbox`, which is `gitRunnerFor`'s own condition named — so
the environment can never describe one filesystem while the git that reads it
runs in another. Both follow a channel coming and going, together.

The session gitconfig splits into data and write. `sessionGitConfig` returns
path/content/env; `sessionGitEnv` writes it and now REFUSES a sandbox target,
because a synchronous write of `/run/agentconnect/git/...` lands on the daemon's
disk — creating the file a check would look for while the pod still has none.
The pod's copy has to travel through the shim's materialize channel.

Two smaller pieces the pod side needs: the `[include]` of the operator's
~/.gitconfig is dropped for a sandbox (it would resolve to nothing and read as
if the operator had no config), and `AC_GITCRED_SOCKET` carries the tunnel's
socket path, since a helper in a pod has no daemon root to derive one from. Both
CLI helpers honour it.

No behaviour change on either daemon today: every caller of these pointers is
gated on a git-repo workspace, which `--k8s` still refuses. This removes the
daemon-path assumption and puts the sandbox target under test so that lifting
the refusal is a small change rather than a large one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(docker): ship the git credential helper in the runtime sandbox image (#857)

Git spawns a credential helper as a PROCESS, once per operation, and the runtime
image carried no such executable: it has the shim and nothing else, no daemon
CLI and no `gh`. So the pointer PR #856 puts in a pod's git config named a path
that did not exist.

The helper is now its own bundle beside the shim, wrapped by a three-line
`/opt/agentconnect/bin/git-credential` — root-owned and unwritable by the runtime
for the same reason the shim is: one the runtime could rewrite is one it could
replace with a helper that asks the daemon for credentials in its name.

One implementation, two entry points. `gitcred/helper.ts` is the helper with the
socket as a PARAMETER: the daemon CLI derives it from its own root, and in a pod
the same code dials what the shim's tunnel serves. Its only imports are node
builtins and `gitcred/env.ts`, because the in-sandbox bundle is asserted to
import nothing else — which is also why the env names moved out of
`cp/gitcred-server.ts` (it pulls the daemon's credential cache) and are
re-exported from there for every daemon-side caller.

Two build decisions the packaging forced, both learned by doing it wrong first:

- Its own entry rather than an argv mode of the shim. The shim entry pulls in the
  WebSocket client, and loading the whole channel graph per `git fetch` is waste.
- TWO tsdown builds rather than one build with two entries. Two entries make
  rolldown hoist what they share into a chunk, and the image copies each artifact
  as a single file — so that chunk is a third file nothing copies and the helper
  dies at startup on a missing module. Sharing `tunnel.ts` made it 136 KB of zod.
  `SANDBOX_TUNNEL_PATHS` therefore lives in the leaf `sandbox-paths.ts`, where
  "paths the image fixes" belongs, re-exported from `tunnel.ts` typed against its
  own enum so the two cannot name different sets. Result: index.js 299 KB,
  git-credential.js 7 KB, both node-builtins-only.

The tests run REAL git — `git credential fill` against the wrapper contract over
a real socket — because every part of this was unit-testable while the feature
did not exist: a token round trip, the env identity outranking a stale
`.git/config` id, a denial failing loudly rather than answering git with nothing,
an unreachable socket naming itself, and no request at all for a non-github host.
They spawn asynchronously on purpose: `execFileSync` blocks the event loop, so
the in-process socket server cannot answer until the child has given up — a
deadlock that reads exactly like a broken helper.

assert-self-contained checks both bundles; verify-runtime-image checks the
wrapper's ownership, mode and executability, and that it exits 1 with an
actionable message when no socket answers.

feat(daemon): prepare a git-repo workspace on the sandbox pod's own volume (#862)

* feat(daemon): prepare a git-repo workspace on the sandbox pod's own volume

`--k8s` refused git-repo workspaces outright, which is what made a private
GitHub repository unreachable in cluster mode regardless of credentials: the
clone/pull/audit flow mixed daemon and pod coordinates, so a clear error was
better than a mystery one from git inside the sandbox. With the socket reachable
(#855) and the helper in the image (#857), the refusal is what is left.

`prepareClusterWorkspace` is a separate function rather than a branch inside
`prepareWorkspace`, because the two differ at every step that touches a
filesystem, and the local path — the one every self-hosted daemon runs — must not
acquire new ways to be wrong:

- whether a checkout exists is asked of the POD, as `rev-parse --git-dir` through
  the runner. A file test answers about the daemon's own empty directory, which
  silently means "clone again, every session". `rev-parse` also answers the
  question that matters: a half-written clone has a `.git` and fails it.
- the clone target is RELATIVE to a cwd the shim fences. An absolute target is
  argv the fence never looks at, so it could land anywhere on the volume.
- a failed clone is emptied through the materialize channel, because there is no
  `rmSync` that reaches a pod. Left behind, git would refuse to clone into a
  non-empty directory forever while the probe kept reporting no checkout.
- the checkout goes one level below the mount (`/agent/repo`). The mount is also
  HOME, so a working tree at the root would sit on top of `.claude`/`.codex`,
  where git reports them as untracked and `git clean` would delete them.
  from-scratch keeps the root: no tree to confuse, and moving it would strand
  every volume already provisioned.

The shim now also re-checks a clone's target against its own root, in the
exec-handler tradition that a check which only runs across a channel protects
nothing on the near side. The relative target makes it moot in practice, which is
the point at which it is cheap to enforce.

Two things this deliberately does NOT do, both now stated where an operator
looks. Skills are not installed for a cluster agent — acquisition, the ledger and
stale-executable removal are local-filesystem work, and pointing them at a pod
path would write them onto this daemon's disk. Session isolation stays refused:
its worktrees need a daemon-owned parent, `worktree add` in the sandbox, and a
retention GC that reads the pod's tree.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): converge a resumed volume's origin, and single-flight its clone

Self-review of the cluster path against the local one it mirrors, before review
had to. Two things the local path does to an EXISTING checkout that this did not:

- **Converge the origin.** The CP follows a repository rename by numeric id, so a
  rename appears as a new canonical URL while a resumed volume still points at the
  old one; without repointing it, that reads as a different workspace. More
  importantly the same step REFUSES an origin that is not a trusted GitHub remote,
  fail-closed — a volume that survived from somewhere else must not have
  daemon-managed git run against whatever origin it carries. The convergence is now
  split from its `existsSync` gate, because establishing existence is the only part
  that differs between the two filesystems; what follows has to be identical.
- **Single-flight the clone.** Per-agent preparation is already serialized by the
  daemon's own queue, so this is the belt to that braces: two clones into one
  volume is a half-written checkout, and preventing it costs a map lookup.

The first was caught by the tests immediately — the recording runner reported no
origin, which the new check correctly refused — so the fake now answers
`remote get-url` and two cases pin the behaviour: a rename is followed in the pod,
and an untrusted origin is refused before any pull.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): refuse in-place cluster workspace replacement, and key the clone lock once

Two review findings, both real.

**Activation bypassed the pod-aware path.** `prepareWorkspaceForActivation` is
reached by every workspace edit and by staged/reconnect repair, and it never went
through session preparation: it stages a clone at `agent.workspace.path.clone-*`,
a daemon-absolute path. With a channel attached the runner sent that to the shim,
where the new target fence rejects it with an error about containment that
explains nothing about what was attempted; with no channel it cloned onto the
daemon's disk for an agent whose workspace is elsewhere.

Refused for a git-repo workspace under `--k8s`, rather than implemented, because
the contract is what makes it hard: a staged clone beside the target, `renameSync`
for an atomic swap, `readdirSync` to prove the destination is still empty at the
boundary, and a rollback that restores the previous tree. The shim can write and
clear — not rename, list or stat — so keeping the rollback guarantee across the
channel needs new shim surface, and that belongs in its own change rather than
half-done here. from-scratch is untouched: its activation only creates and empties
the daemon-side directory that IS the bookkeeping identity, and the pod's volume
is not involved.

The mode is registered explicitly rather than derived from the git-runner
resolver, because that resolver answers per AGENT and is undefined before a
channel binds — a guard on it would take the local path for a cluster agent that
merely has no pod yet.

**The clone lock computed its key three times.** `cloneKey` is state-dependent:
it includes the agent id only while a sandbox runner is attached. A clone that
failed BECAUSE the channel dropped therefore computed a different key on the way
out, deleted nothing, and left its own rejection cached under the original — so
every retry after reattachment re-awaited a dead promise until the daemon
restarted. Captured once now, and used for get, set and delete.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): refuse only a cluster workspace CONVERSION, not its rollback or repair

The previous refusal was too broad, and the review is right that it made the
failure permanent rather than preventing it. Activation is also how a rejected
edit is rolled back, how a staged agent is recovered, and how a same-workspace
repair runs — all three arrive with `reconcileWorkspace` set. So a rejected
git→git edit restored the original row, re-activated it, hit the same refusal,
and left the agent staged and offline.

The distinction is REPLACING AN EXISTING CHECKOUT, which is the only case needing
the contract a pod cannot offer: a staged clone beside the target, `renameSync`
for an atomic swap, `readdirSync` to prove the destination is still empty at the
boundary, and a rollback that restores the previous tree. That is refused. A
first activation is not — with no previous marker there is nothing to replace, and
`replace` is true precisely then, so keying on it alone would have made a git-repo
cluster agent impossible to create. Everything else is a no-op that keeps the
marker honest; session preparation is what converges the volume.

Three tests, and I checked each fails under the blanket refusal rather than
passing by construction: a first activation resolves and stages nothing, a repair
and a restoration both resolve after a marker exists, and only a changed
repository on an existing marker is refused.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): record what the pod volume holds, so a repair is not refused for a stale marker

Review found the sequence: an agent moves away, its repository is renamed while
it lives on another daemon, and it moves back. Ordinary placement activation asks
for no reconciliation, so nothing on this daemon refreshed its materialization
marker — cold preparation converged the shared volume to the new URL while the
marker still named the old one. A later repair then read that as a materialization
CHANGE and hit the conversion refusal, staging an agent whose checkout was already
correct.

The marker records what the VOLUME holds, and cluster preparation is the only
place that knows, so it records it there. Best-effort: the volume is prepared
either way, and failing a session over bookkeeping would trade a stale marker for
no session at all.

The test walks the whole sequence and I confirmed it reproduces the stranding
without the refresh — it fails with the conversion refusal, which is exactly what
an operator would have seen.

test(cp): retry the integration truncate when it loses a deadlock (#868)

* test(cp): retry the integration truncate when it loses a deadlock

The per-test TRUNCATE deadlocks intermittently in CI (Postgres 40P01).
A previous test's app can still have a query in flight on another
pooled connection when the next test starts — background loops outlive
the request that started them. That reader holds AccessShareLock on one
table and wants a second; the TRUNCATE holds AccessExclusiveLock on the
second and wants the first, so Postgres kills one of the pair.

Reordering the table list cannot fix this: the reader's lock order is
not ours to choose. So the truncate retries when it is the victim —
the reader always completes, and the retry then takes every lock
uncontended. Bounded at five attempts with a small linear backoff, and
only for deadlocks, so a real failure still surfaces immediately.

fix(daemon): record a cluster marker only when the volume provably matches (#866)

* fix(daemon): record a cluster marker only when the volume provably matches

Follow-up to #862, whose marker refresh I made unconditional. Review found the
sequence that makes that worse than not recording at all:

A volume sits on branch A. The configuration now names a divergent branch B.
`pullWorkspaceRef` pulls INTO the current branch rather than switching, so its
ff-only pull of B fails, the failure is swallowed as ordinary offline degradation
— and the marker was then written as B anyway. Every later activation reads that
as "nothing changed", so the conversion is never detected and the agent runs the
wrong branch indefinitely. Silently, which is the property that makes it
expensive: the refusal added in #862 exists precisely to surface this case.

Provable now means one of two things. A fresh clone: its `--branch` decided HEAD,
so it matches by construction. An existing checkout: HEAD IS the configured
branch, established by asking the pod (`rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`) rather than
inferring it from a pull that does not switch branches — plus, when convergence
had to REWRITE the origin, a pull that then succeeded, because a rewritten URL
says nothing about the tree that was already there and a branch name can match in
both repositories.

Anything else leaves the marker alone and says so. The change stays visible, and
the next activation refuses it with a message naming what to do — which is the
honest outcome for a volume that cannot be converted in place.

Three tests, and I confirmed the two new ones fail against the merged behaviour
rather than passing by construction: a divergent branch leaves the marker and
stays refused, a rewritten origin without a successful pull likewise, and a volume
genuinely on the configured branch records and proceeds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): prove the repository from the STORED marker, not from this call's rewrite

Review found that my proof did not survive a retry. `remote set-url` is durable
while the flag recording it was per call: after a first attempt rewrote the origin
and its pull failed, a second attempt found the origin already correct, concluded
nothing had been rewritten, and would record a marker for a repository no pull had
ever reached. The reconciliation that should have caught it is then disarmed, and
the old tree runs indefinitely — the same failure the previous commit was about,
one attempt later.

Only something written down survives a retry, and the marker is the thing written
down. So the requirement is now: record only when HEAD is the configured branch
AND the tree is attributable to the configured repository — either a stored marker
already attests that repository, or a pull from it just succeeded. The per-call
rewrite flag is gone; `convergeOriginInPlace` returns void again.

This also closes a case the flag never covered: a daemon with no marker adopting an
existing volume knows nothing about where that tree came from, so `origin` matching
proves nothing. It now needs one successful pull before it will record anything.

Three tests. The rewritten-origin case runs preparation TWICE with a failing pull,
which is the sequence that exposed this, and then a third time with it succeeding to
show the proof does arrive. I confirmed both new cases fail with the repository term
removed rather than passing by construction.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): stop activation seeding the marker preparation reads back as proof

Review found the circle, and it was mine: activation recorded the TARGET
materialization for a cluster agent, and cluster preparation then read that as
attestation of the repository. So an existing, uninspected volume with a failing
pull was accepted as proven — on the strength of a marker written moments earlier
by code that had not looked at the volume either.

The marker was doing two jobs. For a cluster agent it now does one: it means "the
volume held this". Activation no longer writes it, so the only writers are cluster
preparation, on proof, and the detach seed — which is a different statement and
stays, because it names the definition the agent has been RUNNING on rather than
one being proposed.

Leaving it absent is safe by construction: the conversion refusal already requires
a previous marker, so no marker means no refusal, which is the right answer for a
volume nothing can vouch for.

The tests that used activation to establish a marker were asserting against
exactly the seed being removed, so they now establish it the legitimate way —
`withProvenMarker` runs a preparation that proved the volume (a fresh clone, whose
`--branch` decided HEAD). The new case walks the bot's sequence: activate with
reconciliation, prepare with a failing pull, and confirm a conversion is still
detectable. I checked it fails with the seed restored.

feat(operator): separate a missing credential Secret from pod startup delay (#871)

CredentialReady exists to report whether the daemon's required Secret mount let
the kubelet start the pod, but every not-ready pod read as
False/DaemonPodNotReady, so a missing Secret looked like ordinary startup.

Classify the observed daemon pods instead. A missing Secret-backed volume is
only ever visible as a FailedMount Event — the pod just sits Pending with
ContainerCreating — so the pass reads those events, scoped server-side to
Pod-involved FailedMount, matched to the daemon pods by name and to the
credential by the wordings the kubelet uses to name a Secret it could not read.
An Event is believed only while it is still being re-emitted (a window sized to
the recorder's throttled cadence, not the kubelet's retry) and the pod is still
awaiting container creation, so one retained past its fix cannot describe a
mount that now works. The read is best-effort: a forbidden events read warns and
keeps the pass. An unplaced pod reports Unknown/DaemonPodUnschedulable without
reading events at all.

Because an Event can be written after the pod's last update, and the controller
watches only Deployments and Pods, the queue gains a delayed follow-up: a pass
may return requeueAfterMs, any earlier wake cancels it, and only the provisional
DaemonPodNotReady verdict asks for one — so a settled org never polls.

The envelope ClusterRole gains events read verbs; there are still no Secret
verbs anywhere and no new watch.

The control plane becomes the writer of the `AgentConnectOrg` CR the cluster
operator reconciles (docs/designs/agentconnect-org-operator.md). One path
serves a self-hosted cluster install and a hosted deployment; only the policy
inputs differ.

write would be rejected.

Envelope status is never mirrored there — the status route reads it live off
the resource, so a row can never disagree with the cluster. `targetNamespace`
is derived once from the install prefix and the org id because the CRD marks
it immutable, and writes are server-side apply under this process's own field
manager so the operator's manager is untouched.

* fix(cp): fence concurrent cluster settings writes and widen the release closure

permanently apart: each request applied its own upsert snapshot, so

A, and nothing heals it — the operator reconciles the CR, not the row, and this
module has no timer. Every write now bumps `specRevision`, and the provisioner
applies the CURRENT row and re-reads that revision: a change means a peer
superseded the snapshot it just applied, so it applies again.

The control-plane and setup release-input closures still listed only the old
workspace deps, so a source-only change to `k8s-client` or `connection` could
alias an older control-plane image under a new version. Both packages join
`CP_PATHS`, `SETUP_PATHS`, and `SETUP_IMPORTERS`.

slug it reads, which is what lets the convergence loop be unit-tested.

* fix(cp): tear the org's cluster envelope down before deleting the org

Deleting an organization cascaded `org_cluster_execution` away without touching
its `AgentConnectOrg`. That row holds the only copy of the envelope's immutable
`targetNamespace`, so the operator kept reconciling a namespace, daemon, and
sandboxes that nothing left could name — and the daemons-present guard cannot
catch it while the envelope is suspended or its daemon has never connected.

`DELETE /orgs/:orgId` now deletes the resource before the cascade. The call is
idempotent, and a cluster that refuses it refuses the whole deletion with 502,
so the row and the name it carries survive for the retry.

Kubernetes rejection becomes an upstream failure, now that two route files

* fix(cp): tombstone the org envelope inside the delete transaction

The previous fence still had two holes. A process running with
CLUSTER_EXECUTION_MODE=off skipped teardown entirely even though an earlier
enabled run had left a row and a CR, and a concurrent PUT could apply after
teardown returned but before the cascade — both orphaning the envelope again.

transaction that deletes the org, mirroring the crypto-shred tombstone beside

feat(daemon): suspend an idle agent's pod, and delete a removed agent's volume (#883)

* feat(daemon): suspend an idle agent's pod, and delete a removed agent's volume

An agent's Sandbox had exactly one ending: a runtime-image rollout. Everything
else kept its pod forever. An agent that went quiet held a pod running nothing,
and an agent that was deleted held a 10Gi volume nobody would ever read again —
`removeAgent` existed for the second case and was called only by the runtime
probe's teardown.

Two rules, one each:

Quiet ⇒ suspend, keep the volume. The idle sweep already reclaims a host with no
recent activity and no in-flight turn; it now also suspends the Sandbox of any
agent it holds a launch for that no longer has a host. The pod goes, the object
and the workspace volume stay, and the next message resumes onto the same
checkout — no new knob, and no wake path, because `bindChannel` already patches
Running before it waits for readiness. The sweep reads the driver's launches
rather than chaining onto host reclaim: a launch outlives the host it was made
for (a bind for workspace preparation makes one before any runtime exists), and
a rule evaluated from state each tick cannot be stranded by a teardown that
failed.

Removed ⇒ delete the claim, and the volume with it, at exactly the point where
the local path deletes the checkout. Removal only. A detached or moved agent
keeps its volume: both are reversible, and the source daemon is never told that
a move committed, so deleting on detach would trade a leaked volume for a lost
workspace on every rollback. Its pod still goes, through the idle rule.

Suspension turned out to need a prerequisite fix, which is the reason
`forgetLaunch` had no callers. A lost session is terminal — `attach()` is a
no-op once closed — while a cached launch keeps its generation, so a re-bind
that matched generations re-attached the dead session and handed the resumed pod
a channel that could never serve a request. The resume path was therefore broken
for every cause of a departed pod, not just this one; only nothing exercised it,
because nothing suspended. Losing the channel now ends the launch, so the next
turn claims a fresh generation — the fence the replacement pod is bound against.
The regression test fails without that change.

One consequence, recorded rather than papered over: a socket that returns AFTER
loss was reported (a blip longer than the rebind grace, pod still alive) is
bound to a generation nothing awaits, and the launch recovers at the shim's next
credential renewal. Closing it to force an immediate re-dial is not done — a
first bind is indistinguishable from it at that point, and every pod would
re-dial into a close loop after a daemon restart.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): exclude work from an idle suspend instead of merely counting it

Review found the race: `busy` counts holders, it does not keep new ones out. The
check-then-retain pair was atomic against work that had ALREADY acquired the
sandbox, and did nothing about work admitted during the Kubernetes write that
follows — that dispatch acquires the same launch, loses its pod underneath
itself, and then finds its launch forgotten by the suspend's own success path.

The suspend decision is now published before the first await, and acquisition
waits it out in `ensureSandbox` rather than racing it. Publication is
synchronous with the `busy` read, which is what makes the pair atomic in the
other direction too: a holder either shows up in that read, or arrives to a gate
that is already closed. A waiter then resumes into the ordinary path — the
suspend forgot the launch, so it claims a new one, which is the resume it would
have performed a moment later anyway.

The regression test drives exactly that interleaving: a suspend held open inside
the mode write, a bind admitted while it is in flight, and the assertion that the
bind waits and then resumes at a new generation rather than binding the pod that
is going away.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): lease the probe sandbox across its request, not just its bind

Review's second finding, and it is not confined to idle suspension: the probe
releases its bind lease before `session.request('probe')`, which then runs for
up to three minutes with nothing marking that sandbox as in use. Both suspension
paths read exactly that lease to decide a pod is spare — so a rollout's drain
could already pull the pod out mid-probe, and the idle sweep (60s default, no
host, no dispatch, no activity row) would now do the same. Losing the pod fails
the probe, and a daemon whose probe failed advertises no runtimes and does not
retry: it stays useless until someone restarts it.

The lease now covers the whole request. Filtering the reserved probe id out of
the sweep's candidate set was the alternative, and is worse twice over: it fixes
only the sweep, leaving the drain hole open, and it teaches core a reserved name
instead of letting the lease mean what it says.

The first version of this test asserted during the BIND, where the sandbox is
held either way — it passed with the fix reverted, so it was worth nothing. It
now waits for the probe REQUEST to arrive (the shim handler signals it) before
asking to suspend, and fails with `expected 'suspended' to be 'busy'` when the
lease is removed.

feat(console): PR actions — one Auto-fix turn and Merge-when-ready auto-merge (#884)

* feat(console): PR actions — one Auto-fix turn and Merge-when-ready auto-merge (M6)

The design's headline loop closes: read the review, hand it to the agent, arm
the merge (webchat-side-panels.md M6, §5.2).

Auto-fix is ONE action over the whole unresolved set, not a per-thread state
machine (§5.2's scope decision): the panel builds one structured instruction —
every thread's location, author and body — and posts it through the LIVE
composer path (browser→relay→daemon; no CP route). Its only follow-up is a
single refresh=true re-read on the turn's falling edge, where the agent's
GitHub write-back (resolved threads, pushed fixes) landed and the CP TTL would
hide it; the wait is armed per press, consumed once, and reset per scope. A
session with no live composer gets no button — absent, not disabled.

Merge-when-ready is the one backed write: POST
/sessions/:id/pull-request/auto-merge flows getOrgViewableSession → the owning
run → the RUN's agent, mints an installation token clamped to that agent's
repository tier (pull_requests + contents write — GitHub performs the eventual
merge under the same grant; the comment tier that may COMMENT-review is
excluded, since arming merges code), and drives
enable/disablePullRequestAutoMerge by node id, idempotently — a fresh node read
decides whether the mutation runs, and the cached view drops either way. The
read projection gains autoMergeArmed (shared, GitHub's fact) and
canArmAutoMerge (per-caller, Postgres-only, computed in the route like the
overlay facts — never cached), so a read-tier agent sees a disabled checkbox,
not a failed call. Refusals map to statuses the box can show as data: 403 for
the clamp, 409 for GitHub declining the state change, 429/502 for rate limit /
outage. There is deliberately NO Merge button — nothing backs a direct merge,
and M3's absent-rather-than-inert rule applies.

Every new behavior is mutation-pinned: the falling-edge re-read (never fires /
rides the TTL / never consumed), the merge write's re-read, the tier gates on
both mint and capability flag, idempotency, and the 404/authorization matrix on
the new route.

feat(cp): become the key authority for cluster execution envelopes (#881)

* feat(cp): become the key authority for cluster execution envelopes

The operator names the daemon's credential Secret and mounts it required, so
the kubelet gates pod startup on it — but the operator has zero Secret verbs
anywhere and can never write it. That writer is the control plane, and until
now it did not exist: an enabled envelope could never start a daemon.

`POST /orgs/:orgId/cluster-execution/credential` (owner-only) mints the org's
daemon key, publishes it as the Secret's `config.json` — the same document a
hand-run daemon reads, pointed at the same WebSocket URL onboarding renders —
and bumps `credentialRevision`, which the operator projects into a pod-template
annotation to force a Recreate. The key is never returned; it exists only
inside the cluster Secret.

Three orderings carry the design. The Secret is written BEFORE the revision
bump, so a failed write leaves the running pod on its old, still-valid key
rather than rolling it onto a credential that was never published. The
superseded key is revoked LAST, after the rollout has been asked for, so no
window exists in which no valid key works. And the daemon identity is created
once and reused, so a rotation re-keys the org instead of orphaning its
sessions and agents under a new daemon row.

A missing envelope namespace is the ordinary "just enabled" state — the
operator creates it from the CR — and answers 409 without recording anything,
so a retry after NamespaceReady starts clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): make the cluster credential transition retry-safe and exclusive

Three review findings, all about what happens when a step fails — which matters
here because daemon keys never expire.

A credential could be issued for a DISABLED envelope: the check only asked
whether a settings row existed. While the namespace still exists during
finalization, that published a fresh Secret and stored a fresh active key,
undoing the retirement disabling had just performed. Issuing now requires an
enabled envelope.

A failed Secret write leaked the key it had already minted, and on a first
issue left the provisioned daemon unrecorded — so every retry provisioned
another daemon and another live key. The identity is now recorded before
anything can fail, and the unpublished key is revoked on the way out, so a
retry re-keys that same daemon.

Two concurrent rotations could write Secrets in one order and commit them in
the other, leaving the row and the Secret naming different, both-live keys; and
overwriting the only handle to the previous key before revoking it lost that
key forever if the revoke failed. `credentialRotationAt` is now claimed by a
conditional write, so exactly one caller mints and publishes across every
instance — a lease, so a process that dies mid-rotation cannot wedge the
envelope. Revocations are recorded in `pending_daemon_key_revocation` before
they are attempted and cleared only once they land, and the maintenance loop
retries what is still owed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): fence the credential transition with a token and stage it durably

Three more review findings, all the same root cause: a multi-step distributed
transition needs a durable record at every interruption point.

An expiry timestamp is not a fencing token. A holder that ran past its lease
could resume after a successor took over, commit its own credential, and then
release the successor's claim — both writers publishing again. Every write in a
transition is now conditional on a `credentialRotationToken`, so an expired
holder can neither commit behind its successor nor unlock it, and a takeover
adopts whatever the dead holder left staged.

The revocation record was still created too late. A Secret that published and
then failed to commit left a live key in neither the settings row nor the
queue; and overwriting the previous key before queueing it lost that key
forever if the queue write never happened. The minted key is now staged BEFORE
it is published, and promoting it is one transaction with queueing the key it
supersedes.

Disable persisted `enabled: false` and only then deleted the CR and retired the
credential, so an unavailable cluster left a disabled row beside a live pod
holding a live non-expiring key with nothing queued. Disable now takes the same
exclusive claim — fencing an in-flight rotation out — and does all its durable
work in one transaction before the cluster is touched. Re-enabling cancels the
teardown it recorded.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): make every credential write a real CAS and order the Secret publish

Three more findings, all in the same seam.

The token check was a separate SELECT followed by an unconditional update, so
under Prisma's default isolation a stale holder could validate its token, lose
the claim to a successor, and still land the write. `commitCredential`,
`retireCredential`, and `abandonStagedCredential` now carry the token in the
`where` clause — the predicate IS the write. `commitCredential` additionally
requires `enabled: true`, so no rotation can land a live key on an envelope
disable already retired.

Disable persisted `enabled: false` before it owned the transition, so an issuer
holding the lease left the row disabled with its credential never retired.
Disable now claims first and clears `enabled` inside the same transaction that
drops the credential, queues its keys, and records the teardown.

A database token cannot fence a request already in flight to the API server: a
publish stalled past its lease could land after its successor's and restore a
key the row no longer names. Publishing is now a `resourceVersion`-guarded
read-modify-write stamped with a monotonic `credentialRotationSeq`, and refuses
to overwrite a Secret already carrying a higher one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): settle ambiguous publishes and fence teardown against re-enable

Three more findings.

A publish that threw was assumed rejected, but a write whose response is lost to
a dropped connection still commits — and revoking that key would leave the
daemon pod mounting a dead credential. The Secret now exposes its published
sequence, and a failed publish is settled against it before anything is
revoked; a read that fails too is treated as "may have landed", since keeping a
key alive one rotation too long is far cheaper than killing a live one.

Clearing the teardown tombstone did not cancel a drain that had already listed
it, so a re-enable could apply the resource and then watch that drain delete it,
leaving `enabled: true` with no envelope. Both sides now take the org's
credential claim: the enable path holds it while it cancels the tombstone and
applies, and the drain takes it per org before deleting.

The documented deployment grant said `create`/`patch` on Secrets, but publishing
became a resourceVersion-guarded read-modify-write. It is `get`, `create`,
`update`, and `delete`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): claim before enabling, fence the teardown delete, keep every key handle

Round-five review findings.

Enable changed `enabled` before it owned the claim, so a concurrent disable or
drain could observe a state change nobody had exclusive rights to. It now
claims first and upserts under the claim; an org with no row yet is created
disabled purely so there is something to claim.

A teardown whose lease expired could still have its DELETE in flight when a
re-enable applied a new generation, removing what the re-enable just created.
The drain now reads the resource and deletes with its `uid`/`resourceVersion`
as preconditions, so the API server rejects a stale delete instead.

Adopting a crashed rotation's staged key at claim time made it revocable before
any successor had published over it. Adoption moved to the point where the key
is actually displaced or superseded — `stageCredentialKey` and
`commitCredential` — so the handle is never lost and never handed over earlier
than it has to be.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): never revoke a key the Secret may still be carrying

A key displaced out of the staged slot was queued for revocation the moment
its successor staged a replacement — before that replacement had published
anything. The maintenance loop, or the successor's own failure cleanup, could
then revoke the key the Secret still held and leave the daemon pod mounting a
dead credential.

The queue now distinguishes NAMED from REVOCABLE. A key that may be in the
Secret is queued `held`: durable, listed by nothing, drained by nothing.
`commitCredential` releases every held key for the org — that commit is the
higher-sequence publish they were waiting on, and its `specRevision` bump is
the rollout request — and retiring the envelope releases them too, since a pod
that is going away has no credential left to strand. A key whose publish landed
but whose commit lost the claim is now held for the same reason, instead of
being revoked out from under a pod that may restart onto it.

Bootstrapping a first enable is also insert-only now. Two callers could both
observe no row; the loser's upsert would take the update branch and force the
winner's freshly claimed row back to `enabled: false` on its way to a 409.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): a committed credential is not a rolled-out one

`commitCredential` bumping `specRevision` is durable intent, not a rollout: the
pod keeps authenticating with its old key until the CR itself carries the new
`credentialRevision`. Releasing the superseded keys inside that transaction
therefore let the maintenance loop revoke a key the running pod was still
using whenever the apply that followed failed — and nothing would have
re-requested the rollout afterwards either.

The commit now records `credentialRolloutPending` and leaves the predecessor
held. `completeCredentialRollout` — after `converge()` has actually applied the
resource — is what drops the obligation and releases the keys. A request that
dies in between leaves both the obligation and a working credential, and
`drainCredentialRollouts` re-applies under the same per-org claim every other
transition takes, so the retry is durable rather than dependent on the caller
coming back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): drain the owed rollout through the convergence fence

The rollout drain applied the snapshot it captured and then closed the
obligation. A settings write needs no credential claim, so one can persist and
apply a newer spec while that apply is in flight — leaving the CR reverted to
the older spec with nothing recorded that anything was still owed.

It now runs the same convergence loop every configuration writer runs. The
credential fields only move under the claim the drain holds, so whatever row a
peer supersedes it with still carries the revision being rolled out.

fix(k8s-client): stamp Lease times as MicroTime so leader election works (#873)

The API server parses a Lease's acquireTime/renewTime as MicroTime — RFC3339
with exactly six fractional digits. Date#toISOString emits three, so every
create and renew came back 400 and no Lease was ever written: the operator
elected no leader and its control loop never started.

Found installing charts/operator on a live cluster, where both replicas logged
`lease tick failed ... cannot parse ".103Z" as ".000000"` once per renew
interval while no coordination.k8s.io Lease appeared. With the stamp padded to
six digits the same install elects a leader, watches its CRs, adds and removes
the org-envelope finalizer, and fails over to the survivor in about a second.

The fake API server stored timestamps as opaque strings, so no unit test could
see the mismatch. It now rejects a mistyped stamp the way the real server does,
which turns six existing election tests into regression guards for the format.

fix(operator): report CredentialSecretMissing while the daemon pod is stuck at init (#891)

The credential Secret is mounted by the install-config initContainer alone, so a
missing Secret leaves the pod at Init:0/1 with no container ever created. The
kubelet names the fault only in a FailedMount Event, and the gate that lets that
Event be read looked for a ContainerCreating status — a reason a pod that
declares an init container never reports, because every uncreated container is
PodInitializing instead. CredentialReady therefore fell through to the generic
DaemonPodNotReady, the one condition whose purpose is naming this failure.

Accept both reasons, and require all container statuses to carry one: a pod whose
init container is stuck on a blocker of its own has mounted the Secret already,
and its main container's PodInitializing must not re-blame the credential off a
retained Event. Precedence and the freshness bounds are unchanged.

feat(operator): derive the org envelope namespace from the CR name (#892)

`spec.targetNamespace` was required, so every CR named its own namespace:
two of them could name the same one, or one outside the install's prefix,
and the operator could only notice afterwards (`NamespaceOutsidePrefix` →
Degraded). Make the namespace a function of install-time constants plus the
CR's identity instead, so a collision is impossible by construction.

The field stays as a deployment-level escape hatch, now optional and still
immutable (the CEL rule tests presence on both sides, so an org can move
neither between namespaces nor between derived and overridden):

- unset — the normal path, and what the control plane always writes — the
  operator resolves `<AC_ORG_NAMESPACE_PREFIX><CR name>`, unique because the
  name is unique within the control namespace;

docs(design): give an in-cluster daemon a Kubernetes identity instead of a key (#903)

* docs(design): give an in-cluster daemon a Kubernetes identity instead of a key

has one: the audience-scoped ServiceAccount token the kubelet projects into
its pod, which the control plane can verify and map back to the org through
the namespace the operator published. This is the shim handshake run
backwards — a sandbox already proves itself to the daemon exactly this way.

The provisioner then writes one object, the CR, and needs no permission in
any org namespace; the round trip that waited for status.namespace before
publishing a Secret disappears, and with it the minting, the credential spec
fields, the rotation Recreate, and the fencing/sequence/staging machinery
that existed because a publish could half-fail. API keys stay for daemons
with no Kubernetes identity.

Records the rejected alternatives with their reasons — publish into the org
namespace, move a Secret through the control namespace, seal the credential
into the CR, bootstrap a long-lived key — and why revocation, the strongest
objection, does not survive contact with a deployment model where the daemon
is a workload this system can simply delete.

feat(daemon): let webchat agent posts continue a multi-agent conversation (#549 parity) (#906)

* feat(daemon): let webchat agent posts continue a multi-agent conversation (#549 parity)

Closes #904. A multi-agent webchat conversation stalled after one round per
human message: agent posts reached the peers only as transcript context, per
the pre-#549 design ('context frames never activate'). PR #549 had reversed
that rule on the platform ladders, so the same counting relay ran to
completion on Slack and died in webchat.

Parity, at the narrowest seam webchat has: the relay 'context' frame is
already the pre-addressed per-participant copy of a committed post with the
author excluded, so it becomes the continuation activation. The commit
boundary stamps the authoring turn's chain depth on the post
(WebchatPost.author.hopCount); the receiving participant's daemon charges one
+1 transition against the shared MAX_AGENT_CALL_HOPS budget (refusal at the
cap is recorded; a depth-less post from a pre-parity daemon never coerces to
zero and stays transcript-only), admits exactly-once per (post, target)
through the durable activation rendezvous, checks the directional call policy
per edge, and dispatches a post-only wake whose CallMeta installs the depth —
so the reply it commits advances the chain by one and an alternating
conversation terminates by reaching a limit, not by an agent declining to
address anyone.

Final-events-only is structural (rd/webchat-post exists only for a committed
reply; streaming rides rd/chat), and the coarse loop guard is deliberately
not charged, mirroring usesLoopGuard on the platform continuation path. The
wake presents as a conversation post rather than a direct agent call (new
CallMeta.conversationContinuation keeps the direct-call reminder off), so a
silent observer still declines with AC_NO_RESPONSE — committing no post and
fanning nothing out — while its wake spends the hop.

Single-agent webchat, playground sessions, and the platform ladders are
structurally unreachable from the new seam and unchanged.

fix(daemon): let a cluster agent's workspace be edited (#895)

A workspace edit is a replacement, and the local path implements it with a staged
clone, an atomic rename and a rollback that restores the previous tree. None of
those exist through the shim, and the step that needs them runs at agent/activate
before the CP has acknowledged the edit — so --k8s refused every conversion of an
existing checkout outright.

Split it across the two places that can each do half. Activation records the
intent and destroys nothing; cluster preparation performs it from the pod's own
side — empty the checkout, then materialize the configured workspace. The marker
is dropped before the destructive clear and written only when preparation proved
the volume, so every failure in between leaves a volume nothing claims to
describe and the definition that arrives next re-materializes it, rollback or
retry alike. The intent is therefore only ever set, never withdrawn.

Also fixes additionalWorkspaceDirectories, which realpathSync'd a POD path on the
daemon's own filesystem and threw on every cluster git-repo session.

On the CP side, a rejected workspace edit's rollback replayed the pre-edit row,
whose revision is older than the one the target had just applied — the daemon's
fence refused it, so every rejected edit ended fail-closed with the agent staged
and offline. It now replays the restored row and carries the daemon's rejection
reason into the message.

* feat(control-plane): provision an org's cluster envelope with the org

Managed execution was reachable only through an owner-only toggle, so an
organization's AgentConnectOrg existed just where someone went looking for
the switch. Provision it with the org instead, and give the console a
convergence point for the ones no create route ever saw.

  else a kubeconfig, else the pod's own ServiceAccount. Setting nothing
  but the switch is the in-cluster case, with CRs in the pod's namespace.

  is no pod namespace to derive and guessing one would provision every
  envelope into the wrong place.
- ClusterExecutionService.ensureProvisioned: idempotent, enables only an
  org with NO settings row (a disabled row is an owner's decision),
  re-applies the spec when the CR went missing, and issues the first
  credential once the operator publishes status.namespace.
- POST /orgs calls it best-effort after the create commits, and
  POST /orgs/:orgId/cluster-execution/ensure exposes it so the console's

* fix(control-plane): retire the envelope's own daemon when an org is deleted

Provisioning the envelope with the organization meant every organization
got a daemon row, and org deletion is refused while any daemon survives —
a RESTRICT-FK barrier rechecked inside the delete transaction. That guard
exists so someone detaches the physical machines explicitly, and the
envelope's daemon is not one of those: the control plane provisioned it,
and no Daemons page could be asked to detach it. Left in the count it made
every auto-provisioned organization undeletable.

The delete route now excludes it from the guard, switches cluster
execution off — revoking the key and handing the envelope to the
operator's finalizer — and removes the row before the delete. A cluster
that refuses the disable does not fail the deletion: the tombstone written
inside the delete transaction is what teardown hangs on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): address review — Secret liveness, ensure retries, unbounded I/O

Three lifecycle regressions from the review of #901.

The stored `credentialRevision` was treated as proof that the envelope
holds a credential. It is not: deleting a CR hands the envelope to the
operator's finalizer, which removes the namespace and the Secret in it. A
pass that recreated the CR and then trusted the revision left the new
daemon pod blocked forever on a Secret nobody was going to write. Ensure
now asks the cluster whether the Secret is actually published, and re-keys
when it is not — a rotation the daemon identity survives. A namespace that
is not published or created yet reads as absent and answers
NamespaceNotReady, the ordinary "come back later".

The Daemons page recorded an org as checked before the request resolved
and never cleared it, so the deferred credential the endpoint documents
(200 with no `credentialRevision` while the operator is still publishing
the namespace) and every failure both suppressed the follow-up visit that
was supposed to finish the job. An org is now recorded only once the
answer is final — credentialed, disabled, or a 404/403 that cannot change
on a revisit — with a separate in-flight guard against a double send.

`POST /orgs` awaited Kubernetes I/O that has no bound: K8sHttp installs no
socket timeout and the call passes no abort signal, so a blackholed API
server could hold the request open after the org row had committed,
leaving the caller with neither an org nor a safe retry. Provisioning is
now off the response path entirely; the Daemons page ensures the same
thing, so a dropped attempt costs a page visit, not an envelope.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): detach the envelope daemon through the full removal sequence

Retiring the envelope's daemon on organization deletion did a bare row
delete. The foreign key does half that job and none of the visible half:
`Agent.daemonId` is SetNull but nothing touches `Agent.status`, so relays
keep collaboration entries naming a dead daemon and compiled hook rules
keep failing delivery with `daemon_offline`. That is observable because
the delete can still answer 409 afterwards — `review_cleanup_pending`, or
losing the preflight race to a daemon registered in between — leaving a
live organization holding `active` agents with nowhere to run.

The sequence `DELETE /daemons/:id` already ran moves to
`http/daemon-removal.ts` and both callers share it, so a partial copy in
either cannot drift. What survives a 409 is now an organization with
cluster execution switched off and its agents properly unplaced: the state
a manual disable produces, and one the owner can re-enable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): treat a staged credential as incomplete, not published

The Secret-liveness check accepted any positive published sequence, which
is not proof the row is settled. A publish whose response was lost still
landed, so `issueCredential` deliberately leaves that key STAGED and its
predecessor live rather than revoking a credential the pod may be holding;
recovery is a successor claim that publishes, commits, and retires both.
Nothing here runs on a timer, so calling that state complete stranded it
forever — the key the Secret carries uncommitted, the one the row names
never retired, and the console settling the org for good.

A staged key now reads as incomplete whatever the cluster says, so the
successor recovery path still runs. A committed revision whose CR apply is
still owed is a different case: the maintenance loop drains it, and the
ensure pass has already re-applied it through converge on the way there.

* fix(control-plane): answer ensure settlement explicitly instead of letting the console infer it

`ensureProvisioned` returns the pre-attempt settings when a peer owns the

No settings value can carry that meaning, so the pass now answers it:

it lands additively: the API-key path is untouched, and a daemon with no
Kubernetes identity still uses it.

control-plane audience and the envelope daemon's ServiceAccount name — plus the
path the token is projected at. Kept in one place because a constant duplicated
across the operator and the control plane eventually holds two values, and the
rename that causes it passes every build and fails only at runtime.

The daemon reads the token at each connect rather than caching it, since the
kubelet rotates it roughly hourly. The control plane reviews it against the org's
cluster and refuses unless the audience, the ServiceAccount name, and the
subject's namespace all match what the operator published on `status.namespace`.

TokenReview proves an org, not a daemon, so the verified identity is bound to a
daemon record: `daemon.clusterIdentity` is unique, JIT-provisioned on the first
authenticated connect and resolved on every reconnect — the shape the control
plane already runs for an OIDC subject. One record per identity, and a rebuilt

An envelope daemon is now born able to dial. `spec.controlPlane.url` — a new
required CR field the control plane writes and the operator only passes through,

contract copy and `buildSpec`. `CredentialReady` retires rather than being

namespace, silently assuming the control plane runs there. `daemonEgressNamespaces`

piping it into `kubectl apply` feeds it corrupted YAML.

Move the body to `charts/operator/crd/agentconnectorg.yaml` and reduce the
template to the gate plus `{{ .Files.Get }}`, the arrangement
`templates/agent-sandbox.yaml` already uses for the vendored upstream manifest.
Out-of-band installs now `kubectl apply -f` the file itself, which the chart
README documents where `installCRD: false` is explained.

Still a template rather than a `crds/` directory: `crds/` cannot be conditional
and Helm never upgrades it, which a v1alpha1 schema still in motion cannot
afford. The rendered output is unchanged apart from the explanatory comment.

Both CRD parity tests — the operator's zod tree and the control plane's writer
contract — now read the standalone file instead of parsing the template and
dropping every line containing `{{`. They assert against the exact text the API
server receives, with nothing filtered out.

feat(operator): render the master SandboxTemplates from chart values (#913)

`ensureSandboxTemplates` deep-copies a master SandboxTemplate named
`<masterTemplatePrefix><tier>` out of the control namespace into each org
namespace, overriding the container image, `AC_SHIM_ENDPOINT` and the network
policy. Nothing created those masters — the first end-to-end run used a
hand-written one — and a tier whose master is missing is skipped with a warning,
so the org gets no template, no warm pool, and its daemon has nothing to claim
from.

Add a `runtimeTiers` value and render one SandboxTemplate per entry into the
release namespace, named to match the lookup. Each entry carries a tier name, a
container image, resource requests/limits and the workspace claim's size and
StorageClass; the default ships small/medium/large, mirroring the operator's
built-in daemon tier names so the control plane's `CLUSTER_DEFAULT_RUNTIME_TIER`
resolves against a real master when it is left unset.

The rendered shape is what the operator inherits rather than overrides:
`automountServiceAccountToken: false` with a projected, audience-restricted
`serviceAccountToken` (the only service-account token the sandbox-baseline policy
admits), a non-root securityContext on the runtime image's fixed uid, the
workspace `volumeClaimTemplates` entry mounted at the image's workspace root, and
`volumeClaimTemplatesPolicy: Disallowed` so no claim can add volumes and bypass
warm-pool adoption. The three per-org fields carry placeholders.

The chart README explains that these are blueprints rather than per-org objects,
which parts the operator replaces, and why a first install on a cluster that has
never run agent-sandbox needs `--set runtimeTiers=null` before an upgrade with
the tiers.

refactor(control-plane): remove the daemon key-delivery path (#914)

* refactor(control-plane): remove the daemon key-delivery path

An in-cluster daemon authenticates with its projected ServiceAccount token
(#907-#909), so the control plane has nothing to publish into an org namespace
and no second interaction after the CR. Everything that existed because a
Secret publish could half-fail goes with it: the Secret client, the daemon
config-json builder, the credential route, the staged-before-published slots,
the cluster rotation sequence, the owed-rollout flag, and the held-revocation
queue plus its maintenance drain.

Kept, because it was never about the credential: the per-org transition claim
(renamed `envelopeTransition*`) still fences enable, disable and the teardown
drain against each other on one row, and `specRevision` still fences two
concurrent spec writers.

`ensureProvisioned` no longer answers `settled`. With one object to apply and
nothing delivered after it, a pass either applies the CR or throws, so the
flag would be constant true — and a client branching on a constant is worse
than no field. `POST …/ensure` returns the settings; a failure is the retry.

`credentialDaemonId` survives as `legacyKeyDaemonId`, still the adoption source
for an envelope provisioned before the token path. It also fed the org-delete
guard, which now recognizes the envelope's own daemon by its identity binding
and falls back to that pointer until the pod reconnects — without which every
org holding a token-path envelope daemon would have become undeletable.

The migration revokes the keys the queue still owed, plus each envelope's
committed and staged one, before dropping the columns: daemon keys never
expire, so deleting the last thing able to revoke them is not the same as
revoking them.

chore(operator): remove the Helm chart while it is iterated on the deployment side (#915)

Temporary removal, not a deprecation. The chart moves to the deployment
repository so it can be developed alongside the environment that consumes it,
and it is expected back here once managed execution is proven end to end.

Why it has to be somewhere else for now: the control plane and the operator must
agree on a set of install-time constants — control namespace, org namespace
prefix, runtime tier, storage class, the control plane's ServiceAccount. A
mismatch does not fail at deploy time. Every object applies, the release reports
success, and it surfaces later as a daemon whose AgentConnectOrg reports Ready
while its registration never completes. Those constants only exist together on
the deployment side, so that is where the chart can be written once and checked.

This commit only deletes:

- charts/operator, except crd/agentconnectorg.yaml;
- scripts/vendor-agent-sandbox.mjs, which regenerates the vendored
  agent-sandbox manifest and travels with it;
- the chart publish step in the release workflow's finalize job, and the
  checkout that existed only to feed it;
- the chart lint step in the operator-image job;
- charts/operator from the operator component's path list, since chart changes
  no longer affect that image's effective version.

The CRD stays. It is the operator's API contract, and both the operator's zod
schema and the control plane's contract copy are parity-tested against that
exact file — moving it would leave a public package's contract untested. Its
path is unchanged, so no reader needed touching.

The operator image still ships from this repository's release train. Nothing
about how it is built or published changes.

Prose that points at the chart is deliberately left alone: the pointers are
correct again when the chart returns, and churning them twice helps nobody.

fix(control-plane): re-apply AgentConnectOrg specs on a timer so drift converges (#918)

* fix(control-plane): re-apply AgentConnectOrg specs on a timer so drift converges

Applying an org's CR only ever ran from a settings write, from `ensure`, or
from the teardown drain, so an envelope was rewritten only when its own row
changed. But `spec.controlPlane.url` is rendered from control-plane
CONFIGURATION, not from that row: every envelope created before a deployment
learned to write it kept a CR without it. The operator had nothing to inject,
the daemon pods came up with no `AC_CP_URL`, and each sat in local mode — CR
`Ready`, pods `1/1 Running` with zero restarts, one INFO line as the only
evidence. The silence was as much the bug as the staleness.

Make CR writing level-triggered, the way the operator's own reconcile already
is. The existing maintenance loop gains a second pass that re-applies a
bounded, rotating slice of the enabled envelopes: 100 per pass, keyed forward
by org id, so a fleet of any size converges over consecutive passes without one
pass holding the API server.

- Each org goes through the same convergence loop a request takes, so the pass
  applies the row as it reads NOW; one disabled or deleted since the slice was
  listed is reconciled to that instead of to a stale snapshot.
- The listing skips orgs under a live transition claim, using
  `beginTransition`'s own takeover predicate so a crashed holder cannot exclude
  its org from convergence forever.
- Re-applying an unchanged spec is a server-side-apply no-op: nothing writes the
  row, so `specRevision` does not move and the API server stores no new
  resource version.
- Failures are per envelope. One unreachable org costs the rest of the pass
  nothing, and each is logged at error with its org id every pass until it
  converges — an envelope stuck on a stale spec is exactly what silence already
  cost once.

`spec.daemon.image` stays pinned per org: the pass renders it from the row, so
fleet-wide daemon upgrades remain the product decision they were.

A daemon started with `--k8s` now logs a refused control-plane connection at
error rather than info, naming the missing piece. In an envelope the control
plane provisioned, running local is a misconfiguration and not a mode, and info
is why these ran unnoticed.

* fix(control-plane): carry the pass totals on a re-apply failure line

One failing envelope and an API server refusing every write produced the same
per-org error. Including how many the pass converged, and how many it did not,
separates them without a second log line.

fix(shared-bot): route direct conversations to one owner (#919)

* fix(operator): let the org daemon reach its own control namespace

The envelope's daemon egress policy allowed DNS, 443 and 6443 only, on
the assumption that the control plane and relay are reached over public
HTTPS. An in-cluster deployment serves them on their own service ports,
so the daemon's registration WebSocket never completed: the pod ran, the
envelope reported Ready, and the org was silently orphaned from its
control plane, with only `cp: connect/handshake failed` in daemon logs
to say so.

Adds an egress rule to the control namespace, mirroring the ingress rule
that already lets the relay forward in. Confirmed on a real cluster: the
handshake timed out until this rule existed, then the daemon adopted its
daemonId from auth/ok and reported READY.

fix(console): name session branches after people, and make the Git/PR tabs match the worktree (#912)

* fix(control-plane): name a session branch after the person, not their email

A webchat token's `user` claim is the handle the daemon puts on the transcript
author line AND in the session worktree's branch, and it was the sign-in email —
so a session opened from the console checked out
`dev/allendragon-gmail-com/<words>`, which names a domain nobody asked about and
reads as noise where a person's name belongs. The mint now prefers the profile's
display name, falling back to the email and then the user id, so the same
session becomes `dev/jane-doe/<words>`.

The daemon keeps the fallback honest: a handle that IS an address reduces to its
local part, so a user who never set a display name gets `jane-doe` rather than
`jane-doe-example-com`. A handle that merely contains `@` is not an address and
keeps every character it has.

* feat(daemon): list a checkout's own commits, not the base branch's history

`workspace/gitlog` answered `git log HEAD`, so the console's commit list for a
session worktree was the repository's history with the session's one or two
commits on top — the base branch's newest commit is not this session's work, and
a reader looking for what a session produced had to guess where it stopped. The
read now lists `<base>..HEAD` and returns that ref, where base is
`origin/<the workspace's configured branch>` — exactly the start point the
worktree was created from, and what its work will be reviewed against. This is
what webchat-side-panels.md §3.3 asked for by "commit log vs base".

Three cases keep the whole history, because excluding anything there would be
wrong or a guess: no configured branch, HEAD already on that branch (the agent's
primary checkout, whose own history IS the answer), and a base ref this checkout
never fetched — where `<missing>..HEAD` would fail the read outright rather than
degrade.

* feat(web): give the dock's Git and PR tabs a working order

Three console changes over the same session worktree, which #897 gave a real
branch and the panels had not caught up with:

The Git tab showed the PRIMARY checkout's branch for a session, because a
session worktree used to be detached. It now names the branch the worktree is
actually on, and only falls back to the primary's when HEAD really is detached.

Commits moved BELOW the changed files and the commit box, and start collapsed: a
reader stages and commits here, and an expanded history pushed both controls off
a 480px dock. The closed row still carries the count — the log is read either way
— with a `+` when the page is a floor, and the header names the range
(`Commits ahead · vs origin/main`) so a count can never read as the whole
repository.

The PR tab no longer vanishes without a pull request. It keeps its tab over a
real checkout and says what it found: `No upstream configured` for a branch that
tracks nothing, with the sentence that names the next step, and a Create-pull-
request action that posts one turn on the Auto-fix path — there is no CP route
that could open a PR, and the agent already has `gh`. The branch facts come from
the Git tab's verdict, so the state costs no extra read. The tab is dropped only
where a pull request is not a thing the session could have: no probe-able session
id, or a workspace that is not a checkout at all — settling §12's open question 6
the other way from "hide it".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): keep the PR panel's create action in its own session's scope

Two findings from review on #912, both real:

The branch facts fed to the PR panel came from the Git tab's verdict, which
follows HEADER FOCUS — while the PR panel is keyed to the open session, on
purpose (§3.4). In a merged conversation, focusing another participant therefore
put that participant's branch in this session's create-pull-request turn. The
facts now cross only when the two scopes are the same worktree; anything else
passes null, and the instruction says "this session's branch", which is what the
turn acts on anyway.

The action also dead-ended: PR identity comes from the run that owns the session,
and a PR the agent opens from a conversation creates no such run, so the probe
keeps answering 404 after the pull request exists — and the panel kept offering
creation as though nothing had happened, inviting a second PR for one branch. It
now remembers the ask (per session), says the agent replies with the URL in the
conversation and why this tab may never link it, and relabels the control to
"Ask again". The instruction is idempotent too: report an existing pull request
rather than opening another, checked where it CAN be checked — on the agent.

Linking a self-opened PR needs a durable session↔PR binding or a by-head-branch
read source; both change §3.4's identity contract and belong in their own change,
which the design doc now records.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): keep the dock's PR writes to one agent and one scope

Second review round on #912, both findings real and both about a multi-agent
conversation:

The create-pull-request turn went through the conversation composer with no
`@mention`, and an unnarrowed webchat turn is delivered to EVERY participant (the
relay's own default, which `onPgSend` already documents). One press in a
three-agent conversation would therefore have three agents each publish their own
worktree and open their own pull request — and Auto-fix, which rides the same
callback, would have each of them fixing the same threads. `onPostTurn` is now
withheld above one participant, so both controls render absent rather than
fanning out; the composer's mention chips remain the surface for asking one
agent. The panel is session-keyed and holds no agent identity, so narrowing from
inside it would mean inventing one.

The tab's no-PR eligibility also read the header-focused participant's git
verdict, so participant B's checkout could put session A's action on screen. It
now requires the same scope the branch facts do — a git read of THIS session's
own worktree. A linked pull request still keeps its tab whatever the git scope
is: that identity comes from the run, not from a checkout.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): open the session's pull request against its workspace base

The Create-pull-request turn told the agent to open the PR "against the
repository's default branch", but a workspace can be configured onto
another branch — `release` while the default is `main` — and the same
change already measures a session branch against exactly that base
(`origin/<configured branch>`). On such a workspace the press opened the
review against the wrong base, dragging in history the branch never added.

The Git verdict now carries that base, reduced to the branch a pull
request can target, and the PR panel names it. Where the read names none
— no configured branch, HEAD already on it, or a base ref never fetched —
the turn has the agent derive its base instead of being handed the
repository default, which only the first of those three would make right.
The base travels on the same scope gate as the branch facts, so a focused
participant's checkout still names nothing here.

feat(cluster): authenticate a cloud daemon with its Kubernetes identity (#930)

* feat(cluster): authenticate a cloud daemon with its Kubernetes identity

A cloud daemon serves every org, so neither existing credential fits it: an
API key is bound to one org and one daemon, and the envelope path's
namespace-to-org mapping has no namespace to read. It authenticates with the
same projected ServiceAccount token anyway, and the ServiceAccount name is the
discriminator — `ac-cloud-daemon` in the install's cloud-daemon namespace
versus `ac-daemon` in an org namespace.

What differs after verification is only who names the org. An envelope
daemon's namespace decided it and a disagreeing claim is refused; a cloud
daemon states it on the connection (`auth.orgId`), which is safe here and only
here because the identity is an install-level principal already authorized for
all of them. Each (identity, org) pair keys its own daemon record, so
placements, fencing, routing, and visibility stay org-scoped as before.

The relay hop runs the same check from the other end: `rd/hello` already
carries the daemonId, so it is forwarded with the token and the control plane
requires that record to be one this identity owns. That door never creates a
record — an org's first one is minted on the control socket.

The org id reaches the daemon through the data-plane mount, beside the schema
locator the same orchestration already supplies, and a daemon that mount
identifies as a cloud daemon refuses to connect with an API key at all.

feat(control-plane): duty_group ledger for k8s daemons (#937)

* feat(control-plane): add the duty_group ledger for k8s daemons

One claimable row per connected component of the agent↔daemon-held-bot graph
(an enabled cron counts as an edge), with a derived membership projection whose
composite primary key makes one-home-per-agent/bot a database invariant.

- (holder, term, expiresAt) is the lease: every grant path bumps the monotonic
  term (the fencing token); renewal never does. Vacancy is temporal — a dead
  member simply stops renewing, so holder carries no FK.
- claimVacant is a single CAS statement (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED): racing
  claimants take disjoint vacancies, first valid claim wins.
- applyReconcile runs a pure planner (connected components + a deterministic
  identity-assignment rule) inside one transaction under a per-org advisory
  scope: held groups that change composition are re-granted to the same holder
  at a bumped term, merges keep the larger held group (ties break to the lower
  groupId), and the returned plan names the superseded holders.
- claimAgentHome covers botless first triggers: claiming creates the lease,
  re-claims by the incumbent are idempotent, and a losing claimant is told the
  live holder.

Ledger primitives only — nothing is wired into the runtime yet; the heartbeat
lease exchange and daemon-side duty registry build on this in follow-ups.

* fix(control-plane): fence duty-ledger lease mutations against reconcile and stale refreshes

Review found two concurrency defects in the ledger primitives:

- applyReconcile's advisory scope only serialized other reconciles; its
  unlocked snapshot could go stale under claimVacant/renewHeld/release, letting
  the apply delete a freshly granted group without a supersession or rewrite a
  held group's membership without a term bump. The snapshot now takes FOR
  UPDATE row locks on the org's ledger rows, so lease writers commit either
  before the snapshot (and are planned over) or after the apply; SKIP LOCKED
  claimants simply pass a locked org by.
- claimAgentHome's idempotent refresh updated by group id only, so a lease
  moved between the read and the write could be extended by a stale reader. It
  now shares the org advisory scope (fencing row creation against reconcile),
  takes a FOR UPDATE lock on the home row, and CASes the refresh on the
  observed (holder, term); a miss reports the row as it now stands instead of
  claiming a stale grant.

either loses (locked row skipped, nobody superseded) or wins and is named in
the plan's supersessions — never a silently destroyed grant.
