fix(daemon): resolve the console's git root where the workspace actually is (#933)

* fix(daemon): run the console's git in the pod, not on the daemon's disk

The Git panel reported "not a git checkout" for every cluster agent, over a
checkout that was there all along.

`createWorkspaceGit` resolved its root from `agent.workspace.path` — this
daemon's own filesystem — while the runner seam correctly routed the invocation
into the agent's sandbox. So the shim received a cwd like
`/var/lib/agentconnect/agents/<id>/workspace`, its cwd fence refused it as
escaping the workspace root, `isRepo()` swallowed the refusal the way it
swallows every git failure, and the seam answered `isRepo:false`. The console
draws that as a from-scratch workspace: no files, no commits, no commit box, and
all four writes declined as data. The ACP path had this right already
(`resolvePreparedWorkspace` → `clusterWorkspaceCwd`); only the panels went
without, so the two halves of the same rule sat one function apart.

`consoleWorkspaceGitRoot` is that missing half, next to its sibling and reusing
it: the daemon-local resolution still decides WHETHER there is a workspace to
name — absent stays absent, so a shared-workspace sessionId is refused exactly
as before, and a session-isolated one still refuses loudly — and only the
coordinates change.

Two reads in the seam still went to the local filesystem, which the corrected
root then made visible:

- `exists` on a path with no changes in scope came from a `realpath` of the
  workspace root, which under --k8s resolves nothing at all, so every unchanged
  path answered "no such file". It is now asked of git (`ls-files --cached
  --others`) when the workspace is on a sandbox volume; an ignored file is the
  one case that answers absent.
- `lastFetchAt` is `.git/FETCH_HEAD`'s mtime and no git subcommand reports it,
  so it answers "unknown" for a sandbox workspace rather than stat-ing a path
  that belongs to another filesystem. Restoring it needs a shim stat.

Tests pin the coordinate mapping and reproduce the cluster shape without a
cluster — a root in pod coordinates that exists nowhere locally, with git
running in a real checkout through the resolver. Reverting the `exists` change
fails two of them.

The Files panel and the local-skills list are NOT fixed here and stay empty for
a cluster agent: both answer from `node:fs`, and the shim serves `materialize`
but no read or list, so there is nothing to route them to yet. §2.6 records
that alongside the skills gap it already had.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(console): say a sandbox is asleep instead of calling its workspace empty

With no bound channel, both workspace seams fell through to this daemon's
filesystem and answered about a path in the POD's coordinates: the Git panel drew
"Not a git checkout" and the Files tree drew an empty workspace. Both describe an
intact checkout as absent, which is the one degraded answer a reader cannot act
on — nothing is wrong, the pod is suspended, and it comes back on the agent's
next turn.

`sandbox-unavailable` joins `WorkspaceErrorReason` and both seams refuse with it
when the workspace is on a sandbox volume nothing can currently reach. It is the
only reason in that vocabulary that is TRANSIENT rather than a bad request, so
the CP answers it 503 — like an offline daemon, because that is the shape of it —
but WITH the code. Both halves of that matter: a 400 (what every other coded
reason gets) tells the console to stop retrying, and a bare 503 (what a
reasonless rejection gets) is indistinguishable from a daemon that may never come
back. On the write path the 400 would be worse still: it reads as "your edit was
rejected", sending the reader to fix content that was never the problem.

The reachability question is asked per agent, which is deliberately NOT how
placement is decided — `setSandboxWorkspaceMode` exists precisely because "is
there a pod yet" must not choose the filesystem to clone into. A read has no such
hazard and this is exactly its question, so the predicate says so in a comment
rather than looking like the mistake that one warns about.

Web: a fourth git outcome, `asleep`, because it is the only one that resolves
itself — the copy must not read as an outage or as an empty checkout. The tree's
per-directory state now carries the failure's `code` alongside its status, since
status alone cannot separate this 503 from the offline one.

Not done here, and still worth doing: waking the pod on a console read. The
console re-reads on every session page view, so that would resurrect a suspended
pod on each visit and fight the idle sweep — it needs a policy decision about
when a read may cost a pod, not a patch.

Reverting either guard fails a test: the daemon's (the git seam goes back to
reporting "not a git checkout" for a sleeping pod) and the web's (the panel goes
back to drawing the offline story).

* fix(daemon): never read a lost shim channel as git's answer

Review on 32893ed7: resolving the runner once stops the daemon-local fallback, but
it does not preserve `sandbox-unavailable` across a ROUTINE renewal. The shim
re-dials at half its credential TTL and `ShimSession.attach` fails the requests in
flight — with a plain Error, which `isRepo()` swallowed like any other git failure.
So an ordinary renewal settled as "not a git checkout", and stage/commit/push
returned non-repo no-ops: the misleading outcome this PR removes, reintroduced from
the transport instead of from a wrong path.

Three changes, smallest first:

- `ShimChannelLostError` types what `abort()` rejects with. `attach()` already
  documents that a renewal fails in-flight requests and the caller may simply ask
  again; that instruction is only actionable if the caller can tell it apart from a
  reply.
- The remote runner retries ONCE, and only a read. The abort says a reply was lost,
  not whether the request landed, so repeating `commit` risks a second commit. The
  repeatable set is a list of READS rather than of idempotent commands — `add` is
  idempotent and still excluded, because the question is what a repeat can cost and
  the cheapest way to never get it wrong is to repeat nothing that writes. `config`
  is out for the same reason even though this seam only reads it.
- Anything left becomes `GitTransportError` — the runner contract's own vocabulary,
  so the console seam needs no shim import — and the seam wraps every runner it
  hands out to translate that into the transient `sandbox-unavailable` refusal. One
  wrapper rather than a check per operation, because the failure is routine and the
  callers that would misread it are the ones that treat a git error as an answer.

`isRepo` now rethrows the transient refusal and swallows only git's own answer,
which is the whole of the reported bug: a request that never reached git is not
evidence about the cwd.

Reinstating the swallow fails the test that asserts a permanently lost channel
reports transient rather than "no checkout"; the retry has its own test, and a
third asserts no mutating argv is ever sent twice.

feat(protocol,control-plane): duty lease exchange riding the heartbeat (#939)

* feat(protocol,control-plane): duty lease exchange riding the heartbeat

The wire half of dynamic duty ownership for k8s daemons, dormant until a
daemon sends it:

- The heartbeat gains an optional duties field — the member's held digest
  ({groupId, term}, terms as decimal strings) plus its remaining headroom.
  Absent ⇒ single-org daemon, nothing changes.
- New frames: duty/grant (C→D EVT; granted or re-confirmed groups with org,
  term, members), duty/revoke (C→D EVT; superseded = another member holds the
  group now, gone = its edges were removed), duty/release (D→C REQ → ack;
  drain returns groups without waiting out T_reassign). All three are
  install-wide — duty groups span orgs on one member, grants carry per-entry
  orgId.
- CP DutyLeaseService: renewal IS the heartbeat (one batched expiry refresh),
  then a digest diff — stale or missing terms are answered by re-issuing the
  grant at the current term (lost-EVT recovery: confirm the terms or
  supersede, never both), unknown digest entries are classified and revoked —
  and vacancy grants up to min(headroom, per-tick cap), suppressed during the
  startup recovery grace so a CP restart cannot misread quiet members as dead.

* fix(control-plane): gate the duty lease exchange to install-wide connections; make allocation coherent

  other orgs' member refs — claimVacant selects vacancies install-wide. The
  heartbeat path now runs only for frame-mode connections (conn.orgId null);
  duty/release from an org-scoped connection answers SCOPE_DENIED.
- Missing-from-digest regrants (restart / lost grant EVT) occupy new local
  slots but were not charged against the reported headroom, so recovery could
  allocate up to twice the member's capacity. Fresh claims now spend
  max(0, headroom - missing); stale-term re-issues stay free (already local).
- Lost digest entries were classified before the vacancy claim, so a lapsed
  group re-taken in the same beat could be granted and revoked at once. Lost

  revoke sets are disjoint by construction.

fix(daemon): buffer shim frames on sockets accepted before the channel FSM attaches (#940)

After a bound shim channel drops, the daemon's redial and the sandbox's
re-attach race on independent jittered backoffs. When the daemon won,
ShimServer queued the accepted socket with no message listener, so the
daemon's shim/hello was silently dropped and binding stalled for the full
timeout — the root cause of the flaky "waits for the replacement
connection while a bound channel is reconnecting" test (an ~40% failure
rate under load, and a real rebind stall in the production shim).

ShimServer now captures inbound frames (and a close) from the moment a
socket is accepted and replays them when the channel FSM attaches, so the
hello survives the unclaimed window. The reconnect test runs both sides
on injected zero-jitter millisecond backoffs (new backoff factory dep on
ShimDialer), exercising the race deterministically instead of sleeping
real seconds, and a regression test pins the replay at the ShimServer
seam. Verified 20/20 repeated runs (10 under full-suite load) vs 6/10
before.

The daemon half of the duty exchange, completing the loop the control plane
has been running against nobody:

  mirrors the CP's own list, and it exempts outbound duty/release from org
  resolution, since duty groups span orgs).

  platform consolidators re-derive from it, so sockets open on a grant and
  close on a revoke with no per-platform change. Cron and dream schedules move

checkout that was there all along.

`createWorkspaceGit` resolved its root from `agent.workspace.path` — this
daemon's own filesystem — while the runner seam correctly routed the invocation
into the agent's sandbox. So the shim received a cwd like
`/var/lib/agentconnect/agents/<id>/workspace`, its cwd fence refused it as
escaping the workspace root, `isRepo()` swallowed the refusal the way it
swallows every git failure, and the seam answered `isRepo:false`. The console
draws that as a from-scratch workspace: no files, no commits, no commit box, and
all four writes declined as data. The ACP path had this right already
(`resolvePreparedWorkspace` → `clusterWorkspaceCwd`); only the panels went
without, so the two halves of the same rule sat one function apart.

`consoleWorkspaceGitRoot` is that missing half, next to its sibling and reusing
it: the daemon-local resolution still decides WHETHER there is a workspace to
name — absent stays absent, so a shared-workspace sessionId is refused exactly
as before, and a session-isolated one still refuses loudly — and only the
coordinates change.

Two reads in the seam still went to the local filesystem, which the corrected
root then made visible:

- `exists` on a path with no changes in scope came from a `realpath` of the
  workspace root, which under --k8s resolves nothing at all, so every unchanged
  path answered "no such file". It is now asked of git (`ls-files --cached
  --others`) when the workspace is on a sandbox volume; an ignored file is the
  one case that answers absent.
- `lastFetchAt` is `.git/FETCH_HEAD`'s mtime and no git subcommand reports it,
  so it answers "unknown" for a sandbox workspace rather than stat-ing a path
  that belongs to another filesystem. Restoring it needs a shim stat.

Tests pin the coordinate mapping and reproduce the cluster shape without a
cluster — a root in pod coordinates that exists nowhere locally, with git
running in a real checkout through the resolver. Reverting the `exists` change
fails two of them.

The Files panel and the local-skills list are NOT fixed here and stay empty for
a cluster agent: both answer from `node:fs`, and the shim serves `materialize`
but no read or list, so there is nothing to route them to yet. §2.6 records

* feat(daemon): serve the console's workspace files from the pod they live on

A cluster agent's Files panel listed an empty directory and its skills list
reported "not prepared yet", both about a machine the workspace was not on.
`WorkspaceReader` answered from `node:fs` and `createLocalSkillsReader` probed
`existsSync`, while the files were on the sandbox pod's volume — and a scratch
edit was published to the daemon's own disk, where nothing would ever read it.
The `read` capability has been in the grant vocabulary since the channel was
designed ("read a bounded file back out (BFF workspace reads)") and is already
in RUNTIME_GRANTS; only the handler was missing.

Rather than drive remote filesystem primitives from the daemon, the four
operations move whole. `workspace-files.ts` is the placement layer — list, read,
write, delete, with the containment, the atomic hard-link publish and the frame
budgets — and the shim runs THAT, unchanged, on the volume it has mounted. Two
reasons it is shared rather than reimplemented:

- A primitive set fails on both counts that matter. A 200-entry listing becomes
  200 round trips, and the atomic publish's checks — whose whole point is that
  they sit adjacent to their rename — would straddle a WebSocket.
- The shim's rule is that a check on the far side of a channel is not a check on
  this side. Sharing the implementation satisfies it more strongly than a second
  copy would: the containment is not a re-derivation of the daemon's, it is the
  same lines executing where the files are.

So the daemon keeps the policy — which agent, which root, whether the workspace
is writable, serialising against the runtime — and sends the answer with the
request; the shim fences that root against its own workspace root and enforces
the write gate again. `workspaceLocation` now resolves in execution coordinates
for BOTH the file reader and the git seam, because the directory the console
browses and the one it commits are the same directory.

Two refusals travel as data in the reply rather than as an error frame: a
containment violation with its machine-readable reason, and a stale-mtime
conflict. A shim error frame carries only a string, and the console has to tell
"that path is not readable" from "the daemon may be offline" — flattening them
would make a contained path escape read as an outage. The daemon rebuilds them
as the same classes the local path throws, so the dispatcher cannot tell the two
filesystems apart. Everything else stays an error frame, which is what a bad
root or an unexpected EIO should read as.

Skills: a cluster agent's are whatever its repository committed, reported as
`repo` — the daemon installs none into a pod, so there is no ownership ledger
for one, but `.claude/skills` in the checkout is real and is what the harness
loads. The sandbox walk is a separate traversal on purpose: the local one
streams its dirents so a hostile checkout with a million entries is never
materialized, and no channel can stream a directory. It shares the caps, the
name dedup and the ordering through one accumulator, and inherits containment
from the shared operations, so the difference stays traversal-shaped.

`wire-slice.ts` moves up one directory: the placement layer needs it and
`workspace/` importing from `cp/` would have the dependency backwards.

Not addressed, and now documented in §2.6: a console workspace read needs a
BOUND sandbox, and with no channel the panels answer "absent" rather than waking
the pod. The console re-reads on every session page view, so waking would
resurrect a suspended pod on each visit and fight the idle sweep. Git already
behaved this way; the two surfaces agreeing beats one being quietly more eager.

The shim bundle grows 300 kB → 331 kB (gzip 66 → 75) and stays a single
self-contained file with no external imports. It does NOT pull in the skills
ledger or the YAML parser — asserted by inspecting the built bundle — which is
why the sandbox skills walk lives on the daemon side of the channel.

* fix(shim): bind a pinned read to the directory's inode, not to its path

Fifth review round, same containment boundary and a later window: the operations
validate a name, then do path-based I/O after an `await`. The runtime owns the
volume, so it can rename the checkout aside and put something else at the same
path after `canonicalUnder` returns, and `readdir`/`open` follow the replacement.
Re-resolving the name cannot notice — the path still resolves, still canonically,
still inside the mount. Only the inode differs.

So a pinned read now carries the directory's IDENTITY, captured at validation and
re-checked before anything is returned. What that buys, precisely: the work may
touch a replacement, but it cannot produce a RESULT from one — entries, bytes and
mtimes are all discarded on mismatch. The mutations check it immediately before
their publish (the `link`, the `rename`, the `unlink`) rather than after, since a
write that has already landed in a replaced parent cannot be taken back. And the
pinned file open adds `O_NOFOLLOW`, which `canonicalUnder` has just proved is a
no-op unless the target BECAME a symlink — the one window looking again cannot
cover.

This is the binding Node affords: it has no fd-relative `readdir`, so the sequence
is resolve → act → verify rather than open-once-and-operate. What is irreducible
is a swap inside the final syscall pair, which now produces a refusal rather than
data, and which the daemon's own instance does not carry at all — its workspace is
not on a filesystem an agent controls, so it keeps the unpinned path and its two
extra `lstat`s.

Pinned by a test that renames a different directory onto the validated path —
renamed rather than deleted and recreated, because a freed inode can be handed
straight back and the test would pass for the wrong reason.

the pod side is now its own implementation. That reverses this PR's earlier
argument, and the reason is that the argument was wrong: sharing the daemon's
code made the containment "the same lines", but those lines resolve names, and
the two halves stand on filesystems with different owners. What they still share

so a console cannot learn which filesystem its agent is on from a reply's shape.

feat(control-plane): recompute duty groups when their inputs change (#949)

* feat(daemon): hold duty leases and serve only the agents they cover

The daemon half of the duty exchange, completing the loop the control plane
has been running against nobody:

- DutyRegistry (cp/duty-registry.ts) tracks the groups this daemon holds. A
  grant REPLACES its group, so a bumped term or a re-issued grant converges
  without special cases; the registry derives the agent and bot projections
  everything else reads.
- The heartbeat carries {held digest, headroom} — but only on an install-wide
  (frame-mode) connection, so a single-org daemon sends exactly what it sent
  before and the CP-side path stays dormant for it.
- duty/grant and duty/revoke dispatch as install-wide EVTs (the frame set now
  mirrors the CP's own list, and it exempts outbound duty/release from org
  resolution, since duty groups span orgs).
- transportAgents() filters by held duties, which is the whole gate: all five
  platform consolidators re-derive from it, so sockets open on a grant and
  close on a revoke with no per-platform change. Cron and dream schedules move
  the same way through one syncAgentSchedules helper — a cron is an ingress
  edge, so it fires only at the holder.
- Losing a duty is NOT a removal: the light teardown stops turns, schedules,
  and the ACP host, and deliberately never touches the workspace, the agent
  registry entry, the CP-drop latch, or the removal tombstone — a re-grant
  needs nothing from the CP to revive service.
- A whole-daemon drain surrenders its leases with duty/release so a survivor
  can claim immediately; best-effort, since the fallback is lease expiry.

Enforcement is opt-in behind features.dutyEnforcement (default false). The
exchange itself always runs on a pooled daemon — the ledger needs the digest
to converge — but until the flag is on a grant or revoke only moves
bookkeeping, so the ledger can be watched converging before it gates a single
platform connection.

feat: the duty activation rendezvous (#951)

* feat(protocol,control-plane,daemon,relay): the duty activation rendezvous

A trigger for an unheld duty group had nowhere to go: the ledger names no
holder for a group nobody has claimed, and the relay cannot ask a question it
has no frame for. The design's answer (§4.4) is that members volunteer — the
relay routes to any connected member, that member claims on receipt, and a
loser names the winner so the trigger re-routes in one more hop.

- protocol: `duty/claim` (D→C REQ) → `duty/claim/ok`, carrying either the grant
  to install verbatim or the incumbent that won. `RdAck` gains the typed
  `not_holder` reason plus an optional `holderDaemonId` — the first NAK on this
  wire that carries a redirect target, modelled on how `childSessionId` returns
  data the caller could not derive.
- control-plane: the claim handler resolves the org from the agent itself (a
  claimant never asserts one) and runs through the lease service's per-daemon
  lane, so a claim cannot interleave with that member's own heartbeat exchange.
  This is the first caller of `claimAgentHome`, which has been sitting unwired
  since the ledger landed.
- daemon: an inbound `rd/msg` for an agent whose duty this member does not hold
  now claims it — winning re-enters the normal dispatch path, losing answers
  `not_holder` with the winner. The verdict is deliberately not cached in the
  dedup map: a later grant must not keep replaying a refusal. A CP blip answers
  with no holder, so the router retries rather than re-routing into the void.
- relay: one `sendWithRendezvous` helper behind both IM paths, and the same
  re-route for webchat turns. It re-sends the SAME msgId so the true holder's
  own dedup still protects against a double delivery, and it stops after one
  hop — chasing a stale ledger is the retry's job, not the router's.

Reachable only under `features.dutyEnforcement`, which stays off by default:
until it flips, no daemon refuses a trigger, so none of this fires.

* fix: gate rendezvous claims on capacity and drain, and stop claiming a retry that does not exist

Review found three correctness issues in the activation rendezvous:

- The claim path bypassed the member's own capacity gate, so a full daemon
  could take another group — including a multi-agent one — and sit over
  `maxAgents` indefinitely. Headroom is now one function shared by the
  heartbeat digest and the claim, and a claim at zero headroom refuses
  without asking the CP.
- Claims were not fenced by draining. A member could take a fresh lease
  during its own release handoff and ack the drain still holding duty, or pin
  duty to an agent whose gate was about to drop the very turn that triggered
  the claim. Both are now refused before the CP round-trip.
- The relay claimed "the router's ordinary retry covers that window". It does
  not: HTTP IM ingress has already acknowledged and deduplicated the provider
  callback by the time an ack comes back, so nothing upstream re-presents the
  message. A trigger the rendezvous cannot place — no holder named, holder not
  on this relay, or the redirect target refusing in turn — is now counted in
  the per-bot drop counter and logged as the drop it always was, and the
  comment says plainly that bounding this window is the ledger's job, not the
  router's.

* fix(daemon): judge rendezvous capacity and drain on the claim's result, not before it

The gates added in the previous commit were themselves wrong in two ways, both
caught in review:

- Refusing to ask the CP at zero headroom suppressed the one answer that makes
  a stale delivery routable — the incumbent's identity — so a full member
  turned a re-routable trigger into a drop. It also could not enforce what it
  claimed: concurrent claims each read the same headroom, and the group a claim
  wins may cover several agents, not the one it asked about.
- The drain check was a point-in-time test before an async round trip, and a
  whole-daemon drain reopens `draining` BEFORE the leases are surrendered, so a
  claim could still start during the release handoff and install a grant the
  release snapshot had already passed.

Both gates now run after the round trip: a full or draining member still asks,
and hands back anything it wins (`duty/release`, falling back to lease expiry).
Capacity is judged against the agents the granted group actually brings that
this member does not already cover, with one slot reserved per in-flight claim
so concurrent ones cannot collectively overshoot. A new latch covers the whole
whole-daemon drain — including the window after `draining` reopens — so no
claim can outlive the handoff.

* fix(daemon): remove the phantom duty slot and join in-flight claims on drain

Two defects in the previous fix, both caught in review:

  zero, so a full member read one slot of capacity that did not exist and
  accepted another agent; concurrent claims each did the same to the same slot.
  The pending-claim view is now computed unclamped and excludes only this
  claim's own reservation, so a full member comes out negative and refuses.
- The drain latch blocked new claims but never joined the ones already awaiting
  the CP, and with an empty local registry `releaseAllDuties()` returned
  without any barrier at all — so a drain could finish and clear the latch
  while an older response was still in flight, installing a grant after
  `drain/done`. The release now joins every in-flight claim first, inside the
  latch, so each one sees it and hands back whatever it won.

count, and its members are what a drain awaits.

`maxAgents: 0` means unbounded, but the wire still needs a finite headroom, so

id→org maps. An install-wide member has no connection org, its maps only
cover agents it has already installed, and an `agent/detach` payload is

frame. In test this surfaced as an agent whose placement committed while

four agent-lifecycle senders now take it explicitly and thread it through
`request`/`send`, which already accept an org override for exactly this

still wins.

* fix(protocol): state key-server validity as durations, not instants

Review found both time checks broken, and they share one cause — the
response spoke in absolute instants.

chronological: '…00.001Z' sorts before '…00Z', so a refresh scheduled
after its own expiry passed and the valid inverse was rejected.

keyGrantViolation subtracted the caller's request-time clock from an

counted as granted validity — a server honouring 3600s exactly was

it lacks, the member asks the CP for exactly that agent's bundle
(`duty/fetch` → `duty/fetch/ok`) and installs it.

- protocol: `DutyFetch { agentId }` and `DutyFetchOk { bundle? }`, where
  the bundle is the same `{agentId, spec, integrations, crons}` trio
  `agent/activate` carries. An absent bundle is the "you do not hold it,
  or it is gone" answer — never an error frame.
- control plane: `duty/fetch` handler modeled on `duty/claim`. Holding the
  duty IS the authorization — a new `DutyGroupRepo.holdsAgent` join
  answers only for an unexpired lease on a group covering the agent, so a
  member gets exactly the agents it has won. The bundle is assembled by
  reusing `AgentMoveService.snapshot()` + `activationDefinition()` through
  a new public `bundleFor(agent)`, so nothing is duplicated.
- daemon: `CpClient.fetchDutyAgent` plus `installGrantedAgents`, which
  applies the bundle the way `applyAgentActivate` does (revision fence,
  integrations, crons, exact dependents, reconcile) minus the move fence
  and workspace preparation, inside `queueAgentLifecycle`. Agents staged
  for a move or pending removal are skipped, and failures are logged, not
  thrown into frame dispatch.

`applyDutyGrant` fires the install; the rendezvous claim AWAITS it before
answering `granted` — that path exists precisely because a trigger arrived
for an unserved agent and the turn is dispatched right after, so answering
early would reproduce the bug.

Deliberately out of scope: `features.dutyEnforcement` stays off, the grant
policy stays `incumbent`, and placement/`agent.daemonId` semantics and the
reaper are untouched. This adds the missing capability only.

* fix(duty): drop a granted group whose install fails

Review finding: a failed install was swallowed. `claimDutyForTrigger` still
answered `{granted: true}` and dispatched the turn into an agent that was
not there, and nothing ever retried — the member had already applied the
grant, so its heartbeat digest reported that group at the matching term and
the lease exchange had nothing to say ("confirm the terms or supersede,
never both"). The agent stayed permanently absent while the member claimed
to serve it. Only a reconnect recovered it.

A duty this member cannot serve must not be held. On install failure the
whole granted group is now dropped from the local `DutyRegistry` (a group
may cover several agents, and a member missing one cannot serve its work).
The digest then omits it, the CP sees a group it leases to this member that
the member does not report, and its existing missing-regrant path reissues
the grant — that IS the retry, paced by the heartbeat rather than a private
loop. The lease is deliberately NOT released to the CP: the term stays
stable, and under the soak-phase `incumbent` grant policy an explicit
release would leave the group vacant rather than move it.

- `DutyRegistry.drop(groupIds)` — the local half of a revoke, which
  `applyRevoke` now delegates to. The daemon's `dropUnservableDuties` uses
  the same `stopServingAgent` path a `duty/revoke` takes, never the removal
  path, so workspace, sessions, and the registry entry survive (#948).
- `claimDutyForTrigger` answers `{granted: false}` on install failure, and
  only AFTER the local drop, so the answer and the local state agree.
- A per-agent failure stamp suppresses re-fetching for one heartbeat
  cadence, so neither regrants nor inbound triggers can spin the pull
  faster than the beat that offers the group back. Each attempt warns.

* fix(duty): install before opening the serving gate

Two review findings, one shape: the serving gate opened before the agent
was servable.

Applying a grant is what makes this member ROUTABLE for its agents — the CP
and the relay resolve triggers to whoever holds the group — so a grant
applied while its install was still in flight advertised service the daemon
could not yet give. A trigger landing in that window was dropped, and could
not even be re-routed, because the holder it resolved to was this member.
And an empty `duty/fetch/ok` was treated as success, though it is the CP
saying "you do not hold this duty, or the agent is gone" — the strongest
signal available that local state disagrees with the ledger.

Both are fixed by ordering rather than by a second gate: `admitDutyGrants`
installs first and applies the grant second, and an empty bundle now fails
the install like any other error. A group that fails is never applied at
all, so the digest omits it, the CP sees a lease this member does not
report, and its existing missing-regrant path reissues it — the same retry
as before. Checked rather than assumed that nothing needs the group present
in the meantime: `renewHeld` renews by holder alone, and `transportAgents`
(the only other digest reader) filters BY held duties, so installing first
means a granted agent's sockets open exactly once, after it exists.

An agent already present needs no fetch, so the common path is unchanged;
only a genuinely new agent waits, and waiting is correct. A group is served
as a unit, so its bots wait on its agents too — that is the point.

This also collapses round 1's drop path: with the grant never applied there
is no group to drop, so `dropUnservableDuties` and `DutyRegistry.drop` are
gone and `duty-registry.ts` is back to untouched. The per-agent failure
stamp stays, so a permanently broken agent cannot outpace the heartbeat.

`claimDutyForTrigger` follows the same order — install, hold, then answer —
and answers `granted:false` without ever having held the group when the
install fails or comes back empty.

feat(duty): self-fence held duties when the CP link outlives the lease horizon (#976)

* feat(duty): self-fence held duties when the CP link outlives the lease horizon

The duty ledger's no-split invariant is `T_reassign > T_fence`: a member must
stop serving its duties BEFORE the CP can hand them to a successor. Only the CP
half existed — a lease dies at `lastRenew + leaseMs` and `claimVacant` may then
reassign it — while the daemon kept every grant on losing the link. A partitioned
ex-holder therefore served the same agents a successor had already claimed.

The horizon is SENT, not duplicated. `auth/ok` already hands the daemon one
timing constant (`heartbeatSec`); the lease horizon rides the same frame as an
optional `dutyLeaseMs`, sourced from the CP's own `DUTY_LEASE_DEFAULTS.leaseMs`.
A copy on the daemon could drift from the value the CP actually reassigns on,
and that drift is precisely what the invariant forbids. Optional, so a new
daemon against an old CP and an old daemon against a new CP both stay defined.

The deadline is anchored on the last heartbeat that CARRIED DUTIES on a live
socket — the same event the CP renews from — never on the moment of disconnect,
which would overshoot the CP's expiry by up to one cadence when the socket dies
just before a due beat. The fence fires at 3/4 of the horizon past that beat;
the remaining quarter absorbs clock skew, the beat's in-flight delivery, and a
beat the CP dropped. The inequality is documented where the constant lives.

The fence is gated on `dutyEnforced()`. With `features.dutyEnforcement` off (the
production default) duties gate no service at all, so a fence that tore down
platform connections would drop live traffic for no reason. With enforcement off
there is nothing to fence and nothing happens.

Teardown is a local `duty/revoke`, never a removal (#948): held groups are
cleared and `stopServingAgent` stops the platform connections, schedules, and
running host, while workspace, sessions, and the registry entry survive. No
private recovery path: an empty digest is what recovers it — on reconnect the CP
sees leases it holds for a member reporting none and its existing
missing-regrant path reissues them, which re-installs the agents through #972's
`admitDutyGrants`.

The fence lifts on a lease exchange, not on an open socket: the next heartbeat
carrying duties re-anchors the deadline and cancels the timer, and a reconnect
with a fence pending beats immediately rather than waiting a full cadence, so a
healthy link is never fenced.

With no horizon in `auth/ok` the daemon fences on a built-in 120s fallback and
warns once per connection. Silently never fencing would disable a safety
mechanism without saying so; every CP that ever shipped uses exactly this value,
and the warn names the guess.

Tests: a control-plane restart bumps `sessionEpoch` and fences nothing (#955's
acceptance run); the fence fires after the horizon with the link down and leaves
the held set empty with the agents unserved; workspace, sessions, and registry
survive it; a re-grant restores service without re-fetching; enforcement off is
a no-op; and the deadline is pinned to the last heartbeat rather than the
disconnect. Each assertion was mutation-checked.

Out of scope: `features.dutyEnforcement` stays off, the grant policy stays
`incumbent`, and placement and the reaper are untouched. This is one of three
gates on the enforcement flip, with #973 and #975.

* fix(duty): anchor the self-fence on confirmed renewals and close the sockets

Two review findings, each of which defeated the mechanism.

**1. The anchor was evidence we queued a frame, not evidence the CP renewed.**
`lastDutyBeatAt` advanced when the daemon SENT a duty-carrying heartbeat. On a
half-open socket `send()` succeeds locally, the frame never arrives, `renewHeld`
never runs — and the daemon pushed its deadline forward anyway. The CP's expiry
was anchored on the beat it processed, ours on the beat we queued, and on a
half-open socket those diverge without bound.

The CP now answers every duty-carrying beat it actually processed with
`duty/renewed { leaseMs }`, a sibling of the grant/revoke the exchange already
replies with, emitted right after `renewHeld`. The horizon is RELATIVE — "your
leases live this much longer, from when I renewed them" — so the daemon anchors
on RECEIPT and the two sides never compare wall clocks: receipt is strictly
after the CP's renew, which is what makes the daemon's deadline conservative,
and both ends of its subtraction are its own clock, so skew cannot enter. A beat
the CP dropped (its per-daemon lane drops one that overlaps a running exchange)
produces no confirmation, and the countdown correctly keeps running.

That also retires the fraction as a guess about the peer: the horizon is told to
the member on each renewal, and the remaining quarter is now pure slop —
one-way delivery of the confirmation, scheduling delay, and the teardown itself.
Breaking the invariant would take a confirmation delivered more than a quarter
of the horizon late (30s at the shipped 120s).

The fence is consequently armed while the link is UP, re-armed by each renewal,
rather than armed on disconnect: a half-open socket produces no close event, and
only a running deadline fences it. The reconnect cancel became "cancel on a
confirmed renewal": a reconnect beats immediately, and the confirmation that
elicits is what lifts the fence.

Compatibility is unchanged in shape. A CP too old to announce a horizon in
`auth/ok` is a CP too old to confirm renewals, so that single field is the
capability signal: absent, the daemon warns and falls back to the built-in
horizon AND the weaker send anchor — strictly worse on exactly this failure, and
still better than silently never fencing.

**2. The fence was logical but not physical.** Verified in the code: the
platform consolidators run only when `connectionsDirty`, which is derived purely
from the agent-file diff (`toStart` / `toStop` / `change.integrations`). A duty
change moves no agent file, so a fence — and `duty/revoke` before it — cleared
the registry and closed no socket. Direct platform ingress has no per-message
duty check (`transportAgents` IS the gate, and the only other gate,
`handleRelayMsg`, covers relay traffic only), so a partitioned ex-holder went on
receiving and processing platform traffic for agents a successor already served.

`onDutyChanged` now marks connections dirty and the next reconcile pass converges
them, which fixes the fence and the revoke path together. The flag is claimed per
pass, so a duty change landing mid-pass is honoured by the coalesced re-run.

Also: `duty/renewed` had to be added to the CP's install-wide frame allowlist.
Without it `organizationFor` raised SCOPE_DENIED on a pooled connection and
aborted the whole exchange — caught by the existing handler tests.

Tests, both mutation-checked:
- a half-open socket where every beat is sent and none is answered: the deadline
  does not move and the fence fires on schedule (restoring the send anchor fails
  this test and no other assertion in the suite);
- a real Slack socket in the pool is stopped and evicted by the fence (removing
  the duty-driven convergence fails exactly this test);
- the CP confirms each processed beat with the horizon it just wrote, and a beat
  with nothing to grant or revoke still carries the confirmation;
- the daemon adopts each announced horizon, never arms before a renewal it could
  lose, and the older-CP fallback still fences.

* fix(duty): close the three edge paths that still bypassed the self-fence

**1. The confirmation is emitted last, after the exchange it belongs to.**
`duty/renewed` went out right after `renewHeld`, before the exchange knew which
of the member's reported groups no longer belonged to it. A delivered PREFIX of
the exchange then extended the fence even when the CP had renewed none of them —
the fence is global while renewal is per-group.

Ordering closes it, and ordering alone is enough: `renewHeld` and `listHeldBy`
use the identical `holder = <daemon>` predicate and run back to back in the same
exchange, so a digest entry is renewed if and only if it appears in `held`.
Everything else lands in `lost` and is answered by a revocation (or by a grant
that re-took it) in this same exchange. One socket delivers in order, so "the
confirmation arrived" now implies "everything that supersedes what I hold
arrived first". Making the confirmation enumerate the renewed groups would carry
the same information at the cost of a per-group payload, so the smaller fix is
the whole fix. A truncated exchange, or any throw before the last line, simply
leaves the fence running — the safe direction.

**2. A won rendezvous claim arms the fence.** `duty/claim` creates this member's
lease (`claimAgentHome` writes `expiresAt = now + leaseMs`) and it serves that
agent immediately — frequently before any heartbeat has been confirmed, so the
fence had never armed and losing the link right then fenced nothing. A granted
`duty/claim/ok` now anchors on receipt exactly like a renewal, and is
conservative for the same reason: the CP wrote `expiresAt` strictly earlier.

The reply does not need to carry the horizon. `claimAgentHome` leases for the
same `DutyLeaseConfig.leaseMs` the exchange uses and `auth/ok` announced, in the
same process on the same connection, so the value already held is exactly right;
adding a field would put the same number on the wire twice. The old-CP fallback
needs nothing special either — the claim path arms through `armDutyFence` like
every other anchor, so it inherits the built-in horizon.

A lost claim anchors nothing: no lease was created here.

That test also caught a sentinel bug of my own: `lastLeaseRenewalAt` used 0 for
"never renewed", so a renewal at clock time zero armed nothing. It is now
`undefined`.

**3. The convergence request survives a failed reconcile.** The dirty flag was
cleared at the top of `runReconcile` and neither restored nor retried when the
pass threw, so one failed reconcile left a fenced agent's sockets — and its
direct ingress — live indefinitely: exactly the condition the previous round was
about. Replaced with a requested/converged counter pair: a pass CLAIMS the
requested value and publishes it only after the platform layer has actually
converged. A pass that throws leaves the request outstanding, a duty change
landing mid-pass stays outstanding (the claimed value is published, not the
current one), and `convergeDutyConnections` retries with a doubling backoff to a
30s poll rather than giving up — any other reconcile trigger satisfies the same
request and ends the loop. The retry timer is cleared on shutdown.

Tests, each mutation-checked:
- the confirmation is the last duty frame of an exchange whose digest entry was
  reassigned (emitting it first fails this and one other test);
- a won claim arms the fence with no prior renewal, and a lost one does not
  (dropping the claim anchor fails only the won-claim test);
- the fence's socket is closed on retry after a reconcile pass that throws, with
  the test asserting the connection is gone, not that a counter moved
  (consuming the request up front fails only that test).

* refactor(duty): give the self-fence a deadline per group, not one global one

The two remaining findings were one structural flaw: a single global deadline
over per-group leases. A fresh grant delivered without its confirmation left a
group serving with no deadline at all, and a granted claim for B reset the one
deadline A was relying on, carrying A past its own unchanged CP expiry. Both are
unrepresentable now rather than patched.

`CpClient` keeps `dutyDeadlines: Map<groupId, {anchoredAt, deadline}>`:

- **`duty/grant` receipt** sets that group's deadline, before admission (which is
  async) — the grant's own receipt is what arms it, so a lost confirmation, a
  first grant, and a group granted back after a fence are all covered.
- **A won `duty/claim/ok`** sets only the claimed group's deadline. The claim
  renewed nothing else.
- **`duty/renewed`** sets a deadline for every group in the daemon's digest —
  correct because `renewHeld` renews by holder with no id filter, so one
  confirmation genuinely does refresh them all. It is also where the map is
  pruned against the authoritative held set, which is why it collapses back to a
  single value after every confirmation and costs nothing in practice.
- **`duty/revoke`** drops the deadlines of groups that are no longer ours, so a
  revoked group cannot fence twice or hold the timer earlier than a live one.

The timer targets the minimum. When it fires, `fireDutyFence` sheds only the
groups whose own deadline has passed, drops those entries, and re-arms at the
next earliest; a group whose lease the CP still honours keeps serving.

`Daemon.fenceDuties(groupIds)` fences a subset through `DutyRegistry.applyRevoke`
— literally the local `duty/revoke` path, so the teardown is identical and #948
holds: workspace, sessions and registry entries survive. Using `applyRevoke`'s
`agentsLost` also fixes something the old whole-set version got wrong by
construction: an agent covered by two held groups keeps serving when only one of
them is fenced.

Everything built earlier stays: receipt-anchoring, the enforcement gate, the
`auth/ok` horizon with its old-CP fallback, the duty-driven connection
convergence with its claim-then-publish retry.

Swept for other assumptions of one global anchor, as asked:
- the reconnect immediate-beat now triggers on "any deadline is running"
  (`dutyDeadlines.size > 0`) instead of the old scalar sentinel, which also
  retires the `undefined`-vs-0 sentinel entirely;
- the flapping guarantee is now structural rather than a latch: a fenced group's
  entry is deleted, so only a fresh grant or renewal can re-arm it;
- the fence log names the groups shed, how long they went unconfirmed, and how
  many are still leased, instead of implying the whole set went.

Tests: a grant with the confirmation lost still fences on time; a grant after a
fence re-arms; claiming B does not move A's deadline; a partial fence sheds only
the expired group and fences the other at its own deadline; one renewal refreshes
them all; a revoked group stops holding a deadline; and on the daemon side, one
group is torn down (socket, schedules, host) while the other keeps serving, and
an agent shared by two held groups stays in service.

* fix(duty): make a withdrawal landing mid-admission beat the admission

Deadline tracking and every withdrawal are synchronous; grant admission is
deliberately asynchronous (`duty/fetch` + install before the serving gate opens).
Between grant receipt and `duties.applyGrant` a group therefore sits in a gap:
it has a fence deadline but is not in the digest, and nothing can withdraw it
because nothing holds it yet. Both reported sequences ended the same way — the
confirmation pruned the pending group's deadline against the digest, or the
deadline fired and found no held group to shed — and then the admission
committed and service started with no future fence.

This is not fence-specific. A `duty/revoke` and a drain release landing in the
same window have the same outcome, which is finding 1 of #975. One guard, not
three:

- `dutyAdmissions: Map<groupId, admissionSeq>` marks the groups an admission
  owns, set synchronously before the install and cleared in its `finally`.
- `withdrawDutyGroups(groupIds)` drops those marks. Every withdrawal calls it
  BEFORE its own held-set filter, because a pending group is not held and would
  otherwise be filtered out of the very withdrawal meant to stop it:
  `fenceDuties`, `applyDutyRevoke`, and `releaseAllDuties` (which withdraws
  every pending admission, since the existing claim join covers the rendezvous
  path only).
- `admitDutyGrants` re-checks the mark immediately before `applyGrant`, with no
  await in between, and refuses any group whose mark is gone or belongs to a
  newer admission. Refusal is one more term in #972's existing `servable` filter,
  and refused groups join the returned set, so `claimDutyForTrigger` already
  answers `granted: false` for them.
- `CpClientDeps.dutyPending` exposes the marks so a renewal's prune keeps
  "what we intend to hold" = digest ∪ pending. Pruning a pending group's
  deadline is precisely what left an admitted group unfenced.
- `releaseDuties` now forgets the released groups' deadlines, so a drain leaves
  no stale deadline pinning the timer either.

A refused admission leaves nothing held, nothing serving, and no deadline; the
retry story is unchanged, because the CP still leases the group, does not see it
in our digest, and reissues it through missing-regrant. A refused admission is
just another way of not holding it.

Tests exercise the handoff itself — the admission is held open at the
`duty/fetch` round trip so the withdrawal lands inside the window: a fence, a
revoke, and a drain release each refuse it, leaving it neither held nor serving
nor marked; an untouched admission still applies (the guard refuses nothing on
its own); a confirmation arriving mid-admission keeps the pending deadline, and
still prunes a group that is neither held nor pending.

fix(duty): apply a refused replacement's removals instead of keeping the old composition (#977)

A `duty/grant` entry REPLACES its group, so it carries removals as well as
additions. `admitDutyGrants` installs what an entry covers and then applies only
the entries that came back servable — and when a replacement of an already-held
group cannot be installed, the whole entry was filtered out and the previously
held entry survived at its old term AND its old composition. Keeping the servable
agents running is right (#976). Keeping the ones the replacement DROPPED is not:
an agent reassigned elsewhere stayed serviceable here until some later grant
succeeded, so two members could serve it at once — the split the duty ledger
exists to prevent.

"Refuse the new members" and "keep the departed members" stop being the same code
path. On a refused replacement of a held group the removals are applied on their
own: `DutyRegistry.shrinkToGrant` shrinks the held entry to the members both
compositions name and keeps the OLD term. An addition is what failed, so the
removals were never in doubt, and applying them alone can only ever reduce what
this member serves.

The old term is the retry. The digest keeps reporting a term the ledger has moved
past, so the exchange's STALE-TERM branch reissues the whole replacement each beat
(`dutyLease.exchange`: `stale` → `deliverable(stale).map(toGrantEntry)`), not the
missing-regrant branch — which matters, because a stale re-issue is already local
and is not charged against the member's reported headroom, while a surrendered
group would be. Surrendering the group whole would also close the split, but it
would stop serving agents this member can still serve.

Teardown is the revoke teardown, never the removal path (#948): `stopServingAgent`
per agent that is in no held group any more, so workspace, sessions and the
registry entry survive, and an agent another held group still covers keeps serving
untouched. That settling is now shared with the servable branch, so a replacement
that installs CLEANLY sheds what it dropped through the same path instead of
leaving schedules, sockets and a running host behind it.

The #976 withdrawal guard still wins: a group a revoke, a self-fence, a drain
release, or a newer admission took away mid-admission is not shrunk either — it is
not this admission's to write any more.

feat(daemon): make duty enforcement reachable from the environment (#980)

`features.dutyEnforcement` is a daemon-local, operator-owned rollout switch
that defaults to false, and it was unreachable in the deployment it was
written for. A `--k8s` pool member's state root is an emptyDir, so its
config.json is auto-created from schema defaults on every Pod start and any
edit dies with the Pod; nothing under `features` had an environment override.

Add `AGENTCONNECT_DUTY_ENFORCEMENT`, exported as `DUTY_ENFORCEMENT_ENV`
alongside the existing `K8S_RUNTIMES_ENV` precedent. The env outranks the
config file for this one key — a value that lost to a machine-generated file
could never be stated — and it is applied after the parse, so the auto-create
and optional (no file) paths carry it too.

Parsing is strict: `1`/`true`/`yes`/`on` and `0`/`false`/`no`/`off`
case-insensitively, blank or unset means "not stated", and anything else
throws at startup instead of reading as a silent off.

The daemon logs the switch at startup and, once the control-plane connection
is up and the organization scope is known, reports which of the two states it
got — enforcing, or configured-but-inactive on a non-frame connection.

The default is unchanged and nothing is turned on: this only makes the switch
reachable.

feat(duty): route agent updates and the reconnect roster to the duty holder (#978)

* feat(duty): route agent updates and the reconnect roster to the duty holder

`duty/fetch` (#972) lets a member install an agent it won a duty for, but
every subsequent update was still routed by placement. A holder that is not
the agent's `daemonId` installed one bundle and then served it frozen — and
on reconnect that install was a stale-replica candidate, so it could be
pruned outright.

- One resolution seam. `orchestrator/agentDelivery.ts` answers "which daemons
  must receive this agent's updates" — the placement, plus every member
  currently holding an unexpired duty lease covering it — and fans
  `agent/upsert`/`agent/remove` out over it. All six replicate sites (the
  agent routes, the icon, skill-source, organization-environment and
  organization-knowledge fan-outs, and the GitHub-rename convergence) go
  through it; none of them reads `agent.daemonId` to decide delivery any more.
  The lifecycle sends keep their explicit `orgId`.
- The reconnect roster is `pinned-to-me ∪ agents in the duties I hold`, and so
  are its integrations and crons — a served group whose sockets the reconcile
  dropped serves nothing. A duty-held replica is therefore never a
  stale-replica candidate, which is where the pruning happened.
- A freshness signal. `DutyMemberRef.configRevision` carries the CP's current
  spec revision for an agent member; the daemon refetches when what it holds
  is older, instead of skipping any agent it merely has. A refetch is an
  ordinary admission: same install path, same revision fence, same withdrawal
  guard.

Closes #973 — the last gate before the `features.dutyEnforcement` flip.

* feat(duty): route integration and cron updates to the duty holder too

The seam owned `agent/upsert` and `agent/remove`, but the dependent lifecycle
sends still resolved `agent.daemonId` directly. A connected non-placement holder
therefore received no integration or cron update at all — and since those
mutations do not advance `Agent.configRevision`, the grant-time freshness stamp
gave it no reason to refetch either. It kept stale credentials, stale bind rules,
or a stale schedule until it happened to reconnect: the same frozen-bundle
failure as a stale spec, one level down.

Route them through the resolver that already exists. `AgentDelivery` grows
`integrationUpsert`/`integrationRemove`/`cronUpsert`/`cronRemove`, and every
dependent sender goes through it: the cron routes, the integration routes, the
two bot installers, the derived gating convergence, and the HTTP-bot send-only
spec plus its revoke removal. Each of the six `ControlSender` lifecycle senders
now has exactly one call site in the whole control plane, inside `AgentDelivery`,
so no site outside it reads `agent.daemonId` to decide where anything goes.

Two boundaries stay put, both routing rather than replication: the relay's own
`rc/assign` target, and `cron/run`.

* fix(duty): carry the record's org on integration and cron removals

`integration/remove` and `cron/remove` carry only their resource id. On an
install-wide connection the org is resolved from the connection (absent by
construction), then the payload (an id alone), then the id→org map `register`
built — and a holder that acquired the resource through `duty/fetch` never
registered it, so the map has nothing. SCOPE_DENIED was raised before either
frame left the process: the integration delete returned 500 after the row was
already gone, the cron delete logged and returned success, and either way the
holder went on serving a deleted resource.

Take the record's own `orgId` through `AgentDelivery` and `ControlSender`, which
is the pattern #965 established for the agent lifecycle frames. The org is on the
record in hand at every call site.

The upserts needed nothing, but not for the reason it looks: `IntegrationSpec`
and `CronUpsert` declare `orgId` optional, so the schema does not force it. What
holds is that `projectSpec` and `cronToUpsert` — the only producers of either
payload — always stamp the row's org, which `organizationFor` then reads AND
remembers. Both guarantees are now pinned by tests.

`duty/fetch` also records the bundle's agent, integrations and crons into the
connection's id→org maps. Those maps are otherwise built only from the register
snapshot, so every other frame carrying a bare id — the BFF reads keyed on
agentId, cron/run, integration/forget — had the same hole for a resource
installed mid-session. It is a scoping hint, never an authorization: holding the
duty is what authorizes, and the removals do not depend on it.

fix(duty): derive a duty group for every agent, not only for edge-bearing ones (#983)

With duty enforcement on, an agent with no socket-transport integration and no
enabled cron flapped forever: the activation rendezvous minted its singleton
duty group on the first trigger, the next recompute sweep saw the agent in no
computed component and planned the group as a delete, and the revoke that
followed ran `stopServingAgent` — interrupting the agent's in-flight turn. The
next trigger minted the group again, so every webchat-only, A2A-only or
otherwise botless agent was unusable on the pool.

The two halves were fighting because ownability was being read off the edges.
`computeInputs` derived components from `integration` rows on socket bots plus
enabled `cron_def` rows, while `claimAgentHome` minted a home for any agent at
all. Seed the component set from the org's `agent` rows instead and let the
edges merge them: an edge only forces co-location, it is not what makes an
agent ownable. Crons need no input of their own — a cron's agent is an agent.

Recompute now derives what the rendezvous used to mint, so the planner sees no
orphan, a group is claimable proactively rather than only after a message, and
"claiming creates the lease" becomes the fallback for the window before an
agent's first sweep. Agent create/delete join the existing kick seams.

The incumbent grant policy filters the resulting vacant population inside
`claimVacant`, so groups for agents on org-scoped daemons cost no grant budget.
The placement fence now also requires that some agent of the group is actually
placed somewhere: a group whose agents are all unplaced has no rival incumbent,
and vacating it every sweep would only trade the delete flap for a supersede one.

definitions travel separately, and both were still resolved by placement. A duty
holder that is not the agent's placement therefore installed an agent referencing

policing DNS.

feat(duty): make the pool heal itself by making placement a target (#991)

* feat(duty): make the pool heal itself by making placement a target

Enforcement surfaced a defect the mechanism was supposed to prevent: a rollout
replaced a member, its lease lapsed, the duty group became a claimable vacancy —
and nothing claimed it. The grant policy was `incumbent`, which pins a vacancy to
the member the group's agents are already placed on, and after a rollout that id
names a Pod that no longer exists. Healing waited for a trigger; for webchat the
trigger could not even be sent, because readiness reads the same dead id (#987).

`incumbent` was soak-phase scaffolding, but it was also the only thing keeping
pool members off the agents local daemons serve, because the ledger had no notion
of which agents belong to the pool. So it is replaced rather than widened:

- `Agent.placementKind ∈ {daemon, pool}` — additive, defaulted, so every existing
  row keeps meaning what it means and reduces to the old incumbent rule exactly.
  A `pool` placement clears `daemonId`: no member id is durable.
- One resolver answers eligibility (`domain/placement.ts`) and one answers who
  serves an agent right now (`orchestrator/placementResolver.ts`). Both claim
  paths, the placement fence, delivery, the roster, the peer directory, hooks,
  relay ingress and the daemon-originated authority fences read them; nothing
  else branches on the placement kind.
- A member may claim a group iff it may hold EVERY agent in it, so a group mixing
  a pool agent with a machine-placed one is claimable by neither.
- `grantPolicy`/`incumbentOnly` are deleted. `vacateNonIncumbent` is re-derived as
  `vacateIneligible` and runs unconditionally — `renewHeld` renews by holder
  alone, so nothing else notices a holder that stopped being eligible.
- The CP bounds a group one member cannot install: consecutive absences from the
  digest hand the lease back and back that member off, so it reaches a member
  that can serve it instead of wedging on the one that cannot.

The move route takes a pool target and validates it against the union of live
members; the reaper leaves a pool agent placed; the console submits the pool as
itself and reads a server-computed readiness.

fix(duty): scope the routing confirmation to the grant it proves (#992)

#991 gated ingress addressing on the holder reporting the group in its heartbeat
digest, but recorded that as `confirmedAt` — a bare timestamp that knows THAT a
holder confirmed, never WHICH hold it confirmed. Any later state that looked the
same inherited it, and each case reopens the terminal A2A miss the gate exists to
close:

- a lapsed lease re-taken by the SAME member kept its confirmation, though the
  member may have fenced and dropped the group in between (#976) and be
  re-installing;
- an in-place composition rewrite kept it, so agents the rewrite ADDED inherited
  a confirmation the member never gave for them;
- `confirmHeld` accepted a digest carrying an old term as proof of the current
  one.

The key is now `(confirmedHolder, confirmedTerm)`, and confirmed means
`confirmedTerm = term AND confirmedHolder = holder`. `term` is already the
fencing token — every grant path bumps it, renewal never does (#939) — so it is
the identity this needed, and two of the three cases fall out with no new rule.
The third is `confirmHeld` comparing the digest's term to the row's, which is the
same rule the exchange already applies to renewal: confirm the terms or
supersede, never both.

A composition rewrite is INVALIDATED rather than cleared: `applyReconcile`
already re-grants in place at a bumped term, so the bump is the invalidation and
there is no second reason for the confirmation to move. A split's newly created
row is no longer pre-confirmed either — the member has never reported that group
id, and it re-confirms on the beat after it admits the re-grant.

`reportDutiesNow()` still lines up: after admitting a re-grant the member's digest
carries the new term, so confirmation re-arms on the immediate beat.

Migration replaces `confirmedAt`, carrying currently-true confirmations across as
(holder, term) so the deploy does not blank live ingress routing.

docs(designs): daemon groups — the tenancy axis for org-scoped member sets (#994)

* docs(designs): daemon groups — the tenancy axis for org-scoped member sets

The k8s pool is the degenerate case of a daemon group: a named set of members
within which an agent's duty may be claimed. Every prerequisite the pool design
listed for generalizing it has landed — shared data plane, self-fence,
placement as a target — and the pool has run enforced end to end, so the
"future direction" stub in k8s-daemon-pool.md §14 becomes its own document.

Almost all of it is "reuse X": install-on-grant, the fence, holder-following
delivery, proactive re-grant are keyed on the holder and do not care whether
it is a Pod or a laptop. The one new thing, and the reason this is a design
rather than a PR, is the tenancy axis. Today only install-wide connections may
touch the ledger; a local group's members are org-scoped connections, so that
door must open — narrower, never wider: a group agent may be held only by an
org-scoped connection of the agent's own org that is a member of that group,
install-wide members are never eligible for group agents, and org-scoped
daemons are never eligible for pool agents. `claimScopeOf` becomes three-valued,
`mayHold` gains one arm, the SQL mirror one join; the three duty handlers turn
`SCOPE_DENIED` into "scope is none".

Also records why the pool is not a group row (no org to put on it), what the
operator owes a local group (shared Postgres, re-cloneable workspaces), and the
load-bearing tests, including the same rollout test the pool passed.

* docs(designs): say why the pool is unified with groups in reading, not in row

* docs(designs): the pool is one per install and cross-org, never per org

* docs(designs): daemon groups — one member-set concept, the pool folded into it

Rewrites the model on the shape chosen after weighing both: instead of a
`group` placement kind beside `pool`, there is one concept — a member set —
and the pool is one row of it. `member_set(id, orgId NULL-able, name)` where
null means cross-org, never unassigned; the pool is the one org-less row per
install; a local group is a row with an org. Two write-time invariants on
membership (org-less set ⇔ org-less daemons; org set ⇔ that org's daemons)
carry the tenancy narrowing, so the read path collapses to a single rule —
"claimant ∈ agent's set" — and the resolver ends with fewer branches than it
has today. `daemon` stays its own kind: a pinned machine has no replaceability
and every set ritual would be pure cost.

no behavior change, proven by every #991 test passing unchanged; `{kind:'pool'}`
stays as API sugar at the edge), then org sets. Records the three-kind shape

* fix(knowledge): authorize the suggestion replay through the live serving seam

The sync handler still built its allowed set from `agent.daemonId === conn.daemonId`.

fix(knowledge): authorize organization reads through the serving member (#1004)

The four read handlers — `knowledge/search`, `knowledge/list`, `skills/org` and

`agent.daemonId === conn.daemonId`. A pool agent names no machine, so on an

refactor(control-plane): fold the pool into the unified member-set model (#1003)

Zero behaviour change. The install-wide pool stops being a `placementKind`
value and becomes one row of a new `member_set` table, org-less, with every
org-less daemon row enrolled as its member — which is the proof that the pool
was a set all along (docs/designs/daemon-groups.md §2, §3, §6 "PR 1", §8).

- `member_set(id, orgId, name)` — `orgId` NULL means CROSS-ORG, never
  "unassigned"; a partial unique index keeps it to one row per install.
- `member_set_member(setId, daemonId PK)` — a daemon in at most one set,
  cascading with its daemon row so a retired member is never eligible.
- `Agent.placementKind ∈ {daemon, set}` with `Agent.setId` as the `set` ref.
  The migration mints the pool row, rewrites every `pool` agent onto it,
  enrols every org-less daemon, then contracts the enum.

Three write-time invariants carry the tenancy that used to be a read-path
branch: an org-less set takes only org-less daemons, an org set only that
org's, and a `set`-placed agent may reference only the org-less set or one of
its own org. All three are enforced in the transaction that writes the row, so
`dutyEligibility`/`mayHold` collapse to one membership lookup and the ledger's
SQL mirror becomes one join to `member_set_member` on `(agent.setId, holder)`.
The claimant's scope is now READ from the ledger's own tables instead of being
asserted by the caller, so `DutyClaimScope` leaves the repository signatures.

Pool membership stays automatic: `upsertOnAuth` enrols an org-less row in the
org-less set in the same transaction that mints it, and never enrols an
org-scoped one. `{ kind: 'pool' }` stays accepted API sugar at the edge, so the

fix(control-plane): bind a skill source's repo identity server-side (#1002)

* fix(control-plane): bind a skill source's repo identity server-side

`AgentSkillEntry` requires `githubRepoId`, so a skill source without one is
dropped by the projection: the console shows it enabled, the daemon never hears
about it, and nothing is ever installed. The only trace is a CP warn line.

The value could only come from the request body, and no console entry point
sends it — Import from GitHub, Edit, and Install from skills.sh all omit it, and
the web client has no read that would surface it (`/skill-sources/preview`
returns branches/tags/skills only). Every source created through the supported
UI was therefore permanently non-installable, and `PATCH` had the same gap, so
an existing NULL row could not be repaired either.

Resolve it in the route instead. The lookup was already happening on both paths
for the private-repo guard and was throwing the id away: `getRepoMeta` wraps
`repoRefFor`, which returns exactly `{repoId, private, defaultBranch}`. One
`resolveRepoBinding` now answers all three questions per write, replacing two
duplicate round trips.

The installation token only covers repos an org installation can see, which the
commonest source of all — a skills.sh hit like `anthropics/skills` — is not. So
the binding falls back to an anonymous `/repos/{owner}/{repo}` read: the same
public endpoint the daemon already uses to verify identity before acquisition,
no credential involved.

A write that cannot bind is refused rather than persisted: 400 when GitHub says
the repository does not exist, 503 while GitHub is unreachable — the two must
not be confused. `PATCH` re-binds when the source changes or the row never had
an identity, which repairs the NULL rows already in the wild; an unchanged
bound row is left alone, so a `skills`-only edit still succeeds while GitHub is
down. Clearing the id is refused: that is precisely the broken state.

Fixing this in the CP rather than in the web modals covers the API and all
three console entry points at once.

* fix(control-plane): store the canonical repo slug with the bound identity

Review catch: GitHub follows rename and transfer redirects, so

fix(daemon): start the shim loss window when the sandbox pod is up (#1011)

* fix(daemon): start the shim loss window when the sandbox pod is up

A sandbox cold start pays PVC provisioning and an image pull, so its shim
cannot answer a dial at all until the pod is Running. The plane counted that
time against a fixed 20s rebind window, revoked the binding, and reported the
launch lost — and the ACP host torn down with it was never rebuilt, so every
later turn failed with "ACP connection closed" until the member was replaced.

The window now starts from the right event. `K8sDriver.sandboxReadiness` reads
the Sandbox the driver already watches, and a loss check that finds the pod
still coming up waits and re-reads instead of reporting; the pod's arrival
restarts the whole grace window, and the driver's own pod-up timeout is the
ceiling, so a pod that never arrives is still reported lost.

The teardown is also paired with the rebuild: a runtime that reaches terminal
exit — a lost sandbox channel is exactly that — reclaims its host through
`stopHost`, so the next message starts a fresh one on the ordinary path rather
than prompting a closed connection forever. Finally, a dial's "next connection"
promise is pre-observed, because a revoke or a supersede rejects it whether or
not anything awaits it; that rejection surfaced as an unhandled rejection.

Closes #1010.

* fix(daemon): bound the readiness read by the loss watch's own ceiling

The Kubernetes client has no request deadline, so a Sandbox GET the API server
accepts and never answers would hold the loss check open indefinitely — the
launch pinned, its session lost, its ACP host dead, and `onChannelLost` never
reached to release any of it. That is the stuck-forever outcome the pod-aware
window exists to remove, reintroduced through the read the window depends on.

Each readiness read now carries `AbortSignal.timeout(remaining)`, where
remaining is what is LEFT of the watch's ceiling — the same abort seam a watch
uses, threaded through `SandboxApi.getSandbox`. No new constant: an aborted or
failed read counts as "still coming up" for that tick, and the ceiling check
that follows it decides, so a read that stalls to the ceiling reports loss the
moment it unblocks. A watch already past its ceiling reads nothing at all.

runner the poll wins that race, so `clock.advance` fires with no timer

fix(daemon): allocate shim binding generations from the shared store (#1017)

The k8s driver counted launch generations in a per-process Map, so every
daemon started an agent's sequence at 1. A sandbox pod's shim client records
the highest generation it has ever bound and closes any later hello below it
with `4403 stale generation`, which held only under the original assumption
of one daemon per sandbox for the sandbox's life.

The pool breaks that assumption: agents are held by duty leases and move to
another member on every rollout while their Sandbox keeps running. A member
that launched an agent twice against one pod left it bound at generation 2;
its successor dialed 1, was refused, and every turn ended in
`LaunchTimeoutError: no shim channel bound for agent ... in time` until the
pod happened to be suspended and resumed.

Generations now come from `LocalStore.nextSandboxGeneration` — one atomic
upsert on a `sandbox_generations` row, so a successor continues the sequence
and two members allocating at once cannot tie. Pool members share that store
on Postgres, a local daemon keeps it in SQLite. The row outlives the claim on
purpose: the number fences a pod, and a warm-pool pod can be reused.

Nothing about the fence semantics moves. `ensureSandbox` still returns the
cached launch without allocating, so an equal-generation re-bind is still the
reconnect `ShimBindingRegistry.bind` expects, and channel loss still forgets
the launch so the next turn claims a fresh generation.
