feat(daemon): drain duty groups on SIGTERM with acknowledged releases and a draining bit (#1021)

* feat(daemon): drain duty groups on SIGTERM with acknowledged releases and a draining bit

A daemon-pool rollout should surge the whole pool and let the old members drain slowly,
with no capacity dip and each agent moving at most once. Two application-side properties
make that true (#1016):

- A draining member claims nothing. `Daemon.stop()` latches the claim gate first (no
  rendezvous claim, no grant admitted, zero headroom) and reports `draining: true` on
  its heartbeat digest at once. The control plane keeps the bit sticky for the
  registration: `claimVacant`, `claimAgentHome`, and the missing-regrant re-issue all
  skip a draining member until it registers afresh, so a vacated group can only land
  on a member that is staying. Renewal continues meanwhile.
- Drain is real, slow-safe, and acknowledged. Each held group is withdrawn locally and
  handed back with a `duty/release` that is awaited and retried until acknowledged, one
  group at a time, the moment that group is idle — idle groups immediately, a busy group
  when its last turn settles — all before the CP socket closes. Previously `stop()`
  never released duties at all, so a rollout waited out the lease horizon. In-flight
  turns are not cut to speed the rollout up; the whole drain is bounded by the new
  `limits.poolShutdownDrainMs` (5 min default) and ends with one summary log line
  (groups/agents released, acks, releases that timed out).

The CP also logs a warning when a group's term moves twice inside a window, so a
double move is visible on the next rollout without a dashboard.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): release late grants on shutdown and ack only after teardown is real

Two gaps in the shutdown duty drain, from review:

- A grant that wins after the shutdown latch (an exchange that began before the SIGTERM) was
  dropped, leaving the ledger believing the exiting member holds it until refusal accounting or
  lease lapse. It is now handed straight into the acknowledged release path, never installed,
  and awaited before the CP socket closes.
- A group's release was sent while its host stop and platform-connection convergence were only
  scheduled. The release now waits for the agents' hosts to stop and for the duty-connection
  convergence to run; if that cannot be confirmed by the drain deadline the group is not
  released and its lease is left to lapse, counted as such in the summary.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): only never-served late grants are released early; a failed host stop lapses

Three lifecycle gaps in the shutdown duty drain, from review:

- A late grant is released immediately only for a group this member never served. A grant for
  a group already held, mid-admission, or in its teardown window is a replacement, and the
  group's own release path (busy wait, withdraw, confirmed teardown, ack, else lapse) owns it;
  a group already left to lapse stays so.
- The CP-commanded rebalance drain ignores grants that land while suspended again, as before;
  only the shutdown path hands late grants back with an ack.
- A rejected host stop no longer reads as teardown done: `stopServingAgentSettled` propagates
  the failure, the release loop leaves that group unreleased and counts it as left to lapse.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): one path for late grants on shutdown, with observable host teardown

A grant that lands after the shutdown latch is no longer classified by local state (which missed
a teardown a revoke or fence started moments before the SIGTERM). Every late grant takes one path:
wait for the release loop to withdraw the group if it is still held, prove it is not served here
with the same host-stop and convergence primitives the loop uses (confirmDutyTeardown), then the
acknowledged release — or left to lapse. Host teardown is observable per agent (dutyHostStops):
the fire-and-forget wrapper and the settled variant register there, later callers chain behind a
pending stop, and a failed stop stays unconfirmed for the rest of the process.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): settle late shutdown grants only after the release loop is done

A grant that lands during the shutdown duty drain is now simply recorded — never installed,
never acknowledged early — and released acknowledged only once the release loop has finished
with every held group, when nothing is served here any more; a late grant covering an agent of
a group left to lapse (or one whose host stop is still recorded as pending or failed) lapses too.
This replaces the per-case teardown proofs for late grants, at the cost of a small delay bounded

per-member state that outlived the duty. An ex-holder kept an agent's
launch after a revoke, fence or drain, its `busy` read zero, and its idle
sweep patched the Sandbox to Suspended underneath the pod the new holder
was serving. After a rollout the opposite held: nobody had a launch, so an
idle pod was never suspended.

  gate `transportAgents` uses) and floors idleness at the time the launch

fix(control-plane): authorize hook and review reports through the placement resolver (#1047)

Hook dispatch already addressed the serving member through PlacementResolver, but
every acceptance fence behind it still compared `agent.daemonId`. A set-placed agent
names no machine, so that column is null and the comparison never held: the relay's
accepted delivery was refused, `hook/start` came back SCOPE_DENIED (non-retryable),
the review broker denied every action, and a manual GitHub redelivery was never
admitted. GitHub hooks and PR review were therefore permanently dead for those
agents, not degraded across a rollout.

Authority is now the same seam the organization reads use: placement plus the duty
leases a member currently holds. PgHookRepo resolves it once per fenced write —
before the transaction opens, so the ledger read never holds a pooled connection —
and re-reads the hook's agent inside the transaction, so the pre-read cannot widen
authority. The redelivery claim captures the routable member as its dispatch target
instead of the placement column. GithubReviewBrokerService asks the resolver at each
authorization checkpoint. No fence reads a placement kind.

fix(daemon): recover only the interrupted work this member owns (#1046)

Boot-time crash recovery still assumed "if I am starting, nothing else is
running". Two passes read the whole store with no owner predicate and rewrote
every unfinished row as wreckage from the process that just died. On a daemon
pool that store is shared and a member starts while every other member keeps
serving, so "unfinished" means "a peer is working on it".

- Webchat remote-MCP grants. `webchat_mcp_grant_ledger` gains `ownerId`,
  stamped by every record/queue write. The startup sweep
  (`markOwnedWebchatMcpGrantsRevoking`) now revokes only the grants this
  incarnation recorded — the descriptors and plaintext that died with it — so a
  live conversation no longer loses its authority because an unrelated member
  booted. The revocation drain reads only the rows this member is answerable
  for, which also stops a non-hosting member from resolving the org for an
  agent it does not have and warn-looping on the failure.
- Dreams. `dreams` gains the same `ownerId`. The boot sweep fails only what
  this incarnation left in flight, and the recovery write is CAS'd on
  `status IN ('pending', 'running')`, so a losing race can no longer overwrite
  a peer's completion with a `daemon_restart` failure (nor announce one).

A genuinely stranded row is reclaimed on the duty grant instead of at boot: the
CP handing this member an agent (`settleDutyChange`'s `agentsGained`, beside the
sandbox adoption #1045 put there) is the authoritative "this work is mine now",
mirroring `recoverPermissionRequests`. An owner id is a process incarnation, so
a fresh pod owns nothing at boot — which is the point; its predecessor's rows
return through the duty path.

Local single-daemon stores keep today's semantics exactly: with
`shared === false` the boot sweeps still recover everything, because an
exclusively owned store is itself the proof that the previous process is gone,
and the duty-scoped reclaims are no-ops there.

Store schema v4 adds both `ownerId` columns through a migration step.

Refs #1033.

A button or card action was addressed from the same routing projection an

returned whatever came back. Once that member had handed the agent's duty on —

long before the ack came back, so interactive controls on existing messages
silently stopped working for the length of the window while ordinary messages to

do. A member that no longer holds the duty names the one that does and the SAME

idempotent against live gate entries, so a gained agent with no backlog costs

feat(daemon): publish a real pool-member readiness signal (#1056)

* feat(daemon): publish a real pool-member readiness signal

A pool member's process is up long before it can serve anything: it still has to
register with the control plane and learn from a sandbox what the runtime image
provides. With no signal for that gap, the deployment side can only stand in for
it with a fixed minReadySeconds, which is either too short (the rollout scales
old members down before their replacements can take the duties) or wastefully
long.

Under Kubernetes the daemon now publishes one predicate, readinessState(), on
the two sinks a pod probe can read: an HTTP /readyz on AC_READINESS_PORT (off
unless set) and a file at AC_READINESS_FILE (default /var/run/agentconnect/ready)
for a plain exec probe. It is ready only once the CP registration is
acknowledged and the install-wide sandbox runtime probe has returned, and false
again the instant the SIGTERM latch closes, so the endpoints controller stops
routing while the pod keeps running for the whole drain.

Refs #1043, #1016.

* fix(daemon): clear the readiness marker before startup can block

The gate started only after `--k8s` startup had awaited the control-plane
registry, but the file sink is what clears a stale marker — and with the exec
probe the marker lives on a mounted path that outlives the container that wrote
it. A replacement process therefore read as ready while still unregistered, and
indefinitely so while the CP was down.

The gate is now the first thing `start()` does, before any await that can block,

older control plane still decodes: the daemon then attributes the push to

perf(control-plane): cut the integration suite's per-test DB reset and balance its shards (#1059)

The `beforeEach` reset was the suite's fixed floor. `TRUNCATE … RESTART IDENTITY
CASCADE` over 22 named tables expands to a ~70-table closure through `org`, and
pays relfilenode + catalog + WAL work per table whether or not the table holds a
row — ~60ms on an idle database, before any test does its own work.

Replace it with one server-side sweep that reads the table list from `pg_class`
and only DELETEs the tables that actually hold rows, with FK triggers suspended
for the statement so no dependency order is needed. Measured against a local
Postgres: 60ms → 2ms idle, 76ms → 11ms after a test that wrote an org plus two
daemons, and 353.70s → 233.16s of test time over the full 1322-test suite (-34%),
with no degradation over a 400-iteration soak.

Reading the list from the catalog also closes an isolation hole the hand-kept
list had: it named 22 tables and leaned on CASCADE for the rest, which left
`waitlist_entry`, `slack_platform_install`, `feishu_app_registration`,
`github_install_state`, `pending_key_shred`, `shared_thread_agent`, and
`shared_thread_participant` — 7 of 78 — surviving between tests. All 1322 tests
pass with those now swept, so nothing was leaning on the leak.

`--shard` split by file count, which is blind to cost: the heaviest file runs
~30x the cheapest, so the shard holding the expensive half absorbs every slow
minute a degraded runner adds. Pack the shards by a static `it(`/`test(` count
instead (longest-processing-time greedy, no timing manifest to keep fresh) —
109.8s/125.4s of test time by hash becomes 116.4s/116.6s packed, and re-packing
a recorded 1600s/652s CI run by the same weight lands at 1158s/1094s.

fix(daemon): compensate the cron and dream fires a duty handover swallows (#1053)

* fix(daemon): compensate the cron and dream fires a duty handover swallows

Both schedulers are process-local croner jobs armed only while this member holds the
agent's duty, and a freshly constructed Cron knows nothing of a moment that has already
passed — so a fire landing between the old holder unregistering and the new one arming
ran nowhere, with no error, no late run and no log line. cron_runs was declared for
missed-fire compensation but only ever re-reported to the control plane, and dreams had
no durable last-fired at all.

Gaining an agent's duty now replays the one occurrence its stamp says ran nowhere: the
newest missed moment only (never a backlog), inside a grace window of one interval capped
at an hour, and only where servesAgent holds. Each replay is a CAS on the stamp row, so
two members racing the same handoff fire it once. Dreams get dream_runs, the twin of
cron_runs, stamped by every tick ahead of the lifecycle gates. A local single daemon
never settles a duty change and is unchanged.

* fix(daemon): tie a schedule stamp to the definition that wrote it

A catch-up could not prove the persisted stamp belonged to the schedule now in
force. Cron ids are edited in place and dreaming policies are mutable, so "daily,
last stamped 03:00" then "switched to hourly at 12:30" replayed a 12:00 occurrence

fingerprint equals the active one — enforced in missedOccurrence and again in the
CAS claim, so a legacy NULL row and a stale peer are both refused — and the
reconcile that arms the schedules retires a stamp whose definition has moved,
re-stamping now so the new definition starts clean.

fix(control-plane): read a session's transcript from any daemon holding its store (#1019)

`GET /sessions/:id/messages` and `/tool-body` proxy strictly from the daemon
recorded on the session row, so both 503 the moment `daemonId` is null. That was
right when every daemon kept a private sqlite store. A cluster pool member does
not: its store is the install-wide data-plane Postgres its peers share. Members
are bound to a Pod UID and reaped 15 minutes after they go silent, and the FK
SetNulls the column — so a pool rollout detached every session those pods had
recorded and the console reported "the owning daemon may be offline" for
transcripts that were still fully present, one query away from any live member.

Content readers are now a property of the STORE, resolved through
`domain/session-content.ts`: the recorder first, then the members of the
session's own `contentSetId`. Nothing about the agent enters it. Not its
placement — an agent can move into a set, out of one, or between two long after a
session ran, and a store that never held the session answers an EMPTY page rather
than an error, so a wrong reader dresses a lost transcript up as an empty one.
Not its live duty holder either — an idle pooled agent holds no lease at all,
which is the ordinary state, while its transcripts stay exactly as readable.

`contentSetId` is stamped from the recorder's own membership in the same
statement that pins `daemonId`, and only while the reporter IS the recorded
owner, so a daemon that merely serves the agent now cannot claim its rows. Only
the org-less install-wide pool qualifies as shared; an operator-built org set may
be self-hosted machines with private stores.

Two consequences of reaching a peer that never served the agent. It resolves no
org from `orgByAgent`, so both read frames now take the authorized org
explicitly, as the agent frames do — otherwise SCOPE_DENIED before the frame
leaves the CP. And fall-through covers `ConnectionClosed` as well as
`NoConnection`: a socket dying between the registry lookup and the reply is
ordinary during a rollout.

The migration converges databases that ran the reverted #1018 attempt rather than
assuming a clean one. Its second backfill is an inference, confined to that
one-time recovery, with the sequence that defeats it named in the SQL.

fix(daemon): key the runtime model catalog cache by its owning member (#1058)

The runtime catalog cache is per-member state in a table every pool member shares, so
two image generations in a rollout read each other's fingerprint as a change, re-probe,
reset complete, and prune each other's model rows — and boot hydration could bring a
member up advertising models its own image cannot run.

ownerId now leads both primary keys, (ownerId, runtimeId) and (ownerId, runtimeId,
modelId), and every catalog read and write is scoped to the store's own member. A
single-daemon SQLite store owns the one '' partition forever, so its behaviour, including
cross-restart hydration, is unchanged.

gcRuntimeCatalog keeps the 30-day window for the caller's own catalogs and takes another
member's at 7 days, since an ownerId dies with the process that minted it. Staleness is a
property of one whole (ownerId, runtimeId) catalog — meta row and model rows together —
so a phase-1 refresh can never leave a complete meta standing over a pruned model set.

the CREATE block rebuilds both tables owner-keyed.

fix(control-plane): accept a hook completion from the member serving the agent (#1061)

`recordReport` fenced a completion on the run's recorded `dispatchDaemonId`, so a
pool member retired mid-run took its completion with it: the member that serves the
agent afterwards reclaims the row but the control plane answered a permanent
CONFLICT, and the reclaim path could only preserve the body, never deliver it.

Authority is now the same seam every other hook fence uses since #1047 — placement
plus the live duty leases, resolved once before the transaction and re-checked
against the agent the transaction reads. The accepted dispatch target stays on the
row as provenance instead of acting as the fence. A daemon that neither dispatched
the run nor serves its agent is still refused, and a machine-placed agent is
unchanged: its placement is by definition the serving daemon.

Closes #1051

fix(daemon): keep the agent's unrun inbox on a duty handoff (#1064)

Closes #1050. `stopServingAgent` interrupted the agent's turns with
`interruptAgentTurns(..., 'stop')`, which purges that agent's durable inbox
rows. On a pool member the inbox is the shared data-plane store, so a
graceful revoke, self-fence, withdrawal or drain release deleted the
admitted-but-unrun rows the successor holder is supposed to replay — the
one case a crash handled better, because a crash purges nothing.

`reason` cannot express the difference: removal and a duty handoff are both
`stop`. So `interruptAgentTurns` takes an explicit disposition,
`terminal` (the default: pause, removal, host respawn) or `handoff`, and
only `stopServingAgentSettled` passes `handoff`. A handoff skips
`purgeAgentInbox` and threads the intent into `interruptTurn`, which
otherwise deletes the interrupted head's row and every row queued behind
it. Retention is latched on the queue entry, so the cancelled turn's later
settle through dispatch's own terminal paths does not delete the row
either; the live claim is still dropped, so a re-grant here replays it too.

Nothing changes for a single daemon: `stopServingAgentSettled` returns
early unless duties are enforced, and every other interrupt keeps the
terminal default.

fix: the per-member assumptions collected in #1041 (#1063)

* fix(daemon): stop persisting the CP routing map on a shared store, and merge usage under a CAS

Two of the per-member assumptions collected in #1041, both in the shared
store.

`cp_routing` is one install-wide row (`CHECK (id = 1)`) and
`CpRoutingLayer` serializes its whole in-memory map on every mutation, so
every member's write erased every other member's, and each boot hydrated
whichever map was written last — a foreign `routingEpoch` with it, which
then made `applyUpdate`'s stale guard discard legitimate global-rule
updates until the real epoch caught up.

A shared store no longer reads or writes the row at all. The issue also
offered partitioning it per member, and that was the first attempt here,
but `ownerId` is a process incarnation (`randomUUID()` per
`PostgresDataPlane.open`), so a per-owner key changes on every restart:
it would leak an abandoned row each time and still hydrate nothing. There
is no stable member identity available at store-open time — the CP assigns
`daemonId` later, at auth/ok — and inventing one is a placement decision,
not a bug fix. So the honest fix is the one the issue named second, and it
costs nothing a per-owner key would have bought.

The result is safe in the direction that matters: a shared member starts
from an empty map at epoch 0, which accepts the first `route/update` it is
pushed rather than discarding pushes against a foreign epoch, and
`converge()` restates assignments from the CP snapshot on register/ok. An
exclusively owned store is untouched — it is the one store where the row
genuinely survives a restart, and it still does.

`sessions.usage` accumulation was a read-modify-write over one JSON blob,
so `addTokenUsage` and `addCost` — genuinely additive — lost the loser's
increment whenever two members touched one session across a handover. A
single relative UPDATE is not expressible in SQL both backends speak, but
a compare-and-set is: all four writers now go through one merge that
retries on a lost race and degrades, on the last attempt, to exactly the
blind write it replaces.

The usage CAS is verified on both backends — the daemon suite for SQLite,
including a test that interleaves a peer's whole write between the read
and the CAS and fails against the old read-modify-write, and a run against
a real PostgreSQL server for the dialect.

Refs #1041

* fix(control-plane): ask the placement resolver, not the daemonId column, for pool agents

Three more per-member assumptions from #1041, all the same shape: a
question about "which daemon" answered off `agent.daemonId`, which a pool
agent never fills because its placement names a set.

`findThreadOwner` required a non-null `agent.daemonId`, so the pull-on-miss
fallback that routes un-mentioned thread follow-ups never fired for a pool
agent at all. It now answers with the AGENT and nothing else; `lookupThread`

`lookupThread`'s other leg still returns `SharedThreadAgent.daemonId`

so that half is left as known-deferred.

The `channel/agents` ownership bind was made against `resolveDirectory`,
which is the ingress projection and names confirmed holders only. Between a
grant and the member's first confirming digest a member that genuinely held

returned roster stays the projection. The bind alone was not enough to
deliver the fix: `visibleToRequester` fails closed on a requester missing

  including after the git awaits.

for an agent this member does not serve is skipped — the CP would ACK a

deliberately preserves the member's local gate state.

never sends a gate twice; the daemon is idempotent by revision regardless.

cannot see; the interruption half that followed only walked this process's own

stopping the peer's live turns. The purge now skips rows whose agent this member
does not serve, exactly like the sweeps and the replay path, and a member stops
its own turns once per latch on the first admission its open circuit refuses.

The counters were a JS read-modify-write followed by an absolute upsert, so two
members charging the same conversation both read n and both wrote n + 1 — the
undercount is worst exactly when the loop is fastest. Both the charge and the
latch are now single relative, window-aware statements with `RETURNING`, so the
verdict is computed from what was actually stored and the latch is a CAS that
elects exactly one owner for the trip's side effects.

That also removes the path's dependence on an exclusive writer, which the shared
store cannot give it: the Postgres facade rewrites `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` to a plain
`BEGIN`. The remaining transaction buys atomicity between the charge and the
inbox marker only, and the rewrite now says why a shared-store statement has to
be a CAS or a relative write.

Local single-daemon behavior is unchanged: with no duty enforcement every agent
is served here, so the purge still clears the whole conversation backlog.

fix(control-plane): make the hook redelivery sweep cover the window it claims (#1071)

* fix(control-plane): make the hook redelivery sweep cover the window it claims

The redelivery reconciler is the recovery path for a delivery that never
produced a HookRun, but three things kept it from reaching one: it read a
single 100-item delivery page (minutes of traffic on a busy App, against a
30-minute window), it then advanced its coverage cursor to the window ceiling
regardless — declaring a slice swept that was never listed — and its first
sweep came a full interval after boot, so a process that restarts more often
than that never swept at all.

- `listHookDeliveries` walks the `rel="next"` cursor to `deliveredSince`,
  bounded by a page budget, and reports whether it got there. `nextPath` is
  only followed when it stays under the same API base.
- The sweep asks for its whole look-back window and, on a truncated listing,
  advances coverage only to the oldest delivery actually listed — so the next
  sweep resumes exactly where this one stopped instead of sliding past the
  unlisted slice. A short-but-complete listing (a quiet App) still advances
  normally: the distinction comes from the walk, not from the row count.
- The first sweep of a process runs after 60s, not a full interval.

Tests: cursor walk stops at the floor, truncation is reported and never
followed off-base; the sweep requests the whole window, a truncated listing
resumes at its own floor while a complete one advances, and the first sweep
fires early.

fix(relay): hold GitHub authorization and run reports across a CP reconnect (#1067)

* fix(relay): hold GitHub authorization and run reports across a CP reconnect

A GitHub PR-lifecycle delivery that lands while the relay's CP link is down
disappears without a trace. The live maintainer-permission lookup is the gate
for `pull_request:opened`/`synchronize`, it fails closed the moment the link
is not READY, and the compensating "review request required" report is emitted
on that same dead link and dropped. No HookRun row, no Check, nothing on the
PR — and GitHub never retries a delivery it considers served.

- `authorizationRequest()` is the one seam both GitHub authorization RPCs go
  through: it waits up to 30s for the link to register, and re-issues a request
  exactly once when the wire failure was retryable (the link itself). A settled
  error REP stays terminal, so a refusal or an old CP still fails closed on the
  first answer. Both callers are already off GitHub's HTTP request, so the wait
  costs nothing but a pending promise.
- `emitRunReport` queues instead of dropping, and the queue replays in order on
  READY (bounded at 200, oldest dropped first). A delivery refused pre-dispatch
  never reaches a daemon, so no late `hook/report` converges its row: that
  report is the only trace it will ever get. `firedAt` rides along, so a
  replayed row keeps its real ingest time.

Tests: authorization rides out a restart, re-issues a swallowed request exactly
once, still fails closed when the link stays down for the whole window; run
reports replay oldest-first and the queue bound drops the oldest.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(relay): buy the authorization retry with a replaced connection, not a flag

`err.retryable` is not proof the link died: `ReqRep` marks its single-shot ack
timeout retryable, and the CP answers retryable `error` REPs for its own
GitHub/DB blips while the connection stays READY. Both would have reached the
second attempt over that same live link and duplicated the upstream permission
lookup — the opposite of the single-shot-per-link contract.

A registration counter now identifies which connection a request rode. The
retry waits for a replacement and gives up on the original error when the
generation is unchanged, so only a request the CP demonstrably never answered
on a now-dead connection is re-issued.

fix(daemon): fence pool-store transcripts on the owning org (#1075)

The daemon pool's shared store keyed transcripts on (channel, thread) alone,
while the org-fenced pair the data plane declared was constructed and never read
or written. Platform channel and thread ids are unique only inside one org, so on
a pool store one org's INSERT OR IGNORE could swallow another org's message on
the same coordinates, and a (channel, thread) read could serve one org's rows to
another org's console.

transcript and transcript_recipient gain orgId (NOT NULL): it joins the recipient
primary key and prefixes every transcript index. Writes resolve it from the row's
recipient, else its sender, else the agent that made the thread live; a store no
pool shares owns one partition forever and behaves exactly as before, while a
shared store resolves through the daemon's agent registry and refuses a row it
cannot attribute. Reads key on (org, channel, thread), taking the org from the
calling agent — the callers were already agent-scoped, and no placement-kind
branch is involved. telegramThreadForMessage stays unfenced by design and says
so: it runs before routing names an agent, its key is the physical-bot-scoped
channel one org owns, and it returns a thread id rather than content.

Schema version 11 adds the columns, rebuilds transcript_recipient for its new
primary key, and drops the transcript indexes so the CREATE block re-emits them
org-first. A store no pool shares keeps every row on its single partition; a
shared store drops its transcript rows, because nothing in the store records an
agent's org and only test data exists on any shared store today.

The data plane's own transcript pair goes away, with a second data-plane
migration dropping the tables and the sequence, so one store carries the fence.

feat: wake a cluster agent's sandbox from the console instead of explaining (#1077)

* feat(protocol,daemon): add agent/wake to bring a cluster agent's sandbox up without a turn

A cluster agent's files live on its pod's volume and are only readable through
a running sandbox, so a console read that refuses with `sandbox-unavailable`
needs an explicit way to start it — a GET must never wake anything (#1070).

`agent/wake` (C→D REQ → `agent/wake/ok`) is the first half of what a turn does
before it prompts: claim the duty if this member does not hold it (the same
activation rendezvous a relay trigger uses), then bring the sandbox to Running
and bind its shim channel — and deliberately not the second half: no host is
started and no ACP session opened. The daemon answers what it observed, never
a promise: `running` when the channel is already bound, `starting` when the
bind was kicked off (coalesced per agent, so a burst of wakes costs one resume),
`unsupported` on a daemon that runs no sandboxes. Only a `--k8s` daemon
advertises `agent-wake-v1`; elsewhere there is nothing to wake and the control
plane answers without sending a frame the daemon would ignore.

The memory reader is deliberately left as it is: managed memory (`memory/`,
`channels/`) is written by the daemon's own memory provider under the member's
state root, not on the sandbox volume, so reading it "through the sandbox"
would read nothing. That is the storage gap #955 M1 already records, and it
wants its own fix rather than a nicer refusal here.

* feat(control-plane): POST /orgs/:orgId/agents/:id/wake, debounced and resolved through dispatch

The console's "start this agent's sandbox" (#1070). Authorized like every other
agent write (viewers refused, `canEdit` on the agent), the route resolves the
DISPATCH daemon rather than the serving one: a pool agent whose lease lapsed is
served by nobody for one horizon, and the wake is exactly the trigger that gives
it a holder again — it reaches a live member, which claims the agent the way a
turn would. The frame is org-scoped explicitly, since that member's connection
has no entry for an agent it does not hold yet.

Answers with what the daemon observed: 202 `running` / `starting` (poll the
workspace read), 200 `unsupported` when the daemon does not advertise the wake
(a machine-placed agent, or a daemon that runs no sandboxes) — nothing is sent
in that case. Wakes are debounced per agent in `AgentWakeCoordinator`: one in
flight is joined by every caller, and one settled within 30 s is answered from
its result, so a Files and a Memory tab opened together cost the daemon one
frame. A failed wake is not remembered.

* feat(web): wake a sleeping sandbox from the Files tab and poll the read

When the workspace root read refuses with the sleeping-sandbox code (or the
agent is known to run on the pool and the tab is opened), the panel presses the
wake once, shows a calm "Starting the agent's sandbox…" line instead of an
error, and re-issues the read with backoff (2 s → 10 s) until it answers or
90 s pass. Then the existing not-available copy returns with a Start button
that presses the wake again; a daemon with nothing to wake (`unsupported`)
keeps the copy without one. A refused press (403/404) gives up at once; any
other failure lets the read decide, since the wake may simply have raced.

`useSandboxWake` is one hook shared by the agent page's file browser and the
dock's Files panel, with `SandboxWakeNotice` carrying the two shared notices so
the copy cannot drift. The Memory tab is not wired: its reads never refuse as
asleep, because managed memory lives on the member's state root rather than
the sandbox volume (the storage gap noted in the daemon commit).

* fix(web): wake and poll only while the Files tab is actually selected

The session dock keeps every panel mounted (a hidden one is `display:none`),
so the Files panel's hook saw its hidden root read refuse as asleep and
pressed the wake just from opening a session page — a pod start as a side
effect of a page whose reader had not asked for the files.

`useSandboxWake` takes an `active` option: while false it neither presses nor
polls, and a poll interrupted by hiding resumes on the next activation. The
dock's Files panel passes its tab's selected state through; the agent page's
file browser is on screen whenever it is mounted and keeps the default. The
Start button still presses when the panel is visible.

* refactor(daemon): run the orphan reconciler as a one-shot CronJob

* fix(daemon): fail the reconcile job when a delete failed

A delete that fails is counted in the sweep summary rather than thrown, so the

leak would simply be back on the next run with nothing in the cluster's history

daemons therefore had one plane between them: the second daemon inherited the

entry points, so every caller and every behavior is unchanged; the next step
threads an explicit instance down from the owning Daemon and removes both.

fix(control-plane): settle in-flight duty recomputes instead of leaking them across tests (#1084)

`duty recompute kick (real Postgres) > stop() cancels a pending kick` failed
intermittently on CI with `expected [ { …(6) } ] to deeply equal []`.

with a probe over the real FakeClock, which sees zero recomputes entered even

have fixed nothing, because the failing test starts no async work of its own.

refactor(daemon): one rule table for store retention, plus the pool's orphan proof (#1085)

* feat(daemon): reap orphaned per-member store rows in the same reconcile job

The Kubernetes half of the orphan reconciler collects sandbox objects nobody will
ever remove. The same leak exists one layer down: a pool member writes a row into
a per-member outbox on the shared data-plane store, dies, and no peer can drain
it. Rather than one retention rule per table, `store/orphan-reaper.ts` sweeps
them all inside the existing `agentconnect-daemon reconcile --once` CronJob, on
the same batched `agent/exists` answer the cluster half already asked for.

Four tables, one predicate: `inbox` hook-completion reports,
`session_metadata_outbox`, `session_purges`, and `webchat_mcp_grant_ledger` —
everything carrying an `ownerId`/`claimedAt` lease. A row is collected when the
control plane no longer knows its agent (nobody can ever report it), or when
nothing has written it for the single 7-day horizon (a live owner renews its
claim on every drain attempt, so an untouched claim means its owner is gone).
Every delete carries the clock the row was judged on as its CAS, so a row a
member claimed between the read and the delete is left alone. Dry run by
default, opt in with `AC_STORE_ORPHAN_DELETE`, one summary line per run.

A local single-daemon store is skipped outright: it has one owner forever, so
its rows are its own. The store methods are plain portable SQL and the suite
runs in the `store-postgres` project as well as on SQLite.

On the control plane, `PoolMemberReaper` gains the counterpart. Retiring a member
no longer cascades its agents' webchat MCP delegations away now that the row is
agent-keyed, so each sweep revokes the ones nothing serves. The predicate is
exactly `PlacementResolver.servingDaemons(agent) === []` — neither placement
column names a target and no unexpired duty lease holds the agent. No dry run:
such a row is already inert, since the live authority check answers
`placement_mismatch` on every use, so the write only records what is true.

* refactor(daemon): retire the ad-hoc session-purge retention the reaper replaces

`drainSessionPurges` ran its own 30-day prune of `session_purges` on every
sweep, with its own constant, its own warn line and its own idea of how long an
unreportable receipt is worth keeping. The reaper now answers that question for
every per-member outbox table from one horizon, so the special-purpose copy goes
and retention has one home.

Deliberately kept: the in-process set that holds a peer's permanently rejected
hook report out of THIS daemon's drain. It reads like retention but is not — it
stops a member that serves the agent from re-attempting a report the control
plane can only ever refuse. The reaper bounds how long the row survives; that
set bounds how often it is retried in the meantime.

* refactor(daemon): make store retention one rule table and delete the per-table prunes

The reaper sat next to the cleanup it was meant to replace. Retention across the
daemon store was a private constant and a `DELETE … WHERE … < x` wherever each
table's writer happened to live, so "how long do we keep X" had as many answers
as there were writers, and a table nobody remembered simply grew.

`store/retention.ts` is now the one home: a rule per table
(`{ table, key, clock, where?, agentColumn?, ownerColumn?, horizonMs,
foreignHorizonMs? }`), one sweep loop, one summary line. The sweep composes both
the SELECT and a re-fenced DELETE from the rule, and the clock the row was judged
on rides the DELETE, so a row anything wrote in between survives. A rule's clock
is the last write ANY process made to the row, so a live owner that renews a
claim or re-stamps a cache is never collected.

Deleted, their semantics now rule rows:

- `pruneSessionPurges` — gone in the previous commit, now a 30-day rule.
- `gcRuntimeCatalog` and its two cutoff arguments, plus the startup call: the
  30-day own window and the 7-day departed-owner window are `horizonMs` and
  `foreignHorizonMs` on the two catalog rules, and the per-catalog clock that
  kept a phase-1 refresh from stripping its own model rows is the rule's `clock`.
- the terminal-row purge inside `expireMemoryCaptures`, with
  `MEMORY_CAPTURE_TERMINAL_RETENTION_MS`, the `terminalRetentionMs` option and
  the maintenance deadline behind it. What is left there is a state change with a
  redaction and a metric, which is not retention.
- the settled-record delete inside `expireActivations`, with
  `ACTIVATION_RETENTION_MS`.

Two callers, one table. The daemon's own hourly sweep runs the rules age-only, so
a local single-daemon install keeps exactly the retention it had — the CronJob
never ran there, and retention was never about ownership there either. Only
`reconcile --once` has the `agent/exists` answer, so only it applies the
agent-gone proof, still dry-run behind `AC_STORE_ORPHAN_DELETE`. The horizon
proof always deletes: it is the retention these rules replaced.

Left alone, because they are lifecycle rather than retention: the redaction half
of `expireMemoryCaptures`, `pruneRuntimeModelCaps` (one discovery's
set-difference), the ownership takeovers, the session TTL/GC sweeps (worktrees
and CP receipts), `loop_guard`'s cleanup (its cutoff is the caller's window, and
it rides the charge statement), and the per-agent caps on permission-request
history, acknowledged hook receipts and memory `.history` — real-time caps with
no age and no owner.

Tests follow the same move: the per-routine prune tests are gone with the
prunes, replaced by rule-table tests that drive the engine and run every declared
rule against the real schema on both SQLite and PostgreSQL.

fix(daemon): survive an oversized frame on the shim accept paths (#1100)

* fix(connection): terminate an accepted socket that errors instead of crashing

WsServerTransport bridged `message` and `close` off the accepted socket but
never `error`. The `ws` library raises `error` when a peer exceeds the
`maxPayload` cap, and an unlistened `error` event is an uncaught exception in
Node, so one oversized frame from a peer that has authenticated nothing took
the whole process down rather than the connection.

ClientTransport has guarded exactly this on the dial side since it shipped;
this is the accept-side equivalent, armed in the constructor so it is live from
the moment the socket is wrapped. `terminate()` folds the fault into the normal
`close` path, which every connection FSM above already handles.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): survive an oversized frame on both shim accept paths

The sandbox shim has two WebSocket accept paths, and both set
`maxPayload: MAX_FRAME_BYTES` while registering no `error` listener on the
accepted socket. An unlistened `error` is an uncaught exception, so exceeding
that cap was process death rather than a closed connection — and the peer
raising it need not have presented an identity, a token, or anything at all.

- ShimListener, the daemon side a pod's shim calls back into, attaches the
  guard as the first statement of `accept()`, before anything can await, and
  logs the fault against the address it came from.
- ShimServer, the in-sandbox side the daemon dials, gets it through
  WsServerTransport, now constructed first in the upgrade callback.

Both http servers also drop their bind-failure listener once `listen()`
succeeds, which leaves a post-listen accept error unheard and therefore fatal;
each now keeps a warning listener, as the tunnel host already does. The
`WebSocketServer` itself needs none: in `noServer` mode it emits no `error`,
and it aborts an unlistened `wsClientError` handshake on its own.

Tests, one per accept path: an oversized frame from an unauthenticated peer
closes that connection, discloses no frame to it, and leaves the listener
binding the next one. With either guard removed the frame becomes an unhandled
error that fails the whole run — which is why #1096 could not ship the case it
found.

fix: clear a pool member's stale staged-move fence on a move back onto the pool (#1098)

* fix(daemon): release a stale staging fence on a token-less agent/activate

A pool member that sourced a move onto a machine keeps its staged-move
fence by design, but a later move back onto the pool leaves that fence
stale: a duty grant then skips the fenced agent and the member holds the
lease while serving nothing (#1093).

`agent/activate` now accepts a frame with no move token as an
authoritative unstage: with a staging fence armed it adopts the stored
token and runs the normal activation flow, with no fence it acknowledges
as a no-op, and it never clears a removal tombstone or races a pending
removal. Tokened activates keep exact-match fencing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): clear stale member fences when a move commits onto a set

`unstageEligibleSources` released only the fences the CURRENT move had
staged, so a two-hop move (pool -> machine -> pool) left the first hop's
fence on a still-alive member; the ledger could then grant that member
the duty group, `installGrantedAgents` skipped the fenced agent, and the
member held the lease while serving nothing (#1093).

A commit onto a set now also broadcasts a token-less `agent/activate` to
every READY member the move never staged (best-effort, bounded by pool
size), `ensureActive` repairs a set placement the same way on retry, and
a member that was offline at commit time is unstaged from its reconnect
staged-fence report when it is an eligible holder of the set placement.
Fences on machines and on members of other sets stay armed.

Closes #1093

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): keep an authoritative unstage from starting a non-holder host

The token-less unstage reused the FULL activation flow, so a pool member
that does not hold the agent's duty would start an ACP host and bind the
agent's exclusive sandbox channel. When the ledger then granted the duty
to another member, that member was the only one authorized for ingress
but could not bind — an unavailable agent. The reconnect backstop
entered the same path right after `mayAct` returned false.

An unstage now clears, applies and commits the fence with the stored
token but leaves the host stopped unless this member already holds
serving authority, read from the same predicate the duty paths use. A
later grant installs and starts it through the normal path, and the
member's replica is current at the granted revision, so that install
skips the fetch. Tokened activates keep proving their host: the target
is the placement, or a one-hop source whose duty the move never
released.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): read holdership at the host-start boundary, not before the awaits

The unstage host gate was captured before the bundle apply, the reconcile
and the workspace preparation. A `duty/revoke` landing inside those awaits
made it stale: `stopServingAgent` finished stopping the host, and the
activation then reached `ensureHostAsync` with a `true` it had read one
lifetime earlier, restarting the host as a non-holder — under `--k8s`
binding the exclusive sandbox against the member just granted the duty.

The predicate now sits in the same synchronous step as the host start, so
a revoke that won during activation keeps the host down. The window inside
`ensureHostAsync` needs no second check: a racing `stopHost` bumps the
host-start generation, and `startHostWithRetry` re-checks it after
`host.start()` and reaps the child. Tokened activations stay unconditional.

feat(control-plane): pool capacity gauges — the vacant-duty alarm (k8s-daemon-pool.md §12) (#1102)

* feat(control-plane): pool capacity gauges — the vacant-duty alarm (k8s-daemon-pool.md §12)

The pool design leaves the CP one observability job: "it only refuses invalid
claims and alarms on vacant-duty age. A human scales the Deployment." Nothing
emitted that signal, so "is the pool big enough" had no observable at all.

Adds `DutyGroupRepo.poolTelemetry` — one read per member set giving live
members, the duty budget they can spend, the budget spent, and the unmet
demand — projected onto seven observable gauges by
`observability/pool-metrics.ts`. Two paired signals: headroom leads (scale
before it hurts), vacancy age lags (something is already unserved).

The read reuses the claim paths' own predicates rather than restating them, so
the gauges say what a claim would decide:

- Eligibility, set-wise. Most `duty_group` rows are singletons of machine-placed
  agents and are vacant by design, forever (§6); counting them would pin the
  alarm high permanently. A vacancy counts for a set only when every resolvable
  agent in the group is set-placed into that set — so a group mixing a
  set-placed and a machine-placed agent is demand for nobody, exactly as it is
  claimable by nobody.
- Liveness is the lease horizon, the ledger's one notion of it.
- Deliverability. An oversized group is undeliverable on the wire at ANY pool
  size (§5), so it is reported on its own gauge and kept out of both the
  claimable count and the age — scaling would never clear it.

A collection that cannot read the ledger observes nothing rather than zeros: a
zeroed headroom gauge is indistinguishable from a full pool, so a database blip
would otherwise fire the capacity alert.

Every replica observes the same install-wide totals, so these aggregate with
`max by (set)`, never `sum`.

* fix(control-plane): model an unbounded pool member as unbounded, not as zero capacity

maxAgents <= 0 is the daemon's sentinel for NO ceiling, not a ceiling of zero:
Daemon.dutyHeadroomForPendingClaim returns +Infinity for it, and the finite
number on the heartbeat is only a batching hint. The wire schema is a bare
z.number().int(), so negatives reach the ledger too.

Summing the persisted value folded that sentinel into the budget, so a member
that accepts everything contributed nothing. A set with no ceiling reported
zero capacity and negative headroom, and the "pool is full" alarm would have
fired permanently on a pool that can never be full — the signal inverted, which
is the exact failure the oversized-group split already guards against.

Capacity and headroom are now not reported at all for a set holding an
unbounded member, rather than reported as a number that means the opposite.
The capacity sum covers bounded members only, which also keeps a negative value
out of the arithmetic. A new agentconnect.pool.unbounded_members gauge makes the
gap legible instead of looking like a broken exporter, and the headroom alert
already treats absent data as OK.

docs(designs): the dial-in handshake fences on the generation, not the duty term (#1110)

* docs(designs): the dial-in handshake fences on the generation, not the duty term

Section 7 specified three term rules at the shim — a higher term supersedes and
closes the current connection, a lower one is refused, an equal one is accepted
only from the same holder. The shipped handshake enforces exactly those three
rules, but over the binding generation: `ShimBindingRegistry.authorize()` answers
`superseded_generation` for an older one and `generation_claimed_by_another_pod`
for an equal one from a different pod. No term reaches the shim. Supersession is
also not a shim decision — its listener refuses any second dial `4403
unavailable` while one is live, and the dialer drops its own older dial when a
newer launch record arrives.

The design is corrected to what ships rather than the code to the design. The one
observable difference is recorded as an accepted trade-off: while a half-dead
ex-holder's socket is still established, the successor's dial is refused until
keepalive or timeout closes it, so takeover is bounded by the transport timeout
instead of being immediate. Nothing unsafe follows — the sandbox is fenced by
generation and the store by ownership — and it matches the neighbouring posture
that treats an unreachable sandbox as a placement problem. Carrying the term in
the hello would close that window and is deliberately not built: the delay has
not been observed, and the rollout that looked like it root-caused elsewhere.

Closes #1097

* docs(designs): name the right fence for the lingering-socket window

Two corrections from review. The generation is not what protects the sandbox
while a half-dead ex-holder's socket lingers: the listener refuses the successor
before its hello is read, so its higher generation never reaches `bind()`, and
the requests still arriving on the old socket carry that socket's own credential
at its own matching generation and pass `authorize()` unchanged. The generation
fences the ex-holder's rebinding once the socket closes; the duty gate and row
ownership carry the interval itself. Stated in §7 and in the failure-model row.

And the three generation rules belong to `ShimBindingRegistry.bind()`, together
with the pod-identity rule. `authorize()` is the per-operation check on an
already-issued credential — exact generation, expiry, capability — and binds
nothing.

perf(daemon): batch store round trips and coalesce the streaming tool writes (#1113)

A pool member's data-plane store has a concurrency of exactly one: every runtime
statement crosses into a worker thread holding a single PostgreSQL client, and
the main thread blocks on Atomics.wait until it answers. The member's ceiling is
one over the round-trip time, shared by every agent it serves, so the lever is
round trips per unit of work, not statements.

Two semantics-preserving changes:

- StoreDatabase gains batch(): one hand-off carrying an ordered statement list,
  one ordered result array back. The worker still runs each statement on its own
  in autocommit, so failure semantics are unchanged — an error names the
  statement that failed and abandons the rest, exactly as the equivalent run of
  single-statement calls would. The single-statement path is untouched.
- updateToolCall is the store's only per-chunk writer, and each of its writes is
  a full latest-wins overlay of the merged tool body rather than an append, so
  writing only the last state of a superseded sequence leaves exactly the row
  the per-chunk path left. The burst is coalesced per row and flushed before any
  other store statement, on a 200 ms timer, at a row or byte bound, at turn end,
  and on drain. Every read goes through a facade that drains first, so the
  buffer is invisible to a reader.

A representative turn — one inbound message, six tool calls of five streamed
updates each, three reasoning blocks, one reply — costs 84 store round trips
before and 17 after. updateToolCall alone accounted for 60 of the 84.

test/store-round-trips.test.ts pins the counts, so a change that reintroduces
per-chunk chatter fails a test instead of quietly costing latency.

feat(control-plane): org-scoped member sets — the mechanism (daemon-groups.md §6 PR 2) (#1114)

* feat(control-plane): org-scoped member sets — the mechanism (daemon-groups.md §6 PR 2)

An organization can now form a member set out of its own daemons, point agents at it,
and get the lease-driven failover the install-wide pool already has. The ledger did not
change: PR 1 (#1003) already made eligibility one membership lookup, so this opens the
door and nothing else.

- The door. `duty/claim`, `duty/fetch`, `duty/release` and the heartbeat admit any
  connection that is in a member set; `SCOPE_DENIED` now means "in no set" rather than
  "not install-wide". Tenancy is not re-checked there — the write-time invariants on
  membership already decide what being in a set means, so `mayHold` stays one rule.
- The announcement. `auth/ok` carries the daemon's set, and that is the daemon's whole
  duty-enforcement predicate: a member serves only what it holds a lease for, a daemon
  in no set owns its agents outright. Membership is never negotiated on the wire.
- The converse invariant. A `daemon` placement may not name a machine that is in a set —
  such an agent would be placed and unservable at once.
- Set CRUD and membership as an org-scoped REST surface (`/orgs/:orgId/member-sets`),
  and the daemon read model carries its set. The console surface is still to come.

Membership transitions take the design's safety rule — never commit while the old
authority might still be serving — but pay for it with preconditions rather than
choreography: a daemon with directly placed agents may not join, and one holding a live
duty lease may not leave (drain it, or let the lease lapse, which is strictly later than
its own self-fence). Both admitted transitions leave nothing running to disturb, so the
daemon relearns its set the one way it ever learns it: the socket closes 1012 and the
reconnect's `auth/ok` carries it. The one-action enrol-with-agents and drain-and-leave
are what still owe the correlated withdrawal and the transition generation.

* fix(control-plane): fence the member-set preconditions against their concurrent writers

Every precondition guarding a membership change was a check in one transaction and
the write it justified in another, so each could be re-decided under it. Two fences,
both ordinary Postgres taken inside the writing transaction, so they hold across
control-plane instances rather than only within one process:

- Per daemon, an advisory transaction lock every writer of "is this daemon in a set"
  and every reader acting on that answer now takes: enrolment, withdrawal, the
  `daemon`-placement guard, and the ledger's two claim paths. Without it a placement
  reading "in no set" and an enrolment reading "nothing pinned here" both commit and
  leave a set member with an unservable pinned agent; or a claim lands a live lease
  on a member a withdrawal has just decided was idle.
- Per set, the `member_set` row itself — `FOR SHARE` on every path that adds a
  reference, `FOR UPDATE` on the delete — so a placement cannot land after the
  reference count and be silently `SET NULL`ed instead of producing the promised 409.

Both operator preconditions move into the repository, next to the row they guard:
`enrollOperator` refuses `DaemonHasPlacedAgents`, `withdraw` refuses `DaemonHoldsDuty`,
and the route just maps them to 409.

Membership is also re-read once the connection is in the registry. Reading it only
during `authenticate` left a window where a change committing mid-handshake closed
nothing and the socket kept the stale set indefinitely; now such a change is either
seen by that read or finds the connection and closes it.

* fix(control-plane): renewal is a lease-creating write, so withdrawal must fence it too

Renewal carries no expiry predicate — "the CP confirms the same terms" means it REVIVES
every group its holder still names. So a beat landing just after a withdrawal read
"nothing live" made every lapsed group live again under a daemon that was no longer a
member. It now takes the same per-daemon fence the claim paths do.

The commit side was missing its half as well: withdrawal deletes the membership row and
now also vacates what the daemon still nominally holds, which is what the transition in
the design says. Every one of those is already lapsed — the precondition just proved it —
so this takes nothing from anyone; what it removes is the ex-member's ability to revive
them. `term` is untouched: monotonicity is the whole token.

* fix(control-plane): the settled-membership read fails closed

That second read is the ONLY guard on the window between the membership lookup that
builds `auth/ok` and the connection reaching the registry, so swallowing a repository
error and keeping the old value re-opened exactly the hole it exists to close. It now
closes 1011 like the lookup that preceded it — transient to the daemon, which retries.

A pod reports Ready when its container process starts, not when the shim is
accepting on its port, so the duty holder's first dial of a resume is routinely
refused. That refusal was then retried on the shared `Backoff` default — base

milliseconds later was met roughly 1.3s later instead, on every wake path.

inside a pod it just created (base 100ms), and after one it is waiting on a peer
that went away (the shared default, unchanged). The injected `backoff` factory
now takes the phase, so a test can still pin both in milliseconds.

smaller attempts inside the same deadline, and the `LaunchTimeoutError` path and
`readyTimeoutMs` semantics do not change.

feat(control-plane): a daemon with agents on it can join a group (#1130)

* feat(control-plane): a daemon with agents on it can join a group

Enrolling such a machine answered "move its N placed agents onto a group first" — but the
only way to move an agent onto a group is for that group to have a live member, and the
member you are trying to add is the one that would be it. A dead end, and one the design
never asked for: §3 says the pinned agents come WITH the join, as the existing move
convention run once per agent, and the operator sees one action.

So they do. `enrollInSet` takes each agent's move gate, detaches it on the machine — the
same confirmed step a machine-to-machine move uses, which is what stops runtime authority
before the placement changes hands — and then commits placements and the membership row in
ONE transaction. Either half alone is a state the invariants forbid: a member with a pinned
agent, or agents on a set with nothing in it. Nothing is activated; the machine is a member
now, so it claims those groups back on its next beat from replicas it still has.

A machine that cannot acknowledge is refused, and `force` commits on the operator's
assertion that it is permanently stopped — the move's own contract, and the only boundary
a machine outside the ledger has, since it holds no lease and runs no self-fence.

The dialog says what will happen ("Its 2 agents move onto the group with it") instead of
refusing, and offers the force path only once a machine has actually failed to confirm.

`AgentMoveService`'s wiring moves to `http/agent-moves.ts`: group enrolment is its second
caller, and a second hand-built copy of that bundle is a copy that drifts.

* fix(control-plane): enrolment settles the same authority every move does

Five gaps in the enrolment transition, four of them the same mistake: it did the parts of
a move that were obviously about placement and skipped the parts that are about who is
allowed to keep serving.

- Session affinity survived. The existing move releases the assignment rows and the hot
  owner entries after each detach; this did not, so the machine's next register replayed
  them and affinity traffic kept arriving at a daemon another member may now hold the duty
  for. It releases them per agent now, exactly as the move does.
- The placement write was raw SQL, so it skipped the settlement both `setPlacement` and
  `movePlacement` perform: webchat MCP delegations are placement-bound grants, and a hook
  dispatch compiled before the change has to read stale. That settlement is now one
  helper with three callers instead of two copies and an omission.
- `?force=false` parsed as TRUE. `z.coerce.boolean()` truthy-coerces the string, so
  spelling out a refusal asserted the very thing it declined — on the one switch that is
  the operator's safety boundary. `z.stringbool()`, which this DTO already documents as
  the reason not to use the other one.
- The dialog applied one machine's force to every later one in the loop: confirming A is
  stopped waved B past a failure nobody was shown. The assertion is carried per daemon.
- A create-mode retry called `createGroup` again. Names are not unique, so the second
  attempt made a second group and left the first empty; the created id is retained now.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: enrolment rebuilds HTTP ingress, and forcing states what it costs

Two gaps in the join transition.

An `rc/bot-assign` table names the daemon the relay forwards public callbacks to,
and it is compiled rather than resolved per callback. Enrolment detaches the agent
from that machine, so leaving the table alone kept ingress arriving there for the
whole window before the ledger grants the duty back — exactly the window where a
peer may already have won. The convergence now carries the pinned agents' HTTP bot
ids, resolved through a helper shared with the duty-side converger so the two paths
cannot drift. One rebuild per bot, since an assign table already covers every agent
on it.

Forcing a join is disaster recovery on the same terms as a force reassign, so it
now asks for the same thing: an explicit confirmation that the machine is
permanently stopped and cannot reconnect, and that both copies may process messages
if that is wrong. The button alone asserted it on the operator's behalf. Editing the
membership retracts a pending assertion — it was made about one machine in one plan.

fix(control-plane): hash org/user ids into the connector profile name (#1136)

The open-connector connection profile was `<orgId[0..8]>--<userId[0..8]>--<name>`.
An 8-char cuid prefix is `c` plus a base36 millisecond timestamp, so it only
resolved creation time to ~36ms buckets: two orgs created in the same bucket,
whose creating users also were, and that both picked a common connection name
composed the SAME profile.

That profile is what the relay sends as `connectionName` on every action run, and
what the create route provisions the credential under. A collision therefore meant
one org's save overwrote the other's stored credential, after which that org's
agents executed actions with it.

Each id is now 64 sha256 bits as fixed-width base36 — inside open-connector's
charset, alphanumeric-led, and at most 62 of its 64 connection-name chars.

No migration is needed. A profile is composed only at create and is then persisted
as the connection's alias binding marker, which reconnect and relay-binding replay
read back rather than recomposing, so connections provisioned under the older
scheme keep resolving under their stored name. An integration test pins that.

fix(control-plane): joining a group leaves pinned agents alone (#1148)

* fix(control-plane): joining a group leaves pinned agents alone

The join was built on a premise that does not hold. #1130 stopped every agent
pinned to a machine and re-placed it onto the group, on the reasoning that a
machine which enforces duties serves only what it holds a lease for, so a pin
would go dark the moment the membership row landed.

But duty eligibility for a `daemon` placement is `agent.daemonId = holder`, with
no membership term. Joining a group does not widen who may hold a pinned agent —
its machine stays the only one that may. It serves them through a lease now
instead of outright, and that lease is one no peer can take. So the join is a
membership row, and the agents keep running where they are. No detach, no
cancelled turns, no force, no split-brain to warn about.

The converse falls out of the same predicate: an agent may be pinned to a machine
that is in an organization's group. Only the install-wide pool still refuses one,
and for a different reason — a pool member is a Pod the reconciler retires without
notice, so a pin to it names something that stops existing. That is about
replaceability, not membership, and the comment now says so.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): duty reporting follows member-set membership, not the org mode

A member gates service on holding a lease. It has to ask for one on the same
predicate, and it did not: the heartbeat digest and `reportDutiesNow` were gated
on `organizationMode === 'frame'`.

That was the same answer only while the install-wide pool was the one set that
existed. An org's own daemon authenticates with `organizationMode: 'connection'`
(authService.ts), so the moment an organization could own a group, its members
went duty-gated and silent — `dutyEnforced()` true, no digest ever sent, so the
control plane granted them nothing and every agent on them went dark. A later
restart made it visible a second way: transportAgents and syncAgentSchedules
filter against an empty duty registry, so platform sockets and crons stay down.

Both sites now read membership, the same thing `dutyEnforced()` reads.

Also carries the corrected pin rule through the console paths that still enforced
the old one: the daemon page no longer presents joining as blocked by pinned
agents, and both placement pickers offer a machine that is in a group.

fix(daemon): report each runtime probe as it lands, stop starving package launchers (#1153)

* fix(daemon): report each runtime probe as it lands, stop starving package launchers

A curated runtime distributed through a package launcher could never be admitted
on a host that had not already built its npx install tree. Three things stacked
up, measured against @openma/deepseek-harness-acp (the DeepSeek Harness adapter,
~700 packages once its harness deps are resolved):

- The probe sweep applied every result at one barrier, so the runtimes that
  answered in seconds waited for the slowest one before their admission and
  facts frame landed.
- The per-probe deadline was a flat 30s covering spawn + initialize +
  session/new. A package launcher spends ~210s resolving and linking its tree on
  first use, so the probe timed out every sweep, forever.
- The disposable probe HOME dropped every npm_config_*, so each sweep started
  from an empty package cache and re-paid that ~210s (and ~300MB) from scratch.

Results are now applied and emitted per probe — facts/daemon-runtimes is an
idempotent REPLACE fenced by `seq`, so a slow runtime delays only itself, and
the sweep's last frame still carries the same snapshot it used to send once at
the end. With that in place the deadline is only a hang reaper, so npx/uvx
runtimes get a budget that fits a real first install.

Probe launches also keep npx/uvx on the HOST package cache: the bytes are
content-addressed packages rather than user state, and the npx install tree
lives inside the cache root, which is what turns every later probe into a
~4s launch. Agent launches deliberately do NOT get it — a probe never runs a
model turn, so its confined tool use must not be able to write the install trees
other runtimes launch from. Sandboxed probes carve the cache back writable under
the same rule shared credential roots use: it may sit below a protected root,
never contain one.

Verified on a bwrap host: cold sandboxed install builds the tree in 208s and
every probe after that admits dsh-acp in ~4s with its models.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): restamp curated admission when the sweep completes

Recording each curated result as it landed started its five-minute freshness

sweep from sweep COMPLETION. A runtime that answered in ~4s therefore expired
~300s later while the next probe was ~508s away on the measured cold path — for

feat(control-plane): one usage report interface for two authenticated ingresses (#1162)

* feat(control-plane): one usage report interface for two authenticated ingresses

Session usage reached the CP through exactly one door — the daemon's
`usage/report` EVT — so a deployment that meters sessions upstream of any daemon
had nowhere to report them. This adds the second door without letting the two
drift apart.

Both adapters now hand the SAME cumulative payload to one `UsageWriter` port and
each stamps the `source` itself, so a caller can never claim to be an ingress it
did not authenticate as:

- the daemon EVT keeps its placement check and writes `daemon`;
- `POST /api/v1/internal/usage/reports` takes a batch behind a deployment-shared
  service secret and writes `gateway`. Unset secret ⇒ the route is never
  registered, so an unconfigured deployment answers 404, not 401.

`session_usage` and `session_spend` gain that trusted `source`, defaulting to
`daemon` — which is also the correct backfill, since every existing row came
from a daemon.

Two storage semantics the batch door forced into the open, and both now hold for
the daemon door too:

- a LATE report still lands its own timeline checkpoint but can no longer roll
  the snapshot back to an older `lastActivityAt`;
- a report for an agent that no longer exists is dropped rather than raising a
  foreign-key error, so one stale row cannot wedge a caller's retry loop.

Writes stay cumulative upserts, so redelivery of a whole batch cannot
double-count and no per-item receipt is needed.

* fix(daemon): report an interrupted hook fire on a duty handoff instead of retaining its row

A duty handoff keeps an agent's admitted-but-unrun durable rows for the successor
holder (#1050), but a hook fire cannot be handed over: the control plane fences
`hook/start` and every review action to the accepted `dispatchDaemonId`, so no
other member can re-run one with authority. Two paths let a hook row through that
retention anyway.

A pool member releases its duties while SIGTERM drains it, and the `!draining`

only a handoff sets the latch.

A row whose holder never reported at all — a crash, or a member whose restart
minted a new Pod-bound id — was re-admitted by whichever member gained the duty.
That turn ran without review authority (the orchestrator self-fences on the same
field) and then reported as if it had, so a maintainer saw a passing Check for a
review that never happened; a row already past one redelivery instead had its
report refused and waited for the reaper. `replayInbox` now reports the handover
for a foreign accepted dispatch rather than re-prompting. Maintenance replays that
need no review authority — deleted-event no-ops and worktree cleanup — stay ahead
of the fence and still run on the successor.

* fix(daemon): let the daemon that writes a hook receipt own its outbox row

one-shot. The row was redacted — no model rerun — but the handover report itself sat
until an unrelated reconnect, which is exactly the immediate outcome the fence exists

open. Those turns could refresh their context onto a message the daemon had
never delivered, act on the phase change, and have the reply charged to their

budget never happened, so a day's discussion and its votes piled onto one
window and every circuit latched at MAX_AUTOMATIC_TURNS_PER_WINDOW.

six-round `round_limit`, or play-it-out / two-round `completed` — and the

holds them, so `nextDeliveries()` publishes the thread row, the world event,
and the ingress as one atomic step at emit time. Each echo outcome also
reports its room, so `peer.wake` records which circuit was charged.

artifact of the bug: seven seats never exhaust the budget once every phase
arrives as a delivered referee turn. Rewritten as the complement of the
twelve-seat test, asserting invariants instead of a magic number — nothing
latches, no wake is gated, no player takes MAX_AUTOMATIC_TURNS_PER_WINDOW

are charged in the den, and every speech follows a DAY post while every vote
follows a VOTE post. That last one fails directly if a referee message ever

fix(control-plane): re-serve a still-leased grant when a session-access check cannot run (#1181)

* fix(control-plane): re-serve a still-leased GitHub grant when the access check cannot run

An external-visibility session is authorized solely by its provider scope — no
role, not even owner, widens that. The GitHub session-access check re-decides
every recheck period, and for a repository that needs a per-viewer permission
check that means a live identity lookup plus a live GitHub permission read, on
the request path. Any failure in either leg became `unknown`, which drops the
scope, which the session routes serve as a plain 404. So a few seconds of
provider trouble rendered as "session not found" to a viewer who had been
reading that session a moment earlier — and because the snapshot cache above
holds whatever the sweep resolved to, one blip stretched into minutes.

An unverifiable check is not a denial. Keep a bounded record of the scopes a
viewer was really allowed on, and re-serve that grant when the check cannot run.
Nobody who was never allowed is admitted; the price is that a revocation landing
during the outage takes up to one extra lease to bite.

Two rules keep the grace from becoming a back door. Only a decided allow arms
it, and a graced serve never re-arms it, so an upstream that stays down expires
the grant on schedule instead of renewing it for as long as it is down. And a
decided deny disarms it outright, so an outage after GitHub has answered "no"
cannot resurrect what that answer took away.

Also give this check the degraded logging the Slack one already has: it
swallowed every failure with no trace anywhere, which is what made an
intermittent blip indistinguishable, after the fact, from a real denial. The
cause is recorded as an error code or class name, never a message.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): extend the same grace to the Slack and Feishu access checks

Both had the identical gap the GitHub check just closed: any failure reaching
the provider collapses to `unknown`, the scope is dropped, and the session
routes serve that as a plain 404 — so a few seconds of provider trouble hides a
conversation from someone who was reading it a moment earlier. Slack had already
been given the observability half of this treatment and never the availability
half; Feishu had neither.

Slack mirrors GitHub directly: it already keeps a per-principal verdict, so the
grace is armed beside it and read when a re-decision cannot run.

Feishu needed the record invented. It caches the chat's member list, shared
across viewers, and derives each verdict by intersecting that list with the
caller's union_ids — so nothing there remembers that a PERSON was admitted. The
grace record is that, and only that: it caches no audience, and the decision
stays derived.

The two rules that keep it from becoming a back door hold in both. Only a
decided admission arms the grace, and a graced serve never re-arms it, so a
provider that stays unreachable expires the grant on schedule. A decided
exclusion disarms it, so an outage after the provider has answered "no" cannot
resurrect what that answer took away.

Slack counts what the grace absorbed and reports it as one line per resolve,
matching its existing counts-not-targets discipline — a graced serve is not
`degraded`, so without the count a Slack that stays down would go quiet in the
logs at the moment it starts costing something. Feishu gains a `warn` seam for
