test(control-plane): synchronise the mid-flight snapshot race properly (#1321)

The usage-report ingress test that proves a report cannot publish its snapshot
while its checkpoint waits on a row lock started its writer without waiting for
the holding transaction to actually take the lock, then slept a fixed 300ms.

On a loaded runner the holder had not reached its FOR UPDATE yet, so the writer
ran unblocked, finished inside the sleep, and the mid-flight read saw the new
value: a fail with no defect behind it. The interleaving the test names went
uncovered on exactly the runs that were slow enough to change it.

The holder now signals only after FOR UPDATE returns and the writer starts after
that signal, racing the transaction so a failure there surfaces instead of
hanging. The sleep is replaced by a wait for the writer to be genuinely queued on
the row lock, which is also the proof its snapshot statement already ran, so the
read is the mid-flight instant by construction rather than by timing. Same house
pattern the other row-lock races in this suite use.

Verified by delaying the holder 500ms: the old arrangement reads 999 (the CI
failure), the new one still reads 10. The file passes 13/13 repeats, four of them
under CPU load, and the full integration suite is green.

docs(designs): agent-authored attachments (#1326)

* docs(designs): agent-authored attachments

Design for the half of outbound files that #1323 did not cover: an agent
sending a file it produced, and sending a file into the conversation the user
is actually in.

The first draft extended sendMessage and stopped, which fails the primary
case: sendMessage has no in-thread form by design, so an image a user asked
for in a thread would land at the channel root as a new conversation. The
design therefore adds shareFile - a coordinate-less tool that posts into the
session's own conversation from trusted context, carrying identity but no
response metadata - plus an attachFile field on sendMessage for the
cross-conversation case, both over one workspace-fenced, images-only,
size-capped resolver.

The pod split is stated rather than hidden: a sandboxed agent's workspace is
behind a 256KB text-only shim channel, so phase 1 is host agents, and the
wire work for pods is phased behind it. Markdown-driven uploads, a URL
source, composition, and A2A files are considered and rejected with reasons.

* docs(designs): rework agent-authored attachments after a multi-lens review

* feat(daemon): let an agent forward a received image to Slack

An agent could read a shared file but never send one: attachments were
inbound-only on every platform, and no outbound surface accepted bytes. An
image arriving on one platform could be described elsewhere, never relayed.

Slack cannot carry bytes in chat.postMessage at all, so add the three-step
external upload to SlackConnection (files:write, already requested in the app
manifest). Sharing with channel_id is what turns the hosted file into a
message; the caption rides as initial_comment and the agent keeps its own
username/icon, with the same chat:write.customize fallback the text send has.

Expose it as an optional uploadFile port on MessageGateway - the mirror of
downloadFile - and let sendMessage's toUser and channel branches name an
attachment. The name is the one the agent already reads in its [attached: ...]
marker; the daemon resolves it against its own transcript for the caller's
conversation, so an agent forwards only what it received and the bytes never
pass through the model. It reuses the bounded copy kept for console replay, so
a forwarded image can be smaller than the original.

Slack answers a file share with the file and no message ts, so such a send has
no post anchor: providerPostId stays undefined and every consumer of it
degrades on the path a gateway returning no id already takes - no thread
materialization, no channel-root session seed, no paired wake. An unresolvable
name or a target platform without the port fails the whole send rather than
delivering the caption alone.

* fix(daemon): harden the Slack upload path and stop blaming the file name

The byte POST had no timeout while running inside the serial send queue, so a
stuck upload URL could block every message on the connection for undici's 300s
defaults - the exact failure the WebClient's own 30s bound exists to prevent.
Both now share one constant. That request also built a ProxyAgent per upload
and never closed it, leaking a keep-alive socket pool per forward wherever a
proxy is configured; it is closed in a finally.

The caption skipped the file's one markdown seam. initial_comment is mrkdwn
while a text post goes through markdownBlock, so the same message string
rendered differently depending on whether it carried a file - bold, links,
headings and fenced code all came out literal on a forward. The share now
carries the same markdown block, with the comment left as the notification
text.

Refusing an unresolvable name claimed the name was wrong. It usually is not:
the [attached: ...] marker lists every file on a message, while only one
retained image is forwardable, so an agent naming a PDF or a second image was
told to check a spelling it had got right and would retry it. The refusal now
states the real rule, the tool description says images only, and
product-conventions records it.

* fix(daemon): never claim nothing was sent while the caption is in the chat

Telegram and Feishu cannot carry a file and its caption as one message, so
they send two - and both sent the caption FIRST. A failure on the file then
returned undefined, which the caller reports as "nothing was sent" while the
agent's words are already in the conversation. The agent retries and posts
them twice. On Feishu this was the common case, since an image message never
carries a caption; on Telegram it needed a caption over 1024 characters, and
an image Telegram rejects for its own reasons.

The ordering is the fix: both now send the file first, so a failure before
anything lands really did land nothing. The port states that as its contract -
undefined means nothing was posted - and gains a warning for the remaining
partial, a caption lost after the file arrived. sendMessage surfaces it
through the notice channel the root-post relation already uses, so the agent
learns inside the same turn; notices are collected rather than assigned, since
a forward can raise both.

Discord already satisfied the contract by attaching the file to the first
chunk, but silently dropped later ones; it reports them the same way. Feishu's
anchor moves from the caption to the image as a consequence, which is also the
better anchor - it is the post the send is about.

feat(daemon): shareFile — post a workspace image into the current conversation (#1330)

* feat(daemon): shareFile - post a workspace image into the current conversation

Phase 1 of docs/designs/agent-authored-attachments.md. An agent could obtain
image bytes (curl, its file tools) and could forward a received image
elsewhere, but had no way to put a file it produced in front of the person
who asked - the ordinary reply is text-only and every sendMessage post lands
at a channel root. shareFile is the missing surface: a coordinate-less tool
that posts into the active turn's own conversation.

The model supplies a workspace-relative path and an optional caption;
everything else is trusted context. The path resolves through the workspace
browser's own fence (canonicalWorkspacePath - lexical containment plus
realpath re-verification) in a single-shot read; the accepted set is PNG,
JPEG, WEBP by magic bytes, with GIF refused BY NAME since sendPhoto would
silently de-animate it; the outbound filename and MIME come from the sniffed
type, never the model-supplied path, so Discord's extension-only rendering
cannot land a chart as a non-previewable blob. Two synchronous caps bound it:
a per-file limit (its own knob, defaulting to maxAttachmentBytes) and a
per-turn budget charged before the read so concurrent tool calls cannot race
past it.

The anchor is one rule with four platform shapes, so the uploadFile port
gains one: an anchor of {thread, replyTo}. Telegram places by replyTo - the
turn's reply target, without which every plain-group share lands at the chat
root - applied to the photo and the overflow caption alike; Feishu now
REFUSES an anchor it cannot honor instead of silently posting a new topic;
Slack and Discord read the thread they always did. The port's failure is now
typed (missing_scope | too_large | not_found | forbidden | indeterminate |
platform_error), where indeterminate is the send queue abandoning a
still-running upload: the one outcome that must say "may have landed - do
not retry" because a retry double-posts. Every classification uses material
the connections already had.

Three gates run before any file I/O: a headless turn posts nothing, a
postless A2A child has no conversation despite its live gateway, and a
platform without the port gets a named refusal. The share never seeds or
re-anchors a session - the thread already has the one this turn runs in -
and its transcript row carries provenance (path, sniffed type, size, digest)
plus the bytes when they fit the transcript budget, so the console renders
the agent's chart exactly as it renders a user's upload. Captions are
bounded, single-message, and mention-neutralized; Discord additionally
suppresses pings natively via allowedMentions.

The three shipped tool descriptions that steered agents wrong are edited in
the same change: sendMessage's speak-in-this-conversation pointer now names
shareFile, and the claims that an agent cannot produce an attachment are
retracted where they stopped being true.

Sandboxed (cluster) agents refuse with a deferral message - their workspace
is phase 2, over the workspace-fs channel the design already located.

fix(daemon): repair a broken runtime install and name the real refusal cause (#1309)

* fix(daemon): repair a broken runtime install and name the real refusal cause

A Codex agent died at every start with `Missing optional dependency
@openai/codex-linux-x64`: npm had reified an in-place upgrade inside the agent's
private `npx` tree, dropping the old aliased platform package without installing
the replacement. The tree kept a correct lockfile and a node_modules that cannot
run, so all three start attempts failed identically, `agent/activate` staged the
agent out of the roster, and every later webchat turn was refused `no_agent` —
which the console renders as "unavailable (no live daemon)" even though the daemon
was live and answering.

Two fixes:

- A start failure that names a missing runtime package is now repaired once, in the
  tree the child actually resolved, and earns one extra start attempt. The repair
  only reinstalls what an installed lockfile already declares and never runs npm
  lifecycle scripts: the tree lives in the agent's own writable HOME, so running
  them would execute agent-authored code as the daemon, outside the sandbox the
  adapter itself is confined to. Cluster launches resolve packages in the agent's
  pod and are skipped.
- When a start does fail terminally, the daemon remembers the cause and refuses
  later turns with `start_failed` plus one bounded, path-free line naming it, so the
  console says the agent could not start and why instead of blaming a daemon that
  answered. `no_agent` now means what it says.

Verified: new unit tests for the detection/plan/repair seam and the detail
redaction, daemon retry-budget tests, and the webchat refusal; protocol, relay, and
web suites green; daemon suites covering the changed paths green (the full daemon
run exceeds this box's local time budget and is left to CI).

An agent may carry its own HOME in its environment, so read the value the child was

repair that looks in the wrong tree silently does nothing.

Bound the reinstall at five minutes: a start waits on it, so a hung registry must
fail the start rather than park a turn behind a stalled npm.

Review found the `start_failed` refusal unreachable in the very scenario it was

read it. The cause now survives a staging fence and is dropped where a genuine
removal takes its tombstone. The webchat test drives the real stage-out instead of
an id that was never in the roster — it fails against the previous code.

Also from review:

- Agents on a non-isolated runtime share one npx tree, so simultaneous failures

feat(daemon): shareFile reaches a pod agent's workspace (#1331)

* feat(daemon): shareFile reaches a pod agent's workspace

Phase 2 of docs/designs/agent-authored-attachments.md. Phase 1 refused
sandboxed agents because the daemon cannot read a pod's volume directly - but
the fd-anchored workspace-fs channel already carries chunked base64 reads
under the read grant every sandbox holds, so the gap was one port shape:
WorkspaceFs typed its read as text.

The port gains readFileBytes(path, maxBytes), bounded by the outbound file
cap rather than by a frame: over-cap answers {tooLarge} from the FIRST
reply's size without transferring, absence answers undefined. The shim
implementation avoids the two traps the design review named. A request sized
to REPLY_BUDGET would expand 4/3 past the frame when the pod base64-encodes
exactly the requested slice, losing the channel instead of refusing - so
chunks request floor(REPLY_BUDGET/4)*3 raw bytes. And independently-encoded
slices carry their own padding, so their joined strings are not one valid
base64 stream - each chunk is decoded separately and the buffers
concatenated, with the same mtime/size staleness restart the text read uses.
Daemon-side only; the wire and the pod bundle are untouched, so running pods
are compatible.

shareFile's resolver takes the pod arm when the agent is cluster-placed: the
workspace scope already composes the root in pod coordinates, the daemon
contributes the lexical fence (which carries the .git rule the pod-side
check lacks - the symlink guarantee is the pod's own fd-anchored descent),
and the bytes come over the channel. The sandboxed refusal now means only
"sandbox unreachable", and says so.

Tested end to end over the real chunk protocol: a 400 KB binary that forces
multi-chunk reassembly and would corrupt under either trap, the one-frame
over-cap refusal, and the port's bounded read on both implementations via
the shared suite.

fix(console): resolve a session's pull request where the agent actually runs (#1334)

Debugging a live session whose PR panel was still empty (a webchat session on
`cloud-test-2`, which had just opened #1332) turned up two reasons #1294's
branch fallback never fired on the test deployment.

**The branch read went to `agent.daemonId`.** Every workspace route resolves its
daemon through the PLACEMENT (`getServingAgent` → `placementResolver`), because a
pool- or cluster-placed agent has no `daemonId` column at all — and in that
deployment none of them do. So `readSessionBranch` bailed before asking anyone,
and the fallback could not have worked for any agent there, session worktree or
not. It now resolves the serving daemon the same way the routes beside it do.

**A shared-workspace session got no fallback.** The session in question reports
`workspaceIsolation: shared`: the agent has one checkout, which is exactly the
tree the Files and Git tabs already show that session. Refusing to read it left
this tab permanently empty for every shared-workspace agent rather than
protecting anything. It is read now — but only for the agent's most recently
active session, because one tree has one branch and it moves: handing an older
session the newest session's pull request, checks and threads is worse than an
empty tab, since the branch that carried its own work is long gone from that
checkout and nothing here can find it. `SessionRepo.latestSessionIdForAgent`
answers that question on the existing `session_meta_agent_activity_page_idx`, and
a stale session is refused before the daemon read, so it costs nothing.

The DTO says which checkout answered (`linkScope: 'session' | 'shared'`) and the
panel says it in words: a shared tree's pull request may carry more than this
session's work. Only the session-worktree read needs the daemon feature gate; the
primary checkout is a read every daemon has always answered.

`rejected:paused`. The rule stayed in the relay pool regardless, so each delivery
still travelled the whole path to buy a rejection — and for a github hook it also
opened a review projection, which published a Check that reports nothing anyone
can act on. One agent paused twelve days ago had accumulated 2366 projections
this way, 1273 of them settled as `skipped`, one per pull request revision the
repository saw while it was doing nothing.

models for a hook that must not dispatch — disabled, unplaced, or with no valid
installation to attribute events — so `broadcast()` converges to a removal, and
resuming compiles and re-assigns with no further machinery.

else recomputed them: routing convergence runs on placement and duty changes, and
pause is neither.

fix(daemon): read a spend limit as an exhausted quota, not a generic failure (#1347)

A provider that stops a turn because the organization is out of money phrases it as
"You've hit your org's monthly spend limit". That reached neither `PROVIDER_QUOTA_CODES`
nor `PROVIDER_QUOTA_MESSAGES`: the usage-limit pattern allowed a single lowercase word
between "hit your" and "usage limit", so a possessive plus a qualifier missed, and no
pattern mentioned spending at all.

The turn therefore reported the catch-all `turn_failed`. Everything downstream that reads
the reason lost the only fact worth having: the GitHub Check said "Review could not be
completed", the console's delivery list said `turn_failed`, and the actual sentence
existed solely in the daemon log. Observed live on 2026-08-21, where every review turn
for one agent died in under a second for two and a half hours and read as a broken
trigger rather than an empty balance.

Widen the two usage-limit patterns to cover spending and to tolerate the possessive.
Classification stays message-driven on purpose: the same payload carries an
`errorKind: "rate_limit"`, which an ordinary transient rate limit carries too, so a test
pins that the kind alone still resolves to `turn_failed`.

fix(control-plane): let a settled review projection leave the reporter's queue (#1350)

The Check worker claims the 25 oldest rows whose due time has passed, ordered by
that due time. Nothing ever took a row out of that set. A projection whose Check
already shows the desired state, with no write in flight and no newer intent, fell
through every early return in `process()` and reached the write path, so it minted
a token and re-PATCHed a Check that was already correct — then stayed due, and did
it again.

Two costs, both observed live. The queue only grows, because every projection ever
created remains in it: 3680 rows due, 3027 of them with nothing to publish. And
because the claim is a bounded FIFO, real work waits behind that. A pull request
whose review had finished and approved sat at `desiredState=success`,
`observedState=in_progress`, `attempts=0` — never once attempted — with 3671 rows
queued ahead of it, while GitHub showed the check as still running.

Settle such a row instead: clear its due time, release the lease, and drop the
stale error code. Any later work re-arms `nextAttemptAt` through the paths that
already do, so leaving the set is not the same as being forgotten. The check is
re-read under the row lock before it commits, so a converge that landed while the
worker held the lease is not silently discarded.

This does not explain why 3671 rows shared one due timestamp to the millisecond —
something re-arms them in bulk and is still worth finding — but a bulk re-arm is
now harmless: each row settles once, cheaply, and leaves.

fix(daemon): key skill ownership by the real directory, not the harness name (#1355)

* fix(daemon): key skill ownership by the real directory, not the harness name

A CLI-derived skill root is whatever the pinned skills CLI picks for the
runtime, so moving an agent between harnesses changes the path string
(.claude/skills vs .agents/skills). A repository may legitimately expose one
as a link to the other, and contained skill root aliases (#796) already taught
the mutation layer to resolve that. The install ledger, however, still compared
ownership by the literal relative path: after a runtime switch it owned the
same directory under its other name, so reconciliation lstat'd the bundle it
had written itself, did not recognize the path, and refused to overwrite an
unowned skill. That refusal was fatal, so every later delivery to the agent
failed before the agent could start.

Canonicalize the root through the existing contained-alias resolver before it
is compared or recorded, on the candidates, on the recorded set, and on the
legacy hints. Canonicalizing the recorded set is what lets an existing ledger
migrate instead of colliding on the first run after an upgrade. With both sides
naming one directory, a runtime switch now renames the receipt instead of
installing under the new root and then removing the old one, which resolves to
the same directory and would have deleted the bundle just written. A root whose
canonical form is not a valid receipt path keeps its original value.

An unowned destination also stops being fatal. That candidate is skipped,
returned in the new conflicts field, and reported through the existing warn
sink the workspace manager already routes to the daemon log. Skipping leaves
the path untouched, which is what the refusal wanted; the difference is that
one foreign directory no longer costs an agent its other skills or its startup.
Containment is unchanged: an alias resolving outside the workspace still fails
closed at the write layer, and unowned content is still never adopted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): keep a skipped skill conflict retryable

Skipping an unowned destination still committed the ready ledger with the full
desired-plan fingerprint, so the plan looked satisfied when it was not. The
unchanged fast path re-hashes only the bundles actually recorded as owned, and
the skipped one is absent from that set, so the next preparation returned
unchanged: the conflict was reported exactly once, and clearing the foreign
directory afterwards would not install the skill until some unrelated source or
config change moved the fingerprint.

Record a non-matching fingerprint while any conflict remains, the same way a
failed install already does. The next preparation re-checks the destination,
reports the conflict again while it persists, and installs the skill as soon as
the path is clear.

feat(control-plane): publication lease and operation records for code-host reviews (#1384)

* feat(control-plane): publication lease and operation records for code-host reviews

Formal GitLab reviews (design 15) publish through one shared service
account, so the publication lease is a correctness boundary: this adds the
CAS-acquired lease with its monotonic fence, the single-use operation record
ledger that permits exactly one outbound request per record and locks an
ambiguous attempt indefinitely, the provider-neutral review authorization
and result frames behind codehost-review-v1, and the body-free attempt
outcome store. The daemon review adapter is the follow-up slice.

* fix(control-plane): a review outcome releases the lease only through the ledger

Round 2: recording a terminal outcome no longer clears ownership by itself —
release re-runs the same transfer classification under the subject lock, so
an attempt with an outstanding or ambiguous operation record stays owned
fail-closed, and settling that record later is what lets the lease settle.

* fix(control-plane): the terminal review operation stays idempotent after release

Round 3: settling or returning the last outstanding record releases the
lease in the same transaction, so a retransmitted identical request now
resolves the durable record first and answers with its committed state and
the lease phase — instead of reporting a lease it can no longer find.

* fix(control-plane): a replayed terminal operation reports its own fence's phase

Round 4: the idempotent replay no longer echoes the live subject row, which
a newer fence may already own — when the lease has moved past the record's
fence, the reply derives its phase from the old attempt's durable terminal
state, so a lost acknowledgement can never dress a completed release in a
successor's lifecycle.

feat(daemon): give a session an outward id of its own, minted before its runtime (#1354)

* docs(session): sessionId and acpSessionId are one session's two names, each with its own scope

§1.1 already listed all three identifiers, but the sentence binding them
was ambiguous enough that the implementation read it as "the outward id
IS the ACP id" — and the protocol's own comments hardened that reading
into a contract ("opaque ACP session id (agent-assigned; NOT a wire
UUID)"), which is the opposite of what the section intends.

The doctrine, stated so neither direction can drift again: `sessionId`
is the identity everywhere OUTSIDE the ACP hop — the control-plane wire,
the console, sendMessage targets, the # Agent block, and the credential
claims the gateway verifies — and it must exist BEFORE the runtime,
because a credential is minted to start that runtime. `acpSessionId` is
what the runtime knows the session by, needed in both directions on that
hop, and never discardable. They normally hold the SAME value: the
daemon mints the id when the slot resolves and proposes it on
session/new; a runtime that insists on its own leaves the daemon holding
both and translating at that one boundary.

Also names what the section rules out — reporting the ACP id or anything
derived from `sessionKey` as the outward identity — and records the debt
at the site that does exactly that: the key-server call hashes the slot
key, so gateway-metered spend lands under an identity nothing outside
the daemon can resolve. The protocol comments now state the doctrine AND
that the daemon still fills the field from the ACP id today, rather than
claiming a state the code has not reached.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(daemon): give a session an outward id of its own, minted before its runtime

§1.1 says a session has two names for two scopes. The code had one: whatever the
ACP hop called it. That could not be the outward name, because the moment the
outward name is first needed — issuing the model credential that STARTS the
runtime — no ACP id exists yet. So `issueKey` sent a hash of `sessionKey`
instead: stable, and opaque enough to keep platform coordinates out of the
gateway, but resolvable by nothing outside this daemon. Every gateway-metered
request landed under an identity the console could not match to the session that
spent it, which is why per-session gateway spend was unreadable.

The store now mints the outward id when the slot resolves — at `upsertSession`,
or earlier via `ensureOutwardSessionId` when a credential is needed before the
session row exists — and keeps it for the slot's life. A rebuilt ACP hop is a
new runtime instance of the same session, so `acpSessionId` is overwritten while
`sessionId` is not.

Outbound, every frame that names the SESSION now carries that id: metadata

feat(control-plane): give every agent its own GitLab service account (#1418)

* feat(control-plane): give every agent its own GitLab service account

The runtime identity becomes one group service account per (organization,
agent, top-level group) instead of one account per project shared by every
agent (gitlab-com-integration.md §7.2, M8). Each agent now has its own GitLab
face: notes, reviews, approvals, and pushes are authored by an account named
after the agent, and two agents on one merge request are two GitLab users with
disjoint draft sets.

Persistence replaces the binding's account columns outright. `GitlabAgentAccount`
holds the deterministic username, the display-name fingerprint, the credential
epoch, the administering connection, the mutation lease, the lifecycle
generation, and the lifecycle state; `GitlabAccountMembership` records
authorization as an external fact; `GitlabProjectCredential` is re-keyed to the
issuing account. The migration is plainly destructive: nothing is carried
forward, so an existing binding reconverges exactly like one whose account is
missing, with its hooks and grants disabled until it is ready again.

Lifecycle follows authorization. A binding that gains an agent consumer — a
workspace or a hook — ensures that agent's account exists in the project's
top-level group and adds it as a project member at the role the workspace
gitAccess clamp derives; losing the last consumer removes the membership, and an
account with nothing bound in its root retires with its PATs revoked. Deleting an
agent retires every account it earned. Account and PAT mutations run under an
account-level lease, never a binding's, and a membership insert commits only
against the row's current active generation while retirement compare-and-swaps
active→retiring in the transaction that verifies the set is empty — so a bind
racing a retirement loses deterministically and re-provisions a fresh generation.

Consumers follow the same resolution: gitcred grants and the effect lease serve
the requesting agent's own account, the compiled rule names the hook agent's
account and vetoes every account bound to the project, and the review
publication coordinator keys on the acting agent's account. A refused creation
lands the account row in a translated failure state — including the top-level
group's account quota — and never falls back to a human credential.

Console work is a separate change; the project DTO exposes its member accounts
so the existing bot chip stays meaningful. Transferring administration of an
account between connections is left for a follow-up.

joined and the one left. The backoff that outwaits a peer's provisioning
lease moves onto the provisioner, so both callers share one implementation.

The unbind pass now keys on the authorization set rather than on which
accounts converged this run, so a transient failure — a contended account
lease, an upstream blip — can no longer read as authorization removal and
delete a live project membership.

Reactivating a lifecycle generation deletes the credential rows the
interrupted retirement left behind, in the same transaction: those PATs
belong to an identity that may already be revoked or deleted, so keeping

fix(daemon): let the Slack SDK own the file upload transport (#1422)

* fix(daemon): let the Slack SDK own the file upload transport

The external upload's middle step POSTs bytes to a reserved URL that is not a
Slack API endpoint and has no published wire contract. Driving the three steps
by hand cost two live failures in a row: the reserved URL answers HTTP 500
unless the multipart part is named `body`, and fixing that alone still left the
POST refused. Each round was a guess against an undocumented shape.

So stop reimplementing it. `uploadFile` now calls `files.uploadV2`, which owns
all three steps and inherits the agent, proxy, and timeout configuration the
rest of this client already takes from `WebClient`.

Two consequences worth stating rather than discovering later:

- The share loses its identity decoration. `username`/`icon_url` are documented
  for the completion step but absent from the SDK's argument type, and
  `uploadV2` builds its completion arguments from an explicit key list that
  omits both. That decoration was never confirmed against live Slack and was
  already dropped on any rejection, so this gives up nothing that worked. The
  design already recorded file posts as not identity-stamped on any platform.
- `uploadV2` hides which step threw. Only a Slack `{ok:false}` and the SDK's own
  byte-POST rejection prove nothing was published; every other failure is now
  `indeterminate`, so a share whose outcome was never confirmed still cannot be
  reported as "nothing was sent" or retried into a double post.

* fix(daemon): stop claiming an upload failure can name its own step

Review caught that the pinned SDK is 8.0.0, not the 7.19.0 copy also present in
the tree, and that in 8.0.0 `makeRequest` raises `WebAPIHTTPError` for every
non-200 before the `Failed to upload file ...` branch can run. So that string is
unreachable for an HTTP failure, and the comment, the test, and the design note
that leaned on it all asserted something that cannot happen.

Drop the branch instead of repairing it. An HTTP failure genuinely cannot prove
which step raised it: the same error type covers the reservation, the byte POST,
and the share, so a rejected upload and a lost response to an already-accepted
share are indistinguishable. Only Slack answering `{ok:false}` counts as proof
that nothing was published; everything else stays `indeterminate`, which was
already the behavior — this only removes a dead path and the false claim.

the upload it happened.

named `body` carrying an untyped `Blob`, which the hand-written POST already
matched — so the multipart shape was never what the reserved URL refused. The
one divergence left was the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header the SDK sends

fix(control-plane): provision an agent's GitLab account before the write that acts as it (#1423)

* fix(control-plane): provision an agent's GitLab account before the write that acts as it

Found in live testing: picking a GitLab project in the workspace editor and then
replacing the workspace always failed. The edit activates the workspace through
the daemon, activation mints credentials from the agent's own service account
(§7.2), and no account existed yet — so activation was refused and the edit
rolled back. The convergence that would have created the account only ran after
the write, and the rollback meant it never ran at all. Repair could not help
either: the agent never became a consumer of the project, so binding convergence
had no reason to provision an account for it. The flow could not succeed.

The identity is now provisioned inline, to completion, before the write that
will act as it — in both gitlab workspace arms and both gitlab hook arms. Each
runs under the same binding lease a full converge takes, and the account
mutation lease and generation fence stay where the account service puts them; a
contended attempt is retried on a short request-appropriate bound rather than
outwaited for minutes. A definite refusal becomes a 409 carrying the account's
own repair category, so a group that is out of service-account slots says so
instead of failing at activation.

Create provisions after the agent row exists and withdraws the row if the
account cannot be provisioned, because the reverse order would leave an account
no agent owns, while this one leaves an agent the next convergence adopts. A
workspace edit that rolls back for any other reason converges the project it had
just bound, so the membership does not outlive the edit. The post-write kick
stays for the retarget's leave-side cleanup.

The role a workspace authorization derives now has one definition shared by the
consumer query and the write paths, instead of the same rule spelled twice.

forwarded text message always worked. The difference is that a text reply goes

out through the external upload, whose completion answers with the FILE and no
timestamp at all. The share was therefore recorded under a synthetic local id,
so when a human replied under it the daemon saw a thread whose root it did not
recognize as its own and had nothing to wake.

the documented place that record lives. The read is best-effort by
construction: the file is already in the conversation by then, so a failure
degrades to an unanchored share rather than to a failed one — reporting
"nothing was sent" about a file the channel is displaying would invite exactly
the retry that double-posts it.

fix(control-plane): fence the GitLab run projection on the acting agent's account epoch (#1428)

Found in live testing: every merge-request status-note write was refused with
`stale_credential_epoch`, leaving projection rows completed-but-unobserved with
no note, while formal reviews and ordinary replies from the same agents worked.

The daemon fences the note write by comparing the epoch of the effect lease it
minted against the epoch the projection frame carries. Since per-agent identity
the lease is minted against the acting agent's own account, so its epoch is that
account's; the projection was still filled from the binding's counter. Two
counters that advance on entirely separate schedules, compared for equality —
so the fence refused every write, permanently.

The projection now resolves the agent's account on the project the same way the
effect lease does and carries that account's epoch. An agent with no ready
account there cannot write the note at all, so no projection opens — fail closed
like the other missing-authority early returns rather than recording a row whose
write can never pass.

The daemon is unchanged: the fence is right, it was being handed the wrong
counter. Auditing the other fields per-agent identity left on the binding's
counter found no second case — the compiled rule and the review lease carry
account identity but no epoch, and the binding's own counter now feeds only
console display, where nothing compares it.

feat(control-plane): open a private agent's DM to the people it is shared with (#1433)

* feat(control-plane): open a private agent's DM to the people it is shared with

Closes #558.

Conversation gating makes every conversation of a restricted agent default Off,
because the platform has no per-user ACL and only an editor can vouch for a
channel's membership. That is right for a room and wrong for the person the
agent was shared with: their own DM answers a "not enabled" notice until an
editor - often the same person - goes and enables it. The gate protects nobody
there; it just makes a private agent feel broken to its own audience.

So a 1:1 DM now seeds to the ordinary DM default instead of Off when its
counterpart is BOTH in the agent's own sharedWith audience AND carrying a linked
Slack identity in that bot's workspace. Both arms are load-bearing: an unlinked
audience member and a linked non-member each keep today's Off. Share an agent
with a, b and c, and each of the three who has linked gets their own DM opened.

A 1:1 DM is the only conversation seeded, because it is the only one whose
entire human membership is known at discovery - one bot, one person. A channel
is a place and a group DM is a room, so both keep going to an editor.

Mechanism: the reporter adds the counterpart's member id to the conversation
report (IntegrationChannel.dmUserId, persisted as control metadata of the same
class as the row's name); both report paths carry it. The CP resolves the
audience's own linked identities - each a cached per-subject read - and matches
the reported counterpart against them, so no reverse index from a platform
member id to a console account is built. Every unresolvable case fails closed to
the Off default: no sign-in configured, no workspace on the bot, an oversized
audience, or an upstream that cannot answer.

Deciding only at discovery would fire only for people whose link and audience
seat both predate their first DM - the opposite of what happens, since people
link because they were refused. So the two writes that can make the answer true
later, a landed identity link and a widened audience, re-ask it for the Off DM
rows already on record. The catch-up is one-way: a stored trigger is
indistinguishable from an operator's own choice, so re-deriving a close would
revert decisions this never made.

Known edge, recorded in the design: the edge decides admission before the CP has
the row, so the first message of a brand-new DM still gets the one-time notice;
the conversation is open from the next message on.

Design: docs/designs/resource-visibility.md section 14.8. The stale "proposed"
status on section 14 is corrected to implemented in the same pass.

* fix(control-plane): exhaust the GitLab listings a recovery predicate reads

`gitlabListServiceAccounts` asked for one `per_page=100` page and never
followed `x-next-page`, yet it is the only read behind the Section 7.2
per-agent account convergence: it supplies the `createAttemptKnownIds`
snapshot, the candidate search in `claimFromAttempt`, the durable-key lookup
by `serviceAccountUserId`, and the foreign-account check. All four read an
account that is merely further down the pages as absent.

Section 5 puts Premium service-account quantity at unlimited and Section 1
scopes this integration to Free and Premium, so a root past one page is
inside the supported scope. There the convergence degraded badly: an account
GitLab had created was not on page 1, so nothing could claim it, the username
check did not see it either, and the code opened a fresh window, re-created,
was refused for the taken username, and surfaced a generic retryable
`gitlab_409` instead of the promised `username_taken`. Worse, an incomplete
snapshot could let the claim predicate adopt a pre-existing foreign account,
handing somebody else's account this agent's credentials.

listing: a mid-listing failure, a header that does not advance, and the
runaway page bound all raise a typed error instead. The non-2xx mapping moves
into `gitlabError` so both it and `gitlabRequest` share one path.

The two sibling single-page listings get the same treatment for the same
reason. A stray PAT the sweep misses stays live with its plaintext lost, and
a project webhook the adoption misses is read as absent, so the converge
creates a duplicate and cleanup orphans it. `gitlabListProjects` is
deliberately untouched: its paging is the picker's, driven by the client.

exercises the real header. All three new provisioning tests fail without this

fix(control-plane): let an asynchronous GitLab account deletion finish (#1438)

* fix(control-plane): let an asynchronous GitLab account deletion finish

Found in live testing: an account whose last project was unbound entered
retirement, GitLab deleted it — the user 404s and the group's service-account
listing is empty minutes later — yet the row sat at retiring / cleanup_pending /
gitlab_unreachable indefinitely with nothing revisiting it.

GitLab removes a user asynchronously. The retirement asked for the deletion and
then immediately re-read the group's service-account listing as its positive
evidence, so on the normal path it found the account still there and treated a
deletion in flight as a refusal. It threw an internal error carrying status 0,
which the reason mapping reads as "GitLab unreachable" — false, and it hid what
was actually happening.

An account still listed right after an accepted delete now records
`deletion_pending` and returns, and a background sweep re-reads the listing on a
bounded cadence and closes the retirement out on the absence the design asks
for. The sweep re-drives the whole retirement rather than only observing it, so
a run that failed part-way is finished rather than stranded, and its worklist is
keyed on the lifecycle rather than on a reason — a row must not fall out of the
sweep by failing differently.

`gitlab_unreachable` is now reserved for a real transport failure, which is the
only thing the request wrapper reports as status 0. Positive-evidence failures
carry their own category instead of borrowing that one.

Auditing the binding removal saga for the same shape: its webhook deletion is
synchronous and has no immediate re-check to defeat, and its remaining evidence
check is local state rather than a provider read — but it shared the wrong
status-0 reason, and it blocked on the account retirement it triggers. It now
reports `deletion_pending` honestly, keeps its claim while the deletion is in
flight, and completes once the sweep proves the account gone.

A retirement awaiting deletion released the account lease while the row stayed

retirement that ended and revives it. A consumer arriving in that window would
therefore adopt a GitLab user whose deletion had already been accepted, mint
fresh PATs against it, and attach a membership — and when GitLab's worker

dead credentials that the sweep no longer watched. A pending deletion is now a

detach and the obligation now commit in one transaction, before any provider
write, and binding the account again clears it in the same way.

* fix(control-plane): make the GitLab retirement lifecycle itself the durable fence

Review follow-up on two gaps that made the previous fixes non-durable, both
caused by keying a lifecycle decision on a field a later attempt overwrites.

The revival fence read `stateReason`, but the sweep replaces that reason after
any later provider or transport failure while the row stays `retiring` in its
worklist. A deletion GitLab had already accepted could therefore stop matching
the fence, and a consumer arriving before it settled would revive the doomed
user and recreate the dead-credential outcome. The fence is now the lifecycle:
a retirement in progress is never revived, whatever its latest reason says. Its
row is a work item until the retirement deletes it, and only then does the next
attempt provision a genuinely fresh account — which is what the generation fence
has always meant by waiting and re-provisioning. Reviving a retiring row is no
longer possible anywhere, so that repository operation is gone with it.

The obligation transaction wrote its marker but left the emptied account
`active`, so a process exit between it and the external attempt left a row that
neither worklist selected: the marker survived but nothing resumed it, and a
retried removal could release the claim with the account still alive. That
transaction now performs the `active`→`retiring` transition too — it has just
verified the membership set is empty, which is exactly the condition that
transition requires — so the row is a durable work item before any provider
call. Its worklist keys on the lifecycle alone, since a finished retirement
deletes its row and any surviving one is by definition unfinished.

A consumer waiting on a retirement now says so in its own words rather than
borrowing the deletion's, because a retirement can be waiting on repair rather
than on GitLab.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): lock the GitLab account row before the removal detach counts it

Review follow-up. The detach that empties an account deleted and counted its
memberships before taking the account row lock its final update needs, while a
bind takes that lock first. Under read-committed a concurrent bind could hold
the lock with a membership this count could not yet see, and the transition to
`retiring` would then land on a row that has one — an account no consumer may
use, because every retiring row is fenced, and that no retirement may finish,
because a membership remains. A permanent deadlock, reachable whenever a bind
for another project races a removal.

The detach now locks the account row first, exactly as the bind and the
retirement CAS already do, so the two serialize: the bind either commits before
the count and keeps the account, or waits and loses the generation fence.

The regression test races the two against real Postgres over several rounds and
asserts the invariant either way; it fails on every round without the lock.

feat(web): key the GitLab card by bot (#1430)

* feat(web): key the GitLab card by bot

The Integrations card listed projects with their bot accounts inside, which
inverts how every chat-platform card reads and leaves an account whose last
project went away with nowhere to appear. It is now keyed by bot: one row per
agent service account with its avatar, name, handle, top-level group and
health, and the projects it is a member of underneath, carrying the role each
membership derives and the project-level actions on the project line. A project
two agents consume appears under both bots, and one no bot is a member of keeps
its own group at the end — a binding outlives its last consumer, still owning
the webhook and the claim.

Serving that needs the whole roster in one read, so the API gains
GET /orgs/:orgId/gitlab/accounts: every account the organization owns with its
agent, group, health and memberships, visibility-gated so a bot whose agent the
caller cannot see is absent rather than redacted. No token material.

The card asks again only while the server says convergence still owes the
organization work: an account mid-flight, a membership no consumer justifies,
or a consumer whose membership is missing or held at the wrong role. The
console cannot judge that itself — it cannot see an agent's hooks or workspace
— and a roster that merely looks settled proves nothing, since a membership can
change while the project set does not. A refused account is excluded, because
it waits for a human and counting it would ask forever. Repair, take-over and
an unfinished removal each re-read the roster, since they change accounts while
the project set stays put.

Two things also stopped reading as problems that were not problems. A project
with no trigger wants no ingress at all, so the binding now reports the webhook
state itself — not needed, installed, repairing, or failed — and only the two
worth acting on are shown. And each project line says why the bot holds it, its
workspace access and enabled trigger families, so deleting an agent's triggers
cannot leave its working workspace looking like a leftover. Taking a project
over is offered only where administration has lost its authority.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): owe a detach whatever shape the account is in

Two ways the GitLab card could settle on something that was no longer true.

The refusal exemption in the convergence answer covered every non-ready
account, in both directions. It is only ever right for a membership that
cannot be CREATED until someone repairs the account — a bot the group's quota
refused. A membership already recorded and no longer justified is a detach the
saga still owes, and exempting it meant a bot with rotation trouble that lost
its last consumer reported settled while the project sat under it for good. An
actual membership no consumer justifies is now always convergence; only
desired-but-absent on a refused account rests.

The webhook state was a snapshot taken with no regard for whether convergence
had run. Enabling a trigger commits before the run it fires, so a healthy
project with no webhook yet reported a failed one — and since the card read
projects once at mount and polled only the roster, whose answer knew nothing
about webhook work, a successful install could not clear the badge without a
reload. A binding still reporting healthy has simply not been converged for
this desire yet, which is transient; failed now means a run completed and left
the binding degraded. Pending webhook work counts as convergence, and the
projects ride the roster's poll while it is, so the badge clears on its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): take one last project read when GitLab convergence settles

The roster poll refreshed the projects only while the answer still said work
was owed, and the interval drops to zero on the same answer that says it is
not. So the response reporting settled — the one actually carrying the
finished state — was the one read that got skipped, and a webhook that had
just finished installing kept its transient badge until someone reloaded the
page.

The pending-to-settled edge now earns a read of its own: exactly one, and only
after an answer that owed work. A write in flight still owns the projects and
leaves the edge unconsumed, so the settling read happens once the write is
done rather than being lost to it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): let only the newest GitLab project read commit

Each roster answer launched its own project read, so several were in flight at
once and the network chose the order they came back in. A slow read taken while
a webhook was still installing could answer after the one that saw it finish,
painting the transient badge back over the settled state — and by then polling
had stopped, so it stayed. Nothing tied a response to the organization it was
launched for either, so a read could outlive the switch away from it.

Commits are now fenced on a monotonic generation captured when the read starts:
only the newest may set the projects. An organization switch and every write
bump that generation too, since both know something no read already in flight
does — a write's own outcome is the truth, and a read launched for another
organization has nothing to say about this one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): fence the GitLab project read taken at mount

The read that fills the card on arrival committed under its unmount guard
alone. It is launched before the roster surface is enabled, so every fenced
read that follows races it: it could snapshot a webhook still installing, a
later read render the finished state, and then the first one answer last and
put the transient badge back — with polling already stopped for good.

It now takes a generation at launch and commits only while that is still the
newest, exactly like the reads the roster poll launches. The unmount guard
stays, since it answers a different question: whether anyone is still looking,
not whether this answer is the current one.

fix(web): GitLab sessions are GitLab, not generic webhooks (#1440)

Found in live testing: a GitLab-triggered session showed its source as the
generic "Webhook", and the Agents list popped a "GitLab events" tooltip on its
integration mark — the only mark in that cluster with a hover title.

The cause is that the hook-kind vocabulary was hand-copied into every consumer,
so a code host could be left out of a mapping and inherit the generic arm with
nothing failing. GitHub needed the same fixes by hand months ago.

The vocabulary now has one source: `HOOK_KINDS` in
`packages/protocol/src/code-host.ts`, derived from `CODE_HOST_PROVIDERS`, with
`isCodeHostHookKind` answering which kinds are code hosts. Everything that
classified a hook by hand reads it instead:

- the session integration facet and `sessionPlatform` promote a code host out of
  the generic bucket by asking the vocabulary rather than listing hosts;
- the source label, trigger filter-group heading, filter face, and the list marks
  are `Record<HookKind, …>` mappings, so a new host fails type-check until it is
  given each one — verified by adding a third provider, which produced six errors
  across the session projection and the console and none anywhere else;
- the Sessions trigger menu buckets facets by hook kind from that vocabulary
  instead of hand-written switch arms, which is how a GitLab facet used to be
  collected nowhere and vanish from the menu;
- the wire and DTO enums (`HookContext.source`, `RcHookAssign.kind`, and the four
  session/agent DTO fields) build their `z.enum` from the same tuple.

`webhook` is now the mapping for the generic kind, and for a hook whose
definition can no longer be resolved. It is never the fallback for an unmapped
code-host kind.

Also removes the hook-kind tooltip so the integration cluster stays silent on
hover like every other mark in it, and names an unnamed hook by its source in the
Sessions channel and trigger cells instead of calling every kind a webhook.

Tests walk the whole vocabulary rather than the hosts that exist today, on both
sides of the wire, plus a negative control per surface.

working across two groups read as two bots. It owns two accounts because a
GitLab bot account cannot cross a top-level group, but that is one bot with two

stays is the group for projects no bot holds: a binding outlives its last

use rather than text buttons.

link in the integration row and the bot on the Workspace source line. GitHub
names nothing there, and GitLab now matches; the roster lives on the

lookup that existed only to feed them.

project rows leaves the wire, and the card keeps only what tells a held binding
from an orphaned one. Convergence polling stays exactly as it was, because bot
health — creation, rename, retirement, a refused quota — is what it was always

* fix(web): carry held-project health on the bot row, and survive a half-done batch

Dropping the project rows dropped an axis with them. A project's own state and
its webhook are independent of the accounts on it: every account can be ready
while the project is no longer reachable, has no administering account, or has
a webhook that failed to install. With no row of its own and no reading of it
left on the agent page either, such a project became indistinguishable from a
healthy one, and the always-present repair control offered neither a signal nor
a cause. The bot row now counts the projects it holds that need attention and
reveals them with their repair and take-over; a bot whose projects are all
healthy still says nothing. An account's own repair instruction moves out of
the hover title and into rendered text, because that sentence is the one that
says what to do and a touch screen never sees a tooltip.

The bot-wide repair and take-over sent one request per project and treated the
batch as one operation. A single rejection threw away every response that had
already succeeded and skipped the refresh, so the card could report a failure
over rows still showing their old administrator — and a mixed outcome is
expected for a take-over, whose own dialog promises it happens where access
allows. Both now settle every request, always re-read the projects, bots, and
connections afterwards whatever happened, and say how many of the batch landed
instead of naming only the first failure.

* fix(web): survive a failed reconciliation, and keep the attention count fresh

Reconciling a batch awaited the bound roster revalidation, which rejects by
default, and both batch handlers cleared their busy flag and dialog only after
that await. One transient revalidation failure therefore left Repair disabled
for good, or the take-over dialog sitting at "Working…", until someone
reloaded. Reconciliation no longer throws — it reports whether it managed to
re-read everything — and the cleanup runs in a finally either way. A reconcile
that could not read the result now says so, rather than leaving the card
quietly showing state it never confirmed.

The attention count on a bot row reads the project list, and that list had been
left with only its read at mount once the roster stopped driving one. A project
degrading — or healing — after arrival never reached the badge. The
generation-fenced re-read is back on the roster poll, including the one last
read on the answer that reports convergence finished, which is the answer
carrying the finished state and the one that stops the poll. It exists for the
attention signal now rather than for project rows, but it is the same
mechanism, and every commit into the project list stays fenced so a slow read
cannot paint over a newer one.

refactor(control-plane): key the session integration filter by code-host provider (#1441)

The session facet projection promotes any code host out of the generic hook
bucket automatically, but the filter READ path still named the two hosts by
hand. A third provider would therefore be emitted as a facet and offered in the
console's integration dropdown, then rejected by the query it selected — the
asymmetry a reviewer caught on #1440.

The read path now iterates `CODE_HOST_PROVIDERS` end to end:

- `SessionFilterQueryDto.integration` builds its enum from the routing platforms
  plus the shared provider list, so a promoted host is selectable as soon as it
  can be emitted;
- `codeHostHookFilters` resolves definitions per provider and returns one
  `Partial<Record<CodeHostProvider, HookId[]>>` instead of a field per host;
- `SessionFilterQuery` carries that one keyed field, so a new provider needs no
  new port field;
- `integrationSql` asks `isCodeHostProvider` rather than testing each host, and
  `integrationFacetSql` builds one CASE arm per provider that has ids.

`githubRepoId` stays GitHub-specific: the numeric repository-id collapse really
is GitHub's alone, and a repository filter still resolves that host only.

This is a shape change, not a behavior change — github and gitlab resolve, filter,
exclude, and project exactly as before. Verified by temporarily adding a third
provider: the filter path compiles and serves it with no edit, and the only
errors left are the two places a human must act anyway, a display label and the
database enum. Nothing degrades silently.

The route tests now walk the provider list instead of asserting on two named
fields, so they cover every host at once: each is accepted as a filter value and
handed its own ids, and the generic hook filter excludes every promoted host.

feat(control-plane): snapshot the hook kind on the session row (#1444)

Found in live testing: GitLab-triggered sessions rendered as generic webhooks
once their hook had been deleted and recreated. The source kind was read from
the hook definition at display time, so a session pointing at an id that no
longer resolves lost its identity — the row, its label, its facet, and its

session cannot be counted twice.

live hook exactly as they do today, which means a code-host session older than
the column still degrades to the generic rendering once its hook is gone. The
column is additive and nullable, so the migration is safe to apply ahead of the

feat(control-plane): authorize additional GitLab projects and enforce the hook precondition (#1445)

* feat(control-plane): authorize additional GitLab projects and enforce the hook precondition

Section 8.3 of the GitLab design states that creating a hook never creates a
repository grant, and that the watched project must already be the workspace
project or an explicit additional authorization. GitHub enforced that on hook
create and on a binding-changing edit; GitLab did not, and there was no way to
authorize a GitLab project at all. Found in live testing: a review-enabled
GitLab trigger on an unauthorized project fires, the review's exact checkout
cannot obtain credentials, and the agent posts a "could not review" note.

Provider-qualify the grant. `AgentRepoAuthorization` gains a `provider` column
defaulting to `github` (every row on record is a GitHub grant, so the default is
the backfill) and its unique key becomes `(agentId, provider, repoId)`: the two
hosts number their repositories independently, so a bare numeric id stopped
being an identity the moment GitLab grants existed. Every reader that matched on
`repoId` alone is qualified the same way, including the workspace-collision
checks, which now compare `workspaceMode` as the workspace's provider.

Add the gitlab arm to `POST/PATCH/DELETE /agents/:agentId/repos`. The body is a
plain union rather than a discriminated one so a provider-less github body still
validates. The project is named by numeric id and validated against the
organization's own binding — a grant never creates a binding, exactly as a hook
never does. Authorizing makes the agent a consumer of the project, so the arm
takes the same identity bracket the workspace and hook arms take: the account
and membership are provisioned first and the grant row commits under the binding
lease. Revoking converges the membership away. The convergence query that
computes the desired membership set now unions grant rows, without which the
next converge would unbind the membership the grant had just bound.

Enforce the precondition for both hosts in the shared place: `watchRepoAuthorized`
becomes provider-aware and the gitlab hook arms call it on create and on a
binding-changing edit, matching GitHub's grandfathering of existing rows. The
409 names the fix in the reader's own vocabulary — project for GitLab.

Serve the credential. The GitLab grant resolution accepted only the workspace
project; it now resolves either authority and clamps to the grant's tier. On the
daemon, an additional-repository entry carries its provider (absent means github,
so an older control plane's list still decodes) and a named GitLab project is
asked for with its numeric id, without which the request resolved to the
workspace grant and the daemon's own echo check rejected it. Secondary workspace
roots stay GitHub-only and skip GitLab entries rather than cloning them from the
wrong host.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(web): offer GitLab projects in the additional-repository picker

The picker only searched GitHub repositories, so the precondition Section 8.3
states — a watched project must already be the workspace project or an explicit
additional authorization — was unsatisfiable for a GitLab project from the
console. Choosing the code host now comes first, and the GitLab arm lists the
connection's Maintainer-or-Owner projects merged with the ones already added,
setting up a project that is not added yet before the selection lands, exactly
as the workspace and trigger pickers do. It submits the numeric project id, and
speaks GitLab's nouns: project, merge request, pipeline. A project the agent
already holds is named as taken rather than offered again, and grant rows carry
their host's mark wherever they are listed.

The trigger wizard says the same refusal where the pick is, and names the two
ways to satisfy it, rather than letting the create reach the identical message
from the server at the last click.

Docs: Sections 8.3, 13.1, 18.1, and 18.2 record the provider-qualified grant
identity, the two credential authorities an agent now has, the picker and
wizard behavior, and the one half deliberately left out — an authorized GitLab
project receives credentials but is not materialized as a secondary workspace
root, because that layout is still `owner/repo` on github.com.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): finish provider-qualifying the grant readers and rename convergence

Review found three functional gaps in the provider-qualified grants, all of them
places where a numeric id was still treated as an identity on its own.

A GitLab project rename converged the binding, the catalog, and gitlab-workspace
clone URLs, but not the authorization rows. That path is what the daemon maps a
NAMED project back to its numeric id with, so a rename orphaned the new path,
and an ask under the old one was answered with the binding's new path and then
correctly rejected by the echo check. Rename convergence now refreshes both
halves in one transaction and bumps each affected agent's revision exactly once,
so a spec never carries half a rename; its owners join the same fan-out the
workspace agents already did. The method is renamed to match what it converges.

Two GitHub readers still matched on a bare `repoId`. The create preflight read
any same-numbered row as a duplicate, so holding GitLab project N blocked
authorizing GitHub repository N even though the unique key permits both. The
rename refresh in `refreshGithubRepoFullName` was the damaging one: it read and
updated grant rows by number alone, so a GitHub rename could overwrite a
same-numbered GitLab grant's path and replicate the corruption to the daemon.

On the daemon, `erase` derived the provider only from the workspace while `get`
routed a named GitLab project to a provider-qualified key. For a scratch or
GitHub-workspace agent, Git presenting a rejected GitLab token invalidated the
GitHub entry and left the rejected one live until its TTL. Provider resolution
now happens before the op split, so both branches address the same key.

Also closes the rollout hazard the review flagged as non-blocking: the §17.3
projection gate derived its requirement from `workspace.mode` alone, so an agent
whose only GitLab-shaped content was an additional repository could be served to
a pre-GitLab daemon. That daemon strips the unknown provider key, leaving a
two-segment project path to read as an `owner/repo` GitHub entry and be cloned
from the wrong host. The predicate now also reads the assembled
additional-repository list, and delivery judges on the assembled spec, which is
the only place grants are visible. Placement still judges on the agent row and
would need a grant read to match; that is left for the rollout work.

Each fix carries a regression test, and each was confirmed to fail with its fix
reverted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): commit a GitLab authorization at the path the provider answers with

Review found the last place a numeric id and its display path could disagree.
`authorizeGitlabProject` read the binding BEFORE taking the provisioning lease and
its commit closure wrote that captured path. The lease's own project read already
fetched the current `path_with_namespace` and discarded it, updating neither the
binding nor the catalog. A rename between the two reads therefore persisted and
replicated the losing side, and since the grant path is what the daemon maps a
NAMED project back to its numeric id with, the checkout could never be found: the
old path resolves to the binding's new one and fails the consumer's echo check.

The lease's read is now the single answer everything takes. The durable path
convergence the full run already performed — binding, catalog, and every
projected path — is extracted and also run inside the account lease, and the live
path is handed to the commit closure, so the row that lands and the replicas that
describe it cannot disagree. The redundant pre-lease catalog upsert goes with it.

The gitlab workspace edit takes the same live path for its clone URL. It built one
from the same pre-lease binding read, so once the lease converges the projected
paths, committing the capture would have put the stale one straight back.

The hook identity bracket is unchanged: its commit ignores the argument, and a
hook's `repoFullName` is display-only and never matched on.

Regression test: the project is renamed at the provider after the binding is
written and before the authorize call, and the persisted grant, the binding, and
the catalog all carry the new path. Confirmed to fail with the fix reverted.

* fix(control-plane): recompile a project's rules when an authorization adds a bot

feat(daemon): admit GitLab merge-request revisions through the shared queue plan (#1448)

* feat(daemon): admit GitLab merge-request revisions through the shared queue plan

GitHub hook deliveries have long contended for the next generation of one
pull-request lane: a newer head supersedes queued turns and preempts an active
older-head turn, a re-request collapses onto the newest delivery, and one
submitted review's inline comments coalesce into a single batched turn. GitLab
had none of that at the turn level. Every push to a merge request queued a full
turn on the per-thread session, and a stale head's review only died at the
review adapter's head fence just before publishing -- correct, but a whole
generation of wasted work -- while notes never batched at all.

Extract the provider-neutral shape from the working GitHub implementation and
add GitLab as its second implementer, in one change:

- `codehost/hook-admission.ts` is the contract: lane identity, revision stream
  and its recency/contest rules, head, re-run predicate, comment batch stream,
  batch opening, item identity, batch prompt, and whether a sealed batch
  publishes each item itself. A delivery resolves to a module through the
  frame's discriminated provider member, so core never names a provider.
- `codehost/queue-admission.ts` is the pure planner, moved off the GitHub
  module and routed through that seam.
- `github/hook-admission.ts` keeps everything GitHub-specific behind it --
  check-run re-run semantics and submitted-review batching are not in the
  contract.
- `gitlab/hook-admission.ts` is the new arm: the lane is (hook, project, MR
  IID); `merge_request:opened`/`synchronize` establish a head, while a reviewer
  request and the console `rc/hook-rerun` pin to the head already current.
  Preemption reuses GitHub's criterion unchanged rather than inventing one.
  Notes on one merge request coalesce under the same three gates and render a
  GitLab batch prompt.

GitHub behavior is unchanged. The one place the providers genuinely diverge is
publication: GitHub's sealed batch hands publication to its per-thread reply
tool and withdraws the ordinary reply target, while GitLab has no such tool, so
its batch keeps the target and the daemon publishes exactly one note. That fact
is a contract member, which also keeps the batch-reply tool closed for GitLab
and keeps per-item publication accounting off its terminal outcome.

Design docs travel with it: the webhook design records that the admission seam
now has two implementers, and GitLab section 12.3 records the implemented
behavior -- including that note batching, previously declined for want of a
durable review identifier, now uses the merge request itself as the batch key
with the timing gates bounding it, and what that costs.

* fix(daemon): seal a review batch only after an in-flight coalesce lands in it

The durable coalesce awaits in the middle of folding a follower delivery into
the leader's batch: it snapshots the leader hook, commits the row that reports
the follower `coalesced_review_batch`, and only then assigns the new context.
The leader's own seal could run inside that window. It would build and dispatch
the prompt from the pre-coalesce snapshot, and the late assignment would then
overwrite the sealed context -- so the follower was durably reported as folded
into a generation whose prompt never carried it, and its comment went
unanswered.

lock, so a leader that sealed while the delivery waited refuses it and the
follower runs as its own turn; a coalesce that gets there first blocks the seal
until its row commits, and the seal then reads the batch that includes it. A
turn with no batch takes no lock at all.

open, advances past the quiet window so the seal is due, and asserts the

fix(control-plane): stop a lost GitLab convergence fence becoming a degraded binding (#1446)

* fix(control-plane): stop a lost GitLab convergence fence becoming a degraded binding

Found in live testing: the bot-level Repair reliably left a project at
`admin_degraded` / `account_busy`, showing "setup incomplete" and the attention
badge, and it never healed — the next Repair raced the same way.

Repairing a bot re-runs convergence per project it holds, and two bots sharing a
project double that, so several convergences ran at once against one account
mutation lease. The losers reported the retryable `account_busy`, and the
outcome was persisted verbatim: a race became a sticky verdict about the
binding, clearable only by another race. The repair route made it worse by
running a single attempt with no contention retry at all.

Three changes. Convergence is now coalesced per (organization, project): a
caller that finds one in flight joins it and asks for a trailing pass, rather
than racing it for the same leases — so concurrent repairs of one project do one
run, and a joiner's own write is still converged. A contended outcome is no
longer persisted at all; the binding keeps the state it had, because a lost
fence says nothing about the binding. And a pass that exhausts its contention
budget schedules a follow-up convergence, so it settles without anyone pressing
Repair again. The repair route goes through that path with a request-sized
bound, handing off to the follow-up instead of holding the connection.

Any contention reason still reachable now reads as in-progress in the console
rather than as a setup failure. The card's per-bot repair also runs its
per-project requests sequentially: they share one bot account, so firing them
together only made them queue on its lease. That is a mitigation, not the fix —
the server is correct whatever the client does.

* fix(control-plane): owe a follow-up for every contended GitLab pass, and say so

Review follow-up on two liveness gaps left by not persisting contention.

Not persisting a lost fence is only half the answer: something has to come back
for the convergence that never happened. A pass with its own retry loop owns
that, but a create, a takeover, or a single repair has no loop — and a bot-wide
takeover launches one transfer per project, so projects sharing a bot account
contend exactly as repairs do. A contended transfer reported success, kept its
previous state, and was never converged again, leaving a formerly ready binding
falsely healthy with its membership drift unrepaired. Every contended pass now
arms a follow-up, at one place that all three paths run through; only the
retrying loop suppresses it, because it is the follow-up.

The console asked the database whether convergence still owed the organization
work, which reads settled while a follow-up is pending — so the roster could
stop polling one refresh before the binding actually healed, leaving the card
showing the state the contended pass had preserved. It now also asks what is
still in flight or armed, and keeps watching until that is empty too.

convergence was still owed lived in this process's timer — a restart erased both
the obligation and the console's signal, and a takeover preserved as `ready`
could keep unrepaired membership drift with nothing to rediscover it by. The
obligation is now a neutral marker on the binding, written before the timer is
armed and cleared by the pass that settles. A sweep re-drives whatever still
carries it, and the console reads the marker too, so its "still converging"
answer survives a restart as well. The in-process follow-up re-reads the marker
before running, since anything that converged meanwhile has already discharged

The pre-activation ensure a route write runs had its own short budget while a
background convergence can hold the binding lease for minutes, so back-to-back
writes on one project could refuse on pure contention with a healthy convergence
in flight. That path now JOINS the run it collides with rather than spending its
budget losing the same race — when the run finishes, the account it provisioned
is usually the one the write needs — and only past a request-sized bound does it
report, still as a transient "try again", never as a degraded binding.
