feat(control-plane): the GitLab instance base URL as one host axis (#1450)

* feat(control-plane): the GitLab instance base URL as one host axis

The instance a deployment talks to becomes one configuration value beside the
OAuth application registered on it, not a mode: absent means `https://gitlab.com`,
so an existing deployment changes nothing and no code path branches on "is this
GitLab.com". `GITLAB_BASE_URL` joins the managed environment keys with the same
no-document fallback as the client pair, and the deployment document's GitLab
entry gains `baseUrl` (a deliberate strict-schema bump). A base URL without an
OAuth application is a configuration error, exactly as a half client pair is.

Normalization happens once, where the application configuration is resolved, and
produces the only value downstream code sees: HTTPS only, userinfo/query/fragment
refused, host lower-cased, an explicit non-default port kept, trailing slash
stripped, and a path prefix preserved — a relative URL root is a first-class
install shape.

The GitLab API module becomes a client bound to that resolved base at container
build time; the module-level host constant is gone, so nothing can address
another instance. URL composition is concatenation onto the normalized base,
never `new URL(absolutePath, base)`, which silently discards a path prefix. The
three functions that bypassed the shared request helper — the OAuth token
exchange, the paginated project list, and the avatar upload — fold onto one
dispatcher, so there is a single place a GitLab URL is built.

Clone URLs are no longer composed. The three places that synthesized
`https://gitlab.com/<path>` now read the persisted `CodeHostRepository.cloneUrl`,
which is the provider's own `http_url_to_repo` and therefore already correct on
any instance; the rename convergence and the workspace-edit commit take the
lease's live value the same way.

Finally, the axis is immutable while GitLab state exists. Connections, tokens,
numeric project ids, claims, and cleanup obligations carry no instance
provenance, so retargeting would send one host's credentials and host-relative
ids to another. A write that changes the effective base URL — including
unsetting it — is refused with `gitlab_base_url_locked` while any binding,
account, hook, live connection, or claim tombstone exists, raised inside the
deployment-document write's own advisory lock so a concurrent connect cannot
slip past it. A `disconnected` connection row is credential-free history and
does not hold the axis, so the ordinary disconnect path really does free it.

* fix(control-plane): close both sides of the GitLab host-axis fence

Review found the immutability guarantee open in two places, and both let one
instance's credentials and host-relative ids be presented to another after a
restart.

First, the fence only ran when a previous document existed. The no-document
environment fallback is supported, so `deployment_config` can be absent while
GitLab connections and bindings are already live; an `expectedRevision: 0`
write could then select any base and retarget all of it. The baseline is now
the axis in effect at write time — the previous document when there is one, and
otherwise the process-level `GITLAB_BASE_URL` fallback, normalized. That value
is injected rather than read from the environment inside a repository, so the
comparison stays a property of the composed store.

Second, taking the advisory lock only on the config writer did not serialize
its state count with state creation: a connect committing just after a count of
zero left credentials from the old instance behind a document that already
named the new one. The key is now two-sided. The document writer keeps it
exclusively around the count, and the transactions that can create
first-of-its-kind GitLab state — the OAuth callback's connection upsert and the
binding's claim creation — take it shared and then verify the persisted axis
still matches the base their in-flight operation composed against, refusing
with `gitlab_base_url_changed` when it does not. Either commit order is now
safe: the state write blocks until the retarget commits and then sees the new
axis, or the retarget blocks until the state commits and then counts it.

Agent accounts and gitlab hooks deliberately stay outside the shared side.
Neither can be the first GitLab state — both require a binding that the count
already sees — so a lock there would add contention without closing a window.

repository funnel so the enabled and disabled paths are covered by one rule,
and a gitlab-kind write that arrives without one is refused rather than
silently unfenced. The account upsert gains a transaction for the same reason:

feat(control-plane): the GitLab 18.11 version floor and the Setup Server probe (#1451)

* feat(control-plane): the GitLab 18.11 version floor and the Setup Server probe

Group service accounts became generally available on every tier, Community
Edition included, at 18.11; below that the Free-tier answer hides behind
instance feature flags the API does not report. So the floor is a hard
admission gate, enforced in two stages.

Parsing is a pure module: `MAJOR.MINOR` read through the suffixes GitLab
actually reports (`-ee`, `-pre`, `-rc`, a four-component build), the `-ee`
build suffix recorded as the edition, and anything unreadable treated as
below the floor. An instance that will not say what it is has not proven it
can serve the contract, so the failure is closed rather than optimistic.

The authenticated half is the first credentialed call the Control Plane makes
after a successful OAuth callback: `GET /api/v4/version` through the
base-bound client, recorded on deployment-level instance state, then the
verdict. Below the floor the callback returns `instance_version_unsupported`
and never reaches the connection upsert, so no administration identity, no
service account, and no webhook exists to clean up — the observation is still
recorded, because a refusal an operator cannot read is a silent one. The
state is keyed on the normalized base URL, so a re-target after a full
disconnect cannot inherit another instance's version, and the connection DTO
carries the non-secret `instanceUrl` and `instanceVersion` off it.

The reconciliation pass re-reads and re-records the same value, and the
refusal sits at the top of both provisioning entry points — the binding
convergence and the inline pre-activation account ensure, which is new
provisioning too. An instance downgraded under live bindings therefore stops
getting new accounts, credentials, and webhooks while everything already
provisioned keeps serving until its credentials expire: the floor gates
provisioning, not runtime.

The Setup Server gains the instance base URL field and the unauthenticated
half. Saving the URL issues `GET <base>/api/v4/version` with no credentials; a
healthy GitLab API root answers 401 with its own JSON error body, which proves
DNS, TLS trust, and shape — the things that fail far more often than the
version does. Only `invalid_url` refuses the save. `unreachable`,
`tls_untrusted`, and `not_a_gitlab_api_root` come back beside the saved
revision as warnings, because the Setup Server and the Control Plane need not
share a network position and a refusal here would be one process guessing
about another's network. The card's save also stops dropping the persisted
base URL, which had silently unset the axis on every write, and a change of
instance now demands the application secret the way a change of client id
already did.

- `AgentSpec.gitlabHost` — the instance every GitLab consumer on the spec
  addresses.
- `host` on the compiled hook rule's gitlab member and on the trusted hook
  metadata the relay forwards — the turn-time fence.
- `host` on the git-credential grant — an echo the consumer verifies alongside
  provider and project id.
- `gitlab-instance-v1`.

Absent means GitLab.com everywhere, so a peer reading an older control plane is
correct with no second negotiation.

The derivation lives in one function beside the spec assembler: the axis rides
the spec whenever ANY consumer does — a gitlab workspace, a gitlab additional
repository, or an enabled gitlab hook — carrying whatever value the axis holds,
so nothing branches on "is this GitLab.com" (section 24.1). Only the gates read
the value, and a default one gates nothing. The hook consumer is the one no
other projected field reveals, so the assembler takes a hook read, skipped
entirely when GitLab is unconfigured, and the agent-move bundle pins it like it
pins skills.

Four gates, all keyed on the configured value:

- placement — the direct-placement route checks, now asking the domain
  predicate instead of one feature string;
- projection — a second pass over the ASSEMBLED spec in the reconcile snapshot,
  because the additional-repository list and the host exist only there. That
  also closes the same hole for a gitlab additional repository, which the
  pre-assembly pass over domain records could never see;
- hook assignment — the relay broadcast and the per-channel replay;
- hook dispatch — the rule compile refuses a target daemon that has not
  advertised the bit, which is how one omission covers delivery, the relay's
  retry ladder, and an authorized re-run alike. A hook may fire at an agent
  whose workspace never passed the placement gate, so the target needs its own
  gate; it reads the daemon's PERSISTED advertisement, not its live socket, so a
  momentarily disconnected daemon does not have its rules torn out of the pool.

The two feature lists stay apart. Projection and hook assignment extend the
existing gitlab-com-v1 requirement; the dispatch-target daemon — never gated on
gitlab-com-v1 — is gated on the new bit alone, so a GitLab.com fleet behaves
exactly as it does today. Fail-closed by omission throughout: a peer without
the bit never sees self-managed work, so it cannot fall back to GitLab.com for
it.

The relay's entire share is pass-through: it copies the rule's host onto the
metadata it forwards and never parses it.

Tests: protocol round-trips for all four members with the absent-means-GitLab.com
resolution asserted where decoding happens; mixed-version control-plane
integration in both directions across all three consumer sources, including an
additional repository on a scratch workspace and a hook firing at a
non-GitLab-workspace agent; and byte-compatible GitLab.com behaviour for a
daemon advertising nothing.

* fix(control-plane): close the four gaps review found in the GitLab host carriage

All four are real gaps introduced by the carriage change, not pre-existing.

1. The production relay never advertised `gitlab-instance-v1`, so the assignment
   gate dropped every self-managed rule for every real relay while the test
   masked it with a hand-built channel. Carrying the host through IS the relay's
   whole share of the work, and it does that now, so it advertises the feature —
   registration and handshake assertion together.

2. A hook write is a SPEC edit. An enabled gitlab hook is a GitLab consumer, so
   it puts `gitlabHost` on its agent's spec even when the workspace is scratch or
   github — but the CRUD routes only converged the relay rule, so the rule could
   be exposed while the daemon's local spec still resolved the host to GitLab.com.
   The routes now re-project through `AgentDelivery.upsert`, ordered against the
   rule: the agent GAINING the consumer before the rule is exposed, the one
   LOSING it after the rule is gone, and on a retarget joining before leaving —
   the same order, for the same reason, that a repo retarget uses. Covers create,
   enable, disable, delete, and retarget.

3. Console reruns carried no host, so an N3 daemon would have resolved every
   rerun to GitLab.com and refused it. The compiled rule's host now rides
   `RcHookRerun.gitlab` (the relay already forwarded the object unchanged), and
   the rerun walk takes the host into its relay ELIGIBILITY rather than only its
   frame: a relay denied the self-managed rule holds none, so asking it would
   collect a `replay_pending` refusal — and the first answered verdict is final,
   so that refusal would have ended the walk before an eligible peer was asked.

4. The dispatch-target gate was a compile-time decision, which cached the
   daemon's advertisement. That advertisement changes under a standing rule in
   both directions: a daemon gaining the bit stayed ruleless until an unrelated
   hook or relay event, and one losing it kept a live rule — the very thing the
   gate exists to prevent. Convergence-on-capability-change would fix the
   staleness but stays racy, since a daemon can re-register between compile and
   dispatch. So the gate moves to a DISPATCH-time fence at the relay, beside the
   `gitlab-com-v1` fence it mirrors: on the live connection, re-read per delivery
   attempt, so a rollout heals with no convergence pass and a downgrade cannot
   leave a rule serving. Both the webhook path and the authorized re-run reach it
   through the same `dispatchHookFire`, which is what keeps one fence covering
   delivery, retries, and re-runs alike. The compile-time gate and its async
   daemon-features seam are removed rather than kept alongside, so there is one
   mechanism and no cached capability anywhere.

`isSelfManagedGitlabHost` moves from the control plane's domain layer to the
protocol beside `GITLAB_DEFAULT_BASE_URL`: the relay reads it now and the daemon
will in N3, so the rule about what an absent host means belongs on the wire
contract rather than in one consumer.

* fix(control-plane): order the hook spec projection inside the rule convergence

Review found the route-level ordering was too late to hold. The GitLab
provisioning bracket commits the hook row inside `provisionAgentAccount()` and
its `onConverged` callback rebroadcasts from there — so the updated,
secret-bearing rule could be assigned before execution ever reached the route's
awaited spec push, and a hook firing in that window reached a daemon with
neither the new config revision nor `gitlabHost`.

A route was the wrong seam because a route is not the only thing that assigns a
rule. `HookService.broadcast` is: it is the one place every assignment passes
through — the CRUD routes, the provisioning rebroadcast, and a placement
re-converge alike. So the ordering moves there and becomes one sequence rather
than a discipline each caller has to remember: project, then assign; remove,
then project. `replayTo` is deliberately untouched, so a relay reconnect still
replays rules without re-projecting every agent behind them.

The routes keep only the two cases an assign cannot see: the agent a retarget
moved the hook OFF, and a delete, which leaves no row to converge.

Also fixes a real CI failure this uncovered: the gitlab hooks harness left its
`onConverged` rebroadcast untracked, so `settled()` could return while the chain
was still querying and `afterEach` closed the pool under it — an unhandled
"Cannot use a pool after calling end on the pool" that failed the shard with
every test passing. It is tracked like `convergeProject` now. Reproduced on CI
across two runs of the same commit, so not a flake.

The retarget test now asserts the guarantee that actually holds: the gaining
agent carries the host before the rule is assigned to it, which convergence
makes atomically, while the losing agent's timing against that assign is free —
no rule points at it any more.

* fix(control-plane): drop a retargeted hook's old host only once the rule moved

Review was right and my previous reasoning was wrong. `converge()` is
fire-and-forget, so awaiting the losing agent's projection immediately after
calling it ordered nothing: the broadcast could still be compiling, or projecting
the gaining agent, while that push dropped the old agent's last `gitlabHost`. The
pool still holds the old rule targeting that very agent until `hookAssign` runs,
so a delivery in that window is refused. "No rule points at it any more" is only
true after the assign, not after the call.

`converge` therefore takes an `afterAssigned` continuation and the retarget's
losing projection rides it, so it lands strictly after the rule moved. The whole
chain stays fire-and-forget, so a relay push failure still never fails the CRUD
request.

The continuation is deliberately skipped when the broadcast REJECTS, because the
old rule may then still be live and dropping the host it depends on is the unsafe
direction. Leaving that state stale is safe, and the register/ok roster
reconciles it.

The retarget test asserts the order rather than an exact event list: the webhook
converge legitimately rebroadcasts, and a later assign of the already-moved rule
no longer names the agent that left, so what must hold is that the losing
projection follows the assign that moved the rule.

feat(daemon): resolve the GitLab instance from the spec instead of two literals (#1453)

* feat(daemon): resolve the GitLab instance from the spec instead of two literals

The daemon side of self-managed GitLab (gitlab-com-integration.md §24.4/§24.5).
The `'github.com' | 'gitlab.com'` classifier is retired: the managed host is now
a resolved `{provider, baseUrl}` pair carried on each workspace root, derived
from the spec's provider plus its `gitlabHost` (absent ⇒ GitLab.com), and a
clone URL is checked against it rather than being the source of it. The
`.git`-suffix canonicalization, the trusted-origin check and the workspace
materialization key all read that answer.

The credential helper stops gating on two literals. It receives a host table on
`AC_GITCRED_HOSTS`, minted beside the capability at injection time and stripped
from the daemon's own inherited environment so an ambient value can never be
read as a hint. Each entry carries the full normalized base including a path
prefix, because with `useHttpPath` git hands the helper `gitlab/group/project.git`
on a prefixed install; the prefix is stripped on an exact segment boundary
before the project path is parsed, and a host that is a prefix or suffix of a
managed one does not match. The gitcred consumer verifies a grant's echoed
`host` against the spec exactly as it verifies provider and project id.

The `glab` wrapper gets a `GITLAB_HOST` session export so the real CLI targets
the instance, and its target resolver compares against an explicitly passed
expected host — read off the same injected table, never off the exported value —
deferring only on a genuine mismatch. The four GitLab API clients resolve their
base per turn from the carried host. A hook delivery whose metadata host
disagrees with the session's spec is refused as `gitlab_host_mismatch` rather
than re-targeted, because a warm session's environment cannot be edited after
spawn.

The boot warning keyed on the GitLab.com literal becomes a spec-admission
refusal: a GitLab workspace whose origin the operator's `workspaceGitAllowedOrigins`
excludes is refused on the `agent/upsert` ack, naming the origin to add. The
operator list stays authoritative and is never widened. Only the degenerate
case — no https origin permitted at all — survives as a boot warning.

`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `SSL_CERT_DIR` and `GIT_SSL_CAINFO` join
the existing narrow forwarding allowlists so a private authority reaches the
workspace clone environment, the skill acquisition environment, the runtime
probe and the install repair. No skip-verify flag anywhere.

The slice is complete, so the daemon advertises `gitlab-instance-v1` on both the
control connection and `rd/hello` — the relay's dispatch fence reads the latter.

Tests cover the table (GitHub, GitLab.com, a prefixed non-default-port instance,
near-miss hosts, an unknown host), the grant host echo including absent-means-
GitLab.com, the warm-session fence, the spec-admission refusal, and a real clone,
push and `glab` invocation against a TLS `git-http-backend` served on an
ephemeral port behind a path prefix through the injected table.

* fix(daemon): keep the gitlab `.git` rule for an anonymous remote

Keying the suffix canonicalization on the spec's credential provider alone drops
it for an ANONYMOUS remote, and a public GitLab clone needs it as much as a
managed one: GitLab 301s the suffix-less HTTPS probe and daemon git refuses
redirects, so the clone fails and the materialization key of an existing
checkout changes under it.

an anonymous remote CHECKS the address against the deployment's GitLab instance

so nothing changes there. `gitRepoOf`, the materialization key and the console

about which remote a checkout is on.

* feat(daemon): pin the helper for a repo-bearing gitlab consumer

The injected host table only CLASSIFIES a credential request. Git has to select
a configured helper before any table can route it, so an agent whose GitLab
consumer is not its workspace — an authorized additional repository on a scratch
or GitHub workspace — had no `credential.<instance>` block and its clone or fetch
of that repository never reached the helper at all.

The session config now pins the helper for the instance whenever the spec
carries a REPO-BEARING GitLab consumer: a GitLab workspace, as before, or at
least one GitLab additional-repository authorization. Such an agent already
accepts that the managed identity owns that host's credential path — a GitLab
workspace has cut ambient credentials for unauthorized projects on its instance
since §13.2 — and extending the same rule to an additional-repository grant is
exactly the case the pre-spawn host carrier was introduced for.

A HOOK-ONLY host deliberately does not pin. A hook authorizes a turn, not a
repository, so pinning would move such an agent from "falls through to whatever
credentials this host has" to "our helper answers, the control plane refuses,
git fails" with nothing to serve in its place.

Only the SESSION channel widens. A daemon-run clone, fetch or push always knows
its exact target, so `cloneGitEnv` and `workspaceGitRemoteTarget` still pin one
host — the operation's own.

Tests pin all four shapes: both blocks for a GitHub or scratch workspace holding
a GitLab additional-repository grant, one block for a GitLab workspace whose
instance is already its own host, no instance block for a hook-only agent, and
the helper serving the authorized project while DECLINING an unauthorized one on
the same instance — the failure mode the second block introduces, asserted
explicitly rather than left implied.

feat(gitlab): self-managed creation authority, the PAT expiry clamp, and its surfaces (#1457)

* feat(control-plane): classify withdrawn GitLab creation authority and clamp PAT expiry

A self-managed instance can refuse service-account creation outright, and it
can cap access-token lifetime. Both were previously read as ordinary upstream
trouble, so an operator learned about them from a bot going silent.

Creation authority now has its own persisted account state. A 403 from group
service-account creation, or from minting or rotating a PAT on an account that
already exists, lands the row in `service_account_creation_forbidden` rather
than `admin_degraded`: it is a settled verdict, so the inline pre-activation
ensure stops retrying it and waits for a human, and because it is not
`admin_degraded` an account that was already provisioned keeps serving its
unexpired credentials until authority returns. The rotation reason is named
specifically, so the horizon warning says the authority was withdrawn instead
of reporting a bare status. Repair re-attempts once the instance allows it.

An expiry EARLIER than requested is now accepted as legitimate instance policy
and becomes the recorded one, so the rotation horizon is re-derived from what
was granted: a 30-day cap rotates on a 30-day cycle. A null or later expiry
stays out of policy, revoked and failed closed exactly as before, and a create
rejected for exceeding an instance maximum lifetime gets its own reason.

The connection DTO carries whether the observed version clears the floor and
what floor is enforced, so no second version parser has to live in a browser.
The integration fake gains an admin-only mode and a lifetime-cap mode.

fix(console): arm Merge when ready at the edge instead of GitHub auto-merge (#1345)

* fix(console): arm Merge when ready at the edge instead of GitHub auto-merge

GitHub's `enablePullRequestAutoMerge` refuses every pull request whose
mergeStateStatus is not BLOCKED — "clean status" once the checks pass,
"unstable status" while they run on a repository with no REQUIRED status checks.
On such a repository (this one included) there was no state in which the box
could be armed, so the control reported `github graphql error: Pull request is
in unstable status` rather than doing anything.

Merge-when-ready is now an AgentConnect watcher that runs where the agent runs:
a process in the agent's pod for a cluster-placed agent (new `automerge` shim
capability + `/opt/agentconnect/shim/auto-merge.js`, one child per armed pull
request, its own clamped gh token per tick over the existing gitcred tunnel), or
a loop in the owning daemon for a local one. It squash-merges once the pull
request is open, undrafted, conflict-free, has no failing or running check and
nobody has requested changes; REVIEW_REQUIRED deliberately does not block, since
a repository with no required reviewers reports it forever. Every tick judges the
CURRENT head and pins the merge to it, because merge-when-ready has to allow the
commit that turns the checks green — and a failing tick keeps the watcher armed,
surfacing its reason in the panel instead of giving up.

Nothing is persisted. The armed set is in memory at the edge, so a reclaimed
sandbox or a restarted daemon genuinely stops watching and the box reads back
unchecked. The CP relays `automerge/set` / `automerge/state` — scoped
request/reply frames like `task/list`, gated on `auto-merge-v1` — and stores no
intent, runs no loop and replays nothing; `autoMergeArmed: null` means nobody
could be asked, which the panel draws differently from a confident "not armed".

Its own shim capability rather than a widening of `exec`: that channel is
git-only and enforced inside the pod on purpose, and reaching `gh` through it
would turn a deliberate boundary into an arbitrary-execution surface. A pod from
an image that predates the entry answers `unsupported-image`, which the CP relays
as a 409 naming the resume rather than a 503 that would read as "try again".

fix(control-plane): make usage totals the org's, and the withheld part a residual (#1459)

* fix(control-plane): make usage totals the org's, and the withheld part a residual

`GET /usage` applied ONE predicate to everything, so hiding a restricted agent
also took its money out of the totals. That is wrong in the direction that costs
someone money — the same argument the settlement credential already rests on —
and the org's own spend is in any case published to every member by the billing
ledger. What a viewer may not learn is WHOSE spend it was.

So the viewer predicates stop being a WHERE and become a SELECTed boolean. A row
the reader may not attribute still lands in `totals` and in the ingress rollup,
but folds into one id-less `unattributed` rollup instead of into its agent's row.
The Analytics table renders it as a row, so the breakdown adds up to the card
above it again and the % column reaches 100 — today it would silently do neither.

The residual is aggregated INDEPENDENTLY, never `totals` minus the visible rows.
That distinction is the whole point: a subtraction is a plug figure that absorbs
any attribution bug and leaves the page adding up perfectly, where a fifth
grouping of the same deltas turns `Σ agents + unattributed = totals` into an
invariant a bug BREAKS. `aggregate()` now checks it — exact integer equality, no
tolerance — counts a metric and throws, for the reason the window guard beside it
already throws: the alternative is a money figure that is wrong and looks right,
on a page whose job is to be reconciled against an invoice.

Scope, deliberately:

  - `agents` / `models` carry attribution and stay viewer-scoped.
  - `sources` counts every row: `daemon` vs `gateway` names nobody, and keeping it
    whole preserves `Σ sources = totals` for the settlement reader.
  - the `series` stays viewer-scoped, per-bucket total included. A residual
    resolved per hour IS a restricted agent's spend curve — when it ran, how much
    it cost — which is attribution by another route. So the chart does not sum to
    the card, and says "visible agents only" when the two actually differ.
  - `unattributed` is absent, never zeroed, when nothing was withheld, and carries
    no COUNT of hidden agents — that would tell the caller the residual is one
    agent's spend.

The residual is an accepted inference channel: with a single restricted agent it
is that agent's window spend, and no k-anonymity rule can help, because an
accurate total implies it by subtraction. Accepting it knowingly, bounded to one
window figure, is the trade; it is recorded in session-visibility.md, whose Usage
row promised the opposite invariant and now states this one.

fix(setup): carry the target origin's port when re-hosting a discovered URL (#1463)

Setup runs OIDC discovery through the Logto management endpoint, so the process
needs no public egress, and then re-hosts the discovered authorization and token
endpoints onto the public issuer origin before handing them to a browser.

`urlAtOrigin` did that by assigning `protocol` and `host`. The WHATWG `host`
setter leaves whatever port the URL already carried when the assigned value names
none, so a discovery answer served on an explicit port kept that port at an origin
that serves 443 — and the browser was sent to `https://<public host>:3001/oidc/auth`,
where nothing is listening. Sign-in ended in ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED with every
other part of the configuration correct.

A hosted Logto tenant is reached at a port-less origin, which is why this only
appears when the management endpoint is an in-cluster address with an explicit
port — the self-hosted shape.

Assigning `port` from the target as well makes the rewrite take the origin whole,
in both directions: a target that names a port still applies it, which is what the
JWKS path relies on.

fix(daemon): reach the directDestination migration by bumping SCHEMA_VERSION (#1461)

#1456 appended the `directDestination` step to SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS but left
SCHEMA_VERSION at 12, so `upgradeSchema` stopped one short of it. Fresh databases
got the column from the CREATE block and every test passed; every ESTABLISHED
store stayed at v12 without it, and each `getSessionClassification` — one per
dispatch — failed with "no such column: directDestination". The daemon logged
`relay im dispatch failed` and the agent never answered a mention.

The bump makes the step reachable, and the two are now asserted to stay in
lockstep at module load: a step that cannot be reached is dead code, and this
failure mode is invisible to a suite whose stores are all freshly created.

The upgrade fixtures drop the column before replaying, the way each already
drops the one its own step adds, plus a v12 case that walks the read and write
path the missing column broke.

explicitly supports — left an earlier `OPENAI_MODEL_BASE_URL` in place, so the
member ran a real provider key against a gateway that never issued it. The
inverse assembles an old key with a new base URL.

Nothing can fix that per entry: the kubelet resolves each `secretKeyRef`
independently, and the chart cannot see which entries a Secret holds. So the
Secret becomes exclusive — naming it refuses any of those eight variables in
`daemonPool.extraEnv`, and refuses `modelEgress.clients`, both at render time
with the reason. An install that wants a gateway names its base URL and key as
Secret entries like any other credential.

fix(daemon): join the catch-up fires instead of sleeping for them (#1472)

schedule-catchup.test.ts was intermittently flaky on CI, always on the same
assertion: `expected [] to deeply equal [ 'bot-a' ]` for the replayed cron.

The catch-up compensates two schedules, and only one of them is observable
when the settle returns. The dream half is awaited inside
catchUpMissedSchedules, so its recorder is populated by the time the duty
change settles. The cron half is dispatched off that path -- it runs a whole
turn, and duty convergence must never wait on one -- so the promise was
dropped on the floor. The test bridged that gap with a 30 ms sleep, which is
a wall clock racing an unbounded dispatch rather than a completion signal.

and never the dream one.

so it stays joinable for its own lifetime, and let the test await the fires
themselves. Negative assertions get stronger too -- a wrongly launched fire
is now joined and observed rather than possibly missed by a short sleep.

Timing is unchanged: registering a promise does not move when it runs.

Verified by making the stubbed dispatch slow: with the join the file passes
10/10, with the old sleep it reproduces the CI failure verbatim. 20/20 clean
runs of the file afterwards.

feat(daemon): stream Slack turn output natively (#1483)

* feat(daemon): stream Slack turn output natively

Slack's two status APIs — assistant.threads.setStatus and
agents.sessions.setStatus — write one UI slot, so the last writer decided the
whole presentation: custom progress text and per-agent authorship, OR the native
processing UI and its in-message stop button, never both. Nothing could resolve
that while both wrote the same slot.

chat.startStream does. It creates the session and sets it processing itself, and
chat.stopStream releases it, so a streaming turn makes no status call of either
kind and gets native UI, the native stop control, and per-agent authorship at
once.

OutputConverger gains a streaming axis beside mode and emits stream-start /
stream-append / stream-stop instead of post / live-reply / final-live-reply /
progress; the body still reaches the transcript through the paired recordOnly
posts, and the attribution footer rides the one closing stop. SlackConnection
grows startTurnStream / appendTurnStream / stopTurnStream / streamingLikely, all
on the existing send queue, with two error classes: a capability refusal latches
streaming off for a five-minute re-probe, a contextual one degrades only its
turn. A stopped stream is unrecoverable, so its handle is dropped the moment it
ends — by our stop, by a refused append, or by the person's Stop — and
continuation past the 12k block limit is a new message by construction.

Everything that cannot stream keeps today's pipeline unchanged: no thread_ts, no
human initiator in a channel, output mode none, and — until the closing
response-finalization edit is verified on a live workspace — shareable
multi-agent bots, where agent-to-agent routing depends on that edit.

Design: docs/designs/slack-streaming-turn-output.md

* fix(daemon): close three correctness gaps in the Slack stream

Review found three ways the streaming path could show the wrong thing.

Re-anchor across chronological boundaries. The daemon already marks live chrome
to continue below a newly posted permission card or visible agent-authored
message; the stream ignored that marker, so post-boundary text grew a message
whose timestamp sits above the card and the conversation read out of order. A
boundary now triggers the same rollover the 12k limit does — settle, reopen,
tail below the card — on order instead of on size, and lazily, so an empty tail
keeps the current message and its footer.

Replay the uncommitted display tail on a mid-turn append refusal. Production and
application are separated by the apply chain, so later appends and often the
terminal stop are already queued when a refusal lands. Flipping the converger's
axis therefore left the queued actions to no-op away the text they carried,
while the axis owns the display cursor and the transcript cursor advances on a
slower clock — resuming ordinary posts from the transcript buffer re-posted the
overlap. Truncation and duplication from the same change. The converger now
keeps streaming and keeps its cursors, and the APPLIER redirects: every stream
action from the refusal on feeds a fallback buffer, delivered at the closing
stop through the ordinary reply boundary with the footer, response metadata and
the response-finalization anchor.

Keep a stop retryable until Slack accepts it. Both the turn handle and the
connection's entry were retired before the call reported success, so a rate
limit or dropped connection left the message streaming and the session
processing with nothing for settlement to retry — the exact state the backstop
exists to prevent. A handle is now retired only on a definite answer: success,
or message_not_in_streaming_state / stopped_by_user. The unaccepted stop is
remembered verbatim so settlement reissues that stop rather than a bare abort,
which would settle the message but drop its footer.

fix(daemon): settle the streaming state machine edges (#1487)

* fix(daemon): settle the streaming state machine edges

Three failure-path follow-ons from the Slack streaming review (#1483), each a
case where the state machine kept a handle it should not have reused, or reused
an outcome that meant two different things.

A failed ROLLOVER stop no longer reuses the old message. The handle is retained
for the settlement retry, which made the already-queued replacement start skip
and sent the post-rollover tail back into the message the rollover was trying to
leave — above the boundary, or past the size cap — and, since the converger has
already reset its per-message text, the closing edit would then have replaced
the combined message with just the tail. The tail now degrades to the ordinary
post boundary and lands below, which is what the rollover wanted; the old
message keeps its prefix and settlement keeps retrying its stop.

A refusal that dropped only task chrome no longer strands the answer. It opened
an empty fallback and aborted the accepted stream, so a body-then-tool-card turn
ended with no footer and nothing for response finalization to close. Degradation
now moves the response only once the buffer actually holds body text, and a
chrome-only refusal leaves the stream open for its terminal attributed stop.

An append refusal and a user Stop are no longer the same answer. appendTurnStream
returned one boolean for both, so a stop racing its own event could have its
buffered tail posted as a fresh reply into a conversation the person had just
ended. It now answers ok / refused / stopped; stopped ends the turn's output with
no buffer, no post, no replacement message, and no closing edit. The connection
also remembers which conversations the person stopped, so a queued append
arriving after the event is answered stopped rather than refused.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): keep fallback response ownership across stop retries

Whether the fallback owns the turn's response was inferred from the fallback
buffer's length, and the buffer empties on every flush. In the double-failure
sequence — a rollover stop left unresolved, its tail degraded and posted, then
the terminal stop also left unresolved — settlement replays the owed stop after
the flush, reads an empty buffer, and concludes the stream still owns the
response. The retained old message would then be settled as the final one:
footer and response metadata onto the wrong message, and lastResponse/lastReply
restamped with the old ts carrying the tail's text, breaking both the
bare-old-message rule and the response anchor.

Ownership is now explicit state, set the moment real body text lands in the
buffer and never cleared for the rest of the turn, so no retry can hand the
response back to a stream the fallback has already replaced.

fix(daemon): render Slack streaming as a collapsed plan and keep it after the turn (#1489)

* fix(daemon): render Slack streaming as a collapsed plan and keep it after the turn

Seeing the first version in a real workspace showed four presentation faults,
three of them from reasoning about the API by name instead of by behaviour.

Streams now open in `plan` display mode. `timeline` renders every task card flat
and separate, burying the answer under a column of tool chrome; `plan` collects
them into one collapsed-by-default container whose label is a `plan_update`
title. The container gets a small arc: a working label while the turn runs, and
a counted summary at the terminal stop — Completed N steps, plus a failure count
when there is one. Counted, not narrated, so it needs no second model call and
cannot disagree with the cards inside it.

The task-card fields do not all behave alike, and that was the `****` bug:
`title` and `status` replace per id, but `details` appends server-side. Streaming
a thinking line into `details` on every chunk therefore concatenated rather than
refreshed, and card fields render as plain text, so repeated emphasis markers
arrived literally. Anything that appends is now written once — a tool's result as
`output` at completion, nothing per line on the thinking card, which carries
title and status alone — and emphasis is flattened out of every card label.

The §5.5 finalization moves onto `chat.stopStream`. The closing `chat.update` it
replaces was the most destructive call in the pipeline: chat.update replaces a
message's whole content, so it erased every card the turn had rendered and left
the answer marked "(edited)". stopStream takes both things that edit was for —
blocks, appended below the streamed content rather than replacing it, and
metadata — so no edit is issued at all. Safe because the only consumer is
agent-to-agent routing, which happens only on shareable bots, which do not
stream; the carve-out lift now owes ingress a stop-time reader first. Legacy and
fallback turns keep the closing edit unchanged, and a retried stop rebuilds the
same blocks and metadata.

Finally, the loading state comes back for the window before the stream has
anything in it. Writing no status at all read well on paper but left a cold start
showing an empty bubble and nothing else. The documented shape — and what the
official templates do — is to set the free-text status while working and let the
message carry the content, so a streaming turn now writes that text once, clears
it explicitly at the first visible chunk, and writes nothing further. The session
enum is still never touched: startStream owns it, and it cannot carry text.

feat(cli): install several daemon services on one host (#1465)

* feat(cli): install several daemon services on one host

The instance identity was already `<root>` — config, `daemon.lock`,
`state/local.sqlite`, `run/mcp.sock`, logs, agents dir and the whole version
store are root-relative, and `daemonId` is minted per root, so the CP already
registers two same-host daemons as two daemons. The unit name was the one
host-global name left, so a second `install-service` overwrote the first
instance's unit and `uninstall-service` then removed the survivor.

Add `--instance <name>`: unit `agentconnect@<name>.service` /
`md.agentconnect.daemon.<name>`, root defaulting to `~/.agentconnect-<name>`.
The default instance keeps its historical unit names byte-for-byte, so existing
installs are never orphaned. `install-service` records `{ instance, label }` in
`<root>/service.json` so a `--root`-only command — notably the CP-commanded
`upgrade --to <v> --root <root>` the daemon spawns — addresses that instance's
unit instead of the default one. `agentconnect instances` lists what is
installed by scanning the OS's own unit directory.

Two root-binding bugs that multi-instance turns into data corruption:

- `includeRootEnv` was gated on whether a `--root` flag was typed, so an
  `AGENTCONNECT_ROOT`-driven install wrote a unit with no root at all and the
  service silently started on `~/.agentconnect`. It now follows the RESOLVED
  root.
- the unit bound its root purely through inherited env while the run shell
  launches the daemon through the user's interactive login shell, so a profile
  exporting `AGENTCONNECT_ROOT` could pull a service onto another instance's
  root, lock, sqlite and socket. `--root` is now explicit in
  ExecStart/ProgramArguments, and the flag beats env.

ExecStart tokens and the root env assignment are now quoted/%-escaped when they
need it, so a root containing a space or `%` produces a valid unit.

fix(web): switching org from a detail view lands on home, not a 404 (#1486)

* fix(web): switching org from a detail view lands on home, not a 404

A session, agent, cron, daemon or conversation id belongs to ONE org, and the
switcher carried the whole sub-path over — so switching org from a detail view
went straight to the other org's not-found page. Sessions answer 404 rather
than 403, so it was not even a hint about what had been there; it just looked
like the console had lost the page.

`switchOrgPath` decides where a sub-path lands: the same path, or `/home`. It
denies by default — anything deeper than one segment is a detail view — and
allows the few deep paths built from static segments only. So a new `[id]`
route is covered without touching this, and forgetting to list a new static
deep route only sends someone home.

Deliberately NOT `subPath`'s job: that one also canonicalizes a bare URL inside
the SAME org (`/sessions/abc` → `/acme/sessions/abc`), where dropping the id
would break every deep link into the console. A slug rename keeps its path for
the same reason — same org, same resources.

Review caught a regression the previous commit introduced. Both switchers
render the active org as a clickable row, so re-selecting the org you are

pushed `/<same-slug>/home`, throwing away the page the user was reading on a
click that switched nothing. Before the rule it re-pushed the same URL, which

The guard goes where the decision already lives rather than inline in the

path, or NULL when this is not a switch at all — and the callback just obeys.
The no-op arm is checked FIRST, ahead of the path rule.

feat(web): attribute a billing usage row to the agents that spent it (#1493)

* feat(web): attribute a billing usage row to the agents that spent it

The billing service already sends a per-agent split on every debit row; the
console dropped it on the floor. A usage line now shows who spent the money.

Each part gets its own chip: the agent's avatar and label when the console can
resolve it, a default avatar and the amount when it cannot. The roster decides
whether a part is NAMED, never whether it appears.

That distinction is the authorization boundary. The billing service authorizes
on org membership alone, so the `agentId`s it sends are the ORG's and not the
viewer's — naming one to every member is the resource-existence disclosure
`session-visibility.md` §5 forbids, whose rule is that withheld usage comes
back id-less. So the split is resolved against the viewer's own visibility-
scoped `/agents` roster and an unresolvable id is dropped in the reduction, key
included: it never reaches the component, let alone the DOM. An unloaded or
failed roster fails closed — default avatars, no names.

One gap stays open, and it is the service's to close: `/agents` scopes agent
visibility but cannot apply the Session predicate, so a visible agent whose
spend came from a session this viewer may not read is still attributed. Closing
it needs a viewer-scoped split from the service, the way `usage.ts` returns an
`unattributed` rollup.

The console cannot derive the missing half, but it does not have to — the CP's

fix(daemon): exit an in-cluster daemon whose control-plane credential is rejected (#1499)

* fix(daemon): exit an in-cluster daemon whose control-plane credential is rejected

A terminal 4401 made the CP client fatal and left the process alive. For an
API-key daemon that is right: the credential is minted by a human, a rejected one
stays rejected, and redialing it forever is noise.

An in-cluster daemon authenticates with its projected identity token, and there
the same behavior strands the process. That token is re-read from the pod's volume
at every boot, nothing in-process ever redials after a 4401, and boot blocks on
the first registration — so a container that took one can never become servable,
and all that shows is a member that stays unready.

On the identity path the client now asks the daemon to exit non-zero, which puts
the retry on the supervisor's restart backoff. A rollout that races a control-plane
restart converges on its own instead of needing a second step to bring members up.

* fix(daemon): drain before the fatal-auth exit, as the data-plane exit does

Review nit: the data-plane failure path sets the draining flag before asking to
exit, and this one did not. Inert while the exit seam is a synchronous process
exit, but the flag is what stops new work arriving, so it should not depend on
that.

The host member is named for the one thing it does rather than left as a generic
exit call that secretly drains: exitFatal(code) drains and then exits, and the
identity-path 4401 is its only caller.

fix(web): a billing period holds many charges, not one (#1498)

* fix(web): a billing period holds many charges, not one

#1493 shipped a blank usage feed. Verified against a real org: August has
THREE separate debit rows — $0.006822824, $0.015224848, $0.001036384 — each
carrying `period: "2026-08"`, together summing to exactly what `/usage`
reports for the month, $0.023084056. The merged code computed each row's
residual as `rowAmount - Σ named` against that MONTHLY projection, so every
row came out negative, hit the "not reconcilable" guard, and rendered nothing
at all. One debit is a charge, not a period.

Reconciling a period aggregate against a single charge was never going to
work, so the two sources go back to answering the questions they can actually
answer. The AMOUNTS come from the billing service's split — the only thing
that knows how one charge divides — and the projection supplies the
PERMISSION to put a name beside one.

That permission is `complete`, not membership, which preserves what #1493's
review was right about: `/usage.agents` lists an agent when ANY of its spend
is readable and hides the rest in one id-less residual, so membership alone
would let an agent with $1 readable and $99 private be named for charges
covering the $99. Only a period whose projection withholds NOTHING makes a
name safe — then this viewer may already attribute every dollar in it, and a
chip discloses nothing new. Any residual, and the whole period falls back to
id-less rollups. It stays `source=gateway`, the ingress a charge settles from.

Also: no chips while the projection is in flight. Rendering the fail-closed
answer first told the reader they had no access to an agent and took it back
seven seconds later — a wrong statement, not a slow one. Fail closed is for a
missing answer, not a pending one.

Verified in the browser against the test backend: all three rows render the
agent's avatar, name, and exact per-row amount, with no default-avatar flash.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): read the usage residual's PRESENCE, not its amount

`complete` treated a present-but-zero `unattributed` as though nothing had been
withheld, which is backwards from the contract it was reading. The CP sets that
rollup from `unattributed.sessions.size > 0` — withheld SESSIONS, not cost —
and omits it rather than zeroing it for exactly this reason, in its own words:
"a reader must be able to tell 'nothing was hidden' from 'something was hidden
and cost 0'" (session-usage.repo.ts). Aggregate amounts are derived by
subtraction and a downward correction can net a hidden row to zero, so the
zero-check qualified periods whose hidden usage is the hardest to notice, and
let raw per-charge billing amounts carry an agent's name through it.

Gating on absence is the whole fix. The test that comes with it fails against
the old expression, so the next reader gets a regression, not a comment.

* docs: demote daemon-centric from headline to one deployment mode

The architecture document described only one way to host a daemon —
self-hosted, on a machine someone operates — and never mentioned the
managed pool, so "daemon-centric" read as the whole architecture rather
than one case of it. It is not even the common case any more.

- Rename to architecture.md / architecture.svg / system-detailed-design.md
  and retitle both documents; every referrer is updated.
- New "3.1 Deployment modes": self-hosted daemon vs managed daemon pool,
  compared on host operator, process lifecycle, ownership, durable store,
  agent runtime, and host credentials, with pointers to k8s-daemon-pool.md,
  cloud-data-plane-postgres.md, and cluster-spawn-and-shim.md.
- Scope the claims that were only true self-hosted: who starts the daemon
  process, where the agent runtime runs, and the operator trust model.
- Correct the ACP claim. "In-process, no network hop" is the self-hosted
  case; in the pool the daemon dials the sandbox pod. The invariant that
  actually holds in both is that ACP never crosses the Control Plane.
- Reword the four places that named the label instead of the invariant.
- Delete the superseded 1.6 MB raster diagram, unreferenced since the SVG
  replaced it, per the diffable-source-over-raster convention.

* docs: make the two renamed documents honest about both modes

Review was right: the renames made these documents canonical and
deployment-neutral in name while their bodies still described only the
self-hosted daemon, which teaches the very topology this branch corrects.

architecture.md is now mode-neutral where it can be and marked where it
cannot: §2's goal, §4.2, §6.1's two flows, §10's trace path, and §11's
runtime-crash row no longer assert local IPC or a local restart, and the
SVG's painted labels follow — "Daemon-owned ACP / local IPC, or one hop to
a sandbox" and "child process or sandbox pod" replace "Local ACP",
"in-process / local IPC", and "local model processes", with the accessible
description matched.

system-detailed-design.md takes the other option offered: it keeps the
component model, which does hold in both modes, and declares its concrete
forms self-hosted up front, routing pool readers to the three mode-specific
documents. D7's runtime form, D11's store choice, §5's storage row, §6.3,
§7's sequence, and the §2 topology each carry the pool substitution inline
so a reader who lands mid-document is not misled either.

* docs: finish the ACP transport split in §4.4 and its siblings

§4.4's first bullet still said ACP arrives "locally from the daemon,
through an in-process call, local IPC, or a local socket" while the bullet
under it had already been split — folded into the same framing.

Swept the rest of the class so it stops resurfacing: the components table
no longer says the adapters "drive models locally"; §2's goal, §4.1, and
§11's adapter row say sessions continue and the daemon retries on the
daemon rather than "locally"; the detailed design's D6 and D7 carry the
pool substitution their own runtime-form bullet already had; and README's
daemon row says daemon-owned ACP.

* docs: correct what a runtime crash actually recovers in the pool

The failure table claimed an agent-runtime crash produces a fresh sandbox
generation. It does not: reapTerminalHost reclaims the exited host so the
next message re-spawns the runtime, and forgetLaunch — which drops the
generation — is reached only from suspendIfIdle and onChannelLost. An
ordinary runtime exit keeps the agent's bound sandbox and session.

feat(platforms): acknowledge a trigger with a reaction as the turn starts (#1537)

* feat(platforms): acknowledge a trigger with a reaction as the turn starts

An answer arrives late by nature, and until it does whoever mentioned the agent
cannot tell "working on it" from "never saw it". A Slack assistant thread has a
status bar and Telegram has a typing hint, but a message in a channel has
neither, and an issue or pull request has nothing at all until one comment lands
at the very end of the turn — minutes later for a review.

Every turn with a real inbound message now reacts to that message as it starts,
on GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Telegram, Discord and Lark. The reaction lands on the
exact comment that fired the turn, and on the issue or pull request itself only
when the subject is what fired. Origins with no inbound message — a schedule,
another agent's wake, the console — acknowledge nothing.

Core names an INTENT (`seen`) and each module picks its own glyph, because a
reaction vocabulary is platform vocabulary: an emoji shortcode on Slack, a
literal emoji from Telegram's allowed set, a `GLANCE` emoji_type key on Lark,
`eyes` on both code hosts. The chat side is a new optional Layer-1 facet,
`react(container, messageId, intent)`; the code-host side is a two-implementer
seam in `codehost/ack.ts`, since GitHub and GitLab differ only in path, auth
header and body.

`container` is the message's NATIVE container, not its normalized channel: a
Discord message inside a thread reports its parent channel there, and only the
native pair can address the message at all. `nativeMessageCoordinates` is the
inverse of the same msgId minting and yields nothing for an id no normalizer
made, so an anchored hook delivery never reacts to the daemon's own post.

The trusted comment id rides the signature-verified webhook — new optional
`GithubHookMetadata.issueCommentId` and `GitlabHookMetadata.noteId`; nothing is
derived from the model-visible excerpt. Both are optional, so a mixed-version
fleet decodes unchanged and simply acknowledges the subject instead.

It is chrome, not output. Nothing awaits it, a failure is one warning, the
single-writer rule is untouched, and it is never withdrawn: it records that the
turn was seen, which stays true even when the turn later dies with nothing to
publish. A redelivery whose comment already published does not re-acknowledge,
and every host treats an already-present reaction as success, so it keeps no
state. No new permission is needed anywhere — the grants each platform already
requests cover it, and an installation missing one simply shows nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): tolerate relay-filtered siblings in the redelivery claim

The delivery summary names only event, action, and repository, so the
reconciler's candidate set for an issue_comment GUID lists both
comment-family sibling rows while the relay lands a run only for the
subject family that matched. The retryable claim's exact-fanout equality
then rejected the landed row and cleared its retry schedule — retryable
comment failures were never redelivered once an agent watched both
families.

The claim now requires the landed runs to be a subset of the candidate
set, each an active side-effect-free retry row; a landed run from
outside the set still blocks. An unlanded candidate is the relay's own
precise filtering (subject family, mention text, labels), which the
immutable payload reproduces on redelivery, so it is tolerated — except
a candidate hook created after the delivery was ingested, which would
read the redelivery as a first run of a stale event and keeps blocking.
Liveness and dispatch-authority checks narrow to the landed rows.

Also adopt the destination sibling's session-key prefix when a row is
reassigned between agents on one repository, not only on a repository
re-target — a grandfathered owner/repo prefix would otherwise split the
destination agent's family rows into two session namespaces.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): fence unlanded redelivery candidates on lastModifiedAt

The subset claim tolerated an unlanded candidate because the immutable
payload reproduces the relay's filtering — but that proof holds only
while the rule itself is unchanged. A candidate whose definition moved
after the delivery was ingested (created then, re-enabled, or a
mention/label filter relaxed) might treat the redelivery as a first run
of a stale event. Every user-facing edit bumps lastModifiedAt, so the
fence now reads it instead of createdAt, which it subsumes.

Regression test: a sibling that filtered the original event via
mentionOnly and was relaxed before reconciliation blocks the claim.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): restrict redelivery tolerance to same-agent siblings

The lastModifiedAt fence covered HookDef edits but not the compiled
rule's other inputs: an agent pause removes and re-adds the rule and a
rename changes what the mention gate matches, and neither touches the
hook row. An unlanded candidate is therefore tolerated only when it
shares an agent with a landed run — the run proves the agent was live
and routing at ingestion, and family uniqueness plus the per-row shape
gate keep a sibling family from ever matching the event. Hook-level and
agent-level lastModifiedAt (bumped by every user-facing PATCH, rename
and pause included) stay as defense in depth. Every other unlanded
candidate — cross-agent ones above all, whose pause and rename history
the claim cannot reconstruct — blocks the request, exactly as the
pre-split exact-fanout rule did. Deleted candidates stay tolerated: the
relay holds no rule for them.

Regression tests: a cross-agent same-family candidate blocks even with
clean timestamps; a post-ingestion agent PATCH blocks the same-agent
tolerance.

fix(sandbox): drop the DeepSeek web_search a pod key cannot use (#1556)

The harness's search provider deliberately ignores DEEPSEEK_BASE_URL and takes
DEEPSEEK_API_KEY to api.deepseek.com itself, so a sandbox whose key is a gateway
credential answers every web_search with an invalid-key error the model retries.

The tool is a row in the AGENT PRESET, and a preset is only ever edited as a whole
file: the host-plane patch layer cannot reach into a preset subtree, and disabling
the host `web` service instead makes the preset refuse to mount, because a row
waiting on a service the composition never supplies fails the roster's audit. So
the image bakes a copy of the shipped `standard` with the tool deregistered —
generated from the adapter THIS image pins, since a vendored copy in the repo
would rot one bump later — and the shim seeds it into the pod's $DSH_HOME before
launching that runtime, naming it the settings default. A deployment whose sandbox
key reaches the real API sets AC_DEEPSEEK_WEB_SEARCH=on
(daemonPool.runtime.deepseekWebSearch) and keeps the shipped preset.

The baker accepts every layout the adapter has shipped dsh in — hoisted beside it,
nested under it (0.4.16, what this image pins), or a vendored archive (0.4.26) —
because only building the image proves which one is there: resolving the vendored
one alone failed the pinned build.

Verified by capturing the tool schemas dsh-acp sends the model against a mock
endpoint: the seeded $DSH_HOME drops exactly web_search out of 25 tools and
changes nothing else, and the session header records agentPreset

produces a root-owned, read-only 16-row preset.

fix(daemon): survive a runtime binary that cannot be spawned (#1558)

`LocalDriver.launch` attached no 'error' listener to the ACP child process.
A command that cannot be executed emits 'error' and never 'exit', and Node
rethrows an unhandled 'error' event as an uncaught exception — so a single
broken runtime on PATH terminated the whole daemon and every agent it hosted.

This is easy to hit through the startup runtime probe, which spawns every
curated runtime whose command resolves on PATH. A leftover `hermes` wrapper
whose venv interpreter had been removed was enough:

    [agentconnect] INFO  probe: sweeping 1 runtime(s): hermes-agent
    Error: spawn /Users/me/.local/bin/hermes ENOENT
        at ChildProcess._handle.onexit (node:internal/child_process:286:19)

Note that the file existed and was executable; the ENOENT came from its
missing shebang interpreter, so no pre-flight existence check would have
caught it.

Fail the launch instead of the process:

- Handle 'error' and destroy the stdio pipes with it, so the real errno
  reaches whoever reads the stream pair — the only failure channel this seam
  has. `probeRuntime` then records `{ ok: false, error }` as intended.
- Fire `onExit` on 'close' as well as 'exit', since a child that never
  started emits only 'close' and lifecycle waiters would hang.
- Return early from `stop()` when the spawn failed: there is no pid to
  signal, and the old path burned the full deadline and then warned about a
  SIGTERM that no process ever ignored.

fix(daemon): install a whole Git skill collection in a sandbox (#1559)

* fix(daemon): install a whole Git skill collection in a sandbox

A cluster agent with a Git skill source silently got no skills. The
cluster path snapshotted the acquired source with
`inspectLocalSkillSource`'s DEFAULT profile — 64 files, 4 MiB — which is
sized for one installed bundle, while the local path has always used the
wider Git profile. A collection repository (obra/superpowers: 194 files,
1.7 MiB) tripped `skill source has too many files`, the per-source catch
turned that into a warn, and the reconcile published an empty set. Same
config on a self-hosted daemon installed fine.

The Git profile now lives next to the default in skill-source-snapshot.ts
and `ClusterSkillSnapshotSource` carries per-source limits, so a Git
collection gets the wide profile at both inspect sites — daemon.ts and
the coordinator's upload manifest — while managed and Dream bundles keep
the tight default.

Raising the caps meant removing what actually bound them:

- `captureSource` retained every file body, and `inspectLocalSkillSource`
  discarded them all immediately. On a 2 GiB daemon pod that made the
  byte cap a memory question. Inspect no longer retains, so peak memory
  is one file.
- The whole manifest rode in one `begin` frame, so
  MAX_CLUSTER_SKILL_CONTROL_BYTES capped the count near 800 rows. A new
  `manifest` op pages it; the client splits on bytes as well as count,
  and the receiver enforces the totals no single page can see.

Snapshot and wire limits now mirror each other: 16,384 files, 1 GiB,
16 MiB per file. The upload chunk goes to 128 KiB (~175 KiB base64,
under the 256 KiB frame), which matters at that size.

A daemon takes over a running pod, so it can outrun the image it binds.
The new `cluster-skills-v2` feature and `skills-wide` grant carry that:
a v1 image still gets a single-frame manifest clamped to its own limits,
refused with a clear message rather than an opaque frame rejection, and
daemon.ts degrades an oversized source to a warn instead of failing the
launch.

fix(console): accept a public repository when replacing a workspace (#1561)

* fix(console): accept a public repository when replacing a workspace

Agent creation has always accepted a GitHub repository that no App
installation covers: the daemon clones it anonymously, so it is read-only
and carries no catalog repository identity. Replacing a workspace never
had that arm — `PUT /agents/:id/workspace` looked the owner up with
`liveByOrgAndAccount` and refused anything it did not find, and the
console's editor offered no candidate for it. Two consequences: a public
repository could not be picked when replacing a workspace, and an agent
whose workspace already had no installation could not be edited at all,
because the same uncovered-owner gate disabled the save for a branch or
working-directory change.

The workspace route now applies the rule agent creation applies: a
repository granted by an installation stays App-backed, and one granted by
none is accepted as the anonymous checkout, read-only (`gitAccess: write`
still returns 409). Nothing verifies the repository first, exactly as at
creation — a non-public target fails at clone time, where the daemon
reports it. `AgentMoveService.setWorkspace` required a resolved numeric
repository for every GitHub workspace; that requirement now applies to the
credential-minting arm only, which is what the nullable column already
documented.

Both surfaces now share one repository picker (`useGithubRepoPicker` +
`GithubRepoPickerOptions`), so they offer the same candidates on the same
credentials: the synced installation roster, one exact owner/repo resolved
through the installations past a truncated roster, and public GitHub for
anything no installation grants. A public pick is badged and pins access
to read. The two routes also share one binder for the App-backed arm, so
the catalog convergence and the identity gate have a single definition.

that, and the picker's exact-name lookup asked every installation when
none matched the owner — so typing a public repository outside the
organization's installations produced an "Available through the GitHub

suppressed (the public rows are dropped for a name the App row already

Installations are per-account, so the endpoint now answers 404 for an

repository no installation covers falls to the anonymous public read that
already existed, which is what the `public` badge and read-only clamp are

  newest: agentSessionStopped now resolves the full admitted-session list

fix(workspace): default an unstated access tier to what the target carries (#1567)

Creating an agent and replacing its workspace disagreed on the default
access tier: creation reads `gitAccess ?? 'write'`, while
`SetAgentWorkspaceBody` declared `.default('read')`. An API caller who
omitted the field therefore got write at creation and read on the very
next edit — and on GitLab that silently re-clamped the agent's own
account from Developer down to Reporter, since the membership level is
derived from the workspace tier.

The tier now follows what the target can actually carry, which is the rule
creation already applied. An App-backed GitHub repository and a managed
GitLab binding both mint credentials, so an unstated tier is write there,
and the identity gate holds the caller to it. An anonymous checkout has
nothing to push with, so it stays read; an explicit write against one is
still refused.

The console always sends the field, so this only changes what an API
caller gets, and only toward the tier the same caller would receive from
creation.

fix(daemon): let the native Slack Stop cancel a turn that is still cold (#1569)

Slack renders the agent-session Stop control the moment a turn sets

session row is written. Both stop transports resolved the thread's sessions
through the store alone, and that lookup requires a persisted ACP id — so a
click inside the cold window cancelled nothing, still reported the session
`active` (the control disappears, as if it had worked), and the turn ran on.

- slackThreadSessions reads the dispatch gate alongside the store: for every
  agent the conversation admits, a gate-owned logical key joins the resolved
  rows. The `!stop` / `!cancel` path already did exactly this; the native Stop
  was the one entry that never got it.
- cancelSessionByKey resolves the agent from the gate's admitted head as well.
  A cold head has no row and is not queued behind itself, so it bailed even
  when handed the right key.

Covered by a regression test: a turn blocked in `session/new` is cancelled
through the native Stop path and never reaches `prompt`.

carries no session id and agent_session_stopped names no agent — while
participant fan-out legitimately runs several sibling turns against it. Two
review follow-ups from #1563 fall out of that mismatch: the first sibling to
finish cleared the slot, hiding the native Stop while another sibling still
worked, and the displacement path's detached `processing` re-assert could land
after the successor's terminal `active`, leaving a phantom Stop control with no
owning turn.

  failure, cancel, or being the stop's target — re-asserts the newest surviving
  sibling's `processing` under that sibling's identity instead of clearing, so
  the row keeps naming who is actually still working (verified live: a fresh
  `processing` also resolves a pending "Stopping…" back into a working row).
  Only an empty thread transitions to `active`. Stateless — it reads `pending`.
- The native Stop cancels the turn the row is naming: the connection records the
  last `processing` writer per (channel, thread) as the slot's displayed owner
  (`SlackStatusOptions.sessionKey`, never sent to the API, and part of the
  dedupe key so an identity-identical handover still refires), cancels that one
  turn — falling back to the thread's newest session, cold gate keys included —
  and hands settlement to the daemon. Stopping B returns the row to a
  still-working A; stopping the last turn clears it. The relay arm is
  untouched: each daemon applies the same local semantics to the forwarded stop.

feat(daemon): stream Slack tool-call chrome as a native plan card (#1570)

* feat(daemon): stream Slack tool-call chrome as a native plan card

A medium/high Slack turn's tool activity is an in-place `progress` message the
daemon rewrites on every update. Slack's streaming methods render the same thing
natively: one collapsed container of task cards, with the platform's own working
row and Stop control beside it.

Body streaming was tried and reverted (#1483/#1487/#1489, reverted in #1495)
because a channel stream is visible live to exactly ONE recipient — everyone else
sees a placeholder until it stops. That is fatal for an answer and close to
irrelevant for chrome, which is the part of a turn a reader wants folded away. So
this change splits them: the answer keeps `chat.postMessage`/`chat.update`
untouched, and only the tool-call chrome rides `chat.startStream` in chunks mode
with `task_display_mode: 'plan'` and zero `markdown_text` chunks.

One `task_update` per ACP toolCallId, plus one "Thinking" card per thinking run.
`medium` sends title and status; `high` adds the tool result once at completion.
The stream opens LAZILY, at the turn's first task — a turn that runs no tools
never calls startStream and is byte-identical to today, as are `none`, `minimal`
and `low`, which have no tool chrome at all.

Live-verified on 2026-08-28 and relied on here: `chat.startStream` requires
`thread_ts` even in a DM; stopping with cards still `in_progress` makes Slack
render "Something went wrong", so every stop is preceded by a settle append
(terminal statuses plus a counted `plan_update`); the native Stop does NOT end
the stream server-side, so the daemon's own cancel seam settles in-flight cards
as errors under a "Stopped" label; a channel turn with no human initiator may
name the bot itself as recipient; and a finalized card renders the fixed text
"This message contains interactive elements.", which ingress and thread backfill
now refuse to read as a message body.

Degrade is cheap because the body never moved: a capability refusal latches for
five minutes and the turn falls back to today's `progress` message, carried on
the same action; a refused append just drops that card update.

No config knob, no env kill switch, no manifest change, and no change to the
relay, control plane, protocol, web, other platforms, or `setSessionLifecycle`.

Design: docs/designs/slack-streaming-turn-output.md

* fix(daemon): close five ways a Slack chrome stream could be left open

Review found five paths that strand a streaming message — Slack keeps rendering
a working row nobody can ever close.

Key stream bookkeeping by MESSAGE, not by conversation. One connection can host
sibling turns in the same (channel, thread) — same-message multi-agent fan-out,
and displacement deliberately lets the displaced turn coexist while it settles —
so a conversation key let the second open clobber the first handle and orphan it.

Treat a send-queue timeout as INDETERMINATE. The queue rejects at 30s while the
queued task keeps running, so a timed-out chat.startStream can still open a
message after the turn has degraded and stopped watching. The open's real answer
now rides its own promise: a late ts is settled and stopped immediately rather
than left unowned.

Make the terminal settle and the stop one indivisible unit. As two actions, a
transiently refused settle fell through to a stop that still had `in_progress`
cards — the "Something went wrong" rendering the design exists to avoid. The
settle now rides the stop action, and SlackConnection.settleAndStop appends it,
stops only if that landed, and re-arms itself on a bounded backoff keeping the
settle content verbatim.

Give an unresolved stop an owner that outlives the turn. Pending is dropped at
turn settlement, so a stop that failed twice had nobody left to retry it; the
per-connection sweep above is that owner, and the applier retires the turn's
handle the moment it hands the pair over so the two can never race.

Open the stream from the terminal settle when cards are pending but nothing was
appended yet. A tool that started AND finished inside one 750ms coalescing
window left a medium/high turn with no tool chrome at all.

docs(design): the host-neutral git workspace model (#1573)

* docs(design): the host-neutral git workspace model

The workspace discriminant is the code host today (scratch|github|gitlab),
which bakes a UI notion into the wire, the database, and two independently
written route validations — the root shared by #1561 and #1567. The daemon
never adopted that model: it collapses the arms into git-repo|from-scratch
plus an independent gitCredential on arrival.

This design promotes the daemon's model outward: mode answers "is there a
repository", a credential union answers "who vouches for it". Provenance
is derived server-side by one function shared by creation, replacement,
and a resolve endpoint the console's badges call, so the picker can no
longer disagree with the write path. Provider tiles stay in the console —
they carry lexicon and guidance — but all produce the same payload, and a
"From a Git URL" tile plus GitLab public-project candidates fall out of
the neutral shape. Rollout is readers-first behind a workspace-git-v1
daemon feature so an old daemon never receives an arm it fatals on.

Records the decided rules: provenance fixed at write time and never
auto-upgraded, bare Git rides the anonymous arm on host credentials,
unstated access takes the highest tier the target carries, and a covered
owner's ungranted repository refuses rather than degrading to anonymous.

fix(daemon): stop the shutdown duty drain retrying a permanently closed CP client (#1579)

A bootstrap-delivered upgrade retires the CP connection before the
daemon's shutdown drain runs: the client latches `stopped`, closes the
transport, and never redials. The drain's acknowledged-release loop then
retried `duty/release` every 5s against "control plane unreachable
(client CLOSED)" until the full pool drain budget (300s) elapsed - five
minutes spent on releases that could never be delivered, while the duty
self-fence interrupted the surviving turns at its horizon anyway. The
install itself takes under a second; the wait was all retry ladder.

Give CpClient a `terminallyClosed()` predicate (stop() ran, or a fatal
auth close latched - the bootstrap path sets `stopped` before invoking
the restart) and have `releaseDutyAcknowledged` give up at once when it
holds: the lease lapses now instead of at the drain deadline, the same
outcome five minutes sooner. A DEGRADED client still retries, since a
redial may yet deliver the release. Turn draining is untouched.
