perf(daemon): create the store schema in one transaction, not 58 (#1598)

* perf(daemon): create the store schema in one transaction, not 58

`initializeSchema` hands 58 CREATE statements to a single `exec`, and a multi-statement
script commits each statement separately. Under WAL with `synchronous = FULL` — the
node:sqlite default this store keeps — that is 58 flushes to bring up an empty database,
and every daemon pays them the first time it boots.

One transaction, so one flush. `synchronous` is untouched: this removes commits, not
durability. The version stamp joins the same transaction, which settles what the comment
it replaces could only work around — a creation that fails halfway now leaves no schema
at all, rather than a partial one the stamp was careful not to bless.

Measured on the store-heavy suites (macOS, `tests` time, stable across runs):

    local-store.test.ts      1.21s -> 0.64s   (103 cases)
    session-manager.test.ts  2.24s -> 1.50s   (97 cases)

A daemon-booting file barely moves (~4%): it opens one store per case and spends its time
elsewhere. So this is worth most where a flush costs most — on the Windows job, the slice
it addresses is the 16 files that open a store directly, 429 s of that suite's 2374 s.

Postgres is behaviorally unchanged: a multi-statement script already ran in one implicit
transaction there, and schema creation is serialized by the advisory lock the data plane
holds across `LocalStore.open` either way. `test:store:postgres` is green.

fix(daemon): stop the skill installer's own bundles from pinning session worktrees (#1604)

* fix(daemon): stop the skill installer's own bundles from pinning session worktrees

The installer writes skill bundles into the checkout, where Git reports them as
untracked. The session-retention GC, which must never auto-delete untracked
work, then refuses to reclaim any session worktree it prepared. Registrations
grow without bound until the runtime's sandbox profile — one deny path per
registered worktree — overflows the OS exec argument limit, and no command in
that agent can spawn at all.

owned bundle roots go into the checkout's `info/exclude`, anchored at the
checkout root so an `agentDir` agent's cwd offset is carried, and `git status`
goes clean again for the existing GC to act on.

pull ran under rather than whichever preparation ran git last.

test(control-plane): stop gitlab follow-up timers leaking across tests (#1608)

Every contended provisioner pass arms a 30s converge follow-up via
`clock.setTimeout`. The gitlab integration harnesses wired in the real
`systemClock`, so that timer outlives the test that armed it — and when it
fires it re-resolves the binding by (orgId, projectId), both constants: the
seed re-creates the same org id before every test and the fixtures reuse one
project id. The per-test DB sweep therefore cannot isolate it: the leaked
background converge lands on the CURRENT test's freshly created rows and
races its leases. That is the intermittent CI failure in "a binding entering
cleanup owes no more convergence" — `beginCleanup`'s CAS (opOwner
null-or-expired) meets the leaked run's live op lease and returns false, and
`claimLease` can likewise meet a leaked run holding the account lease.

Fix: `trackedTestClock()` — identical to SystemClock, plus an afterEach that
cancels every still-pending timer — wired into all six gitlab integration
files in place of `systemClock`. No test runs anywhere near 30s, so in-test
timer behavior is unchanged; cross-test firing becomes impossible.

Reproduced deterministically before the fix by shrinking FOLLOW_UP_DELAY_MS
and stretching the leaked run's lease-held window with per-page fake latency
(`onListPage`), which produced the exact CI assertion failure. Production
lease logic is untouched — the race only exists in the test environment,
which resurrects identically-keyed rows under a live process's timers.

Co-authored-by: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(daemon): let the retention GC reclaim review-snapshot worktrees despite scratch state (#1610)

A formal-review worktree is a daemon-owned snapshot: every delivery re-fetches
the exact revision and hard-resets the tree (`reset --hard` + `clean -ffdx`),
so its dirty files and local commits are disposable by construction. The GC's
dirty/unique-commit protections — which exist to guard user work in ordinary
session worktrees — were retaining these snapshots forever over scratch files
the next delivery would discard anyway, feeding the worktree pile-up behind
issue #1603.

removeRootSessionWorktree now probes for the worktree's fetched review refs
(refs/agentconnect/reviews/<id>/* in that root), lazily and only when a
protection would otherwise retain. A probed snapshot skips both protections and
is removed with --force; its generated branch goes with it, since the next
reset would discard those commits regardless. Ordinary worktrees — including
the reference-root worktrees riding along the same review session, whose roots
hold no such refs — keep the full protections, and a probe failure reads as
"not a snapshot".

feat(daemon): deliver the drain-cycle narration instead of dropping it (#1623)

* feat(daemon): deliver the drain-cycle narration instead of dropping it

When a background task settles after the turn, the Claude runtime keeps its
"you will be notified" promise in-process: it self-wakes a drain cycle and the
model narrates the completion there. That cycle has no Pending, so every one
of its content updates was discarded — the narration (often the very output
the human asked for) was lost, and the completion wake had to ask the model to
say everything again, which it does only probabilistically (observed live: it
re-sent the second output and silently gave up on the first).

Capture and deliver it instead. While the lease reads `running` with no
pending dispatch, answer-chunk text accumulates on the lease (capped); the
running→idle edge — or the next real dispatch, which claims the buffer
synchronously — posts it as agent speech (name, icon, author id) with a
transcript row. The sentinel, closed sessions, and `none` mode keep their
semantics; a session with no platform connection keeps the old drop and does
not claim delivery. Deliveries spend their own counter against the wake cap,
bounding a model that keeps self-continuing by starting tasks from each drain
— a loop the wake budget alone cannot bound.

The wake stays armed (a drain may narrate nothing) and now reads
`drainDeliveredAt` at fire time: when the narration landed, it says so and
asks only for what is still owed, instead of "nothing you said reached

feat(web): let a schedule's times be read in either clock, the viewer's by default (#1630)

* feat(web): let a schedule's times be read in either clock, the viewer's by default

A schedule card showed its two halves on different clocks and said so nowhere:
`cronHuman` renders the expression as a bare wall time, while `cronNext` honours
the stored timezone and renders the result in the viewer's. A schedule kept on
one clock and read on another therefore showed "At 09:00 AM" directly above a
next run eight hours away, with nothing on the card to explain it.

The expression's reading now names the timezone it is interpreted in, and every
INSTANT on the schedule surfaces — next run, and each run's start — renders in
whichever clock the viewer picks. The choice is a per-device preference stored
beside the other console ones, defaulting to the viewer's own.

The expression itself is never converted, which is why the switch governs
instants only: `0 2 * * MON` in one zone is a different weekday in another, and a
zone that observes DST has no fixed offset to convert by. So its reading always
names its own zone, and the switch decides what the times around it mean.

The switch renders only where there is a second clock to switch to — a schedule
already on the viewer's zone offers two identical readings — and only after
mount, since the viewer's zone is unknown on the server.

* fix(control-plane): stop guessing a schedule's timezone from the server

A schedule fires by its timezone, and the server was picking one for any caller
that did not send it: `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone`, which
is the control-plane PROCESS's zone — UTC in a container, the developer's own
zone in a test. So "every morning at 9" could mean 9am somewhere the person
asking has never been, and the meaning of a stored schedule depended on where
the control plane happened to run.

it optional with a bare "IANA timezone name" description, so a model asked
through a connector for "a daily 9am job" had no reason to send one — which is
how a schedule ends up on UTC without anyone choosing it. That field is required
now, and says whose zone it must be and to ask when it is unknown.

Two changes behind it, both at the one place a zone is decided:

- An omitted zone on CREATE stores `UTC` — a constant rather than the ambient
  process zone, so a schedule means the same thing wherever the CP runs.
- An omitted zone on EDIT keeps the one the schedule already had. It used to
  overwrite it with the process zone, quietly moving a live schedule off the
  clock it was authored on.

The REST body stays optional so existing callers keep working; it is the
agent-facing tool that is strict, since that is the caller with a person to ask.

* fix(daemon): tell a scheduled turn which clock it fired on

A schedule carries a timezone and fires by it, but nothing carried that into the
turn. The daemon host runs its own clock — UTC in a container — so an agent
asked for "today's digest" reads today from the host and dates the file to
yesterday whenever the two zones straddle midnight. A schedule firing at 01:58

timezone was on the CronDef the whole time; it just never reached the turn.

zone-less expression, and so does one naming a zone no formatter accepts — a
hand-authored cron is not validated against IANA, and the stamp must not be the
thing that throws. The clock is assembled from `Intl` parts under a pinned

A runtime may compose several messages inside one uninterrupted answer run —
Codex does, and names each with `messageId`. The convergers appended every
`agent_message_chunk` into one buffer and flushed it at a boundary in the WORK
(tool call, thought, plan), so a run that only speaks had no boundary at all and
its messages arrived glued: "…without any Reddit account activity.The collector
returned 46 candidates…".

Worse than the run-on sentence, a leading `#` on the next message lands inside
the previous paragraph and stops being a heading — a digest reached its channel
with its title rendered as literal text.

The id was already on the wire and already read on one path: the GitHub reply
collector groups by it to pick a turn's final answer. The same update object
reaches the chat convergers, which ignored it. Each now closes the current
message where a NAMED id replaces a different named one, through the same
`flush`/`closeSegment` a tool boundary uses, so per-platform mode semantics are
untouched.

A runtime that names nothing keeps today's behavior exactly, which is what keeps
this from undoing #323: a reply that merely streams in pieces is one message,
not one per chunk.

Staged turns are covered for free — `commitStagedSegment` replays the original
update objects through the same converger, so the boundary applies to a replayed
turn identically. That makes a staged segment able to commit as more than one

feat(slack): give agents thread reads, reactions, canvases, and scheduled sends (#1644)

* feat(slack): declare capability scopes without fencing installs on them

The app manifest and the install fence were one list, so every scope we ask
for is a scope an existing installation is marked broken for not having. That
is right for the scopes without which the app cannot receive or answer a
message at all, and wrong for a scope that unlocks one optional tool: adding
one would put every already-installed workspace into `reinstall_required` for
a feature it never asked for.

refuses a short grant against; `SLACK_CAPABILITY_BOT_SCOPES` is declared in the
manifest and never fenced on, so a workspace that installed before a capability
existed keeps working and only the one tool that needs the scope refuses, with
Slack's own `missing_scope`.

The first six are `reactions:read`, `canvases:read`, `canvases:write`,
`channels:manage`, `groups:write`, and `mpim:write`. The last two also close a
standing gap: `conversations.leave` has always needed one of them, the adapter
comment has said so since it was written, and the manifest never asked.

seam rather than three.

the connection — it is how the daemon rebuilds mid-thread context — and was
simply never handed to the agent. `getThreadHistory` exposes it, needs no new
scope, and pairs with `getChannelHistory`, which already reports each message's

empty list the daemon's best-effort backfill settles for.

turn chrome, where core names an INTENT and the module picks the glyph. That
design is right for chrome and wrong here, so `addReaction` is a separate
member: the glyph comes from the model, which already knows which platform it is
speaking on, and no core-side vocabulary is invented to translate. `getReactions`
reads the tallies back.

`readCanvas` / `updateCanvas` for a page that outlives a message and is edited
in place; `scheduleMessage` for a post the platform delivers at a wall-clock
moment; `createConversation` for a channel or a group DM.

never by its name, and each tool's `platform` enum narrows to the declaring
platforms — Slack declares all six ports today, so an agent without it is
injected none of them. Adding a second implementer is a registry line plus the
adapter members. The bespoke channel-history helpers collapse into one generic
`platformsWithPort` lookup on the way past.

stay the only delivery paths for the agent's own voice, so `scheduleMessage` is
channel-root only for exactly the reason `sendMessage` is. And Slack takes no

identity — said in the tool description rather than discovered in the channel.

nothing else, so `readCanvas` returns metadata and anchors always and the body
only when the ordinary credentialed file path serves it.

refactor(cp,web): split the daemon read by how fast each half changes (#1652)

* refactor(cp,web): split the daemon read by how fast each half changes

`GET /daemons` carried a daemon's liveness, its capabilities and every runtime's
full model catalog in one payload, and the console polls it every 15 seconds. On
a nine-daemon fleet that is ~104 KB per poll of which ~1% — status, health, load,
last-seen — is what the poll is actually watching. The catalogs alone are 68%.

Split the read by change rate rather than by "summary vs detail":

- `GET /daemons` keeps the liveness row.
- `GET /daemons/capabilities` answers what each daemon can run — capabilities,
  runtime profiles, configured MCP servers. Readers of these need every daemon at
  once (the pickers' runtime list, the per-agent login warning, a set's runtime
  union), so this stays a fleet-wide read; it just leaves the fast poll.
- `GET /daemons/:id` is new and is the only read carrying a runtime's model
  catalog, which is how its readers already use it — one daemon at a time.

The catalog cannot be shared or deduplicated: it is probed from the ACP binary on
each host, so two daemons on the same runtime version legitimately differ.

The console stitches the first two halves back into one `DaemonRow` in the data
context, so views are unchanged; only the four surfaces that read a catalog now
resolve the daemon they are configuring through `useDaemonDetail`.

fix(daemon): read a memory component dropped mid-walk as absent, not an escape (#1658)

`walkContained` canonicalises the parent chain one component at a time and
rejects anything whose realpath lands outside the memory root. That check
assumed the only way to leave the root is to escape it. On Windows a component
a concurrent rm has already unlinked can still realpath successfully — to the
volume root rather than to an ENOENT — so a benign deletion race surfaced as
`MemoryPathError: path resolves outside the memory root`.

It is the cancel-wins path that races: cancel removes a dream's staging while
`stagedFiles()` is resolving it. Missing staging is data there — the review
screen wants null, which is the right answer once cancel won — but the
containment check threw before the absence could be reported. That is the
intermittent `Unit Test (Windows)` failure in `dream-runner.test.ts` >
"cancel-wins when it lands during staging"; the same commit passed on a re-run,
and the PR it failed on touched no file under this package.

A failed containment check is now re-probed with lstat before it is called a
violation: only a path that is still present has escaped, and a dropped one is
absence, which stays data on the read side. The write side's two
re-verifications go through the same helper, so a concurrent rm during a publish
surfaces as its own errno instead of a false security signal.

Both sides of the comparison were already normalised the same way — each is a
`realpath` output, and `path.relative` is case-insensitive on Windows — so the
short-vs-long-form and case asymmetries were not in play; the vanished component
was the whole defect.

`canonicalWorkspacePath` and `canonicalUnder` both took a failed containment check
as proof of an escape. On Windows `realpath` can answer for a path a concurrent
`rm` has already unlinked with one OUTSIDE the root — the volume root — instead of

conversion) surfaced as a path-escape violation rather than "not found". The same

still checked), `exists:false` from a listing, a conflict from an edit. A non-vanish

feat(slack): give agents bookmarks and lists, and batch the reserved scopes (#1661)

* feat(slack): give agents bookmarks and lists, and batch the reserved scopes

Six tools on the existing port mechanism, plus the scopes that back them.

BOOKMARKS — `listBookmarks` / `addBookmark` / `removeBookmark`, the links pinned
at the top of a conversation. The write says plainly that a bookmark outlives
the task: it is channel-visible state an agent can create, and the model needs
that in view rather than discovering it from a complaint. Only `type: 'link'`
is offered; Slack's other kinds name existing entities by an id a model has no
way to hold.

LISTS — `readList` / `addListItem` / `updateListItem`. These repeat the canvas
lesson exactly. A value is addressed by `column_id` and keyed by that column's
TYPE, and Slack publishes no schema endpoint for a list, so the columns are
derived from the rows a read returns and handed back with them. The read is not
a convenience before the write; it is the only source of the ids and types the
write needs, which is why both write descriptors point at it.

RESERVED, and labelled as such: `channels:join`, `team:read`, `users:read.email`
have no caller. That is a deliberate exception to the rule this repo just
adopted, and the reason is the rule's own consequence — with one scope list,
every addition costs a reinstall of every installation, so batching the ones
already in view is one reinstall instead of three. Recorded in the constant and
the design doc as an exception taken once, not a licence to declare scopes
speculatively.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(slack): match the real Lists wire contract, and stop borrowing a foreign channel

Three defects, all from writing against a shape I had not checked closely enough.

FIELD PARSING. A List field carries `key`, `value` and often `text` ALONGSIDE
the typed property, and Slack's own examples put `key` first — so reading "the
first property that is not column_id" returned `['key', 'rich_text_notes']`.
Every cell lost its value and reported a type the write endpoints reject, which
means the advertised read→write flow could not have worked once. The type is now
recognized from the documented set rather than taken positionally, and
`include_list: true` supplies the authoritative column schema, which also sees a
column no row has filled in yet — the old derivation could not.

UPDATES. `slackLists.items.update` takes no top-level id; the row is named per
cell as `row_id`. Every call would have been refused with `row_id_not_provided`.

BOOKMARK CHANNEL. `ctx.channel` belongs to the SESSION's platform, and defaulting
to it ignored which gateway resolved. A Telegram session whose agent also has
Slack, calling with `platform: 'slack'` and no channel, would have handed Slack a
Telegram id and failed as `channel_not_found` far from the cause. The resolver
already reports `sameConvo`; the default now honours it, and the tools say the
channel is required when the target is elsewhere.

The tests carry Slack's documented fixtures rather than the tidy shapes I had
assumed — a field with its metadata in front, a schema-only column, and the
per-cell row id — so the same mistakes cannot pass again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(slack): normalize List schema types to the keys a write accepts

A column's schema `type` is not always the key a request may use, and the case
that matters is the one every list has. The primary column is always a text
column, and Slack is explicit: "you may see the `text` property appear in a
response as a fallback, but it is not accepted in the request payload" — writes
must be `rich_text`. Reporting the schema type verbatim handed the agent the one
key the write endpoints reject, on the column it reaches for first.

So schema types cross a table on the way out, and the response recognizer goes
through the same one: a value read as `text` still reports `rich_text`. `message`
was missing from the writable set and is added.

Six schema types are computed by Slack and no request may set them —
`created_by`, `last_edited_by`, `created_time`, `last_edited_time`, `vote`,
`canvas`. They now come back marked `readOnly` rather than carrying a key that
would be refused, and the write tools say to skip them.

Same root cause as the last round: I read the shape of a response and assumed the
request mirrored it. The fixtures now include a primary column typed `text` and a
computed column, so the assumption cannot come back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(slack): map the task column aliases, and make the vocabulary checkable

Slack's task columns come back from the schema as `assignee`, `due_date` and
`completed` — `todo_assignee`, `todo_due_date`, `todo_completed` in todo-mode
lists — and are written as the ordinary fields they are made of: `user`, `date`,
`checkbox`. Reporting the schema name meant every write to a task list was
refused, and a task list is the common case.

This is the fourth round of the same shape of defect, so the fix is not another
entry in a table nobody can check. `LIST_SCHEMA_TYPES` now enumerates every
column type Slack documents, and a test asserts the mapping answers for ALL of
them — a type Slack adds later fails there instead of silently passing through
as a write key. A second test asserts nothing maps to a key the item endpoints
reject, which is what `text` was doing.

The bug was never a mapping anyone got wrong; it was a vocabulary nobody had
enumerated. Enumerating it is the repair.

feat(cp): Linear platform provider skeleton and storage (#1670)

* feat(cp): register a Linear platform provider over its own token storage

Linear is a chat-kind platform whose ingress is relay-terminated and whose
egress is daemon-direct, so it implements the control plane's provider
contract like its four peers -- with two differences the design calls for:

- the generic credential path is REFUSED. A connected workspace is one shared
  bot for the deployment's single OAuth app, and a member integration must
  never exist outside one, so `validateConfig` sends the operator to the
  connect flow and `credentialBodySchema` stays vestigial;
- `projectIntegrationConfig` is the async projector the contract was made
  async for: it loads the workspace's short-lived access token out of the
  provider's own `linear_token` table by the bot's generic identity, and
  answers fail-closed when there is no grant.

Storage lands with it. `linear_token` is keyed by the connection identity
(org, client id, workspace) rather than by the bot row, which is what lets the
callback write the grant before the bot exists and keeps member churn away
from the credential; both values pass through the existing cipher seam.
`linear_install_state` is the connect funnel's nonce row and holds no secrets.

The contract grows one optional member for the disconnect edge core had no
home for: `sideEffects.onBotDelete(bot, secrets)`, best-effort like
`postCreate` and consulted only for a platform that declares it. It runs after
the bot row is actually gone, so a refused delete never tears down a live
install; Linear's implementation drops the identity's grant, which hangs off
no row and nothing else would ever collect.

The connect funnel, its OAuth callback, the token exchange/refresh service and
the credential broker are deliberately not here.

* fix(cp): redeem the Linear nonce atomically and withhold a spec with no grant

Two lifecycle holes from review, both cases where a check and the action it
guards were separable.

**The connect nonce is one-shot, so redeeming it must be one statement.**
`LinearInstallStateStore` exposed `get` + `delete`, which lets two concurrent
callbacks -- a double-clicked authorize tab, or a replayed redirect -- both read
the same live row before either deletes it, and both go on to mint a workspace.
The pair is replaced by `consume(id)`: a single `DELETE ... RETURNING`, so the
loser blocks on the row lock, re-evaluates against a row that is gone, and gets
null.

**A provider with no deliverable payload must withhold the integration, not
ship an empty one.** `projectIntegrationConfig` answering `undefined` produced a
spec whose `config` was absent, and that spec still rode the roster: its id
stayed in the desired set, so it never reached the prune list, and the reader on
the other side refuses a payload-less spec while KEEPING the entry it already
holds. A revoked or swept grant therefore revoked nothing -- the integration kept
running on the last good credential.

`undefined` now means absence. `integrationToSpec` / `httpIntegrationToSpec`
answer null, which is the same fact -- and the same exit -- as the roster's
existing "no secret, no bot" guard, so the reconcile snapshot omits the
integration and the prune list carries it. The live shared-transport path goes
further and pulls the send-only bundle, the teardown a workspace-side revoke
already performs. A move refuses, like a missing credential row. Every other
platform always returns a payload, so nothing else changes shape.

feat(cp): let a shared bot pin its default agent (#1665)

* feat(cp): let a shared bot pin its default agent

The HTTP-bot compile derived `defaultAgentId` as the earliest non-gated member,
so the agent that catches a bare mention, a DM, or a delegation was an accident
of install order and nothing could move it. Bot gains a nullable
`preferredAgentId`; the compile prefers it while it still resolves to a placed,
non-gated member of that bot, and otherwise falls back to the derivation
unchanged — a stale pointer degrades instead of silencing the bot.

PATCH /bots/:id takes the field (null clears it) beside the existing sharing
flip, refusing an agent that does not use the bot with the same wording the
per-conversation default agent uses, and rides the same syncRoutes re-broadcast.
The FK is SET NULL because the bot row outlives the agent, so nothing else would
clear a deleted agent's pointer.

Platform-free by construction: any shared bot has the knob.

* fix(cp): apply both halves of a bot update or neither

PATCH /bots/:id wrote the preferred default agent and broadcast the recompile
before the sharing half was validated, so a body carrying both fields could
answer 409 — manifest gate, transport, disable-while-shared, or a lost mutation
lease — with the default already moved and shipped to the relay pool. A refused
request must change nothing.

Every refusal now precedes both writes: membership, then the manifest gate, then
the lease, then the locked re-read's transport and capacity checks. Only after
all of them do the writes run, sharing first because its row-locked recount is
the last thing that can still refuse, and a single syncRoutes broadcasts the
result once. The lease is still taken only when the capacity flip needs it.

* fix(cp): commit both bot columns in one transaction

Reordering the validation left one gap: `shareable` and `preferredAgentId` were
still two repository calls, and the mutation gate is in-memory — it does not
exclude a concurrent agent DELETE. One landing between the calls let the sharing
flip commit and the preferred write then fail its foreign key, so the request
errored with half the body applied.

`setShareable` and `setPreferredAgent` collapse into one `BotRepo.update(orgId,
id, patch)` that writes both columns in a single statement inside the existing
row-locked transaction, keeping the `BotStillShared` recount where it was. A lost
foreign key now rolls the capacity flip back with it. The install path's silent
promotion to shareable rides the same member, so there is one locked writer for
the bot row rather than two.

* fix(cp): answer a lost preferred-agent FK with the membership 409

The transaction rolls back correctly when the preferred agent is deleted between
the route's membership check and the write, but the foreign-key violation reached
the client as a 500. The agent's Integration goes with it in the cascade, so it
has genuinely stopped being a member — the honest answer is the refusal a body
naming a non-member already gets.

`BotRepo.update` types that violation as `BotPreferredAgentMissing` rather than
leaking a Prisma code past the persistence seam, and the route maps it beside its
`BotStillShared` branch to the same copy its up-front membership check uses. No
new status code: 409 was already declared.

* chore(cp): settle the bot default column against the Linear provider

Rebasing onto the Linear platform provider brings a new `BotRecord` fixture that
predates this column, so its literal gains the same one-line `preferredAgentId:
null` every other platform fixture carries.

The migration moves to 20260921000000 so it still sorts last: the Linear tables
landed at 20260920000000 while this branch was in review, which would otherwise
have left an earlier-named migration arriving after one already applied.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): send reasoning deltas and exempt the Linear settle from the cap

Two functional bugs found in review, both from carrying an in-place renderer's
assumptions onto an append-only feed.

`drainReasoning` never cleared its buffer. The chat renderers keep a cumulative
one because they EDIT a single message, but Linear appends, so on medium/high
every idle flush re-posted the whole turn's thinking — duplicated content and a
budget burned on repeats. It now emits the delta since the last flush, with the
same accumulation cap and tail clamp as before.

The hard per-turn activity budget also counted and blocked the settling
`response`/`error`. A busy enough turn would therefore drop its own final answer
and leave the Linear session active until it went stale — the opposite of what
the cap is for, which is bounding progress chrome. A settling activity is now
exempt and draws nothing from the budget, so the cap can never be what loses the
answer.

Both are pinned: two idle flushes of a growing reasoning stream must not overlap,
and a turn whose budget is exhausted must still post its response, and its error
on the failure path, and nothing else.

feat(daemon): Linear Layer-1 connection and config schema (#1674)

* feat(daemon): add the Linear Layer-1 connection and its config schema

Linear's daemon-side edge unit, Layer 1 only (linear-integration.md §9.4).

`platforms/linear/connection.ts` is a per-integration egress client over plain
GraphQL `fetch` — no SDK dependency, since the agent surface is two mutations
(`agentActivityCreate`, `agentSessionUpdate`) and two queries. There is no
socket to open: ingress is relay-terminated, so `start()` only warms the token
and `stop()` clears the refresh timer.

Token custody follows §4.4/§7.3. The connection starts from the spec's ≤24 h
access-token snapshot, caches it in memory, and re-requests over
`linearcred/request` once it is within a 2 h margin of expiry, single-flight so
concurrent sends issue one request. Renewal failure degrades rather than
breaks: the cached token keeps serving until it actually expires, and only then
does a send fail. Token material never reaches a log line, and the daemon never
holds the client secret or the refresh token.

Outbound writes share one `PlatformSendQueue` per integration with a 1 s
minimum interval (§5.3). The read port answers what Linear affords —
`getChannelInfo` resolves the issue, `getUserProfile` the Linear user — and
answers empty elsewhere; there is no bot-channel enumeration, no leave
affordance, and attachment download is deferred.

The `linear` `CONFIG_SCHEMAS` line flips `capabilities.platforms`, so the
registry-drift test now names Linear as awaiting its composition lines. That
list is asserted exactly: the moment the turn-output surface, command chrome
and connection pool land, the plain equality passes again and the exemption
must go.

Out of scope and arriving separately: the Layer-2 turn output and converger,
the message strategy and pre-spawn ack, and the `daemon.ts` composition and
reconcile wiring.

* fix(daemon): harden the Linear connection's renewal and rate-limit handling

Three resilience defects from PR review, each reproduced before fixing and each
pinned by a test that fails against the previous code.

The refresh chain ended at the first failure. `scheduleRefresh` armed one timer
whose callback cleared the handle and then swallowed the outcome, so a transient
renewal refusal left the integration with no timer at all — recovery could only
ever be found by a live send, inside Linear's 10 s ack budget. The failure path
now re-arms, the callback re-arms whatever the outcome, and the delay is the
later of the expiry margin and the end of the backoff.

The renewal backoff was conditional on the cached token still being valid, so it
fell open exactly when it mattered: once the snapshot expired, every send
re-drove a `linearcred` REQ through the outage. The backoff now holds
regardless; a send inside it fails fast with the token-unavailable error and one
request is made per backoff window, not one per send.

Linear reports a rate limit as HTTP 400 with `RATELIMITED` in the GraphQL
errors, and the client threw on the status before ever parsing the body — so a
rate-limited final `response` was classified terminal and dropped. The body is
now parsed before the status is judged, the error code decides retryability, and
`Retry-After` is carried on the error. The existing rate-limit test used a 200,
which is why it passed over the broken path.

Rate-limit classification is only useful if something acts on it, so the paced
egress path gains the bounded retry section 11 already describes: up to three
attempts inside the caller's queue slot, preferring the provider's `Retry-After`
over its own backoff and capping it so one write cannot eat the queue's task
budget. Terminal refusals still fail on the first attempt, and read-port calls
do not retry — they already degrade to a default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): key Linear activity creation so a retry cannot double-post

The bounded send retry made an append-only create unsafe. `agentActivityCreate`
appends a row per call — a second create with identical content stacks a second
row rather than updating the first — and a transport loss or a 5xx is
indeterminate: the write may have committed before the response went missing. So
the retry could publish the same thought, action or final response twice under
two server-generated ids.

Activity creation now carries its own idempotency key. A UUID is minted once per
LOGICAL activity, before the first attempt, and rides the mutation input's
optional `id`; every retry of that activity reuses it, so the second write
addresses the same row instead of appending a new one. The factory is injectable
so tests assert on fixed ids rather than real UUIDs.

A retry refused because that id already exists means the earlier attempt landed,
so it resolves as success. The detection is deliberately narrow: only a refusal
whose message clearly says the id is taken counts, it counts only on a retry —
on a first attempt the same refusal means a caller reused a key across two
logical writes, which must surface — and anything ambiguous is still thrown.
Silently swallowing an unclear error would drop a real activity, which is the
worse of the two failures.

`agentSessionUpdate` needs no key and is unchanged: `plan` and `externalUrls`
are full-array replaces, so a retry converges on the same state.

* feat(cp): re-stamp the deployment Linear credentials onto every workspace bot

The setup card can rotate the deployment Linear app, but the relay never reads
that config: it verifies `Linear-Signature` with the copy the connect tail
stamped into each workspace bot's `BotSecret` row and shipped in the
`rc/bot-assign` secrets bag. Rotating therefore moved the source of truth and
left every stamped row behind, so each workspace kept failing verification until
someone reconnected it by hand.

This is the re-stamp §10.6 of the design specifies. A provider-owned convergence
loop compares the current deployment app against each Linear bot's stored slots
— `botToken` carries the client secret, `signingSecret` the webhook secret — and
for every row that drifted writes both through `BotCredentialWriter.install`,
the same atomic seam the connect tail uses, which advances `credentialRevision`,
then re-broadcasts the assignment through `syncBot`. A matching row is untouched,
so a second pass is a no-op.

It is declared as a `backgroundLoops` member rather than a bespoke boot hook, so
`startBackground()` and shutdown drive it without naming the platform. The pass
`start()` runs immediately is the load-bearing one, since the credentials arrive
through the environment and can only move across a restart; the interval is a
self-heal for a re-stamp whose broadcast found no connected relay.

`BotRepo.listForPlatform` is the worklist. It is deliberately unfiltered by
install state, unlike `listHttpActive`: a workspace whose members are all gone
still holds the stale secret its next `syncBot` would broadcast, so skipping it
would defer the drift rather than remove it.

* fix(cp): scope the Linear re-stamp to the current app's live installs

The re-stamp walked every `linear` bot, which crossed two lifecycle edges it has
no standing to decide.

A bot whose durable `externalAppId` is a PREVIOUS client id is a different app's
install — the setup card permits changing the client id, and such a workspace
authorized the old app while its `linear_token` row stays keyed by it. Stamping
today's secrets there fused two identities into a row neither app could serve.
Those bots are now skipped, and counted once per pass into a log line naming
them as awaiting reconnect. A NULL app half takes the same arm: an unattributed
row is not evidence that it is ours.

A revoked bot was worse than useless: `install` advances the generation through
`bumpCredential`, which clears `revokedAt`, and the seam offers no no-unrevoke
variant — so rotating a deployment secret silently resurrected a workspace that
had revoked or uninstalled the app. Un-revoking belongs exclusively to the
reconnect flow, which re-proves the grant first, so a revoked bot is skipped too.

Covered both ways: unit cases for the previous-app row, the unattributed row, the
revoked row, and a mixed fleet where only the live workspace moves; integration
cases asserting the previous-app and revoked rows keep their stored secrets and
`credentialRevision` with no broadcast, the revoked one keeps `revokedAt`, and a
three-workspace fleet publishes exactly the live bot.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): retry the Linear re-stamp broadcast until a relay is told

The durable rewrite and the relay broadcast are two steps, and a failed second
one was forgotten. The next pass compared the row this loop had already fixed,
found it current, and skipped the bot — so connected relays kept verifying with
the old signing key indefinitely, with nothing in the database left to say so.

The retry is now remembered rather than re-derived: a successful install marks
the bot pending, the mark is only cleared once `resync` resolves, and every pass
retries the pending set independently of the drift comparison. The broadcast sits
after the drift branch rather than inside it, so a bot that both drifted and owed
a retry publishes exactly once per pass.

The mark is process-local by design. A CP restart replays every assignment to
each relay as it registers, and that same register replay covers a `resync` that
returned having broadcast nothing because no relay was connected — only a THROWN
resync is a debt. Persisting this would add a table to re-implement a guarantee
the register path already gives.

Two marks are dropped rather than retried: a bot that has become another app's
install, or that has been revoked. Once a row leaves this loop's standing,
publishing it belongs to the revoke and reconnect paths. Marks for bots that
disappear between passes are pruned so the set cannot grow without bound.

feat(cp): Linear workspace connect funnel and token custody (#1675)

* feat(cp): connect a Linear workspace through an OAuth funnel and own its token

A Linear bot cannot be born from pasted credentials -- the deployment owns the one
OAuth app -- so this adds the only flow that mints one, plus the custody the
resulting grant needs.

The funnel (org scope) records the chosen default agent behind a one-shot `state`
nonce and returns the authorize URL, gated on core's relay-availability 409 and the
daemon's `linear` capability: Linear has no dial-out transport, so a workspace bot
exists only on `http`. Nothing else is written -- no Bot, no Integration -- because
an http bot is synchronized the instant it is created, which would drive
`projectIntegrationConfig` before any grant existed.

The unauthenticated callback redeems the nonce before it spends the code, exchanges
it, resolves `viewer { id organization { id name } }`, and then runs the design's
exact order: upsert the grant under the connection identity FIRST, then the shared
create tail. That ordering is implementable only because the grant is keyed by
`(orgId, clientId, organizationId)` rather than by the bot row -- `installNewBot`
mints the bot id internally -- and it is what makes the tail's own `syncBot` find a
durable token. A workspace already connected in this organization takes the
reconnect arm instead: the same upsert replaces the dead grant in place and the
members are untouched. A tail refusal after the upsert leaves an inert row the next
connect overwrites.

Redemption is a single compare-and-set on the funnel row, so two concurrent
callbacks -- a double-clicked tab, a retried redirect -- cannot both reach Linear:
the loser blocks on the winner's row lock and matches nothing. `consume` CLAIMS
rather than deletes, because the row is also the console's only completion signal;
the OAuth tab is a throwaway, so the identity and workspace fences, which refuse
after the grant is already written, have no other channel back. The claimed row is
then `settle`d with the outcome, and the status poll reads it through a member named
`peek` that is documented as strictly read-only: reading a row and then acting on it
is the exact race `consume` exists to close.

`LinearTokenService` is the single durable writer of a credential that rotates:
refresh runs behind a per-identity single-flight, persists the rotated pair BEFORE
replying, and treats a rejected rotate as "someone else rotated first" by reloading
the row once -- only then does the workspace count as needing a reconnect. An
unreachable Linear never spends that retry and never flips the state.

Two collectors close the loop. The disconnect edge now revokes upstream before
dropping the row, but only when no organization's Bot holds the identity: the fences
are global while token rows are org-scoped, so a loser's teardown must never revoke
the grant backing the winner's live install. The orphan sweeper applies the same
split on a grace window -- org-scoped selection, unconditional local delete, global
revoke -- and is the backstop for both a refused tail and a failed disconnect.
Neither needs to push a daemon-side teardown: both only ever collect grants whose
organization holds no bot, so no integration for them can exist.

Reconnect does need one, and it is pinned as frames. Now that a provider answering
"no payload" means true absence, a dead grant pulls the send-only bundle; rotating a
row is therefore no longer enough to claim a workspace is repaired, so the test
asserts the sync emits `integration/remove` with the grant gone and that the
reconnect callback brings the entry back carrying the fresh access token.

* fix(cp): close four lifecycle holes in the Linear reconnect and sweep paths

All four are cases where a step looked complete on its own but left a neighbouring
piece of state behind, and they interlock enough (one migration, one changed
selection shape) to land together.

**Reconnect must restore the revoked lifecycle, not just the grant.** The way a
workspace actually ends up needing a reconnect is the `OAuthApp revoked` doorbell,
and `revokeBot` both stamps `Bot.revokedAt` and flips every membership to
`revoked`. `agentIds` is active-only, so re-broadcasting after that saw an EMPTY
member set: the sync unassigned the bot while the funnel settled `completed`,
leaving a green console over a workspace that answers nothing. And with
`credentialRevision` unmoved, a revoke report still in flight for the replaced
grant would pass the fence and kill the credential that had just replaced it. The
arm now goes through the same writer the Slack platform-app re-install uses --
store, advance the generation, restore exactly the memberships revoked WITH the
generation being replaced, one transaction -- before `syncBot` re-broadcasts.

**A reconnect nonce is bound to its workspace.** The row recorded only org and
user, so it meant "any workspace of this organization": an operator repairing A
who authorized already-connected B rotated B's grant and was told it worked, while
A stayed dead. The row now carries the expected bot and the callback checks the
granted workspace against it BEFORE the step-1 upsert, so a mismatch rotates
nothing and settles `wrong_workspace`. This also subsumes the old
`default_agent_required` answer for a reconnect aimed at an unconnected workspace,
which was a true statement about the wrong thing.

**The sweep's batch counts orphans, not scanned rows.** The oldest stale grants in
any real deployment are overwhelmingly healthy installs -- a workspace that simply
has not needed a refresh in an hour -- so taking the oldest N and filtering
afterwards let those N fill every pass and starved the orphans behind them forever.
The org-scoped ownership test moved inside the selection, which is also where the
global one now sits, so the two scopes the design separates are the query's two
subqueries.

**The sweep claims a row before acting on it.** The grace window is a heuristic,
not a lock: a retried connect's step-1 upsert can re-grant a long-stale identity
between the snapshot and the act, and the sweep would then revoke the FRESH token
upstream and delete the row backing the install that retry had just repaired. Each
row is now deleted under a condition on the `updatedAt` it was selected with, in
one statement that returns what it removed; zero rows affected means skip, and the
revoke uses the token that claim returned rather than a re-read.

* fix(cp): decide the Linear orphan revoke under a per-identity advisory lock

The last window the row-level guard cannot see. A different organization can
complete a connect for the same `(clientId, organizationId)` at any moment, and
doing so touches NONE of the losing organization's rows -- so the updatedAt-guarded
delete still matches, and a `claimedElsewhere` computed back at listing time is by
then a lie. The sweep would revoke the app-workspace grant the winner had just
obtained.

The mistake was structural: an answer about OTHER organizations was being carried
down from a snapshot, alongside answers about this row that a row-level guard can
legitimately protect. So `claimedElsewhere` is gone from the candidate type
entirely -- keeping it would leave the cheap, stale version within reach -- and the
global question now has exactly one home, asked durably at the moment of acting:

  withIdentityOwnership(identity, act)

takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on `(clientId, organizationId)`,
re-queries ownership under it, and runs `act` inside. `put` -- §7.1 step 1, every
claimant's FIRST durable write -- takes the same lock, which is what makes the
answer stable while `act` runs; and because §7.1 fixes that write before the create
tail, locking it fences bot admission too, without wrapping a transaction around
`installNewBot` and its relay broadcast.

The lock is deliberately not org-scoped. Every other lock family here keys on an
organization because its invariant is tenant-local; this one asks whether ANY
tenant relies on the grant, because a revoke acts on the app-workspace
authorization rather than on one tenant's copy of it. `owned` is therefore true for
any organization's Bot on the identity OR any other organization's token row --
the second disjunct catching a winner that is mid-callback, having written its
grant but not yet its Bot, which a bot-only test would miss entirely.

The revoke stays INSIDE the lock: releasing first would only narrow the window,
since a winner admitted in between still loses its grant. That means one bounded
HTTP call inside a transaction, so the Linear client gained a per-request timeout
(it had none -- Node's fetch does not) sitting well under the transaction's own
budget, and a call that never returns now surfaces as `unreachable` instead of as
an expired transaction. An ownership query that answers nothing fails closed.

`onBotDelete` had the same shape -- a plain `getByExternalIdentity` read, then a
revoke -- and moves to the same seam, which retires its `bots` dependency.

* fix(cp): collect a Linear orphan inside one hold, and let a waiter outlast it

Two boundary gaps left over from moving the revoke decision under the identity
lock.

**The claim was still outside the lock.** The ownership question deliberately does
not count the caller's own organization -- a disconnect must not see the row it is
itself removing -- so a same-org retry that committed a fresh grant in the gap
between the conditional delete and that question was invisible to it: the sweep
read "unowned" and revoked the authorization backing a grant that was seconds old.
The `updatedAt` guard does not catch this, because by then the guard has already
passed.

So the claim, the ownership question and the upstream revoke are now one
uninterrupted hold. `deleteIfUnchanged` and `withIdentityOwnership` are gone as
separate store methods and reachable only from inside `withIdentityLock`, which
hands out a section with `claim` and `owned`: making them unreachable outside the
lock is the point, since either one used on its own is exactly the bug. A `put`
racing the sweep can now only land wholly before the claim (which then matches
nothing and the candidate is skipped) or wholly after the decision.

The test that pins this asserts the structural property as well as the behavioural
one -- the collection takes ONE acquisition, and no re-grant lands while it is
held. Asserting only "fresh grant intact, no revoke" was not enough: that ordering
passes on the split implementation too, because a `put` before the claim merely
moves `updatedAt`. Verified by re-splitting the hold and watching it fail.

**A waiter could expire behind a holder.** The callback's step-1 `put` waits for
this same lock, and `pg_advisory_xact_lock` blocks INSIDE the transaction, so the
ceiling that matters is its `timeout` -- left at Prisma's default it could expire
while queued behind a sweep that legitimately holds the lock across a bounded
upstream call. That failure is not retryable: the callback has already spent its
OAuth authorization code, and Linear will not honour it twice.

The three numbers are now one documented ordering next to the lock -- API request
timeout < maximum hold < waiter budget -- with a unit test asserting it, including
the slack between the last two, so shaving any of them fails a test rather than
surfacing months later as a workspace that will not connect.

* test(cp): pin that both Linear convergence loops survive composition

The re-stamp and the orphan sweep arrived from different branches and each
declared `backgroundLoops`. Merged as two object spreads that reads as additive
and is not: the later key replaces the earlier, so one loop silently never starts
and nothing fails. The merge itself is resolved in the commits below; this is the
test that keeps it resolved.

Three assertions, at both levels. The provider suite pins the pair when both slots
are composed and each one alone when only its slot is -- so the presence-follows-
slot-presence property survives too -- and the connect suite pins what the fully
composed container actually publishes, which is where a wiring regression would
land rather than a shaping one. That last assertion previously read "the
provider's only loop", which was true when the sweep was the only one and is now
exactly the claim a second loop should have invalidated loudly.

* fix(cp): remove the Linear token row inside the disconnect's identity hold

Round 3's finding, on the teardown path. `onBotDelete` asked the ownership
question and made the revoke decision under the identity's advisory lock, then
released it and deleted the organization's token row. A `put` queued on that lock
publishes a fresh grant the instant the hold ends, and the trailing unconditional
delete removes THAT row -- leaving the create or reconnect tail behind it
believing its grant is durable when it is already gone.

So the removal moves inside the section, as `LinearIdentitySection.remove()`: one
uninterrupted hold for the whole disconnect decision, mirroring the sweeper's
claim. Under it nothing can interleave, so the row removed is exactly the one the
revoke decision was made about. `owned()` stays BEFORE the removal on purpose --
it excludes the caller's own organization, so it already reads the world as it
will be once the row is gone.

The test asserts the STRUCTURAL property -- that the removal happened while the
hold was open -- rather than only "the fresh grant survived". The behavioural
assertion alone does not discriminate: once the hold releases, the queued `put`
and a trailing delete are two round trips with no ordering between them, so the
buggy version passes whenever the delete happens to win, which it did on the
first attempt. Confirmed by re-splitting the section and watching the structural
assertion fail.

feat(cp): broker Linear access tokens on the daemon socket (#1682)

* feat(cp): broker Linear workspace access tokens over linearcred/request

The last control-plane leg of the Linear integration (linear-integration.md
§4.4, §7.3): a daemon may now pull a fresh workspace access token instead of
running out the ≤24 h snapshot its `agent.json` carries.

The handler mirrors `gitcred`'s seam exactly — core owns the frame family and
the scope check (a Linear integration of the frame's org, whose agent this
daemon currently serves via placement or a held duty), and the provider's
token service owns the work: single-flight refresh when the stored grant is
near expiry, durable persist of the rotated pair before the reply. Refusals
follow the frame module's vocabulary: SCOPE_DENIED for a foreign daemon, a
non-Linear integration, or a control plane with no Linear app; a terminal
LEASE_DENIED for a grant only an operator reconnect can repair; a retryable
INTERNAL for an unreachable Linear, which is never proof the grant is dead.

`LinearTokenService.accessToken` now reports whether its answer is newer than
the pair the caller read. A rotated grant rides the shared integration
converge — the same re-push a visibility flip takes, whose http-bot arm
re-syncs the workspace bot — so every member's `agent.json` converges, not
just the requester's. Best-effort and after the reply: a grant that already
landed must not fail on a fan-out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cp): compare-and-set the Linear refresh write instead of upserting it

`refreshOnce` read the row and called Linear before it wrote, so the world
could move inside that round trip and the write would flatten it. Two ways
that bites: a disconnect's locked revoke+remove completes mid-refresh and the
delayed upsert recreates the row, handing a live grant to a workspace whose
install is gone; or a reconnect stores a new grant and the older rotation
overwrites it.

The refresh now writes through `LinearTokenStore.rotate` — an UPDATE, never an
upsert, matching only while the row still carries the `updatedAt` the flight
read, the same CAS token `LinearIdentitySection.claim` guards with. An UPDATE
cannot create a row, so resurrection is impossible whether or not the remover
took the lock; a moved `updatedAt` means the rotation matches nothing instead
of clobbering a fresher pair. The caller adopts what it finds instead of
retrying into it: gone, so `not_connected` and a terminal LEASE_DENIED at the
broker; superseded, so the newer grant is served. That is deliberately the arm
a rejected rotate already took — a lost CAS and a spent refresh token are one
event noticed at two moments.

Chose the guarded write over holding the identity's critical section across
the upstream call. The refresh is on a daemon-driven path that fans out with
the fleet, unlike the sweeper's one bounded background loop, so holding would
pin a pool connection per refreshing workspace across a call bounded only by
the API timeout — on the pool the BFF and the daemon socket share. A slow
provider would become control-plane-wide connection starvation, which is worse
than the bug. The narrow write also needs no upstream I/O under the lock at

feat(daemon): compose the Linear platform end to end (#1680)

* feat(daemon): compose the Linear platform into the daemon

Lands the enumerated composition set the Linear design leaves for the daemon
(linear-integration.md §9.4), so an advertised platform is also a served one.

- daemon.ts registrations, no new branches: a `linear` connection map plus its
  bind lambda, `reconcileLinearConnections` at both shared reconcile call sites,
  one turn-output surface, one command-chrome surface, and one platformAction
  decoder for the stop payload.
- Message strategy (§8): the delivered message plus the round-tripped adapter
  bag become the prompt — a daemon-authored trusted header, the member's text
  verbatim, workspace-admin guidance, and the issue body and earlier comments
  inside the shared untrusted fence with a truncation note.
- The issue-less surface (§4.5) answers once and starts no turn, after the
  durable inbox admits the delivery.
- The pre-spawn acknowledgement (§10.1) posts at admission and only on the
  first one, so replayed and concurrent deliveries of the same message id
  collapse onto a single feed row; `none` mode stays silent.
- Stop (§5.1) interrupts the addressed session and settles it with a response.

The drift test's composition exemption is gone: the registries now agree by
plain equality.

* fix(daemon): settle and deduplicate a Linear turn on every path

Four review findings on the Linear composition, all in the ingress/turn seam.

The acknowledgement deduped on the ordinary durable-inbox row, but that row is a
replay queue for work IN FLIGHT: core deletes it the moment the turn reaches a
terminal state. Linear's redelivery ladder is 1 min / 1 h / 6 h, so every
redelivery that matters arrives after the row is gone — re-acking an append-only
feed and re-running the whole turn. It reproduces deterministically by
redelivering once the turn has settled; CI hit it because the first turn had
finished between the two deliveries and the local run's had not. A born-completed
inbox row under its own id namespace is now the record that outlives the turn,
`INSERT OR IGNORE` is the CAS that keeps concurrent deliveries to one winner, and
a retention rule ages it out — nothing drained such a row before.

Admission is `requireDurable` for Linear now: the acknowledgement's whole dedup
argument is that durable row, so a swallowed write would let a redelivery
double-post. Refusing the delivery is the correct trade — the relay retries.

Turn FAILURE reached the feed on neither path. A warm failure enqueued a
Slack-shaped action the Linear applier has no arm for, and a cold one (a failed
spawn or handshake, before any turn record exists) has no reply transport at all
— so the settling `error` that moves the session out of `active` never posted and
the session looked busy forever. Warm failures now route through the converger's
own failure rule; cold ones through a registered per-platform failure sink, so
core still branches on no platform name.

The command seat resolves a Linear connection too. It was excluded with the reply
path, which left a registered command-chrome surface nothing could reach:
`/status` was consumed in silence, and so was `!resume` — the only way out of an
open loop-guard circuit.

* fix(daemon): resolve the Linear token broker at call time, not at construction

On an ordinary startup the platform connections open before the control-plane
socket connects, so the client captured when the Linear connection was built was
`undefined` for that connection's whole life. Every renewal then failed once the
snapshot token aged out — a break that only shows up a day after deploy, on a
connection that looked healthy the whole time.

Read the current client inside the token thunk instead.

* fix(daemon): admit a Linear delivery and its receipt as one, and lease its transport

Three things the delivery receipt still got wrong, and the CI flake in the test
that was meant to prove it.

The BARRIER. The redelivery tests waited for the durable row to be 1 and then 0.
That row exists only between admission and teardown, so a fast turn is inserted
and removed between two polls and the wait for 1 times out — which is what CI
saw. `dispatch` settles its promise only after `removeInbox`, on both the success
and the failure path, so holding that promise is a signal that cannot be missed;
the tests hold it instead of sampling anything. The acknowledgement is
fire-and-forget and no promise covers it, so it is drained through the store's
own mutex rather than slept past. No test polls for a transient state now.

The RECEIPT was written after admission and outside its fence, so a receipt the
store refused still let the turn run — and once the ordinary row was removed at
settlement, the next redelivery ran the same turn again. It is now minted inside
dispatch's admission fence: the hook is awaited and a rejection refuses the
delivery, the relay ACK waits for that outcome instead of outrunning it, and the
refusal reaches the provider so its retry ladder recovers. The fast admission
branch now also drops the durable row when admission throws, as the queued branch
already did — otherwise a refused delivery would still replay at startup.

The TRANSPORT was held by nothing. Linear's output does not go through
`replyConn`, so no lease existed and the prune pass could stop the client
mid-turn, losing the settling activity that ends the session. A turn now captures
its egress port at turn start and holds a lease on it, so reconciliation drains
before stopping; capturing also means an integration unbound mid-turn still
settles through the transport the turn already holds.

* fix(daemon): commit a delivery and its receipt atomically, and lease one transport

Two races left in the Linear composition, both from doing one thing twice.

The RECEIPT was a second store write after the admission row. A crash between
them left an ordinary row that replays at startup with no receipt ever minted,
so the next redelivery was unrecognizable and ran the same turn again; and a
receipt-CAS loser only fell silent while its admitted turn still ran.

Both rows are now one transaction. `appendInboxWithReceipt` inserts the receipt
first as the CAS and the admission row second, so an admission row cannot exist
without its receipt and a failure leaves neither. Losing the CAS makes the
delivery a plain duplicate: nothing is admitted, no turn starts, no activity is
written. `dispatch` carries this as a generic `receiptId` option — a provider
whose redelivery ladder outlives the turn needs it, and the mechanism is not
Linear's.

The EGRESS TRANSPORT was resolved twice — once to take the lease, once when the
output surface seeded its turn state — with session opening in between, so a
rebind landing in that window left the lease on one client and the output on
another. One lookup now yields the connection, takes the lease, and is handed to
the surface already resolved; the turn-output context carries the transport
rather than an id to look up again.

feat(cp): gate pool claims on the member's platform capabilities (#1686)

* feat(cp): gate duty claims on the member's advertised platforms

A pool member claimed vacant duty groups with no regard for the platforms it
can actually run. A daemon resolves an integration's config through its own
platform-module registry and fails closed on an id it has no module for, so a
member of an older image that won an agent whose integrations name a newly
added platform took that surface dark with no error anywhere, until the group
moved again. Every new platform's rollout window has that hole.

Both claim paths now also require the group's active-integration platform set
to be a subset of the member's advertised capabilities.platforms, stated once
as SQL next to the placement predicate and shared by claimVacant and the
activation rendezvous. Fail-closed on both sides: a member whose capabilities
carry no platform list advertises nothing, and a group no live member can serve
stays vacant rather than being served by a member that would drop it. An agent
with no active integration requires nothing, so webchat, cron and A2A
singletons never meet the gate. Deliberately kept out of the placement fence,
where the same read failing closed would tear down live service.

The pool gauges follow in lockstep, through the very same predicate: a vacancy
no live member of the set can serve leaves the claimable demand count and gets
a series of its own, exactly as an oversized group does, because scaling the
pool cannot clear it. A set with no live member proves no gap and keeps its
vacancies as ordinary demand. A member that left claim budget unspent logs one
line per passed-over agent naming the platform ids it lacks, since a capability
refusal is otherwise invisible: the claim simply matches fewer rows.

The install-time gate now reads the same pure predicate, so install and claim
cannot disagree about what "this daemon can run that platform" means.

* fix(cp): scope the rendezvous capability gate to what it grants

The activation rendezvous checked the capability predicate at its entry, against
the TRIGGERED agent only, and a duty group is a connected component: a shared
socket bot puts several agents in one. So a member advertising slack but not
linear passed the check for a slack agent and then took the whole vacant group
containing a peer that needs linear, going dark on exactly the surface the
vacancy claim now refuses. The early return also answered before the group was
read, so a capability refusal for a group under a live lease named no incumbent,
costing the relay the one-hop re-route the rendezvous exists to provide.

The gate now rides the statements that grant, each at that statement's own scope.
The mint path creates a singleton for the triggered agent, so it carries the
agent-wise predicate in the INSERT's own WHERE beside the rollout barrier; the
take path takes an existing group, so it carries the group-wise predicate the
vacancy claim already uses, in the UPDATE's WHERE. The entry keeps the placement
predicate alone, so a refusal now falls through the ordinary branches: a
live-held group answers with its incumbent, and a refused take reports the row as
it stands, exactly as a rollout-barrier refusal already does. An idempotent
re-claim by the member already holding the lease takes nothing and stays ungated,
for the same reason the placement fence is.

Three cases cover it: a group holding a peer the member cannot serve is refused
for a triggered agent it can; that same member still mints the singleton it can
serve; and a capability-refused rendezvous for a live-held group still names the
holder. The pool gauges and their parity claims are untouched.

* fix(cp): name only a live holder when the rendezvous refuses

Vacating keeps the `holder` column — only `expiresAt` decides — so the terminal
read of `claimAgentHome` handed that column back verbatim, and a capability-refused
take of a lapsed group answered with the member that used to serve it. The relay
treats a named holder as the sole re-route target, and the ingress behind a
rendezvous was acknowledged upstream before it got here: pointing that one hop at
a disconnected former holder is a drop, not a retry. The rollout barrier's own
refusal had the same shape.

The refusal now names a holder only when the row still carries an unexpired lease,
read through `liveHold` — one predicate, used by the branch that decides whether
the group is taken at all and by the terminal read that reports it, so the two
cannot drift. It is the row-wise complement of the vacancy predicate every claim
statement carries, and both fail closed at the boundary: a claim refuses rather
than double-serving, a refusal reports no incumbent rather than a stale one.
`granted` is unchanged in meaning, now stated as "live and mine". `groupId` and
`term` still ride along — the group WAS read, which is exactly what the contract
distinguishes from an entry-level refusal.

Covered by a vacancy whose stale holder column still names the previous member:
the capability-refused claim answers `holder: null`, and the member that carries
the platform takes the same group. The live-incumbent case still names it.

docs(linear): the workspace is the channel (#1690)

* docs(linear): the connected workspace is the channel, not the issue

Map a connected Linear workspace onto ONE channel: channel = the Linear
organizationId, thread = the AgentSession UUID, and the issue demoted to
display metadata (session title, threadUrl, the prompt's trusted header).
Issue-as-channel judged an issue by its shape (a container of threads) rather
than by what a channel is for here — the configuration mount point a dispatch
default and gating hang on. Issues are unbounded, born with their traffic, and
never configured; every configuration fact belongs to the workspace.

Consequences recorded across the affected sections: the workspace's dispatch
default is the ordinary per-conversation owner the routing ladder already
resolves first, so the bot-level persisted preferred default this design asked
core for is withdrawn and the compile's earliest-member derivation survives
only as the pre-first-report backstop; the daemon reports the workspace eagerly
as its single observed conversation; rows are born 'mention' for every member,
private agents included, because integration and conversation granularity
coincide and linking is the consent act, which leaves Linear with no trigger
control and no Off state (muting is unlinking); the connect flow loses its
default-agent step and starts from an agent's integrations page; and the
console splits unlink-self (the agent's Linear card) from whole-workspace
Disconnect (the org-level Bots card). Dedup keys are unchanged, being
content-derived. Section 15 carries the dated decision record.

* docs(linear): the workspace owner rides the default rung, and the CP seeds its row

Three corrections from review, all in the workspace-is-the-channel model:

Routing. The conversation row is the storage and console carrier of the
dispatch default, not a route. Compiling its owner to a channel-scoped route
would put it on the ladder's FIRST rung, ahead of thread continuity and the
unscoped keyword slug — shadowing @<agent-name> on every mention and dragging
bound sessions onto whoever the row currently names. The compile maps the owner
onto the group's defaultAgentId, the addressed-gated last rung, and emits no
channel-scoped route; the resulting order is now stated as a table (named
create to the keyword slug, bound follow-up to thread continuity, bare create
to the row's owner, pre-row backstop to the earliest non-gated member).

Seeding. The row is written by the CP synchronously in the install paths — the
connect tail and each add-member — seeded 'mention' and published by the
syncBot those paths already end in. The daemon's conversation report is demoted
to a name refresh and missing-row backstop: seeding a default from a live
daemon leaves it absent in exactly the window a bare delegation arrives in.

Naming. channelName is the workspace name, period: it is the display slot of
the channel coordinate, so an issue-derived name would relabel every sibling
session on each event. Issue identity lives in the session title and threadUrl.

Both new behaviors read one manifest axis, soleConversation, rather than a
Linear branch in core; section 15 and the test lists follow.

* docs(linear): record the gated-member arm of the sole-conversation axis

The axis carries three co-varying reads, not two. The third is gating itself: a
restricted member of a bot whose install names the only conversation it can
reach is not conversation-gated, because linking the agent already was the
per-conversation consent the gate waits for. It is one predicate,
gatesNewConversations(platform, agent), computed where the compile builds its
placed set, so the member's keyword rung, its eligibility to hold the default,
its continuity gating, and its relay attribution move together instead of being
patched fence by fence — and de-gating is per bot, so the same agent stays
gated everywhere else.

Section 6.2 also records the alternative that was rejected: scoped keyword
routes for gated members put name selection above thread affinity, so a
follow-up naming another member would hijack a bound session — the rung-order
bug the owner route has, through a different door.

The seed read now names its seats, since the point of it is that they share one
predicate: the compile's ensureConversationOwners, the read-side GET
/integrations projection, the channels-report handler, and the install paths.
Section 15 and the CP integration test list follow.

* docs(linear): the trigger-write surfaces refuse what nothing reads

Fourth read of the sole-conversation axis, and the one that closes the loop: a
setting nobody reads must be a setting nobody can write. The generic
per-conversation PATCH and the setChannelTrigger tool reject a trigger write on
such a platform and name the unlink path instead, while the owner change rides
the same route untouched — that being the one setting the conversation
actually has. Without the guard the install-time seed and the vacuous gating
read stay quietly editable back into the state they exist to prevent. Slack and
every other platform keep both writes.

Recorded in the section 9.1 axis description (three reads to four), section
4.3's no-trigger bullet, the section 15 record, and the CP integration test
list: trigger write refused, owner change succeeds, Slack untouched.

feat(daemon): add OpenClaw as a curated ACP runtime with an external-execution sandbox exception (#1678)

* feat(daemon): add OpenClaw as a curated ACP runtime with an external-execution sandbox exception

OpenClaw 2.0's `openclaw acp` is a thin stdio bridge: execution lives in the
machine-local OpenClaw Gateway (ws://127.0.0.1:18789 by default), which owns
model credentials and sessions; the bridge reads the gateway address + token
from ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json. The curated entry gates availability on the
real `openclaw` binary plus an initialized state root (~/.openclaw, honoring
$OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR / $OPENCLAW_HOME / $OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH), seeds only
openclaw.json + .env into the private probe HOME, pins $OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR
there, and redacts the seeded gateway token from probe diagnostics. The
gateway connection env (OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL/_TOKEN/_PASSWORD) is treated as
provider credentials: inherited by launches and allowlisted for probes.

Sandboxing the bridge would contain nothing — the Gateway executes — while
SRT's --unshare-net severs the loopback dial the bridge exists for. So
RuntimeDef gains `externalExecution`: such a runtime launches like any
unsandboxed runtime, an agent's optional sandbox request is downgraded with a
warning, and security.requireSandbox refuses the launch and its admission
probe, keeping the runtime unadvertised on hosts that demand confinement.
Model-catalog enumeration (sandbox-only by design) skips it; the probe-derived
model list stands. skills@1.5.21 audits `openclaw` as a native identity, the
local-Gateway config model needs no account-app switch, and the console gets
the curated display mark.
