feat(linear): the workspace is the channel (#1692)

* feat(linear)!: the workspace is the channel

Re-base Linear's conversation coordinates on the connected workspace. `channel` is
now the Linear organizationId, `thread` stays the AgentSession UUID, and the issue
becomes display metadata only — it rides `threadUrl` and the §8 trusted prompt
header, never the coordinates. The issue-less fallback (channel = session UUID) is
gone: the channel is always the workspace, and an issue-less session is just a
thread whose bag carries no issue metadata, which is what the unsupported-surface
answer now keys off.

A connected workspace behaves like one Slack channel with several agents on it. The
mechanism is one new manifest axis, `soleConversation` (linear: true, fail-closed
false), declaring that an install NAMES the single conversation it can reach. Two
pre-dispatch reads follow:

1. Route projection. The workspace conversation row's owner maps to the group's
   `defaultAgentId` — the ladder's last, addressed-gated rung — and the HTTP-bot
   compile emits NO channel-scoped route for it. A scoped `mention` rule would be
   the FIRST rung, and every Linear event marks the app as mentioned, so it would
   shadow `@<agent-name>` selection and hijack a bound session's follow-ups.
   Precedence is therefore: named create wins on the keyword rung, a bound
   follow-up wins on thread affinity, a bare create falls to the row's owner.

2. Install-time seed. The connect tail and each add-member synchronously write the
   `(integrationId, organizationId)` conversation row — owner = the linking agent
   on the first write — born `mention`, published by the `syncBot` those paths
   already end in. Link-is-consent overrides the restricted-agent `off` seed, so
   there is no window where an agent is linked but unroutable and no wire-contract
   change. The daemon's eager report is demoted to a name refresh and a backstop:
   the report carries no trigger and the snapshot write preserves the stored one,
   so it cannot fight the seed.

Private agents: rather than patch each gated fence, the compile computes a member's
gated flag from `gatesNewConversations(bot.platform, agent)` at the single seat that
builds the placed set. On a `soleConversation` bot a restricted member is simply not
conversation-gated — the gate's purpose is already met by linking — so it keeps its
keyword rung, can hold the default, and satisfies the scoped-route requirement that
thread continuity and `agentTarget` impose. This was preferred over emitting
channel-scoped keyword routes per member, which would have placed name selection at
the channel rung ABOVE thread affinity and let a follow-up naming another member
hijack a bound session. The de-gating is per bot and derived from that bot's
platform, so the same agent stays fully gated on an ordinary bot and its name routes
nowhere else.

Also: the stop decoder's local session lookup is channel-scoped again now that a
channel coordinate exists, and the observed-conversation seam is typed by a
platform-neutral `ObservedChat` rather than the Telegram-named record.

Nothing is released, so this changes semantics directly with no compatibility shim.

* feat(cp): refuse a trigger write where the install is the conversation

The generic `PATCH /integrations/:id/channels/:channelId` still accepted `off`/`any`
for a workspace whose platform declares `soleConversation`, and `updateConversation`
copies the value to every sibling row and publishes it through the mute fences — so
a caller could silence a workspace without unlinking, contradicting the axis's own
"the conversation's trigger IS the link".

The write is now refused with a 400 naming the unlink path, read through
`allowsTriggerControl(platform)` — a sibling of `gatesNewConversations` on the same
manifest axis. Refuse rather than canonicalize to 'mention': a silent rewrite would
hide a caller bug, and the caller that asked for Off wanted something the platform
cannot express. An `agentId` (owner) write on the same conversation is untouched —
that is WHICH member answers, not whether the workspace answers at all.

One enforcement seat covers both surfaces: the `setChannelTrigger` MCP tool proxies
to this route, so the gate applies there too; its description now states the rule so
the tool's model-facing contract does not promise a write the route refuses.

The other trigger writers were checked and need no gate: `linkedDmReconcile` and the

fix(daemon): carve back the owner checkout's Git metadata for session worktrees (#1695)

An isolated session runs in its own worktree, but that worktree's index — and
every ref and object its commits write — live in the OWNER checkout's `.git`,
which sits outside the cwd. No carve-back covered it, so a confined runtime
could not run a single Git write in its own worktree: `git add` died with
"Read-only file system" on the index lock, and even `git status` failed. The
same asymmetry hid it during review — a non-isolated session's cwd IS the
checkout, so its `.git` was writable by accident of containment.

Derive the Git metadata roots from the trusted agent layout (the primary
checkout plus every materialized secondary checkout), add them to the sandbox
write set, and close `hooks` and `config` inside them explicitly: the sandbox
runtime's own mandatory protection is derived from the cwd, where an isolated
worktree's `.git` is a link file rather than a directory.

The inner Codex profile carve-back had the same blind spot for the same reason
and now shares those roots. Its `.git`-is-a-directory test could never pass for
a worktree cwd, so the list it built was always empty there.

fix(daemon): open Git metadata to an unsandboxed Codex launch, hooks and config excepted (#1703)

Codex's `:workspace` permission profile makes each session's own cwd writable and
protects `.git`. A session with `workspaceIsolation: session` runs in its own
worktree, whose `.git` is a link file — the index it writes, and every ref and
object its commits create, live in the owner checkout's `.git`, outside that cwd.
So every Git write failed while reads kept working.

The sandboxed path already reopened those directories. The unsandboxed path did
not: it applied the permission profile with `protectedRoots` only, and only when
the agent-scoped credential channel happened to be enabled.

Carve the same metadata directories back there, computed from the agent root and
the daemon-named primary checkout rather than from the cwd, which is the primary
checkout for every session the host serves. Two differences from the sandboxed
path, both because no outer boundary exists to fall back on:

- The profile itself denies `hooks` and `config` inside each root it opens. On
  the sandboxed path the outer boundary closes them; here the profile is the only
  confinement, so a bare write grant would let model-authored code plant a hook
  that a later host-side Git invocation executes. The deny is emitted beside the
  write on the agent profile alone, leaving `agent-full-access` — the deliberately
  unconfined mode — unchanged.
- A checkout that resolves outside the agent root is skipped rather than refused.
  Refusing would break a launch the operator already chose to run unconfined.

The trigger widens from "has the credential channel" to "is Codex", because the
bug does not depend on that channel. Nothing changes for a launch with no Git
metadata to reopen: the profile builder still returns nothing to apply.

Verified against the vendored Codex with its `codex sandbox` subcommand, which
runs a real command under the same OS sandbox a session gets. With a plain
`:workspace` profile, reading the owner checkout's `.git` succeeds while writing
its worktree index fails; feeding it the config this change generates, the index
and refs become writable while planting a hook and rewriting `config` are both
denied. The probe was an ordinary exec'd binary, not an editing tool, so the
filesystem table demonstrably governs the exec sandbox and not just file edits.
That run was on macOS/seatbelt; the Linux backend was not exercised.

* feat(console): approval bell fed by a revived agent/activity frame (#1704)

unread "Approval needed" item and flips it to a read "Approval resolved"
item when the wait ends. The console had no cross-agent pending signal, so
this revives the protocol's dead `agent/activity` frame end to end.

- protocol: `agent/activity` carries the outward `sessionId`; `launchId`
  is optional. Only `awaiting_permission`/`idle` are emitted.
- daemon: the permission coordinator emits `awaiting_permission` when the
  first answerable request parks on a session and `idle` when the last one
  settles, across editor-path permissions, elicitations, and chat cards.
  Live waits are re-asserted on every (re)connect; emits are serialized.
- control-plane: handles the frame, persists `SessionMeta.activityState`
  fenced to the reporting agent, publishes a `session-state` SSE event,
  and resets a daemon's waits on disconnect and on the session `end`
  milestone. `GET /sessions` gains an `activityState` filter and the
  list DTO carries the field.

  reconnect (no poll), filtered to agents with `canEdit`. New
  client-local `approval` category: pending ⇒ unread + toast, deep-link
  to the session page; resolved ⇒ read, no decider name or decision.
  A decision made in the current tab flips its item to read at once.

Design recorded in slack-approval-dm.md §7, rewritten in place.

Closes #1704

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): order a reconnect's approval replay behind the disconnect clear

The old socket's clear of a daemon's approval waits ran unfenced after the
registry guard, so a fast reconnect could replay `awaiting_permission` and
then have the late clear commit `idle` over it, with nothing left to heal
the row. The clear is now queued per daemon in the connection registry and
the `agent/activity` handler waits for that queue before writing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): one per-daemon tail for every approval-state write

Two ordering gaps remained after the disconnect-clear barrier: an accepted
`agent/activity` write could still be in the database while its own
connection's close clear ran, and a daemon's reconnect replay could reach
the CP before the session's `start` snapshot had drained from the outbox,
so the wait was dropped for lack of a row and never re-asserted.

The registry's chain is now a general per-daemon tail: the handler's
persist, the close clear, and a new silent clear on `register` all run on
it in arrival order, so a connection's last mutation is always its clear
and a superseded socket's leftovers cannot outlive it. The daemon replays
its live waits only once the session-metadata outbox drain has settled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): re-assert an approval wait when its session's snapshot is acknowledged

The reconnect replay ran after the outbox drain resolved, but the drain
also resolves on its ordinary retry paths with rows still pending, so a
wait could reach the CP before the session row existed, be dropped for
lack of one, and never be re-asserted once the retry landed the row.

The outbox now tells its host when the CP acknowledges a snapshot, and the
daemon re-emits `awaiting_permission` for a live wait on that session. The
acknowledgement is the reliable trigger, whichever attempt lands it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): re-check a wait is still live right before emitting awaiting_permission

The ack-time re-assert snapshotted the live waits, awaited the outward id
lookup, then emitted. A request that settled during that await had already
queued its `idle` ahead, so the stale `awaiting_permission` landed last and
left the bell falsely pending. Every `awaiting_permission` emit now asks the
coordinator whether the wait is still live after the lookup, with no await
before the send.

feat(slack): let an agent search the workspace's public channels (#1646)

Message search is the one Slack capability a bot cannot reach the ordinary way:
`search.messages` accepts user tokens only. The bot path is the Real-time Search
API, `assistant.search.context`, which brings a credential, a data policy, and a
reach that all had to be measured rather than read off the docs — the docs are
wrong in both directions.

**The credential.** A bot search is refused without the ephemeral `action_token`
Slack attaches to events where the app is addressed (verified: with scopes and no
token, `invalid_action_token`). It is a credential, and the normalized message it
arrives on is persisted to the durable inbox and replayed after a restart — so it
never goes there. Ingress lifts it into the platform adapter's memory, bounded and
TTL'd; core carries only the triggering message's id, and the adapter resolves id
→ credential internally. On the HTTP transport the relay saw the event, so it
forwards the token BESIDE `rd/msg`'s payload, never inside it, for the reason §8.2
already keeps the `trusted*` assertions out of it plus the persistence one.

**The reach: public channels only.** Slack's scope reference calls
`search:read.private` / `.im` / `.mpim` user-token only. A workspace grants all
three to a BOT — and they return nothing. With the bot a MEMBER of a private
channel, no combination of `channel_types` (including omitting it) surfaced a
message posted there, and a DM's text matched nothing at all while a semantically
similar public message matched twenty. Anthropic's own Slack app makes the same
split: bot search is public, private and DM search is a per-user grant. So the
manifest asks for `search:read.public` / `.files` / `.users` and no more, arriving
WITH the tool that calls them, which is the rule `SLACK_BOT_SCOPES` states.

Neither `channel_types` nor `context_channel_id` narrows anything — asking for
`private_channel` returns public content, and the same query with and without a
context channel returned identical results. Nothing is described to the agent as
a filter, and an earlier revision that bound the tool to its own conversation was
reverted: a bot cannot search the private channel or DM it is talking in, so
binding returned an empty list wherever an agent is actually addressed.

**The results.** Slack forbids storing what this API returns, while every other
tool result is ordinary transcript material — so the result is stamped and
`session/ephemeral-results.ts` redacts any body carrying the marker before the
transcript row is written, keeping the call, status and the agent's own query.
Detection is a substring scan of the serialized body rather than a field path,
because a runtime may echo a result in `rawOutput`, in `content` blocks, or nested
in either. The copy that survives in the ACP runtime's own history is accepted and
argued in the design doc rather than papered over, with the fallback scoped.

Three limits are stated to the agent because they are structural: public channels
only including not the current conversation; hits may sit in channels the bot
cannot read; and only a turn some human addressed can search, which excludes cron,
agent-to-agent wakes, and channel messages that did not name the app.

fix(daemon): keep Git's config readable and open the worktrees subtree in the Codex profile (#1715)

Two defects in the Codex agent profile, both settled against the vendored Codex on
Linux with `codex sandbox` driving a real session worktree.

command without reading its config, so every Codex session with a Git workspace lost

fix(daemon): stop a lost start gate from failing a finished skill helper (#1739)

The confined workspace mutation helper is handed a "GO" byte on stdin only
after `registerHelper` durably records its process group, but that gate is
real only inside the sandbox wrapper: on a host without one the helper is
launched directly, never reads stdin, and starts work immediately.
`registerHelper` runs a SQLite immediate transaction that retries a busy
database every 50 ms, so on a loaded machine the helper can finish and exit
before the write happens and the gate lands on a closed pipe. The resulting
EPIPE was recorded as the run's failure, so a mutation that exited 0 with a
valid receipt came back as "confined skill workspace mutation was refused" —
one unit-test flake seen so far, one skill install refused for nothing on a
busy daemon.

The helper's own exit status and output are the verdict, so a failed gate
write is not itself a failure: a wrapper that never got its byte still exits
non-zero or hands back no receipt. Killing on that error was wrong twice
over, since signalling an already-exited group answers EPERM, which the kill
path then recorded as the failure instead; `close` already kills whatever
survives.

writers of the row are not equally authoritative, and the write did not say so:
an absent icon meant "leave the stored one" for both, so a team whose icon was
removed in Linear kept the old one, while the reconciler's comparison saw the
mismatch and re-ran the same no-op write on every tick.

`ReportedChannel.icon` / `.color` are now a tri-state. Absent is "unknown" and
still leaves a drawn row standing — a daemon lookup that resolved nothing may
not blank one — and an explicit `null` is "the platform says it has none" and
clears it. Only a writer that ENUMERATES the platform's own state may send

`IntegrationChannel` has no null. `upsertConversation` keys the update on
`!== undefined` rather than truthiness so the clear reaches the column.

is one component of emoji syntax, not the whole of it: a flag is a PAIR of
regional indicators and a keycap is a digit plus U+20E3, and neither carries the
property, so both fell through to the initial — and a code-point read of either
draws half of it. The mark now segments with `Intl.Segmenter` and tests the
whole grapheme against `RGI_Emoji`, with an explicit union (pictographic base,
regional-indicator pair, keycap sequence) for an engine without `v`-mode
sequence properties. The team's initial is a grapheme for the same reason.

tri-state at the repository against a real database, and a flag, a keycap, a
modifier, a ZWJ sequence and a Linear icon name at the mark — plus the fallback

A delivery-assembled turn — a Linear delegation, a GitHub or GitLab event — stores the whole
prompt as the transcript row's `text`, which is also what the console shows. Splitting the
two needs a durable second seat for what the model read and for the facts a formatter can
render, and this change adds it without changing anything visible yet.

- protocol: `UserTurnBody` — an optional `prompt` (the model text when it differs from the
  row's text) plus `LinearTurnFacts` / `CodehostTurnFacts` — rides `SessionMessage.body` on
  a text row, next to the tool and plan bodies.
- daemon: `NormalizedMessage.turnBody`; the transcript ingest, the observer and the coalesce
  paths persist it as `body`, and it upgrades in place when an observer row won the insert;
  the session manager prompts from `turnBody.prompt ?? text`; replay renders the persisted
  prompt through `transcriptPromptText`, fail-closed like the quote sidecar; the review
  orchestrator and the review batch keep the prompt in step when they rewrite the turn.
- hook and Linear strategies fill the body: today `prompt === text`, so the model reads
  exactly what it did before and the console changes nothing. The session reader carries a
  text row's body inline, dropping only an oversized prompt.

The next step swaps the row's text for the member's words and lets the console format the
facts behind a "more" fold.

feat(web): label session isolation by its effective boundary, not the stored flag (#1756)

* feat(web): label session isolation by its effective boundary, not the stored flag

`workspaceIsolation: 'session'` promises each session its own directory, but
how that directory is made depends on whether an OS boundary encloses the
runtime (git-workspace-model.md §11): a linked worktree when nothing does, a
per-session clone when something does. The console called it a "worktree"
either way, which is wrong for a sandboxed agent and for every managed-pool
one — a pool runtime is enclosed by its own pod and advertises no `sandbox`
capability at all, so the stored flag says "no sandbox" exactly where the
boundary is strongest.

`lib/session-isolation.ts` is now the one place that decides:
`sessionIsolationLabel({ pool, runInSandbox, sandboxSupported, sandboxRequired })`
returns "Worktree" only when nothing encloses the runtime and "Session
isolation" otherwise, folding in the same
`sandboxRequired || (sandboxSupported && runInSandbox)` the agent modals
already gate their toggle on. `agentSessionIsolationLabel(agent)` is the
form for an agent the console already holds, whose sandbox triple the control
plane projected against the daemon it is placed on.

The surfaces that NAME the mode take it from there: the workspace form's
toggle, the checkout picker's heading, counter, loading and empty states, and
the composer chips on Home and session detail.

Diagnostic copy that merely refers to the session's own directory cannot see
the boundary from where it stands, so it drops the mechanism and says
"checkout" — the file viewer, the files and git panels, and the git-write
failures. Sentences that assert something true only of a linked worktree (a
detached HEAD, a `.git` shared with the primary) are left alone: they
describe the unconfined tier's real behavior and change with the runtime
work, not with a label.

Verified at the unit and component level: the helper's three cases are
covered, and swapping its two labels turns every one of them red.

feat(daemon): launch managed ACP adapters from a daemon-owned tree, not npx into the agent HOME (#1757)

* feat(daemon): launch managed ACP adapters from a daemon-owned tree, not npx into the agent HOME

An ACP adapter is the runtime's PARENT process, outside every inner tool sandbox, so it must not
load its code from anywhere the model can write. `npx -y <spec>` did exactly that: it resolved the
dist-tag and installed into `$HOME/.npm/_npx/<hash>` under the agent's own private HOME, at every
host spawn. One session could plant code there that the next session's runtime parent executes.

The daemon now installs each adapter it supplies itself into `<root>/runtimes/<package>@<version>`
and launches the package's declared bin with node directly. The dist-tag is resolved once, at
daemon start (an upgrade restarts the process); a spawn never resolves anything. An unreachable
registry falls back to the newest tree already installed, and with none the launch is refused with
an error naming the tree rather than silently falling back to npx.

Which launches move: every spec the daemon itself supplies (curated, ACP registry, managed) whose
command is `npx`. Explicit operator `config.runtimes` stays the final authority and is untouched,
and a pool member still resolves its packages inside its own sandbox pod.

Startup stays bounded by installing only the adapters this daemon's own agents run; a runtime
assigned after boot is installed once, before its first host start.

The outer sandbox denies the daemon root, so the tree is carved back read-only through the
runtime's trusted read roots. runtime-install-repair now repairs the store tree instead of an npx
tree under a HOME, and npm runs with the daemon's own HOME so the `.npmrc` it reads is the
operator's, still through the existing env allowlist.

feat(daemon): one ACP host per session for a confined self-hosted launch (#1758)

* feat(daemon): one ACP host per session for a confined self-hosted launch

git-workspace-model.md §11, PR 2 of the rollout: a self-hosted daemon whose
sandbox is effective now runs one ACP host per (agent, session) instead of
multiplexing every session through the agent's host. Everything else keeps one
host per agent: a pool launch dials the agent's one sandbox pod, and an
unconfined launch never needed the split.

The predicate is exactly `!k8s && effectiveRunInSandbox(...)`, in
`Daemon.perSessionHost`. Hosts are keyed by a new `HostKey`
(`src/acp/host-key.ts`): the agent id for the shared host, agent id + logical
session key for a session-bound one, with `hostKeyDirName` giving the
filesystem leaf later PRs carry into launch preparation.

- Every per-host map (`hosts`, `hostStartedAt`, `hostRuntimeHome`, the start
  generation/abort/ready/stopping state) is keyed by `HostKey`; a new
  `hostLaunch` records each host's agent dir and launch cwd. `hostConfigFiles`
  stays per agent because the materialized files live in the agent dir and are
  shared by its hosts, so they now go with the agent's last host rather than the
  first one to stop.
- `stopHost(agentId)` stops every host of the agent (reconcile eviction, removal,
  drains, memory-connection fences all go through it); `stopHostByKey` is the
  per-host teardown that scopes lease/binding cleanup to the sessions the host
  served and removes the host's sandbox policy directory. A host bound to a
  session is also stopped when that session's worktree is removed, when
  retention deletes the row, and when the TTL closes it.
- Ordering: for a session-bound host the session workspace is prepared inside
  the cold-host gate (`startHostWithRetry`) before the spawn, and the host
  launches in that directory; `SessionManager` receives the bound cwd and opens
  the runtime session there, ahead of any other cwd source. A cwd the daemon
  already verified (GitHub exact-ref reviews) is handed to `hostFor` so the
  host launches in it rather than in a re-preparation.
- `writeSandboxSettings` writes `<agentDir>/.agentconnect/sandbox/<host>/settings.json`,
  one directory per host, so two hosts of one agent spawning together no longer
  overwrite each other's policy while the provider reads it; the directory is
  removed with the host. The symlink validation is unchanged. Dream hosts and
  key-server model-session hosts get their own leaf too.
- `session/load` after a restart re-spawns the resumed session's own host under
  the per-session key and loads it there.
- Capacity: gates keep counting agents; per-session hosts are bounded by session
  admission. The heartbeat's load now counts agents with a live host rather than
  hosts, so a confined agent with several sessions does not over-report.
- The idle reaper judges a session-bound host by its own session's activity,
  in-flight turn and background work.

Tests: per-session key + pre-spawn preparation + bound cwd; per-agent key when
unconfined and when the mechanism is absent; two concurrent sessions produce two
hosts and, at the launch layer, two policy files each anchored on its session
cwd as write root and Git safe directory; stopHost and a spawn-signature
reconcile stop every host; the policy directory goes with the host; resume after
a restart; and a k8s daemon keeps the shared host even with a mechanism forced
on. Both halves of the predicate were mutation-checked against these tests.

feat(sandbox): preinstall the browser an agent-browser turn needs (#1762)

* feat(sandbox): preinstall the browser an agent-browser turn needs

A browser turn in a pod started from nothing: the skill's `npm i -g agent-browser`
EACCESes as uid 10001, and the Chrome it then downloads cannot start, because the
image carries none of the 25 shared libraries `ldd chrome` asks for and
`agent-browser install` installs them with `sudo apt-get`, which the runtime user
has no way to run.

So the image now carries all three parts: the library closure (+32 MB standalone,
+18 MB here — libgtk-3-0 and xvfb are deliberately out, headless CDP was verified
end-to-end without them), the pinned CLI with the six foreign-platform native
binaries pruned (89 MB to 15 MB), and Chrome for Testing itself, version- and
sha256-pinned in its own download stage for the reasons gh's is.

AGENT_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH is the CLI's only browser-location hook, so it is
what makes the baked copy authoritative. `install` ignores it and downloads
anyway, and its skip cannot be seeded either — that is keyed on whatever version
Google's last-known-good feed names that day, so a pinned image goes stale within
a Chrome release. Hence a wrapper beside the gh one, answering a BARE install and
execing the real CLI for anything else.

Chrome costs +183 MB pulled and, unlike the 391 MB per workspace VOLUME it
replaces, one copy per node. Its modes come from the download stage: a `chmod -R`
in the runtime layer rewrites all 391 MB into a second layer.

feat(relay): a webhook caller can key deliveries into one session per subject (#1765)

A generic webhook hook could only choose between a fresh session per
delivery and one shared session for the whole hook, and the tempting
X-AC-Delivery-Key header cannot group deliveries: the daemon dedups on
(sessionKey, msgId) and both carry the delivery key, so a reused key is
absorbed as a redelivery rather than appended. External subjects — a
service-desk ticket and its comments — therefore had no way to
accumulate one session.

key) and the relay computes `<hookId>:subject:<key>` as the session
key, while msgId keeps the delivery key so idempotency is untouched. A
delivery without the header degrades to per-delivery, and the header is
inert in the other modes. The GitHub kind's perThread is exactly this
pattern minted relay-side; this hands it to generic callers.

Enum joins the wire schema (relay-cp), the CP DTO/ports vocabulary, and
the Postgres enum (additive ALTER TYPE migration). The console's
webhook create form gains a session-continuity select; docs decision
list and the General Webhook sessionMode section describe the new mode
and the affinity-vs-idempotency split.

feat(daemon): one sandbox pod per session on the pool — the host's pod is its own (§11) (#1766)

* feat(daemon): one sandbox pod per session on the pool — the host's pod is its own

git-workspace-model §11's pool row: an isolated session on a pool member is
the confined tier, so its host launches into a pod of its own instead of
dialling the agent's one pod. The `!this.k8s` stopgap in `perSessionHost` goes;
on the pool the session row's isolation keys the host (shared → the agent host
and pod, session → its own host and pod).

The k8s driver is re-keyed by a `SandboxSubject` — the agent id for the agent
pod, `<agentId>/<session leaf>` for a session pod, derived from the host key.
A session claim is `agent-<id>-<16 hex of the leaf>` (kept under 63 chars),
its pod labelled `agentconnect.md/agent` AND a separate
`agentconnect.md/session`, and the same labels ride the claim's metadata so a
member can list an agent's session claims. `SpawnRequest` carries the host
key; the shim binding registry, dialer, channel binder, loss watcher, tunnel
binder and lease gate are keyed by subject, so a session pod's suspension
never gates its siblings or the agent pod.

Storage: the session's clones and HOME live on the session pod's volume at
`<mount>/sessions/<leaf>/{workspace,repos,home}`, prepared by the same
blobless-clone path a confined self-hosted session uses; the agent pod keeps
the primary checkout, secondary roots and managed memory. The plane routes
every workspace path to the pod that owns it, and a session runtime holds the
agent pod as its companion for its life so memory, merge-when-ready and the
console's primary reads keep their reachability.

Lifetime: the claim lives as long as the session row — idle suspend per pod
keeps the volume, retention judges the clone on its own pod and deletes the
claim with the row, a replaced workspace retires every session pod, agent
removal deletes them all. Admission keeps counting agents.

* fix(daemon): the session-volume discard runs with the conversion, and a sleeping session pod stays addressable

Three review findings on the one-pod-per-session change.

Session volumes are no longer discarded when a workspace edit is activated.
That call precedes the acknowledgement and its sandbox-mode rollback is empty,
so a later rejection restored the previous definition after every session
claim -- clone and HOME with it -- had already been deleted, irreversibly. The
retirement moves onto the volume, into the conversion that empties the primary
checkout: it runs only once the marker no longer proves the workspace, spares
the leaf being prepared (whose own directory is emptied so it clones afresh),
and is fail-closed, so a retirement that raised leaves the marker unproven and
the next preparation retries it. An isolated session's preparation reaches the
agent pod's half for that conversion alone; with none due it still never
consults the primary checkout.

A workspace path now names its pod by the path itself rather than by the
live-launch registry. An idle-suspended session pod leaves that registry while
its claim and volume survive on purpose, so a console read of
`<mount>/sessions/<leaf>` was routed to the agent pod, where the directory does
not exist. The routed reads wake a sleeping session pod instead -- but only
beside a bound agent pod, since the console's wake is agent-scoped, and only
onto a claim the cluster already holds. `RoutedWorkspaceFs`/`RoutedWorkspaceFiles`
resolve their target asynchronously for it, and a git runner for a sleeping
session directory is deferred rather than withheld.

The session bind and its companion hold are settled together. With the
session's rejection propagating on its own, the launch's catch drained its
holds while the companion was still binding, and the retain it then took
belonged to no runtime and no exit callback: the agent pod stayed busy until
the process restarted. The companion still degrades rather than failing the
launch.

* fix(daemon): a read resumes the claim it observed, and keep-alive judges its own pod

Two consequences of the wake-on-read fix in the previous round.

A routed read that names a sleeping session pod checked `hasClaim` and then went
on to `ensureBoundChannel`, which is not atomic with it: retention, a workspace
conversion or an agent removal can delete the claim in between, and `ensureClaim`
would then make a fresh empty one — a console read resurrecting a session sandbox
whose row and volume are already retired, as a live agent's orphan. The wake is
now a resume-only driver operation (`resumeBoundChannel`) fenced on the uid the
router just observed: the same suspension, takeover and release fences as
`ensureSandbox`, then a READ of the claim that name holds, re-judged against the
object after the round trip. A claim that is gone or replaced refuses. The path
cannot create, so a read can lose a race with a retirement but never win one.

The keep-alive was still gated on `runsInSandbox(agentId)`, which this work made
true for any bound pod of the agent, so a bound agent pod carried a suspended
session's poll into `workspaceGit.status` and the deferred routed runner woke that
session's claim — a visible clean page undoing the idle sweep every 60 seconds.
The decision now names the pod this page's worktree lives on, resolved through the
same scope and routing rule the status read uses, and that pod is HELD across the
read (`holdIfBound` -> `K8sDriver.retainLaunched`) rather than only checked before
it: the idle gate reads its `busy` count synchronously, so the hold excludes the
sweep instead of racing it. `SandboxHolds` is now keyed by sandbox subject, and
each reason leases the pod it is about — the dirty tree its own, an armed merge
watcher the agent's, since that is the pod it runs in. The idle sweep asks for the
subject it is judging, so one dirty session no longer pins its siblings.

* fix(daemon): keep-alive judges the watcher's pod and the tree's pod independently

Review follow-up on the previous commit, which was a regression it introduced.
A page whose isolated session pod had gone to sleep returned early, so it skipped
`armedFor` and released this holder's lease on the AGENT pod — the pod an armed
merge-when-ready watcher actually runs in. The sweep could then take that pod
while the page was still visible, silently disarming the box the operator ticked.

The two facts are now judged independently, one pod each, under the same

fix(daemon): a bundle the checkout no longer holds is a first install, not a failed restore (#1772)

* fix(daemon): a bundle the checkout no longer holds is a first install, not a failed restore

The skill ledger lives in the daemon state directory and is keyed by workspace
realpath and inode, so it outlives the contents of the workspace it describes. A
session clone that is re-checked out in place keeps that key and loses the
bundles under it, and the ledger then planned the next installation as a
replacement of a prior set that is no longer on disk.

The reservation refused it with "owned skill disappeared during reservation",
and recovery answered that by restoring a prior it had never quarantined, so the
helper raised a bare ENOENT on the journal's own quarantine name. What reached
the log was "the prior executable set could not be restored", which named
neither the real failure nor the path that caused it.

An absent recorded bundle is not stale executable content: there is nothing to
quarantine and nothing foreign to protect, so its path is now planned as a first
install. Recovery drops a prior that is at neither of the two addresses it could
be found at, and drops the fingerprint with it so the next plan cannot skip the
reinstall. The atomic no-clobber mkdir inside the confined helper still makes the
replace decision, so a bundle that reappears is still refused.

Nothing that used to fail closed now succeeds. A prior that is present but
unowned is still refused, a quarantined prior that cannot be put back still
fails, and the trusted-receipt path used by the cluster coordinator proves every
receipt before this prune can see it. Two diagnostics improve with it: a restore
with an empty quarantine says so instead of surfacing an ENOENT, and the failure
that started a recovery is now named alongside the recovery's own.

Observed on a self-hosted daemon using per-session workspaces, where it cost
every code review its exact checkout.

* fix(daemon): a pruned recorded set must not carry the fingerprint that described it

fix(daemon): a confined host's temp dir is short enough for its SRT socket (#1770)

* fix(daemon): a confined host's temp dir is short enough for its SRT socket

Since #1763 gave a confined session its own runtime HOME, no sandboxed
session-isolated agent could start its ACP host at all: three attempts, each
"ACP connection closed", with "listen EINVAL: invalid argument" one line
earlier.

The provider set TMPDIR to <private HOME>/.tmp and SRT opens its multiplexer at
<TMPDIR>/srt-mux-<pid>-<n>.sock. That socket name plus its separator is 23
bytes, so TMPDIR has to fit in 84 of the 107 usable bytes Linux allows in
sun_path. The session tail /sessions/session-<24 hex>/home/.tmp is 52 of them by
itself, leaving 32 for the daemon root plus the agent name, which no realistic
install fits, so bind() returned EINVAL for every confined session host. The
managed pool never saw it: its mount is short enough that the same socket fits.

A host's temp directory is now one short leaf of the agent directory:

- The daemon composes <agentDir>/t/<8 hex of the host key>, creates it 0700 and
  passes it in the launch env. The provider uses that path and keeps its
  existing guard, that the temp root must be an explicit SRT write root, instead
  of recomputing it from HOME. A typical install lands around 82 bytes against
  the broken shape's 124.
- It is inside the agent dir like every other writable root, so sandboxBoundary
  keeps its rule unchanged and needs no exemption; the temp parent is resolved
  and required to be a real directory before anything is created under it.
- Short is not the same as bounded, and this is the honest cost of staying
  inside the agent dir: a deep enough daemon root plus a long agent name still
  overflows. The launch is now refused at preparation with the path, its byte
  count and the limit, rather than dying as an opaque EINVAL three ACP start
  attempts deep. That check covers the pre-existing <agentDir>/home/.tmp ceiling
  too, which an agent name of about 35 characters already crossed.
- It is dropped with the host's policy directory when the host stops, and a
  probe or model enumerator gets its temp dir inside the disposable scope its
  caller already deletes, so nothing accumulates per launch.
- Ownership is proven, never inferred from the name. `t` is short, not reserved:
  an agent's workspace.path resolves under the agent dir too, so an operator may
  already have data at exactly that path. The daemon writes a marker file when it
  creates the temp root, refuses to launch against one it did not create, and at
  boot removes only the <8 hex> leaves of a root carrying that marker — never the
  parent, and nothing at all under someone else's directory.

The audited offline skills helpers keep the private-HOME temp they have: their
HOME is already a short mkdtemp under the system temp root, so the same overflow
cannot reach them. A launch in a sandbox pod keeps its own temp dir too: the pod
supplies it, and this daemon must not name a path on a machine it is not on.

fix(daemon): one rule decides whether a session is confined (#1776)

* fix(daemon): one rule decides whether a session is confined

"Is this session confined?" was answered in three places by three rules that
disagreed the moment an agent's settings changed:

- the host key asked only whether a boundary was available, never whether the
  session was isolated;
- workspace preparation asked whether the session's directory was on disk;
- the launch asked whether the host key carried a session key.

So a sandboxed agent set to shared still got a per-session host, HOME and temp
dir, and turning sandboxing off left preparation on the clone tier while the
launch was on the worktree tier — every turn then died on the cwd containment
check, in a directory the launch half did not believe in.

There is now one rule, in WorkspaceManager.confinedSessionTier: the session's
own directory on disk is the record, and a session that has one keeps the
confined tier until it retires. A session that stands nowhere yet takes what a
session created now would get — isolation with a boundary around the runtime,
its own pod on a pool member and the effective OS sandbox otherwise. A session
counts as isolated when either the agent's standing setting or the session's own
isolation says so, which keeps a formal review isolated on an agent that
defaults to shared and keeps a from-scratch agent's setting meaningful, since
its rows always report shared. The host key, preparation, the review stand-in,
the launch HOME and its Git grants all consult that one answer, and the launch's
own derivation is gone.

The transition is sticky one way and is now written into git-workspace-model
section 11: removing the boundary keeps a session in its clones (its work is
there, and unconfined a shared .git adds nothing), while adding one moves a
session still on a linked worktree, because leaving it would keep it writing the
owner checkout's .git. Nothing is destroyed either way — retirement still judges
what is left under the same dirty and unique-commit rules.

An empty worktrees/<id> directory is now absent rather than a third state: a
review with no trusted checkout stages its empty stand-in on the session's own
tier instead of the other one's parent, which is where these came from, and a
confined preparation reclaims a leftover with a single rmdir.

The tier now comes from what was recorded when the session was created, not
from the agent's current settings and not from an inference: the session's own
workspaceIsolation says whether it has a tier of its own at all, and the clones
or worktree it already stands in say which. So changing an agent's runInSandbox
or workspaceIsolation reaches only sessions created afterwards. An empty
worktrees/<id> directory is neither of those records — it has no .git for
anything to read, and counting it pinned a session to a tier nothing served,
which is how one stopped being able to recover at all.

feat(daemon): the orphan reconciler collects a session pod whose session row is gone (§11) (#1767)

* feat(daemon): the orphan reconciler collects a session pod whose session row is gone

git-workspace-model §11 gives an isolated pool session its own pod, and its
claim lives as long as the session row. So a pod whose agent lives but whose
session the shared store no longer has is an orphan exactly as one whose agent
is gone. The reconciler reads the separate `agentconnect.md/session` label off
a claim or Sandbox, asks once per run which of those sessions still have a row
— after the live-agent test and before the grace test — and collects the rest
under the same grace. Fail-closed: no store to ask, or a store that will not
answer, keeps every session pod of a live agent; a gone agent's session pods
fall to the agent rule without a question.

`reconcile --once` opens the shared store BEFORE the cluster sweep and answers
the question from it (`sessionKeysForAgent`, leaves derived the way host keys
derive them), so no control-plane frame changes: the store — not the control
plane — is what holds the daemon's session rows.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): admission and the orphan sweep share the claim's own version

The reconciler's absence proof is a snapshot taken before its deletion loop. A
session row can come back after it, and that admission REUSES the leaked claim
rather than creating one -- so its uid and resourceVersion stood, the object was
already older than the grace, and the preconditioned delete took a live pod and
its volume. Neither the age rule nor a same-name replacement check could see it,
and a second row read would only have narrowed the window.

So admission writes, and the two fence on the object's own version.
`ensureSandbox` stamps every claim it takes with
`agentconnect.md/last-admitted-at` -- on the claim's metadata, never in its spec
or its pod's, so warm-pool adoption is untouched -- and `ensureClaim` merges that
stamp onto the claim even on the path that only reuses one. Two things follow.
The grace now runs from the later of creation and last admission, so a
re-admitted leaked claim is young again and is no candidate at all. And the
stamp's write moves the resourceVersion, so an admission that landed after the
sweep listed the object makes its delete fail: reported as replaced since it was
listed, pod and volume left alone, and the next run decides again.

`claimVacant` is not touched -- that ledger is the control plane's duty layer,
not this one.

* fix(daemon): a refused admission stamp degrades the fence, never the launch

The admission stamp the previous commit added is a merge PATCH on the claim, and
the Role shipped for pool members granted `sandboxclaims` only get/list/watch/
create/delete. Every admission that reused an existing claim would therefore have
gone POST 409 → PATCH 403, so a suspended claim could not resume at all: a
permission gap turned into an outage on every resume, which is worse than the
race the stamp closes.

Two halves. The Role now grants `patch` on `sandboxclaims`, with the render
contract asserting the new verb set. And the daemon degrades rather than
depending on it: a 403 on the stamp falls back to a plain read, the claim is
admitted and the sandbox launches, and the driver says once that the orphan sweep
now judges that claim by object age alone until the verb is granted. Only a
permission refusal takes that path — any other rejection is this call failing and
stays fatal, so a malformed patch is not silently swallowed.

* fix(daemon): the stamp says a claim is in USE, not merely that it was admitted

An admission-only marker left a hole the reviewer found: `ensureSandbox` returns
from the launch registry without touching the API, and `adoptSessions` caches a
Running claim this member never admitted, so a member can serve a session
indefinitely while its claim is never written. A sweep that snapshotted that
session's row as absent would then still match on uid and resourceVersion when
the row came back, and its preconditioned delete would take a live pod's volume.

So the stamp is refreshed on a tick, not only at admission: `refreshAdmissionStamps`
re-stamps every claim this member holds a launch for, and the runtime plane runs it
at a third of the sweep's default grace, so two missed ticks still leave a held
claim young. The reconciler needs no change — it already runs its grace from the
later of `creationTimestamp` and the stamp — but the annotation now reads "last
seen in use by a member", which its contract comment says.

Best effort by construction: it is off every turn's path, one claim's failure never
stops the rest, a claim retired underneath the member is not an error, and a Role
without `patch` degrades exactly as an admission does, reported once.

* fix(daemon): a launch is stamped when it is published, on a cadence the grace sets

Two holes in the fence, both where the periodic re-stamp does not reach.

A takeover writes nothing to the claim it adopts, and `setInterval` does not fire
for a whole period, so for that first window an adopted claim looks untouched
while a returning delivery is already served from the launch registry. A sweep
holding that claim's old version would still match and delete a pod in use. The
stamp now lands BEFORE the launch is published, in `adopt()` and in the resume
path alike: `resumeSandbox` records a launch straight from the claim it read, so
it publishes an unadmitted launch exactly as a takeover does. The periodic pass
keeps steady-state freshness; it is no longer what a new launch depends on.

The cadence was a constant of its own, a third of the DEFAULT grace, while the
sweep honours any configured `AC_K8S_ORPHAN_GRACE_MS` — so an install that
shortened the grace let a held claim age past it between two ticks. It is now
derived from the same number (`stampRefreshMsFor`), and the chart puts that value

cannot read different windows. The render contract asserts both surfaces carry

The stamp helper turned every PATCH failure into success. That was right while it

fix(daemon): a confined session can write its own HOME, but never the credential in it (#1780)

write. The inner policy did not: Codex extends `:workspace`, whose writable
root is the cwd, and HOME is a SIBLING of the cwd, not below it. So the package
caches the session layout puts there were unwritable and pnpm/corepack failed
inside a confined session.

back out of it as `deny` by the same most-specific-match idiom the Git-metadata
entries already use for `hooks` and `config`. The carve-out is the whole
directory, not a narrower set: `auth.json` there is a LINK to the shared host
credential, and the rest is the ACP parent's own state, written from outside
this sandbox. That deny is a no-op on behaviour — the caller's protected
credential roots already deny the same path — so it preserves today's boundary
rather than widening it, and it survives the new, more specific parent grant
whatever order the entries are composed in.

emitted only for a HOME the outer policy already made writable.

judged there against a small, deliberate subcommand list -- the process that
spawns git is the only one whose check is a control. `checkout` is not on that
list. The worktree tier never needed it (`worktree add -b` creates the branch and

with `checkout --no-track -b`, which the sandbox refuses. A self-hosted daemon

either, and its refusal was swallowed by the probe's own catch, so a dirty review
clone on a pool member was retained forever instead of removed; it now reads the
head ref with `show-ref --verify`.

The rest of the confined path was enumerated against the inventory and is clean:
clone, config, check-ref-format, remote, ls-remote, fetch, update-ref, rev-parse,
rev-list, show-ref, symbolic-ref, branch, reset, clean, status, log, diff.

is enforced in the loop rather than stubbed: a confined session is prepared,
reviewed and retired across that channel, and every subcommand it issues is

fix(daemon): move the session hook policy onto the gitconfig file channel (#1787)

* fix(daemon): move the session hook policy onto the gitconfig file channel

sessionGitPolicyEnv pinned core.hooksPath and core.fsmonitor through the
indexed GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/KEY_n/VALUE_n channel, which the module header had
already ruled out for anything the model's git reads: the indexed vars do not
merge across processes.

Read per process inside a runtime pod, the ACP runtime carried COUNT plus both
KEY/VALUE pairs while its own child carried COUNT alone. Git then reads "there
are 2 command-line settings", cannot find KEY_0, and refuses every invocation
with "unable to parse command-line config" — so the agent had to unset the
variables to get any git working, and the two settings that failed to arrive
are the ones that stop a repository's hooks from running.

Both settings now live in the per-agent gitconfig that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL
names, after the host [include] so an operator hooksPath cannot outrank them
and before the credential blocks so the helper reset ordering is untouched. A
git-repo workspace with no managed credential gets the same file for the
policy alone, with no credential pointer and no socket capability.

The move is global scope where the pins were command scope, so a repository
that sets core.hooksPath in its own .git/config now wins. Daemon-run Git keeps
its command-scope pins and a confined runtime cannot write .git/config or
.git/hooks; an unconfined agent's own git in such a checkout is the uncovered
case, and assertSafeWorkspaceGitConfig deliberately allows core.hooksPath, so
it does not close it either. A test pins that consequence.

hidden from the runtime — and git reads a hidden global config as no config at
all, so the pins would vanish silently rather than fail.

whenever the launch names one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): key the session gitconfig by what it contains

A credential-stripped host writes the same per-agent gitconfig as the warm

policy-only content. That host keeps pointing GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at the path,
so its nested clones and submodules lost the helper and the reset entry until
it was rebuilt — and on a local daemon could fall back to helpers from the
included host config. The two coexist by design and share a pod on the pool,
so this was reachable rather than theoretical. Introduced by the move of the
hook policy onto this channel: the previous env-only policy had no file to
collide on.

`elicitTarget` had no kind for it, so every surface declined. Webchat has an
input; Slack's button row still does not, so `SLACK_ELICIT_KINDS` is unchanged

Two kinds join the surface-capability set of #1801 — `text` (a string with no

refuses a source over 200 chars and every quantified group whose body itself
quantifies or alternates ((a+)+, (a|a)*). A refused pattern makes the property
unrenderable, so the form declines rather than being accepted unchecked — the
expression is never run at all.

refuse it: pre-populating an answer the card cannot submit helps nobody.

schema, which is what the screen exists to prevent.

alone still leaves a hole: a screened pattern carries at most three quantifiers,

feat(console): webchat consents to URL-mode elicitations (#1810)

* feat(console): webchat consents to URL-mode elicitations

ACP reserves URL mode for the asks that must never transit the LLM context, a
chat card, or the Control Plane — credentials, API keys, OAuth, payment. We did
not advertise the capability at all, so a runtime could not reach that seam and
fell back to form mode for exactly the things form mode forbids.

The daemon now advertises `elicitation: { form: {}, url: {} }`, and webchat
renders the consent card that earns the declaration. The card shows the full URL
for examination and fetches nothing about it — no favicon, preview, title
lookup, or prefetch hint — emphasizes the host so a lookalike is visible, flags a
Punycode (`xn--`) host and a link that is not encrypted, and opens only on the
reader's own click into a plain new tab, never an iframe or an in-app webview.

`accept` here means the user consented to OPEN the URL, not that the flow behind
it finished: the ACP request resolves at consent, Decline is the spec's explicit
`decline`, and the turn ending is still `cancel`. ACP's `elicitation/complete`
carries no session, so a consented card is parked under its `elicitationId`
within the agent host that raised it and re-labelled Completed if the
notification ever arrives; an unknown or already-completed id is ignored. (MCP's
`-32042 URLElicitationRequiredError` has no ACP counterpart — the daemon is an
ACP client and never calls tools on the agent — so it is out of scope here.)

Only http/https reach a card; every other scheme is declined rather than handed
to a browser tab. `elicitTarget` still returns null for a non-form mode, so every
form-only surface keeps declining and Slack gains no consent card. Slack's form
card also stops autolinking a URL in the agent's own message, which the spec's
server-side rule says belongs on a URL-mode ask alone.

Wire: `elicitation` gains an optional `url`, following #1801/#1803/#1807. A
reader that does not know it sees an optionless card it can only Dismiss — read
as `decline`, never as consent. `elicitation_resolved` gains a `completed`
outcome; an old reader drops that one frame and keeps showing the consented card,
so the losing direction is a missing label, never a wrong verdict.

* style(daemon): spell the elicitation key separator as an escape, not a raw NUL

The consented-URL map key embedded a literal NUL byte in its template literal.
The runtime string is the right choice — NUL cannot occur in either component,
so the separator is unambiguous — but writing it as a raw control character made
the whole file read as binary: `file` reported `data` and grep refused to search

`\x00` in the literal produces the identical string and keeps the file text.

* fix(console): split a consent URL by position, not by its normalized host

The card split the original URL by searching it for `parsed.host`. The URL
parser lowercases an uppercase host and punycodes a Unicode one, so for
`https://Billing.EXAMPLE.com/pay` or `https://例え.jp/authorize` the normalized
host does not occur in the original string at all, the search failed, and the
card rendered with no URL and no Open link — only Dismiss. The daemon accepts
those requests, so the reader was left unable to consent to a flow the agent had
legitimately asked for.

or `#`. The original bytes still reach the reader unaltered, which is the point

fired while telling the reader their host "is written in Punycode" when what
they see is not. It now tests the shown host too and names both the spelling

feat(daemon): agentconnect auth logs a runtime in, and the console hands over the command (#1818)

* feat(daemon): agentconnect auth logs a runtime in on the daemon host

A runtime's credential lives in that runtime's own state directory on the host sessions are
seeded FROM, and every login flow it offers wants a human at a terminal — a browser consent
URL, a pasted API key, or its own interactive CLI. So this is an operator command, not
something the daemon can do for itself.

`agentconnect auth [--runtime <id>] [--method <id>]` (delegated verbatim to the daemon bin)
lists what is installed on the host, annotates each row with a REAL login probe rather than an
on-disk heuristic, and then walks whichever ACP method was chosen: a `terminal` method by
handing the operator's own terminal to the agent program (advertised via the new
`auth.terminal` client capability), an `agent` method through `authenticate` plus the
request-scoped URL/form elicitations the auth phase asks over.

The runtime deliberately runs UNSANDBOXED against the operator's own HOME: a private-HOME
launch would write the login into a directory thrown away with the process.

Also here, because a login needs them:
- request-scoped elicitation reaches an `onAuthElicit` hook instead of being declined, and
  `auth.terminal` / `elicitation.url` are advertised only when the caller can service them.
- a loopback-redirect paste fallback, so a headless host can finish an OAuth flow whose
  127.0.0.1 listener no browser can reach (Google retired the OOB flow in 2023).
- stop() gives the child an EOF grace window before signalling, so a runtime that dumps a
  stack trace on SIGTERM no longer makes a successful login look like a crash.

green, and both paths run for real against the installed runtimes on this host —

* fix(daemon): auth releases its prompt, answers the form it was asked, and awaits probe teardown

* fix(daemon): a DM root really answers its card, and Slack's link markup is decoded

Two P2s from review, both reproduced.

**The DM exception was dead code.** Slack normalization sets `thread` to
`thread_ts ?? ts`, so it is never absent and a root message carries its OWN ts
there — while the match tested `msg.thread !== undefined` to tell a root from a
reply. Every DM answer therefore took the threaded branch, compared its own ts
against the card's thread, and missed: a card at 100.001 with a top-level `42`
at 200.001 was not an answer, and the DM card was exactly as unanswerable as it
would have been with no exception at all.

The fact was never lost in normalization, only mis-read, so it is derived rather
than preserved: a message whose `thread` equals the ts inside its own `msgId` is
a root. No new normalized field, because `thread` has some forty readers across
daemon, relay and control-plane whose meaning must not shift under them, and a
wire field would need a skew window on both ingress paths for something already
in hand. The different-thread exclusion is unchanged and still tested: a reply
under another root of the same conversation — DM included — answers nothing.

keeps `<https://example.com/>` and `<mailto:a@b|a@b>`, so a `uri` or `email`
field refused the reader forever for following the card's own instruction.
`decodeSlackReplyValue` recovers what the reader typed, beside
`stripLeadingSelfMention` as the second pure step before any schema check: the
destination is the part BEFORE the pipe (a label is display text and is never
the value) and `mailto:` comes off, so an `email` field gets `a@b`.

DECODING, not extracting: only a reply that is one link and nothing else is
unwrapped. Prose with a link inside is returned whole, because choosing which
PART of a sentence is the answer is the guess this route refuses to make. It
also undoes the three entities Slack escapes in message text, which is lossless
and is where a wrong value would otherwise have passed `uri` silently — a query
string arrives as `?a=1&b=2`. Inbound only: nothing here touches the
outbound defusing of agent-authored text (#1810/#1819).

row. Answer opens a modal carrying one `input` block per field, in schema order:
`static_select` for an enum and for a boolean, `multi_static_select` with
`max_selected_items`, `plain_text_input` with `min_length`/`max_length`,
`number_input` with `is_decimal_allowed` and its bounds, and
`initial_value`/`initial_option` from `default`.

itself, exactly as `open-config` has opened the status modal all along. Nothing
is pre-rendered anywhere: the view is built on demand from the card's own pending

by construction, and it dies with the card. What round-trips through Slack is the
opaque session target the card's `block_id` already carried, echoed in the
modal's `private_metadata` beside the request id.

since per-field errors exist only as a `view_submission` response. It rides

* fix(daemon): anchor SRT's mandatory-deny scan at the private HOME, not the checkout

SRT resolves its built-in deny names (`.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, `.profile`,
`.gitconfig`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, `.mcp.json`, `.vscode`, `.idea`,
`.claude/commands`, `.claude/agents`) against the helper's own process.cwd(),
and for a missing name it has bwrap create a zero-byte mount point there so the
sandboxed process cannot create the file itself. The provider chdir'd into the
workspace before wrapping, so every host launch left eleven zero-byte
placeholders in the checkout root. SRT deletes only the ones it created in that
run and only on a graceful exit, so one SIGKILL made them permanent: a shared
checkout in the wild showed nine of them untracked, all stamped by a single
launch five days earlier and untouched by every restart since.

Those names are HOME's, so the scan now runs from the private runtime HOME —
where the placeholders are nobody's untracked file — and the process moves to
the workspace only for the spawn, since bwrap runs where the helper stands and
SRT passes no --chdir. Nothing depended on scanning the checkout: its
`.git/config` and `.git/hooks` have been denied explicitly per Git metadata
root since #1695, which is also why the workspace `.claude` pre-create for a
Claude runtime is no longer needed (its config dir is in the private HOME).

The provider also sweeps the old scan's leftovers from the checkout root before
launching: only a zero-byte regular file or an empty directory of those exact
names, so real content is never touched.

the Control Plane for no benefit, and measuring them settled both.

Dream staging is a whole proposed store per retained dream: on one install's
busiest agent 1.6 MB of live Markdown in 219 files against 12 MB of staging in
602, and across eleven agents 5.8 MB / 246 files against 23.5 MB / 1728 — four

model and mostly discarded. A draft is also the one part of the tree that need
not survive a move. It stays on the daemon's disk under either home, which is
also what leaves MemoryFs.root an honest path: the extraction host's cwd is
built from it, and a database has no directory to run in.

The change log is row-shaped already — one record per write, read filtered by
path and paged by cursor — and as a file it is rewritten whole on every write
and reaches its 2 MiB cap in practice. It becomes its own org-fenced table,
appended in the same transaction as the write it records, retention enforced
as a delete. A daemon home keeps today's sidecar file.

average about 7 KB against a 128 KiB chunk, so an ordinary write is one append
and one commit. The pod's op set stays worth reusing and CpMemoryFs stays an
adapter rather than a third implementation — recorded as its own paragraph so
the choice is not re-litigated from the op names alone.

fix(message): surface Slack Lists, canvases, and file mentions to the agent (#1862)

A List mentioned in a Slack message reached the agent as nothing it could act
on. Slack delivers the mention three ways at once, and each one lost the
reference on our side: the `rich_text` element is a `list_record`
(`{ file_id, url }`), a type `richElementText` did not model and rendered as an
empty string; the fallback `text` spells the mention as the bare file id, which
is what survived — `can you see F0…`; and the `files` entry (`filetype: list`)
became `[attached: list (application/vnd.slack-list)]`, a marker with no id and
no link that suggests a download. The agent asked which list, then said there
was no attachment, and only found the List once the user had repeated the word
enough times to make the bare id guessable.

`extractSlackMessageText` now renders these references so a model can act on
them, always naming the kind and the id the tool takes:

- `list_record`, `canvas`, and `file` elements become
  `<url|title (Slack List F…)>` (a `record_id` adds the row);
- `message_mention` and `canvas_message_unfurl` become the channel and ts a
  thread read takes;
- `tag` and `color` keep their text, and every leaf type the extractor does not
  model — `attachment_mention`, `work_object_mention`, `workflow_mention`,
  `citation`, whatever Slack adds next — keeps the `text` / `url` it carries
  instead of vanishing;
- a List or canvas shared on the message with nothing in the body mentioning it
  is rendered the same way from its `files` entry, title and permalink.

The fallback-vs-layout dedupe learns that a rendered reference and its bare id
are one mention, and keeps the rendering that spells more, so the two views of
one message no longer both survive. `toSlackAttachment` drops List and canvas
files, so the attachment marker stays about bytes.

The thread-history read reuses both functions, so backfilled context gets the
same rendering.

feat(control-plane): the managed memory home in the Control Plane — two tables and the store handler (#1877)

* feat(control-plane): the managed memory home in the Control Plane — two tables and the store handler

Step ③ of the managed-memory `home` rollout (memory-evolution.md §3.2.1). The
`control-plane` home gets its two tables — `agent_memory_file`, one row per file
keyed (agentId, path) with directories implicit, and `agent_memory_history`, the
change log as an event table keyed by the record id — and the two D→C handlers
that serve them: `memory/store` runs one memory-fs op as one SQL transaction under
a per-agent advisory lock, `memory/history/append` files a batch and retains by
deleting (newest 100 per file, then the store's 2 MiB, oldest first).

Two constraints the table adds, both required by the conditional write
unified-memory-interface.md §5 later builds on this transaction: the `mtime` a
commit stamps is strictly monotonic per (agentId, path) — GREATEST(now, previous +
1 ms) inside the commit — and staged rows an abandoned append sequence left are
swept by a bounded periodic loop once they are an hour old.

Authorization mirrors `knowledge/search`: org from the frame or the connection, the
agent served by this daemon (`placementResolver.mayAct`), and its home resolved to
`control-plane`; otherwise SCOPE_DENIED, which is what makes the CP the write fence
across daemons. `fitToBudget`/`utf8Boundary`/`encodedBytes` move into protocol so
both carriers cut the same slice; the daemon re-exports them.

Not here: the `agent-memory-store-v1` advertisement, `memory/home/migrated` and the
binding rules (step ④), and the daemon-side adapter (step ⑤).

feat(daemon): the one-way memory home migration, and the forced return that keeps nothing (#1888)

* feat(daemon): the one-way memory home migration, and the forced return that keeps nothing

When the daemon holds a managed binding whose `home` is `control-plane` and
still carries the CP's `homeMigration: 'pending'`, `MemoryHomeMigrator` copies
`memory/` and `channels/` from the `daemon` home into the CP once — every file
by path, overwriting, mtimes kept, the sidecars sent as change-log rows with
the daemon's ids — and reports `memory/home/migrated`. Triggered at the end of
every reconcile pass (a binding that arrived with the marker), once at a time
per agent, retried with backoff, and re-run from the start on CP READY. On a
`--k8s` member the source is the sandbox volume, read inside `withMemoryHome`
so the pod is bound; an empty volume is a legitimate empty source. The copy is
restartable by doing nothing clever: the source is frozen from the flip, the
target is served to nobody until the CP holds the completion, and a re-sent
batch is the same rows. The source tree is never deleted.

On `{ accepted: true }` the registry drops the marker from the local replica
ahead of the CP's next push, and reconcile rebuilds the session boundary the
way any memory-binding change does: a managed home and its pending copy are
now part of the host-spawn signature. `CONFLICT` stops the copy and touches
neither tree; `SCOPE_DENIED` and connection failures leave the marker in place
for the retry.

The forced return, `control-plane` → `daemon`, archives the pre-switch local
tree aside before the binding goes live — `memory/`, `channels/` and
`memory-backups/` under `<agent dir>/memory-archive-<timestamp>/`, with
`memory-dreams/` left where it is — so the agent starts from an empty tree and
nothing is resurrected.

fix(control-plane): re-issue a Check write whose marker never reached GitHub (#1897)

Once a write marker is durable, `reconcileAmbiguous` only ever GETs the Check
and looks for the marker. That is right while GitHub lags an accepted mutation,
but a worker killed between committing the marker and sending the request
(every rollout can do this) leaves a row that reconciles forever: the marker is
never on the Check, so every pass ends in `ambiguous_write` with the mutex held
and the desired state never published. A required review Check then stays
`in_progress` until someone pushes a new revision.

Bound the recovery on evidence plus time. When GitHub returns the Check (update)
or a complete name listing (create) without the marker, and the write is older
than a 10-minute grace window, the request provably never took effect: release
the write mutex with `ambiguous_write_reissued` so the next pass mints a fresh
marker and re-issues the same desired state. A capped listing, a GET failure, or
a marker whose encoded state cannot be decoded keeps the mutex as before. Rows
already stuck for days converge on their next pass under the same rule.

fix(daemon): drain microsandbox terminal events before disposal (#1899)

After an output-limit failure, closing a microsandbox connection immediately after sending SIGKILL can deliver the old command's output and exit event to the next command. The pinned relay reuses client IDs before the guest has finished terminating the old process. A real-VM probe reproduced `sleep 30` returning an unrelated exit event and stale stderr before cancellation.

Keep draining the killed process until its terminal event, then close the client and release the execution. Cleanup has a deadline covering both the kill send and terminal drain. If transport is lost or termination cannot be confirmed, fence and stop the VM before allowing reuse; also reject launches already being prepared when the fence occurs. The retained disk remains available after restart.

Follow-up to #1894; related to #1884. The SDK connection cap, auth handling, and default SRT behavior are unchanged.

Validation:
- All 20 microsandbox driver, guest, and launch tests passed, including delayed terminal disposal, concurrent in-flight launch fencing, and retained-VM recovery.
- Daemon typecheck, ESLint/Prettier, and the self-contained daemon build passed.
- Real manager/guest-bridge stress: 192 sequential plus 64 concurrent executions beside a live stream; clients returned from 3 to 3, peak 19, no connection-limit rejection or forced GC.
- Repeated timeout/stdout-limit/stderr-limit/failure/cancellation chains passed without stale output. Reader cancellation, TERM/KILL, retained restart, and forced transport-loss recovery also passed with the test file preserved on disk.

* feat(daemon): a Telegram question that must be typed gets a box

A `text` or `number` elicitation was declined on Telegram because a keyboard
accepts no characters. It has something better than a keyboard for this: a
`force_reply` opens the reader's own compose box aimed at one message, and the
reply comes back naming it — the nearest thing the Bot API has to an input
box, and a per-card answer channel by construction.

So the card carries one button that opens the box, plus Dismiss. There is no
Confirm: the reply IS the submission, and a second tap would only be a chance
to lose it. The prompt REPLIES to the card, which is also what keeps it inside
a forum topic — Telegram places a reply where the message it answers is, so no
thread coordinate is re-derived. Settling the card edits the prompt too, so no
reader is left typing into a question that is over.

The words go back as the field's own carried value under the same block id a
Confirm uses, so a typed answer is validated by the SAME re-derivation every
other answer is: a number that is not a number, a string breaking its own
`pattern` or `format`, are refused with the field's own words and the card
left live — and the box stays open, because the reader who was just told what
was wrong is typing into it.

`claimReply` on the facet is how a message becomes an answer instead of a
prompt. Core offers each typed message to the live cards of its own
conversation before thread canonicalization reads it as continuing the session
and before command parsing reads `!stop` typed into the box as a control. A
surface that asks nobody to type claims nothing, which is what Slack's does.
Agent-authored traffic never claims: "anyone who can see the card may answer
it" is about people.

A form of several questions is still declined — one prompt at a time is a
state machine across fields, and a reader who walks away mid-way leaves half a
form standing. That, and the select-with-Other companion, are #1794's next
Telegram items.

* feat(cli): an upgrade prunes the versions it replaced

Installing and upgrading grew `<root>/versions` without bound — only a manual
`version prune` ever removed an old bundle. Every install/upgrade now prunes the
store once the new version is in place, keeping three versions in total by
default, and `--keep <n>` (0 to keep everything) overrides it.

keeping N *on top of* them, so "keep 3" means three directories on disk; both
stay protected. Cleanup is best effort: a failed removal is reported and never
fails the install or upgrade that produced the new version.

* fix(cli): automatic cleanup keeps the target and any running bundle

Review found two ways the new prune could delete a version that is still needed.

`version install <v> --keep 2` with `current` and `previous` both set spent the
whole budget on the protected pair and deleted the bundle it had just unpacked —
an install deliberately does not switch `current`, so retention alone dropped it.
The automatic prune now protects the version the operation installed, on the same
budget-overflow terms as `current`/`previous`.

`current` and `previous` track selection, not what the live daemon is executing:
node resolves `current` at load time, so a daemon launched under 1.0.0 keeps
loading files from that bundle across later upgrades that never restarted it.
Repeated `upgrade` without `--restart` therefore deleted a bundle in use. The
automatic prune now defers while `<root>/daemon.lock` names a live process, and
only the prune after a restart that passed its health check treats the store as
idle. Deferred versions are reported and reclaimed by a later prune.
