feat(daemon): steer a mid-turn message into the running turn over ACP _session/steering (#1910)

* feat(daemon): steer a mid-turn message into the running turn over _session/steering

A message for a session whose turn is still running was always queued behind
it and, at best, folded into the turn-final regeneration after the candidate
answer was already finished. Both managed runtimes now implement the
_session/steering ACP extension, so the daemon steers instead (#1847).

- AcpHost reads _meta.steering.supported at initialize (steeringSupported())
  and exposes steer(), sending idleBehavior: promptRequired so a steer that
  races the turn end is declined rather than becoming an unadmitted turn. The
  runtime probe records and logs the capability.
- The queued admission branch offers an eligible arrival to the live prompt
  before placing it: an ordinary human chat message, not !queue, hooks,
  scheduler wakes, agent-to-agent calls, or barrier-holding entries. injected
  settles the entry like a coalesced one (steered_into_turn), releases the
  durable row, and marks the row absorbed and claimed so neither context fence
  re-prompts it; failed, an RPC error, a spent per-turn budget
  (MAX_STEERS_PER_TURN), a runtime without the capability, or the
  features.sessionSteering switch off falls back to today's queue path.
- The Linear ack says the message was added to the running task instead of
  queued; onAdmission reports steered for that.
- Product conventions and the turn-final refresh design record the behaviour.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(webchat): steer a composer message into the running turn instead of queueing it

The console composer held a message typed during a running turn in a
browser-side queue and sent it once the turn ended, so the daemon's new
steering (#1847) never saw it. For an agent whose runtime can steer, the
composer now sends at once and the daemon steers it (#547).

- The daemon's webchat status frame carries `steerable` while the live turn's
  host advertised _session/steering and the feature is on.
- A browser turn frame may carry `steer: true`; the relay passes it through
  and copies the daemon's `steered` verdict back on the ack. Such a turn is
  steer-or-refuse: `dispatchWebchatTurn` awaits the admission verdict and acks
  `steered`, plain accepted when the turn had already ended (it runs as its own
  turn), or `busy` when the runtime declined - then no queue entry, stream, or
  transcript row is left behind and the browser keeps the message.
- The provider steers when the daemon declared the turn steerable, nothing is
  already queued, the message is text-only and the conversation has one agent;
  otherwise it queues as before. A steer opens no stream lane: its `done`
  (`steered_into_turn`) settles it, a `busy` refusal puts it back at the head of
  the queue, and a late ack without `steered` on an idle lane opens the lane
  for the turn it became.
- The session view renders a steered message as a user bubble labelled as
  steered into the running reply, and the reply that continues after it starts
  a fresh block below it instead of merging into the block above.
- Product conventions describe the console behaviour.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(webchat): keep a steer across socket drops, restore refusals in send order, let tool updates cross it

Three regressions review found in the composer steering path (#547):

- A socket that dropped after a steer was sent but before its verdict lost
  the message while it stayed labelled as steered. A pending steer now keeps
  its wire frame: a reconnect re-sends it under the same turnId, and the
  daemon confirms a copy it already steered idempotently instead of refusing
  it as a duplicate; when no reconnect follows (idle close, exhausted
  retries) the steer goes back to the composer queue.
- Two steers refused `busy` were prepended one after the other and came back
  as [B, A]. Composer sends now carry a sequence number, and a refused steer
  is inserted at its own position among queued messages.
- A `msg` row appended mid-turn fenced the tool_update and plan lookups, so a
  call started before a steer stayed in progress forever in the live view.
  Steer rows still fence text grouping but no longer stop same-turn tool,
  plan, or supersession updates.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(webchat): reconcile a re-sent steer with the delivery it may already be

Review found two reconnect paths that could run one message twice:

- A reconnect copy of a steer arriving while the original admission was still
  deciding got `busy`, which the browser took as a refusal and queued a fresh
  turn even though the original then steered. The transport now keeps the
  pending steer admission per stream and a copy joins it, receiving the same
  verdict; a copy of a steer that became its own turn is reported accepted,
  never `busy`. `busy` is now the daemon's definite refusal only.
- Giving up on reconnecting (or an idle close) turned an unacknowledged steer
  into a fresh turn with a new turnId, losing the identity the daemon dedups
  on. An unacked steer now keeps its turnId: the provider reconnects for it
  even when no turn is busy, re-sends the frame on every new socket, marks
  the delivery uncertain when retries run out, and requeues only on a
  definite `busy`. A copy reported accepted opens its lane and resumes it, so
  a turn already streaming is replayed rather than waited on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(webchat): open a late steer's lane once the older lane retires

After a reconnect, the browser can still hold the previous turn's lane while
the daemon has finished that turn and admitted the re-sent steer as its own
turn. When the copy's plain accepted ack arrived before the previous turn's
replayed `done`, settleSteerAck returned without opening the late turn's lane
and nothing revisited that ack, so its reply stayed on the dead connection.

The accepted transition is now retained on the pending steer, and whenever
the last lane of a session retires (a `done`, a lane rejection) that steer's
lane opens and is resumed instead of the session going idle. Opening a
steer's own lane and resuming it share one helper with the immediate case.

feat(daemon): a Discord elicitation is answered in a dialog (#1961)

* feat(daemon): a Discord elicitation is answered in a dialog

Discord declined every elicitation, and it turns out to be the best surface we
have for one. A Discord MESSAGE takes buttons but no typed box; a MODAL takes
`Label`-wrapped text inputs and select menus. So the reader gets the whole form
as one dialog, submitted atomically — closer to what `elicitation/create`
describes than any message-level card can be.

Verified against what is installed rather than assumed: `discord-api-types`
`APIComponentInLabel` admits a select menu, radio group, checkbox group and
text input inside a modal, and `discord.js@14.27` both sends raw modal JSON
(`showModal`) and reads every one of them back (`ModalSubmitFields.getField`).

The card in the channel carries one Answer button and Dismiss; Answer opens the
dialog. The one exception is the one every surface makes: a lone single-select
or boolean stays a row of buttons, because one tap already answers it and a
dialog would be a round trip for nothing.

Select menus do the option fields, not radio or checkbox groups, though the
modal takes those too. A radio group is prettier but holds 2-10 options against
a select's 25, and its arity is a different COMPONENT rather than a different
bound — so choosing it would buy nicer pixels for two more code paths and two
more cliffs. One control, one bound, one read path.

Nothing Discord-shaped survives into the answer: every option carries its
POSITION and every field is keyed by the same `elicitFormBlockId` a Slack
Confirm submits under, so a dialog is a different PLACE to answer and never a
different answer. `submitElicitEditor` reconciles one thing on the way in — a
list-taking control answers with a list even where it was configured to take
one, and the FIELD says which it was.

This is NOT the Slack modal removed earlier in #1794. Slack has message-level
input state, which made its modal a second way to do what the card already did;
Discord has no way at all to type into a message, so the dialog is not a choice
between surfaces but the only surface that can take a typed answer.

Two things stay declined: a reduction of more than five fields, which is more
than a modal holds — declined whole, since a dialog missing a question would
collect an answer to a form the reader never saw — and URL mode, whose consent
a Discord link button could never report.

Refs #1794

* fix(daemon): a permission card offers every option or none

`buildPermissionCard` did `params.options.slice(0, 5)`. An agent offering six
options rendered five buttons, and whichever the reader tapped came back as
their decision on the FULL request — they never saw what was cut, and the agent
could not tell the decision was made from a truncated set. The identical defect
#1794 gap 7 fixed for elicitation cards, on the adjacent seam.

The 5 was neither a platform limit nor a row's: Slack holds 25 elements in one
`actions` block and this card puts nothing else there. So the cap is the
block's own, and the card offers all 25.

Past that it builds NO card, and the honest outcome needed no new decision —
`resolveAcpPermission` already has a path that keeps the request open and
answerable. A list the card cannot offer whole now fails the
`chatApprovalEnabled` gate, so it takes `awaitEditorPermission`: the request
stays open, every option is on the Agent page, and chat gets the neutral notice
that path already posts. Better than either option the issue floated —
declining silently, or resolving `cancelled` — because nothing is decided and
nothing is lost.

The approval DM shares the builder and gets the same treatment it already gives
an unrenderable elicitation: the ask plus where the options can be seen, rather
than an intro with a truncated button row under it.

Severity as filed, not inflated: the ACP standard set is four options
(allow_once / allow_always / reject_once / reject_always), so this was latent
rather than firing. What made it worth fixing before the cosmetic items is that
a permission decision misreported from a partial menu is closer to a safety
question than a rendering one.

* feat(web): page earlier history into the composer's prompt recall

The recall pool is only the loaded transcript window, and the transcript pages
earlier rows in on demand. Two consequences the first cut missed: Up at the oldest
loaded prompt stopped with no hint that earlier prompts existed, and a page
prepending rows while recalling moved the numeric index, so the label and the
next step pointed at a different entry.

Entries now carry a stable row key (webchat `postId`, else source session + `seq`),
and the hook keeps its place by key across a prepend. Up at the oldest loaded entry
calls `loadEarlier` and lands on the newest prompt the page brings; pages with none

* test(web): an inline import type is not a value import of protocol

The leaf scan's second matcher exists for side-effect `import 'x'` and dynamic `import('x')`, the two forms with no `from` clause. It also matched TypeScript's inline import type, `import('@agentconnect.md/protocol').MemoryEntryCapabilities`, which sits in a type position the compiler erases and never reaches a bundler. `lib/api.ts` uses about fifteen of them and value-imports nothing from protocol - its one protocol import is `import type { HookKind }` - so the scan read it as a barrel importer and failed the leaf check on main.

A match is now ruled out when the token in front of it opens a type position: `:` `<` `|` `&` `typeof` `keyof` `extends` `as` `satisfies`. `=>` and `,` are deliberately absent. They front an arrow body or a call argument far more often than a type, and the two directions do not cost the same: over-counting a type is a false failure someone reads and fixes, while under-counting a real dynamic import would let this scan go blind on the very thing it guards. Across the console the change drops exactly one pair, the `lib/api.ts` false positive, and keeps the other six importers.

fix(daemon): a dropped control-plane socket no longer consumes the turn's formal review (#1979)

`submitCodeReview` authorizes each attempt with the control plane before it
writes anything at GitHub. When that socket closed mid-request, the correlator
rejected the call with a retryable "connection closed" and the orchestrator
marked the turn `done`: the review was lost for the rest of the turn, and a
second tool call answered "already has a formal review attempt" even though
GitHub had never seen the request.

A retryable wire failure at authorization is a proven no-effect. Keep the same
attempt id, return the turn to `idle`, and tell the caller to retry. The retry
re-authorizes the SAME attempt (the lease treats a repeated attempt id as its
own renewal) and goes marker-first before any POST, so it can never
double-submit. Non-retryable failures still consume the attempt.

* fix(daemon): a sandbox that is down is not a daemon that has none

One bit answered two questions. A daemon advertised the `sandbox` capability
only while its sandbox was HEALTHY, so a microsandbox that failed to start
looked exactly like a host that never had a sandbox — and those two states have
opposite meanings. A host without one runs agents unconfined; a host whose
configured sandbox is down refuses those sessions outright.

The console believed the wrong one. It showed a sandboxed agent as running in
"its normal environment", and the daemon detail view filed it under the host
runtime, while every launch was in fact being refused. Worse, creating an agent
on such a daemon silently stored `runInSandbox: false`, turning a transient
outage into a permanent setting change nobody asked for.

A daemon now advertises the capability from its CONFIGURATION and reports the
outage separately: `capabilities.sandboxUnavailable` carries the reason it
cannot serve one right now. Supported stays true, so the stored preference
survives and enabling it is still a request the operator may make; the console
reads the reason and says the sandbox is unavailable, quoting what the daemon
reported, instead of describing an unconfined run that is not happening.

fix(daemon): start microsandbox VMs one at a time so disk locks cannot leak (#2018)

* fix(daemon): start microsandbox VMs one at a time so disk locks cannot leak

A starting VM flocks every named disk volume it attaches and clears CLOEXEC on
those fds so its own supervisor inherits them. Any other process spawned beside
that start inherits them too, so a second sandbox's supervisor ends up holding
the first one's locks and keeps them after that VM stops. The stopped
environment can then never start again — every turn fails with `volume "..." is
already attached with an incompatible disk mode`, and restarting the daemon does
not help because supervisors are detached.

VM starts are now serialized, which closes the window that spawns one supervisor
beside another. When a start still hits the lock, the driver identifies the
holding process through /proc, suspends it when it is an idle environment of
this daemon, and retries once; a holder with work in flight is left alone and
the failure now names the volume and the holding pid instead of repeating the
SDK sentence.

Fixes #2013.

fix(daemon): an upgraded daemon stops hoarding the image it no longer boots (#2017)

* fix(daemon): an upgraded daemon stops hoarding the image it no longer boots

Each release pins its own sandbox image, so every upgrade pulled a new one and
kept the old one forever: nothing had ever removed a cached image. A host a few
releases along was holding several full images it could never boot again.

Startup now collects the image cache before it pulls. It keeps the configured
image and every image a persisted binding still records, which a retained VM
validates when it starts, and removes the rest one reference at a time. Whole
cache pruning is deliberately not used: the backend prunes any image no sandbox
has booted, which includes the image the daemon just pulled and has not started
a session on, so it would re-download the current image on every restart.

Removal is non-forcing, so the backend refusing an image a sandbox still boots
from is a second guard behind the keep set. A refused removal is kept and
logged, and a cache that cannot be read is logged without failing startup.

The preparation VM moves from a random name to a stable one and is reclaimed
before it is recreated. A start interrupted before its teardown used to leave a
VM behind that pinned a retired image for good, which would have defeated the
collection above.

The SandboxTemplate's podTemplate referenced the install-wide
`.Values.imagePullSecrets`. Those pods are created by the agent-sandbox
controller in `daemonPool.sandboxNamespace`, and the kubelet resolves a pull

release namespace, the reference names a Secret that is not there and every
sandbox logs FailedToRetrieveImagePullSecret. The pull still succeeds, because
the runtime-sandbox image is public and the kubelet falls back to an anonymous

misconfiguration, and the event it prints is the kind that trains an operator
to ignore pull-secret warnings.

default, so the default render names nothing at all. An install that hosts the
runtime-sandbox image privately sets that value and creates the dockerconfigjson

install-wide value could never express, since one value cannot name a Secret in
two namespaces.

Every other template keeps `.Values.imagePullSecrets`: those pods render into
the release namespace, where that Secret does exist, and the SandboxTemplate was
the only chart object placing a pod anywhere else.

chart-rendered pod carries the install-wide value, a sandbox pod carries its

feat(webchat): render MCP Apps interfaces in a sandboxed console frame (#2021)

* feat(webchat): render MCP Apps interfaces in a sandboxed console frame

An MCP server may ship an interactive HTML interface for one of its tools (MCP
Apps, SEP-1865): it predeclares the interface as a `ui://` resource, links it to
a tool with `_meta.ui.resourceUri`, and the host renders it in a sandboxed iframe
that talks back over MCP's own JSON-RPC. This makes AgentConnect that host, and
webchat the one surface that renders one.

THE DAEMON HOSTS, because nothing else can. A configured MCP server is attached
to the RUNTIME today, and the runtime never advertises the UI extension (so a
server never registers its UI tools), never issues the `resources/read` the HTML
lives behind, and has no ACP frame meaning "render this". So a `ui: true` server
is dialed by the daemon itself and its tools are re-exposed through the bridge
the runtime already mounts — namespaced `<server>__<tool>`, so nothing can shadow
a product tool — which is what puts the daemon on the call when `_meta.ui` comes
back.

WEBCHAT-ONLY ON PURPOSE, said once rather than discovered later: an iframe cannot
live in a Slack message, a Telegram keyboard, a Discord modal or a Feishu card.
This is not a fifth `ElicitCardFacet` implementer and must not become one. Every
other surface DECLINES out loud through the standing notice #1794 built, and the
tool still runs and its text still reaches the model, so no turn breaks for want
of a frame.

TWO DELIBERATE NARROWINGS OF THE SPEC, both recorded in the design:

- No `allow-same-origin`. The spec assumes app HTML is served from an origin that
  is not the host's; the console's is, so a `srcdoc` frame granted it could read
  the browser auth session out of `localStorage` and call the CP as the signed-in
  user. v1 runs on an opaque origin and an app gets no storage; a dedicated app
  origin is the follow-up.
- The CSP is built from what the resource declared and nothing else, restrictive
  by default, and a declaration can only widen its own directive.

A frame's bridge is authorized entirely from the daemon's own record of the card:
the payload names what to do, and the card names what may be reached — which
server's tools, which conversation's stream, whose post a `ui/message` becomes.
The stream is HELD on the card because a frame outlives the turn that opened it.

Caps come from the wire: the card rides the same `rd/chat` frame every reply
chunk does, so a 96 KiB template and a 160 KiB card sit under the 256 KiB frame
budget even at JSON escaping's worst case. An oversized card sheds its tool
result first (the model already received it) and is declined only if it still
will not fit.

Design: docs/designs/webchat-mcp-apps.md. Part of #1966.

Verified: typecheck and lint clean; protocol (528), relay (42) and web (2557)
suites pass; 30 new daemon tests pass. The daemon suite's 8 remaining failures
(daemon-smoke gitcred, skill-install, acp-matrix) reproduce with these changes

* fix(webchat): make an MCP App frame work against the real SDK

Five findings from review, all reproducible, all fixed.

THE INITIALIZE RESULT WAS REJECTED OUTRIGHT. `McpUiInitializeResult` requires
`protocolVersion`, `hostInfo.version` and `hostCapabilities` — and
`hostCapabilities` is not `capabilities`, which is what was being sent. The
official SDK's `App.connect()` validates the result, so an SDK-built app never
finished initializing and nothing downstream could have worked. The reply now
carries all four required fields, and declares only what this host truly
decodes: the four daemon-served methods, links, logging, and TEXT content in
both directions. The `tool-input` notification also carries its arguments under
`arguments`, because a bare object parses to empty params and loses them, and
the `tool-result` notification always carries `content` since the schema
requires it.

APP EVENTS DIED WITH THEIR TURN. A frame outlives the turn that opened it — the
reader is still looking at it and its bridge is still served — so the daemon
keeps sending replies and settlements on that card's original turnId. But the
browser's ordered turn cursor is retired at `done` and `admitsLane` refuses to
reopen a completed lane, so every one of them was dropped: a button pressed
after the agent finished hung to its timeout, and a closed card kept rendering
as live. `app_rpc_result` and `app_resolved` now bypass stream admission, which
is sound rather than a shortcut — an RPC result is correlated by its own callId
and a settlement is idempotent on appId, so neither needs the cursor.

A TOOL NAME NEVER SELECTS A SERVER. A view calls its tool by the name its own
server gave it (`refresh`); it has no business knowing an operator configured
that server as `charts`. The prefix check rejected every such call as
`wrong_server`. The server is now `app.server` from the card, always, and the
name is resolved against that server's own tool list — which is strictly
stronger: `secrets__read` is looked up on this card's server, not found, and
refused. A lexical check could not have done either job, since it cannot tell a
genuine upstream name containing `__` from an attempt at another namespace.

VIEW CALLS LOST THEIR STRUCTURED RESULTS. `callForView` reused the
model-oriented path, which drops `structuredContent` — precisely what a refresh
or pagination tool answers with. View calls now take an upstream-result path
that preserves it.

THE TWO REQUEST PAYLOADS WERE THE WRONG SHAPE. `ui/message` sends
`{ role, content: ContentBlock[] }` and `ui/update-model-context` sends
`content` and/or `structuredContent`; neither is the string field being read, so
both valid SDK requests returned `invalid params`. Both are now decoded from
content blocks, with the structured half serialized rather than dropped, clamped
to the wire bound instead of refused by it.

Adds 4 card-lifetime regression tests driving the real provider socket, and
raises the suites to 31 daemon / 19 card / 56 provider cases.

fix(daemon): make a purged session's pod and volume actually go with it (#2031)

* feat(daemon): give back the workspace volume of an agent nobody has used

Suspension reclaims an idle agent sandbox's CPU and memory. It reclaims no
storage: the claim keeps a provisioned workspace PVC, and the only path that
ever deleted an agent claim was deleting the agent. Session pods already had a
reclamation path — the retention GC deletes a session's row and its claim
together — so an install accrued exactly one live volume per agent anyone had
ever used, forever. The orphan reconciler cannot collect those: their agents
are alive, which is precisely the case it refuses to touch.

`idle-volume-reaper.ts` is a second sweep in the reconciler CronJob, not a job
of its own, because it needs strictly less than the orphan half: no scheduler,
no lease, no control-plane read — the same claim listing plus one store query.
It collects an agent pod's claim, and the volume with it, only when all four
hold: the claim is an agent pod's and no session pod of that agent is present;
its Sandbox reads `operatingMode: Suspended`; the agent has NO session row left
in the shared store; and the claim is older than the window (default 7 days).

The third is the load-bearing one. A session row's existence is what keeps a
session pod's claim (git-workspace-model.md §11), and the retention GC deletes
a row only after judging that session's worktrees — including REFUSING to
delete one that still holds uncommitted or unpushed work. "No session rows"
therefore reads as "session retention has already judged and released every
session of this agent". The agent's own checkout is not judged: the pod is
suspended and judging would mean waking it, which is the cost the sweep exists
to avoid, so the window stands in for that. Two consequences: an install with
`sessions.retention: never` collects nothing, which is correct rather than
broken, and the effective idle time is max(retention, this window).

Deliberately NOT fenced on `last-admitted-at`, unlike the orphan grace: that
stamp means "last seen in use by a member" and a rollout re-stamps every claim
it adopts, so a window of days measured from it would be reset by every deploy
and never elapse. It still fences the DELETE — a wake moves the claim's
resourceVersion and makes the preconditioned delete fail rather than take a
volume a member just woke. Dry-run by default, on its own flag, because this
half collects volumes of agents that still exist.

Also mounts the members' data-plane Secret into that CronJob, read-only. Two of
its three sweeps ask the store a question — which session pods still have a row
(§11), and now which agents have none left — and without the mount
`openSharedStore()` returns undefined, so every session pod read as live and the
store-retention half was skipped outright, a clean-looking run with two sweeps
silently disabled. The render contract asserted the mount must NOT exist ("a
one-shot sweep holds no agent state"), which is what locked that in; it now
asserts the opposite and says why.

* fix(daemon): make a purged session's pod and volume actually go with it

Two things stood between "this session's row is deleted" and "its pod and its
workspace PVC are gone", and both were invisible: one silently disabled the
sweep that is supposed to catch the failures, the other could create a failure

summary line where it should print two, so the backstop for a session pod whose
direct teardown failed has never run in a cluster. The render contract asserted
the mount must NOT exist ("a one-shot sweep holds no agent state"), which is
what locked it in; it now asserts the opposite and says why.

**A purge that could not stop its host abandoned the claim.** The cluster branch
deletes the session row first and then stops the host and deletes the claim, and
that stop was unguarded: a throw escaped the purge, aborted the rest of the
sweep, and left the row gone with the claim alive AND this member's launch still
cached. That last part is the one leak the reconciler can never collect — a
cached launch keeps re-stamping the claim, and a stamp inside the grace reads as
"in use" forever. The stop is now logged rather than thrown, so the claim delete
always follows the row delete and one session's failure is not the next one's.

refactor(protocol): read code-host frame members through one discriminated view (#2040)

* refactor(protocol): read code-host frame members through one discriminated view

The hook, run-report, and rd/msg frames carry `github` and `gitlab` as
optional siblings, and every consumer branches on the sibling it knows.
A third code host would turn those two-way branches into three-way
switches in core code.

Keep the wire exactly as it is (an older peer must keep decoding today's
frames, and a new member is only ever sent to a peer that negotiated its
feature) and add a decode-time view over the members instead:

- `codeHostHookMetadataOf` derives one provider-keyed arm, with the
  rename-stable `(provider, externalId)` repo key, from a frame's
  metadata members and fails closed when a frame carries none or more
  than one;
- `codeHostHookRuleOf` does the same for a compiled `rc/hook-assign`
  rule, whose `kind` names the provider; the two rule members become
  named schemas (`RcGithubHookRule`, `RcGitlabHookRule`) with no wire
  change;
- `pickCodeHostHookMembers` copies the members forward for a frame that
  forwards trusted metadata rather than reading it.

The hook/report and hook/start one-of refinements count the same arms.
Both view types are written as one object type per provider so a
generic reader keeps `provider` and `metadata` correlated without a
cast.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(relay): verify and route Gitea webhook deliveries

`hooks/gitea/` implements `POST /webhooks/gitea` on the GitLab ingress skeleton:
a 1 MiB raw-body cap, a bounded first parse for `repository.id`, a rule lookup by
`(gitea, id)`, then a timing-safe bare-hex HMAC-SHA256 check of `X-Gitea-Signature`
against every matching rule's signing key — which is what keeps a table holding
both the current and the next key lossless mid-rotation. Only then is the body
decoded. Unmatched, malformed, and forged deliveries all answer 404. Gitea sends
no timestamp header, so there is no replay window: the daemon's durable
`(sessionKey, msgId)` inbox and the unique `(hookId, deliveryKey)` run row absorb
retries, keyed on `X-Gitea-Delivery`.

Every routing decision reads `X-Gitea-Event-Type`. The legacy `X-Gitea-Event` is
lossy in both directions — it collapses the sync and reviewer-request types into
`pull_request`, and labels a review `pull_request_comment`, which is also an
ordinary timeline comment's own type — so it is never consulted.

The mapping normalizes to the provider-neutral pattern universe: `issues:opened`,
`merge_request:opened`, `merge_request:synchronize` (`pull_request_sync`),
`merge_request:review_requested` (only when `requested_reviewer` names the bot,
the one event type where that field means what its name says), `note:created` for
issue and pull-request timeline comments, `push`, and the relay-authored
maintenance pair `issues:closed` / `merge_request:merged`. A review submission
arrives as one delivery carrying only the summary, so it normalizes to
`review:commented`, `review:approved`, or `review:changes_requested` — the verdict
is the only part of the correlation the relay can carry — and is gated by the
pull-request comment family rather than by an event pattern. Edited-comment noise,
draft toggles, label churn, and assignment are vetoed as they are for GitLab.

Gates: the bot's own deliveries never re-trigger, except a same-repository
revision it authored, which stays relay-trusted like a push; cadence, comment
families, and the mention gate run before the live `rc/codehost-membership-authz`
call, which carries the actor's login beside its numeric id because Gitea looks a
permission up by name. An external pull request never starts automatically — its
author fails the gate and a denied revision leaves a durable, actionable row.
Maintenance deliveries bypass the actor gate and open no model turn.

Session keys are `gitea:<repoId>:<issue|pull>:<index>` and
`gitea:<repoId>:push:<ref>`, always from the signed subject and a positive index,
never a display path or a delivery id. `dispatchGiteaRerun` serves the `gitea` arm
of `rc/hook-rerun` through the same dispatch path.

Fixtures are shaped by real captured deliveries and carry only synthetic
identifiers.

* fix(daemon): clear a Gitea review lock from durable coordinates

The ambiguous_locked exit depended on an in-memory map owned by the
process that made the ambiguous request: after a daemon restart, or when
the next attempt ran on another daemon, a refused attempt never checked

* fix(control-plane): keep the newest Gitea head current when an older run reports late

The status coordinator superseded every other head on every lifecycle
edge, so a terminal report from an older head that arrived after a newer
head had been accepted superseded the newer head and then revived its own
row through the same-run upsert and a terminal setDesired.

Rank heads by their run's acceptance (HookRun.startedAt, stored as the
projection's queuedAt on every edge): the coordinator establishes the row
first, then supersede(..., acceptedAt) preempts only strictly older heads,
the caller's own row included when a newer head is already there, and
setDesired and the mid-write parking path refuse a superseded row. An edge
whose row already belongs to a newer run of the same head moves nothing.

feat(daemon): a bridge tool asks its own host instead of guessing (#2016)

On the ACP wire we are the client and every chat surface renders the card (#1794).
On the MCP wire the role is reversed: the daemon is the server, and its tools
resolve missing information by inference or by failing. This adds the MECHANISM
for a tool to ASK the agent's own host (Claude Code, Codex) instead. It ships with
no product call site: the tools that will ask land in the changes that follow, so
nothing in the shipped tool set changes behaviour with this piece alone.

`capabilities.elicitation` is a CLIENT capability no server may declare, so
`bridge.ts`'s `{ capabilities: { tools: {} } }` is unchanged. What the bridge does
instead is READ the client's declaration, by the server SDK's own lenient pre-mode
rule — a bare `elicitation: {}` counts as form support, which is exactly what the
Claude harness sends, so a strict `elicitation.form` read would have disabled every
ask on that runtime while codex kept working.

The mechanism is a RETURN VALUE, never a daemon→bridge request: the MCP IPC has one
undiscriminated id space minted only by the bridge, so an inverted direction would
collide with a live tool call's id. `askHost` throws `AskRequired`, the control
server answers the frame with an `mcpAsk` marker, and the bridge turns that into the
SDK's `input_required` result — which on this 2025-era connection the SDK's own shim
fulfils as a server→client `elicitation/create` before re-calling the tool.

Four rules the seam enforces:

- the emitted `requestedSchema` carries no root key beyond type/properties/required,
  because codex re-parses it with a deny-unknown-fields type and a root `title`
  alone kills the forward inside codex core before ACP ever sees it;
- the guard against an OLD in-sandbox bridge (image skew is the normal case) is
  structural, in `McpControlServer.handle`: a tool can only mint an ask through
  `deps.ask`, and that port exists only when the frame declared a form-capable host;
- a tool may only ask BEFORE it does observable work, or must be safe to replay —
  the answer arrives on a fresh `tools/call` that re-runs the whole handler;
- a decline is a usable tool error, and the ask leg's timeout is pinned to 120s
  rather than inheriting the SDK's 600s default, so the replayed round meets the
  turn gate rather than a long-dead turn.

With no product caller yet, the seam is proven end to end by a test-only tool
(`test/ask-stub-tool.ts`) routed through the real `executeTool` — which is also how
it reaches the ask port `McpControlServer` injects per call, the thing under test.
`shareFile` takes no destination by design and `sendMessage`'s target channel is
required input, so neither guesses; `sendMessage` is out of this seam's scope by
product decision and raises no card, filed separately.

fix(webchat): make MCP Apps work against a real third-party app (#2088)

* fix(webchat): make MCP Apps work against a real third-party app

Tested against a genuine published app — openwork's `get-time`, which inlines the
official MCP Apps SDK — rather than against a template we wrote ourselves. Four
of the five things that stopped it were bugs in the shipped feature, and one was
a limit derived from the wrong number.

THE TEMPLATE COULD NOT ARRIVE. A real app's template is several hundred KiB (this
one is 328) because it inlines the SDK, and the card carried it inline in one
`rd/chat` frame — which is capped at 256 KiB, so the cap was not merely low, it
was below the floor of what a real app is. Templates past 48 KiB now arrive as
ordered `app_template` chunks on the same stream and are reassembled by the
browser, so the document cap (1 MiB) can describe what a page may reasonably be
instead of what one frame happens to hold. The frame is armed only once the
declared `htmlBytes` has been assembled: handing an iframe half a document
renders a broken page, which is the outcome the cap existed to avoid.

THE CSP WAS NEVER IN FORCE. Every real template is a complete document, and the
policy was PREPENDED to it — which drops the doctype (quirks mode) and lands the
meta outside `<head>`, where browsers do not honor `http-equiv` CSP at all. So on
exactly the templates §7.2 exists for, the policy was present in the bytes and
enforced by nobody. It is now injected into the head, with the three template
shapes handled explicitly; a bare fragment is wrapped, which also gets it out of
quirks mode. The sandbox's opaque origin always held, so this was a missing
layer rather than an open door.

THE CARD DID NOT PERSIST. §8 said a card "is persisted in the daemon's transcript
as an `app` row". There was no `upsertApp` and no writer — the row was designed
and never written, so every card vanished on reload. Adds `LocalStore.upsertApp`
(the peer of `upsertElicit`), written at open and rewritten at settlement, plus
the console's history rendering for it. The template is deliberately not stored:
history is the record of a decision, not a page to re-run.

AN UNAVAILABLE INTERFACE WAS SILENT. §7.4 said an oversized template "is declined
with a notice"; the code logged a warning and returned, so the reader was
promised an interface, shown nothing, and told nothing. A declared-but-unproducible
interface now declines out loud, while a tool with no interface stays quiet.

And the card header read `get-time` where the server declared "Get Time" — the
upstream `Tool.title` is now used.

Also fixes a leaf-import violation this feature introduced on main: the console
value-imported the protocol barrel, which drags sixty relative modules into its
bundle (`protocol-imports.leaf.test.ts` catches it; I had not re-run the full web
suite after the review fixes). The MCP Apps constants move to a bundler-safe
`protocol/src/mcp-app.ts` leaf that `frames/webchat.ts` imports from, so the
wire's bounds and the browser's are the same numbers by construction.

Verified end to end with the real 328 KiB template: admitted under the cap, 7
chunks whose worst encoded frame is 59 KiB against the 256 KiB limit, reassembled
byte for byte, doctype preserved and the policy parented to HEAD.

`integrationId` it had no way to obtain. They ask the agent's own host instead.

The guard is `ambiguousIntegrations`, which moves here with its first caller: this
session's own bot is the trusted tiebreak, and it is the bot an unqualified
`sendMessage` resolves to, so the ids a read returns stay reachable. A same-platform
multi-bot session therefore asks nothing and reads its own bot's history — strictly
better than the empty list it used to get — and the ask is left to the case with no
tiebreak at all: a cross-platform read where the agent has several bots on the target
platform and none of them owns this conversation.

Making the answer matter needed a prerequisite in the same change: `observedChannels`
and `observedUsers` took only `(agentId, platform)`, so a named bot had nowhere to go.
They now take an `integrationId`, and the daemon resolves it to that ONE bot's
`transportScope` — what the session store's history has always been keyed by (a session
that spanned several bots carries a `mixed:` scope and belongs to none of them).

Three consequences worth stating: an explicitly passed `integrationId` now scopes the
fallback too, which is the very repair the note used to ask for and then ignore;
`listChannels` reads a delivered answer BEFORE the live enumeration, because the
replayed round would otherwise spend a second platform API call on a list the asking
round already found empty; and an answer lives only in the SDK's per-call state, so a
later `tools/call` asks the same human again — accepted, and softened by reporting an
empty human-disambiguated read as that bot's empty history rather than as a
platform-wide `[]` the model would want to retry.

feat(daemon): a cross-platform call asks which bot to act as (#2022)

The second consumer of the ask mechanism (#1965 Gap A), and the resolution itself.
`resolveGatewayForPlatform` ended in
`candidates.find((i) => i.id === ctx.integrationId) ?? candidates[0]`: for a
same-platform call the first arm keeps the session put, which is right, but for a
genuine cross-platform call with several bots on the target platform the fallback took
whichever came first, silently. That was the audit's only silent WRONG answer —
everything else unresolved in the bridge either throws or defaults to something a tool
descriptor documents. The resolver can now ask instead, behind the same
`ambiguousIntegrations` guard, which stops about fifteen read and action tools guessing
at once. The `ctx.platform` action tools are inside that set, not outside it:
`ctx.integrationId` is optional (a memory-only turn, a cron wake, a session resumed
after a restart registers without one), so a session that NO bot owns makes the guard
non-empty on its own platform too.

The ask is OPT-IN. Only a call site that passes `ask: true` puts a card in front of a
human; every other one of the function's ~16 callers keeps today's first-candidate pick
BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by remembering to switch a default off — an opt-out default
would mean any call site added later silently acquires a human-facing card, which is
exactly the failure this seam already produced once on `listChannelMembers`.
`sendMessage` is the one caller that does not opt in, and it is untouched here: its
effect is visible and irreversible, so a card that steers it is a product question
`docs/product-conventions.md` would have to admit first, filed separately.

The ask lives in the resolver, not at its call sites: the function is synchronous, and
making it async-and-three-outcomes would oblige every caller to propagate a question it
has nothing to say about. `AskRequired` is a typed sentinel `McpControlServer` catches
centrally, so the helper raises it and stays synchronous.

THE OFFER IS THE TRUSTED SNAPSHOT AND NOTHING ELSE — in particular not the subset whose
connection is live at this instant. `gatewayFor` may rotate, so a liveness-filtered
enum is computed from a value that can differ between the round that mints the card and
the round that carries its answer: pick B, lose B's connection while the card is open,
and the answering round finds B outside its freshly filtered enum, discards the human's
answer as un-offered, and acts as A. That is the very silent wrong bot this ask exists
to remove, reachable on the visible-effect tools too (a reaction posted as the wrong bot
cannot be taken back), so the offer is round-stable instead. The untrusted-input guard
is unchanged in force — an id outside the session snapshot is still refused — and a
chosen bot that cannot act by the time the answer lands fails with the ordinary
`no live connection` naming the id the human chose, the same error an explicit
`integrationId` would have got. It is also what lets the resolver and the
history-backed reads share one key honestly: both legs now offer the identical set.

A question the ask must not put is one no answer can repair, and the rule is positional:
a refusal derived from the ARGUMENTS ALONE reads the same whichever bot the human names,
so it belongs ABOVE the ask. Its sharpest form is the channel default — a call whose
`channel` defaults in only for this session's own bot cannot be repaired by ANY answer
when no channel was named, because the ask fires exactly when no candidate owns this
conversation, which is exactly when `channel` becomes required — so `askOnlyWithChannel`
opts in only when a channel was named. The same rule hoists the argument checks of
`createConversation` (`name`/`users`), `scheduleMessage` (`postAt` and its two bounds)
and `updateCanvas` (per-edit shape) above their resolve: each otherwise spent a card, and
one of the two rounds the bridge allows, to arrive at the message the call always gave.

`listChannels` names its bot on the LIVE branch too, not only the observed one. A live
channel list is one bot's ids as much as a remembered one is, and moving the ask above
the enumeration is exactly what makes a human-chosen bot's live list reachable — so
without the id there the model would hold chat ids only reachable through a bot the next
unqualified call does not pick. Same rule as #2020's: omitted only where nothing was
picked, which is a single bot on that platform.

ONE key per platform per tool call (`integrationId.<platform>`), shared with the
history-backed reads, because the bridge allows two rounds per call and `listChannels`
does both halves. The key is shared; the message is not — each caller passes the verb
phrase the card names. Sharing it also deleted the read-the-answer-before-enumerating
workaround: the ask now sits ABOVE the live call, so the asking round spends no platform
call and the answering round spends exactly one, on the bot the human named.

A decline, a cancel, an answer naming an id we never offered, and a host that cannot
render a card all keep the first-candidate pick.

feat(mcp): let a CP-managed provider be daemon-hosted, so its interfaces render (#2090)

* feat(mcp): let a CP-managed provider be daemon-hosted, so its interfaces render

MCP Apps shipped reading DAEMON-LOCAL config only, so a provider registered in the
console could never render an interface no matter what it declared. This closes
that: `ui` becomes a real field on the provider, projected onto the pushed
definition, and the daemon's Apps host resolves servers per organization.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY IN THE WAY. Three things, and only the third was the one the
design doc named:

1. The wire could not express it — `McpServerSpec` had no `ui` field at all, so
   the CP had no way to say it even if it knew.
2. The CP had nowhere to keep it: no column, no API field, no projection.
3. The Apps host read `this.mcpServerDefs` (local config), while CP definitions
   live behind `cpMcpDefs.effective(orgId)` — a path it never consulted.

THE STATED REASON FOR THE LIMIT WAS HALF WRONG, and the doc is corrected rather
than quietly amended. §4 claimed hosting a CP definition would move a CREDENTIAL
BOUNDARY. It does not: a CP provider is pushed as a relay-proxy def whose `url`
is the relay and whose `headers` carry a scoped grant key, while the upstream url
and upstream secrets never leave the relay — and the daemon already holds that
grant key, because it hands it to the runtime today. Hosting it exposes nothing
new.

What was real is the ORG SCOPE. A connection may not be keyed by server name
alone: two organizations can each have a `charts` pointing at different proxies
under different grants, and one map keyed by name would let one org's connection
answer the other's calls. Connections are now keyed by `(orgId, name)` and every
host method takes the org it resolved in — including the view bridge, which reads
it off the card rather than re-deriving it.

Two consequences fall out. CP definitions arrive with `register/ok`, not at
construction, so only local servers can be warmed at startup and
`onMcpDefsChanged` warms the rest as they land — keeping the dial off the path of
the next session's synchronous tool composition. And nothing about the relay
needed changing: its proxy forwards JSON-RPC verbatim with no method allowlist,
so `resources/read`, the extension negotiation and `_meta.ui` already passed
through.

THE FLAG IS EXPLICIT, AND NOT BECAUSE DETECTION IS IMPOSSIBLE. A daemon could
dial a provider once and read `_meta.ui` off its tool list. The reason is that the
flag decides who CONNECTS, and connecting is what renames the server's tools to
`<server>__<tool>`; detection would let an upstream's later change silently
re-home a server and rename tools underneath an agent whose prompt names them.
Probing to DEFAULT the field is the natural follow-up and needs this column
either way — it is what stops the decision moving on its own.

* fix(mcp): warm a pushed definition, share a local one, re-dial a rotated grant

Three ways a daemon-hosted provider could be present and still never work,
found in review. Each regression test was confirmed to fail against the previous
commit.

THE RECONNECT SNAPSHOT NEVER ANNOUNCED ITSELF. `applyReconcileSnapshot` converged
CP definitions without calling `onMcpDefsChanged`, and that is the path EVERY
daemon start takes — so a `ui: true` definition arrived, was stored, and had its
connection dialed only if some later unrelated push happened to report a change.
Its tools were simply missing from every session until then.

A DAEMON-LOCAL SERVER WAS HIDDEN FROM CP-MANAGED AGENTS. Connections were keyed by
the CALLER'S org, but a local definition is one server every organization shares:
warmed under the local scope, it could never be found by a lookup from an org, so
a CP-managed agent silently lost its local UI tools. Connections are now keyed by
the definition's OWNING scope — an org for a CP-pushed definition, nothing for a
local one — which also stops two organizations sharing a connection authorized
for only one of them.

A ROTATED GRANT KEPT THE OLD BEARER. `connect()` returned the cached client
without comparing the definition it was dialed for. The CP rotates a proxy def's
bearer while its name and url stay put, so the connection went on presenting a
credential the relay had already retired — and outliving sessions, it failed new
ones too. A connection now carries its definition's fingerprint and is re-dialed
when that changes.

The scope and fingerprint decisions are exported as pure functions and tested
directly: the connection cache cannot be populated without a real dial, so
testing them through it would have needed a client seam extracted for tests
alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(mcp): a rotating grant must not join the dial it is replacing

The fingerprint guard only covered a COMPLETED connection. A dial already in
flight was joined by any caller, including one that wanted a different
definition — so a grant rotated mid-dial waited on the attempt carrying the key
it was replacing. When the retired grant is refused, as it is once revoked, the
fresh definition never got a dial of its own and the provider stayed absent from
every later session.

A running attempt now records which definition it is dialing and is joinable only
by a caller wanting that one; anything else starts its own. Installing moved out
of `dial` and into `connect`, which owns the cache and can therefore refuse a
superseded attempt that succeeds anyway — it is closed rather than left open, and
never overwrites the fresher connection.

The regression test drives the ordering directly (old dial open, definition
rotated, second dial started, retired grant refused) by overriding `dial` on the
instance rather than adding an injection seam to production. Confirmed to fail
against 2749fda: one dial attempt instead of two.

fix(daemon): cancel a turn whose runtime has gone silent (#2085)

* fix(daemon): cancel a turn whose runtime has gone silent

A model request that stalls at the network layer — a live TCP connection, no
bytes arriving — hung a turn forever: the session stayed `prompting`, every
later message queued behind it, and nothing noticed. The idle sweep skipped
it deliberately, because a running prompt keeps the SDK-lifecycle lease busy.
Recovery meant killing the runtime, clearing acpSessionId in SQLite by hand,
and restarting the daemon.

- Stall watchdog: each in-flight prompt records its last runtime signal (the
  prompt going out, any session/update, an SDK lifecycle message, a human
  answering its card). The idle sweep checks those stamps; past
  `limits.turnStallTimeoutMs` (30 min default, 0 disables) the daemon logs a
  warning naming the session, posts the same "Agent failed to respond" notice
  a failed turn gets, and cancels through the `!stop` path — session/cancel,
  the cancelBackstopMs force-stop if the runtime ignores it, queued messages
  fail-stopped. A pending permission or elicitation card does not count
  against the budget.
- Safe recovery: a prompt rejected with "Session not found" drops the host's
  claim and clears the row's acpSessionId, so the next message opens a fresh
  session instead of repeating the failure.
- 'stalled' joins TurnInterruptReason; daemon-detailed-design.md §7.3
  documents the knob, the transition, and the mechanism.

Closes #1915

  approval meter into syncApprovalActivity, which every card kind reaches when
  its gate closes — ordinary forms and URL consent included — so an answered

- The exact turn is owned before any I/O: tripStalledTurn suppresses its

feat: OAuth-authorized custom MCP providers (#2095)

* fix(relay): contain an upstream MCP auth challenge at the proxy

The MCP proxy relayed an upstream 401/403 verbatim — `www-authenticate` was
never in STRIP_RESPONSE_HEADERS. That hands the agent's MCP client the
upstream's own RFC 9728 challenge, so it runs the upstream's OAuth discovery
against the proxy url: it learns the upstream identity the proxy exists to
hide, and the `Authorization` it eventually presents is stripped by
forwardRequestHeaders along with the grant key, killing the provider for that
session. Reachable today with a wrong API key on a custom provider.

Contain it the same way an upstream 3xx already is: strip
`www-authenticate`/`proxy-authenticate` and answer an opaque 502. The injected
credential is the binding's, so a rejection is the CP's to repair, never the
caller's. The relay's own grant-key 401s stay 401 so the two remain
distinguishable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(control-plane): SSRF-guarded outbound HTTP for CP-originated calls

MCP-provider OAuth makes the CP dial hosts a console user typed — protected-resource
metadata, authorization-server metadata, dynamic client registration, and every
token/refresh exchange. Until now the CP only fast-failed such a url at write time
(`blockedUpstreamUrl`) and left the authoritative egress guard to the relay.

Restate the relay's two guarantees for CP egress: refuse a name if ANY resolved address
is unreachable from the public internet, and pin the socket to the address that was
validated so it cannot be re-resolved between check and connect. A 3xx comes back as an
ordinary response rather than being followed, since following it re-resolves past the
pin. Failures are opaque reason codes, because a request built here carries client
secrets, authorization codes and refresh tokens that must never reach a log line.

The allowlist is the CP's own deploy permission, never the relay's — the two egress
permissions must not be merged. No caller yet; the OAuth discovery module lands next.

* feat(control-plane): MCP authorization discovery and client registration

The client half of the MCP 2026-07-28 authorization spec, as pure logic over an
injected dial so every branch is unit-testable without a network.

Discovery is three steps, each a normative MUST and each one a place where being
slightly wrong fails silently much later: POST an unauthenticated `initialize` and read
the Bearer challenge (a GET misses most servers); fetch protected-resource metadata from
the challenge pointer or the well-known fallback order; then fetch authorization-server
metadata by the spec's exact URL priority, refusing any document whose `issuer` is not
byte-identical to the one the URL was built from.

`resource` canonicalization cuts both ways and the direction is easy to reverse: the
published string goes out verbatim as the RFC 8707 audience, while deciding whether a
document describes the registered url ignores a single trailing slash. Getting the second
one strict is how a provider completes authorization and then never presents its token —
the same trap `http/oauth/base.ts` records from the server side.

Registration prefers operator-supplied credentials and falls back to RFC 7591 DCR.
Client IDs are bound to their issuer, so a moved authorization server means re-register,
never retry. Client ID Metadata Documents belong between the two and are not in P1;
the metadata already carries the capability flag for them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(control-plane): persistence for a provider's CP-held OAuth grant

The `auth` mode on a provider row (headers | oauth2) plus the three tables an OAuth
grant needs, on the GitlabConnection pattern: non-secret discovery and client state in
`mcp_provider_oauth`, the sealed client secret and token pair in a side-table no DTO
read can reach, and one-shot start → begin → callback rows carrying a sealed PKCE
verifier and the issuer recorded for the RFC 9207 comparison.

Two properties the whole design rests on are enforced in the repo's transactions
rather than above it. A token pair is only ever published together with the
`tokenVersion` it was minted against, so no reader observes a connected row holding a
stale or missing pair. And every write that changes user intent — prepare, connect,
disconnect — advances that version, so a refresh already in flight loses its CAS
instead of resurrecting a grant that was just replaced or revoked. Re-running the
funnel therefore voids a pair minted against the old client identity, which is what the
spec's authorization-server binding rule requires.

`resource` is its own column rather than being derived from `McpProvider.url`: the
authorization server matches the string it published, byte for byte.

14 integration tests cover the CAS, the lease hand-off on expiry, the org fence through
the parent provider, and the once-only browser binding and consumption of a state row.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(control-plane): the authorization request, token exchanges, and token custody

Three pieces, all pure over an injected dial.

`authorize.ts` builds the authorization request — PKCE S256, and the RFC 8707 `resource`
on the authorization request as well as the token one — and implements RFC 9207 issuer
validation as the spec tabulates it, including the deliberate row where a present `iss`
is compared even from a server that never advertised the capability. The comparison is
byte-exact: no case folding, no trailing-slash or default-port normalization. It gates
error responses too, so a mismatched error is never displayed or acted on.

`token-endpoint.ts` redeems a code and renews a grant. Its failure taxonomy is
load-bearing rather than cosmetic: a 4xx is a definitive refusal and means the grant is
dead, while an unreachable server or a 5xx means we learned nothing and must not flip a
working provider into reauth_required over a blip.

`token-service.ts` is the custody, on the LinearTokenService pattern because the hazard
is the same — refreshing may rotate the refresh token, and spending a rotated one twice
strands the organization. Single-flight per provider collapses concurrent callers into
one upstream call; a database lease plus a tokenVersion CAS elects the one durable
writer, since a refresh token outlives the process; and the pair is persisted before any
caller sees it. A lost CAS takes the peer's write rather than re-applying its own. The
refresh margin is half the token's observed lifetime rather than a constant, because a
fixed skew tuned for a two-hour token is useless for a five-minute one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(control-plane): the three-hop MCP provider authorization funnel

`McpProviderOauthService`, on the `gitlab/oauth.service.ts` shape and for its reasons.
Start is authenticated: it discovers, resolves a client identity, records what it learned
and mints a one-shot state row holding a sealed PKCE verifier plus the issuer the response
will be compared against. Begin is an unauthenticated top-level navigation that stamps a
browser-binding cookie exactly once before redirecting. Callback consumes the row once,
requires the same browser, validates the RFC 9207 `iss` — before acting on an error
response, so a mismatched error is never shown — redeems the code, and commits the grant.

Two refusals that look pedantic and are not. A grant with no refresh token is rejected
rather than stored: it would work for an hour, then fail with nothing able to repair it
and no way for an operator to tell that from the server being down. And a deployment with
no PUBLIC_CP_URL is refused up front rather than deriving an origin from request headers,
because the redirect_uri is registered once and cannot change afterwards.

A client identity is reused across re-runs when the issuer is unchanged, and re-registered

would ever unassign it. That is a revocation bypass. The chain moved to its own module for
this second consumer, re-exported where routes already import it.

A refresh re-pushes the RELAY binding only, with every active grant hash. Re-pushing the

* fix(control-plane): five defects review found in the OAuth path

All five reproduce; each fix ships with the test that shows it.

everything it returns, so a server that declines to rotate handed back a plaintext value
that went straight into the commit — silently stripping its at-rest encryption on the
first such refresh under a real cipher. It is re-sealed like a fresh one now.

sweep applies `refreshDue`, the same predicate the resolve path uses, so the two cannot
disagree about what is due.

definition is the agent-facing proxy url and grant key, neither of which a disconnect
changes, so every enabling daemon lost the server until some unrelated sync ran.

has no static headers, so either operation republished its binding with no Authorization
at all. Every live publication now resolves through the one auth-aware resolver; a
provider with no grant publishes its definition and no binding, because a binding with an
empty credential is worse than none.

fenced on the generation its funnel started at — the same discipline as a refresh commit,
for the same reason: the exchange takes real time and intent can change inside it.

fix(cli): make Linux daemon services survive logout and reboot (#2102)

* fix(cli): make Linux daemon services survive logout and reboot

The Linux unit was installed under `~/.config/systemd/user` and started with
`systemctl --user enable --now`. With `Linger=no`, logind stops the user manager
once the last login session ends, and `Restart=always` cannot revive a daemon
whose manager is gone: closing the last SSH connection took the daemon offline
and reconnecting brought it back, so it read as intermittently offline.

Install a system unit instead — `/etc/systemd/system/<unit>`, `User=<the
operator's account>`, `WantedBy=multi-user.target` — so only the unit file
belongs to root while agent execution keeps the ordinary user's permissions.

Privilege stays confined to the two commands that change what is installed.
`install-service` and `uninstall-service` re-execute themselves through sudo;
`up`/`down`/`restart` remain unprivileged via a polkit rule scoped to one unit
name, one account, and the lifecycle verbs. `enable`/`disable` are outside that
rule — boot persistence is an install-time decision, which is why install does
the `enable` and `up` only needs `start`. Hosts without a polkit rules.d backend
are detected and told that `up`/`down` will need sudo there.

The elevated argv is rebuilt from resolved intent rather than rewritten from the
caller's, so no option-parsing quirk can cross the sudo boundary; `sudo -E` is
avoided so the invoking user's environment never reaches a root process. `PATH`
travels as an argument because sudo's `secure_path` replaces the environment
one, and `sudo -n true` is probed first so a passwordless-less non-TTY run
refuses with the exact command instead of blocking on an invisible prompt.

Discovery now scans both scopes, so an existing per-user install stays fully
drivable. `install-service` retires it first and unelevated — `systemctl --user`
reaches only the caller's own manager — and refuses outright if one is still
present when already elevated, so a single root is never driven by two enabled
units. Lingering is never enabled or disabled: it is shared by all of that
account's services.

Because a unit is enabled at install, `down` on a system unit now means stop
now, not stop and stay down across a reboot; `uninstall-service` retires an
instance. macOS launchd behaviour is unchanged.

Closes #2051

* fix(cli): chmod root-written service files and hand <root> back to the daemon account

`writeFileSync`'s `mode` is masked by the umask, so under `umask 077` the system
unit and the polkit rule both landed 0600. A 0600 unit is unreadable by the daemon

fix(control-plane): refuse a pin to a pool Pod by identity, not by membership (#2114)

`assertDaemonNotInSet` read the pool's membership row under the daemon fence, and
the enrolment took the same fence but never looked at pins. The lock only ordered
the two writers; it refused nothing. When a pin reached the lock first, both
committed, and an agent ended up pinned to a Pod the reconciler retires without
notice.

daemon — and no enrolment changes it. The guard now reads that instead of the
membership row, so a Pod is refused before it enrols, the placement transaction no
longer waits on the daemon fence, and `pinnable` on the daemon DTO becomes the same
predicate the console already uses for `cloud`, dropping a pool-set lookup from the
daemon reads.

The race test this made order-dependent — green only when the enrolment won the
lock, which is what usually happened, and red on CI when it did not — becomes a
deterministic one: a pin is refused before and after enrolment. The one test that
relied on pinning through the window activates its agent directly instead.

* fix(mcp-oauth): let a path-less issuer differ from its metadata by a trailing slash

feat(slack): let the session lifecycle acknowledge a turn, reacting only when it could not (#2134)

A behaviour change, with the product convention changed alongside it. "A trigger is
acknowledged before it is answered" (docs/product-conventions.md) had every platform place
a 👀 reaction on the triggering message (#1537). On Slack the daemon already produces a
durable turn-start signal — the agent-session lifecycle marks the thread "is working…" with
the Stop control for the whole turn and withdraws it when the turn ends — so a Slack turn
showed two acknowledgements, and the one that never goes away stayed on every answered
message, in workspaces where 👀 already carries a meaning between people.

The convention now reads: the reaction is the default acknowledgement, and Slack's lifecycle
indicator IS the acknowledgement where Slack confirms it took the `processing` write; the
reaction falls back in only when that write was refused, so a Slack turn never shows neither.
A typing hint is not an indicator in this sense, so Telegram and Discord react as before, and
code-host turns are untouched.

Implementation: `SlackConnection.setStatus` (and `setSessionLifecycle`) now resolve `true`
when Slack accepted the write or the slot already showed that state, `false` when the call
failed — the failure is still absorbed, only reported. `showActivity` returns that outcome
for Slack and `false` for every transient indicator; the turn start hands it to
`acknowledgeTrigger`, which on Slack reacts only when it resolves `false` or rejects, and
elsewhere reacts at once as before. Other `showActivity` callers ignore the promise as they
always did.

fix(cluster): let an ACP write survive a shim channel renewal (#2136)

A bug fix for a cluster agent that stops answering for good after one unlucky credential renewal: every turn — new sessions and replies alike — failed with `⚠️ Agent failed to respond: shim channel renewed` for hours while the sandbox pod sat there healthy, until someone deleted the pod by hand.

The shim credential renews at half its TTL, and `ShimSession.attach` aborts the requests in flight on the socket it replaces. That is documented and correct: the reply was lost, ask again (`ShimChannelLostError` is typed for exactly that). The ACP stdin write is the one caller that could not act on it. Its request rides inside the `WritableStream.write` of `createRemoteRuntime`, and a `WritableStream` that rejects a write stays errored — every later `write()` rejects with the same stored error object. The `ShimSession` survives the renewal, the runtime never exits, so `AcpHost` stays warm on a dead stdin and every subsequent turn dies on its first byte.

Asking again is only safe if the pod can tell a re-send from a new write — ND-JSON applied twice is a corrupted frame. Terminating the ACP stream is not acceptable (it ends the runtime, and the write in flight is usually the turn), so this stream buys the missing property instead:

- `shim/acp-stream.ts` — chunks carry an optional per-stream `seq`.
- `shim/acp-runner.ts` — a `seq` is applied at most once, recorded after the write so a failed write is still owed. Chunk writes run in arrival order so a re-send cannot overtake the attempt it duplicates.
- `shim/client.ts` — the `open` reply announces `resumableWrites: true`. Against a shim that predates it the daemon must not ask twice.
- `k8s/remote-runtime.ts` — writes are numbered; a write rejected with `ShimChannelLostError` is re-sent unchanged once the session is attached. When it cannot be re-sent the runtime is ended deliberately, closing the sandbox stream first so no adapter is orphaned in the pod, and `reapTerminalHost` respawns on the next message.
- `shim/session.ts` — `waitForAttach(timeoutMs)`.

Backward compatible in both directions: an older shim ignores `seq` and does not announce, so the daemon falls back to the terminal path; an older daemon never sends `seq`, so the new shim's dedupe is inert. `docs/designs/cluster-spawn-and-shim.md` §6 gains a subsection on why the ACP stream re-sends where the tunnels terminate.

fix(mcp): read a native surface's intent from ACP's specified content channel (#2144)

* fix(mcp): read a native surface's intent from ACP's specified content channel

A Console dialog opened from webchat never appeared on a `dsh-acp` agent — and
`dsh-acp` is what the built-in AgentConnect agent runs on, so every
configureIntegration / installSkill / manageAgentTools card was silently lost.
Not one `app` row exists across 1888 recorded tool calls.

`nativeUiFromToolUpdate` read the intent out of `rawOutput`, which ACP defines as
`unknown` — a passthrough of whatever the harness's own tool layer produced. Each
adapter therefore leaks its own internal shape: codex-acp a `{result, error}`
envelope, claude-acp bare content blocks, and dsh-acp
(`@openma/deepseek-harness-acp`) a flattened `{output: "<text>", isError}` that
drops `structuredContent` entirely. The reader recognized the first two, so the
third fell through and returned undefined.

ACP does specify a channel for this: `content: ToolCallContent[]`. All three
adapters populate it with the same wrapped text block, and the intent was sitting
there the whole time. Read it first, keeping every `rawOutput` spelling as a
fallback so the adapters that do carry structure keep their fast path.

Two smaller repairs alongside:

- A text candidate was capped at 4096 chars, but a write tool's card rides beside
  its own full record — an observed `createAgent` envelope is 6157. The cap is now
  the card's own budget.
- The projection returned silently when it found no intent, which is why this
  survived so long. A result that names a `ui://agentconnect/` surface and still
  yields nothing now warns, scanning only the text candidates the reader itself
  looks at rather than stringifying a result that can hold a whole file.

* test: anonymize fixtures copied out of a real environment

Four test files used values taken from a running deployment rather than
reserved examples: in-cluster Service origins and a namespace in the key-server
address table, host home-directory paths in two link-flattening suites, and a

which resolve nothing and never leave the process. The link suites assert the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): let a model credential outlive the session it belongs to

The daemon asked for a one-hour credential, and a session that stays
continuously busy never gets to replace it: the refresh is checked when a turn
asks for a host, and skipped while the session's SDK work is still live — a
started host is authoritative for its whole working life, and nothing swaps a
runtime out from under work in flight. So the credential a session starts with
is the one it keeps, and an hour later that session dies mid-run.

Default to a hundred years instead, and stop treating `exp` as the control. Any
finite window breaks exactly the sessions that matter most, and a larger finite
number only moves the date it happens on. What stops traffic is the gateway's
per-request question to the issuer, which reads the org's standing rather than
anything about the credential.

The window is now a deployment choice rather than a constant:
`--key-server-ttl <seconds>` / `KEY_SERVER_TTL_SECONDS`, alongside the two
key-server settings already there. The issuer may only narrow, so lowering it
always binds and raising it past the issuer's ceiling does nothing. A value that
is not a positive integer is ignored with a warning naming the window actually
in force, rather than refusing to start a daemon whose other agents are fine.

The tradeoff is recorded in key-server.md §3 rather than left implicit: nothing
retracts a credential in flight, and the per-request question is org-level, so a
leaked credential stays usable for as long as its org is allowed. The levers
against one are stopping the org and rotating the signing key — which is exactly
what an install that wants a real expiry sets the new flag for.

placement, roster size — which is what the design says it is.

* fix(cluster): let an agent that moved off the pool release its pods, volumes and sessions

An agent moved to another daemon left everything behind and nothing could
collect it: releasing it drops the launches the idle sweep reads and that
sweep is the duty holder's alone, the retention sweep is holder-only too, and
`agent/exists` reports the agent as perfectly alive — while the daemon that
holds it now reads a different store. One pod and one PVC per move, forever.

Two halves. `agent/detach` now suspends the departing agent's own pod and every
session pod it can adopt before releasing them, keeping the claims and volumes;
best effort, never a reason to fail the ACK.

And placement, not existence, is the question the pool's reconciler asks:
`agent/exists` takes `placedOnSetId` and answers `elsewhere`, gated on the new
`agent-placement-v1` server feature, with the set read from `auth/ok` before the
observer registration withdraws that membership. On that answer a departed
agent's claims age out on their own window (`AC_MOVED_AGENT_GRACE_MS`, default
7 days — a move is reversible by design and the volume left behind is that
promise, so this is where the promise ends), its expired session rows are purged
through the ordinary `deleteSession`, and its store rows collect on a new
`agent-moved` proof beside `agent-gone`. Everything rides the existing dry-run
flags, and a control plane that cannot answer placement leaves the sweep exactly
as it was.

scheduled observer cannot infer an unobserved round trip from the current
placement alone.

placement writer cannot record the columns and forget the clock. `agent/exists`

feat(hooks): trusted users — vouch for a user the role gate would refuse (#2150)

* feat(hooks): trusted users — a maintainer's vouch admits an actor the role gate refuses

Every code-host hook gate keeps its live repository-role check, and now reads one
more thing beside it: a per-repository list of users a maintainer vouched for.
Someone on it fires the repository's hooks exactly as a role-holder would — as the
commenter, as the subject author of an unmentioned continuation, and as the author
of a pull request that would otherwise wait for a maintainer request. Nothing about
the resulting turn changes; the vouch is the same human decision as granting triage
on GitHub, made without touching the repository's own permission model, and it is
the only way on GitLab and Gitea — whose bars are push permissions — to let a
non-committer fire an agent.

Entries are matched by the host's numeric user id, never by login. The console
takes a login; the control plane resolves it through the repository's own
credential and stores the id with the login as a display hint, so a login that
was renamed away vouches for nobody. The list is read only for an actor who fell
below the bar, so a role-holder costs no extra request, and on Gitea a failed
identity re-resolution is never rescued by it.

An explicit @-mention by an actor neither gate admits now earns one fixed-text
reply on its thread, posted by the daemon as a relay-authored maintenance
delivery: no model turn, nothing the actor wrote on the wire, and a per-thread
receipt so a thread is told once. Dispatch is gated on `hook-notice-v1`, since an
older daemon would run the delivery as a prompt.
