fix(gitea): admit team-granted write when the collaborator permission reads back read (#2153)

Gitea 1.24 (go-gitea/gitea#34128) stores a General Access team's flat access
mode as `read` whatever its units grant, and the collaborator permission
lookup answers that flat mode, so every member of an ordinary team was refused
by the membership gate and automatic pull-request reviews never started.

When the flat answer is below write and the actor is not a trusted user, the
gate now lists the repository's teams, keeps those whose `repo.code` unit is
write or above (or whose flat mode is admin/owner), reads each team and then
asks its roster for the login, admitting a 200 that carries the delivered id.
A team the bot cannot read admits nobody; when no qualifying team is readable
the denial logs `team_lookup_unavailable`, since that is the bot's standing
(it must be in the organization's Owners team), not the user's. A token
rejection on a team route still flips the connection as before.

The teams listing is one unpaged body on every supported Gitea version and
answers 405 for a personal repository, which the gate treats as no teams.

Fixes #2148

Co-authored-by: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(daemon): read the whole echo in the ACP write-resume tests, not its first 100 ms (#2156)

The three AcpRunner cases in shim-acp-write-resume.test.ts spawn `cat` as
the runtime, write to its stdin, sleep a fixed 100 ms and then assert what
came back. On a loaded runner `cat` has not echoed anything by then, so the
assertion reads '' — the stable Release run for 00bc89fe4 failed on exactly
that (`expected '' to be 'first\nsecond\n'`).

End the child's stdin and wait for its 'close' instead. `cat` exits on EOF
and 'close' only follows the end of stdout, so every byte the runner wrote
has been echoed before the assertion runs. No timing is left in the check,
and the dedupe assertions get stricter: a duplicate that landed after the
old 100 ms window now fails them too.

fix(daemon): never signal a shim runtime that failed to spawn (#2163)

When the runtime command cannot be spawned (ENOENT), Node leaves
`child.pid` undefined and reports the failure on a later tick. A
`close()` that ran before that tick fell through to `child.kill()`,
which libuv turns into `kill(0, SIGTERM)` for a process that never
started, signalling every process in the shim's own process group.

That ordering is reachable when an `open` for a missing command and a
`close` or `shim/cancel` for the same stream arrive in one socket read,
because both frames are then handled in one macrotask.

`close()` now returns when the child has no pid. A child with a pid
keeps the existing group-then-child signalling, and `finish()` already
guards its group sweep on the pid.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(daemon): run the microsandbox runtime and its helper tunnels through the shim (#2161)

The local microsandbox backend now starts its ACP runtime and serves its
gitcred and mcp helper endpoints through the VM's shim, the shape the cluster
pool already uses: the shim starts with the VM, is granted acp and tunnel,
the runtime runs on createRemoteRuntime and the tunnels on TunnelProxy, and
the guest helper configuration points at the shim's socket paths. The Python
AF_VSOCK socket bridge, the vsock devices on new VMs and the exec-stream ACP
spawn are removed, so there is one microsandbox mode.

Shared code: createRemoteRuntime holds events until the open reply names its
stream, slices writes into 128 KiB numbered frames so a large prompt no longer
exceeds the socket's frame limit, and accepts a cwd; the shim's ACP runner
gains a completeEnv mode used only by a shim started with its identity on
stdin, which only the local VM does. No wire protocol change.

A new "Sandbox (microsandbox VM)" job boots a real VM on pull requests that
touch this path and drives ACP plus both tunnels through cold start, a running
VM and a resume. Measurements are recorded in the pull request.

Preparation for docs/designs/session-executors.md §4, which now states the
unified shape.

fix(daemon): name the session by its outward id on the code-host hook/start barrier (#2166)

While a Gitea review ran, its commit status linked Details to a session the
console could not find. The provider-neutral hook/start barrier that GitLab and
Gitea share sent the runtime's ACP session id; the control plane records that id
on the run and builds the in-progress status (Gitea) or note (GitLab) link from
it, but the console knows a session only by its outward id (session-concept.md
§1.1). The terminal hook/report already translated, so the link healed once the
review finished.

The turn already resolves its outward id once, so the barrier now takes that.
A regression test covers both affected providers, and GitHub's barrier, which
has translated since the outward id was introduced, is pinned alongside.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(relay): apply the CP replay that arrives with rc/registered (#2164)

The CP answers rc/register and immediately replays the relay's pool
configuration: hook rules, HTTP-bot assignments, MCP and memory
bindings. The relay only turns READY in the continuation of its awaited
register request, while the ws client emits every frame of one socket
read synchronously. A replay frame that shared a read with
rc/registered therefore reached onText while the link was still
REGISTERING and was refused with PROTOCOL_STATE, silently on both ends.

A relay that is slow right after it starts hits this. The first rule
the CP replays never reaches its table, and every event for that rule
is answered 202 and dropped until the relay registers again. A pull
request opened in that window gets no review until the CP's
redelivery sweep happens to route the delivery to another relay.

Hold the controls that follow rc/registered and apply them once the
link is READY, after onReady, which clears the memory bindings the
replay restores. The daemon's post-register queue already does the
same. A refused control is now logged; it was invisible before.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(daemon): renew the local VM's shim channel daily, not every five minutes (#2165)

* fix(daemon): renew the local VM's shim channel daily, not every five minutes

Since the local microsandbox backend moved its runtime and helper tunnels
onto the shim, the VM's shim channel renews at half the default ten-minute
binding TTL, like a pool pod's. A renewal ends any tunnel stream with a
daemon-to-guest data frame in flight, and when that stream is the in-VM
MCP bridge's connection the bridge exits and the agent loses its tools
until the harness restarts it.

The local VM's identity is a one-time random token this daemon hands the
shim over stdin, checked by a constant-time compare against the same
in-memory value. A renewal presents that token again, so it re-proves
nothing, and it rotates a session credential that lives in the same shim
process as the token itself. Give the local VM a 24-hour binding TTL so
renewals happen twice a day instead of every five minutes. The pool keeps
the default TTL.

A new test holds a daemon-to-guest tunnel frame in the guest's real shim,
forces a renewal, and shows that stream closing while an idle stream on
the same tunnel survives. A second test pins the VM binding's lifetime.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(daemon): renew the fake VM's shim through its own renewal path

The microsandbox shim harness forced a renewal by closing the guest's
server socket directly. A real half-TTL renewal goes through the shim's
own path, which drops the binding before hanging up. With the socket
closed from outside, the shim kept its binding and kept sending events
into the closing socket, and ws drops those silently.

Under CI load, the ACP renewal test's mid-renewal write sometimes reached
the shim inside that window. The shim applied the write and the runtime
echoed it, but the echo was lost. The daemon's re-send of the write was
then deduplicated by seq, so the echo never arrived and the test timed out.

Delaying guest-to-daemon bytes by 300 ms after the renewal reproduces the
timeout every time with the old fake. With the shim renewing through its
own path, the same delay passes.

feat(memory): conditional entry mutations on native-writable managed homes (#2168)

* feat(memory): conditional entry mutations on native-writable managed homes

The entry interface served create, update and delete only on a home with the
transaction primitive, so a managed tree on the daemon's own disk, in a
sandbox shim, or behind an older Control Plane was read-only through the
console's entry browser and through the createMemoryEntry family the model
already saw advertised. Those homes now serve the same three operations
through the compatibility writer's guarantees: the revision precondition is
checked and the one file replaced under the per-directory lock every
daemon-side writer takes, with the filesystem's absent/mtime guard against an
out-of-band edit, and the stored text is normalized and stamped as every
managed write is. The index and the sidecar change log follow the write as
they do for a compatibility write; the receipt is minted in process and kept
nowhere, so a lost answer is uncertain and never replayed; there is no
source-turn capture fence on such a home. Nothing emulates
atomicTransaction: a home that has it still takes the transactional path,
and both share one precondition and content preparation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(memory): keep the revision fence through a filesystem delete

The filesystem mutation path checked the revision and then removed the
file unconditionally, so a native writer replacing the topic in that gap
would have lost its newer content behind a "completed" conditional delete.

replace: the regular file is re-read right before the unlink and must still
carry the mtime the caller saw. The entry writer deletes only through it,
and a managed view advertises delete on a non-transactional home only when
its port has it, so a sandbox shim or an older peer offers create and update
without delete rather than an unconditional removal. The race test covers
the delete gap beside the update gap, with a distinct mtime per intrusion.

The compatibility writer checks a revision under the daemon's per-directory
lock and guards the replace or unlink with the filesystem's mtime, which
refuses a stale daemon-side write and catches an out-of-band one on a
best-effort basis; it is not the home authority's atomic compare-and-commit,
and the memory system plan says homes without the atomic store do not
advertise that guarantee. A non-transactional managed home now describes
its mutations as last-write-wins: a revision is optional there and checked

behind a verified unlink. A transactional home is unchanged.

unchanged: a shim or older Control Plane can apply the commit and lose its
reply, and the file can change before the log, index or receipt that follow
it fail. Those were mapped to UNAVAILABLE, which a caller may retry, and a

A native dialog reported through the app bridge, so its report expired with the card
that opened it: a reader who pressed Create after the card was settled — by the session
ending, by a fifth card in the conversation, or by the page being closed — got the agent
they asked for and a conversation that never heard about it, waiting on something that
already existed.

name its own sender, so everything it can reach is looked up from the card the daemon
itself opened. A native dialog has no such question to answer — it is the Console's own
form, running on the reader's session under their own JWT — so that gate buys nothing
there and only loses the report. It now reports the way the composer sends, and the way
an approval decision already did: an ordinary webchat turn, addressed by conversation and
agent, with no card in the path.

changes when its live steps become persisted rows, which REMOUNTS the card under a dialog
the reader is still filling in. The old callback belonged to the unmounted instance and
returned at its first line, reporting nothing and showing nothing; the cleanup had already
closed the dialog, and the module-level open-once guard kept the remounted card from
putting it back. Per-open deduplication now lives in the dialog's own closure, and a

carrying the other: a delivered report closes the card, which is what keeps a fresh

feat(session-executors): the executor owns the generation, and nothing needs a shared store (#2197)

Spreading a session no longer depends on a shared data-plane store, which the
daemon opens only under --k8s and shares across every agent on the machine.

  its own environment and persists what it applied. `executor/prepare` carries
  the holder's `launchId` instead, and the `ready` reply names the generation
  the executor allocated. The same launch id returns the same reply with
  nothing rotated; a new one means generation + 1, a fresh key and the old
  pipe closed.

  the Control Plane makes true: the last duty read and the relay's send are
  adjacent with nothing awaited between them, and every relay to one executor
  leaves over its single control connection, so arrival order is
  authorization order. The executor applies prepares in arrival order too.

  gated by neither consent, so a holder can still clean up after a group's
  switch or a machine's share setting goes off.

  and this machine's session retention measured from the last prepare or dial,
  persisted so a restart does not reset the clock.
- `executor/candidates` may name a session, and the answer hints where the
  Control Plane last saw it run, so a successor attaches to the environment
  its predecessor left.

issue #2188 tracks making the store backend a setting of its own.

* docs(send-message): spec an in-thread update form for sendMessage

An agent can read any thread it can reach (`getThreadHistory` is explicitly
for "a thread the agent is NOT answering") and react in one (`addReaction`
takes any channel + messageTs), but cannot write in one. The withheld
capability is the write, and a thread coordinate is no more dangerous in a
post than in a reaction.

The case that makes it concrete is the crossposted message: one request
lands in several channels, the agent answers in one, and the status update
the others are waiting for can only go to each channel's ROOT — detaching it
from the discussion it answers and leaving those threads looking unanswered.

The form was removed for agent-routing reasons (§2.1 covers the current
thread, §2.3/§3.2 cover activation between agents), and neither reason
speaks to placing an update in a human conversation elsewhere.

Specced in §2.4, with the four rules the form actually needs:

- Routing is the ordinary §2.3 ladder, unmuted. The asymmetry with a root
  post is thread state, not safety: a root post reaches nobody because the
  thread it creates has no participants yet.
- Hop is INHERITED from the posting turn. An update minted at depth 0 would
  let a cron-woken agent re-arm a conversation every tick, and §2.3's
  "terminates because it hits a limit" would stop holding.
- Fences are unchanged: per-recipient `!stop`, Off/gated, call policy, and
  no lifting a mute.
- Anchoring answers the return path, which is the real reason the form was
  unsafe: an update joins its author to the thread and seeds a session
  keyed there with the posting session as origin, so a human's reply
  resumes a session with lineage instead of one §8.6 refuses to synthesize.

Refusals never fall back to the root: a non-root thread, a thread-less
platform, and the caller's own thread are each rejected.

Implements send-message-routing-rework.md §2.4. The bare-`channel` branch
takes `thread`, and the post lands inside that conversation instead of at

fix(daemon): compose a placed session's launch in its executor's coordinates (#2203)

A session placed on another machine of the group was composed like a local
one. An unconfined launch inherited the holder's whole environment and a
private-HOME launch named the holder's HOME and XDG paths, so the runtime ran
under a HOME that is a path on the daemon that is not running it. A holder
whose own backend is microsandbox also composed it through its VM path, which
replaces protected credentials with placeholders whose secrets never reach the
executor.

The holder now composes a placed session's HOME, XDG and runtime state roots
on the session HOME its executor seeded (ExecutorPlane.homeFor, beside
mountFor and rootsFor), sends none of its own environment, seeds nothing on
its own disk, and wraps no boundary of its own around it: the executor's
strategy is the boundary. Provider credentials and agent secrets travel as
the launch's values over the TLS-PSK link. The executor's HOME seed now also
answers where that machine keeps a sign-in the HOME only points at (Claude's
credential directory), and its shim fills that in beneath the holder's env.

The coordinate is `append:<epochMs>` (§3.2) — a timestamp, not a counter, because

derived from what survives would reset and re-mint a coordinate whose transcript
is still on disk. It lives in a reservation row resolved by one atomic
INSERT-OR-IGNORE-then-read (§3.3), so two messages arriving together into a
conversation with no session converge on one value rather than minting two; `!new`
will advance it by compare-and-set, and a loser does not advance again.

Where the coordinate is resolved is the load-bearing part (§3.1). It cannot be
stamped at ingress — one inbound message fans out to several agents, and two in
one channel may not share a mode — and it cannot wait for the session manager,
because the durable inbox lane and the serial gate have already keyed on the
result by then. It resolves in the per-target step beside the target's own mute
key and transport scope, and is carried from there: `sessionThreadOf()` is the one
place every session key, transcript coordinate and revision fence reads it.

The delivery coordinate is untouched, so an answer still lands in the room the
message came from. Everything that talks to a provider — chrome, reply targets,
drain narration, thread titles, Telegram's reply chain — keeps reading `thread`,
and the two §6.3 reads that have no synthetic equivalent degrade: no provider
backfill for a session that spans many threads, and no permalink for a coordinate
no message has.

fix(daemon): finish composing a placed session's launch where it runs (#2206)

* fix(daemon): write config-file secrets where a pod or placed session runs

A `*_DATA` config-file secret (KUBECONFIG_DATA, DOCKER_CONFIG_DATA) was
materialized under the holder's agent directory for every launch, and its
pointer named that path. A runtime in a pool pod, or in a session placed on
another machine of the group, runs on a filesystem where that path does not
exist, so kubectl, helm and docker got a pointer to nothing.

The daemon still decides which secrets become files. Only where they are
written moves. When a launch's runtime runs through a shim on another
filesystem, the holder plans the files under `<runtimeRoot>/config-files`
there: the pod image's runtime root, or the one the executor reported. It
points KUBECONFIG and DOCKER_CONFIG at that directory and carries the files
with the launch. The driver empties the directory and writes the files before
the runtime starts, as it already writes the session gitconfig. Emptying it
first keeps the local rule that a deleted secret leaves no file behind.
Nothing is written on the holder's disk, so such a host no longer registers
config-file state for the idle sweep.

This replaces materializeConfigFilesThrough, which nothing used.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): start a placed session's adapter from its executor's own install

A daemon launches a registry or managed ACP adapter from its own adapter
store: its `process.execPath` plus a bin path under its daemon root. A
session placed on another machine of the group used the holder's catalog
entry as is, so the executor was asked to start a node and a tree that exist
only on the holder. That only worked when both machines had the same Node at
the same path and the same adapter version installed under the same root. A
session in an executor's VM was worse off: the adapter it needs is the one
the image declares, not any host's store.

`executor/prepare` now names the session's runtime, and the executor's
`ready` reply carries `runtimeLaunch`: the command and arguments the
environment it prepared starts that runtime with. For `host` that is what a
local agent of that machine would start, installed in its own store first if
it has not been yet, as for an agent assigned after boot. For `microsandbox`
it is the entry its image declares. The holder launches with that command
and keeps the rest of its own definition (ExecutorPlane.runtimeDefFor), and
its launch log says which one it used.

Both fields are optional. A CP or executor that predates them drops them, and
the holder keeps its own definition, which is today's behavior. An executor
with no such runtime, a failed install, or an answer the frame cannot carry
also leaves the answer out, so the environment is still prepared.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): let Codex commit in a placed or pool session's own clones

Codex's `:workspace` profile pins a checkout's `.git` read-only, so a
confined session needs an exact write grant on each of its clones' `.git`
(git-workspace-model §11). A local session gets it: the launch reads
`sessionGitDirsIn` from this disk. A session placed on another machine of the
group got none, and neither did a pool session. The holder's disk has no such
clones, so model tools could not commit in `workspace/` or `repos/<a>/<b>`.

Before a session host starts, the holder now lists the session's clones
through the filesystem that holds them, which is the executor's shim or the
session pod's. It uses sessionGitDirsUnder, the WorkspaceFs twin of
sessionGitDirsIn. That `stat` follows no symlink, so a `.git` that is a link
is refused there as it is here. The launch reopens each `.git` found, with
hooks and config read-only, in that filesystem's coordinates: beside the
private-HOME profile for a placed session, and in the pod's unconfined
profile for a pool session. A session on this disk is unchanged. A listing
that fails is logged and grants nothing, so the host still starts.

feat(daemon): add !new — start over, in whichever way this conversation means it (#2214)

* feat(daemon): add !new — start over, in whichever way this conversation means it

Stage 4 of channel-session-mode.md §7. One gesture, two mechanisms, because
"start over" means different things when a session IS a thread and when it is not.

In `append` it advances the reservation by compare-and-set. Nothing else is
written: the reservation is authoritative and no resolver reads the sessions
table, so the bare row §7.1 described would serve nobody — the doc is corrected.
The retired session keeps its row, outward id, CP metadata and transcript, and
ages out through ordinary retention. Work already admitted finishes on the old
coordinate, since coordinates are resolved at ingress, which is what the reply
says.

In `createNew` the thread is not going anywhere, so the session keeps its key,
coordinate, outward id and workspace, and loses its context. That is the
acpSessionId/lastDeliveredTs reset the session manager already performs for two
other reasons, with one deliberate difference: those null the cursor, which makes
the next prompt replay the whole thread — restoring exactly what a clear removes.

The cursor is the load-bearing detail, and the first version got it wrong: it is
compared against the transcript's own ts, and the replay path discards a cursor
its platform cannot order, falling back to a full catch-up. A wall-clock stamp is
an id no platform issued, so !new was a silent no-op on Slack — the platform `!`
exists for. It is derived from the !new message itself now, and the test that
pins it drives the real command through a real Slack message rather than handing
the store a hand-shaped cursor.

Three guards the operation earns: the write is pinned on the runtime session id
the command read, because the in-flight refusal is otherwise check-then-act; a
!new the latest-session fallback retargeted to another thread is refused, since
the reply would land somewhere the cleared thread's people never see; and it
takes !resume's trusted-actor gate, because it cannot be undone.

fix(daemon): keep /dev usable under Codex full access in a sandbox (#2217)

A sandboxed Codex session in "Full access" could not open /dev/null, so
git, shell redirections and most tooling failed. The full-access profile
granted a writable `:root` alongside the deny entries that hide the runtime
credentials. The deny makes Codex's Linux sandbox take its restricted path:
it read-only binds `/`, mounts a minimal `/dev`, then binds each writable
root, and binding `/` again covers that `/dev` with the host's, remounted

bwrap directly: that order refuses /dev/null, and binding only subpaths
writable, or `/` before `--dev`, does not.

profile's own writes (the session's clones, its HOME, shared stores) and
keeps its open network. With nothing to deny, the writable root is Codex's
full-disk policy, which mounts `/dev` after it, and stays as it was.

for longer than `limits.agentMaxLifetimeMs`. The write is conditional on
the row being unchanged since it was read, and `updatedAt` keeps its last
activity, so the TTL close in the same pass closes it. Nothing is reset at

Removing a sandboxed session's directory suspends the VM that mounts it,
and the suspend refused whenever that VM still ran a process: "microsandbox
environment <agent>/session-<leaf> has 1 active executions". On a
review agent this failed nearly every merged pull request's cleanup, so each
review checkout stayed on disk until the seven-day retention window.

and the cleanup has already judged the session inactive under the
workspace admission fence. So the mount release now drains that VM: it

through its ordinary terminal-exit path, and stops the VM. The agent's
own VM, which several sessions can share, is suspended exactly as before.

fix(daemon): suspend a sandbox pod again when its wake never binds (#2279)

* fix(daemon): suspend a sandbox pod again when its wake never binds

A wake patches the Sandbox to Running and then waits for the pod. When
the pod cannot schedule, the wait times out, but nothing set the mode
back. The launch also stayed recorded. Its claim kept being re-stamped,
the next read waited on the same Pending pod again, and each stuck pod
kept its CPU request until no wake on the node could schedule.

A failed bind now marks its Sandbox. Once the last hold on it is
released, the driver suspends it through the idle-suspend path. It
skips this when the launch was replaced or a channel to the pod is
still attached.

The idle sweep judges a host-less session pod by the whole agent's
activity, so a busy agent kept stuck pods alive. The sweep now also
suspends a recorded launch that never bound a channel and whose pod is
still not Ready a full pod-up timeout after the launch was recorded.
This covers pods that were stuck before the upgrade or were taken over
while stuck.

Fixes #2275

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): fence the stalled-wake suspend on the launch it judged

The sweep read a stalled-wake verdict and then called suspendIdle,
which acts on whatever launch is current. The readiness read in
between can outlive the verdict. A console wake could bind the pod
during that read, or the launch could be replaced, and the suspend
would still land on a pod that had just become usable.

suspendIfStalled now makes the whole decision. After the readiness
read, it checks again that the same launch is current and still
unbound. In that same tick it opens the lease's suspension gate
against that launch. The sweep hands it every pod inside the activity
window instead of acting on a boolean. The failed-bind put-back
suspends its own launch the same way.

* fix(daemon): collect the sandbox image cache after retention, including flat leftovers

Image collection only ran in the startup probe, while the previous
release's session VMs were still retained and pinned its digest. Nothing
ran it again once retention discarded the last of those VMs, so a retired
image stayed cached until the next restart after that point.

- MicrosandboxManager.collectImages() is a runtime entry point. It keeps
  the configured image, every binding's image, and every tag created after
  this manager's own pull. An upgrade pre-pulls the next release's tag from
  a separate process while the old daemon runs, and that tag must survive.

  directory, holding the owner's pid. Image removal deletes layer files a
  concurrent pull may already have decided to reuse. A pull waits for the
  lock; a runtime collection skips its round; a dead holder's lock, or one
  left by an earlier process with this pid, is reclaimed.
- Every collection sweeps the flat rootfs store that v1.55 filled and msb's
  removal never touches: refs whose manifest is no longer cached, then
  blobs no remaining ref names.

  discarded at least one session VM.

  usually one of the daemon's own stopped VMs.

  arm landing during the sweep's question is never lost. A pod whose

A group agent's control-plane row names no daemon, so a member that
registers before its lease lands is told to detach the agent: the drop
puts it in the draining and dropped sets and archives the replica. When
the lease then lands on that same member, the grant install brought the

and refused every turn as draining until the process restarted. A grant
carrying the revision already applied fared worse: the unchanged spec did
not rewrite the archived replica, so the agent was never loaded at all.

restores an archived replica, clears the dropped and draining marks unless
a destructive operation is still pending, and lifts the git credential
denial.

does this, and older builds did it whenever retention ran before an agent
had loaded.

The retention pass now also lists each loaded agent's session directories
and retires those that no session row, dream or held host maps to. It
applies the rules a session's own retirement applies: uncommitted work or
a commit no remote has keeps the directory, and a review snapshot is
exempt. Git runs on the daemon's host with its pinned configuration and
never through the session's plane, so the sweep never boots a VM. A
directory that a microsandbox environment still names waits for that VM
to be retired, and an agent whose sandbox manager is down is skipped. An
agent with work in flight is skipped too, and each directory is judged
again inside the workspace admission fence. Pool members are left to the
pool's own orphan reconcile.

as session leaves.

fix(daemon): never follow a link or wait on a pipe the runtime left in a checkout (#2316)

* fix(daemon): never follow a link or wait on a pipe the runtime left in a checkout

with an unbounded read that follows symlinks and blocks on a FIFO. A sandboxed
runtime can write all three, so a symlink to `/dev/zero` or a FIFO in place of

  oversized `info/exclude` is left untouched rather than rewritten.

  with O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK, checks the descriptor with fstat, and reads at
  most one byte past the cap.

feat(relay): probe bot credentials periodically and report two evidence tiers (#2314)

* feat(relay): probe bot credentials periodically and report two evidence tiers

The relay's `auth.test` probe ran only when a bot was assigned, and it
reported every dead-credential answer as a revocation without Slack's code.
`invalid_auth` is ambiguous: Slack also returns it to a caller outside the
app's IP allowlist, where revoking only sends the operator into a reinstall
that cannot help. This is the relay half of the two tiers the Control Plane
learned in #2297.

- contract: `reportRevoked` takes `{ reason, evidence, eventAtMs?, code? }`;
  lifecycle events (Slack `app_uninstalled`/`tokens_revoked`, Linear's
  revoke) are `evidence: 'event'`. The host gains `reportCredentialCheck` and
  `credentialCheckSupported()`, and an ingest may expose `probeCredential()`.
- manager: sends `rc/bot-credential-check` only to a CP that advertised
  `bot-credential-check-v1` and only with a known revision; reports the first
  probe after each (re)assign and afterwards only a change for that revision;
  keeps the latest unacknowledged check per bot, replays it on reconnect and
  on the READY-link retry, and drops it on any reply, on unassign, or on a
  re-assign with a newer revision. It also schedules each probing ingest: the
  first run at a random offset within the interval, later runs at the
  interval +/- 10%, on unref'd timers cleared on stop, unassign and re-assign.
- CP client: `reportBotCredentialCheck`, `advertisedFeature` (answered from
  the last registration while the link is down), and `rc/bot-revoked` without
  `evidence`/`code` for a CP that does not advertise the feature.
- Slack: `account_inactive`/`token_revoked` revoke with `evidence: 'probe'`
  and the code; `invalid_auth` becomes a `rejected` check, or a revocation as
  before when the CP lacks the feature; success is an `ok` check; any other
  failure (network, rate limit, `missing_scope`) reports nothing.
- config: `RELAY_CREDENTIAL_PROBE_INTERVAL_SEC` (default 3600), also listed
  in the chart's relay config.
- docs: preset-agents.md §5.3, shared-bot-relay.md §7.1 and the plugin
  architecture sketch.

* fix(slack): keep each relay's credential observation and aggregate the mark

Slack's `invalid_auth` depends on the caller's address, so relay replicas
can legitimately disagree: one outside the app's IP allowlist is rejected
while another passes. The CP kept one bot-wide watermark and each relay
reported only changes, so whichever first-round report landed last stuck.

- control plane: a new `bot_credential_observation` table holds each
  relay's latest probe of a bot (revision, result, code, observation
  time), cascading with its bot and its relay. A check takes the relay,
  bot and observation locks in that order, fences on the current
  revision, replaces the relay's row only when strictly newer, and
  recomputes the mark in the same transaction: any rejected row for the
  current revision marks the bot (first sighting kept, newest rejected
  code), none clears it. The failover sweep deletes stale relays under
  the same lock order and re-aggregates every marked bot, so a mark held
  only by a relay that is gone clears. `bumpCredential` deletes the bot's
  rows with the revocation and mark. The migration drops the bot-level
  `credentialCheckedAt`, which nothing else read.
- protocol: the semantics changed, so the CP advertises
  `bot-credential-check-v2`; nothing consumed v1.
- relay: gates on v2 (a v1-only CP gets the legacy revocation fallback),
  keeps change-only reporting per relay, and resets that latch on every CP
  registration, so a relay whose row was swept with its old id rebuilds it.
- docs: preset-agents.md §5.3 and shared-bot-relay.md §7.1 describe the

fix(daemon): finish a host stop whose VM still runs another execution (#2318)

After an ACP host stops, stopHostByKey suspends its microsandbox VM. The
manager refuses to suspend while any execution is active, and the stop then
rejected. An execution can legitimately outlive the host: a workspace clone
whose abort is still unwinding runs in that VM, and a sibling host can share
the environment. During shutdown the rejected stop became the drain's
never-settling fail-closed wait, which is how a CP-commanded restart hung.
On the idle sweep it logged a failed stop.

Leave a busy VM running instead. The idle sweep suspends it once nothing runs
in it, and shutdown's stopAll ends its executions and stops it.

fix(daemon): refuse a FIFO or device a runtime left where the daemon reads a file (#2321)

The daemon is one process serving every agent. Eight of its reads open a path a
sandboxed runtime can write with a call that follows links and blocks on a
FIFO: Claude settings.json and the Claude login files in the shared host config
dir, the retained .claude.json and Hermes config.yaml in the runtime HOME, the
shared-login credential comparisons, the local image read under the session
cwd, the console file read and edit sniff, and the shim's descent `childFile`.
A FIFO stalls the event loop on a sync read or a libuv pool thread on an async
one; a link to /dev/zero is an unbounded read. Several sites lstat first, which
only narrows that to a swap race.

- Add `src/fs/regular-file.ts`: open with O_NONBLOCK (and O_NOFOLLOW unless the
  caller follows links; an lstat stands in on Windows), require fstat isFile,
  and read at most one byte past a bound. Every site above reads through it.
- `DirHandle.childFile` opens with O_NONBLOCK and refuses a non-regular leaf.
- A FIFO or device in place of Claude settings, a retained .claude.json, a
  Hermes config or a private login now fails the launch instead of hanging it.
- The console read reports size and mtime from the opened descriptor.

Tests plant a FIFO fed by a separate writer process, so code that blocks reads
the writer's bytes instead of hanging the worker; where the old code checked
first, a stat spy makes the swap after the check deterministic.

fix(daemon): resolve a confined session's additional repositories on the session side (#2319)

A confined session prepared each additional repository's reference root in
the agent's own subtree first: mkdir repos/<a>/<b>, ls-remote for the
default branch, a full clone when missing, .materialization.json, origin
and helper convergence. On the pool that subtree is the agent pod, so every
isolated preparation woke it and could clone the whole repository there,
although the session took only the default branch and the repository-id
attestation from it; its own clone comes from the remote.

A confined session's clone of a secondary root now answers for itself:

- A fresh clone asks its remote for the default branch (ls-remote --symref)
  from beside the clone, so from the machine and over the credential route
  the clone uses, and records {provider, repoId, repoFullName, branch} in
  .git/agentconnect-materialization.json before it is published.
- A resumed clone is judged by that record alone and asks the remote
  nothing. One naming another repository is left untouched and omitted, or
  fails the preparation as the reviewed root: the rule the agent's subtree
  applies to a reused name. Origin and helper convergence are unchanged.
- A clone taken before clones carried a record adopts the agent subtree's
  marker once, if it attests the same repository, through the agent's
  filesystem that preparation still reaches. Otherwise it is omitted.
- A session's console push and log read the branch from its own clone's
  record instead of the agent's marker.
- The local cwd containment check names a confined session's reviewed root
  from the rows rather than from the agent's subtree on disk, which is no
  longer materialized for it.

A new session therefore follows the remote's current default, while the
agent's checkout keeps the branch it pinned when it first materialized.
This covers the whole confined tier (pool session pods, sessions placed on
an executor, local sandboxed sessions), which shares this preparation. The
worktree tier and shared sessions are unchanged.

fix(daemon): cancel workspace Git when the shutdown drain gives up (#2320)

* fix(daemon): cancel workspace Git when the shutdown drain gives up

Admitted workspace preparation ignores its turn's abort by design, so a
later generation never races stale work. A cold turn whose session clone
or checkout outlasts the drain window therefore kept the drain's final
await open. A blobless clone of a large repository can take minutes, and
its `reset --hard` fetches every blob. The daemon neither exited nor
served, until a kill timeout or the fleet-exit bound ended it and left the
staged clone behind.

At the drain deadline nothing later remains to protect, so the workspace
manager now aborts every Git it runs from that point: host, microsandbox
and pod runners alike. The clone fails through its own cleanup, the cold
dispatch settles, and shutdown completes.

fix(daemon): report a cold session as resuming until its turn starts (#2338)

* fix(daemon): report a cold session as resuming until its turn starts

The console shows the status the daemon last reported to the CP. A turn
reports `prompting` only in its start snapshot, which is sent after the
session is open. On a cold host, reaching that point can take minutes:
checkout, sandbox start and session/load. A turn replayed after a restart
always starts cold. Until the start snapshot, the console kept showing the
interrupted turn's `idle`, so the session looked stuck while the daemon was
bringing it back.

When a turn finds an existing session row but no running host, the daemon now
reports `resuming` to the CP before it opens the session. The console already
renders that status. The local row is left unchanged. If the turn ends before
announcing its start, the daemon reports the row's own state again, so the CP
never keeps `resuming`. Warm turns and brand-new sessions are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): commit the resuming status in order with what replaces it

A `plan` snapshot with no pending outbox row is sent as fire-and-forget
`event/session`. The CP runs those frame handlers independently, and its
session upsert has no fence on `status`. So a fast cold-start failure could
commit the following `idle` first and the earlier `resuming` after it,
leaving the session stuck at `resuming`.

The outbox input now takes an `ordered` flag. With it, a `plan` update
creates a durable obligation, like a lifecycle milestone does, and goes
through the acknowledged drain. That drain sends one request at a time and
fences by revision. Both the `resuming` report and the report that restores
the row's state use it. The tests start the second process with an empty
outbox and an ACK-capable CP. They then assert that `resuming` is
acknowledged, never trails a later state, and never goes out as a
fire-and-forget event.

fix(control-plane): stop retrying session PR-link captures forever (#2344)

The Control Plane queues a pull-request link capture when an isolated
session ends, then reads the session worktree's branch from the serving
daemon until a read succeeds. A failed read was retried a minute later with
no cap and no expiry, so a session whose sandbox was removed, asleep or
unserved was read forever, and every stuck row stayed a standing
session-scoped read against the daemon. Due rows were also claimed oldest
first, so a session that had just ended waited behind all of them.

- Read the daemon's `sandbox-removed` refusal as a definitive absence: the
  session's worktree is gone and no wake restores it, so the row completes.
- Owe a capture only while the session's last activity is under a day old.
  An older row is dropped without another daemon read and none is queued;
  a later turn moves `lastActivityAt`, so it queues a fresh capture. No
  schema change.
- Claim due captures by the session's latest activity, so a session that
  just ended is read while its workspace is still awake.

Related to #1896

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(daemon): stop a workspace read from resuming a sleeping session pod (#2346)

On the pool, a file read or git operation that named an isolated
session's directory resumed that session's sleeping pod whenever the
agent's own pod happened to be bound. The rule dates from when the
console's only wake was agent-scoped; #2317 added the session-scoped
wake, so no read needs to resume anything any more.

Left in place, any bound agent pod turned reads into wakes. The Control
Plane's pull-request link capture keeps retrying a `workspace/gitstatus`
for isolated sessions that have ended, and on a test environment each of
those rows resumed its old session pod, one after another, each kept up
for a full idle window. An open session page's Files and Git polls, which
keep running while their tab is not selected, did the same.

A read of a session path whose pod is not bound now refuses as
`sandbox-unavailable`, or `sandbox-removed` once its claim is gone, as
before, whatever the agent pod's state. The session wake is the only
console action that resumes a session pod; preparation, retention and
launch bind their pods themselves, and keep-alive and merge-when-ready
never wake one.

Related to #1896

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(daemon): round the Decision evaluator timeout to whole milliseconds (#2343)

The daemon's evaluator clock is performance.timeOrigin + performance.now(), so the
remaining time before a gate's deadline is fractional. AbortSignal.timeout() rejects
a non-integer delay with a RangeError before any request is sent, and the gate records
that as unavailable/provider and admits the message. Every deadline-bounded Jev
evaluation on a daemon without an injected clock failed this way.

Floor the timeout so it stays inside the deadline, and cover it with a test that uses
the sub-millisecond clock.

feat(daemon): let running turns finish before a config change respawns the host (#2340)

* feat(daemon): let running turns finish before a config change respawns the host

A config change in the host-spawn signature (runtime, model, effort, modes, memory,
env, secrets, skills, description) used to interrupt every running turn at once and
purge its inbox, so the conversation went quiet with no reply and no notice. That
also contradicted the reconciler design ("runtime change -> applies to next new
session; do not interrupt active").

With turns in flight, idle processes now stop at once and each busy process keeps
serving its turns until they settle, bounded by the new limits.configRespawnDrainMs
(5 min). A turn that would start on a retiring process waits for its successor
inside the session startup observer, shown as a new `restart` startup phase: every
new turn of an agent with one shared process, only that session's follow-ups where
each session has its own. A turn still running at the limit, or still starting up
when the change lands, is cut with its durable row kept and replayed on the new
process, and its conversation is told so. A webchat turn has no row and is told to
send its message again. A workspace change still cuts at once, now with the same
notice.

The shutdown drain posts the matching notice when its deadline cuts a turn, whose
row it already keeps for replay.

* fix(daemon): fence retiring processes before teardown, scope grant revokes, notice startup cuts

- Install every busy process's retirement before the first await, so a turn that
  settles while idle processes are still stopping cannot start its follow-up on the
  old process.
- Revoke remote webchat grants per retiring process, when it stops and before its
  held turns resume, instead of all of the agent's grants at the end: a session
  started meanwhile on a fresh process keeps its grant.
- A turn cut while still starting up gets the config-change notice too: "picked up
  again" for a kept row, "send your message again" in the webchat terminal frame.

* fix(daemon): protect still-retiring processes, hold idle ones until their grants are revoked

- A process still retiring from an earlier config change is no longer treated as
  idle by the next one: its grants and model session stay until its own retirement.
- An idle process with webchat grants holds turns bound for it until it has stopped
  and its grants are revoked, so a same-conversation successor cannot reuse or lose
  the old grant mid-turn.

* fix(daemon): keep a model session's respawn hold while its pool entry is released

The pool drops a model session's entry before its host stops and its grant is
revoked, so the owner lookup falls back to the shared host key mid-release. A turn
of that session now also finds a hold stored under its own session key.

fix(daemon): reap the agent's shared host by its own work, not isolated traffic (#2352)

The idle reaper judged the agent's shared ACP host by the activity of every
session of the agent. Once anything started that host (activation without a
key server, a shared session, distillation, the commit-message wand), isolated
sessions' traffic kept it alive, and on a pool it kept the agent pod up too.

- The shared host's clock is now the latest of its start, the last activity
  of the sessions hostKeyFor routes to it, and the end of its last internal
  pass. A session with a host of its own no longer counts; a worktree-tier
  isolated session, which runs on the shared host, still does.
- Distillation and the wand's console seam hold the host (HostPasses) from
  before the pass fetches it until it settles, so the reaper never stops it
  mid-pass. A pass older than agentMaxLifetimeMs is taken as wedged.
- An admitted dispatch of any session still holds every host of the agent,
  because a formal review's preparation is fenced on the shared host staying
  ready.
- Docs: k8s-daemon-pool.md section 4 and background-task-aware-reclaim.md
  section 4 state the rule.

fix(daemon): reach a spread session's files on its executor, and list a key-server host's clones (#2351)

Two follow-ups to the #1896 fixes, each verified before it was changed.

A session placed on another machine of its group (session-executors.md §7)
runs in `<executor root>/sessions/<leaf>`, the root that machine's shim
reports. Its console location composed the primary clone on the pool's
default `/agent` mount instead: a holder with no pool has no runtime root to
offer, while the session directory, its secondary roots and its preparation
all ask the session's own placement. The attachment and image tools also
picked their off-disk filesystem only under --k8s. So for a spread session
`saveAttachment` tried this holder's own disk at `/agent/...` and failed,
`readWorkspaceImage` answered not-found, and a turn's file links into the
primary clone were dropped.

- `consoleWorkspaceRoot` composes a session's root on the mount of the plane
  that holds that session, as `sessionDir` does, falling back to the runtime
  root. On the pool both name the install's one mount, so nothing changes
  there.
- `WorkspaceManager.offDiskFsFor` answers an off-disk scope's filesystem from
  its own plane, or `unbound`, never this disk. It replaces the pool-only
  `poolToolWorkspaceFs`, so the tools reach the executor over the session's
  pipe and refuse as `sandboxed` while it is closed.

A key-server model-session host on the pool was built without the `.git` of
the clones its session pod holds. The ordinary host start lists them since
#2206, because Codex's `:workspace` profile pins a clone's `.git` read-only
unless it is named. So after a key-server host restart (an idle reap and a
resume, a member restart, a provider change) Codex could not commit in its
own clones. The key-server start now lists them through the same helper,
for a host that runs in its session's own pod; shared sessions and internal
passes list nothing, as before. A new session's first key-server host still
has no clones to list, because its workspace is prepared after that launch.

fix(daemon): read a spread session's console files on its executor (#2355)

A session placed on another machine of its daemon group
(session-executors.md §7) could not be browsed in the console Files
view. The holder's files resolver had arms only for the pool and a local
microsandbox. A root it matched inside the executor's directory was
refused as `sandbox-unavailable` even with the session's pipe up, and a
root it could not match by path, which is every root once the pipe goes
idle and the plane forgets it, was listed off the holder's own disk as
an empty tree.

- The console scope's location carries the isolated session's key, and
  the reader hands that key with the root to the files resolver and to
  its off-disk check. A placed session is judged by its key, as its root
  was composed, not by whether its pipe still names the root.
- `ExecutorPlane.workspaceFilesFor` runs a placed session's file
  operations on its bound shim and refuses as `sandbox-unavailable`
  while the pipe is closed. The daemon asks it before the pool and
  microsandbox arms, so the agent's own checkout stays on the holder.
- `RoutedWorkspaceFiles` moves beside the `WorkspaceFiles` seam, so the
  pool and the executor plane share one class.

fix(daemon): run a spread session's console Git on its executor (#2357)

A session placed on another machine of its daemon group
(session-executors.md §7) could not rely on the console Git panel. The
panel resolved its runner by the root's path alone, and the executor
plane matches a path only against the root the session's bound shim
reported. Once the session goes idle the plane forgets that root, so
the holder ran git on its own disk at a path that is not there and
answered with that disk's failure instead of refusing as
`sandbox-unavailable`.

  placed session by its key: its shim's runner while the pipe is up,

fix(daemon): prepare a new pool session before its first key-server launch (#2365)

Codex's `:workspace` permission profile is fixed at spawn and pins a
clone's `.git` read-only unless the launch names it. A key-server host
lists its session's clones before it starts, but the turn path started
a new isolated session's first host before `sessions.handle` prepared
the session's workspace. That launch had nothing to list, so Codex
could not commit in the session's own clones until the host restarted.

A turn whose isolated pool session has no started key-server host now
runs the session's own preparation first. It is the same session-pod
call `sessions.handle` makes, with the same request, and it never
touches the agent pod. The launch then lists the clones that exist, and
the turn hands the prepared cwd to `sessions.handle`, as a formal
review already does, so nothing is prepared twice. A warm host, a
review that prepared its own cwd, and a shared session are unchanged.

`sessionInitiatedBy` now holds the opener rule that names a session's
branch, so the early preparation and `SessionManager` cannot name a
branch differently.

fix(control-plane): hint a session's executor from the relayed ready prepare (#2393)

`executor/candidates` answered a successor holder from `session_meta.executorDaemonId`,
which only the holder's asynchronous `event/session` report writes. A holder that died
after a `ready` prepare but before its report landed left the successor with no hint,
so placement could start the session away from its remote environment.

The CP now records the executor when it relays a `ready` prepare to the current duty
holder, before the holder receives the key, in a small `session_executor_hint` table
keyed by (agentId, sessionKey) that holds ids and a timestamp only. Session reports
write to it too. An observation replaces the recorded one only if it is newer, and a
report also wins a tie, so a stale prepare cannot override a newer report and a re-emit
written before a prepare cannot override it. A stayed-home verdict clears an existing
hint but never creates one. Keys with no hint fall back to the session row as before.

* feat(executor): protect a hosted VM's credentials with the local preparers

A VM hosted for another member of the group now takes the local VM's
credential step. The preparers run against this machine's own environment and
the session HOME it seeds, the VM starts with the recognized keys as
placeholder secrets, the projected files in HOME hold placeholders, and the

launches through the launcher without a second copy.

the runtime's own variable for the key it protects and the variables it binds.

feat(daemon): sync the workspace to its configured branch instead of pulling (#1829)

* feat(daemon): sync the workspace to its configured branch instead of pulling

The session-start pull and the console's pull button both ran `git pull
--ff-only` INTO whatever branch the checkout happened to be on. A shared
checkout an agent had parked on its own branch therefore never came back:
every fast-forward failed, the failure was swallowed as offline degradation,
and the agent worked on a month-old base while the console showed that
branch's HEAD as "the latest commit".

`syncWorkspaceRef` replaces `pullWorkspaceRef`: fetch the configured branch,
then `checkout --no-track -B <branch> refs/remotes/origin/<branch>`. The local
branch ends identical to the remote one — never a merge, so history cannot
fork — and uncommitted edits ride along the way `git checkout` carries them.
Two cases refuse as data instead of losing work: a local commit the remote
lacks (the branch is left alone and the detail says to push or move it), and
an uncommitted edit touching a file the sync would rewrite (git's own refusal,
naming the file). The result names the branch it switched away from.

The console button is now "Sync", its result copy reads "Synced main —
updated N files." / "Switched from X to main — …" / "Already in sync.", and a
request-level failure is explained like every other console git write: the
daemon's "agent is working in this workspace" refusal reaches the browser as
409 `WORKSPACE_STALE` rather than a 503 that read as an offline daemon.

Wire contract and route path are unchanged; the cluster volume's branch proof
keeps its shape, since a refused sync still leaves the volume where it was.

* feat(daemon): run srt sessions on executors inside an SRT-wrapped shim (R1a)

Step R1a of session-executors.md §12: the `srt` strategy on the executor
facet. The shim runs inside an SRT boundary, as a pod or a VM contains it,
so every runtime, bridge and helper it starts inherits the boundary.

- srtLauncher (execution/strategies.ts) is the host launcher with SRT around
  the shim. startHostShim takes a boundary option; srtShimBoundary
  (execution/srt-shim.ts) wraps the shim's command with the provider from the
  shim's own bundle.
- The policy is the executor's: srtShimPolicy composes it from the
  environment (its directory, HOME, writable mounts such as a hosted HOME's
  shared sign-in) and this machine's own paths (the shim bundle, node, the
  runtime store and admitted runtime installs), hiding the daemon root, the
  agents directory, the host HOME, the temp roots and runtime state. The
  holder sends none. The policy file sits beside the runtime root, outside
  everything the boundary can write.
- The three changes the probe found: no AC_SHIM_PARENT_FD under a boundary
  (the provider's owner watch ends the sandbox when the daemon dies); the ACP
  runner copies SRT's proxy variables over the launch's when SRT marked the
  shim; and the policy denies nothing under `.git`, so the holder's Git works
  through the shim inside the boundary. SRT's temp root is a short
  `<runtimeRoot>/t`.
- Stop sends SIGTERM to the shim itself, since SRT forwards no signal inward.
- The facet offers `srt` when its probe passes, its records keep the
  strategy across a restart, and placement spreads `srt` sessions.
- test/srt-shim.test.ts runs the real boundary in the Sandbox (Linux) job.
- Docs: session-executors.md §5, §11 and §12 (R1 split into R1a and R1b),
  and daemon-sandbox-backends.md.

fix(control-plane): wake a PR session at most once per feedback delivery (#2484)

A GitHub redelivery reuses the original delivery GUID, so the relay reports
the same PR feedback delivery key again. Completing a wake cleared the key
from the ownership row, which erased the only dedup state, and every
redelivery re-dirtied the PR and woke its session with an identical
"[GitHub PR feedback]" turn.

Redeliveries are routine: the hook redelivery reconciler re-posts every
delivery that landed no HookRun on each 10-minute sweep, which includes PR
comments the hook matcher deliberately ignores, and its per-GUID attempt cap
is in memory and resets on every Control Plane restart. A single App-authored
comment on a PR therefore kept waking the linked session every ten minutes,
including after the PR merged.

Record each received delivery key once in a new receipt table inside the
enqueue transaction and treat a repeated key as a no-op. Receipts expire with
unowned rows (7 days), past GitHub's three-day redelivery window.

fix(control-plane): persist the GitHub no-run redelivery cap per GUID (#2486)

* fix(control-plane): stop redelivering GitHub events the relay already evaluated

HookRedeliveryReconciler treats any matching delivery without a HookRun as
lost and asks GitHub to redeliver it. A delivery the relay received and
deliberately fired nothing on, such as a PR comment no hook is summoned by,
also has no HookRun, so the reconciler redelivered it every sweep. Its
per-GUID cap of three lived in process memory. Each redelivery shows up in
GitHub's listing with a fresh timestamp, which keeps the GUID inside the
look-back window, so every Control Plane restart started another round of
three. One CP restart re-posted 38 such deliveries at once.

GitHub's delivery listing already records every attempt, including whether it
was a redelivery and the relay's HTTP status. The reconciler now uses that
record:

- Once the relay has acknowledged (2xx) a redelivered copy of a GUID and there
  is still no run, the relay has evaluated the event itself. Another copy
  would be filtered the same way, so that GUID is done. The first redelivery
  of an acknowledged original is kept, because the relay acknowledges before
  it dispatches and can drop a delivery if it dies in between.
- The attempt cap counts the redeliveries GitHub lists, not only the ones
  this process remembers, so a restart cannot reset it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(control-plane): persist the no-run redelivery cap per GUID

Review feedback on the previous commit was right on both counts.

- A 2xx on a redelivered copy only means the relay accepted it. The relay
  acknowledges before it dispatches, so it can still lose that copy, and
  stopping at the first acknowledged redelivery gave up the retries that
  could recover it.
- Counting attempts from the delivery listing misses any attempt older than
  the window the listing walked. After a restart the count could drop below
  the cap.

Drop both inferences. Instead, claim each redelivery of a GUID that landed no
run atomically against a new hook_delivery_recovery row, and stop at three.
This keeps the original recovery budget, and the count now survives restarts
because it no longer lives in process memory. Rows are pruned once their last
request is past twice the look-back horizon.

* feat(daemon): run every local srt host in its own shim (R1b-2b)

R1b-1 moved a confined srt session into its session directory's
SRT-wrapped shim. Every other srt host (the agent's shared host, a
memory or dream pass, a session host with no directory of its own) still
wrapped each runtime alone. Each of those now runs in an agent-scoped shim
of its own, one per host key.

- The environment id is `<agentId>/<host dir>`, as a VM's placement names
  it, and its runtime root is fixed by that id.
- Its root is the agent's directory. `srtShimPolicy` now writes a root only
  where a mount names it, so the agent's agent.json stays hidden and only
  the launch composition's roots are reopened. Confined and hosted
  environments already mount their directory, so they are unchanged; the
  confined-session Git descriptor now names its directory too.
- The sandbox starts in the host's cwd, carried as `cwd` in the descriptor.
  That is where a runtime wrapped alone started, so SRT's own protections
  are anchored where they were and the runtime runs there.
- The MCP spec follows the host key, a pass's included, so each host's
  bridge dials its own shim's tunnel.
- The srt launcher's reuse check compares canonical paths and accepts a
  request inside a granted tree.
- The agent's workspace Git and files stay on this host, as they were.

No daemon host takes the direct per-runtime launch any more; runtime
probes, model enumeration and the local `chat` command still do, and
R1b-2c retires it. The Linux sandbox suite shows an agent-scoped shim keeping
agent.json unreadable and the agent directory unwritten while its
workspace takes the runtime's writes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): stop a dream host's srt shim when its extraction settles

A one-off dream host now runs in its own agent-scoped shim. Neither the
failed-start path nor the settled path stopped that shim, so it stayed until
the idle sweep. Both paths now retire the dream's environment through one
helper: its VM and runtime home, or its srt shim.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(daemon): retire the direct srt launch for daemon hosts (R1b-2c) (#2497)

Since R1b-2b every srt host of the daemon runs in a shim, so the parts of
the direct launch that only a host wrapped alone needed were dead code.

- A sandboxed srt launch with no shim environment is now refused, not
  wrapped alone.
- The per-host policy and temp-directory cleanup at every host stop, dream
  teardown and failed start is gone, and with it `removeHostSandboxState`,
  `removeSandboxSettings` and `removeSandboxTempDir`.
- The grants of this daemon's MCP and git-credential sockets for a
  runtime wrapped alone are gone, and so is the `mcpSocketPath` the launch
  passed for one.

Runtime probes, model enumeration and the local `chat` command keep the
per-runtime wrap: each is short-lived, runs outside the daemon's hosts, and
would pay a shim start per launch. The boot sweep still reclaims a `chat`
run's temp directory.

feat(control-plane): lower a repository or installation grant's access in place (#2498)

* feat(control-plane): lower a repository or installation grant's access in place

The console is getting an inline Read only / Read & write toggle on each
additional repository, but both PATCH routes refused a lower tier with 409
and asked for revoke and authorize again.

Both routes now lower access in place. Raising keeps its behavior: a
repository row re-checks the caller's host permission, an installation
grant stays owner-only. Lowering is refused with 409
AGENT_REPO_INTEGRATION_CONFLICT only while an enabled GitHub hook still
needs the tier for pull request reviews or Checks, the rule a workspace
access edit already enforces:

- A row checks the hooks on its own repository under the agent lifecycle
  and agent/repository advisory scopes every GitHub hook write takes.
- A grant checks the hooks on repositories only it serves: owned by the
  installation's live account, with no row of their own and not the
  workspace repository. A row keeps its own tier, so it does not block.
- A hook write re-checks the row or grant its actions resolve through
  under the same scopes, so a concurrent enable cannot slip past a
  downgrade. A write that keeps or narrows a hook's needs is not refused.

A lowered row serves the next credential request at the lower tier, and a
GitLab project role re-converges, as on revoke. A lowered grant re-projects
the spec with the lower tier, which makes the daemon drop the agent's
cached repository credentials. The row tier is not on the spec, so a token
a daemon already holds for that repository lives out its expiry of at
most one hour, the window revoke documents.

The duplicate-create messages no longer tell the caller to remove a grant
to lower its tier, and the design doc's route table follows the new rule.

Part of #2398.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(control-plane): say what a lowered row leaves on the daemon

A revoke changes the spec and so drops the daemon's cached credentials; a
lowered row does not, so the OpenAPI text no longer says "as on revoke".
The console section of the design doc is left to the change that rewrites
it for the inline toggle.

Part of #2398.

fix(web): send a continued conversation's turn to the picked participant (#2499)

* fix(web): send a continued conversation's turn to the picked participant

A merged multi-agent conversation that can be continued from the console
(a code-host pull request, for one) always continued its representative
member's session: the composer read the first member's detail and sent into
its session, so a reader could never address anyone else in the room.

The composer's roster chips now pick the one member session a send
continues. The representative stays the default, a member whose own session
cannot continue here is not pickable, and a pick that stops being
continuable falls back to the representative instead of locking the
composer. The live lane (stream, busy flag, queue) stays keyed by the page's
session; only the socket's session target follows the pick, and a retarget
drops the socket bound to the previous target. The picked session's rows now
also confirm the live prompt, so a turn sent to another member is not shown
twice once it lands.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web): target a retargeted lane's next turn at its new member

The ready frame caches the relay-verified roster per lane. After a retarget
that cache still named the previous member, so the next send opened its
stream lane for that member while the new socket only reaches the picked
one: the reply landed on a lane nobody opened and the old lane never
closed. A retarget now drops the cached roster along with the socket.

Live-prompt reconciliation also read only the member picked when a tail
fetch landed, so switching back before the fetch settled left an earlier
turn's saved prompt next to its live echo. It now reads every member the
page sent into in this conversation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): mount an overlay base read-only under srt

An overlay mount in sandbox.mounts made the whole srt strategy unavailable
("sandbox.mounts mode=overlay requires microsandbox"). SRT has no
copy-on-write layer, and its launches already treat every non-writable mount
as read-only, so normalization now degrades overlay to readonly for srt
instead of rejecting it. A renamed target is still unsupported under srt.

* fix(daemon): check overlay/bind conflicts on the requested modes

Degrading an overlay to readonly under srt let an overlay and a writable
entry at the same path pass the conflict check and merge to writable, so
srt could grant writes to a base the operator marked as overlay. The check
now compares the operator's requested modes, before the degrade, for every
strategy.

* fix: keep repository access raise-only

Revert #2498. Lowering a repository row's or installation grant's access
in place needed a hook fence, new advisory locks and a hook-side re-check,
and still left a daemon's cached write token usable for up to an hour.
Lowering stays revoke and authorize again, which already retires the

again. The design doc's Web section says the same.

* fix(control-plane): enforce raise-only access at the write

Two PATCHes that both read `read` passed the route's check, so a stale
`comment` committing after `write` lowered the stored tier without revoke
and authorize again. Both writers now update only from a lower tier
(`access in` the tiers below the requested one); Postgres re-reads that
condition after a concurrent raise commits, so the stale write is a no-op
and the response carries the tier that won. A grant's materialize change
in the same patch still applies.

Part of #2398.

* fix(control-plane): re-derive a GitLab role after a stale raise loses

Raising a GitLab row sets the account's project role before the
conditional tier write. A stale `comment` that loses to a stored `write`
therefore left the row at `write` with the account at Reporter. When the
write keeps a higher tier than the request asked for, the raise now
re-converges the project, as a revoke does, so the role follows the stored
tier again.

fix(daemon): review a grant-covered repository at an exact checkout (#2506)

An agent may cover a whole GitHub account with an installation grant
instead of one row per repository. The Control Plane already admits hooks,
mints tokens and authorizes review publication for a repository only the
grant covers, but the daemon's review root lookup read rows alone, so a
formal review of such a repository degraded to the revision-only empty
directory.

Resolve that repository to a root of its own when no row or the primary
names it: the orchestrator passes the hook's repository id beside its name,
and the workspace manager places a row-shaped root through the same
placement a row uses, so subtree, clone URL, credentials and sandbox mount
are a row's. The root serves only that review's working directory, exactly
like an on-demand row's review: it never joins the agent's roots, another

feat(relay,daemon): expose strict im admission through the host seam (#2571)

* feat(relay,daemon): expose strict im admission through the host seam

A platform that must answer its provider from durable admission
(google-chat-integration.md §4) could not read one: the daemon's im ack
reported every deliberate gate as accepted once dispatch began, and the relay
host's `forward` only says the relay handled the message.

- protocol: `RD_IM_ADMISSION_V1` (`im-admission-v1`), advertised on rd/hello;
  the `RdAck` field docs now cover the im path.
- daemon: every pre-addressed im ack, the routed host copy included, fills
  `routeAdmission` and `recoverable` beside the unchanged `accepted`/`reason`:
  admitted for a durable admission or a receipt-settled duplicate; rejected and
  recoverable for durability, draining, capacity, not_ready, not_host and
  stale; rejected and not recoverable for off, muted, no_agent, unauthorized,
  an agent-authored copy and a delivery the strategy settled itself. Any
  admission member on a relay-ingress strategy now makes the ack wait for the
  durable admission, so `admitted` is never reported ahead of the row, and a
  recoverable refusal is no longer cached for replay.
- relay: `RelayIngressHost.forwardStrict` runs the same ladder as `forward`
  and returns a `RelayAdmission` (the rd/route/ack disposition and reason)
  through the mapping the route forwarder uses (`admissionFrom`); a target
  without the feature is answered rejected/unsupported and never sent to, a
  withdrawn grant is rejected, and a fan-out settles on one admission, else
  one retry, else the first rejection. `HandledDelivery.admission` rides
  through `handleInbound` untouched, and `dedupPeek`/`dedupMark` split the
  mark-on-first-sight `dedupSeen` for a platform that marks only after a
  disposition.
- Slack, Linear, webchat and the rd/route leg keep their behavior; the three
  design documents name the new members.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(relay,daemon): report a strict admission only after the durable write

Review found two ways a strict `admitted` could outrun the row it claims:
the shared no-strategy path acked as soon as dispatch started, so a failed
inbox write landed after the ack was cached; and a strategy with only
`receiptId` or `onAdmitted` left `requireDurable` unset, so `persistInbox`
swallowed a failed write and admission still reported accepted. An HTTP
platform reading `forwardStrict` would have answered success and marked its
dedup for a delivery with no replayable row.

- daemon: the shared path (with or without a gate), the woken agent-authored
  copy, and the awaited path's dispatch-resolved fallback keep the legacy
  `{ msgId, accepted: true }` with no verdict, since none of them holds proof
  of a row. The awaited path always dispatches with `requireDurable: true`:
  any admission member means the platform answers from admission, so a failed
  write is the durability refusal and `admitted` follows the row and receipt.
- relay: `forwardStrict` reads an `accepted` ack without a verdict from a
  daemon that advertises `im-admission-v1` as `rejected`/`unsupported`, so a
  platform that forgot its strategy is diagnosable; `admissionFrom` and the
  routed leg are unchanged.
- docs and comments say the verdict rides every im ack answered through a
  platform strategy with an admission member, and that a platform answering
  from admission supplies one with at least `receiptId`.
- tests: shared-path acks are pinned to the legacy shape; a strategy with only
  `receiptId`, and one with only `onAdmitted`, refuse a failed write as
  durability; a verdict-less accepted ack maps to unsupported on the relay.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): ack control commands only after their durable effect

Review found the relay im path acking every control command `admitted` after
`handleCommand` returned, while `!queue` launched its dispatch fire-and-forget:
a failed inbox write was only logged after a strict caller had answered
success and marked the delivery settled. Design §4 asks commands for a
completed, replay-safe disposition too.

- `!queue` rides dispatch's durable admission fence: the relay path hands
  `handleCommand` a queue admission that makes the write required, binds it to
  the platform strategy's `receiptId` when one exists, and acks only from the
  admission result — `admitted` after the row and receipt, `durability` when
  the write fails, the awaited path's gate verdicts otherwise. A redelivered
  `!queue` is a duplicate under the receipt, not a second queued turn.
- Every other command is minted a born-completed receipt under that same
  `receiptId` before it runs, so a redelivered `!cancel` finds it, cancels
  nothing, and is answered consumed; without a strategy receipt the relay
  dedup and the daemon's ack cache keep bounding the replay window as before.
- Handlers report what they did (`CommandEffect`): a durable effect that
  completed before returning is `admitted`; a reply, refusal or no-op is
  `rejected`/`recoverable: false`. `!stop` is applied through its mute latch or
  cancelled verdicts, `!resume` through a reset latch or mute, `!new` through
  the cleared or rotated context, `!cancel`/`!stop` through the interrupted
  turn, `/fast` and the selects through their recorded override; `/status`, a
  usage or list reply, and the Agent-level guard are consumed.
- The two designs describe the command receipt and the outcome.
